en: Victory to Śrī Lakṣmī and Keśava! Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of Obstacles!
[I bow] to the Lord, the nectar for the thirst and fatigue of those traveling the path of saṃsāra, slowly...
Having reflected upon the unimpeded tradition received from his guru in the teaching of Manu,
and having observed that other commentaries do not follow the intention of the author of the text,
Govindarāja has composed this commentary which follows the intention of the author of the treatise. || 1 ||
Approaching Manu as he sat with a one-pointed mind, the great seers honored him according to custom and spoke these words. 1.1.

Here, a certain disciple of Bhṛgu, due to the interruption of the traditional lineage, has uttered this composition for the purpose of recollection: "Having prostrated before Prajāpati Amitatejas, who assumes a body by his own will, I shall declare the various eternal *dharmas* (duties) as set forth by Manu—those which consist of actions to be performed for the sake of unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*), since it is desired that these have their basis in the Veda, with the purpose of attaining the desirable and avoiding the undesirable. Although *adharma*s (unrighteous acts) will also be mentioned, they are not separately promised here because, once one falls from status through the repeated practice of censurable acts, one loses the qualification to perform *dharma*; thus, they are included within the promise of *dharma* itself. The great seer named Manu obtained the title 'Manu' through his knowledge of the entire meaning of the Vedas and so forth; he was authorized to effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, a fact that has reached the ears of all learned men through the tradition of scripture. Regarding the term *svayaṃbhuve*, the fourth case ending is used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), according to the rule that the word *kriyā* (action) must also be supplied. Because the *Smṛtis* are equal to the *Chandas* (Vedas) insofar as they codify the meaning of the Vedas, there may occasionally be a faulty formation of words here according to the rules of the *Chandas*."

Regarding the word "Manu": the great seers (*maharṣis*)—so called because they were "great" due to their possession of qualities such as *aṇimā* (atomicity) and because they had "seen" the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas—approached Manu with devotion and directly, while he was seated with one-pointed attention and an undistracted mind. Having honored him pre-eminently, without transgressing the boundaries prescribed by the scriptures, they spoke these words which are about to be stated immediately hereafter. (1.1)
O Blessed One, you ought to speak to us of the dharmas for all castes, in their proper order and succession, as well as for those born of intermediate origins.

"O Blessed One! For he alone is endowed with all sovereignty and is capable of declaring to us—the twice-born, including all castes from the Brāhmaṇas down to the Śūdras, as well as those born of the intermixture of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others, whether in the natural (anuloma) or inverse (pratiloma) order—all our duties in their entirety, in due sequence, beginning with the rite of impregnation (niṣeka). 1.2.
For you alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true meaning and purpose of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.

"Thou alone art the one. Because Thou alone art the sole author of this entire scripture—which is uncreated and consists of such injunctions as "this must be done" and "this must not be done"—and because that scripture, having been composed, is so profound in its textual content that it cannot be conceptualized as being of such-and-such a nature, and because it is so immense that it cannot be measured as being "only this much," [Thou knowest] that ultimate reality which is of the nature of action and of the nature of what is to be performed; [Thou knowest it], O All-Powerful One. (1.3)
Thus questioned duly by those high-souled ones of immeasurable power, he honored all those great seers and replied, "Listen. 1.4.

"He" refers to Manu, who possessed immeasurable splendor. By those great sages (*maharṣis*)—high-souled ones acting for the sake of others—he, being thus questioned on matters of dharma by those very great sages in that manner, preceded by their approach and accompanied by proper worship, honored them and spoke to them as follows: "Listen. (1.4)
In the beginning, this was as if enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks, beyond reasoning, unknowable, and as if entirely asleep. (1.5)

"It was so. Since the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the world are caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), this treatise must be diligently mastered for its great purpose as a means of explaining them; with this intent, he begins the section concerning the origin of the world. Therein, he first describes the preceding state with this verse: "This world, prior to creation, was as if in darkness. Because everything then existed in a state of destruction as an effect, it was not known through perception. It was "without mark" (*alakṣaṇa*), meaning it could not be inferred because its characteristic signs were absent, since inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception and thus cannot function when that is impossible. It was "inconceivable" (*apratarkya*), meaning it could not even be reasoned about through analogy, such as "the gavaya is like a cow. It was "unknowable" (*avijñeya*), meaning it could not be known even through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), as in the case of inferring Devadatta's presence outside his house from the fact that he is alive but not seen there. If that is so, does it not follow that the world was simply non-existent? To this he says: "as if fast asleep. Its nature is known solely from scripture (*āgama*). Just as the self remains with the operations of the senses and mind ceased during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), so too, upon the total subsidence of all effects, the world then existed in that manner. For deep sleep is the state of sleep devoid of dreaming. (1.5)
Then the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, unmanifest yet making this world manifest, his power active in the great elements and other things, appeared as the dispeller of darkness.

The word "then" (*tataḥ*) refers to the period immediately following the previously mentioned state. The Self (*ātman*), having assumed a body according to its own will, being unmanifest (*avyakta*)—that is, beyond the reach of perception and other means of knowledge because it is accessible only through meditation—brought forth the world. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) such as earth and others, as well as other principles (*tattva*) such as the Great Intellect (*mahat*) and so on, are understood. He, by whom vigor (*ojas*)—the power of creation (*sṛṣṭisāmarthya*)—was attained, became that Light; he took on a body, being the dispeller of darkness (*tamonudaḥ*), the destroyer of dissolution (*pralaya*). || 1.6 ||
He who is perceivable by those beyond the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, consisting of all beings, and inconceivable—he himself indeed arose. 1.7.

"He who is that one" means: he who is that Self (ātman) which cannot be grasped by the mind because it transcends the senses; subtle, because it is perceivable only by a subtle intellect; eternal, because it is permanent; consisting of all beings, because everything originates from it; and inconceivable, because its powers are extraordinary—it was he himself who assumed a body. 1.7
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures from his own body, he first created the waters alone; into them, he cast his seed. (1.8)

"He" refers to that Self (Ātman). Desiring to create various kinds of progeny, he created water itself by mere meditation from his own assumed body even before creation; into those waters, he infused his seed, which is his own power. || 1.8 ||
That egg became golden, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.

"Thus": that *vīrya* (vital energy) became a golden egg, and for that very reason it possessed a brilliance equal to the sun. And within that, by his own will, Hiraṇyagarbha was born. His designation is "the Grandfather," the creator of all worlds. 1.9.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara; since they were his primordial abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (1.10)

The waters are called by the word *nārāḥ* because they are the offspring (*apatyāni*) of that Person known as the Self (*ātman*) in the manner previously described. Since those waters were his first course (*ayanam*), his primordial support—taking the word *ayanam* to mean "that in which he moves" (*eti asmin*)—therefore he is remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*. This etymological definition of his own name is thus provided for the sake of strengthening what was stated before; and according to the rule "the long vowel is seen in other cases as well," *narāyaṇa* becomes *nārāyaṇa*. (1.10)
That cause which is unmanifest, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being—from that was he, the Puruṣa, emitted; in this world, he is celebrated as Brahman. 1.11.

That which has been called "Self" (ātman) and will be described according to the method [to follow]—the cause of all, because it is accessible through the reasonings and scriptures taught in the Vedānta, and because it is not an object of perception and other means of knowledge, it is, while being existent, as if non-existent by nature—the Person produced by that [Self] is celebrated here and there by the word "Brahman. 1.11.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One himself,
through his own meditative power, divided that egg into two parts.
"In that" means: having remained for a year by his own will within that aforementioned egg, Brahmā divided that egg into two halves by means of meditation directed toward his own self alone. (1.12)
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between them, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.

"By those two": by means of those two egg-shells, that Brahmā fashioned heaven with one and the earth with the other. And between them, he created space along with the directions and the intermediate directions—making eight—and the stable abode of the waters known as the ocean. And this he fashioned from the principles (tattvas) beginning with the Great One (mahat). 1.13.
And from himself he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the presiding lord who is the conceiver.

To demonstrate that "it is indeed just so," he says, "He brought forth. According to the Vedānta philosophy, the creation of the principles (*tattva*) proceeds from the body of Prajāpati alone; therefore, [the objection] is irrelevant here. The *pradhāna*, which is the referent of the word, is expressed by the term "Self" (*ātman*). And thus:
"From this [Self] is born the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and all the sense organs;
[and] space, wind, light, water, and the earth, the supporter of the universe."

Thus, by such passages in the Upaniṣads, it is stated that from the Self, which exists in various states of imagined differentiation, all this world arises in an imagined form. That Brahmā drew forth from his own body the mind (*manas*), which—because it is eternally inferable—is, as it were, non-existent in nature; for its existence is understood through the mark of the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions, and thus the mind is both existent and non-existent in nature. First, he drew forth the principle called the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the conceiving subject, characterized by the conceit "I," which is associated with its effects and capable of performing its own functions. (1.14)
And [he perceives] the Self as truly great, as well as all the five sense organs, which possess the three qualities and are the perceivers of objects, gradually. 1.15.

"Manāhatam" (the mind): because it arose from the Self prior to the principle called *ahaṅkāra*, he has extracted it. Those which have been mentioned are endowed with the three qualities known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Likewise, there are the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriyas*)—namely, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—which gradually produce the cognitions of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, according to the sequence taught in the Vedānta. By the word "and" (*ca*), the organs of action (*karmendriyas*)—namely, the anus, genitals, hands, feet, and speech—are also included; since it is stated that they are "graspers of objects" by virtue of being sense organs, the creation of the objects themselves is also implied by implication. 1.15.
But having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [great elements], each possessing immeasurable power, within their own respective measures, he fashioned all beings.

Regarding the word "teṣām" (of them): having joined those subtle components of the six previously mentioned [elements] and the great subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of sound and so forth—which possess immeasurable power and extreme vigor due to their accomplishment of infinite effects—to the portions of their respective functions within the measures of the self (*ātma-mātrā*), he created all beings, beginning with humans. 1.16.
Those subtle components of form which these six take as their support—therefore the wise call that "body" (śarīra), being the form (mūrti) of that [Self]. 1.17.

Regarding the phrase "the components of form" (*mūrtyavayavā*): because the subtle components called *tanmātras* and *ahaṃkāra*, which constitute form and produce its shape, are conceptually differentiated as belonging to that Self; and through connection with whom these elements to be described hereafter take recourse [to it] as effects—therefore, worldly people call that very form, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of that Self, when it has undergone transformation, "the body. This etymological definition of the body is stated for the purpose of strengthening the sequence of origination already described. (1.17)
Then the great elements, together with their functions, enter that imperishable creator of all beings, along with the mind and its subtle components. 1.18

"Into That"—that is, into Brahman existing in the state of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and ego (ahaṅkāra)—the great elements, beginning with space, subsequently enter; that is, they arise from the subtle elements. Together with their functions—namely, support, cohesion, digestion, expansion, and providing space—which are their respective effects, and with the mind as its constituent part consisting of pure and impure volitions, which is subtle because it lacks external visibility; [they enter] "the creator of all beings," because the world originates from karma produced by pure and impure volitions, and [it is] "indestructible," meaning imperishable; they enter [it], for it arises from ego. (1.18)
But from the subtle material constituents of these seven immensely powerful beings, that which is imperishable arises from the imperishable.

Regarding the word "of them": because the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the Great Principle (*mahat*) were previously mentioned, and because the Great Principle was introduced even earlier, [the text says] "of these seven. Since these seven are produced from the Puruṣa, this perishable world arises from the Puruṣas through their imperishable, non-perishing portions that constitute the body. This remaining portion is a restatement intended to demonstrate that whatever is an effect is unstable, whereas whatever is the cause of production is stable relative to its effect. (1.19)
Among these, each subsequent one acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever among them occupies the nth position is traditionally held to possess that many qualities. (1.20)

"From the first of these... means that from among these elements introduced in the preceding verse, each subsequent element, such as air and the rest, takes on the sound and other qualities belonging to each preceding element, such as ether and the rest; the fact that sound and the others are the qualities of ether and so forth will be stated later. Likewise, ether and the others [take on qualities] in succession. Thus, regarding the attainment of double the qualities for the others—excluding ether and the rest—he says: "Whichever one... Whichever among these is the *yāvatitha* (the *n*-th), meaning whichever fills a certain position starting from the second, that possesses that many qualities—such as two qualities, three qualities, and so forth—as recorded by Manu and others. (1.20)
But he, at the very beginning, fashioned the names and the distinct functions of all beings, as well as their separate conditions, from the words of the Veda alone.

"Of all"—that Brahmā created the names of all [beings], such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth, as well as their respective actions, such as Vedic study and the like, individually; those very same [names and actions] which had existed for each in the previous kalpa, he fashioned at the beginning of creation from the very words of the Vedas that appeared to his mind as they had been studied in the prior kalpa, like one waking from sleep—and likewise the various worldly conventions. (1.21)
The Lord created the gods who consist of karma, as well as living beings; he also created the subtle host of the Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.

Regarding the phrase "of those whose nature is action" (*karmātmanām*): [the Lord] created the host of deities such as Indra who possess vital breath (*prāṇavat*) and are constituent parts of ritual action; for there are also deities such as Yakṣas who are without vital breath. Furthermore, he created the host of the Sādhyas—specific classes of gods—and the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, which remain eternal because they are performed even in other Kalpas. The Sādhyas are mentioned separately because of their subtlety. (1.22)
From fire, wind, and the sun, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman—
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas— for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.

"From Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi": although the triad of the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman is eternal, constant, and subtle, he drew it forth from Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi at the beginning by means of his divine power. This is not to be doubted, because it is for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice and because it is based on traditional scripture (āgama). Accordingly, the Brāhmaṇa states: "The Ṛgveda was born from Agni," and so forth. 1.23.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets; the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and the level and uneven terrains. 1.24.

Regarding "time" (kāla): time is that which possesses the activity of obstructing and setting in motion the movements of the sun and other celestial bodies; the divisions of time consist of months and so forth; the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) begin with Aśvayuj; the planets (graha) are the Sun and others; and there are the rivers, oceans, mountains, and even and uneven terrains. Here, the verb "he created" (sasarja) refers to the action to be mentioned later. 1.24.
Desiring to create these progeny, he emitted this creation: austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger. (1.25)

"Austerity" (tapas): "Delight" (rati) is the tranquility of the mind. He created these aforementioned divine and other beings, as well as the creation previously described and mentioned in this verse. || 1.25 ||
For the sake of distinguishing between actions, he separated merit and demerit;
and he joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.

Regarding the phrase "of actions": he distinguished between dharma and adharma separately for the sake of classifying actions such as giving and theft, establishing that "this is dharma, therefore acts such as giving which accomplish it must be performed," and "this, however, is adharma, therefore acts such as theft which produce it must not be done. Furthermore, he joined these creatures with pairs of mutually contradictory states—pleasures and pains arising from the birth and death of children and so forth—which are the fruits of dharma and adharma; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), hunger, satiety, and other such conditions are included. (1.26)
The minute, perishable particles that are said to constitute the five elements—along with these, all this [universe] comes into being in successive order. (1.27)

Regarding the word *anvya*: those which are the subtle measures (*sūkṣmamātrāḥ*), the perishable portions of the five *tanmātras*, because they are subject to transformation—along with these, that which has been stated and will be stated arises. This is because they follow [everything] everywhere in due order. To dispel the misconception that the creation about to be described immediately follows [the previous section] might occur without the *tattvas*, he reminds us once more, in the midst of the description of creation, that [all things] arise from the *tattvas*. (1.27)
Whatever task the Lord first appointed him to perform,
that very same task he himself undertook again and again as he was being created.

Regarding the word "yam": that particular species, such as the lion and so forth, which Prajāpati assigned at the beginning of creation to a specific action, such as the killing of elephants; that particular species, even after the time of the initial creation, whenever it is being produced again by the power of its own accumulated karma, then and there it spontaneously engages in that very same act, such as the killing of elephants, and no longer requires the appointment of Prajāpati, because that [action] has been made by Prajāpati as the inherent nature (jātidharma) of that species. || 1.28 ||
Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—
whatever each [being] had bestowed at the beginning of creation, that very thing entered into him of its own accord.

To explain this in detail, he says: "The violent and the non-violent," and so forth. Violent action belongs to the tiger and similar creatures; non-violent action belongs to the ruru deer and similar animals. Mild action, endowed with compassion, belongs to the Brāhmaṇa and others; cruel action belongs to the Kṣatriya and others. Righteousness (*dharma*) is, for example, the nurturing of offspring by the crow and other such beings. Although their merit does not actually arise from that [act] because it is for the benefit of others, it is figuratively designated as "righteousness. Unrighteousness (*adharma*) is, for example, that of the crane and others. This too, as before, is spoken of figuratively because of its intent toward deception. Truth (*ṛta*) belongs to the gods and untruth (*anṛta*) to human beings; thus it is said: "The gods are speakers of truth, whereas humans are indeed speakers of untruth. Although all of this is already included within the mention of righteousness and unrighteousness, nevertheless, the separate enumeration in pairs is based on the distinction of their specific natures. Whichever action among these Prajāpati assigned—that is, gave—at the beginning of creation, that very same thing the being himself partakes of upon being born at a later time in the creation. As he will state: "The mobile and immobile world was created according to their karma. Therefore, it should be understood that whatever he assigned to each was due to the power of the karma acquired in a previous cycle. (1.29)
Just as the seasons, in their regular succession, spontaneously assume their own respective characteristics according to the season, so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.

Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as): just as spring and the other seasons perform their own characteristic actions by themselves at their proper time, in the same way, living beings perform their respective actions, such as violence and so forth. 1.30.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.

Regarding the phrase "of the worlds": according to the principle to be stated later—that "what is cast into the fire [arises as the world]"—He created the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes from pleasure and the rest, respectively, for the sake of the multiplicity of the worlds beginning with the earth, by means of His divine power (*daivī śakti*). And thus there is the scriptural indication (*liṅga*): "The Brāhmaṇa was His mouth," and so forth. (1.31)
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became male with one half and female with the other; with her, the Lord created Virāj.
"In two ways": that Brahmā, having divided his body into two parts, became a male with one half and a female with the other; and from her, he created the person named Virāj. (1.32)
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person, whom he himself created after performing austerities; I am the creator of all this.
"Tapas. O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj just mentioned, who, having performed austerity, created himself—that creator of all this. 1.33.
Desiring to create progeny, I performed most difficult austerities and,
from the beginning, created ten great seers as the lords of creatures.
Desiring to create progeny, I performed extremely difficult austerities and first created ten Prajāpatis and great Ṛṣis. || 1.34 ||
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. (1.35)
And he said to them: "Marīci. || 1.35 ||
These [Manus], possessing great splendor, created seven other Manus,
as well as the gods and their hosts, and the great seers of immeasurable power.

"These" refers to these ten of great splendor who created seven other Manus, as well as the gods, the classes of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable luster. For all these Manus, each one possesses the authority for creation and so forth during his own Manvantara. (1.36)
And [he saw] yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas; gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
nāgas, sarpas, and suparṇas; and the various hosts of the ancestors (pitṛs). || 1.37 ||

"And the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas. The yakṣas are the ministers of Vaiśravaṇa; the rākṣasas are those such as Rāvaṇa; the piśācas are specific types of beings dwelling in desert lands and similar places. The gandharvas are Citrasena and others; the apsaras are Menakā and others; the asuras are Virocana and others; the nāgas are Takṣaka and other serpents; and the *ahis* are the *suparṇas*, or Garuḍas. The phrase "he created the assemblies of the abodes of the ancestors, such as the Soma-drinkers (*somapāḥ*), and so forth" carries over [from the previous verse]. The same applies to what follows. (1.37)
Lightnings, thunderbolts, and clouds; red-hued flashes and Indra’s bows; meteors, atmospheric crashes, and comets; and celestial lights of various kinds.

"Lightning" (vidyut) refers to what is commonly known as a red meteoric weapon (*śastrotpāta*). The "bow" (*dhanus*) is the rainbow, which takes various colors. A "meteor" (*ulkā*) is a light in the form of a streak that falls from the atmosphere and is sometimes seen at night. A "thunderclap" (*nirghāta*) is an ominous sound arising from within the earth. "Comets" (*ketavaḥ*) are celestial bodies in the shape of staffs and so forth; there are also other celestial bodies, both superior and inferior. 1.38.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and fanged predators. || 1.39 ||

Regarding "kinnaras": *kinnaras* are those with the bodies of *kinnaras* and the faces of horses, while others are the reverse. *Vihangamas* are birds; *paśus* are cattle and the like. Although humans are also animals (*paśu*), they are mentioned separately because of their preeminence. *Vyālas* are lions and the like, possessing both upper and lower rows of teeth. (1.39)
And worms, insects, and beetles; lice, flies, and bedbugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings. 1.40.

"Regarding 'worms, insects, and moths': worms are those that take refuge in the earth; insects are somewhat larger than worms; moths are locusts. The stationary [beings] are of various kinds, distinguished as trees, shrubs, and so forth. (1.40)
Thus, by my command, all this— both the stationary and the moving— was created by those great-souled ones through the application of their ascetic power, each according to their respective karma.

"Thus" means: in this manner, by those sages, at my command, this was created through the power of their asceticism, in accordance with the karma residing in the actions of the living beings being produced. || 1.41 ||
I shall describe to you exactly what kind of karma is proclaimed for each of these beings here, as well as the sequence of their births.

"Of whom" means: for those beings, whatever kind of action they have performed, that very same has been proclaimed here in this scripture. For you, the understanding of their actions comes from the mention of their names alone—such as "gods" (*devatāḥ*) because they shine (*dyotana*) or are the place of shining, or "yakṣas" (*yakṣāḥ*) because of their sacrificing (*yakṣaṇa*), and so forth. Now, some say: "I shall explain by what connection of action they are born. Alternatively: "Whatever kind of action these beings have in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which was also told by the ancients—as for example, 'plants end with the ripening of their fruit'—that I shall describe accordingly, in accordance with the sequence of the teaching. (1.42)
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous predators with two rows of teeth;
as well as *rakṣas*, *piśācas*, and humans—all these are born from the womb. (1.43)
Regarding "animals": those born from the union of the womb and the embryo arise first therein; subsequently, those released from that state are born. || 1.43 ||
Birds born from eggs, snakes, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises—whatever other such creatures there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic. 1.44.

"Born from eggs" (aṇḍaja) means those that first come into being within an egg and are subsequently born from it: the crocodile; the creature called the porpoise (śiśumāra); the tortoise (kūrma); those born on land such as the chameleon and others; and those born in water such as the conch and others. 1.44.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from moisture;
likewise, whatever else is of this kind arises from heat.

Regarding the term "born from moisture" (*svedaja*): moisture is the internal humidity of earthly substances. Furthermore, whatever else resembles gnats and the like, such as ants and so forth—that too is included. Lice, bedbugs, and the like are born from moisture alone. (1.45)
All stationary beings are born from sprouts, growing from seeds or cuttings;
herbs are those that perish after the ripening of their fruit and are endowed with many flowers and fruits. (1.46)

"Trees are born from sprouts. Breaking through the earth upward, trees are produced. Some of these are born from seeds alone; others, however, are born from both seeds and stalks. Branches, when planted outside in the ground, become trees. Now, he demonstrates what was said regarding "the karma of each according to its kind"—namely, "herbs": the end of herbs such as rice and the like comes precisely with the ripening of their fruit, for by that they wither. They attain many flowers and fruits; that is, they become endowed with abundance. (1.46)
Those that bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*. || 1.47 ||
"Flowerless" means that fruits appear on forest trees even without flowers; trees, however, are endowed with both flowers and fruit. || 1.47 ||

Furthermore, there are various kinds of shrubs and clusters, as well as species of grasses; likewise, there are those that grow from seeds and from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines.

Regarding the term *gucchagulma*: those for which a cluster of creepers (*latāvṛnda*) exists from the very root, and which do not have trunks (*prakāṇḍa*), are *gucchās*, such as the *mallikā* and others. *Gulmas*, however, consist primarily of indistinct and short creepers that lack trunks, such as the *puṣpaka* and others. The various kinds of grasses (*tṛṇajāti*) are the *dūrvā* and others. *Pratānas* are those in the form of tendrils (*tantu*), such as the *trapuṣa*, *alābu*, and so forth. *Vallīs* are climbing creepers (*vratatī*), such as the *guḍūcī* and others. || 1.48 ||
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions, these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain. 1.49

Regarding the phrase "by *tamas*": the qualities (*guṇas*) are known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Among these, objects such as trees and so forth are pervaded by *tamas*—which, by its nature, produces various forms of suffering—and have as their cause the evil karma acquired in previous births. Although all beings possess internal consciousness to some degree, these are said to have "internal consciousness" because they lack external signs of consciousness, such as verbal expression and other forms of worldly interaction. Nevertheless, because even a trace of *sattva* and *rajas* exists within them, they are also possessed of pleasure and pain. (1.49)
These destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, are declared to end here within this terrible cycle of existence for living beings, which is perpetually and incessantly moving.

"Ending with this": all the origins of transmigratory existence, which culminate in stationary beings and have Brahman as their primary source, are said to be entirely perishable—characterized by the repeated taking up and casting off of bodies within this eternally dreadful and terrifying cycle of transmigration for living beings, that is, for the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*). 1.50.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew into himself, subduing time with time.

Having thus demonstrated the creation, he now speaks in order to show the dissolution: "In this manner, having created all this and me as well, that Prajāpati of inconceivable power again withdrew into himself. The meaning is that, by casting off his body, he destroys the period of creation through the period of dissolution; and by the force of the karma of living beings and by his own will, he repeatedly performs both creation and withdrawal. (1.51)
When that God is awake, the world thus moves;
when he sleeps with his soul at peace, then everything closes its eyes.

"When he is that God": when that Prajāpati wills, then he brings about the production and maintenance of this world in this manner; but when he does not will, being one whose self is tranquil and whose mind has withdrawn its activity, then it dissolves in this manner—that is, an intermediate dissolution (*antarālapralaya*) occurs. Just as in the body, when the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is awake, then the world consisting of beasts, birds, and reptiles moves and becomes possessed of activity; when he sleeps, then it is motionless—thus, the states of the Self known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are mentioned here as illustrations for the maintenance, intermediate state, and dissolution of the activities of Prajāpati’s waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, since they serve as examples for the causes of dissolution. (1.52)
But when that [Self] sleeps in its own state of composure, the embodied beings whose nature is action desist from their respective activities, and the mind falls into exhaustion. (1.53)

To clarify what was previously stated, he says: "When He, being self-abiding, sleeps. When He is established in cessation, self-abiding, with the mind's activities withdrawn, the embodied beings—the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña)—who possess bodies projected by their karma, cease from their respective actions such as the assumption of bodies; and the mind, devoid of all the senses, becomes free from activity. (1.53)
But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self,
then this Self of all beings sleeps happily and in peace.

Now he describes the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) with the word "simultaneously" (*yugapat*). At that very same time—when all beings dissolve into the Supreme Lord—at that very same time, this one, who has become the self of all beings, being at peace (*nirvṛta*), with the activities of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep ceased, sleeps happily; that is, he experiences deep sleep (*suṣupti*). The meaning is that in that state, the condition of deep sleep and the great dissolution occur simultaneously. (1.54)
Relying upon this darkness, the embodied being remains for a long time with its senses intact;
yet it does not perform its own functions, and then it departs from the physical form.

And in connection with the topic of dissolution, he describes the departure of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) with the words "When [it is] darkness" (tamo yat). When that self, being pervaded by extreme delusion, remains for no small time even with its senses—performing functions such as inhalation and exhalation due to the fact that the senses do not perish even upon the destruction of the body—it then abandons the body. (1.55)
When, having become as subtle as an atom, it enters into union with the seed—both the stationary and the moving—it then casts off its physical form. (1.56)

Does he abandon his form independently of another body? To this he says: "When... When, being of subtle dimension, he presides over either the seed of a stationary being or the seed of a moving being, or some other [seed], then he leaves this body. He is "conjoined," meaning joined with the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, as it is stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "As he departs, the vital breath departs after him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it. (1.56)
Thus, through waking and dreaming, that immutable one incessantly brings this entire world of moving and non-moving beings to life and causes it to perish.

"Thus": that Brahmā, in this manner, by means of his own states of waking and dreaming, incessantly and without interruption, enlivens and kills the moving and the stationary, being himself imperishable. 1.57.
Having composed this treatise himself, he first caused me alone to receive it according to the prescribed rule; I, in turn, [taught] the sages beginning with Marīci.

"This" means: having composed this scripture, this treatise, Brahmā first diligently taught it to me alone by his own self, saying of the nature of the scripture, "This is to be done; this is not. Thereafter, I taught it to the sages beginning with Marīci. || 1.58 ||
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of it from me without exception.
"Regarding this": this Bhṛgu will cause you to hear this entire scripture without omission, because he has acquired all of this in its entirety from my presence. 1.59.
Then, having been addressed in that manner by Manu, the great seer Bhṛgu, with a joyful heart, spoke to all those sages: "Let it be heard! (1.60)

Regarding the word "tataḥ": Bhṛgu, having been addressed by Manu in that manner—meaning he was effectively told, "He will cause this to be heard," rather than being directly told, "You shall cause it to be heard"—thereupon, with his heart gladdened by this honor, that teacher Bhṛgu said to those sages, "Let it be heard. (1.60)
Of this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, there were six other high-souled and highly energetic Manus in his lineage who each created their own respective progeny. (1.61)

Regarding the phrase "of Svāyaṃbhuva": in the manner described, six other Manus—descendants of Manu, the grandson of the Self-born (Brahmā), who were authorized at various times at the beginning of creation, born of his lineage, and sharing his single purpose—produced their own respective offspring. || 1.61 ||
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
And they were as follows: Svārociṣa, etc. (1.62).
These seven Manus of great splendor, beginning with Svāyambhuva, having produced all this world of moving and non-moving beings within their respective intervals, maintained it.

"Those who [descended] from Svāyaṃbhuva": the six just mentioned and Svāyaṃbhuva himself—thus there are seven. These Manus, headed by Svāyaṃbhuva, possessed great splendor; having produced this world of moving and stationary beings during their respective periods of authority, they protected the creatures. (1.63)
Eighteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, thirty of those make one *kalā*,
thirty *kalās* make one *muhūrta*, and a day and night (*ahorātra*) consists of as many [thirty] of those.

Furthermore, as to how long the term of office (*adhikāra*) for each Manu is, he says: "Nimeṣas... A *nimeṣa* is the natural blink of the eyelids, occurring together with the opening of the eyes (*unmeṣa*). Eighteen of those constitute a *kāṣṭhā*. Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are the time known as a *kalā*. Thirty *kalās* are designated as a *muhūrta*. And thirty such *muhūrtas* constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*). From the use of the accusative case [in the verse], the word "one should know" (*vidyāt*) is to be supplied. (1.64)
The sun divides day and night for both humans and gods:
night is for the sleep of beings, and day is for the performance of actions. 1.65

Regarding the phrase "day and night": the sun, the Āditya, divides day and night pertaining to gods and humans; he apportions them. Consequently, for living beings, night serves the purpose of sleep, while the day serves the purpose of exertion in action. (1.65)
For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night, divided into two fortnights;
the dark fortnight is their day for active duties, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep. (1.66)

Regarding the phrase "in the ancestral [month]": a human month is a day and night for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Therein, the division is made by means of two fortnights: the dark fortnight is the day for the purpose of undertaking ritual action, while the bright fortnight is the night for the purpose of sleep. (1.66)
In the case of the gods, a year constitutes day and night; their further division is as follows:
the northern course of the sun (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night.

Regarding the term "daive" (divine): a human year is one day and night for the gods. Within that, the division is such that the northern course [of the sun] is the day and the southern course is the night. || 1.67 ||
Now learn, in brief, the measure of a day and night of Brahmā, and the duration of each of the Yugas in their respective order.
"Of the Brahma" means: listen now briefly and in order to the measure of a day-and-night of Prajāpati and of each of the Yugas. 1.68.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.

"Four" refers to the divine years, because they have been introduced immediately prior, and because it is observed in the Purāṇas that the number of the Yugas is proclaimed by means of the divine measure alone. Manu and others state that the period known as the Kṛta-yuga consists of four thousand divine years. Its *saṃdhyā* (twilight) likewise consists of as many hundreds of years; the *saṃdhyāṃśa* (the period following the twilight) is the partial persistence of the characteristics of the past Yuga and the predominance of the characteristics of the coming Yuga, and it lasts for exactly four hundred years. (1.69)
In the other three [ages], together with their twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.

Regarding the phrase "in the others": furthermore, in the three ages beginning with Tretā, together with their respective junctions (saṃdhyā) and sub-junctions (saṃdhyāṃśa), there is a decrease by one thousand and one hundred years for each. Tretā consists of three thousand years, and its junctions and sub-junctions consist of three hundred years each. In this manner, for Dvāpara and Kali Yuga, along with their respective junctions and sub-junctions, one should understand that there is a reduction of one thousand and one hundred years from each preceding age. (1.70)
This cycle of four ages (caturyuga) which has been enumerated at the very beginning consists of twelve thousand [years]; this is called an age of the gods (devayuga). || 1.71 ||

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): this period of four ages (*caturyuga*), which was previously enumerated at the beginning prior to this verse, multiplied twelve thousand times, is the time known as a *devayuga* or *vedayuga*. || 1.71 ||
A thousand divine yugas, by calculation, should be known as one day of Brahmā; his night is of exactly the same duration.

Regarding the phrase "of the divine [ages]": a thousand of these divine yugas should be understood as one day of Brahmā; the statement that the number of nights is likewise a thousand is a restatement (anuvāda). 1.72.
Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of the same duration. 1.73.

Regarding the word "that": that which has an end after a thousand yugas is a day of Prajāpati; because knowing that is a cause of merit, those who know the night to be of the same duration are "knowers of the day and night," but this does not refer to the knowledge of the day and night of humans and so forth. This praise for the knowledge of Brahma’s day is intended to inspire interest in knowing it. 1.73.
At the end of that day and night, he who was asleep awakens;
having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): that Brahmā, having slept at the end of that day-and-night, awakens. Thereupon, he creates his own mind and employs it for the purpose of creating the world-egg (*piṇḍa*), but he does not produce [the elements] anew; for in this interval, the dissolution has passed, and another great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) has subsequently arisen. Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa: "Endowed with the desire to create, he again directed his mind toward creation. (1.74)
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings forth creation;
from it, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality. (1.75)
Regarding the word "mind" (mana): that mind, belonging to Prajāpati, being impelled at that very moment by the desire to create, performs the act of creation. 1.75.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality. 1.76.

"From space," however: from space, which has become intent upon generating its own modifications, wind is born—carrying fragrant and foul odors, pure, purifying, and powerful. And that [wind] is held by the seers to be endowed with the quality of touch (sparśa). 1.76.
From the air, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness; it is radiant and is said to have the quality of form (rūpa). 1.77

Regarding the phrase "from air": from air, as before, fire arises—resplendent, illuminating others, destroying darkness, radiant, and luminous. And that is said to be endowed with the quality known as its own nature (svarūpa). || 1.77 ||
And from light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning. 1.78.

Regarding "light" (*jyotis*): as before, it is [the element] of fire (*tejas*). Water is traditionally remembered by Manu and others as being born endowed with the quality called taste (*rasa*). And from water, earth is born endowed with the quality called smell (*gandha*). This is the first creation following the dissolution of the intermediate period (*antarālapralaya*). 1.78.
That divine yuga which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand [years],
multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a *manvantara*.

Regarding the word "yat" (which): that which was described as a divine *yuga*, consisting of four *yugas* with the measurement of the *dvāpara*, multiplied by seventy-one, is here in this treatise called a period known as a *manvantara*. This much time constitutes the authority for the creation and so forth of one *sattva*. || 1.79 ||
The Manvantaras are innumerable, as are the creations and destructions;
the Supreme Lord performs these again and again, as if in play. (1.80)

Although fourteen Manvantaras are enumerated in the Purāṇas, nevertheless, when they become infinite through repetition, then creation and dissolution occur. And because this reality known as creation and dissolution abides in the Supreme State characterized by non-return, Prajāpati, the Supreme Lord, performs this again and again as if in play. Not only His will alone is the cause here, but also the karmas of living beings; for this very reason, the word "eva" (indeed/only) is used. 1.80.
In the Kṛta age, the Dharma was complete in its four quarters, and truth alone prevailed;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred through unrighteousness among human beings.

"Four-footed" refers to this entire dharma which has four supports. Likewise, truth existed in the Kṛta age; it is mentioned separately because of its preeminence. And thus, for human beings, there was no acquisition of knowledge or wealth by means other than [rightful] weapons. 1.81.
In the other [ages], Dharma exists by means of scripture, but it is diminished quarter by quarter; through theft, falsehood, and deceit, Dharma likewise departs quarter by quarter. (1.82)

Regarding the phrase "in the others": in the Tretā and subsequent ages, however, due to the coming of the scriptures (śāstra), dharma—the performance of sacrifices and so forth—is, according to the sequence of each age, diminished and reduced by one quarter per age through theft, untruth, and deceit. This is not because of the ages themselves, since theft and the rest are observed in all ages, though not necessarily in equal measure. And thus, as the performance [of dharma] recedes quarter by quarter, the primary dharma—which is the cause of prosperity (abhyudaya) to be accomplished by that performance—also recedes quarter by quarter. (1.82)
In the Kṛta age, people were free from disease, accomplished in all their aims, and had a lifespan of four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan is diminished by one quarter at each stage.

"Free from disease" means they are free from disease because of the absence of unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is the cause of illness; "having all their goals accomplished" means that all desired fruits have been achieved. Because of the absence of obstructing unrighteousness, according to the perspective of the *Purāṇas*, they have a lifespan of four hundred years. Thus it is said: this lifespan is natural, yet by performing actions that procure longevity, they may even possess a longer life. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the statement, "Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years. Furthermore, in Vedic texts such as "Man is indeed a hundred-year-old," the word "hundred" has a plural sense, since both the words "hundred" (*śata*) and "thousand" (*sahasra*) are recorded among the names for "many. Such are the humans in the *Kṛta* age. In the *Tretā* and subsequent ages, however, their lifespan diminishes by one quarter in each successive age. (1.83)
The lifespan of mortals declared in the Vedas, as well as the fruits of ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to the respective age. 1.84.

"Stated in the Veda" refers to: "Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years. Thus, if the lifespan stated in the Veda and the power of the principal optional rites (*kāmyakarma*) are fulfilled, the attainment of a hundred-year life for human beings bears fruit in accordance with the [specific] age (*yuga*). 1.84.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are one thing, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are others,
and those in the Kali age are yet others, according to the decline of the ages.
"Others" means that in the ages beginning with Kṛta, there occurs a difference in the dharma of human beings according to the nature of each respective age. || 1.85 ||
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity is the one thing of importance.

And so it is with austerity (*tapas*). In the Kṛta age, austerity—consisting of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such observances—is practiced primarily and predominantly by human beings, due to the inherent nature of that age; self-knowledge, sacrifice, and charity follow as secondary adjuncts. Likewise, in the Tretā age, knowledge is supreme while austerity and the rest are merely incidental. Similarly, they say that in the Dvāpara age sacrifice is supreme, and in the Kali age, charity is supreme. (1.86)
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.

Regarding the word "of all": that Brahmā, possessed of great luster, for the sake of protecting this entire world—according to the principle expressed in such passages as "The oblation cast into the fire" (*agnau prāstāhutiḥ*)—ordained the various duties, both for the sake of unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*) and for the sake of livelihood (*vṛttyartha*), of the Brāhmaṇas and other classes born from his mouth and the other [limbs]. These are mentioned here as being supplementary to the account of creation. Thus it has been stated: "For the protection of this entire creation. However, the actual injunction (*vidhi*) regarding these will appear later, since this present section is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). (1.87)
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving gifts and receiving them. (1.88)

In this regard, "teaching" refers to the study and instruction of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) and the Smṛtis, as well as reciting and expounding them. "Sacrificing for oneself and officiating at sacrifices" refers to performing sacrifices and acting as a priest for others. "Giving" consists of providing food and water, and removing the suffering of living beings according to one's ability. He ordained that Brāhmaṇas should accept gifts from virtuous persons. 1.88.
The protection of subjects, giving, sacrifice, and study, as well as non-attachment to sensual objects, constitute the duty of a Kṣatriya in brief. 1.89.
"Of the subjects" means: *ijyā* is sacrifice. "In objects" refers to the forms and so forth residing in women and other such things. "Complete avoidance" means: in brief, that is, in summary. (1.89)
The protection of cattle, giving gifts, performing sacrifices, studying, trade, moneylending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya. (1.90)
Trade is the journey for the purpose of commerce by way of land, water, or other routes. Lending at interest is the investment of wealth for the sake of profit. 1.90.
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra: to serve these very classes without malice. (1.91)
"One": that Lord, out of compassion, enjoined the service of Brāhmaṇas and others as a duty and so forth. 1.91.
The upper part of a man’s body, above the navel, is declared to be more pure;
therefore, his mouth has been described by the Self-Existent One as the most pure of all. (1.92)

Now, in order to praise the scripture by way of explaining the distinction between the duties of the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes—praise which results from study, hearing, and practice—he speaks this praise of the Brāhmaṇa: "Above... (1.92). Since it is established that a person is pure in every respect, the Self-existent One declared that the region above the navel is even more pure, and that the mouth is the most pure of all.
Because he was produced from the highest limb, because of his seniority,
and because he upholds the Veda, the Brahmin is, by the very nature of this entire creation, the lord according to dharma.

What follows from this? To this he says: "Because of his birth from the highest limb. Because he was born from the head, because he was produced first, because he is endowed with the sacred teachings and so forth, and because he possesses the most excellent retention of the Vedas, the Brāhmaṇa is the master in the instruction of Dharma for the entire world. (1.93)

For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.

From whose head, then, did he emerge? To this he says: "Him. The Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), having performed austerity from his own mouth, created that Brahmin during the first creation for the purpose of carrying the food of the gods and ancestors and for the protection of the world. 1.94.
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the denizens of heaven always consume the sacrificial offerings (havya), and the ancestors likewise consume the ancestral offerings (kavya)? 1.95.

And thus, as for the phrase "of whom": what being could be more preeminent than that great soul known as a Brāhmaṇa, from whose mouth the gods dwelling in heaven—the celestial inhabitants of immense power—continually consume the *havya* offerings, and the ancestors likewise consume the *kavya* offerings? (1.95)
Among beings, living creatures are the best; among living creatures, those who live by intelligence are the best;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, Brahmins are traditionally held to be the best.

Now, he speaks the verse beginning with "Of beings" (*bhūtānām*) in order to praise the Brāhmaṇa by virtue of his possession of qualities such as learning: "Of all beings," that is, among all living creatures, both stationary and moving, even though they all possess qualities, those such as scorpions and the like who have an elevated consciousness are superior to the stationary beings because of their experience of higher pleasure. Even superior to them are dogs and the like, who live by their intelligence, because of their coming and going in search of food and shelter. Even superior to them are human beings because of their distinguished discernment. Even superior to them are Brāhmaṇas, because of their fitness for the qualification toward liberation (*apavarga*). (1.96)

Among Brahmins, there are those who are learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are refined; among those of refined intellect, those who perform their duties; and among those who perform their duties, those who know Brahman. || 1.97 ||

Regarding the phrase "among the Brahmins": even among them, the learned are superior because they possess the qualification for performing actions that yield great fruit; even more so than them are those of perfected intellect, who have formed the resolve to carry out the meaning of the scriptures; even more so than them are the practitioners, because they are engaged in the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired; and even more so than them are those who have realized the Self, because their fruit is liberation. (1.97)
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.

Furthermore, what is meant by "birth"? For a Brāhmaṇa, birth alone is the imperishable body of dharma, because he is born for the sake of dharma; having been initiated, he becomes one with Brahman through the knowledge of the Self. 1.98.
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born upon this earth, he is born as a lord over all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma. 1.99.

"O Brāhmaṇa! Because the Brāhmaṇa, upon being born, is produced as the one who is superior, unique, and most excellent on earth—being the lord and master of all beings for the sake of preserving the accumulation of Dharma—and because he is born with pure qualities, therefore he is the eternal embodiment of Dharma; this is the reason previously stated. [The word] *kośa* means a storehouse or accumulation of wealth; here, however, the word *kośa* is used figuratively. And his role as its protector arises from his teaching of all Dharmas to the Brāhmaṇas. (1.99)
"Everything that exists in this world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble lineage, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this. (1.100)

"Everything is his own. Because this would contradict the scriptural injunctions against theft and so forth that will be mentioned later, and because this [statement] is primarily intended as praise, it is said that the entire collection of objects existing in the world is like the property of a Brāhmaṇa. In that regard, since the Brāhmaṇa himself—by virtue of his excellence, his noble lineage, and his being born from the mouth—is worthy to take possession of everything, therefore all this is indeed his own property. (1.100)
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the Brahmin’s compassion that other people eat at all. (1.101)

And thus, "it is his own": even that food, clothing, and so forth belonging to others which he provides is considered his very own; this is praise as before. And thus, out of kindness—that is, out of compassion directed toward him—other people provide food, clothing, and so forth. 1.101.
For the sake of discerning his own duties, as well as those of the others in due order, the wise Manu, son of the Self-Existent, composed this treatise. 1.102.

Now he states the fruit of the praise of the Brāhmaṇa mentioned above, beginning with the words "tasya" (of him): This great treatise, which is such as this, was composed by Manu—the grandson of Prajāpati and possessed of excellent intelligence—primarily for the sake of discerning what ought to be done and what ought not to be done for the Brāhmaṇa defined by the aforementioned characteristics, and incidentally for the sake of that same discernment for the rest, from the Kṣatriyas down to the mixed castes. (1.102)
This must be studied with diligence by a learned Brahmin and correctly expounded to his disciples; it is not to be taught by anyone else. 1.103.

Regarding the word "learned" (*viduṣā*): this undertaking is for the purpose of ensuring that a Brāhmaṇa—who desires what is beneficial and avoids what is harmful and knows these things—studies this treatise with diligence. By the inclusion of the term "diligence," the right to study this work is also granted to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; thus, he will later state, "from conception until the cremation ground," and so forth. However, there is no requirement for them to apply the same degree of effort as a Brāhmaṇa. Nor does this imply that the rule applies to the Brāhmaṇa alone, because the word "diligence" is not used as a qualification of the Brāhmaṇa in that context. Nor is the status of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas established by this alone, because if the section beginning with "conception" were not commenced, the word "diligence" would be incapable of conveying such a specific distinction. Furthermore, there is no mention here of Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas. Once this scripture on conception and so forth exists, it follows that the right to study belongs to all twice-born (*dvija*) castes, while the Brāhmaṇa must be diligent. Moreover, this undertaking is for the purpose of establishing the Brāhmaṇa’s right to teach this scripture and to prohibit others from doing so. As for the claim made by some that this verse is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), that is unproven, because its meaning is clearly understood. If the meaning were merely an explanatory praise, there would be no distinction based on diligence. Let us grant that such a distinction might not exist here; however, if this were a mere *arthavāda*, the specific distinction—that the Brāhmaṇa has the right to teach this scripture while others are prohibited—is difficult to establish. As for the statement, "the three castes should study," and so forth, we shall explain that as a restatement (*anuvāda*) concerning the Vedas. (1.103)
A Brahmin who studies this treatise and whose vows are well-praised is never defiled by the faults of action born of mind, speech, or body. (1.104)

"Regarding this": by studying this treatise, a Brahmin who understands its meaning and whose vows are praised—remaining unimpaired in his restraints (yama) and observances (niyama)—is not bound by the sins produced by the non-performance of prescribed duties or the performance of prohibited ones through the mind, speech, and body. 1.104.
He purifies his lineage and seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even alone, he is worthy of this entire earth.

Furthermore, what does he purify? Because of his connection with the row [of diners] during the taking of food, he purifies that row which has become impure; for, by virtue of being established in the scriptures, he possesses the quality of being a "purifier of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*). Likewise, by his lineage, he purifies seven ancestors—his father and so forth—who have passed away, and seven descendants who are yet to come. And he is worthy to receive this entire earth as a gift, because the learned man possesses the capacity to remove the defects inherent in receiving gifts. (1.105)
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect; this constantly brings renown; and this is the supreme state of ultimate liberation. 1.106

Now he directly praises the treatise with the words "This" (idam). This [treatise] is superior to other rites for securing well-being (*svastyayana*), meaning it is preeminently praiseworthy; it is a *svastyayana* because it brings about non-destruction. It increases the intellect through the understanding of the practices that pacify destruction, and through the enumeration of the meaning of the treatise, it expands the intellect. Furthermore, it is supreme because it constantly—i.e., at all times—produces renown by being the cause of fame, and it is the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) because it is the means of achieving liberation (*mokṣa*). 1.106.
In this [work], the Dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions, and the eternal conduct of all four social classes. 1.107

"In this [work]" means: in this [treatise], the dharma based on tradition (smārta) has been stated in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions—both prescribed and prohibited—which result in desired and undesired fruits for the social classes (varṇas). Furthermore, the conduct (ācāra) known as the dharma of persons is mentioned separately in order to demonstrate both its commonality and its predominance. And thus, in this context, the word "dharma" is used in its general sense, referring to such practices as the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) and so forth. (1.107)
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared in the Śruti and in the Smṛti;
therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be constantly devoted to it. 1.108.

Regarding "conduct" (ācāra): that conduct which is declared in the Śruti is called *dharma* for the purpose of proclaiming its universal importance for all persons; and that which is based on the Smṛti is the supreme *dharma*, preferred above sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Aṣṭakā, among both Śrauta and Smārta duties. Therefore, one whose soul is always praiseworthy should be constantly engaged and diligent in conduct at all times. 1.108.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas;
however, one who is endowed with right conduct is declared to partake of the full fruit. 1.109

"Regarding 'from conduct' (ācārāt): A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen away from conduct—that is, one whose behavior has deviated from the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti—does not obtain the fruit of Vedic action. On the other hand, one who possesses good conduct becomes a partaker of the complete fruit. (1.109)
Having thus observed the course of Dharma through right conduct, the sages adopted right conduct as the supreme root of all austerity. 1.110

"Thus" means as follows: by their intellect, the seers perceived that the attainment of Dharma through right conduct (*ācāra*) is superior to—and more excellent than—the fruits of austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*; for it is when this [conduct] exists that austerities become fruitful. Thus, in this context, the praise of conduct is for the purpose of praising the scripture; however, in what follows, it is for the purpose of the actual practice of conduct. (1.110)
And he [taught] the origin of the world, the very rules for the formative processes (saṃskāra),
the practice of religious observances (vratacaryā) and ritual service, and the supreme rule for ritual bathing.
Now, in order to demonstrate that this treatise is endowed with a grand narrative, he states the table of contents: "Of the world... (1.111).
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages, the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha). 1.112.
"Acquisition of a wife," thus [it is said]. 1.112.
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, the vows of a Snātaka,
what may and may not be eaten, purification, and the cleansing of objects.
"Of the mental modifications" (vṛttīnām) || 1.113 ||
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation itself;
the entire duty of kings and the determination of legal cases.
"Regarding the application of the duties of women. (1.114)
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife, the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns (criminals). || 1.115 ||
The procedure for questioning witnesses. 1.115.
[He taught] the conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation.
"The conduct toward Vaiśyas and Śūdras. (1.116)
The journey through saṃsāra, which arises from the threefold karma;
the supreme good resulting from actions; and the examination of the merits and defects of those actions. || 1.117 ||
"Going through cyclic existence" (saṃsāragamana). || 1.117 ||
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of countries, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and groups. (1.118)

Regarding "the laws of the regions" (*deśadharmān*): the origin of the world has been explained as it was stated. The praise of Brahmā and so forth is included within this very category, because they share the same purpose as the praise of the scriptural law (*śāstradharma*). [1.111f] The injunction for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*) is their performance. The practice of vows (*vratacaryā*) is the observance of vows; a vow is that of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). Service (*upacāra*) is the compliance with salutations and other duties toward teachers and others. The compound *vratacaryopacāram* is a singular collective dvandva. Bathing (*snāna*) is a specific purificatory rite for one returning from the teacher’s house; its supreme injunction (*paro vidhiḥ*) is the excellent rule. Marriage (*dārādhigamana*) is the taking of a wife. This includes the definitions of marriage types such as the *brāhma* and others, as well as the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), such as the *vaiśvadeva*. The ritual for ancestral offerings (*śrāddhakalpa*) is the procedure for *śrāddha*. The eternal (*śāśvataḥ*) refers to that which is constant due to its operation as a beginningless stream. The definition of livelihoods (*vṛtti*)—the means of subsistence such as agriculture and so forth—is given. The vows of a *snātaka* householder are mentioned. Edible food (*bhakṣya*) includes curds and the like; non-edible (*abhakṣya*) includes garlic and the like. Purity (*śauca*) regarding childbirth and so forth lasts ten days and so on. The purification of substances such as metallic objects is by means of alkaline substances and the like. The application of duty (*dharmayoga*) for a woman is the performance of religious duties. Asceticism (*tāpasya*) is the activity of an ascetic forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). For a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), liberation (*mokṣa*) and renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) are indeed modes of the mendicant's duty, since worldly existence is the cause [of bondage]. The duty of an anointed king is the determination of legal cases (*vyavahāra*) presented by plaintiffs and defendants, as well as the rules for questioning witnesses. The duty of husband and wife (*strīpuṃsayoḥ*) is their mutual conduct. The duty regarding the division of paternal inheritance is mentioned. Gambling with dice and so forth, and the regulation thereof, as well as the removal of "thorns"—the eradication of thieves and the like—are discussed. The service (*upacāra*) of Vaiśyas and Śūdras is the performance of livelihood (*vārtā*), such as service and so forth. The origin of mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇa*), whether through the direct or inverse order of birth, is described. The instruction on livelihood in times of distress is the "law of distress" (*āpaddharma*). The performance of penance (*prāyaścitta*) follows from the non-performance of prescribed duties and so forth. The origin of the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) occurs through the threefold causes of action, distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior. That than which there is nothing else more auspicious is the "highest good" (*niḥśreyasa*), namely self-knowledge, because it is the cause of the highest bliss. The examination of the merits and defects of actions, both prescribed and prohibited, is detailed. Laws based on specific regions, castes, and families are mentioned. Heresy (*pākhaṇḍa*) consists of wearing sectarian marks based on external philosophical systems. A guild (*gaṇa*) is an association of merchants, artisans, and so forth. [1.111–118]
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me, so also do you now learn it from me. 1.119

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): it is not established that [Manu spoke this] because of the implication of the meaning of the subsequent scripture, namely, "Just as Manu was previously questioned by me and spoke this, so too do you hear from my presence this tradition which has not fallen away. 1.119.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Manvāśayānusāriṇī*, composed by Govindarāja, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mādhava.
Now begins the second chapter.
Understand that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous, who are always free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart. 2.1.

Oṃ, salutations to Sarasvatī! Having thus established the great purpose of the treatise for the sake of study and hearing, [the author] now begins for the purpose of stating the subject matter at hand. In that regard, he first states the general definition of Dharma—which is about to be explained—as a technical term (paribhāṣā) that pervades the entire treatise, beginning with the words "by the learned": "Listen to that Dharma which, being a duty whose purpose is the unseen (adṛṣṭa), is practiced by the learned—those virtuous and righteous people who know the meaning of the Vedas—and who are always free from passion and hatred, and by whom it is approved in their hearts and free from internal conflict. (2.1) Since Dharma has no other source of authority, it is that which is practiced by the learned who understand the meaning of the Vedas; by the virtuous who are righteous; and by those who are always devoid of attachment and aversion. It is that Dharma which is approved within the heart and free from the wavering of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa); it is a duty whose nature consists of an unseen result. Listen to that! (2.1)
To have the self centered on desire is not praised, yet here there is no such thing as being without desire;
for the mastery of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.

He states another objection: "Kāmātmatā" (being motivated by desire). Being motivated by desire is not praiseworthy; it is improper to have a disposition characterized by longing for results. For ritual acts enjoined by the scriptures, when performed while abandoning the longing for results and as an aid to the knowledge of the Self, lead to liberation. However, if they are performed with a desire for results, they become causes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Granted that being motivated by desire is not praiseworthy—by this, the desire itself is prohibited—he says, "And yet not so," considering this point. Without desire, there is no engagement in this scripture, because the acquisition of the Vedas and the connection with Vedic rituals are indeed to be desired. (2.2)
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices arise from volition;
vows, restraints, and duties—all are traditionally held to be born of volition. (2.3)

Right here he states the proof: "Rooted in volition" (*saṃkalpamūla*). Volition (*saṃkalpa*) is a mental operation of the form: "By means of this object, this purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is to be accomplished. And that is the root of desire (*kāma*), for immediately after it, the wish to acquire that object arises; following that, there occurs determination (*adhyavasāya*), which is the exertion of the instruments through physical activity. Thus, sacrifices and the like originate from volition. Since they arise from volition, they must necessarily exist without [prior] desire. From volition, self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and determination proceeds the engagement in action. The duties of restraint (*yamadharmāḥ*) consist of prohibitions. (2.3)
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire. (2.4)

In this very context, he states a worldly illustration: "Of one who is without desire" (akāmasya). Any action performed with deliberate intention that has a visible purpose is never seen to occur in one who lacks desire. Therefore, whatever action one performs, all of that is the movement of desire; the meaning is that it is the effect of will. (2.4)
Behaving correctly toward these, one goes to the world of the immortals and enjoys here all desires exactly as they were intended. (2.5)

To this, he states the resolution: "In those [actions].
