Here, desire is not prohibited; rather, this is the correct conduct (*samyagvṛtti*) that one should perform exactly as it is heard in scripture. One who engages in those actions by abandoning the longing for their fruits does not incur bondage, and thus attains the state of the immortals—that is, the nature of the immortals, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). In this transmigratory world (*saṃsāra*), through the practice of self-knowledge and the possession of the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*), one enjoys all objects as desired. (2.5)
The Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the tradition and conduct of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous, and also the satisfaction of one's own self. (2.6)

Now, for the purpose of enumerating the means of knowledge regarding Dharma, he says: "The Veda. The Veda—characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma—is "entire," meaning complete. Since even the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and others are heard as being syntactically unified with injunctions (*vidhi*), it is the root and authority for Dharma, because it is free from false knowledge and doubt, and because its validity is innate. This is established by logic. This is restated here in order to demonstrate that the Smṛtis and other texts possess authority because they are rooted in the Veda. Likewise, the codification of the Mānava and other scriptures consists of the recollection of what is to be done and what is not to be done by those who know the Veda; "conduct" (*śīla*) consists of the abandonment of passion and hatred; "custom" (*ācāra*) consists of practices such as the binding of the marriage-thread during weddings and so forth; and the "self-satisfaction" (*ātmatuṣṭi*) of the virtuous and righteous consists of a mental contentment regarding matters practiced for invisible purposes (*adṛṣṭa*), pertaining to optional matters. All these are authorities regarding Dharma because they are rooted in the Veda. (2.6)
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone, all that is stated in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge. (2.7)

And thus he demonstrates that these have the Veda as their source—by the words "yaḥ" (who). For some, dharma is based on the authority of scripture (*śruti*), conduct (*śīla*), custom (*ācāra*), and self-satisfaction (*ātmatuṣṭi*); for others, such as the Brāhmaṇas, it has been declared by Manu. All of that is said to be "stated by all the Vedas," because the memory of those [traditions] is rooted in signs (*liṅga*) found in *mantras* and *arthavādas* that have been lost or scattered. For in the communication of supersensuous matters, since no other cause can be apprehended for those who know the Veda, it is only the Veda that can possibly be the source. Since the Veda is the cause of knowledge regarding all perceptible objects, it is "consisting of all knowledge," as if composed of all knowledge. And here, the *aṣṭakā* rites and so forth, which involve great transgressions (*pratyavāya*) if neglected, are included in the text; whereas conduct, custom, and self-satisfaction are not included because they involve only minor transgressions. (2.7)
But having examined all this entirely with the eye of knowledge, a wise man should indeed abide in his own duty according to the authority of the scriptures. (2.8)

"All" means whatever collection of treatises there may be—all that, having been examined in its entirety and without remainder with the eye known as higher knowledge (*vijñāna*), one who knows the scriptures should abide in his own duty (*svadharma*) by means of the authority of the Veda alone. This is because the Veda alone possesses authority regarding *dharma*, and not the authority of non-Vedic Brāhmaṇa scriptures; for knowledge is like an eye, since it delimits the objects of cognition. (2.8)
For a human being who practices the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains renown in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. (2.9)

"Proclaimed by Śruti and Smṛti": A person who practices the dharma declared in the Śruti and Smṛti attains renown in this world and supreme happiness in the next world. This praise of the performance [of dharma] by describing its truly existing qualities is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm; for praise would not proceed without cause or purpose. Thus, it should be understood that this applies to all such praises here. (2.9)
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Smṛti is indeed the Dharmaśāstra;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them the Dharma has shone forth.

Regarding the term "Śruti": this is a statement of matters established in common worldly usage, intended to instruct those of dull intellect, with the practical result of establishing conventions such as the prohibition of Mīmāṃsā and so forth. "Śruti" refers to the Veda, and "Smṛti" refers to the Dharmaśāstras. The inclusion of the term "Smṛti" is for the purpose of indicating that good conduct (*śīla*) and other such factors are also varieties of traditional remembrance. These two—Śruti and Smṛti—are not to be scrutinized through fallacious reasoning regarding any matters, including those whose results are immediate hell, such as the drinking of liquor and the like. Why is this so? Because Dharma, which is beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), has shone forth—that is, attained manifestation—through them alone. (2.10)

Any twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would show contempt for these two roots [the Veda and the Smṛti], should be excluded by the virtuous as an atheist and a reviler of the Veda. (2.11)

Thus, he describes the exclusion of such a performer with the words, "He who would despise those two. One who, having acquired the status of a twice-born solely through the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, yet—by resorting to the treatises of false reasoning—should revile them; one who, holding a settled conviction that "there is no world beyond" and so forth, is a reviler of the Veda, is to be shunned by the learned from all duties to be performed by the twice-born, such as Vedic study and the like. (2.11)
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—they say that this fourfold set is the direct definition of Dharma. (2.12)

Now, in order to demonstrate that the distinction between the types consisting of tradition (smṛti), conduct (śīla), custom (ācāra), and self-satisfaction (ātmatuṣṭi) is not restrictive, he states the fourfold definition of Dharma by means of the inclusion of conduct: "Veda, tradition... (2.12). There is merely a difference in form among the Śruti and the others, but not in substance, since all of them consist of the recollection of the learned (śiṣṭas). And thus he himself said: "The Śruti is to be known as the Veda, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed tradition. Good conduct is the conduct of the virtuous. Self-satisfaction is what is pleasing to one's own self. 2.12.
For those who are unattached to wealth and sensual pleasures, knowledge of Dharma is ordained;
for those desiring to know Dharma, the Śruti is the supreme authority. (2.13)

Regarding the phrase "in matters of wealth and desire": for those who are unattached to the visible human goals known as wealth (*artha*) and desire (*kāma*), and who are devoid of the longing for them, the realization of reality (*tattvāvabodhana*) is prescribed by the scripture. The intention is that if one performs religious duties (*dharmānuṣṭhāna*) merely for the sake of worldly reputation out of a desire for those [visible goals], there is no attainment of the unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*); therefore, what is the use of knowledge of *dharma*? Furthermore, when there is a conflict between the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and so forth, for those wishing to know reality, the *Śruti* is the most excellent authority among the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, etc. Consequently, in the event of a conflict with the *Śruti*, the *Smṛti* is set aside, because inference is weaker when it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (2.13)
But where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of them have been rightly declared as Dharma by the wise. (2.14)

Regarding the phrase "conflict between two Śrutis": where there is a conflict between two Śrutis themselves, such that they express two mutually contradictory injunctions, both of those things to be established by them were declared by Manu and other ancient wise men to be equally valid and correct as options for performance. Since both are taught with equal authority, the abandonment of either is not appropriate here. Thus, by analogy, this same principle is to be understood even when there is a conflict between two Smṛtis; this is the application to the subject at hand. (2.14)
"When the sun has risen, when it has not yet risen, and likewise when the time is between [dawn and sunrise], the sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation. (2.15)

He states an illustration for this: "When [the sun] has risen," etc. Although there are scriptural injunctions regarding mutually contradictory times for the oblation—namely, "one should offer when the sun has risen," "one should offer before sunrise," and "one should offer at *samayādhyuṣita*, the time of night's departure"—nevertheless, everything applies in every way; that is, even if the oblation is performed at another time, the oblation is still accomplished. For it is not proper to repeat the primary act called the oblation merely out of regard for the subordinate factor of time. Such is the Vedic statement beginning with "one should offer when the sun has risen. (2.15)

He for whom the ritual procedure beginning with the impregnation and ending with the cremation ground has been prescribed by means of mantras—only he should be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever. (2.16)

"Niṣekādi" means that for which the ritual procedure (kalpa) beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), performed with mantras, has been declared; and that [procedure] is said to belong to the twice-born (dvija). Therefore, it should be understood that the right to study and hear this Smṛti-śāstra belongs to him, but not to Śūdras and others. Furthermore, since the performance of the rites is enjoined even for those down to the pratiloma castes, it is not prohibited by this [text]. However, it has been stated here that "teaching" (pravacana) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. In the verse beginning with "vidiṣet," the authorities on Dharma and the technical definitions (paribhāṣā) have been stated. (2.16)
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, which was created by the gods, they call Brahmāvarta. (2.17)

Now, for the purpose of defining right conduct (*sadācāra*) and for the purpose of stating the locations suitable for the performance of dharma, he describes the regions with the words: "between the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī. They call the region situated between the rivers named Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī by the name Brahmāvarta. The two terms "river of the gods" (*devanadī*) and "created by the gods" (*devanirmita*) are intended as praises of the region. (2.17)
Whatever custom has come down by way of tradition in that region for the social classes (varṇas) and the intermediate castes (antarālas), that is called "good conduct" (sadācāra). || 2.18 ||

Regarding the phrase "in that": because virtuous conduct generally exists in that region, that conduct which has come down through a continuous succession among Brāhmaṇas and others of noble lineage—transmitted through an unbroken tradition rather than being merely contemporary—is called "virtuous conduct" (sadācāra). 2.18.
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.

Regarding "Kurukṣetra": the Matsyas and other regions, Virāṭadeśa, Pāñcāla, Kānyakubja, Āhicchatra, Śūrasenaka, and Mādhura—this region is known as the land of the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣideśa), being slightly inferior to Brahmāvarta. (2.19)
From a twice-born man born in this region, all men on earth should learn their respective duties. (2.20)
"Born in this region": all people on earth should learn their respective customs from a Brāhmaṇa born in regions such as Kurukṣetra and others. 2.20.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains,
to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is celebrated as Madhyadeśa.

Regarding the phrase "between the Himavat and Vindhya": that region known as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country) lies between the two mountains named Himavat and Vindhya situated in the northern and southern directions; it extends westward from Vinaśana, the place where the Sarasvatī disappears, toward the eastern direction, and westward from Prayāga, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, toward the western direction. (2.21)
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean, and between those very two mountains—the wise know this region as Āryāvarta. (2.22)

"Up to the ocean": the learned consider that region called Āryāvarta to be the middle situated between the eastern and western oceans, and between those two mountains, the Himavat and Vindhya, which extend toward the northern and southern directions. 2.22.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as a land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas. 2.23.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.

"Therefore, these [places]"—because it is possible for them to possess virtuous conduct and fitness for sacrifice, and because they serve an invisible (transcendental) purpose, the twice-born, even when born in other lands, should diligently resort to these very regions. A Śūdra, however, when oppressed by the lack of a livelihood, may dwell even in a region other than these. 2.24.
This source of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief, as well as the origin of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes (varṇas). 2.25.

This is the source, the cause, of Dharma—that which is practiced by the wise and which persists until the bestowal of its fruit; this has been stated to you in brief as its cause. Here, the word *dharma* refers to an unseen impression (*apūrva-ātma-saṃskāra*) within the self. However, in the phrase "practiced by the wise," it is used in the sense of its causes; thus, this usage is observed in both senses. Furthermore, the "origination" or birth of the world has been described. Now, listen to those duties to be performed by the castes (*varṇas*), such as the Brāhmaṇas and others—namely, the duties of caste (*varṇadharma*), the duties of life-stages (*āśramadharma*), the duties of both caste and stage (*varṇāśramadharma*), and those called occasional (*naimittika*)—which constitute five types. The duty of caste is, for example, the prohibition against drinking liquor for a Brāhmaṇa. The duty of the life-stage is, for example, the practice of begging alms for a student (*brahmacārin*), or the carrying of a staff made of *bilva* wood for a Brāhmaṇa. The duty of both caste and stage is, for example, that a Brāhmaṇa’s staff should be made of *pālāśa* wood. The duty based on qualities (*guṇadharma*) is, for example, the protection of subjects by a king endowed with qualities such as consecration. Occasional duties are, for example, expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). (2.25)

The purifying refinement of the body for the twice-born, beginning with the rite of impregnation, must be performed through meritorious Vedic rituals; it is sanctifying both in this world and after death. (2.26)

“By Vedic [rites]”: because they are accomplished by means of Vedic mantras and because they are established on the basis of the Vedas, the bodily consecrations (*saṃskāra*) of the twice-born, beginning with *garbhādhāna*, must be performed through meritorious Vedic and Smārta rites—such as the employment of mantras beginning with “May Viṣṇu prepare the womb”—which are causes of dharma through traditional succession. They are purifying (*pāvana*), meaning they effect purification, because for one who has been consecrated, there is a connection with the fruits of rituals such as sacrifices in the hereafter (*pretya*); and in this world, for one who has been consecrated, there is the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to study and other such activities. The entitlement belongs to the father because of the inclusion of the *niṣeka* (conception rite). However, in the absence of the *niṣeka*, the entitlement might occasionally belong to another person who occupies that position or is appointed to perform it. (2.26)

By means of the fire-oblations performed at conception, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle, the taint derived from seed and the taint derived from the womb are wiped away for the twice-born. (2.27)

Furthermore, from what source does their impurity arise, such that they must be purified? To this he says: "By those pertaining to the womb" (*gārbhaiḥ*). Those rites performed for the sake of the embryo are "pertaining to the womb. The mention of *homa* (oblations) is a qualification applicable to those rites pertaining to the womb according to their possibility; for rites such as *garbhādhāna* (conception) do not consist of oblations, whereas rites such as *sīmantonnayana* (parting the hair) do involve oblations. That which is performed for one who has been born is the *jātakarma* (birth-rite). All these have the nature of being defined in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, because they are mentioned here only in their general form, as this [text] is a general *smṛti*. *Caula* is the tonsure rite; *mauñjīnibandhana* is the investiture with the girdle, i.e., the *upanayana* (initiation). By means of these, the "semen-born" (*baijika*) impurity—the defectiveness of the father's seed due to its being produced from procreative intent—is removed; and the "womb-born" (*gārbhika*) impurity—the defectiveness resulting from dwelling in the embryonic abode—is removed for the twice-born. (2.27)

He now shows, by way of illustration, those actions in which the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the young student are beneficial: "By private Vedic study, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the triple knowledge, by sacrifices, by sons, by the great sacrifices, and by other sacrifices, this body is made fit for union with Brahman. (2.28)

"By self-study" means by the study of the Vedas, by vows such as the *sāvitrī*, by *saumya* rites consisting of the fire-rituals performed morning and evening, and by the vow known as *traividya*, which is taught separately because of its importance. "By sacrifice" refers to the libations offered to the gods, sages, and ancestors during the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*). By means of sons, by the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) such as the *vaiśvadeva*, and by sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma*, the body and the Self residing therein are rendered fit for the attainment of Brahman; through the combination of these ritual acts, liberation is reached. (2.28)
For a male child, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed before the cutting of the umbilical cord;
it includes the ritual consumption of gold, honey, and clarified butter accompanied by sacred mantras.

"Before the navel-cord [is cut]" (*prāṅnābhi*): prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord, the sacramental rite known as *jātakarma* (birth-rite) is prescribed for the male child. At that time, this infant must be made to consume gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by mantras such as "I give to you of honey and ghee" (*pratidadāmi madhuno ghṛtasya*). The mention of "the male" (*puṃsaḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding the neuter; for we see the mention of marriage for eunuchs and others in the passage, "If there should be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and so forth. Furthermore, since there is a prohibition against eunuchs eating at *śrāddha* ceremonies despite being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), it follows that they possess the capacity for procreation. There is no evidence for their capacity for procreation; thus, the author will later state their exclusion from marriage in the verse, "Among those who do not menstruate" (*amantarkāsu*). (2.29)
One should have his naming ceremony performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar date (tithi), at a favorable moment (muhūrta), or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities.

Regarding the phrase "the naming": since it is prescribed under the rite of birth (*jātakarma*), one should give a name to this infant on the tenth or twelfth day from birth, or on another auspicious day, at a favorable moment (*muhūrta*) such as *abhijit*, avoiding the ninth and other *riktā* days, and under a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) endowed with the qualities described in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). This applies when there is an inability [to perform the rite immediately]. However, if capable, he should do it himself, because the *Gṛhyasūtra* states, "The father gives the name. When the earlier time is not possible, one must resort to each subsequent time in order; for there is no purpose in following a fixed sequence. The same should be understood regarding the alternative times mentioned hereafter. (2.30)
Now he prescribes what kind of name should be given, both in terms of its form and its meaning:
"The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya should be connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra should be contemptible. (2.31)
And that auspiciousness belongs to the Brahmin. Their names—Bhadra, Śakti, Dhana, Dīnaka, and so forth—should respectively signify the praise of auspiciousness, power, wealth, and poverty. (2.31)

The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end with a word signifying "shelter," that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word signifying "protection," that of a Vaiśya should be joined with a word signifying "prosperity," and that of a Śūdra should be joined with a word signifying "service. (2.32)

He states [the rule] for the purpose of prescribing the secondary suffixes (*upapada*): "For a Brāhmaṇa, [the name] should end in *śarman*. For these [classes], the secondary suffixes *śarman*, *pāla*, *puṣṭi*, and *dāsa* should be used respectively as words signifying happiness (*śarma*), protection (*rakṣā*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and servitude (*preṣya*). Examples are: Bhadraśarman, Śaktipāla, Dhanapuṣṭa, and Dīnadāsa. (2.32)
For women, [names] should be easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, captivating, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and containing words of benediction. (2.33)

Regarding the names of women: the name of women should be easy to pronounce, expressive of a non-cruel meaning, clear in its sense, pleasing to the mind, auspicious in sound, ending in a long vowel, and joined with a word that conveys a blessing. For example: *Amaradevī*. (2.33)
In the fourth month, the infant’s first outing from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food, or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family.

Regarding "in the fourth": in the fourth month, the child's first outing from the house (*niṣkramaṇa*) should be performed; and in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*). Whatever auspicious rites are desired according to family custom—such as the adoption of a name, titles like *svāmin* and so forth—those should be performed, as well as what was previously mentioned. (2.34)
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to dharma in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Veda. (2.35)

Regarding the *cūḍākarma*: for the twice-born, the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) is to be performed in the first or third year. It must be done according to the law (*dharmataḥ*), that is, by means of the sacred rule (*dharma*), for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "Oṃ, where the arrows fly together like boys with shorn hair. By this, he shows that such Smṛti rules are rooted in the indicative marks of the Vedas. (2.35)
One should perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
that of a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception, and that of a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception. (2.36)

"Regarding the phrase 'in the eighth year from conception': for a Brāhmaṇa, the initiation (*upanayana*), which is the same as the *upanāyana* or the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, should be performed in the eighth year from the year of conception. Likewise, for a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception, and for a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception. (2.36)
The initiation of a Brahmin who desires spiritual luster should be performed in the fifth year;
that of a Kṣatriya seeking power in the sixth; and that of a Vaiśya desiring prosperity in the eighth.

"Of one desiring *brahmavarcasa* (Vedic luster). *Brahmavarcasa* is the splendor produced by excellence in study, knowledge, and so forth. Since a child lacks specific discernment, the father’s desire—"May such a son be born to me"—is directed toward the child; thus, the son is also designated as "one desiring *brahmavarcasa*," because he is the locus of that fruit. For that Brāhmaṇa, the initiation (*upanayana*) should be performed in the fifth year from conception. Similarly, for a Kṣatriya who desires internal strength such as the prowess of arms, elephants, and horses, it is in the sixth year from conception; for a Vaiśya who desires extensive activities such as agriculture, it is in the eighth year from conception, since it is the years from conception that are under discussion. (2.37)
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya of noble birth until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth. (2.38)

He states the secondary rule: "Up to sixteen," etc. According to the traditional teaching of Hārīta, "Initiation occurs at the conjunction of the year [with] the meters and the syllables of the feet. Since the prefix *ā* signifies inclusion (*abhividhi*), initiation—which is the means for the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*—for a Brāhmaṇa does not exceed its proper time until the sixteenth year; for one of Kṣatriya birth, until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, until the twenty-fourth. Furthermore, initiation must be performed as a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for the person, because it is traditionally declared to be a "sacrament of the body" (*śarīrasaṃskāra*). One should not, however, mistakenly assume it to be a "sacrament of Brahman" (*brahmasaṃskāra*) simply because Vedic study is observed to follow immediately thereafter, for in that regard it is merely inferential. (2.38)
Beyond this time, all three of these, having failed to perform the consecration at the proper time, become *vrātyas*, fallen from the *sāvitrī* and despised by the noble ones. (2.39)

"Beyond this" means as follows: if these [boys], according to the time appropriate for each—that is, at the time prescribed for their initiation (*upanayana*)—remain uninitiated even when that time has arrived, they fall from the *Sāvitrī* beyond this period; they are excluded from initiation and become objects of reproach by the learned, thereby receiving the designation of *vrātyas*. The formal establishment of this designation is for the purpose of conventional usage, such as in the rule: "Having performed the sacrifice for *vrātyas*," and so forth. (2.39)
Indeed, one should never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with Brāhmaṇas who have not been purified according to the prescribed rules. (2.40)

As long as these persons have not become purified by performing penance according to the rules and the scriptures, one should never, even in times of distress, enter into any relationship with them—such as Vedic study, giving a daughter in marriage, and so forth—nor perform any ritual acts pertaining to the Brahman. (2.40)
Students of the Veda should wear, in their respective order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat; as well as garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.

Regarding the phrase "those made of black antelope skin, Ruru-deer skin, and goat skin": although "black" (*kārṣṇa*) is a general designation, because it is connected with the Ruru deer, the student should wear as upper garments the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat; this is also because of the Gṛhya rule stating, "the skins are the upper garments. He should wear as lower garments clothes made of hemp, flax, or wool, as is implied by the context. The mention of the sequence is for the sake of order; for, based on the observation in the Gṛhyasūtras that "hemp and flax are for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa," there might otherwise be a misconception that these two belong to non-Brāhmaṇas. Thus, since the numbers are unequal, they are to be correlated respectively. (2.41)
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of Murvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads. (2.42)

Regarding the *mauñjī*: a girdle made of muñja grass, consisting of three equal strands that are smooth, should be made for a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya, however, a girdle made of *mūrvā* fiber—the bowstring—should be made; and in this case, because it would result in the destruction of its nature as a string, it does not possess the quality of being triple-stranded (*trivṛt*), as that is well-established in the earlier texts (*gāndhi-granthas*) regarding the former [girdles]. For a Vaiśya, it is made of hempen thread (*śāṇasūtra*). And here, the state of being triple-stranded continues to apply, because the strands are required and because the number of strands is prescribed in the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*. (2.42)
But in the absence of muñja grass, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja;
they should be triple-stranded with one, three, or five knots. (2.43)

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of *muñja* grass": since three types of religious students (*brahmacārin*) have been introduced as the subject matter and their lack [of specific materials] is equal, commentators explain that the mention of *kuśa* grass and the others is intended to include many such items; thus, "in the absence of *muñja*" means in the absence of *muñja* and the rest. In the absence of *muñja* and so forth, the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes should perform the rites using *kuśa* and other specific types of grass respectively. These [girdles] should be made with three strands and one knot, or with three or five knots. From the use of the word "or" (*vā*), there is no fixed sequential connection between the knots and the classes, such as Brāhmaṇas and so on. Furthermore, this variety of knots occurs even for the primary [materials], because Laugākṣi records the injunction for knots regarding the primary ones in the mantra: "Thou art equal to wealth, thou art the divine knot; do not loosen. And those learned in the three Vedas remember this difference in the number of knots. (2.43)
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya should be made of woolen threads.

"Made of cotton" (*kārpāsam*): that specific arrangement for which the future designation "sacred thread" (*upavīta*) applies must be made, respectively, of cotton, hemp, or wool for Brahmins and the other classes. It should be triple-stranded (*trivṛt*), meaning threefold, and twisted upwards, turning to the right. || 2.44 ||
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of bilva or palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, those of vaṭa or khadira; and a Vaiśya, those of pīlu or udumbara. (2.45)

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha, which states, "The staff of a Brāhmaṇa shall be made of Bilva or Palāśa wood," and because we see here the phrase, "Having taken up the desired staff," the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are entitled, respectively, to two staffs each—alternatively from among those known as Bilva, Palāśa, Vaṭa, Khadira, Pīlu, and Udumbara. (2.45)

The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made to reach the hair at the crown of the head according to its proper measure; that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose. (2.46)

Regarding the phrase "ending at the hair": the staffs of the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes should be made respectively to reach the length of the hair, the forehead, and the vicinity of the nose. (2.46)
All of them should be straight, without blemishes, and pleasing to the sight; they should not cause alarm to men, possessing their bark intact and not damaged by fire. (2.47)

"Upright": those staffs should be polished, free from cracks, devoid of a terrifying appearance, possessed of their bark, and free from defects caused by fire; nor should any living being be startled by them. (2.47)
Having accepted his desired staff and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.

"Having accepted," it means: having taken up the consecrated staff as desired, having meditated upon the sun and circumambulated the fire from left to right, one should consume the food according to the scriptural injunctions. 2.48.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go about for alms using "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, with "bhavat" at the end. (2.49)

To the question "How so?", he says: "Preceded by *bhavat*. A Brahmin should utter the request for alms with the word *bhavat* at the beginning, as follows: "O venerable one (*bhavati*), give [me] alms. Similarly, a Kṣatriya should place *bhavat* in the middle: "O venerable one, give me alms (*bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*)," and a Vaiśya should place *bhavat* at the end: "Give me alms, O venerable one (*bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*). (2.49)
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt—whichever of these will not treat him with contempt. (2.50)

"Mother": the mother's sister is the *mātṛṣvasṛ*. First, he should beg alms from her for the purpose of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and not from anyone else, provided that she does not cause the religious student (*brahmacārin*) humiliation by refusing him. "His own": his uterine [sister]. 2.50.
Having collected that alms-food as much as required without guile, and having offered it to his teacher, he should eat while facing east, pure and having sipped water. (2.51)

Regarding the word *samāhṛtya* (having collected): that alms-food, sufficient for his purpose—that is, the quantity required for satiety—should be collected from many sources without guile, avoiding poor-quality food; having presented it to the teacher and being permitted by him, he should sip water (*ācamya*) and, being pure, eat facing the east. This is the rule regarding direction. The phrase *ācamya upaspṛśya dvijo nityam* (the twice-born, having sipped water and touched [the organs], always... is a restatement of the rule to be explained later, since the specific details of this act will be enjoined there with the words beginning "and the apertures" (*khāni ca*). (2.51)
One who eats facing the east gains long life; facing the south, one gains fame;
facing the west, one gains prosperity; and facing the north, one indeed eats the truth.

Now he states the optional [rule]: "conducive to longevity" (*āyuṣyam*). One should understand that this is the sense of the gerundive suffix (*liṅ*), namely: "one eats facing east food that is beneficial for longevity," for otherwise it would be purposeless. Thus, it is stated that one who desires longevity eats facing east. Likewise, [food] beneficial for fame is [eaten] facing south; one desiring prosperity [eats] facing west. Truth (*ṛtam*) is reality; because it is the cause of its fruit, one eats the "immortal" (*amṛtam*) food facing north. (2.52)
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
after eating, he should likewise sip water properly and touch the cavities of his head with water. (2.53)

"Having touched water": at all times, even after the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), a twice-born man, having sipped water (*ācamya*), should eat his food with a concentrated mind, that is, with no other thought. After eating, he should touch water according to the scriptures. And he should touch the apertures of the senses—the openings in the head—with water; for there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) of Gautama stating, "And he should touch the apertures located on the head. Since the author says "he should touch water" and then separately states "and he should touch the apertures," it is understood from this that by the two words *upasparśana* (touching) and *ācamana* (sipping), the primary act is merely the threefold sprinkling, whereas the touching of the apertures and so forth constitutes the subsidiary procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, *ācamana* is designated as such because the verbal root itself signifies the act of consuming. (2.53)
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way. (2.54)

"One should worship" means that one should always worship food as a deity and meditate upon it as being for the sake of the vital breaths (prāṇas). One should eat this food without disparaging it; having seen it, one should be pleased and become serene. One should abandon weariness even when it arises from other causes. One should welcome it with faith, thinking, "May this [food] always be mine," in every way, in every manner, and in all its forms. 2.54.
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten unhonored, it destroys both of these. (2.55)

"Offered" means that food which is offered bestows capacity and vigor; however, that same food, when eaten without being offered, destroys both. Therefore, one should eat what is offered—this is a praise of the subject matter, as otherwise, if it were for the sake of a specific result, there would be the consequence of it becoming a non-obligatory act.
One should not give the leavings of food to anyone, nor should one eat between [meals];
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating.

"Not with remnants" means that one should not give food that has been left over by anyone. Likewise, "in between" means one should not eat between the two times of evening and morning, since eating is prescribed as appropriate for evening and morning, and because the word *antarā* itself denotes the interval. One should not eat in excess. Furthermore, one who has food remnants on his hands should not go anywhere. (2.56)
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven; it is meritless and despised by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. (2.57)

"Unwholesome" (*anārogya*) means that because it is a cause of disease, it produces ill-health; and because it brings about the production of feces and so forth, it is life-destroying and not conducive to longevity. It is "not leading to heaven" (*asvargya*) because, by its very nature of producing unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it lacks the capacity to fulfill the injunctions of the scriptures, and because it obstructs the enjoyment of heaven acquired through other meritorious acts due to such transgression. It is "demeritorious" (*apuṇya*) because it is the cause of that [unseen demerit], and it is "hated by the world" because people censure one who observes them eating excessively. Thus, by describing these existing defects, this is an *arthavāda* intended to express natural censure for the purpose of creating aversion [to overeating]. (2.57)
A Brahmin should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha; or he may use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya tīrtha. (2.58)

Regarding the word "brāhmaṇa": a Brahmin should sip water for as long as he lives using the *brāhma* (brahmanic) *tīrtha*, or those of Prajāpati and the gods (*daiva*). The phrase "but [using] the *pitrya* [tīrtha] only occasionally" is a restatement of a constant rule (*nityānuvāda*) intended to praise the other two. Since the *pitrya* [tīrtha] is not prescribed [here], it is not obtained [as a primary option]; therefore, the mention of the "Brahmin" is for the purpose of indicating the Kṣatriyas and others as well, because these [other castes] are also under discussion in the context of the rule, "Having sipped water, a twice-born man [should always perform his duties]. (2.58)
They declare that the sacred site (tīrtha) of Brahmā is at the root of the thumb;
the Kāya [site] is at the base of the fingers, the Daiva at their tips, and the Pitrya below those two. 2.59.

Since the meaning is already established, he states the definition: "of the base of the thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhamūlasya*). This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) of Pracetas: "In the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa there are five *tīrthas*. They declare the *brāhma* *tīrtha* to be on the lower part of the base of the thumb of the right hand. The *kāya* [tīrtha] is at the base of the fingers. The *daiva* [tīrtha] is at the tips of the fingers, because the word "tips" (*agra*) requires a reference to those very fingers. The *pitrya* [tīrtha] is below those two; since the phrase "below those two" also requires a reference, it is connected with the previously mentioned thumb and fingers. (2.59)
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should touch the cavities with water, as well as the self and the head. (2.60)

Since the act of sipping water (ācamana) is not something commonly known in worldly practice, he states its essential nature with the word "thrice" (triḥ). First, one should sip water three times through the sacred part of the hand (tīrtha). Thereafter, one should cleanse the mouth twice. Following that, one should touch the apertures of the senses (khāni) with water. Then [one touches] the seat of the self, the heart, and then the head. (2.60)
One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water from a proper source—water that is neither hot nor frothy—while in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north. (2.61)

"By waters that are not hot": according to the Smṛti of Śaṅkha, "by unboiled [waters]," this means by waters untouched by contact with fire and free from foam; a learned man desiring purity should sip water (ācamana) using the aforementioned part of the hand (tīrtha), in a secluded and clean place, facing either east or north. 2.61.
A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity. 2.62.

"What quantity of water should one sip for *ācamana*? To this he says: "With [water] reaching the heart. A Brahmin becomes pure with water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, with water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, with water that has been sipped—that is, reached the palate—according to the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya: "Reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate. A Śūdra [becomes pure] at the end [of the mouth], because *ācamana* is the subject under discussion; thus, with water touched at the extremity of the tongue, lips, and mouth. (2.62)
When the right hand is raised, a twice-born man is called *upavītin*;
when the left is raised, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*. (2.63)

Since the terms *upavītin* and the others are not well-known, he provides their definitions. Furthermore, at the occasion of sipping water (*ācamana*), he specifies that the *upavīta* is "raised" for the purpose of making it an ancillary part of the sipping rite. The *upavīta* should be made of cotton and possess the characteristics already described. When the *upavīta* is suspended around the neck—that is, when it is cast over the neck—one becomes *nivītin*. This being the case, when it is raised on the right arm one becomes *upavītin*; when the left is raised, one is *prācīnāvītin*. These two definitions are established here for the sake of clarity. Likewise, the definition of *nivīta* is for the purpose of human activities, according to the Vedic injunction: "The *nivīta* is for men. *Prācīnāvītī* is the technical name; however, for the sake of metrical conformity, it is stated as *prācīna āvītī*. And this [mode] pertains to rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*). (2.63)
Having cast the girdle, the deer-skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras. (2.64)

Regarding the phrase "the girdle" (*mekhalām*): if the girdle and other such items have been destroyed, one should discard them in water and take up others accompanied by their respective mantras. Accordingly, Baudhāyana has prescribed a mantra for all of them; and because there is a rule for their disposal (*pratipatti*) together with the ritualized taking up (*grahaṇa*) of the girdle and the rest according to the scriptures—expressed as "one should take up others with mantras"—and because the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is also mentioned therein, it is concluded that the water-pot, too, must be taken up according to the scriptures for the purpose of holding water. Furthermore, because they are to be taken up again, it is inferred that these items continue to be used even after the time of initiation (*upanayana*), and not merely as part of the initiation ceremony itself. (2.64)
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a member of the royal caste (rājanya), in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, two years after that. (2.65)

Regarding "the tonsure" (keśānta): the sacramental rite known as the tonsure is prescribed for Brahmins and the other castes respectively in their sixteenth, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth years. (2.65)
This entire series of rites for women must be performed without omission, at the proper time and in the correct order, for the purpose of purifying the body. (2.66)

Since there is no authority for the inclusion of women under the phrase "prior to the growth of the navel" because that mention of the male (*puṃs*) lacks any basis for applying to females, [the author] says, "without mantras. This entire sequence of sacraments (*saṃskāra-paddhati*) must be performed for the sake of the sacraments of women, devoid of mantras, without transgressing the proper chronological order. (2.66)
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and household duties are their tending of the sacred fires. (2.67)

Since it might thus follow that the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for women would likewise be without mantras, he says "the marriage rite" (*vaivāhika*). That very procedure of marriage is their Vedic sacrament (*saṃskāra*) in place of initiation; service to the husband is in place of service to the teacher (*guru-śuśrūṣā*), and household duties are in place of tending the sacred fire (*agni-paricaryā*). (2.68)
This has been declared as the sacred rite of initiation for the twice-born, which manifests their true birth; now learn the application of ritual action.

"This" refers to this rule concerning the initiation (*upanayana*) of the twice-born, which has been declared as that which manifests and reveals [their status]. For even one who is born is equal to one unborn if he is not initiated, because [without it] he lacks the cause for merit. Now, listen to the connection regarding the rite of initiation for one who has been initiated. (2.68)
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.

"Having initiated": Having performed the initiation of the disciple, the teacher should first of all teach him purification (*śauca*), because one who is impure has no qualification for anything whatsoever. He should also teach him proper conduct (*ācāra*), such as rising [from one's seat] to greet others, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) consisting of the casting of oblations into the fire in the evening and morning, and the performance of the twilight rites (*sāndhyakarma*). (2.69)

But when about to be taught, having sipped water according to the scriptures and facing north, he should be instructed with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali*, wearing light clothing, and with his senses subdued. (2.70)

Regarding the term "about to study": the student who is about to begin his studies should have performed the ritual duties prescribed by the scriptures, having sipped water (ācamana), having formed the *brahmāñjali* as will be described below, wearing coarse clothing, with his senses subdued, and facing north; he is thus to be taught. 2.70.
At the beginning and at the end of Vedic study, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the hands together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.

Regarding the phrase "the commencement of Vedic study": at the beginning and end of the daily recitation of the Vedas, one must always perform the clasping of the teacher's feet day after day. Having placed the hands in the well-known position known as *saṃhatau* or *kacchapaka*, one should study; for this is remembered by the sages as being designated by the term *brahmāñjali*. Thus, because it is not something commonly known in the world, the specific nature of the *brahmāñjali* is defined. (2.71)
The clasping of the teacher’s feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. (2.72)

Furthermore, as to how the clasping of the feet should be performed, he says: "with crossed hands. One should approach the teacher's feet with hands placed in opposite directions; the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. (2.72)
But when about to be requested to teach, the teacher, always alert, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should conclude with, "May there be a pause. (2.73)

Regarding the phrase "about to be requested": when a student is about to begin his studies, the teacher, being untiring, should say at all times, "Recite, sir! and having said, "May there be a pause," he should immediately desist from teaching. (2.73)
One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*.
What is not preceded by the *oṃ* slips away, and what is not followed by it falls apart. (2.74)

Regarding the word "brahmaṇaḥ": at the beginning and end of the recitation of the Veda, one should always utter the syllable *oṃ*, both during the time of formal study and at other times as well. For that Veda which is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away—it is forgotten even though it was grasped—and subsequently it falls apart. That for which it is not performed falls apart; it is not mastered at all. (2.74)
Sitting upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he is then worthy of the syllable Om.

Regarding the phrase "with the tips pointing east": because of the traditional teaching of Gautama, "The touching of the vital breaths with *darbha* grass and the sitting upon [grass] with the tips pointing east," he sits upon *darbha* grass with its tips directed toward the east. For this very reason, he is purified by the *darbha* blades themselves acting as purifiers, which touch the heart from the location of the vital breaths; and he is further purified by the *prāṇāyāmas*—which consist of the restraint of the breath—in accordance with the *prāṇāyāmas* prescribed by Gautama as "three *prāṇāyāmas*, each consisting of fifteen *mātrās*. Thereafter, he becomes fit to perform the previously mentioned *oṃkāra*. (2.75)
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. (2.76)
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse. (2.77)

Regarding the injunction, “One should make the *praṇava* [the syllable *oṃ*] the beginning of the *brahman*,” he states its explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) with the words “the letter *a*,” etc. From the three [Vedas], the *praṇava*—consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*—was indeed extracted by Prajāpati. Furthermore, he extracted these three great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), namely *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. This is a praise of the *vyāhṛtis*. Since this praise occurs here unexpectedly, its purpose is to prescribe them for the time of Vedic study. Likewise, the fact that the Supreme Lord Hiraṇyagarbha Prajāpati extracted each quarter-verse of this verse addressed to the deity Savitṛ, beginning with “*tat savitur vareṇyam*,” from the three Vedas respectively, is also an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the *Sāvitrī* intended for the time of study. (2.76–77)
Reciting this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis during the two twilights, a Brahmin learned in the Vedas becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas. (2.78)

The wise Brāhmaṇa who knows the meaning of the Vedas, chanting at the two twilights this imperishable syllable called *oṃ* and this *Sāvitrī* preceded by the *vyāhṛtis* "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," becomes endowed with the merit of the entire Veda; thus, by describing the greatness of the fruit arising from the twilight recitation, there is a praise of the three rules under discussion. 2.78.
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is released from even great sin after a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.

"Thousand times"—this triad, having been practiced by a twice-born man outside the village for a thousand repetitions a day for as long as a month, removes even a great sin such as the killing of a Brahmin, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin; this is a praise of the three prescribed rules under discussion, by way of describing the greatness found in the secret penances. 2.79.
One who is deprived of this Ṛc, as well as of his own timely ritual action, whether born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya lineage, incurs reproach among the virtuous. (2.80)

"By this [verse]" means: one who is deprived of this *sāvitrī* verse—due to the absence of Vedic study—and who is also deprived of his own rite called "initiation" (*upanayana*) at the time of initiation, belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya caste, incurs censure among the learned. Thus, by way of censuring the non-performance [of the rite], there is praise for the threefold injunction regarding initiation. (2.80)
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, together with the three-footed *sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. (2.81)

"Preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*": these three great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛtis*), beginning with *bhūr*, are preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*; they are imperishable and indestructible because their fruit lasts for a long time. And this *Sāvitrī*, "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ," should be known as the mouth of Brahman, the gateway to the attainment of the Veda. Therefore, it should be studied at the beginning of one's private recitation (*svādhyāya*); such is the praise of the subject matter. (2.81)
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space.

"Who" refers to one who studies that Sāvitrī daily for three years without indolence; he, like the wind, possesses a movement unimpeded everywhere, and being of the nature of space (kha-mūrtimat), that is, having the form of ether, he attains face-to-face the Supreme Brahman, characterized as the Supreme Self, because of its all-pervasiveness. Thus, by describing the greatness of the recitation (japa), there is a praise of the ritual rule under discussion.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence. (2.83)

"Ekākṣaram" (the single syllable): this single syllable called *oṃ* is the supreme Brahman, according to the perspective of the Vedānta, which distinguishes between the Brahman of sound (*śabda-brahman*) and the supreme Brahman (*para-brahman*). Prāṇāyāma is a penance superior to penances such as the *kṛcchra*; there is no other recitation more excellent than that of the *Sāvitrī*. Thus, this is a praise of the injunctions concerning the *oṃ*-syllable, prāṇāyāma, and the *Sāvitrī* under discussion. "Truth excels silence": silence merely avoids the fault of falsehood, whereas truth produces spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) through truthful speech; thus, in the context of this praise, there is a praise of the declaration of truth. (2.83)
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
however, the Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as the undecaying Brahman and Prajāpati himself.

"They perish" means that all the performances of *homa* and *yajña* enjoined by the Vedas are perishable, because their fruits are subject to exhaustion. On the other hand, this [syllable] called *oṃkāra* should be known as imperishable (*akṣara*), because its fruit—known as the attainment of Brahman—is imperishable through the means of meditating upon its meaning. And this very [Brahman] is what is designated as Prajāpati. (2.84)

By means of disparaging Vedic ritual—which is the subject matter produced through the perspective of the Vedānta regarding both word and meaning—the praise of the actual subject matter [of this work] is established:
"The sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual injunctions (*vidhiyajña*);
the whispered (*upāṃśu*) is a hundredfold; and the mental (*mānasa*) is recorded as being a thousandfold. (2.85)

Regarding the phrase "vidhiyajñāt" (from the ritual sacrifice): the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is superior by tenfold qualities compared to external rites such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others, because its fruit is ten times greater. That same recitation is a hundredfold more effective when performed in a whisper (*upāṃśu*), which another person does not hear; and it is a thousandfold when accomplished through mental activity alone. This statement regarding the greatness of recitation—exceeding the fruits of Vedic rituals—is for the purpose of praising the present rule, based on the consideration that internal restraint is more difficult to endure than the renunciation of material substances, and that excellence increases with the intensity of practice. (2.85)
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña). 2.86.

The four types of sacrifices, beginning with the *pākayajña* and including the ritual sacrifices (*vidhiyajña*) such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, all together do not equal even a sixteenth part of the value of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*). Thus, by means of this censure of *śrauta* and *smārta* rituals, the greatness of *japa* is proclaimed through the demonstration of its superior fruit for those possessed of self-knowledge; this is for the purpose of praising the injunction under discussion. (2.86)
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin. (2.87)

"By recitation alone indeed. By recitation alone a Brāhmaṇa may attain liberation; there is no doubt at all in this matter. How is it that such a great fruit is obtained with so little effort? Because internal self-restraint is more difficult to achieve than even the renunciation of external objects. And thus he should act; otherwise, he may or may not perform rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma for that purpose, since the scripture declares that a Brāhmaṇa should be devoted to the welfare of all beings. How could one who slays the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma (*agniṣomīya*) be a friend to all? Thus, for a person incapable of performing Vedic or Smārta rituals, the statement that "one intent on recitation attains perfection" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to praise the practice under discussion. 2.88.
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses. 2.88

"Of the senses": one should make an effort to restrain the senses—the eyes and so forth—which, when they operate according to their own will, tend to draw one toward their captivating objects such as forms and the like for the sake of enjoyment; just as a skilled charioteer makes an effort to restrain horses that have already begun to run on the road. (2.88)
I shall correctly explain, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven faculties which the wise of old have taught. (2.89)

Regarding the phrase "eleven": those sense organs which the wise Manu and others of former times have described, I shall explain them to you correctly, in their entirety, in their proper sequence, according to their function, and exactly as they are. 2.89.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth. (2.90)

"And those [are] the ear," etc. "Skin" (*tvak*) refers to the hide; here, the sense-organ of touch is called "skin" by virtue of its location therein. "The two eyes" is expressed in the dual number due to the distinction of their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In the case of the ear and the others, the singular number is used because they take as their objective support the unity of the power that constitutes them. "The anus" is the downward breath (*apāna*); "the generative organ" is the penis. "Speech" (*vāk*) is a specific part of the body that manifests sound. (2.90)
Of these, the five sense organs are the ear and so forth in their proper order;
the five organs of action are said to be the anus and so forth. (2.91)

Regarding the phrase "the organs of cognition" (*buddhīndriyāṇi*): among these, the five beginning with the ear are, in order, the producers of the cognitions of objects such as sound for the intellect; the five beginning with the anus are for the purpose of actions such as excretion—thus the division into two groups is made based on the difference in their functions, as Manu and others declare. (2.91)
The eleventh, the mind, should be known as having a dual nature by virtue of its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.

Regarding the eleventh: the mind (*manas*), by its own quality known as volition (*saṃkalpa*), which is of a nature both auspicious and inauspicious, should be understood here as the eleventh [organ], being of a dual form. When this [mind] is brought under control, these two groups consisting of five members each are said to be controlled, because the activity of the sense organs is rooted in the operation of the mind. (2.92)
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault; but by restraining them, one attains perfection. (2.93)

Now he states the purpose of restraining the senses with the words "of the senses" (indriyāṇām). By attachment to the objects of the senses, a person certainly incurs faults both seen and unseen; but by restraining those very senses, he certainly attains the accomplishment of goals both seen and unseen. (2.93)
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. 2.94

Now, one might ask: "Is the cessation of the senses from their objects not taught because of the thirst for enjoyment? Why, then, is it taught by means of prohibiting attachment? To this he says: "Never" (na jātu). Desire for objects that are being craved never ceases through the indulgence of those objects; on the contrary, it increases even more, like fire fed with clarified butter and the like. (2.94)
Between one who might obtain all these things and one who might renounce them entirely, the renunciation of all desires is superior to their acquisition. (2.95)

"And thus, as for 'whoever'": whether one should indulge in all desires or abandon them entirely without having experienced them at all, for such a person, abandonment is superior even to the enjoyment of all desires. This is because, even regarding those things previously enjoyed, if there is no restraint of the mind, the desire for further enjoyment arises again; and if that [desire] is not fulfilled, suffering is inevitable. Therefore, it is better to abandon craving from its very root. (2.95)
These senses, when addicted to their objects, cannot be restrained by abstinence in the same way as they can be constantly restrained through knowledge. (2.96)

If that is so, then the mere remaining of the body in a state devoid of objects would be the means; therefore, he says "no. These senses, which produce great defects through attachment to objects, cannot be properly restrained by the non-enjoyment of objects such as form and the like, in the same way that they can be restrained at all times through the cognition that contemplates the defects inherent in those objects. (2.96)
The Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances, and austerities never lead to perfection for one whose inner disposition is corrupted. (2.97)
Regarding the Vedas: for one with a corrupt mind, the recitation of mantras, giving, ritual bathing, sacrifices, kṛcchra penances, and so forth, never reach fulfillment.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.

Having heard this: he who, having perceived through his ears, skin, eyes, and nose desirable sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells, does not experience joy, and having perceived those that are contemptible, does not fall into dejection—he is to be known as one who has conquered his senses. (2.98)
But if among all the senses even a single sense leaks away, through that his wisdom flows out, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin. (2.99)

Effort must be made toward the restraint of all the objects of the senses, because [of the rule] "among the senses" (indriyāṇām). For if even a single sense among them proceeds at will toward its own object, then the knowledge resulting from the restraint of one's other senses is also destroyed; just as when water is poured into a leather bag, all the water leaks out if even a single foot [of the seam] is left uncovered. 2.99.
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restrained the mind,
one should accomplish all goals through yoga without wasting the body.

Thus, for one whose senses are not restrained and whose mind is distracted, there is no accomplishment of the Vedas and so forth; therefore, [the word] "under control" (vaśa) is used. Without afflicting the body by means of his capacity, having conquered the aggregate of the senses and having disciplined the mind, he should accomplish all goals such as the mastery of the Vedas.
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but one should always remain seated during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible. (2.101)

"Until the stars appear, remaining silent," according to the *Gautama Dharma Sūtra* (2.11), "from the time when the stars are visible, [he should recite] the *pūrvā* [Sāvitrī]. Although in this context the injunctive suffix is heard following the verb *tiṣṭhati* ("standing"), nevertheless, because its root is found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*), the recitation (*japa*) is the primary element here; standing and sitting, however, are subordinate members (*aṅga*). And so, in the *Yajurveda Brāhmaṇa*, the injunctive suffix is heard following the very root *jap* (to recite). As it says, beginning with: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*)," and continuing: "Standing during the *pūrvā* twilight, he should recite this syllable-by-syllable *Sāvitrī* and these [Vyāhṛtis] preceded by the [Great] Vyāhṛtis at both twilights. The meaning of the sentence is that he should recite [the mantra] preceded by the prostrations and the Vyāhṛtis until the sun is seen. Regarding the *paścimā* (western) twilight, however, he should sit and recite the *Sāvitrī* from the time mentioned in the *Gautama* text—starting from when the stars are visible—until the stars have fully appeared. (2.101)
Standing while reciting prayers during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night; sitting during the evening twilight, however, one destroys the impurity created by day. (2.102)

"Standing during the morning," etc.: standing during the morning twilight and reciting the *Sāvitrī*, one removes the accumulated sin produced during the night; for if it removed all sins, the section on penances (*prāyaścitta*) would be rendered purposeless. Likewise, sitting and reciting during the evening twilight, one destroys the sin committed during the day. (2.102)
But he who neither stands for the morning [prayer] nor performs worship at the evening [prayer] is to be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (2.103)

Thus, since the non-performance [of the rite] might somehow occur even for one who has not committed a sin, he declares its obligatory nature by saying "not so. Furthermore, he who does not perform the morning twilight devotion (*pūrva-saṃdhyā*) or he who does not attend to the evening one is to be shunned like a Śūdra from all duties of a twice-born man, such as Vedic study, giving, and so forth. This censure is intended to ensure that the rite must necessarily be performed. (2.103)
Restrained and established in the daily rule, he should go to the forest and, with a concentrated mind, recite the Sāvitrī near water. (2.104)

For the purpose of explaining the rule for the *brahmayajña*, [the author] says "of water" (*apām*) regarding students (*brahmacārin*) who perform it daily: having gone to a secluded place outside the village, being self-restrained, pure, composed, and with a controlled mind, established in the conviction that "this rule for the *brahmayajña* is obligatory," and having developed a sense of urgency, one should mutter the *Sāvitrī* near water, because of the recitation of other mantras [in that context]. (2.104)

There is no restriction regarding days unfit for study (anadhyāya) with respect to the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, daily private recitation, and indeed the mantras used for burnt offerings. (2.105)

Because the recitation of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*) is a duty (*dharma*), and because the rules for non-study (*anadhyāya*) are prescribed in a different context as part of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), [the author] says "in the case of the auxiliaries of the Veda" (*vedopakaraṇe*) to address the doubt that the prohibition of non-study might apply even to the *brahmayajña* and other such rites. There is no obligation to observe non-study periods regarding the auxiliary sciences that assist the Veda, such as *nirukta*, nor regarding the obligatory daily study known as the *brahmayajña*, nor when reciting mantras for the purpose of a fire-oblation (*homa*). Furthermore, the mention of "auxiliaries of the Veda" and so forth is not made here for the sake of brevity, as it follows from the context. The word "hi" indicates traditional authority (*āgama*). (2.105)
In the daily obligatory recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice.
It is a meritorious offering of the Veda, wherein the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered even during times when study is otherwise forbidden.

Regarding this, he states an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "naityaka. In the case of the *naityaka*—the single *brahmayajña*—there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). Because that is remembered by Manu and others as a *brahmasattra*, it must be performed at all times due to its similarity to the *satras* such as the *gavām ayana*, which proceed continuously. To the question, "What is its similarity to a *sattra*? he replies with "the nature of a *brahmāhuti*" and so forth. A *sattra* is offered with the oblation of *soma*; this [Vedic recitation] also is *brahman* offered with the oblation of the utterance of the Veda. It is like an oblation because it serves the purpose of an oblation and because it is a cause of merit; thus, it is equal to a *sattra*. Furthermore, a *sattra* is joined with the *vaṣaṭ*-call for the purpose of offering; this too is accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call of the non-study period (*anadhyāya*), since one studies even during periods when study is otherwise suspended. (2.106)
For him who, being self-restrained and pure, studies his sacred lesson according to the rule for a year, this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. (2.107)

Regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): he who, being pure and with a restrained mind, studies for a year this self-study known as the *brahmayajña* according to the prescribed rule of going to the forest and so forth—for him, this [deity] constantly bestows milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. And thus, although it is obligatory, a fruit also arises from this through the desire for a result, just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. 2.107.

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, a twice-born man should maintain the sacred fire, practice begging for alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher until his formal return home (samāvartana). (2.108)

"Fire and fuel": the twice-born should perform these acts beneficial to the teacher—namely, kindling the fire, gathering alms, using a wooden bedstead and so forth, eating, and smearing the teacher’s house—with them from the time of the initiation (*upanayana*) until the period of the vow known as the *samāvartana*. This is restated for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), so that these [acts], which are subsidiary (*aṅga*) because they do not constitute the primary rite (*pradhāna*), continue throughout the entire period of studentship (*brahmacarya*). Consequently, only these cease at the *samāvartana*. Other duties, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and others not contradictory to other stages of life (*āśrama*), continue for as long as one lives. As Gautama says: "And this is not in conflict with those who follow the subsequent [stages]" (GDh 3.10). For this very reason, one should perform these until the *samāvartana*. However, there is no restrictive rule to the contrary that these must cease even before that, because that would result in the subversion of the principle that the subsidiaries must follow the primary rite. (2.108)

One who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman—these ten, according to the Dharma, are those who may be taught by the son of the teacher. || 2.109 ||

Regarding the phrase "the teacher’s son": the teacher’s son is one who is devoted to service, a giver of knowledge, habituated to the performance of dharma, endowed with purity through softness, nobility, and so forth, a kinsman, capable of grasping and retaining [the teachings], a giver of wealth even before the formal fee (*paṇa*), possessed of straightforwardness, and initiated by himself—these ten are to be taught for the sake of dharma. One who gives wealth and is desirous of learning is also included, because of the statement: "There is dharma both from imparting knowledge and from teaching, in the form of merit resulting from the observance of rules" (2.109).
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, a wise man should behave like one who is dull-witted in the world. (2.110)

"Nor when unasked": apart from the cases mentioned previously, one should not speak to anyone else who is studying or making errors in pronunciation and so forth if they have not asked; nor should one speak to one who asks for the sake of mere cavil (*vitaṇḍā*). What then? Even though he knows the matter therein, the wise man should behave in the world as if he were deaf. Here, the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) serves the purpose of prohibition. (2.110)
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two perishes or incurs enmity. (2.111)
"Unlawfully" means by transgressing the stated boundaries. Of the two—one who speaks or one who asks—whichever is the transgressor, he dies or incurs hatred in the world. (2.111)
Where neither dharma nor wealth are found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve, there knowledge should not be sown, just as a good seed is not sown in saline soil. (2.112)

In order to demonstrate that among the previously mentioned causes, the triad beginning with *dharma* (virtue) constitutes the means (*upāya*), he says: "Virtue and wealth" (*dharmārthau*). This is because in the case of teaching, there should be no *dharma* [as a motive], nor should there be wealth obtained through a fee (*paṇapūrva*), since teaching for a fee is prohibited as it constitutes being a hired teacher (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*). Service (*paricaryā*) should be commensurate with the teaching, like a well-nourished seed in a plot of ground incapable of producing a sprout. (2.112)
A knower of Brahman should rather die together with his knowledge;
even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.

"And thus with knowledge. It is better that one who has not yet imparted knowledge should die while maintaining the habit of teaching knowledge; however, even in the most dire calamity, or when there is no person fit to be taught as described, one must not sow this knowledge in a barren place (*irina*), which is like saline soil devoid of the production of fruits such as merit (*dharma*). By this, he shows that knowledge must necessarily be given. Otherwise, the statement "one may even die together with knowledge itself" would logically follow as a consequence of the teacher's connection [to the pupil], serving as an indication of the absence [of a recipient]. And so says the Śruti: "He who, having studied knowledge, does not speak it to one who asks, shall be a destroyer of his own purpose. This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding this prohibition takes the form of an ancient narrative (*purākalpa*). (2.113)
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to a scorner, so that I may remain most powerful. (2.114)
