But to that Brahmin whom you know to be pure, self-controlled, and a celibate student—to such a guardian of the treasure who is never negligent, speak of me. (2.115)

Knowledge approached a certain Brāhmaṇa and said: "I am yours. It is said that Knowledge, possessing a physical form, came to a certain Brāhmaṇa and spoke: "I am like a treasure for you; therefore, protect me. And as for protection: do not teach me to one who is envious and unworthy. For if you do so, I shall become exceedingly capable of performing your visible and invisible tasks. Furthermore, he whom you know to be gentle, pure through the use of clay and water and other means, self-restrained, with senses controlled, a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), and abstaining from sexual union with women—this latter qualification is mentioned separately because of its importance—he is the one you should teach: a Brāhmaṇa capable of guarding the treasure of knowledge, of a retentive memory, free from negligence, and not lacking in diligent practice. (2.114–15)
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission becomes guilty of the theft of the Veda and falls into hell. (2.116)

"Brahman. He who would learn the Veda (*brahma*) without having been authorized—neither teaching it to others nor practicing it for the sake of not forgetting it—is guilty of the theft of Brahman and goes to hell. 2.116.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received. 2.117

Regarding the term "worldly" (*laukika*): worldly knowledge refers to subjects such as Āyurveda intended for visible benefit; Vedic knowledge refers to the subject matter of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*); and spiritual knowledge (*ādhyātmika*) refers to the knowledge concerning the science of the self found in Sāṃkhya and other systems. From whomsoever one should learn, one should first salute that person in the manner to be described hereafter, without depending on their verbal address. (2.117)

A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if his essence consists of nothing more than the Sāvitrī verse, is better than one who is unrestrained, even if he has mastered the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all kinds of goods. (2.118)

In this regard, there is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) stating that the Sāvitrī alone is the essence: if a Brahmin is well-restrained—meaning his self is disciplined by the performance of the practice of salutation—then even if he is devoted solely to the Sāvitrī and studies no more than that, he is better and more praiseworthy. One who lacks good conduct, however, is not praiseworthy even if he has mastered the three Vedas; for, being unrestrained, he becomes an eater of all things and a seller of all things. (2.118)
One should not occupy a bed or seat already used by a superior;
rather, while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise and salute him. 2.119.

Regarding "on the bed or seat": one should not sit upon a bed or seat that has been used or is being used by a teacher or someone of superior status. Furthermore, seeing him approaching while seated on a bed or seat, one should rise from there and offer salutation. (2.119)
For the vital breaths of a youth indeed ascend when an elder approaches; one recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him. 2.120.

In this context, there is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) based on the perception of danger. Regarding the word "upwards" (*ūrdhvam*): because when an elder arrives, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the younger person tend to move upwards due to the loss of life resulting from improper conduct, one recovers them once more through rising to meet him and saluting him, which serve as the causes for that recovery; therefore, those two acts must be performed. (2.120)
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase: life-span, merit, fame, and strength. (2.121)

But here is another [benefit] in this very case, seen through the observation of its utility: for one who is habituated to salutation—that is, whose nature is to perform salutation—and who is always and at all times devoted to serving elders, four things—longevity, wisdom, renown, and strength—attain increase. (2.121)
After the salutation, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name. (2.122)

Furthermore, as to how the salutation should be performed, he says: "After the salutation. When performing a salutation to an elder, one should utter one's own name after the words "I salute you" (*abhivādaye*), saying, "I am [Name]," such as "I am named Bhadra. The mention of the *vipra* here and in the formula of the return-salutation is for the purpose of indicating the twice-born (*dvija*), since all three classes are under discussion. (2.122)
To those who do not acknowledge his name when he greets them, as well as to all women, a wise man should simply say, "I am [so-and-so]. (2.123)

Since the recitation of one's own name occurs in all such cases, he says "of the name" (nāmadheyasya). When a greeting is addressed to a name that has been uttered, and those who are to be greeted do not understand it because they are unrefined or ignorant, a wise man should say, "I greet you. And even women, though they may be knowledgeable, should speak in this very same way. 2.123.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the state of being "bhoḥ" is the very essence of names.

Regarding the word *bhoḥ*: in the act of salutation, one should utter the word *bhoḥ* at the end of whatever one’s own name may be. And that [word *bhoḥ*] serves the purpose of addressing the person being saluted; for it is said, "of names" (*nāmnām*). Because Manu and others have declared that the very existence (*svarūpasattā*) of names is the portion consisting of *bhoḥ*—that is, the existence of the word *bhoḥ* itself—therefore, one should utter the word *bhoḥ* to address the person being saluted, taking its place in the position of the saluted person's name. With that, one should perform the salutation in the form: "I am he whose name is Bhadra, sir" (*bhadranāmāham asmi bho*). (2.124)

When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one. Furthermore, at the end of his name, the vowel 'a'—preceded by the final syllable—should be pronounced with a protracted (pluta) accent.

Now he states the rule for the return-greeting (*pratyabhivādana*): "O long-lived one" (*āyuṣmān*). When a greeting has been performed, the person who greeted must be addressed with the words, "Be long-lived, O gentle one" (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya*). Furthermore, whichever vowel—such as *a* and so forth—is at the end of the name of the greeter, that vowel must be protracted (*pluta*), because there is no fixed rule that names must end in the letter *a*. This protracted vowel is either the preceding syllable itself, or it is extracted from the preceding syllable and not an adventitious addition. Thus, the form of the return-greeting is: "O long-lived one, be gentle, Bhadra! (with the final vowel protracted). (2.125)
That Brahmin who does not know the proper response to a salutation should not be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra. (2.126)

Here follows an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "He who does not know the response to a salutation... This means that even a Brahmin—who, despite being learned, does not know how to perform the return-salutation (*pratyabhivādana*) for a salutation performed according to the scriptures—let alone anyone else, should not be saluted by a learned man, just like a Śūdra. Therefore, the established rule is that once one is to be saluted, the return-salutation must be performed correctly after having understood it according to the scriptures; this is a praise of the return-salutation. If it were intended as an injunction, there would be a contradiction with the context, and it would also subvert the statement: "Those who [use] a name... (2.126).
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, regarding his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, regarding his prosperity; and a Śūdra, regarding his health alone. (2.127)

In connection with the topic of returning a greeting, he states another duty for the one who returns the greeting, beginning with the words "A Brāhmaṇa. Having approached the one who has greeted him, the person returning the greeting should ask a Brāhmaṇa, "Is it well with you? (*kuśalam asti*); a member of the Kṣatriya caste, "Are you free from illness? (*anāmayam*); a Vaiśya, "Are you secure? (*kṣemam*); and a Śūdra, moreover, "Are you healthy? (*ārogyam*). (2.127)
One who is initiated is not to be addressed by name, even if he be younger;
one who knows the Dharma should address him using the honorifics *bhoḥ* or *bhavat*. (2.128)

"Regarding the phrase 'he should not address': one who has undergone initiation for the sake of a sacrifice must not be addressed by name—even if he is younger—either for the purpose of returning a greeting or for any other business. What then? One who knows the law should address him using derivative terms preceded by the words *bhoḥ* and *bhavat*, such as *bho dīkṣita* or *bhavat yajamāna*. (2.128)"
But toward a woman who is another's wife and not related by birth, he should address her as "Madam," or "O blessed one," or "Sister. (2.129)

If a woman who is another's wife is not related by birth to one’s own mother or father, then one may address her for the sake of accomplishing the task with the words "O fortunate one" (*subhage*) or "O sister" (*bhagini*), and so forth; specifically, one should say "O fortunate lady" (*bhavati subhage*) or "O mother" (*bhavati mātaḥ*). This is because the word "iti" has the sense of "in this manner," and thus includes the term "sister" (*bhaginī*) according to the appropriate circumstances.
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself, saying, "I am so-and-so. (2.130)

"And [the word] *mātulān* (maternal uncles) means that one should rise before maternal uncles and others who are younger in age and say, 'I am so-and-so, a bhadra. The *ṛtvij* (priest) will be mentioned later. And here, the "guru" refers to the son of the mother's sister and so forth, not the teacher of knowledge (*vidyāguru*), because the latter will be mentioned in the section on childhood."
A maternal aunt, the wife of a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, and a paternal aunt are to be honored like the wife of one's guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru. (2.131)

Regarding the term "mātṛsvasṛ" (mother's sister): mother's sisters and others are to be honored with the clasping of the feet and other such gestures, as will be described later, just like the wife of one's guru; for they are equal to the wife of a guru. (2.131)
The wife of one's brother of the same caste may be saluted every day;
however, the wives of paternal kinsmen and maternal relatives are to be saluted only after one has returned from a journey abroad. (2.132)

"Regarding 'the wife of a brother': because this occurs in the section on salutation (*pūjā*), it refers to the wife of one's elder brother, who is to be touched at the feet, as seen in the rule: "One should not salute her by touching her feet here. A woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*) [is to be saluted] every day. Kinsmen (*jñātayaḥ*)—those on the mother’s and father’s side—and relatives by marriage (*saṃbandhinaḥ*), namely their wives, are to be saluted upon returning from a journey, but not day after day. (2.132)
Toward his father’s sister and his mother’s elder sister as well, he should maintain the same conduct as toward his mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they. (2.133)

"Regarding the father's sister": one should behave toward the father’s sister, the mother’s sister, and an elder sister as toward a mother. Since the acts of honoring such as clasping the feet are already established for the mother’s sister and the father’s sister by the rule itself—"One should treat [them] with equal respect like the wife of a guru"—this statement is intended to extend the conduct toward a mother, such as doing what is pleasing to them. As he will say: "One should always do what is pleasing to those two. And since the superiority of the mother is established precisely through the prescription of both direct (aupadeśika) and extended (ātideśika) conduct, the statement—"The mother is more venerable than these" and "the father’s sister, the mother’s sister, and an elder sister"—is for the purpose of prohibiting the performance of what is pleasing to them in cases where it is forbidden for a mother. (2.133)
Friendship among citizens is established after ten years; among artists, after five years;
and among those learned in the Vedas, after three years. Among one's own kin, however, it is formed even by a very brief acquaintance.

Regarding the phrase "known as ten years": among those devoid of specific qualities who reside in the same city, friendship is said to be established between two people after ten years have passed, even if one is older. Consequently, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama—"A friend is to be addressed as 'O, sir' (bho bhavat)" [GDh 6.14]—he should be so addressed. Similarly, among those who possess arts—that is, those who know music—friendship is said to be established after five years. For those studying the Vedas, friendship is preceded by three years; that is, friendship exists with one who is senior by more than three years. Among kinsmen, however, it occurs in even a very short time. Where there is no reckoning of years, friendship is otherwise; in all other cases here, the practice of seniority prevails. (2.134)
One should know that a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king are like father and son; yet, of the two, the Brahmin is the father.

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya who are both one hundred years of age, there shall be the conduct of father and son in salutations and similar interactions. Furthermore, between those two, the Brāhmaṇa occupies the position of the father. 1.135.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding. (1.136)

Regarding the word "wealth" (*vitta*): wealth, kinship, age, performance of Vedic and Smārta rites, and learning—these are the grounds for respect (*mānya-sthāna*) when they belong to the same social class (*samāna-jātīyatva*), and they must be treated with honor. Consequently, among those who lack these qualities, one who possesses wealth is to be respected. Furthermore, among these [five] qualities beginning with wealth, whichever is mentioned later is more weighty than each preceding one. Therefore, it is established that among those possessing wealth, one who possesses kin is to be respected. (1.136)
Among the three [higher] castes, he who possesses the greatest number of qualities and virtues is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage.

Regarding the phrase "of the five": among the three castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, even one of inferior birth who possesses many—three, four, or all five—out of the five [qualities] such as wealth and so forth, but not only one or two, and if these are virtuous and preeminent, then he is to be honored even by one of superior birth. Thus, the rule "a ten-year-old Brāhmaṇa" applies either to a case where [the other person] lacks qualities or to a case where both possess equal qualities. Likewise, even a Śūdra who has reached ninety years of age is to be honored by the twice-born. In this way, wealth, kinship, and occupation are the grounds for the honor accorded to a Śūdra toward the twice-born; however, sacred learning (*vidyā*) does not exist for him at all.
Way must be yielded to one holding a wheel, to one in his tenth decade of life, to the sick, to one burdened with a load, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom. (1.138)

Regarding the term "cakriṇaḥ": for one mounted on a vehicle such as a chariot, for those who are very old, the sick, or women carrying heavy burdens, and for a Brāhmaṇa who has performed the *samāvartana* bath—because of the proximity of the word "king" (*rāja*) and because this occurs in the section on honors—this is the prescription of a portion of honor for these individuals, namely that they should be allowed to pass by on a path that would otherwise obstruct their progress when they are setting out for the king’s sake or for the purpose of marriage. (1.138)
Among those gathered together, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored;
and between the royal *snātaka* and the [ordinary] *snātaka*, it is the *snātaka* who receives honor from the king.

Regarding the phrase "of them": furthermore, among those such as the king and others who travel on the same path, the *rājasnātaka* is to be honored by means of the wheel and so forth—that is, by yielding the way, which is the subject under discussion. Between a *rājasnātaka* and another *snātaka* traveling on the same path, it is the *snātaka* who receives honor.
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpa and the Rahasyas, him they call an Ācārya.

Because it involves ritual service (*sopacāra*), he says "having initiated" (*upanīya*) to indicate the characteristics of the teacher (*ācārya*) and others, for the sake of the aforementioned variety. Manu and others call him an *ācārya* who, having performed the initiation (*upanayana*), teaches the Veda along with the *Kalpasūtras* and the *Upaniṣads* to a disciple. Since the secret portion (*rahasya*) is included under the term "Veda," it is taught separately here because of its preeminence. (1.140)
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas, for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya. (1.141)

"Regarding 'a single part': he who, for the sake of a livelihood, teaches a portion of the Veda or the Vedāṅgas—namely, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), etymology (nirukta), grammar (vyākaraṇa), astronomy (jyotiṣa), and prosody (chandas)—having first performed the formal rite of dedication (arpaṇa), is called an Upādhyāya. (1.141)
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports him with food, is called his guru.

Regarding the phrase "niṣekādīni" (beginning with conception): that brahmin who performs the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) according to the scriptures, and who supports and promotes [the student] with food, is called a *guru*. And thus, this father is a *guru* because of the mention of *niṣeka* (conception). 1.142.

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.

Regarding the term *agnyādheya*: he who, having performed the prescribed scriptural practices, performs the *ādhāna*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *agniṣṭoma*, and other Soma sacrifices, is called an *ṛtvij* (officiant) in this treatise. Because he too is worthy of respect, he is mentioned here; as it has been said: "The father-in-law and others, the officiants, and the gurus. (1.143)
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as mother and father; one should never bear him malice. (2.144)

"He who covers [the ears]" means he who fills both ears with the Veda, making it unerring and free from errors of accent and so forth; he is to be regarded as one's mother and father. And toward him, one should not commit any act of malice even after the period of study has concluded. (2.144)
Ten preceptors are equal to one teacher; a father exceeds a hundred teachers;
but a mother surpasses a thousand fathers in respect. 2.145.

Regarding the phrase "toward preceptors" (*upādhyāyān*): because of the reason of reverence, the *ācārya* is superior to ten preceptors; the meaning is that the worship due to the *ācārya* should be tenfold greater than the worship due to a preceptor. Likewise, a father—who performs all the purificatory rites and so forth—is superior in reverence to a hundred *ācāryas*. A mother—who causes all the purificatory rites and so forth to be performed—is superior in reverence to a thousand fathers who are merely biological progenitors. (2.145)
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for the Brahmin, both after death and in this world. (2.146)

Regarding the term "progenitor": between the two fathers—the biological father and the teacher who produces [the child] without the need for the performance of rites such as the *saṃskāras*—the father known as the teacher (*ācārya*) is more praiseworthy. This is because that birth of a Brahmin, which consists of the initiation (*upanayana*) for the purpose of receiving the Veda (*brahma*), is eternal and constant in this world, since it serves as the cause for liberation through the traditional lineage. For this reason, when the biological father, the mother, and the teacher are present together, the teacher alone is to be honored first. The mention of the "Brahmin" is intended to indicate the twice-born (*dvija*) in general, as all three classes are under discussion here. (2.146)
One should know that the birth which occurs when his mother and father unite in passion and he is born from the womb is merely his physical origin. (2.147)
But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule with the Sāvitrī—*that* is real; *that* is free from old age and death. (2.148)

Regarding this, there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "out of desire" (*kāmāt*). As for the phrase "but the teacher" (*ācāryas tu*): the parents produce him from mutual desire, not out of a wish to provide him assistance; they merely know his rebirth—that he is born from the womb. The teacher, however, is the one who causes him to study the entire Veda according to the scriptures. That birth or origin which he effects for him through the *Sāvitrī* mantra, which is a constituent part of the initiation (*upanayana*), is "true"—that is, it is of the nature of truth—because it is the cause for performing rites such as those prescribed in the Śrutis. It is "undecaying" (*ajarā*) and "unimpeding" (*abādhakā*) because there is no further diminution of him upon that subsequent birth; and it is "immortal" (*amarā*) because, by way of producing the qualification for the knowledge whose nature is immortality, it is the cause of immortality.

|| 2.147–48 || The wise man should always avoid those who are wicked, even if they are powerful, just as one avoids a snake with a poisoned fang. One should not associate with the wicked, for they cause harm even when they are honored; they are like a fire that consumes its own abode. One should not dwell among the wicked, for they lead to ruin; rather, one should dwell among the virtuous, for they lead to prosperity. Just as a drop of water falling on a lotus leaf does not cling to it, so too the wise man, having abandoned the wicked, does not become defiled by their faults. One should seek out the company of the virtuous, for they are the source of happiness; they are like a cooling breeze in the heat of summer. One should not follow the counsel of the wicked, for it leads to destruction; rather, one should follow the counsel of the virtuous, for it leads to well-being. Thus, having understood this, the wise man should always keep the company of the good and avoid the company of the evil.
One should know that person here as a teacher by whom even a little or much of what has been heard is beneficial, through that very benefit conferred by the sacred learning. 2.149

Furthermore, he states another characteristic of a guru: "even a little for the sake of worship. One should recognize here, in this context of worship, even that person who explains any portion of what has been heard—whether small or great—as being a benefactor through that assistance with the sacred teachings. (2.149)
The creator of the Vedic birth and the instructor of one's own duty—a Brahmin, even if a child, becomes by law the father of an elder. (2.150)

Nor is seniority by age to be considered for the purpose of honoring the teacher of knowledge, because of the phrase "of the Veda" (brāhmasya). Since it is impossible for one who is younger to perform the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the one who performs the teaching and other rites indicated by that [initiation], and who instructs him thus: "This is your duty" (*svadharma*) and "This is the law" (*dharma*), becomes equal to a father—even if he is a child—by virtue of being the cause of the elder's duty, wealth, and religious acts. (2.150)
The child Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his elders;
having embraced them with his wisdom, he said to them, "O little sons! (2.151)
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods about that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."
The ignorant one is indeed a child; he who imparts the sacred mantras becomes a father.
For they call the ignorant one a "child," but the giver of mantras a "father. (2.153)

In this context, there is a further explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the nature of the original form, beginning with the words "he taught" (*adhyāpayāmāsa*). Regarding the phrase "them": a boy named Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, while still a child, taught his father, paternal uncles, and others. Having accepted them as disciples by means of his knowledge of the Vedas and other sciences—which served as the cause—and for the sake of his purpose, he addressed them as "little sons" (*putrakāḥ*) at times such as when calling them. Then those fathers, provoked to anger by being thus addressed, assembled and asked the gods about that matter: "Is this practice of addressing us with the word 'little son' proper? The gods, having gathered to deliberate on this, said to those fathers: "It is fitting that the child spoke thus to you. For even if one is old, if he is ignorant he is a fool; and he who is a teacher, even if he is a child, is equal to a father. For people call one who is unequal to them an "ignorant child," and they speak of the teacher as a "father. (2.151–53)
Neither by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he among us who is learned in the Vedas is great. 2.154

And therefore, "not by years": seniority does not consist in the abundance of age, such as grey hair or wrinkles; rather, our view is that he who is capable of teaching is the superior one—it was thus that the sages established the law. (2.154)
The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas by valor, that of Vaiśyas by grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone by birth. (2.155)

And this being so, regarding the phrase "of the Brahmins": the superiority of Brahmins is by virtue of knowledge; that of Kṣatriyas, moreover, is by virtue of personal prowess; that of Vaiśyas, by virtue of grain, gold, and so forth; and that of Śūdras, by virtue of age. (2.155)
One does not become old merely because one's head is gray; even if young, the gods know him as venerable who is devoted to study. 2.156

One does not become old merely because one's head has turned grey due to the natural process known as the predominance of age. Rather, even if he is young, the gods consider him to be old if he has studied the Vedas; this statement is made for the sake of emphasizing the importance of the subject at hand. 2.156.
As is an elephant made of wood, as is a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three merely bear the name. (2.157)

"Yathā" means: just as a wooden elephant is incapable of combat and the like, and just as a deer made of leather is of no use for hunting and such activities, so too is a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied [the Vedas] regarding those actions performed by a Brāhmaṇa, such as receiving gifts and so forth. And thus, all three of these bear only their names; they do not perform the functions accomplished by actual elephants and the like. (2.157)
As a eunuch is fruitless among women, as a cow is fruitless with another cow, and as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless. || 2.158 ||

Just as one who is impotent, just as a eunuch is devoid of offspring even when approaching women, just as a female cow is devoid of the fruit of offspring due to the absence of mating with a bull, and just as a gift given to an ignorant person is fruitless, so too a Brāhmaṇa devoid of Vedic knowledge is fruitless, because he provides no benefit—either seen or unseen—to the Supreme Self. 2.158
The instruction of living beings toward their own welfare must be carried out through non-violence alone;
and one who desires righteousness should employ speech that is sweet and gentle. (2.159)

In the context of the conduct of the teacher (*ācārya*), he now states a certain rule for the student (*ācārya*) as well, beginning with "only by non-violence" (*ahiṃsayāiva*). Since it will be stated later that there should be a slight striking on the back of the body "with a rope or a bamboo strip," one must avoid excessive beating. Because the term "beings" (*bhūtānām*) is used, this applies not only to the students under discussion but also to wives and others; thus, the teacher must perform the study of the Vedas and so forth for them. And for that purpose, speech itself—free from abuse—must be spoken loudly, according to the instruction regarding Dharma for one who desires Dharma. (2.159)
He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit taught in the Vedānta.

Regarding the phrase "of whom" (*yasya*): for one whose speech and mind are pure and free from modification, they do not undergo turbidity even when [active]; and being properly guarded, once arisen, they never perform their functions with turbidity throughout one's entire life. Such a person attains the complete fruit called liberation, as taught in the Upaniṣads. (2.160)

One should not be a wounder of others even when afflicted, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm others; one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds. (2.161)

And for this reason, one should not be "wounding" (*nāruntuda*). Even when deeply afflicted, one should not touch the vital points (*marmaspṛk*) of others; one should not have the intention to engage in activity for the purpose of harming another. Furthermore, one should not utter that speech by which the world hates him, for such speech is an obstacle to attaining worlds such as heaven. (2.161)
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if it were poison;
he should always long for contempt as if it were nectar. (2.162)
Regarding the phrase "from honor": a Brahmin should feel as much distress from honor throughout his life as if it were poison, and he should always long for contempt as if it were nectar. (2.162)
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in happiness and wakes in happiness; he moves through this world in happiness, while the scorner perishes. 2.163

"Happy" means this: he who is not despised sleeps happily; for one who has been insulted, there arises no mental agitation such as "I have done what was improper. Thus, he abandons sleep with ease and conducts himself easily in the world. But he who causes insult—thinking "I have done wrong"—is destroyed by demerit in this world and the next. (2.163)
By this sequential method, the twice-born man, having purified his self, should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the attainment of Brahman while dwelling with his teacher.

Having thus discussed the duty pertaining solely to the student (*ruṣamātra-dharma*) by way of incidental digressions, he now states the subject at hand with the words "by this": "By this [means], having been initiated according to the aforementioned sequence, the twice-born, while residing in the teacher’s household, should gradually acquire day by day that which has the attainment of the Vedas as its purpose—namely, austerity consisting of observances—and the refinement of the self. (2.164)
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions, must be acquired by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule. (2.165)

Regarding the phrase "by specific austerities" (*tapoviśeṣaiḥ*): by specific austerities—both those already mentioned and those yet to be described, such as kindling the sacred fires and so forth—and by various types of vows prescribed in the *Gṛhya-śāstras* for each Veda, such as the *Sāvitrī* and others, the entire Veda must be studied by the twice-born; that is, all the branches (*śākhās*) consisting of both Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. This is because the term "Veda" is observed to be applied even to a single portion, as seen in the Smṛti rule: "In the case of reciting [a portion], the tongue shall be cut off. Furthermore, since the term "Smṛti" is used for even a single part, the inclusion of the entire text implies the necessity of studying the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*). This is obtained through the force of the injunction to study, since its purpose is the comprehension of meaning; for comprehension of meaning is not possible without the auxiliaries. The "Secret" (*rahasya*) refers to the Upaniṣads; it is mentioned separately due to its preeminence. Moreover, one should not abandon one's own branch (*svaśākhā*) for the sake of a continuous lineage starting with one's father; otherwise, one incurs the sin of abandoning one's own branch, as stated in the Smṛti. And thus: [The verse continues: "He who abandons his own branch and studies another, having fallen from both, becomes a mere Śūdra in this world. He who abandons his own sūtra and conducts himself according to another’s sūtra, making an unauthoritative seer his standard, is likewise joined with unrighteousness.

Thus it is recorded in the *Pariśiṣṭas*. However, a person’s connection to a specific *śākhā* is not determined by their *gotra*. Therefore, whichever *śākhā* has been studied by someone, that alone is his own *śākhā*; and the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) concerns precisely the performance of its meaning. As for the statement that "he who abandons his own *sūtra* is one who abandons the Vedic *śākhā*," that is incorrect. Just as there is a traditional remembrance of a fixed *gotra* in the form "this is our *gotra*," so too do they remember a fixed *śākhā* in the form "this is our *śākhā*," and they record the fault of abandoning the *śākhā* precisely through the abandonment of that [remembrance]. Furthermore, the phrase "having abandoned" refers to the abandonment of the performance of its meaning, namely one's own *sūtra*. That very *śākhā* which has been handed down through the lineage of fathers and ancestors is what must be studied.
But surely, how can these contemporary designations based on the teachings—such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth—be justified as fixed designations like "we [are the Kāṭhakas]" and so on?

True. Who says this? These designations (*samākhyā*) have other causes as their basis. Or who says that designations such as "the Kaṭhas" are non-eternal? How so? This present designation is caused by the study [of the text] after it was proclaimed. And since designations are caused by the act of proclaiming, even though there may be the appearance and disappearance of these designations, there is never any loss of the remembrance of the eternal relationship, because the *śākhā* (branch/section) is eternal. The term "secret" (*rahasya*) refers to the *Upaniṣads*; they are taught separately because of their predominance due to being devoted to the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*). 2.165.
A twice-born man of the highest order, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is said here to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin. (2.166)

In this context, he states the lifelong duty of study with the word "Veda. Desiring to perform austerity (*tapas*) such as restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), a Brāhmaṇa should practice the Veda alone for as long as he lives. For the practice of the Veda is declared in the scripture to be his preeminent austerity, superior to all other forms of austerity. The mention of the "best of the twice-born" is intended to indicate the [other] twice-born classes; it serves as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) because they are the subject under discussion. (2.166)
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even unto his fingernails, who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability. (2.167)

"Indeed, it is so. Even a twice-born man who, though wearing garlands and other ornaments, studies his own Veda daily according to his ability—even while neglecting the Brahmanical observances—performs austerity that pervades him down to the tips of his nails, reaching even those nails which are devoid of life. This austerity is superior to all other forms of austerity because it pervades those very nails. How much more so for one who studies while joined with the prescribed observances? This is praise of the subject at hand; however, there is no study of the Veda possible through the abandonment of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). The particle *ha* indicates traditional scripture. And for that Brahmin who is free from envy, that is the supreme austerity.
When a twice-born man studies even the Rigveda verses as his daily private recitation according to his ability;
First, the acquisition of the Veda; then reflection, practice, austerity, and its impartation to disciples—thus, indeed, the study of the Veda is fivefold. (2.167)
The twice-born man who, having not studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits, quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra while still living, along with his progeny. (2.168)

Regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): that twice-born man who, having been initiated (*upanīta*), exerts himself in the Vedāṅgas and so forth without first learning the Veda, quickly attains a status equal to a Śūdra—even while still living—along with his lineage, because he fails to perform the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) for himself, his sons, and others due to his ignorance of the Veda. By the use of the term "twice-born," there is a prohibition against an uninitiated person studying the Veda or the Vedic auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*). Accordingly, the prohibition will apply specifically to the Veda itself, as in the rule: "One should not utter the *brahman* (the Veda). (2.168)

The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass; the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti. (2.169)

Now, by way of praising the performance of that [Vedic study], he states this stream [of the life-cycle] as "the first birth from the mother": the first birth of a man is from his mother; the second is the tying of the girdle (*mekhalā*); the third is for the sake of sacrifice at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) for one who has become twice-born (*dvija*), because of the injunction of the Śruti: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) indeed make him a fetus again when they initiate him. (2.169)
In that regard, as for his birth as a Brahmin, which is marked by the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass:
therein the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, and the teacher is said to be his father. (2.170)

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): among those three births, that birth of a man which is for the purpose of grasping Brahman—characterized by the tying of the girdle (*mekhalābandhana*)—is such that Sāvitrī is his mother and the Preceptor (*ācārya*) is his father; thus, by means of a metaphorical device (*rūpaka*), he establishes [the nature of] that birth. (2.170)
Because he imparts the Vedas, they call the teacher "father";
for no ritual duty whatsoever is enjoined upon him [the son] prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass. (2.171)

"Because of the imparting of the Veda": they call him the teacher-father because of his teaching the Veda; for prior to that initiation (*upanayana*), no action such as study—which serves as a cause for some degree of excellence—is appropriate. And thus, since he has not yet attained the status of a "twice-born" (*samāna*) prior to initiation, it is logical that his status as an Āryan birth is established through the imparting of the Veda. (2.171)
He shall not pronounce the Veda, except when offering the *svadhā* libation;
for he remains equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born to the Veda. (2.172)

Thus, since there is a prohibition against study prior to initiation (*upanayana*), he states an exception: "He should not utter [Vedic words]. That ritual by which the action accomplished through mantras containing the word *svadhā* is poured out—that is, conveyed—to the ancestors is called *svadhā-ninayana*; with the exception of that ancestral rite, he should not cause the Veda to be recited. Because as long as he is not born [to his status], that is, as long as he has not been initiated, he is equal to a Śūdra. This very point is the indicator for the eligibility to perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha and other rites when there is the death of an uninitiated father. (2.172)

For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the vows is prescribed, as well as the formal reception of the Veda (brahmagrahaṇa), in due order according to the rules. (2.173)

Regarding the phrase "having performed the initiation" (*kṛtopanayana*): for one who has been initiated, it is first required that he be instructed in the vows (*vrata*), such as the *Sāvitra*, which are enjoined by his own particular scripture. Following that, the study of the Veda in its aforementioned form—the study of the mantras and brāhmaṇas belonging to his own branch (*svaśākhā*)—is prescribed in due order, preceded by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other such practices. (2.173)

Whatever skin, whatever sacred thread, and whatever girdle is prescribed for him, and whatever staff and whatever garment—each of these must also be maintained during his religious observances. (2.174)

Regarding the word "which" (yad): whatever types of skin, girdle, staff, and garment were prescribed for a specific student at his initiation (*upanayana*), those very same types—and no others—must be adopted for the subsequent vows (*prativrata*). Since the wearing of what was previously acquired has already been enjoined, the re-specification of them would otherwise be redundant; therefore, it is understood that they must be of the same type but distinct items. Furthermore, because the previous items are no longer fit for their purpose and are as good as destroyed, the rule "he should throw them into water" constitutes their ritual disposal (*pratipatti*). || 2.174 ||
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules, fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit. (2.175)

"One should practice" means that the student (brahmacārī), while living in the teacher's household, having restrained the collection of the senses—that is, the aggregate of the sense organs—should observe these restraints and observances for the sake of increasing his own austerity. 2.175.

Having bathed daily and become pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of sacrificial fuel upon the fire. (2.176)

"Daily" means that having bathed every day and being pure, one should perform the offering of water (udakadāna) for the gods, beginning with Maheśvara; for the sages, beginning with Aṅgiras; and for the deceased ancestors, beginning with the father. Likewise, one should perform the worship of the deities, beginning with Hara, with flowers and other offerings, as well as the placing of fuel-sticks (samidh) into the fire in the evening and in the morning. || 2.176 ||
One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women, all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings. (2.177)

"One should avoid" means: one should avoid honey, meat, garlands, women, and the harming of living beings; likewise, fragrant substances such as camphor and the like, and substances with intense flavors such as molasses and the like. Although the word *rasa* (flavor) already includes honey, it is taught separately for the sake of a specific penance. "Sour things" (*śuktāni*) are those that have acquired their own natural flavor and become acidic through the passage of time or through contact with other substances such as water over time. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of completing the meter; it does not have the capacity to convey any further meaning. As for the Gautama rule stating "or sour speech," there, because of the proximity of the word "speech" (*vāk*), the word "sour" (*śukta*) functions in a different sense. Here, however, if this were intended, one who acts intentionally would consider: "I am uttering all words, which are indeed sour. Even though the prohibition is established for the student (*brahmacārin*) by the rule "and all sour things here," its mention here is for the purpose of making it an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of Vedic study. By this prohibition, if one eats [forbidden food], there would be a mere transgression of the person's duty (*puruṣārtha*), but not a deficiency in the ritual injunction (*vidhivaiguṇya*). What, then, is the status of prohibitions regarding falsehood, violence, and so forth? Furthermore, the prohibition of meat and the like mentioned here is for the purpose of consumption, not for medicinal purposes. Thus, Vasiṣṭha permits meat and the like: "He may eat another [substance] at will, and he may consume the leavings of his teacher for the sake of medicine. (2.177)

Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and carrying an umbrella, as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments—(these are forbidden). 2.178.

Regarding "anointing" (*abhyaṅgam*): one should avoid anointing with ointments, ghee, and the like; wearing shoes or carrying an umbrella; desire, anger, the property of others, and singing or playing musical instruments. "Desire" (*kāma*) refers to an excessive longing for food and such. Since sexual passion (*manmatha*) is already prohibited by the mention of women, it is not repeated here. (2.178)
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, as well as falsehood; gazing at and touching women, and injury to another—[these he should avoid]. (2.179)

Regarding gambling: one should avoid playing with dice and other such games, quarreling with people, proclaiming the faults of others, untruthfulness, embracing women out of a desire for sexual union, and causing harm to another’s property through loss and the like. (2.179)
One should always sleep alone and never let semen spill;
for by spilling semen out of desire, one destroys his own vow. 2.180

"Alone" means he should not lie down with another person—this applies everywhere, whether in the house of his teacher or in his father's house and so forth. Furthermore, he should not discharge semen by any other means than through sexual union with a woman, even if it is into something other than a vagina (*ayoni*). For by intentionally discharging semen, one destroys one's own state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). (2.180)

If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) unintentionally emits semen during sleep, he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with "punar mām. (2.181)

Regarding "in a dream": if a twice-born student (*brahmacārin*) unintentionally emits semen in a dream, he should bathe, honor the sun with flowers and other offerings, and recite three times the verse beginning, "May my virile power return to me. The displacement of this expiation from its immediate context is intended to proclaim the gravity of the student's obligation compared to other rules for the preservation of semen. (2.181)
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass—as much as required—and he should go out for alms every day. (2.182)

"Water-jar" means that he should bring a water-jar, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *darbha* grass for as long as they are needed for his teacher and himself; he should go out for alms every day. He should not live on the following day with food brought on a previous day that has become stale, nor with oily substances, nor with sour gruel and the like, unless there is a specific rule regarding oils. 2.182.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praised for their own duties. 2.183.

Regarding the phrase "with the Vedas and sacrifices": from the houses of those who are devoted to the performance of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, who are praised for their own duties such as teaching and so forth for the sake of their livelihood, and who live by their own proper occupation, the student, being pure, should daily collect alms. (2.183)
One should not beg for alms from the family of the teacher, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives.
However, if other houses are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding house in favor of the next.

"From the teacher," etc.: he should not beg at the teacher's house, nor likewise at the houses of his own father and mother. However, if food is not obtained from houses other than these, he should avoid each preceding one in turn. First, he should beg at the house of a relative; if that is unavailable, then at the teacher's house. (2.184)
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village, restraining his speech and remaining pure, but he must avoid those who have been formally accused. 2.185.

"Everything": even when nothing is obtained from kinsmen, householders, and so forth, he may collect [alms] from among the four castes and others. Being one who has conquered his senses, he should observe silence—avoiding only the utterance of words for begging—and he should avoid those accused of crimes, those well-known as outcasts due to their sins, those whose guilt is certain, and outcasts by association (the *daṇḍāpūpaka* rule). || 2.185 ||
Having fetched fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air;
and evening and morning, he should unwearyingly offer oblations with them into the fire. (2.186)

"Having brought from afar" means having brought fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from the forest, according to the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Alternatively, because "afar" is not strictly limited, one should bring uncut fuel-sticks and place them in the house, a shed, or a similar location, since it is impossible to set them down in the open air (*vihāyas*, i.e., the sky). Being diligent with these, one should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) every evening and morning. (2.186)
If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*. (2.187)

"Having not performed," etc. Because of the gravity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*), begging for alms and the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) are to be combined. If, acting out of desire (*kāmakāreṇa*), one who is not ill fails to perform these continuously for seven days, he who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇī*) shall perform the penance that will be described in the eleventh chapter. How so? Furthermore, according to the individual sequence of Gautama’s rule regarding the kindling of the fire and the practice of begging for alms, if one fails to perform them for seven nights, one must offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*) or fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the two verses beginning with *retasyābhyām*. The term "not ill" (*anātura*) implies that for one who is ill, there is another penance; it does not mean an absence of penance altogether. For this much is understood: this penance applies to one who is not ill, but it does not mean that there is no transgression for one who is ill. The phrase "he should not touch his own apertures" is a qualification within a restrictive injunction (*niyamavākya*), not something by which it would be understood that one who is ill lacks the entitlement [to perform the rite]. Rather, it is a qualification of the penance itself; therefore, there certainly is another penance for one who is ill. Furthermore, the specific mention of this penance is for the sake of brevity; for if it were performed [in the general case], the explicit mention of the term "celibate student" (*brahmacārin*) would have been necessary. (2.187)
Subsisting constantly on alms, the observer of the vow should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the livelihood of one who observes the vow through alms is equal to fasting.

"By means of alms-food": a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should maintain his life-sustenance by means of alms-food for as long as he observes his studentship. However, he should not eat food belonging to a single person. Because his livelihood through alms-food yields a fruit equal to fasting, the phrase "he should subsist on alms-food" is reiterated here for the purpose of stating the reward for this rule. Nor should there be any suspicion of its being optional, since an expiation has been prescribed for its violation. "He should not be one who seeks alms from others, nor should he accept alms-food; alms-food is equal to the drinking of Soma; therefore, he should subsist on alms-food."
Whoever consumes morsels of that alms-food which is pure by its acquisition, sprinkled with water, and offered in sacrifice, that act is equal to performing sacrificial rites.
At a rite dedicated to the gods, he may eat like one observing a vow; at a rite for the ancestors, he may eat like a seer (ṛṣi).
If requested, he may eat at his pleasure; his vow is not thereby violated. (2.189)

"Like one observing a vow" (*vratavat*): at a rite for the gods (*daiva-karma*), for the sake of the vow, [food] is devoid of honey and other such items; and at a *śrāddha*, like a seer (*ṛṣivat*), it should not be village-grown, but wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like. Being invited, he may eat the food of a single person (*ekānna*) at his will if he so desires. For one acting in this manner, there is no violation of the vow. Furthermore, the word "seer" (*ṛṣi*) has its well-known application to Vasiṣṭha and others, and not to a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*); for if it were the latter, there might arise the suspicion that meat-eating is permitted by the authorization of food suitable for him, as in the rule "he may eat even a single [type of] food. Because eating at a *śrāddha* is more blameworthy than ordinary custom, the author states "like a seer" to express an excellence of restraint. (2.189)
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not prescribed in such a manner. (2.190)

Regarding the phrase "of the Brāhmaṇa": this act known as eating food from a single house at rites for the gods or the ancestors is prescribed by Manu and others specifically for the Brāhmaṇa. As for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, they do not prescribe this practice, even though it is a form of accepting alms. Furthermore, the status of being a *brahmacārin* (student) applies to both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well, due to the context. Since the permission to eat alms-food applies to all students, and since the prohibition of eating food from a single house is an exception to that, these two castes are also included in the scope of the topic. Moreover, since the rule regarding "acceptance" (*pratigraha*) has already found its application in the case of Kṣatriyas other than students, this specific prohibition is made only when such acceptance would otherwise be applicable. (2.190)
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged, he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his preceptor. (2.191)

"Urged" means that, whether commissioned by his teacher or not, he should practice the effort of reciting the portions of the study he has received and the effort of serving the teacher for as long as his period of studenthood lasts. (2.191)
Restraining his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher. (2.192)

Regarding the body: having restrained the body, speech, eyes, and so forth—the sense organs and the mind—one should remain standing with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of the Guru. (2.192)
One should always keep one's hand raised, maintain virtuous conduct, and remain well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," one should not sit directly facing the teacher.

"Perpetually": as long as he lives, he should dwell in the presence of his teacher with arms raised, endowed with good conduct and free from laziness. When told by the teacher, "Be seated," he should sit down facing the teacher. (2.193)
In the presence of his teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him. (2.194)

"Having inferior food, clothing, and dress": in the presence of the guru, for as long as he lives, his food, clothing, and ornaments should be inferior to those of the guru in terms of refinement, quantity, and so forth. He should rise before the guru rises from bed, and lie down after the guru has gone to sleep. (2.194)
One should not engage in conversation with a guest while lying down, nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor while facing away. (2.195)

Regarding "responding and conversing": one should not respond to or engage in conversation concerning an order, an acceptance, or a matter of business while lying down, seated, eating, standing, or with one's face turned away. (2.196)

Standing, one should attend to him who is seated; approaching, one should attend to him who is standing; going out to meet him, one should attend to him who is coming toward oneself; and running after him, one should attend to him who is running. (2.196)
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is far off, bowing down before one who is reclining, and standing by the side of one who is giving instructions. (2.197)

How then? [The rule is: "For one who is seated," "for one who has his face turned away," "for one who is sitting and giving an order"—one should stand up to respond or converse. For one who is standing, having gone toward him; for one who is walking quickly, following behind him while walking quickly; for one who has turned away or is standing still, having come face-to-face; for one who is at a distance, having approached him; for one who is lying down, having bowed low; and for one who is standing nearby. 2.196–97.
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat should always be low;
within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases. (2.198)

"Likewise, [he should use] a low bed and seat": in the presence of the teacher, his bed and seat should be shorter than those of the teacher for as long as he lives. Likewise, within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases. (2.198)
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures. (2.199)

"One should not utter [the name]" means that even in the absence of the guru, one should not pronounce his name without the words of veneration (*pūjāvākya*). One should not imitate the guru’s movements—such as walking, speaking, or eating—by saying, for example, "Our guru is going. (2.199)
Wherever censure or even slander of the guru occurs, there one should either cover one's ears or depart for another place. (2.200)

Regarding the word "of the guru": in whatever place some people utter faults against the guru—that is, speak of non-existent defects—one should cover one's ears there and depart for another location from that place. Furthermore, one must not oneself engage in slander or the like. (2.200)
Through slander one becomes a donkey; indeed, the reviler becomes a dog.
One who consumes another's property becomes a worm, and the envious person becomes an insect. (2.201)

Regarding the phrase "from slander": one who slanders is reborn as a donkey in another birth; one who reviles becomes a dog. One who lives off the wealth of a teacher without permission becomes a worm. One who cannot endure the virtues of a teacher becomes an insect; the separate mention of the insect (*kīṭa*) from the worm (*kṛmi*)—the latter being slightly more developed—is intended to show that [slander] must therefore not be committed. Furthermore, it is not logical that this verse, whose subject is hearing, should be considered a statement of the first half [of the injunction], because the word "heard" (*śruta*) is not employed [in the verse]. Moreover, due to its association with the two subsequent [verses] which have the nature of injunctions, [it is part of the injunction]. If it is argued that the prohibition of performing [the act] is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*) once the prohibition of hearing is established, then from what source is the statement of the result [of the transgression] established?
One should not honor him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, one should descend from a vehicle or a seat before saluting him. 2.202.

"Standing at a distance": while standing at a distance, one should not honor the teacher by sending flowers from the hand of another; nor should one honor him when he is provoked to anger, nor should one honor him while he is standing near his wives. And when [the teacher] is situated on a vehicle or a seat, then one should descend and salute him. Furthermore, even when [the student] himself is on a vehicle or a seat, he should rise up and salute him; and in this case, having descended, he should salute him. In that regard, since it is possible for one to descend from a low vehicle or seat without rising, it was said: "he should rise up and salute. Moreover, since rising is also possible for one who is on a vehicle such as a carriage or a cow-drawn cart, it was said: "having descended, he should salute. (2.202)
One should not sit with one's teacher to the wind or downwind;
nor should one say anything at all that cannot be heard by the teacher. 2.203.

"Against the wind" (*prativāta*) means: where the wind has turned toward the front, blowing from the teacher's location toward the student's location; or where the student follows after the teacher, such that the wind blows back toward the teacher's location—in those places he should not sit behind the teacher. Likewise, in the presence of the teacher, in any place where there is no hearing (*saṃśravaḥ*), that is, no overhearing of the teacher, he should not say anything at all to anyone else. (2.203)
One may sit together with one's teacher on vehicles drawn by cattle, horses, or camels; on a palanquin or a stone slab; on mats; and likewise on a rock, a wooden plank, or a boat. (2.204)

"On ox-carts, horse-carts, camel-carts, vehicles, palaces, and straw-mats. When mounted on an ox-cart, a horse-cart, or a camel-cart; in a palace (a white-washed mansion); on a straw-mat or a mat made of reeds by actors and others; on a potter's wheel; and on stones, wooden planks, or boats—one may sit together with one's teacher. This is an exception to the prohibition: "One should not occupy the same bed or seat as a superior person" (2.204).
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
nor, unless authorized by his teacher, should one salute one's own teachers. (2.205)

Regarding the word "of the guru": when the teacher-guru (ācāryaguru) is present with the pupil, he should behave toward him as he would toward his own teacher. Likewise, while staying in the teacher's house, he should not salute his own birth-gurus (parents) without being permitted by him. 2.205.

In the same way, one's conduct toward teachers of sacred knowledge, toward one's own parents, and toward those who forbid unrighteousness as well as those who instruct in what is beneficial, must always be constant.

"Towards the teachers of knowledge exactly so. One should behave in this very same manner toward other teachers of knowledge, such as the *upādhyāya* and others, besides the *ācārya*. Likewise, one's conduct should be constant toward those who are like one's own parents (*svayoni*), namely those teachers who instruct in medicines and other means for averting unrighteousness (*adharma*). 2.206.
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one would toward one's own guru—likewise toward the guru’s son, the teacher, and the guru’s own kinsmen. (2.207)

"In teachers who are superior to oneself in terms of spiritual excellence (*śreyas*), such as through their knowledge and so forth"—this [phrase] "in teachers" (*ācāryeṣu*) is a qualification of the teacher’s sons. By this qualification, Manu’s intention should be understood as follows: one should behave toward the teacher’s sons—whether they are older than oneself, of the same caste as oneself, of a higher caste, or in the highest state—as one would toward the teacher himself. And likewise toward the teacher’s own kinsmen, such as the teacher’s paternal uncles and others. (2.207)
Whether he be of equal age, a child, or a pupil, the son of the teacher who teaches during a sacrificial rite deserves honor just like the teacher himself. (2.208)

Regarding the term "bāla" (child): a student (*śiṣya*) who is younger than a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), or one who is equal [in age] in matters such as sacrificial knowledge (*yajñavidyā*), likewise deserves worship like a teacher while teaching; however, his status as a teacher is not established merely by the fact that he teaches. This is because, among teachers of knowledge (*vidyāguru*), it is understood that this [status] applies exactly in such cases. Furthermore, it is not the case that his treatment as a teacher is based on his being younger, since the designation "child" (*śaiśava*) has already been shown in relation to him. True. However, since it was stated [in verse 2.145], "Or a student in the performance of a sacrifice," the status of being a student in the sense of [receiving] the meaning (*artha-śiṣyatva*) does not apply to one who is teaching; therefore, this statement is made to address a potential doubt in that regard. This very point serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the teacher of the meaning (*arthaguru*) is more venerable than the teacher of the text (*granthaguru*). (2.208)
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing, or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one perform the washing of his feet. (2.209)

Regarding "rubbing": massaging, bathing, eating the teacher's leftovers, and washing his feet should not be performed for the teacher’s son. From this very prohibition, it is concluded that these acts must be performed for the teacher himself, even though they are not explicitly mentioned in that regard. (2.209)
The wives of one's gurus who are of the same caste should be honored like the gurus themselves;
those of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation. (2.210)

"Like the teacher" means that the wives of the teacher who belong to the same caste (sajātīya) are to be honored like the teacher; however, those of a different caste (vijātīya) are to be honored merely by rising from one's seat and saluting. 2.210.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs, and the dressing of the hair—these should not be performed by the wife of one's teacher. (2.211)
Regarding "anointing": one must not perform oil massages, bathing, rubbing with unguents, dressing the hair, or applying fragrant pastes on the wife of one's teacher. 2.211.
But the wife of one's guru, even if she is young, should not be saluted by touching her feet here by one who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults.
Regarding "the teacher’s wife": the young wife of an elder should not be saluted by a youth—even one who understands pleasure and pain—preceded by the clasping of her feet. 2.212.
This is the very nature of women: to corrupt men in this world.
Therefore, the wise do not become heedless on account of women. (2.213)

Regarding "intrinsic nature": this is the very nature of women that they generate an intensification of passion in men. For this reason, a wise person does not indulge in negligence such as physical contact and the like. || 2.213 ||
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger. (2.214)
For women are capable of leading even a man who knows the scriptures well down the path of unrighteousness in this world, if he is subject to desire and anger. (2.214)
One should not sit in seclusion with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a wise man. 2.215

"Thus it is said": one should not sit even with one's mother, sister, or daughter in a secluded place; for the host of the senses is difficult to restrain, and through such association, it causes even one who knows the scriptures to fall away from his discipline. (2.215)
However, one should certainly perform a formal salutation according to the rules before young wives of gurus on the ground, saying, "I am so-and-so. (2.216)

Regarding the word "kāmam": according to this rule—namely, "a youth should perform salutation on the ground before the wives of his gurus with hands crossed"—he should perform the greeting in the manner already described, saying, "I am so-and-so. (2.216)
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher's wives every day and offer salutations, remembering the duty of the virtuous. (2.217)

"Having returned from a journey": one who has returned from a sojourn should perform the clasping of the feet [only] once daily toward the wives of his gurus, merely by way of salutation; doing so while reflecting that "this alone is the proper conduct. (2.217)
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade, so does one who is intent on service obtain knowledge residing in the teacher. 2.218

This is appropriate, [extending] as far as the service of one's teacher, including one's sons, wife, and so forth; for "just as" (yathā): just as a man, digging with great effort using a spade or other tool, obtains water located in the netherworld (pātāla), even so one who is habituated to service obtains the knowledge residing in the teacher, but not through laziness. 2.218.

He may be shaven-headed, or he may wear matted hair, or he may have a single lock of matted hair on the crown; the sun must never set upon him while he is in a village, nor should it ever rise upon him there. (2.219)

Regarding the word *muṇḍa*: he may have all his hair shaved off, or he may wear all his hair tied together so that the strands are interlocked; or his matted locks (*jaṭā*) may consist of his topknot (*śikhā*) alone. And he should act in such a way that, while residing in a village or a town, the sun shall never—at any time—set or rise upon him while he is lying down, as indicated by the mention of "one who is lying down" in the following verse. (2.219)
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting prayers.

Regarding the word "him": if the sun should rise while that religious student (*brahmacārin*) is sleeping according to his own will and thus cause him to be overtaken [by dawn], or if the sun should set while he is lying down due to his lack of understanding of the meaning of the scriptures, then, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) of Gautama—"reciting the Sāvitrī"—he shall not eat for the day while reciting the Sāvitrī. This expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is mentioned here separately from the main context for the sake of brevity; for if it were placed there, the specific mention of the "religious student" would have had to be repeated. (2.220)
For he who sleeps while the sun is setting upon him, or while it is rising, and fails to perform the penance, shall be joined with great sin. (2.221)

Regarding this, there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda): "For he is overtaken by the sun. Being overtaken by the sun—that is, being asleep when the sun sets—means that one who does not perform the penance just mentioned would be possessed of great sin. (2.221)
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend to both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule. (2.222)

Since this is so, therefore [the text says] "having sipped water" (ācamya). Being self-restrained, pure, composed, and with senses controlled, having touched water in a clean place and performing the recitation (japa) according to the procedure prescribed for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana)—namely, "one should attend both twilights as long as one lives"—this is a restatement of the twilight worship in connection with the expiation for the omission of the twilight rites. The requirements of being self-restrained, composed, and in a clean place are for the purpose of a mandatory injunction (vidhi). (2.222)
If a woman or a person of lower birth should perform any virtuous deed, one should practice all of that with diligence; and whatever brings him joy, he should also adopt. (2.223)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): even if women and Śūdras practice that which is for their welfare—which, though to be described later, contradicts the scriptures—one who is disciplined and diligent should observe it after seeing it from them; and he should perform those scriptural acts, such as the recitation of prayers (*japa*), in which his mind finds satisfaction. 2.223.

Some say that the good consists of dharma and artha; others, of kāma and artha; and yet others, of dharma alone. Or again, some maintain that artha alone is the highest good; such is the established position regarding the three aims of life (trivarga). || 2.224 ||

It was stated, “One should practice what is beneficial” (*śreya ācaret*); as to what that benefit (*śreya*) is, he says: “Dharma and Artha. Some say that Dharma and Artha constitute the benefit, because they are, respectively, the causes for [attaining] the next world and this world. Others declare them to be Karma and Artha, because it is perceived through direct observation that these two alone accomplish the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Still others maintain that Dharma alone is the benefit, because it is heard in scripture that both Artha and Kāma have their root in it. Yet others assert that Artha alone is the benefit in this world, since from that alone Dharma and Kāma are accomplished. Having thus stated these various opinions, he states the established position: “But the settled view is the Trivarga. The group consisting of the three—Dharma, Artha, and Kāma—is called the benefit; this is the conclusion. For all three, when not in mutual conflict, accomplish the goals of human life. Nor is the pursuit of Kāma taught for the religious student (*brahmacārin*), because this section is intent upon defining the meaning of the term “benefit. (2.224)
The teacher, the father, the mother, and an elder brother must not be treated with disrespect, even by one who is distressed; this is especially true for a Brahmin. (2.225)

"And the teacher as well as the father": the teacher, father, mother, and elder brother must not be treated with contempt even by a Kṣatriya or others who have been oppressed; this is especially true for a Brāhmaṇa, because the performance of dharma for all others is rooted in them—lest there be an over-extension [of this rule]. (2.225)
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one’s own brother is the embodiment of oneself. (2.226)

"The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman. This designation of [the teacher] as having the body of Brahmā and so forth is based on the commonality of residing in the same womb as the source for the production of instruction in Brahman; it serves as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the injunction under discussion. Brahmā and Prajāpati are the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and Hiraṇyagarbha, who is his uterine brother. (2.226)
The suffering that parents endure for the sake of the birth of human beings cannot be repaid, even in a hundred years. (2.227)

When conception occurs, immediately thereafter, parents experience incessantly the suffering pertaining to their offspring; even by performing services for hundreds of years, it is impossible to attain freedom from that debt, let alone through a single lifetime. (2.227)
One should always perform what is pleasing to those devoted to austerity and to the teacher; for when these three are satisfied, all austerity is fully accomplished. (2.228)

Therefore, regarding the phrase "constantly devoted to austerity": one should do what is pleasing to one's mother, father, and teacher for as long as one lives. And that austerity must not be neglected through attachment to other things or by disregarding their pleasure. For it is only when they are satisfied that the entire fruit of austerity is fully attained.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them. (2.229)

Since this is so, therefore [the text says] "of them. The service of these parents and others is declared by Manu and other authorities to be a penance superior to all other penances. And thus, permitted by them, one should not perform any other religious duty except for those that are obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika). (2.229)
For these three worlds are indeed those three stages of life;
they are indeed the three Vedas, and they are said to be the three sacred fires. (2.230)

"Because they are those": since service to them is the cause for attaining the worlds of earth, the intermediate space, and the world of Brahmā, they are called "those three worlds. And thus, because service to them yields a fruit equal to that of the three stages of life other than studentship (*brahmacarya*), they alone are "the three stages of life. Because attendance upon them yields a fruit equal to the recitation of the three Vedas, they alone are "the three Vedas. Because propitiation of them yields a fruit equal to rites accomplished by means of the sacred fires, they alone are "the three fires.
