Thus it was stated by Manu and others; this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the preceding injunction. (2.230)
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher, however, is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable.

"The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire. From the Gārhapatya fire comes the production of the oblations, and from this father [comes the birth of the son]. And the Dakṣiṇāgni has the status of a subordinate (guṇatva), while the mother is dependent upon the father. The Āhavanīya fire possesses primacy because it effects the completion of the sacrifice; likewise, the teacher possesses primacy because he accomplishes all human goals. This designation of these [three] as "fires" is based on some commonality. And the triad of fires assists them for the sake of protection, as if being more weighty. This too is an explanatory passage (arthavāda). 2.231.
Being heedful in these three, a householder may conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god. (2.232)

Regarding the word "in the three": by being unerring in service toward these three, the householder shall conquer the three worlds to be described hereafter and take possession of them through his sovereignty. Consequently, by means of his own body, endowed with splendor like the blazing sun and other deities, he dwells happily in the heavenly world. The term "householder" is used to show that this duty pertains even to the householder. (2.232)
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world; and by service to one's teacher, one likewise reaches the world of Brahmā. (2.233)
Regarding the word "this": through service to one's mother, father, and teacher, one attains the worlds of the earth, the intermediate space, and the world of Brahmā. 2.233.
All duties are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all his ritual actions are fruitless. (2.234)

"Everything": all religious duties (*dharma*), such as sacrifices and the like, become oriented toward yielding their fruit for him by whom his mother, father, and teacher have been honored and propitiated. However, for one by whom these have not been fully satisfied, all ritual acts such as sacrifices are fruitless; this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the injunction regarding service (*śuśrūṣā*). (2.234)
As long as those three live, he should not attend to anyone else; he should constantly perform service for them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare. (2.235)

While one's mother, father, and teacher are living, one should not practice any other duty. What then? One should always act toward them alone by way of providing present and future benefit; this is an explanatory reiteration (*arthavāda*) of the rule under discussion. The repetition of the phrase "of those three" refers to what has already been established, for the purpose of strengthening the rule at hand. (2.235)
Whatever one may do for the sake of the next world, provided it does not conflict with their interests, that very thing one should announce to them through thought, word, and deed. (2.236)

Regarding the word "to them": whatever one might perform for the sake of the next world or for the sake of sacrifice, in contradiction to their service, that very thing would become their fruit; thus, one should give to them by means of the activities of mind, speech, and body. (2.236)
For it is within these three that a man's duty reaches its completion;
this is the supreme dharma manifestly revealed, while any other is called a secondary dharma.

Regarding the word "in three": because when the mother and the others are propitiated, whatever duty such as sacrifice is to be performed by a person, all of that becomes fulfilled for him. Since this [service to them] is the direct and preeminent dharma, whereas the Agnihotra and so forth are called "secondary" (gauṇa) by Manu and others—this is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the rule under discussion. (2.237)
One who has faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a lowly person; one should learn the supreme Dharma even from an outcaste, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family. (2.238)

"Full of faith" means one endowed with faith may receive superior knowledge—the instruction on self-knowledge and so forth according to the sequence described—even from a member of a lower caste such as a Kṣatriya, and even from a Śūdra he may learn a superior dharma that is not contrary to the scriptures, whatever has been learned by him from anyone. As for what was said [in verse 2.237], "if it be a woman, or if it be a person of lower birth," that is not [the case]; for even if they teach him, he should practice by observing their performance of those acts. And he may take up a superior [woman]—one endowed with the characteristics of non-widowhood and so forth—even from a family of Kṣatriyas, potters, or others. (2.238)
Even from poison, one should take the nectar; even from a child, a well-spoken word;
even from an enemy, virtuous conduct; and even from filth, gold. (2.239)

"From poison": even from poison, one should take the nectar by means of applying elixirs (*rasāyana*) and other remedies that counteract it. By one setting out for a village or elsewhere, even a word uttered by a child should be accepted as an indicator of the successful attainment of the desired goal. Even gold fallen into impurity, though not yet refined, should be accepted. (2.239)
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, dharma, purity, eloquent speech, and various arts—these are to be accepted from all sources. (2.240)

"Women are jewels," and "crafts that are not corrupt. Here, the purpose is to mention the purity of the jewel of women, painting and other such crafts that are not corrupt; likewise, these things, when based on what is virtuous, are indeed to be accepted. 2.240.
In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
however, he must follow the teacher and serve him as long as the study continues. (2.241)

Regarding the phrase "from a non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇāt*): this refers to a time of distress (*āpad-kāla*) when there is no Brāhmaṇa teacher available; alternatively, the reading is *upātkalpa*. In that situation, study from a non-Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the religious student (*brahmacārin*). Although service (*śuśrūṣā*) is already established as part of the duty of study, its re-statement here serves to establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*): namely, that service to the teacher consists solely of following him and nothing else. Furthermore, this lasts until the Veda has been mastered, not merely during the time of recitation, because of the traditional rule (*smṛti*) in the Gṛhyasūtras stating, "having sat down facing the east. This is not the case [with a Śūdra], because there is no going [to follow him] there. Even though a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya might be more similar [to a Brāhmaṇa] than a Śūdra—due to caste status, similarity, and being twice-born—the term "non-Brāhmaṇa" here refers specifically to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, and not the Śūdra; for we see a prohibition elsewhere stating, "a Śūdra pupil and likewise a Śūdra teacher," and because of the observation that even in times of distress, one may live by the duty of a Kṣatriya, as he is the next closest [caste] after the Brāhmaṇa. Thus, it should be understood that first from a Kṣatriya, and in his absence, from a Vaiśya. Since they are designated by the word "teacher" (*guru*) here, and since only a portion of service is permitted, it is concluded that the Teacher does not intend such teaching for Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas either. How then could one who is forbidden to teach be a "teaching teacher" (*adhyāpana-guru*) or one to be served? And in this context, this [study] is for the sake of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa-artha*), whereas for these two [the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya], it would be for the sake of livelihood (*vṛtti*).
"One who, being base by birth, should live by superior occupations out of greed"—because such a transgression will be described [later]. (2.241)
A disciple desiring the unsurpassed goal should not dwell for life with a non-Brahmin teacher, nor even with a Brahmin who has not mastered the Vedas. (2.242)

Thus, regarding the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) who is about to be described, since he might live his entire life without returning home if he were to study under a non-Brāhmaṇa, the author says "not" in order to prohibit that. A lifelong student, desiring the highest goal, should not dwell for life in the house of a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher, nor even in the house of a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of proper conduct, learning, and noble lineage. (2.242)
But if he should desire to dwell permanently in the family of his teacher,
he should attend upon him with diligence until the liberation from the body.

Now, he says "yadi" (if) for the purpose of explaining the rule regarding lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*). If, however, a student (*brahmacārī*) should desire to dwell in the teacher’s house for life, then, becoming diligent, he should serve the teacher until the fall of his body; such a person is called a *naiṣṭhika*. Thus says Hārīta: "If he reaches the final goal (*niṣṭhā*). On the other hand, the other is called an *upakurvāṇaka*, because he is engaged in performing service for the sake of study. Nor should one suspect here a contradiction with scriptural injunctions such as "one should perform the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives," since this [rule on lifelong studentship] also has its root in that very scripture: "The third [type of student] is the lifelong celibate, dwelling in the teacher’s family, exhausting himself completely in the teacher’s family. (2.243)
But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes directly to the eternal abode of Brahmā. (2.244)

He states the fruit of this [practice] with the words "until the end": he who serves his teacher for as long as the body lasts goes directly—by a clear path, unobstructed by any other course—to the imperishable world of Brahmā until the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). The mention of the "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is for the sake of illustration, since all three [classes] are under discussion. (2.244)

One who knows the Dharma should not provide any service to the teacher beforehand; however, when about to bathe and having been commanded by the teacher, he should procure what is required for the teacher according to his ability. (2.245)

"Not previously" means as follows: A student who has not yet acquired the Veda, having been instructed by his teacher that "I will not teach you unless you bring wealth," should not give anything at all to the teacher, for that would entail the fault of being a paid teacher (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*). For this very reason, the author says "one who knows the Dharma. This prohibition applies when [the gift] is not preceded by a sale, because it has been stated [elsewhere]: "Where neither Dharma nor Artha exist... Likewise, Āpastamba says: "When one feeds the teacher and eats the remaining food, that is indeed an excellent oblation; when he offers other substances according to what is available, or even [just] the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), this is the sacrifice of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), performed with constant devotion. However, when desiring to perform the ritual bath (*snāna*) at the time of returning home (*samāvartana*), if he is instructed by the teacher, "Bring this object for me," he must certainly bring the teacher's object according to his ability, since at that time the possibility of being a paid teacher does not arise. (2.245)
Bringing satisfaction to his guru, he may offer a field, gold, a cow, a horse, or at least an umbrella and sandals; or grain, garments, or even vegetables. (2.246)

Regarding the term "field": thus, because the purpose is to generate affection, the mention of land and so forth is for the sake of illustration; ultimately, if anything at all should be produced, it would be a parasol and sandals. 2.246.

But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who is endowed with good qualities, or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, just as toward the teacher himself. (2.247)

The Teacher says "the teacher" in order to prescribe the rule for the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika): "When the teacher has died, one should perform service toward the teacher's son, wife, or sapinda relatives as toward the teacher himself; in the absence of each preceding one, one should serve each succeeding one. (2.248)
When these are not available, one who maintains a steady posture while standing, sitting, or walking, and practices service to the sacred fire, shall perfect his own body. (2.248)

"Even when these are absent" means that if the teacher’s sons and others are not present, one should exhaust one's own body by performing the fire-ritual with devotion—rising, sitting, and moving about—while relying on the fixed rules regarding time. 2.248.
The Brahmin who thus practices the vow of celibacy without violation goes to the highest station and is not born here again. || 2.249 ||

"Thus. Although it has already been stated that "until the completion of the body," this is reiterated for the purpose of summarizing and prescribing the non-falling away from the fruit of the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). He who practices the lifelong studenthood (*brahmacarya*) without faltering in the manner described goes to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) and is not born again in the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). At the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), he is united with Brahman. The mention of the "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is for the sake of illustration, since all three [classes] are under discussion. (2.249)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Rules for the Stage of Studentship," in the commentary on Manu composed by Govindarāja, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mādhava, which follows the intention of the venerable Manu.
The third chapter:
The vow concerning the three Vedas consists of practicing [service] under a guru for thirty-six years; or half of that, or a quarter, or even until they have been mastered. (3.1)

Regarding the student (*upakurvāṇaka-brahmacārin*) who is entitled to enter the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), since there is a question as to how long he must remain in celibacy before entering the householder stage, the author says: "lasting thirty-six years. This means that while residing in the teacher's house, one should observe for thirty-six years the vow—which is a collection of restrictive rules—concerning the three Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma, twelve years for each branch (*śākhā*). Alternatively, half of that is eighteen years, with six years for each branch; or a quarter, which is nine years, with three years for each branch. Or rather, he should observe it for whatever length of time it takes to master the Vedas, whether more or less than the limit stated by Kātyāyana. This option depends on the desired fruit of the observance, according to the Vedic revelation: "That which is studied with fixed observance becomes more powerful (*vīryavattara*)."
Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, two of them, or even one— in the proper order,
and having remained firm in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.

"Regarding the Vedas": having studied the three branches, two, or even one, in the sequence beginning with his own branch, and according to the established order of the succession between the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, he—having maintained unbroken celibacy and not having engaged in sexual union with a woman—enters the state of a householder. 3.2.
One should first honor with a cow that son who is well-known for his own duty, who inherits the father’s Vedic legacy, and who sits upon the couch wearing a garland.

Regarding the word *tam*: he who has completed his period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) is one whose character has become renowned through the persistence of the religious duties undertaken during that stage of life. According to the Vedic text, "Therefore, they say a son who is well-instructed is worthy of the world," the father is the primary candidate for this role. In the absence of a father, the teacher (*ācārya*) should honor him—once he has mastered the Vedas and been adorned with garlands and other ornaments, seated upon a costly couch—with the ritual known as *madhuparka*, which uses a cow as its means and whose nature is described in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. This is performed prior to the formal assumption of the status of a householder (*gārhapatha*). It is called *dāya* because it is given; since the Veda itself is the gift, it is the "Vedic gift" (*brahmadāya*), and he who takes that is the "receiver of the Vedic gift" (*brahmadāyahara*). (3.3)
Having bathed and returned home according to the prescribed rule with the permission of his teacher,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious characteristics.

"By the guru": permitted by his guru, the twice-born man, having performed the rites known as the ritual bath (*snāna*) and the return home (*samāvartana*) according to their nature as prescribed in the *Gṛhya* scriptures and without transgressing the rules of the *Gṛhya-śāstra*, should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious characteristics. (3.4)
A woman who is not a sapinda of the mother and not of the same gotra as the father is recommended for marriage among the twice-born for sexual union. (3.5)

Regarding the term *asapiṇḍā*: the author will also state later that "sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with the seventh person" (MDh 5.60). Therefore, for the twice-born, a woman who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother—meaning she is not born from the lineage of the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) or the great-grandfather (*pramātāmaha*)—and who is born from the lineage of the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*) or the great-grandmother (*pramātāmahī*), and who is not of the same *gotra* as the father; and by the force of the word "and," she who is not born from the lineage of the paternal aunts (*pitṛṣvasṛ*) and so forth, who are *sapiṇḍas*—such a woman is to be employed in marriage rites, such as sexual union and the like. (3.5)
Even if they are prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain—one should avoid these ten types of families when forming a marriage alliance. (3.6)

Regarding the term "great": one should avoid these ten families that are about to be described, even if they are eminent. Likewise, for the sake of avoiding the transmission of their character, diseases, and birth defects to one's own offspring, and by virtue of the injunctions of the scriptures, one should avoid marriage alliances with those who are prosperous in cattle, goats, sheep, buffaloes, and grain, in order to avoid invisible faults. (3.6)

Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic desire, those with hairy anal folds, and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy—[these should be avoided]. (3.7)

"Of lowly conduct" means: one should avoid families that are devoid of sacrifices and other rites, those consisting only of women, those lacking Vedic knowledge, those characterized by excessive and chronic *tomā* (a type of skin disease), those afflicted with diseases known as *ārśas* (hemorrhoids) and the like, and those related to those suffering from consumption (*rājayakṣman*), weak digestion (*mandāgni*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), vitiligo (*śvitrin*), or leprosy (*kuṣṭhin*). (3.7)
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.

"One should not marry" means: one should not take as a wife a girl who is tawny, has six fingers or more, is afflicted by disease, is possessed by a spirit, lacks body hair, is talkative, or is reddish-brown in complexion. (3.8)

One should not marry a girl whose name is that of a lunar mansion, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one with a terrifying name. (3.9)
"No," [he replied]. "One should not marry a girl whose name is that of a constellation, a tree, a river, a barbarian, a mountain, a bird, a snake, a slave, or something terrifying.

One should marry a woman whose limbs are free from defects, who has an auspicious name, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft. (3.10)

"Having unimpaired limbs" means: one should marry a maiden whose limbs are complete, whose name is not inauspicious, whose gait is as graceful as that of a royal swan or an elephant, whose body hair, hair on the head, and teeth are not excessively thick, and whose limbs are tender. This statement regarding the injunctions and prohibitions is for the sake of prosperity when marrying a maiden who is free from defects and endowed with good qualities. (3.10)
But a wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother and whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter). (3.11)

Regarding the phrase "of whom": one should not marry a girl out of the mistaken notion that she is a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) based on the mere intention expressed by the rule of the *putrikā* stated by Manu and Gautama: "Whatever offspring she may have shall be mine for the sake of the ancestral oblation (*svadhākara*). For even if her father is known to be without a brother, she might sometimes have been made a *putrikā* by her father due to the absence of a son. Or, even if there is a well-known fact that she has brothers, one should not marry her out of the mistaken notion that she is a *putrikā* if her progenitor is not specifically known, thinking, "She was produced by this man, but not [as his own son]. For when the progenitor is correctly known, there is a possibility of her being a *putrikā* even if she has brothers from a different father, since brotherhood is established for those who share the same mother; thus, both [the girl and the boy] are qualified by this [prohibition]. Furthermore, a *putrikā* does not possess the full status of a wife, precisely because of this prohibition. This has been explained by the author of the *Nirukta*: "Like one without a brother, she goes toward the ancestors; facing them, she exists for the act of lineage-continuation, namely, for the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*)."

In this context, regarding those injunctions and prohibitions for which there is no connection with visible benefits or defects—as in the case of "she who is not a sapinda of the mother"—if such a rule is transgressed, she does not become a wife, because the word *bhāryā* (wife) is a term denoting a sacramental status (*saṃskāra-śabda*), like the term *āhavanīya* (the consecrated fire). On the other hand, regarding those where the statement of an injunction or prohibition is based on the observation of visible benefits or defects—as in the case of "one whose rites are deficient"—there is no loss of wifehood upon such transgression; rather, because it is merely a breach of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is only the requirement of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Furthermore, that which begins with "nor one named after a constellation, a tree, or a river" (MDh 3.9) and so forth, also follows the same rules of inclusion and exclusion as the preceding section on injunctions and prohibitions, because it is situated within that very context. Thus, after Manu has stated the prohibition regarding *sapiṇḍas* and others, he introduces a separate treatment beginning with "even if they possess great prosperity" (MDh 3.6), and within that same section, he mentions "one whose rites are deficient" and so forth, as well as "nor one named after a constellation, a tree," and so on.
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] may be taken in successive order of inferiority. (3.12)

Regarding the term *savarṇā*: it has been stated that for the twice-born, at the initial taking of the hand, a woman of the same caste (*samānajātīyā*) is appropriate. However, for those who proceed to the act of marriage out of desire, these [wives] mentioned below shall be the best according to the order of castes. (3.12)

A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as a wife for a Śūdra; she and one of his own [caste] are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and one of his own for a Kṣatriya; and those three and one of his own for a Brāhmaṇa. (3.13)

Regarding the term *śūdrā*: for a Śūdra, only a Śūdra woman becomes his wife; he may not have women of higher or lower castes. For a Vaiśya, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman are prescribed by Manu and others as wives. For a Kṣatriya, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra woman are wives. For a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇī, a Vaiśyā, and a Kṣatriyā are wives. According to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha, "Some [allow] even a Śūdra woman, excluding the sacred formulas (*mantra*)," she becomes the wife of these twice-born men without the recitation of the *mantras*. (3.13)
For it is taught that, even in times of distress, a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, regardless of the circumstances. (3.14)

"No," [says the opponent]. In no traditional narrative (itihāsa) is a Śūdra woman described as the wife of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who, for the sake of entering the householder stage, cannot obtain a wife of their own caste. Thus, because of the prohibition of a Śūdra wife, it is understood that when a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya fails to find a wife of their own caste, there is marriage with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman respectively. Furthermore, since the activity of the Kṣatriya class is observed in the case of Dhanañjaya and others, first the Brāhmaṇa marries a Kṣatriya woman; in her absence, he marries a Vaiśya woman. (3.14)
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth quickly lead their own lineages, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras. (3.15)

Regarding this, there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda): "the woman of a low-born caste. Because of the mention of "Śūdra-hood," it is understood that when twice-born men—due to their lack of knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures—marry a Śūdra woman of low birth, they cause their lineages—their descendants and progeny extending over a long period of time through sons, grandsons, and so forth—to fall into the state of Śūdras, since only such [offspring] are produced therein. From the use of the term "twice-born" here, it is inferred that for a Vaiśya as well, who has not performed a marriage with a woman of his own class, there is a prohibition against marrying a Śūdra woman. Furthermore, for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, there is an even greater transgression [for such an act], because of the force of the initial formulation of the prohibition. (3.15)
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by the offspring of that son. (3.16)

They state other opinions as follows: "The one who marries a Śūdra woman" (śūdrāvedī)—this is the view of Atri and of Gautama, the son of Utathya, that he who takes a Śūdra wife becomes an outcast (patita). This is an inference of a prohibition based on censure, for censure does not arise without cause; according to their opinion, this is an absolute prohibition against marrying a Śūdra woman. The opinion of Śaunaka, however, is that one falls [from caste] by the birth of a son from a Śūdra woman; therefore, according to his view, one may approach her during the period favorable for conception (ṛtu). The opinion of Bhṛgu, moreover, is that one falls solely through having offspring from a Śūdra woman; and thus, according to his position, one who has already produced offspring with the other wives may approach the Śūdra wife during her season. (3.16)
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood. (3.17)

Regarding the phrase "a Śūdra woman": the statement that "having approached a Śūdra woman, a Brāhmaṇa goes to hell" is an absolute prohibition (*atyantapratiṣedha*). The remainder is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). The statement that "by procreating a son on a Śūdra woman, he falls from Brāhmaṇahood itself" is an *arthavāda* intended to prohibit the procreation of a son. Thus, in this context, because of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," the absolute prohibition and the prohibition of procreation apply specifically to the Brāhmaṇa class. (3.17)
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are centered primarily on that [wealth], neither the ancestors nor the gods eat; he does not go to heaven. (3.18)

Regarding the phrase "rites for the gods, the ancestors, and guests": the author will state a prohibition [in MDh 9.87]: "But he who, out of delusion, causes those rites to be performed by another woman while his own wife of the same caste is present. Therefore, even when a wife of the same caste is not present, if sacrifices, *śrāddhas*, and gifts to guests are performed by a *śūdra* woman, the ancestors and the gods do not partake of that *havya* and *kavya*. Nor does that householder attain heaven by virtue of that hospitality. (3.18)
For one who has drunk the saliva of a Vṛṣalī, who has been afflicted by her breath,
and who has even begotten a child upon her, no atonement is prescribed.

Regarding the phrase "of one who has drunk the saliva of a *vṛṣalī*": for one who has been kissed by a Śūdra woman, who has been rendered impure by her breath while sharing the same bed or seat, and who has begotten offspring upon her—no purification whatsoever is prescribed. Thus, the first and second halves of the verse constitute an absolute prohibition; according to the opinion of Bhṛgu, they are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*). (3.19)
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women among all four social classes, which lead to welfare or harm both in this world and after death. (3.20)

"Of the four": hear in brief these marriages—which are causes for obtaining a wife—that pertain to some beneficial and harmful matters in both this world and the next, belonging to all four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as they are about to be described. (3.20)
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura; the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest. (3.21)

Regarding the term "brāhma": this designation of these [mantras] as "brāhma" and so forth is intended to convey praise or censure; it does not, however, imply that they possess an exclusive connection with deities such as Brahmā. (3.21)
I shall declare to you all that which pertains to each class according to its dharma, as well as the virtues and faults of each, and the merits and demerits regarding their offspring.

"Those which are the laws of each"—meaning those marriages which do not deviate from the laws of a particular caste, and whatever virtues and defects belong to a marriage that bestow desired or undesired fruits upon the bridegroom, as well as the virtues and defects inherent in the offspring born of specific marriages—all that I shall declare to you. (3.22)
One should know that for a Brahmin there are six [forms of marriage] in order, and for a Kṣatriya four of the lower ones;
for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, however, one should know those same [four] as being lawful and not Rākṣasa.

"Six": one should know that these six, established in their sequence from the beginning—the first four for a Brahmin and a Kṣatriya, and those same ones excluding the Rākṣasa for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra—are not contrary to dharma. || 3.23 ||
The wise know that the first four [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone for a Kṣatriya; and the Āsura for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. (3.24)

"Four": the authors of the *Smṛtyarthasamuccaya* consider the first four to be recommended for a Brāhmaṇa, the one *Rākṣasa* for a Kṣatriya, and the *Āsura* for both Vaiśyas and Śūdras. Here, since the *Arṣa* and other [marriages] previously prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa and others are excluded in this context, they apply optionally when the obligatory ones are impossible; this should be understood likewise in subsequent cases as well. (3.24)
Of these five, three are considered lawful and two unlawful in this world;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.

Regarding the phrase "of the five": here, because the Paiśāca form is excluded, the five beginning with the Prājāpatya are understood. Among these five, beginning with the Prājāpatya, three are not deviating from dharma; however, two—the Paiśāca and the Āsura—are recorded in this scripture as unrighteous (*adharmya*). Those two must not be performed even in times of distress. (3.25)
Whether performed separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa—are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya. (3.26)

Regarding the word "separately" (*pṛthak*): it was previously established that the two forms of marriage called Gāndharva and Rākṣasa, which were mentioned before, are each individually unrighteous for a Kṣatriya. By the statement "those two are remembered as righteous when mixed," it is now declared that they are righteous when combined. In that case, when a maiden, preceded by mutual passion, brings herself away from her suitor through an agreement [of love] or by means of battle and the like, then the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa forms become mixed. (3.26)
Having clothed and honored her himself, and having invited one who is endowed with learning and virtue, the giving away of the daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite. (3.27)

"Having clothed her and honored her"—having clothed the maiden with special garments and honored her with ornaments and the like, one brings a bridegroom who possesses learning and good conduct without solicitation; the giving of the maiden to him is recorded by Manu and others as the Brāhma marriage. (3.27)
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs the ritual,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) dharma.

Regarding the term "yajña": when a sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma has commenced, the officiating priests proceed with the rite; Manu and others call that marriage in which the giving away of the maiden is performed after she has been adorned, the *daiva* form of marriage. (3.28)
Having accepted one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the rule, the giving of the daughter in accordance with the prescribed rite is called the Ārṣa form of marriage. (3.29)

"One [cow]" means: having received one or two cows as a boon according to dharma, on account of a duty that must necessarily be performed such as a sacrifice, the giving of a daughter in accordance with the scriptures is called the Ārṣa marriage (3.29).
Having addressed the words, "May you both practice dharma together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite. (3.30)
"With you"—having spoken these words at the time of giving her away, "may you two perform your duty together," the gift of the maiden preceded by such worship is known as the Prājāpatya rite. (3.30)
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability, the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma. (3.31)

"From the kinsmen": having given wealth according to one's ability to the girl and to her kinsmen, that which is the giving away of the girl, the taking, or the acceptance by her own will—without the [prescribed] rules regarding the Ṛṣis, the amount of wealth, or the caste—is called the Āsura marriage (3.31).
The mutual union of the maiden and the bridegroom through desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it is carnal and arises from passion. (3.32)

Regarding the term *icchayā* (by mutual desire): that union consisting of sexual intercourse arising from the mutual passion between a maiden and her suitor is to be understood as the *Gāndharva* marriage, which is conducive to sexual union and caused by desire. In this case, in the *Gāndharva* and other such marriages, the act of approaching (*upagamana*) itself is primary; this is indicated by the word *tu* (but/however). Nor does this imply a loss of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), because of the statement: "The mantras for taking the hand are established as applicable when [the woman] is still a maiden. This is because sacraments are seen in the definitions of the *sahoḍha*, *kānīna*, and *paunarbhava* sons provided by Manu and Yājñavalkya, such as: "She who is consecrated while pregnant," "The son born of a maiden from her husband," and "Whether she be unconsecrated or already consecrated, she who is consecrated again is a *punarbhū*. Furthermore, in *Gāndharva* and other marriages, the nuptial rite must still be performed, according to the traditional teaching of Devala: "And it should be performed by the three castes with the agreement of the parties, having fire as witness. Likewise:
For those marriages which are Gāndharva, Āsura, Paiśāca, or Rākṣasa,
the fire-oblation is prescribed to be performed after the wedding has first taken place.

This is because of the observation in the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*, and because in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, [the act] is treated like the primary act of approaching [a wife]. And thus, the rule beginning with “the mantras of the taking of the hand” applies to the case of a maiden who has already been enjoyed by another man, based on such statements as “the marriage rite must be performed again. Consequently, for the twice-born (*dvijāti*), a woman who has not undergone the sacramental rites after the act of intercourse does not become a wife; however, for a Śūdra, she certainly does become one, because of the mention of “by the three castes” and because the right to inherit the estate is seen for a son born in such a manner. (3.32)
Having killed, maimed, or wounded [the guardians], and having forcibly carried off a maiden from her home while she cries out and weeps—this is called the Rākṣasa rite. (3.33)

"Having slain" means: having struck down the girl's kinsmen, having crushed them, having cut them down, or having done so without crushing them; having inflicted the amputation of limbs and the like, and having broken through walls and such—when one carries off a maiden from her home while she cries out, "Alas, mother! Alas, father! I am being abducted, helpless!", with her eyes clouded by tears—that too is the abduction of a maiden, the Rākṣasa form of marriage. (3.33)
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged, that most wicked of marriages is known as the Paiśāca, the lowest of all. (3.34)

"Sleeping" means one who is overcome by sleep or intoxicated, whose restraint of character has been destroyed; when one approaches her in a secluded place during such a marriage, that is a cause of sin. Among marriages, this eighth type is known as the Paiśāca. (3.34)
For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is distinguished as the best;
for the other castes, however, it occurs through mutual desire.

"The giving of a daughter to the twice-born is praised as being with water alone"—this means that for Brāhmaṇas, the giving of a daughter is said to be most excellent only when preceded by the offering of water. However, for Kṣatriyas and the others, on the other hand, the giving is desired even by mere word, even without water, provided there is mutual consent. (3.35)
O Brahmins, listen as I correctly proclaim all those virtues which Manu has declared for each of these forms of marriage. (3.36)
"Ya iti" (Regarding "who"): O Brahmins, listen as I duly relate all that fruit of each marriage among these—beginning with marriage—which has been declared by Manu. || 3.36 ||
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who has performed meritorious deeds liberates ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin. (3.37)

"Ten ancestors and ten descendants"—this refers to the son born of a *brāhma* marriage. If he is a performer of good deeds, then he liberates twenty-one individuals from sin: ten preceding ancestors such as his father, ten subsequent descendants such as his sons, and himself as the twenty-first. Nor should one raise the objection here that "the non-performance [of rites] does not cause the destruction of what has been done," for this matter is established by direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), just like the *śrāddha* and other rites. Furthermore, the liberation of these ancestors and descendants occurs through the mere birth of the virtuous son, even though they themselves have not yet been liberated at that time because they have not yet ceased to exist. (3.37)
The son born of a maiden (daivodāja) produces seven generations of descendants, both preceding and following him;
the son born of a woman married according to the ṛṣi-rite (ārṣodāja) produces three; and the son born of a woman married with the kāya-rite (kāyodāja) produces six.

Regarding the term *daivoḍhāja*: a son born of the *daiva* marriage rite liberates seven ancestors, beginning with the father, and seven descendants, beginning with the son, from sin. A son born of the *ārṣa* marriage rite liberates three descendants, beginning with the son, and three ancestors, beginning with the father. Likewise, a son born of a woman married by the *prājāpatya* rite liberates six descendants, beginning with the son, and six ancestors, beginning with the father. (3.38)
In the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma rite, in their proper order, sons who possess Vedic splendor and are esteemed by the learned are born. (3.39)
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned, possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years. (3.40)

"In the Brāhma and other [forms of marriage]" means: "endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue. In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, which are established in their respective order, sons are born who are endowed with the splendor resulting from excellence in study and so forth; who possess beauty dear to the virtuous, characterized by the qualities described in the twelfth chapter; who are endowed with the auspicious virtues of compassion and the like; who are wealthy, famous, and performers of enjoyments such as garlands and ointments; and they live for a hundred years. (3.39–40)
But from the remaining improper marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of the Veda and dharma are born. (3.41)

Regarding the phrase "in others": in the remaining defective marriages, such as the Āsura and so forth—other than the four beginning with the Brāhma—sons are born who perform cruel deeds, speak untruths, and harbor hatred toward the Vedas, sacrifices, and other sacred rites. (3.41)
Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they become blameworthy among men. Therefore, one should avoid those who are blameworthy. (3.42)

"By blameless [means]" means by marriages that are not censured, which are the causes for obtaining a wife; through such [marriages], the offspring of men become blameless, whereas through censured ones they become censured. Therefore, one should avoid those who are censurable; one should not perform them. (3.42)
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste; this following rule is to be known for the marriage rite with women of different castes. (3.43)

Regarding the phrase "the sacrament of taking the hand": the sacrament consisting of grasping the hand is prescribed by the *Gṛhya* texts for women of the same caste who are being taken in marriage. However, when women of a different caste are being led away in the rite of marriage, this procedure about to be described should be understood to take the place of "taking the hand. (3.43)
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden, and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste. (3.44)

Regarding the arrow (*śara*): in the case of a marriage with a Kṣatriya woman, at the place where the hand is taken, the edge of the arrow held by the Brāhmaṇa’s hand must be grasped during the wedding of a Brāhmaṇa. And in the case of a Vaiśya woman, in the wedding of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, the iron-tipped end of a sickle or similar implement held by the hands of the Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya must be grasped. Furthermore, in the wedding of a twice-born man with a Śūdra woman, the hem of the garment appropriate for that particular season must be grasped. (3.44)

He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may go to her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days. (3.45)

"Approaching her during the season": *ṛtu* refers to that state of women in which they are capable of conception. During that time, a man who has not yet fathered a son should approach his wife as a matter of rule, because it is heard in scripture that there is fault in failing to do so. And thus Parāśara says:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; of this there is no doubt."

Furthermore, the Vedic text—"One is born burdened with three debts: to the gods by sacrifice, to the ancestors by progeny, and to the seers by the study of the Vedas"—is the source for this [rule], since it is improper to postulate another source when such a one exists. Accordingly, the Teacher will reveal its basis in this Vedic text through the statement, "He who desires a son should enter [into union]. Thus, because it is rooted in this [Veda], it is determined to be a restrictive rule (*niyama*). However, for one who already has a son, there is no such restriction, because the injunction has fulfilled its purpose with the birth of a single son. This is seen from the passage, "But those born of desire," and from the text, "One should neither give nor receive a single son, for he is for the sake of the lineage of the ancestors. As for the praise of many offspring in the verse, "Place ten sons in her," how could that number of ten be restricted if one must approach his wife during her fertile period even after having a son? Therefore, this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), and not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) intended to prohibit intercourse outside the fertile period.

What, then, is the specific distinction between these two, namely *niyama* (restriction) and *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification)? In this context, a *vidhi* that brings about what has not yet been obtained is called *niyama*. They say it is a "partial obtainment," as in the case of the injunction: "One should sacrifice on level ground" (*same yajeta*). For here, from the very injunction of the sacrifice such as "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*), the obtainment of the level ground—which serves as the locus for the sacrifice—is already present as a partial possibility; this is because a sacrifice cannot logically occur without a locus, and thus this statement remains neutral (*udāste*) toward one who intends to sacrifice on level ground, since he is already spontaneously engaged in it. However, for one intending to sacrifice on uneven ground, when the level ground is not otherwise obtained, this statement becomes purposeful by enjoining the meaning of "levelness. And thus, the Vedic text itself, which is the fruit of the injunction, constitutes the *niyama*.

Others, however, say that the restatement of what is already established serves to establish a restriction (*niyama*), such as: "One should protect oneself from everything. In cases where [an action] is established both here and elsewhere, there occurs an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). For example: "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten. Here, because there is a simultaneous possibility of eating both the rabbit and others due to the impulse of the desire to eat, the others are exclusively specified by the rule that they are not to be eaten. Although exclusive specification is beset by the defects of abandoning its own primary meaning (*svārthahāni*), assuming a secondary meaning (*parārthakalpanā*), and subverting what is already established (*prāptabādha*), nevertheless, since the meaninglessness of the sentence would otherwise result in either case, this very method is resorted to as the better option. Abandoning one's own meaning (*svārthahāni*) means the relinquishing of the injunctive sense even when there is an audible hearing of a word expressing an injunction. In that context, there is the assumption of a prohibition regarding that which was the object of comprehension of the preceding sentence. And the subversion of what is already established (*prāptabādha*) consists in the subversion of the eating of five-nailed animals other than those five, which was prompted by the impulse of the desire to eat.

Thus, since approaching [one's wife] is established as a duty both during the fertile season (*ṛtu*) and outside of it, although a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)—namely, "one should not approach her outside the season"—might not strictly apply because there is no possibility of its being optional, nevertheless, because the hearing of a fault (*doṣa*) for non-approach is recorded, it is logical that this is indeed for the purpose of a restriction (*niyama*). Furthermore, one should always be content with one's own wife and should not approach another woman; thus, while approaching during the season is already established by the general rule of approaching one's wife, this is a restrictive exclusion regarding such approach, excluding the new moon day and other festival days (*parvan*). Even during the season, one who protects his wife and desires progeny should approach her as a matter of rule even without a desire for offspring, out of a desire for sexual union with her. As for what will be stated later, "the new moon day and the eighth" (4.128), etc., that is for the purpose of prohibiting approach on festival days when approach might otherwise be established by the rule "one should approach during the fertile season. He will state this further in the verse beginning "likewise, not outside the season" (3.47). 3.45.
The natural menstrual period of women is said to consist of sixteen nights, together with the four other days that are censured by the virtuous. (3.46)

Regarding the *ṛtu*: together with the four days censured by the noble-born, the sequence of the women’s fertile period (*ṛtu*), produced by factors such as health and so forth, consists of sixteen days and nights. (3.46)
Of these, the first four, as well as the censured eleventh and the thirteenth, are excluded; the remaining ten nights are commended. (3.47)

Regarding the phrase "of these": furthermore, among those sixteen nights, the first four starting from the onset of menstruation, as well as the eleventh and thirteenth, are censured; therefore, one should not approach them. The remaining ten nights would be recommended for approaching. (3.47)
Sons are born from women on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one who desires a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night. (3.48)

Regarding the phrase "on even nights": sons are born to one who approaches [his wife] on even nights—namely, the sixth, eighth, and so forth; daughters are born on odd nights—the seventh, ninth, and so forth. Therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during the fertile period (ṛtukāla) on even nights, because the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) becomes diminished on those nights. Thus says the Āyurveda: "On even nights the menstrual flow becomes diminished, and on odd nights it does not; therefore, the birth of a son or a daughter occurs accordingly. (3.48)
A male is born when the male seed is in excess; a female when that of the female is in excess.
When they are equal, there is a non-male (a hermaphrodite), or both a male and a female; when they are diminished or scant, the opposite occurs.

Regarding the term "male" (*pumān*): when the male seed is predominant, even on uneven nights, a male child is born who may have the appearance of a woman, be weak, or be deficient in limbs, because this is stated in Āyurveda itself. When the female seed is predominant, however, even on even nights, a female child is born who may have the appearance of a man, or be weak, or be deficient in limbs, according to the view of Āyurveda. When the seeds of both male and female are equal, a neuter (*napuṃsaka*) is born, whether on even or uneven nights. (3.49)
Avoiding women on the eight censured nights and the other [inauspicious] nights, he remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) he inhabits. (3.50)

On the six censurable nights and on any other eight nights, he who avoids women in due order and approaches her only when two nights remain—even while dwelling in another stage of life (*āśrama*)—remains a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). There is no fault of violating celibacy for him; thus, for one whose son has died or who is situated in another stage of life, approaching her for two nights by his own will for the sake of a son is justified, since it was introduced [in the text] with the words, "even while living in whatever stage of life, one desiring a son may approach her," and because the son is heard in scripture to be of great benefit. As for those who say this is improper because absolute celibacy is taught for other stages of life—that is incorrect, because even this [case] falls within the scope of the sacred scriptures. (3.50)
A wise father of a maiden should not accept even the slightest bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring. (3.51)

"No," [it is said]. The father of a maiden, knowing the fault in accepting wealth, should not accept even the slightest amount of wealth in the form of a barter for giving away his daughter; for by accepting it out of greed, he would become a seller of his offspring. (3.51)
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property—whether it be her vehicles or her clothing—those sinners go to a downward state. (3.52)

Regarding "women's property": gold, female slaves, vehicles, and clothing belonging to daughters, sisters, or female relatives are enjoyed by the father and others; therefore, those sinful men, performing such acts, go to hell. This is an incidental prohibition against living off women's property. (3.52)
Regarding the rite of the seers (ārṣa), some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price; but that is surely false.
Whether it be small or great, even so, it remains nothing other than a sale. (3.53)

Regarding the term *ārṣa*: some teachers have stated that in the *ārṣa* form of marriage, a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) should be received from the groom as a bride-price (*śulka*). However, that is untrue; for whether it be small because it is accomplished with little wealth, or great because it is accomplished with great value, in every case it remains a sale. Thus, the statement "one pair of cattle" is understood to be the opinion of others (the *paramata*). 3.53.
When the kinsmen do not take a fee for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure benevolence. (3.54)

Regarding the phrase "yāsām" (of whom): when, for certain maidens, their fathers and others do not give a gift for their own sake to the bridegroom, but rather accept what is given for the sake of the maiden by well-disposed husbands and others as a formal offering (*arpaṇa*), that is not a sale. What then? That is an act of worship; it is merely an expression of compassion toward the maidens, entirely devoid of the taint of sale.
These women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant prosperity for them. (3.55)
"By the fathers": by fathers, brothers, and husbands who desire to attain great prosperity, women should be honored and adorned. (3.55)
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all rituals there become fruitless. (3.56)

Regarding the phrase "wherein": in whatever family women are honored by the father and others, there the deities are pleased. On the other hand, where these women are not honored, all ritual acts such as sacrifices become fruitless due to the absence of the deities' favor. (3.56)
Where female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes; but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever. (3.57)

Regarding the phrase "they grieve": that family in which the newly married daughter, daughter-in-law, and others become sorrowful perishes very quickly; however, that family where these women do not suffer from grief prospers at all times. (3.57)
Those households which female relatives, when unhonored, curse, perish on all sides as if struck by a magical spell (kṛtyā). || 3.58 ||

Regarding the word "jāmayaḥ": those houses which are not honored by newly-wedded daughters-in-law, daughters, and others immediately bring curses upon them; they perish with total destruction, like those afflicted by specific malevolent spells (*abhicāra*). || 3.58 ||
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always worship these women with ornaments, clothing, and food, constantly during ceremonies and festivals. (3.59)

Since this is so, therefore these [goddesses] should always be worshipped by men desiring prosperity, both during communal festivals and at celebrations. For that reason, they should be constantly honored with ornaments, garments, and food by people seeking all their desires during communal festivals—such as the Kaumudī and Mahānavamī—as well as at rites such as the initiation ceremony (upanayana). (3.59)
In that family where the husband is always content with his wife and the wife likewise with her husband, prosperity is indeed certain.

Regarding the term "contented": in whatever family the husband is constantly free from desire because of his wife as the cause, and where the wife likewise is constantly free from desire for another man because of her husband as the cause, there exists unshakable auspiciousness. (3.60)
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight the man; and from a lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed. (3.61)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if a woman were not radiant through the application of fragrant unguents and the like, she would not gladden her husband; and due to the husband's lack of joy, conception would not occur. || 3.61 ||
When a woman is pleasing, the entire family is pleased; but when she is displeasing, the whole family is indeed displeased. (3.62)

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "when a woman is radiant": when a woman is radiant through her dress and other qualities, she is pleasing to her husband; because of this lack of contact with other men, her family becomes illustrious. But when she is not radiant, due to being disliked by her husband and harboring thoughts of other men, the entire family becomes disgraced. (3.62)
Through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas,
and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble lineages fall into the state of being base.

Regarding the phrase "by bad marriages": through the absence of the sacramental rites of marriage such as the Āsura and others, through the non-study of the Vedas, and through the failure to honor Brahmins, even renowned families fall into decline. Therefore, this must be avoided. (3.63)
By means of crafts, trade, and solely through the offspring of Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king. (3.64)
Families that are deficient in sacred mantras quickly perish through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, through atheism, and through the neglect of ritual duties. (3.65)

"By craft and by trade," and "by officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice": families quickly fall into degradation through the practice of crafts such as painting, the employment of wealth in crafts, the procreation of offspring from a Śūdra woman alone, the buying and selling of cattle, horses, and chariots, agriculture, service to kings, officiating at sacrifices for Vratyas and others, the non-performance of rites for purification, and the neglect of study. (3.64–65)
But families that are prosperous in terms of sacred mantras, even if they possess little wealth, are reckoned among the great lineages and attract vast renown. (3.66)

Regarding the phrase "by means of mantra": although there is the popular saying that "family [status] is determined by wealth," nevertheless, families that are endowed with Vedic study, comprehension, and the performance of its prescribed rites—even if they possess little wealth—attain respectability among distinguished lineages and acquire great renown. All of this has been stated as a digression following upon the context of marriage. 3.66.
In the marriage fire, the householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking of food.

Regarding the term "pertaining to marriage": the householder should perform, in the fire produced at the time of marriage, the rites prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*—such as the *Aṣṭakā* and others—according to the scriptures, as well as the daily cooking and the performance of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) which are to be accomplished with fire, as will be described hereafter. (3.67)
A householder has five slaughter-houses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water-jar; by using these, he is bound [by sin]. (3.68)

"Five slaughter-houses" (pañca sūnā): the five things belonging to a householder—the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar, and so forth—are like slaughter-houses (*sūnā*) because by employing them for their respective tasks, one becomes connected with sin. Thus, from this mention of "slaughter-houses," and from the mention of "expiation" (*niṣkṛti*) in the phrase "for the sake of expiating those [five]," and from the statement that one is "not tainted by the defects of the slaughter-houses," it is concluded that these [five] are causes of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and that the Great Sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) serve as their expiation; for righteousness and unrighteousness fall solely within the domain of the scriptures (*śāstra*). And this being the case, it does not follow that the Great Sacrifices are non-obligatory (*anitya*), since their obligatory nature is established by such texts as, "The gods, guests, dependents, seers, and ancestors are the deities," and so on. Like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), these [Great Sacrifices] serve a dual purpose. 3.68.
For the sake of expiating all of these in due order, the great seers have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day. (3.69)

Regarding the phrase "of these": for the sake of expiation—that is, for the removal of the sin arising from those slaughter-places such as the hearth and so forth—Manu and others have prescribed the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*) daily for householders. (3.69)

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men. (3.70)

And these are: teaching; "recitation" (japa) and "oblation" (ahuta), which will be described later; by the word "teaching," study is also included—this is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña). Libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña). Offering into the fire is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña). The bali-offering to beings is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña). Honoring guests is the sacrifice to humans (manuṣyayajña). These specific duties to be performed, which are about to be described, are here indicated merely by their essential nature. (3.70)
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability, even while living constantly in the household, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse. (3.71)

"Five": he who does not abandon these five great sacrifices according to his ability is never bound by the sins arising from the slaughter-ground (sūnā) of the hearth and so forth, even while living at home. (3.71)
He who does not offer sustenance to these five—the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—though he breathes, he does not truly live. (3.72)

Regarding the phrase "of the deities, guests, and dependents": by the word *devatā* (deity), living beings (*bhūta*) are also included, for they too possess the nature of deities. Likewise, there is the inclusion of both the *ṛṣis* and the [other] deities, because their status as deities is recorded in tradition. As for the dependents (*bhṛtya*), Manu has declared: "One's aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son—Manu has said that these must be supported even if one has committed a hundred wrongs."
Having said this, he who does not give to these five—the gods and the others—even though he maintains his breaths, does not truly live, because there is an absence of the purpose of living. (3.72)
They declare that the five sacrifices consist of the *ahuta*, the *huta*, the *prahuta*, the *brāhmya-huta*, and the *prāśita*. (3.73)

Thus, by censuring their non-performance, he declares their obligatory nature with the words "the unoffered and the offered. An explanation of these will follow in the subsequent verse. The sages speak of these very five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) under these other names; this presentation of alternative designations is intended to demonstrate that there is only a difference in name, not a difference in substance. (3.73)

Recitation is the *huta* offering; the fire sacrifice (*homa*) is the *prahuta*; the ritual offering to beings (*bali*) is the *bhautika*; the worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya-huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*. (3.74)

Regarding the term *japa*: by the word *ahuta*, the *japa* known as the *brahmayajña* is intended; *huta* is the fire-oblation (*homa*), the *devayajña*; *prahuta* is the offering to beings (*bhūtabali*), the *bhūtayajña*; the *brāhmaṃ hutaṃ* is the honoring of the foremost of the twice-born, the *brāhmaṇa*, which is the *atithiyajña*; and *prāśitaṃ* is the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), the *pitṛyajña*. If, for some reason, the complete performance of these great sacrifices is not possible, then [the following applies]: 3.74.

One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas and to the rites dedicated to the gods here in this world; for it is by being engaged in the rites dedicated to the gods that one sustains this entire world of the moving and the unmoving. (3.75)

“He should be constantly engaged in private Vedic study and in rites for the gods and the ancestors; for he is indeed engaged in both. (3.75). He should always exert himself in the performance of the sacrifice to Brahman and the sacrifice to the gods. Therefore, one who is thus devoted to the performance of sacrifices sustains this world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving. 3.75.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. (3.76)

And so it is said: "The oblation cast into the fire" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.3). An oblation duly offered into the fire according to the prescribed rules, because its nature is to carry the essence [of the offering], reaches the sun. That essence of the oblation, ripened by time, arises from the sun in the form of rain. From that comes food, and through the consumption of that, living beings are born. (3.76)
Moreover:
Just as all living beings depend upon the wind for their life, so do the other stages of life depend upon the householder. (3.77)
Just as all living beings live by depending upon the vital breath, so too do the other stages of life (āśramas) endure by depending upon and taking recourse to the householder’s stage of life. 3.77.
Since members of all three other stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone with both knowledge and food, therefore the householder’s stage is the most excellent. (3.78)

"And thus, because... means: since even the three [other] orders of life, distinct from the householder, are supported by the householders alone through instruction in the meaning of the Vedas and the giving of food, therefore the householder's order is the best. "Gṛha" refers to the wife; "medha" refers to sacrifice. One whose sacrifice (*medha*) is dependent on the home (*gṛha*) is a *gṛhamedhī*. They are called *gṛhasthāḥ* because they stay in the home (*gṛha*). He is a *gṛhī* because he possesses a home (*gṛha*). (3.78)
One who desires imperishable heaven and absolute happiness in this world must strive to maintain that which is difficult for those with weak faculties to uphold. (3.79)

Therefore, this must be maintained by the householder. This stage of the householder (gṛhasthāśrama) is to be practiced with effort by one who desires the connection with heaven and the endless, supreme bliss of enjoying delicious food and sexual pleasure in this world; it cannot be sustained by those whose senses are unrestrained—this is the description of the fruits of the householder’s stage of life. 3.79.
The seers, the ancestors, the gods, all beings, and likewise guests, place their expectations upon householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act for them. (3.80)

And there is no falling into impermanence, because it says "the sages" (ṛṣayaḥ). Since the sages and others seek [their needs] from householders, therefore that which is prescribed by the knower of the scriptures must be performed for them. 3.80.
One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas, the gods with burnt offerings according to the rule,
the ancestors with funeral rites (śrāddha), men with food, and the spirits with the bali offering.

To the question "What is that?", he says: "By Vedic study" (svādhyāyena). Since worship can take many forms, it is not contradictory that Vedic study and the like serve as modes of worship; one should worship the sages, gods, ancestors, guests, and living beings with the aforementioned great sacrifices consisting of Vedic study and so forth, in accordance with the scriptures. (3.81)
Day after day, he should offer the śrāddha with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors. (3.82)

Regarding these, he first speaks for the purpose of defining the sacrifice to the ancestors: "He should give day by day. Producing satisfaction for the ancestors with food, water, milk, roots, and fruits as available, he should perform the *śrāddha* every day. (3.82)
In the performance of the five sacrifices for the sake of the ancestors, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, in this regard, one should not feed any twice-born man specifically for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

"One" means: regarding the purpose for the ancestors included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), one may feed even a single person according to one's ability; however, if possible, one should feed many Brahmins as well. Since the word *śrāddha* might imply that the feeding of Brahmins for the *vaiśvadeva* rite is also included in the boiled rice (*odana*), he says "and not" (*na caiva*). One should not feed any other Brahmin intended for the *viśvedevas*. (3.83)
Every day, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the oblation (homa) into the domestic fire for these deities from the prepared Vaiśvadeva food, according to the prescribed rule. (3.84)

Regarding the phrase "of the Vaiśvadeva": a Brāhmaṇa should perform daily an oblation (*homa*) in the marriage fire—or in a fire established at another time—of food that exists for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva, preceded by the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, such as sweeping (*parisamūhana*) and so forth, for these deities who are about to be mentioned; the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate the twice-born (*dvija*), since all three [classes] are the subject under discussion. (3.84)
First for Agni and for Soma, then for those two together, for the Viśvedevas, and for Dhanvantari. (3.85)
To Kuhū and to Anumati, and to Prajāpati, together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt. || 3.86 ||

And likewise for Kuhū. According to the traditional rule that "oblations have the utterance of *svāhā* as their primary element," one should first perform the oblation to Agni with *svāhā* and to Soma with *svāhā*, and so forth; thereafter, one should perform the combined oblation to Agni and Soma together with *agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*. Following that, having offered to the Viśvedevas, one should offer to Dhanvantari, Kuhū, Anumati, Prajāpati, and Dyāvāpṛthivī; finally, at the end, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Thus, because these are specific fires mentioned in the Gṛhya-sūtra, these oblations ending with the utterance of *svāhā* must be performed. (3.85–86)
Having thus properly offered the oblation, he should at every moment present a sacrificial offering (bali) in all directions to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, together with their followers.

"Thus. Having thus offered oblations to each respective deity according to the procedure described, one should present the *bali* offering to Indra and the others, along with their followers, in all directions starting from the east, turning clockwise: "Obeisance to Indra and Indra’s men in the east; to Yama and Yama’s men in the south; to Varuṇa and Varuṇa’s men in the west; to Soma and Soma’s men in the north. This is because the *gṛhya* texts show this very method; furthermore, the use of terms such as "Indra-antaka" (Yama) is for the sake of avoiding metrical defects. 3.87.
Saying "To the Maruts," he should throw [food] at the door; saying "To the Waters," he should also throw it into the water;
and saying "To the Vanaspatis," he should offer it upon the pestle and mortar.

"To the Maruts" at the door; "to the Maruts" thus at the doorway; "to the Waters" in the midst of the water; and "to the Forest Trees" at the pestle and mortar—because they form a dual compound in the singular, one may optionally offer the bali elsewhere as well. 3.88.
One should offer to Śrī at the head of the bed and to Bhadrakālī at the foot;
one should present the bali offering to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.

Regarding the term *ucchīrṣaka*: at the head-region of the Vāstupuruṣa, in the northeast direction, one should worship Śrī; at his feet, in the southwest direction, one should worship Bhadrakālī and Brahmā-Vāstoṣpati. Although they are mentioned as a pair (*dvandva*) in the middle of the house, there is no mention of the particle *āṅ* (indicating a single deity), and thus they constitute two separate deities. (3.89)
And one should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the beings that roam by day and those that roam by night.

"To all" (*viśvebhyaḥ*) means "to all those belonging to the Viśvedevas"; because of the word "and" (*ca*), this constitutes a single oblation. One should cast it into the space of the name (*nāmākāśe*) with the formula, "To all the gods" (*viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ*). According to the *Gṛhya* texts, there are the formulas "to the beings that roam by day" (*divācarebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ*) and "to the beings that roam by night" (*naktaṃcarebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ*) for the evening. Since no other receptacle is mentioned and the sky (*ākāśa*) has been introduced as the subject, [the offering] is indeed in the sky alone. 3.90.
One should offer the bali-oblation on the back of the dwelling for the prosperity of all food;
however, one should carry all the remainder of the bali toward the south for the ancestors.

"One should make [the offering] on the back of the dwelling. On the roof of the house, or on the back of the house, or in some other suitable place, one should offer the *bali* there with the formula, "Obeisance to all beings who have become food. For the sake of the *bali*, one should carry all the remnants of the ghee and rice toward the southern direction for the ancestors, because of the instruction in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*: "With the formula 'Svadhā to the ancestors,' wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). (3.91)
One should slowly scatter [the food] on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, birds, and insects. (3.92)

"And for dogs" means: after that, having set aside another portion of food, he should gently place it on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, lepers, and so forth, as well as for crows and worms, taking care to avoid scattering dust over it. || 3.92 ||
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by a straight path, embodied in light, to the supreme abode.

"Thus": according to the principle thus stated, he who constantly honors all beings as described by providing food and other necessities becomes one whose body is composed of splendor (*tejaḥśarīra*) and goes to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) by a manifest path that is easily reached—namely, immediately upon the fall of the body. This concludes the description of the fruit of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*); and it has been stated that there is no occurrence of impermanence [for such a person]. (3.93)
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
and he should give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and to a student of sacred knowledge.

"Having performed thus": having performed this *balikarman* in the manner described, one should first honor the guest before those who consume the food of the entire household. One should give alms to a student (*brahmacārin*) who is habitually begging, at the very same time, according to the rule stated by Gautama: "The giving of alms after pronouncing 'May it be well' (*svastivācya*) is not preceded [by other rites]. (3.94)
Whatever merit one obtains by giving a cow to a guru according to the prescribed rule,
that same merit a twice-born householder obtains by giving alms.
