Regarding the phrase "the fruit of merit": by giving a cow according to the rule stated by Yājñavalkya, beginning with "A cow with small horns made of gold," one attains the fruit of merit expressed in the verse, "The giver of a cow reaches the realm of the Sun. That very same fruit a twice-born householder attains by giving alms. 3.95.
One should respectfully offer, according to the prescribed rule, even a portion of alms or a vessel of water to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas. (3.96)

Regarding the word *bhikṣām* (alms): one should offer [food] consisting of fruits, flowers, and so forth, having honored [the recipient], to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the ultimate meaning of the Vedas, preceded by the ritual injunctions such as "let him pronounce a blessing" (*svastivācya*). This is a distinct rule concerning the giving of alms to a student (*brahmacārin*). And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "Having given food to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who is a student... (3.96).
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of men who lack understanding perish, when they are given out of delusion to Brahmins who have become like ashes. (3.97)

"They perish" means that those foods which, out of delusion and due to ignorance of the treatises on giving, are offered by donors to Brahmins who are devoid of the luster of Vedic study, ritual injunctions, and sacrificial performance—those offerings become fruitless for those men who are ignorant of the treatises on giving. (3.97)
An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, who are enriched by knowledge and austerity, delivers one from misfortune and even from great sin. (3.98)

Regarding the phrase "in those enriched by knowledge and austerity": whatever is offered as oblations to the gods (*havya*) or to the ancestors (*kavya*) into the mouths of Brahmins—who are like fires, being endowed with the splendor of wisdom and spiritual practice—protects one here from the difficult-to-cross affliction of enemies, diseases, and the like, and there [in the next world] from great sin. (3.98)
To a guest who has arrived, he should offer a seat and water, and food prepared according to his ability and in accordance with the prescribed rules. (3.99)

Regarding the phrase "to one who has arrived": when a guest presents himself of his own accord, one should honor him as best as possible with a seat, water for rinsing the mouth, food, and various types of fans, and then offer these according to the procedure to be described later in the verse beginning with "seats and lodgings. || 3.99 ||
Even for one who constantly gathers grains by gleaning and offers oblations into the five fires, a Brahmin staying unhonored takes away all his merit. (3.100)

"Even from stones, for one who constantly gleans... This refers to one who, due to extreme poverty and a desire for the excellence of self-restraint in livelihood, gathers even the "stones"—the flaws of the field's produce—or performs the fire-oblation (*homa*) in all five fires, including the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* along with the *tretā*. An unhonored guest takes away the merit earned through the fire-oblations resulting from such total restriction of livelihood. By speaking of the fault of not giving, he describes the observances (*niyamas*). The fire named *sabhya* is called the "great instrument" (*mahāsādhana*); it is established here and there for the purpose of removing weeds and the like. (3.100)
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—these are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous. (3.101)

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the absence of food, [one may give] grasses": grasses, resting places, water for sipping and so forth, pleasant and truthful speech, and [hospitality] in the homes of the virtuous for the sake of a guest are never cut off. Therefore, in the absence of food, these must certainly be given.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest. 3.102

Because [the term] is not well-known, he states the definition of a guest: "one night. A Brāhmaṇa staying for one night in another's house is remembered as a guest (*atithi*); because he does not have a second lunar day (*tithi*) due to his constant state of being away from home, he is thus called a guest (*atithi*). (3.102)
One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin from another village or a traveling companion who has arrived at one’s house, even if one’s wife or the sacred fires are also present there. (3.103)

"Nor one from the same village": he should not recognize as a guest even one who has arrived at that very same village during the time for the *vaiśvadeva* offering—a resident of the same village with whom he has social ties, who lives by means of worldly interaction, whose livelihood consists of various jests and stories, and who has come there along with his wife and sacred fires. (3.103)
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others go, after death, to the state of cattle as those who merely receive food and other gifts. (3.104)

Regarding the phrase "they wait upon": this is intended to demonstrate the result—that those householders who, having gone to other villages for the sake of hospitality, are of dull intellect and, due to gluttony, subsist on the food of others, go to the state of being cattle in the houses of those who gave them food in a future birth because of that consumption of another's food. Therefore, one should not partake of another's cooked food. 3.104.

A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder; whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating. (3.105)

Regarding the term *apraṇodya* ("not to be turned away"): since this guest has arrived with the setting sun, and because he is then unable to go to his own home, he must not be rejected by the householder—that is, the *gṛhastha* who performs the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) prescribed for the home. Whether he arrives at the time of the *vaiśvadeva* offering or thereafter, he must not stay in the house of this householder without eating food. Food must certainly be given to him; and this [verse] is commenced for the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiṣiddhapratiprasava*) regarding guests who might otherwise be prohibited. Otherwise, since the giving of food to a guest in the evening would already be established by the statement to be made later—"For this, called the *vaiśvadeva*, is ordained for both morning and evening" (MDh 3.121)—this present rule would not need to be commenced. (3.105)
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven. (3.106)

"No," [it is replied]. Whatever is pleasing to the guest, one should not eat oneself without having given that to him. Furthermore, the feeding of guests for the sake of wealth or fame leads to an evil heaven; thus, this is a statement regarding the fruit of hospitality (*ātitheya*), but it does not entail the contingency of being non-permanent (*anityatā*), because it has been stated [elsewhere] that "he takes away all one's good deeds" (3.106).

One should provide a seat, lodging, a bed, attendance while walking behind, and respectful service; for those who are superior, one should perform the highest degree of these, for those who are inferior, the lowest, and for those who are equal, that which is equal. (3.107)

Regarding the phrase "seats and dwellings": when many guests are staying simultaneously, one should provide superior, middling, or inferior treatment—consisting of resting places, beds, attendance, and service—relative to one another among those who are superior, middling, or inferior, based on their faith and other qualities. However, the food itself should be equal, as no distinction is heard of in that regard. (3.107)
But when the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been completed, if another guest should arrive,
one should give him food according to one's ability, but one should not perform the Bali offering again.

Regarding the *vaiśvadeva*: when the *vaiśvadeva* has been performed up to the feeding of guests, if another guest should arrive, one should then cook food again according to one's ability and give it to him; however, one should not perform the *baliharaṇa* (offering to the elements) from that food. From this prohibition of *baliharaṇa*, it is understood that the *vaiśvadeva* is intended for the purpose of consecrating the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*). For if it were a rite for consecrating the food (*annasaṃskāra*), how could he permit the eating of unconsecrated food? (3.108)
A Brahmin should not proclaim his own family or lineage for the sake of food;
for by praising them for the sake of a meal, he is called by the wise a "vomit-eater. (3.109)

In this context, he states the characteristic of the enjoyer: "not for the sake of eating. A sage should not speak of his own family or lineage for the purpose of obtaining food; for if one speaks for the sake of food, the wise call him a "vomit-eater" (udgīrṇāśī). || 3.110 ||
A Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa; nor are a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, a kinsman, or even a teacher. (3.110)

"But for a Brāhmaṇa, there is no such thing as a guest. In the house of a Brāhmaṇa, teachers, friends, relatives, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras do not become guests. This is because the teacher holds the position of authority; friends and relatives are equal to oneself; and the Kṣatriya and others belong to lower castes. A Brāhmaṇa may be superior even to a Kṣatriya. Both the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya would indeed be of superior caste; the same applies to the Vaiśya. (3.110)
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may, if he so desires, feed him after the Brahmins have finished eating. (3.111)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if a Kṣatriya, having exhausted his provisions for the journey because he is staying in another village, should arrive at the house of a Brāhmaṇa according to the duty of a guest, then he too should be fed once the Brāhmaṇas residing in that house have finished their meal. || 3.11 ||
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at his household as one who possesses the status of a guest, he should feed them together with his servants, practicing kindness toward them. (3.112)

"Regarding the Vaiśya and the Śūdra": when a Vaiśya or a Śūdra arrive at one's house in the guise of guests, yet without provisions for the journey, they should then be fed together out of compassion. 3.112.
He should also, together with his wife, feed other friends and relatives who have come to his house out of affection, providing them with food according to his means and their station. (3.112)

"Others" refers to those distinct from the aforementioned Kṣatriyas and so forth—such as friends, kinsmen, fellow students, and the like—who have come to the house out of affection. Having prepared food according to his ability, the wife should feed them at the time of the meal. As for himself, this is also the proper time, because it will be stated later: "But what remains, the husband and wife [should eat]. However, for the teacher, the time is not fixed, since he has the authority to determine the time according to his own convenience. (3.113)
He should, without hesitation, provide these very persons—unmarried women, young girls, the sick, and pregnant women—with food immediately after the guests. 3.114.

"Regarding 'married women' (*suvāsinyah*): he should feed the women whose fathers-in-law and fathers are still living, as well as virgins, the sick, and pregnant women, immediately after the guests have been served, without delay; according to the reading *agrata eva*, [this means] even before the guests. (3.114)
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures. (3.115)

"Without having given"—that is, one who, ignorant of the fault of transgression, eats before these guests, down to the servants, does not realize that while eating he is consuming his own flesh, which results in this fruit: being devoured by dogs and vultures immediately upon death. (3.115)
Then, after the Brahmins and their own servants have indeed finished eating,
the husband and wife may afterwards eat what remains.

Regarding the phrase "when they have eaten": when the guests and others, the relatives and connections, and the servants have finished their meal, the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains of that food. (3.116)
Having honored the gods, the seers, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains. (3.117)

Regarding the phrase "to the gods": this restatement, ending with "those pertaining to the household are *gṛhya*," indicates that the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) has already been described. This is a reiterative reference for the purpose of stating the transgression that will be mentioned hereafter. (3.117)
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin; for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice. 3.118.

"Sin" (agham): he who cooks solely for his own sake and does not give to the gods and others, eats only sin because it is the cause of evil; he does not consume even a morsel of food, since this eating of the remnants of a cooked sacrifice is taught as the food of the virtuous. (3.118)
One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, an officiating priest, a graduate, a teacher, a beloved father-in-law, and a maternal uncle, again after a full year has passed.

In connection with the honoring of guests (*atithipūjā*), this specific rule for the honoring of kings and others is stated: "A king, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), one who has completed his studies (*snātaka*), a teacher (*guru*), a beloved [relative], a father-in-law (*śvaśura*), and a maternal uncle (*mātula*). Any twice-born householder should honor with the *madhuparka*—the ritual procedure described in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*—a Kṣatriya consecrated as a ruler of a territory who has come to his home, a mendicant, an officiating priest, a *snātaka* who has mastered knowledge and vows, a disciple his teacher, a father-in-law his son-in-law, a son-in-law his father-in-law, and a nephew his maternal uncle. He should honor these when they have returned to his home after a limited period, that is, once a year has elapsed. As for those who say that the teacher (*ācārya*) should honor the *snātaka* because the latter is already well-known [as a person to be honored], for them, how could the term "after a year" (*parivatsarāt*) serve as a qualification for the *snātaka*? (3.119)

When a sacrificial rite is about to take place, both a king and a learned Brahmin are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is the established rule that this does not apply when no sacrifice is being performed. 3.120.

Regarding the restriction concerning the King and the Snātaka, he says "the King" (rājā). The rule of the scriptures is that the King and the Snātaka are to be honored with the *madhuparka* only when they have arrived for a sacrificial rite (*yajñakarman*), and not at a non-sacrificial occasion, even if more than a year has passed. However, within a year, they are not to be honored even at a sacrifice, because the word "after a year" (*saṃvatsarāt*) is supplied from the preceding verse. And here, because the phrase "but not at a sacrifice" (*na tu yajñe*) is employed, this [verse] is understood to serve the purpose of restricting the honor due to the King and the Snātaka. (3.120)
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer a Bali oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.

"At evening" means that at the end of the day, when food has been prepared, the wife should perform the *baliharaṇa*—known as the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*)—by mentally designating [the offerings] while omitting the mantras beginning with "Salutation to Indra" (*indrāya namaḥ*). For it is precisely this sequence, from the sacrifices down to the eating of one's own meal, that is prescribed for the householder both in the evening and in the morning. (3.121)

But having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha at the waning of the moon, month after month. || 3.122 ||

Regarding the phrase "the sacrifice to the ancestors" (pitṛyajña): having performed on the new moon day the Śrauta rite known as the Piṇḍayajña, one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should perform that very rite as prescribed in the Sūtra—based on the Sūtra statement, "One who maintains the Aupāsana fire, and likewise one who has not maintained the fires, having cooked [the food] for the daily [rites]"—and then perform the Śrāddha called Piṇḍānvāhāryaka, so named because it is offered subsequent to (anu-paścāt) the rice-balls (piṇḍas) belonging to the monthly Piṇḍapitṛyajña. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate the twice-born (dvija), since all three classes are under discussion. (3.122)
The wise know the monthly ancestral rite for the rice-balls to be the *anvāhārya*;
that should be performed with effort using commendable meat. (3.123)

Now, by means of the mention of its name, he establishes this [rite] as occurring immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* with the words "of the *piṇḍas*. That monthly *śrāddha* which is performed subsequently (*anu*) to the *piṇḍas* is therefore considered by the learned to be the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*. And thus it is logical that it should be performed immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. It should be performed with effort using meat specifically prescribed, such as the flesh of a rhinoceros and so forth; in the absence of that, however, with other sacrificial foods (*haviṣya*). (3.123)

In this regard, I shall explain in their entirety those best of the twice-born who are worthy of being fed, those who are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food they should be honored. 3.124
Regarding that: I shall explain all of this—in whom one should feed at that *śrāddha*, whom one should avoid, the appropriate number of guests, and with which foods it should be performed. (3.124)
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not engage in excessive elaboration. (3.125)

Although it might follow from the instruction that "those who are worthy of being fed" should be invited, nevertheless, because there is little to be said, he first states the number: "two. One should feed two for the *daiva* (divine) rite which is an ancillary part of the *paitṛka* (ancestral) rite; or three, intended for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; or one for each of the *daiva* and *paitṛka* rites. One who is capable of feeding more than the stated number should not proceed to offer the *arghya* water for those additional guests. As for the argument that the statement "one for each of all [the ancestors]"—based on the *Gṛhyasūtra* rule "one should invite at least three," and the present mention of "one for each in both [rites]"—is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to prohibit a larger number, that is incorrect. This is because this [rule] is heard as an alternative to the rule "two for the divine rite and three for the ancestral rite. Furthermore, Yājñavalkya prescribes "only one for each," and Vasiṣṭha likewise.
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed?
Having set aside a portion of food from all the prepared offerings into a vessel, [one should proceed].
Having performed [the rites] in the temple of the deity, he should then proceed with the śrāddha ceremony.

Thus, [the rule] is established from the feeding of a single Brāhmaṇa. As for the Gṛhya-sūtra statement beginning with "But not one by one," that refers to a situation where there is a perfect abundance of materials, Brāhmaṇas, and so forth, and is not intended to prohibit others; for immediately after this, the author of the Gṛhya-sūtra says, "At will, even if there is no food," meaning that in the absence of edible food and such, one may at will feed even a single person to all. And likewise, the rule "One should invite at least three" also refers to a situation of perfect abundance of materials, Brāhmaṇas, and so forth, and does not indicate the absolute non-existence of the injunction regarding each individual. The word "vistara" (elaboration) is used due to the requirements of the meter, according to the traditional rule: "Or when the word 'ca' occurs at the beginning."
Hospitality, the proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.

Regarding the phrase "honoring" (*satkriyām*): the honor shown to Brahmins—consisting of a pure location and so forth, the afternoon time, ritual purity, and the presence of virtuous Brahmins—destroys the fault of excessive elaboration (*vistara*). Therefore, one should not perform a Brahmin feast that exceeds what has been prescribed. Because the prohibition of elaboration is based on a specific reason, there is indeed room for feeding more Brahmins when honor and the other requirements are present. Thus it was said by Gautama: "One should not feed inferior Brahmins; or [feed] an odd number, according to one's ability. (3.126)
This well-known performance for the deceased, called the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), occurs at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that [meditation], the worldly performance for the deceased is constantly accomplished. (3.127)

Regarding the word "renowned" (*prathitā*): This rite known as *pitrya*, the ancestral ritual, this *pretakṛtyā*—the performance intended for the benefit of the deceased—is celebrated among all householders at the waning of the moon or in the home, not in other stages of life (*āśrama*). For one engaged in that ancestral rite, devoted to it, there is the worldly, traditional (*smārta*) funeral rite; by means of it, the deceased is benefited through the attainment of a continuous succession of virtuous sons and grandsons. Therefore, this must be performed with diligence. (3.127)
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.

Regarding the phrase "to a *śrotriya*": foods intended for the gods, the ancestors, and so forth, should be given to one who has studied at least the *chandas* (the Vedic meters). Since the term *śrotriya* is applied to one who has studied merely the *chandas*, this rule does not apply with absolute rigidity. However, when such a person is available, the gift should be given to one who has studied an entire *śākhā* (branch) of the Veda. When there is the possibility of choosing according to the injunctions such as, "One should diligently feed a *bahvṛca* at a *śrāddha*," then—provided he is indeed a *śrotriya* and possesses learning, good conduct, noble lineage, and other such qualities—it should be given to that most venerable Brahmin; for by giving to him, it becomes an especially effective means of benefiting the ancestors through the mediation of their satisfaction. (3.128)
One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors;
one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.

Because of the statement "one for each," one should feed even a single person learned in the meaning of the Vedas at both the rites for the gods and the ancestors; for one obtains the full fruit known as the satisfaction of the ancestors. Since it is stated that one does not obtain an abundant fruit by feeding many who are ignorant, it is concluded that here the feeding of the Brāhmaṇa is the primary act, whereas the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) and so forth are merely subsidiary elements. (3.129)
One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; he is the proper recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is considered a guest. (3.130)

"From afar," etc.: According to the principle of examining officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) stated by the author of the Sūtras—"those who are ten generations back on the mother's side and ten generations back on the father's side"—one should examine a Brāhmaṇa who has studied all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*). For that reason, such a Brāhmaṇa is like a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); just as those seeking water go by way of a ford, which is a path for descending into the water, so too do the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and ancestors (*kavya*) reach the gods and ancestors through such a Brāhmaṇa. Such a Brāhmaṇa is remembered as equal to a guest because he yields great fruit. (3.130)
For where a thousand times a thousand who are ignorant of the Ṛgveda may eat, a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, deserves all of them according to dharma. (3.131)

"Regarding the word 'thousand': where, in rites for the gods or ancestors and the like, they feed ten lakhs of Brāhmaṇas who do not know the Ṛgveda, there a single knower of the Veda, having eaten, being pleased and satisfied, by means of dharma—that is, by the production of merit—is worthy (arhati) to take the place of all those others; the meaning is that he produces the same merit arising from their feeding. This is the praise of feeding a learned Brāhmaṇa. (3.131)
Offerings for the ancestors and oblations for the gods should be given to one preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by weeping alone.

Regarding the phrase "to one preeminent in knowledge": sacrificial offerings (*havya*) and ancestral offerings (*kavya*) should be given to those preeminent in learning, and not to others. For just as hands smeared with blood cannot be cleansed of that smear by blood itself, but only by water, so too the self cannot be delivered by giving to the ignorant, but only through the medium of giving to the wise. Thus, by censuring the ignorant, there is praise for giving to the learned. (3.132)
As many mouthfuls as one ignorant of the mantras eats at offerings to the gods or the ancestors, so many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls does that deceased person consume. (3.133)

"However many," etc. This is a statement regarding the fruit of giving to one who lacks knowledge: as many mouthfuls as an ignorant person consumes from the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors), that same number of blazing, massive iron balls known as *śūla-ṛṣṭi* weapons the performer of the present *śrāddha* must consume. Thus Vyāsa speaks of the fruit for the giver alone: "As many balls as one who is unacquainted with the *Ṛgveda* consumes of the sacrificial food, so many *śūlas* shall he consume upon reaching the abode of Vaivasvata. (3.133)
Some twice-born ones are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity; some are devoted to austerity and sacred study, and others are devoted to ritual action. (3.134)

Regarding the phrase "devoted to knowledge": some Brahmins are intent upon the knowledge of the Self; others are primarily devoted to austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance; still others are dedicated to austerity and study; and others are intent upon sacrifices and the like. (3.134)
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be established with effort among those devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) should be given according to the rule to all four [classes] alike.

What does he mean by saying "to those established in knowledge"? To those for whom knowledge is primary, the offerings intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*) should be given with effort; however, the offerings intended for the gods (*deva*), without overstepping the boundaries of the scriptures, may be given even to the four beginning with those established in knowledge. 3.136:

He whose father is unlearned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) but whose son has mastered the Vedas, or whose son is unlearned in the Vedas but whose father has mastered the Vedas— [in such cases, the latter is the one to be honored].
Regarding the term *aśrotriya*: one who is the son of a non-learned man (*aśrotriya*) but is himself learned (*śrotriya*), and one who is the son of a learned man but is himself not learned. 3.136.
One should know the elder of these two to be the one whose father is a Vedic scholar;
however, the other deserves hospitality for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras. (3.137)

Having raised the question of which of these two is superior, he says, "the more eminent. Between these two previously mentioned, one should consider the son of a *śrotriya* who is himself not a *śrotriya* to be more praiseworthy. Subsequently, the son of one who is not a *śrotriya* but who is himself a *śrotriya* deserves honor for the sake of honoring the Veda studied by him; through him, the Veda is honored, but he [the father] is not worthy of such honor. This is for the purpose of examining the learning of the father and others, and it serves the purpose of giving to one who is not a *śrotriya*, because of the rule: "Gifts should be given only to a *śrotriya*. And thus, the statement "one should examine [the guest] from afar" remains intended for the examination of excellence in birth, distinct from learning. (3.137)
One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
That twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend should be fed at the *śrāddha*. (3.138)

One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; rather, one should win him over with other forms of wealth. One should feed that twice-born (*dvija*) at a *śrāddha* whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend. One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*. What then? One should cultivate friendship and affection for him through other means of wealth. Furthermore, one should feed at a *śrāddha* that Brāhmaṇa whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend—that is, one who is neutral. (3.138)
For him whose śrāddha rites and oblations are dominated by friends, there is no fruit after death from those śrāddhas or oblations. (3.139)

Regarding the phrase "of whom": this statement is intended to express the absence of fruit—that for one whose *havya* and *kavya* offerings are devoted solely to assisting friends, there is no reward in the next world—and it implies that one should not give only to a former friend through *śrāddha* and other rites, but rather [to all who are worthy]. (3.139)

That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships through a funeral feast (*śrāddha*) falls from the heavenly world; he is a "friend at the *śrāddha*" and the most base of men. (3.140)

Regarding the word "he": that base twice-born man who, out of ignorance of the scriptures, forms a friendship with a *śrāddha*—thinking, "Through this performance of a *śrāddha*, there will be friendship between me and him"—is called a *śrāddhamitra* because he makes a friend of the *śrāddha*. Due to being motivated by such friendship, he is not even connected to the heavenly world, despite having earned it through other meritorious deeds. (3.140)
That which is called the *saṃbhojinī* is declared by the twice-born to be the *paiśācī* sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
it remains right here in this world like a blind cow in a single house.

Regarding the term *saṃbhojinī*: that sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or gift is called *saṃbhojinī* because it is enjoyed together [with the recipient]. Such a social gathering (*goṣṭhī*), because it possesses the nature of a *piśāca*, is described by Manu and others as *paiśācī*. And because its purpose is merely friendship, it exists only in this world, like a blind cow in a single house; it does not serve for any benefit in the next world. (3.141)
Just as one who sows seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit, so too a donor who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Rigveda does not obtain the fruit. (3.142)

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): just as a farmer, having sown grain in a saline tract of land, does not obtain a fruit, so too a donor, having given the *śrāddha* and other offerings to one who is not a *śrotriya*, does not obtain the fruit. This is stated for the purpose of explaining the futility of giving to one who is not a *śrotriya*. (3.142)
By giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the rule to one who is learned, one makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death. (3.143)

The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given to a learned man bears fruit both in this world and after death. When offerings such as the *śrāddha* are given according to the scriptures to one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, they make the givers successful through the fruit of the hereafter known as the satisfaction of the ancestors, and through the fruit of worldly renown. Furthermore, they make the recipients successful in the next world by means of the fruit of sacrifices and other rites performed with the wealth obtained through that acceptance; for sacrifices and the like performed with wealth acquired through unrighteousness are fruitless. And in this world, they make the recipients successful regarding the fruits of agriculture and other labors performed with wealth acquired through righteousness. This [passage] is intended to state the visible and invisible fruits for both the giver and the recipient of a gift to a learned man.
At a śrāddha, one may certainly honor a friend even if he is not learned, but never an enemy;
for an oblation consumed by a foe becomes fruitless after death. (3.144)

Regarding the word *kāmam*: it is better (*varam*) that, in the absence of another virtuous Brāhmaṇa, one should feed a virtuous friend at a *śrāddha* rather than even a worthy enemy; for food and other offerings consumed by an enemy in a *śrāddha* become fruitless in the next world. This statement is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for a virtuous friend when others are unavailable. Since the term *śrotriya* is applied to one who has studied even a mere portion of the Veda, its adoption here is stated to be obligatory (*naiyamika*). (3.144)
One should diligently feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda, or an Adhvaryu belonging to another Śākhā, or a Chandoga who has completed his studies. (3.145)

Now, however, since it is possible [to find such persons], he states that one should give to those who have studied all the recensions (*śākhās*) for the sake of a specific result, using the word "with effort" (*yatnena*). One should diligently feed at a *śrāddha* such a Bahvṛca (Ṛgvedin) who has studied all the recensions, and likewise such an Adhvaryu (Yajurvedin) and Chandoga (Sāmavedin). Because of their conduct (*vṛtta*), these individuals are appropriately described by various terms denoting the study of the complete collection of recensions. As for those who claim that this [term "all recensions"] serves as a qualification for the rule "gifts should be given only to a *śrotriya*," in order to exclude those who study only a single recension (*chandas*), for them the phrase "only to a *śrotriya*" would be redundant, since that is already established by the present verse alone. (3.145)
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at a person's *śrāddha*, the satisfaction of that person's ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations. (3.146)

"Of these": from among these [reciters], such as the Bahvṛcas and others, if one whose mind is honored should eat at a *śrāddha*, there will be for him an uninterrupted satisfaction of the ancestors extending through seven generations, beginning with the father; this is the statement of the fruit resulting from feeding those who study the entire recension (*śākhā*). For this very reason it is known: "Wherever the ancestors may reside, they dwell happily on the *kavya* offerings brought by their sons and others. Furthermore, this is the fruit of the satisfaction of the ancestors; and in the rite of *śrāddha*, the fallacies of "gaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) should not be raised here, because it is within the exclusive domain of the scripture, just like the case of Vaiśvānara, due to the authority of traditional revelation (*āgama*).
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of oblations to the gods and the ancestors;
however, this secondary rule should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

Regarding the word "this": this is the primary rule concerning the offering of *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors), namely that [the gift] is given to those who are not one's own kin, such as those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and so forth. Furthermore, this rule which is about to be stated should be understood as the secondary rule for when the primary [rule] is absent; it is always practiced by the virtuous (*sādhu*) in the absence of the primary [option]. (3.147)

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the preceptor, the daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a kinsman, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices. 3.148.

"Regarding 'the maternal grandfather' (mātāmaha)": one should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister's son, the father-in-law, the teacher of sacred knowledge, the daughter's son, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one sacrifices. "Viṭ" means offspring; its lord is the "lord of the viṭ" (viṭpati), namely the son-in-law, as well as a kinsman such as one of the same lineage (sagotra). || 3.148 ||
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors is at hand, he should examine him with great care. (3.149)

"No," [says the author]. One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of feeding him at a rite for the gods (*daiva*) merely on the basis of worldly reputation; he should be accepted as such and fed there. But when a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*) is at hand, one should examine him with great care, according to the principle stated: "One should examine him from afar. (3.149)
Manu has declared those Brahmins who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or those who live as atheists to be unworthy of offerings to the gods and the ancestors. 3.150

"Those who are thieves, outcasts, and eunuchs"—Manu has declared that such Brahmins as thieves and the rest are unfit for both *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors). Regarding "thieves," this refers to those other than those who steal a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, because the latter are subsumed under the category of "outcasts. He will describe the "outcast" in the eleventh chapter; [the thief of Brāhmaṇa gold] is included there as an outcast. He will describe the "eunuch" (*klība*) as a neuter person. Those whose conduct is based on the belief that "there is no world beyond" are those of atheistic behavior (*nāstikavṛtti*). (3.150)
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who wear matted hair but do not study, those who are weak, gamblers, nor those who solicit groups of people. (3.151)

Regarding the term *jaṭila*: since there is a rule stating that a *brahmacārin* who has not yet mastered the Vedas should be given food only for the sake of his Vedic study (*śrotriya-yāya*) because he lacks [any other] entitlement, [the term *jaṭila* here does not refer to him]. Likewise, one should not feed those with skin diseases, those who live by gambling, or those who officiate at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, at a *śrāddha*; however, there is no prohibition regarding offerings to the gods (*daiva*). Furthermore, where the author intends to prohibit both [types of offerings], he uses the expression "taking of *havya* and *kavya*" to indicate both cases. (3.151)
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers, and those who live by trade—these should be avoided at rites for the gods and the ancestors. (3.152)

Physicians, temple-priests, and meat-sellers—likewise. Physicians and the others are to be avoided for both *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors). A physician is a medical practitioner; a *devalaka* is one who performs prohibitions not for the sake of dharma, because such acts are prescribed therein. Meat-sellers [are excluded] even if they sell but once. And thus there is the indicative mark: "One falls immediately by [selling] meat. Otherwise, the meaning would already be established by the term "trade" (*vipaṇa*); furthermore, since the word "living" (*jīvantaḥ*) is employed here, it is understood that even a single instance of selling meat is intended. Trade (*vipaṇa*) means commerce. || 3.152 ||
One who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, a usurer, a servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth; 3.153.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, an outcast, a hater of Brahmins, the elder brother superseded by the younger, and one who belongs to a corporate body— [these are not to be invited]. (3.154)

Regarding the term *yakṣmī*: one who suffers from consumption (*kṣayin*) is well known as a cattle-herder for the sake of his livelihood; the *parivettṛ* and *parivitti* will be mentioned later. A *nirākṛti* is one who rejects the Vedas and so forth, and thus is not to be supported; he is a hater of Brahmins, even when in the midst of a group of Brahmins and others. These persons are to be excluded from offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). (3.154)
One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vows, the husband of a low-caste woman, one who has married a second time, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour; 3.155.

"A person of evil conduct" refers to actors, singers, and the like; a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who has engaged in sexual union with women; the husband of a *śūdra* woman; the son of a remarried woman (*punarbhū*), who will be described later; one who is one-eyed; and he in whose house lives his wife's paramour—these are to be avoided at offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught by a paid teacher, one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one who is a teacher of a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka; 3.156.

"A teacher for hire" refers to one who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught for a fee, a Śūdra student, and his own teacher—not one's own [spiritual] teacher, because the latter is declared to be fit to be fed as an alternative [to the forbidden]. A harsh speaker, and the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* (which will be described later)—these are to be excluded from offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). (3.156)
One who has abandoned, without cause, his mother, father, or teacher; and one who has entered into association with outcasts through marriages contracted according to the Vedic rites. (3.157)

"Abandoned without cause": she who has been abandoned without reason by her mother, father, teacher, or preceptor; and one who has entered into association with outcasts through such connections as studying together, giving a daughter in marriage, and so forth—even before a year has passed. For after a year, the purpose [of this specific rule] is already fulfilled by the fact of his outcasting itself, according to the rule: "By [the lapse of] a year, he becomes an outcast. (3.157)
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel belonging to a degraded person, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; || 3.158 ||

"An incendiary of houses" means one who sets fire to a dwelling; one who provides substances for killing; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, as will be described later; a seller of *soma* in its form as a creeper; one who goes to sea; a reciter of panegyrics; a grinder of sesame seeds and the like; and a forger of documents, witness statements, and so forth—all these are to be avoided in both cases. (3.158)
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard, one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a net-seller, and a seller of poison; 3.159.

"Regarding the word *pitṛ* (father): one who is afflicted by disease, one who is accused, a fisherman (*jālika*), a seller of liquids (*rasavikrayin*), one who disputes with his father regarding the scriptures, worldly objects, or property, a gambler, and another who performs sacrifices for others—since the other [categories] have already been mentioned. The reading *kekara* (squint-eyed) is the practice of the reciters. A drinker of intoxicants other than *surā*, a leper, one who has incurred a curse due to committing a major or minor sin even though there is no certainty that he committed it, one who practices dharma under false pretenses, and a seller of liquids—the term *rasa* being well-known to refer to sugarcane juice and the like, and because the word *rasa* is used in the *Arthaśāstra* to refer to poison as well—a seller of such things; these are to be avoided in both cases. (3.159)

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried, one who betrays a friend, one who subsists by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; 3.160.

"Of bows and arrows": one who makes bows and arrows. "The husband of an *agredidhiṣū*" refers to what will be stated later [in verse 3.172]: "of a deceased brother. Due to the requirements of the meter, the word *agra* is used with the elision of the suffix *adhy*, just as *Satyabhāmā* is called *Bhāmā*. As for the claim that, upon examining the text of Gautama, the term *agredidhiṣūpati* yields two distinct meanings—the husband of an *agredidhiṣū* and the husband of a *didhiṣū*—and that therein the *agredidhiṣūpati* is one who marries an unmarried girl while the *didhiṣūpati* is the husband of her elder sister, that is incorrect, because it is not the literal meaning of the word. Nor is the explanation "the husband of a *didhiṣū* and the husband of her [elder sister]" appropriate, as it contradicts the definition of Manu: "of a deceased brother. One who engages in harming a friend; a gambler who presides over a gaming house (*sabhika*); and one taught by his own son, since it is impossible for a son to be the primary teacher of his father. (3.160)

One suffering from bee-like skin eruptions, one with scrofulous swellings, one with vitiligo, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise one who reviles the Vedas—these should be avoided. (3.161)

"One suffering from epilepsy," "one afflicted with the disease called gaṇḍamālā," "one with vitiligo," "a slanderer," "one possessed by the disturbance of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and so forth," "the blind," and "one who reviles the Veda"—these are to be excluded from offerings to the gods and the ancestors. || 3.161 ||
One who trains elephants, cattle, or camels; one who lives by the stars;
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare. (3.162)

"An elephant, cow, horse, or camel trainer" means one who trains elephants, cattle, horses, or camels; one who lives by the science of omens (*jyotiḥśāstra*); one who rears birds for sport after first selling them; and one who instructs others in combat—these are to be avoided in both cases [as bridegrooms and as guests]. (3.162)
One who digs channels, one who delights in obstructing them, a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees; 3.163.

Regarding "of streams": one who breaks the embankments that obstruct the flow of water, or one who leads it to another region by means of breaking them and so forth; one who performs their damming-up; one who lives by the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*); and even a messenger other than one dispatched by a king. One who plants trees for a price—and not for the sake of merit, since there is an injunction such as "one who plants ten mango trees does not go to hell"—[is also liable]. (3.163)
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by hawks, a defiler of maidens, one who is cruel, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for groups (gaṇas). (3.164)

"Śvakrīḍī" refers to one who plays with dogs, one who lives by performing sacrifices for others and similar activities, a reviler of maidens, one who delights in violence, or one who lives as a Śūdra. Alternatively, the reading is "vṛṣalaputra" (son of a low-born man). One who performs sacrifices to the Vināyakas and other deities on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight and so forth—these are to be avoided in both cases.
One who is devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, a constant beggar, one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous—[these are excluded]. (3.165)

"One devoid of proper conduct" means one who has abandoned such conduct as rising to greet others and so forth; "impotent" (*klība*) means lacking energy, since this term is traditionally applied to a eunuch; "one whose nature is always begging. Or, "one who lives on what is not produced by himself," meaning one who subsists [on gifts] even when other means of livelihood such as agriculture are available; "one with elephantiasis" (*ślīpadī*), meaning one whose single foot is swollen due to a specific disease and who is censured by the virtuous for some reason or another. In both cases, these persons are to be excluded from the assembly. (3.165)
A sheep-butcher, a buffalo-herder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and likewise a carrier of corpses—these must be avoided with great effort. (3.166)

A butcher of sheep and buffaloes, the husband of a remarried woman, and one who carries out the dead for a price—not for the sake of dharma—these must be avoided with effort in both places, because [the practice] is not enjoined by the Vedic scripture which states: "This indeed is the supreme austerity: that they carry the deceased to the forest. (3.166)
A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid both these lowest of the twice-born, whose conduct is censurable and who are unworthy of sitting in the row at a meal. (3.167)

"Regarding these": these are those of censurable conduct, such as thieves and the like, in this present life; and those who are one-eyed and so forth [are censured] in a previous birth, because it will be stated later that "they are born thus by the remainder of their karma. Therefore, a preeminent twice-born man who knows the scriptures should avoid these outcasts among Brahmins—who are unworthy of eating in the same row as qualified Brahmins—at rites for the gods (daiva) and for the ancestors (pitrya). (3.167)
For a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes. (3.168)

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": just as a grass-fire is extinguished by the oblation (*havis*) and is incapable of burning the oblation, and consequently the *homa* performed therein is fruitless, so too a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of Vedic study is like a grass-fire; for that reason, one should not give with reference to him, just as a *homa* is not performed in ashes. Since the prohibition of those who do not study is already established by the rule, "Gifts are to be given only to a *Śrotriya*," this statement is intended to permit those who are well-behaved and study the *Chandas* (Vedas)—even if they have physical defects such as being one-eyed—when it concerns rites for the gods (*daiva*). One should avoid one of reprehensible conduct and one who does not study; however, in the case of one who is well-behaved and studies, one need not take into account the presence of physical marks such as being one-eyed, which indicate the persistence of remnants of reprehensible karma acquired in a previous birth. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"But if he is joined with sacred mantras, even if he possesses bodily defects that would defile a company, Yama has declared him to be undefiled; indeed, he is a sanctifier of the company. (3.168)
I shall now describe in its entirety the future fruit that accrues to the giver who bestows gifts upon those unworthy of the company at rites for the gods or the ancestors. (3.169)

Regarding "giving to those unworthy of the company" (apaṅktyadāna): I shall fully explain that sin of the giver which results in the non-production of fruit when an oblation intended for the gods or ancestors is given to one who is unfit to sit in the company at a meal. 3.169.

Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, or likewise by those such as a younger brother who marries before his elder, and by others who are unworthy of the company at a meal—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.170)

When food intended for the gods or ancestors is eaten by those who have not observed the *sāvitra* and other vows for the purpose of Vedic study, as well as by others such as a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), thieves, and other persons unworthy of the company at a meal (*apāṅkteya*), the Rākṣasas consume it by virtue of a mere fragment of their own merit; it does not result in the desired fruit for the donor. From this very prohibition, it should be understood that there is also a prohibition against those who do not observe vows and who study forbidden texts. (3.170)

He who enters into marriage and the maintenance of the sacred fires while his elder brother remains unmarried is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*. (3.171)

Because the terms *parivetṛ* and so forth are not well known, he defines them with the phrase "the taking of a wife and the establishment of the *agnihotra*": he who, while his elder brother remains unmarried (*akṛtadāraka*), takes a wife and brings the domestic, Vedic, and Smārta fires is the *parivetṛ*; and the elder brother is to be understood as the *parivitti*. (3.171)
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him,
and she by whom he is superseded— all these go to hell, with the giver and the officiating priest as the fifth.

In this context, he states the consequence of violating this rule: "The elder brother who remains unmarried," and so forth. By means of which daughter the act of superseding occurs—the giver of that daughter, the officiating priest, and the one who instructs the *homa* for her marriage, with these five as the fifth—they all go to hell. (3.172)
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—even if she has been authorized by the sacred law—is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. (3.173)

Regarding the word *bhrātuḥ*: when a deceased brother’s wife has been lawfully appointed (*niyuktā*) according to the *dharma* to be described below, he who, abandoning the duty of appointment (*niyogadharma*), cultivates passion through the motive of lust, is an *agredidhiṣūpati*. This is because such an act is forbidden. Here, due to the requirements of the meter, the word *agra-* is not employed, just as in the case of the name Satyabhāmā. (3.173)
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa is one born while the husband is alive; the Golaka is one born when the husband is dead. (3.174)

Regarding the phrase "in the wives of others": from the wife of another, two kinds of sons are born, known as the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*. Among them, he who is born of a woman whose husband is still living is a *kuṇḍa*, and he who is born of a widow is a *golaka*. (3.174)
But those beings born in the field of another cause the offerings of *havya* and *kavya* given by the donors to perish, both in this world and after death. (3.175)

"But those born in another's field" refers to those born of another's wife, known as *kuṇḍas* and *golakas*. Because they do not serve any unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) and are merely designated as living beings, the offerings of food and drink given here in this world yield no fruit for the givers; there is an absence of the incidental result called fame in this life, and there is an absence of satisfaction for the gods and ancestors in the next world. Thus, such acts either remain fruitless or are as good as not performed. (3.175)
As many members of a worthy company as one who is unworthy to sit in their row beholds while they are eating, for so many does the foolish donor fail to obtain the fruit of his gift. (3.176)

"Apāṅktyas" refers to those unworthy of sitting in the row; even for them, as many as they see—meaning as many individuals as those unworthy of eating perceive—the donor, being ignorant, shall obtain no fruit there in that *śrāddha* or similar rite. Thus, the result of seeing those unworthy of the row has been stated. (3.176)
An eyeless man destroys the merit of ninety [gifts], a one-eyed man that of sixty, a leper that of a hundred, and one afflicted with a foul disease that of a thousand given by a donor. (3.177)

He states the specific distinctions regarding the blind and others with the word "by looking" (*vīkṣya*). Because the blind man lacks sight, his mere presence destroys the fruit of the meal belonging to ninety persons worthy of the *pāṅktya* assembly. Likewise, a one-eyed man [destroys the fruit] of sixty, a leper of a hundred, and one afflicted with skin disease of a thousand; this is the statement regarding the fruit resulting from the proximity of the blind and others. Precisely because of this variety in number, it is also understood that—based on the observation of the number sixty as mentioned in the phrase "if he is devoid of mantras"—there is a censurable inclination toward feeding those who are one-eyed and so forth, where each subsequent person results in a diminished number. Thus it is said: "In the absence of desire for that, there is a greater censure. (3.177)
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift.

"However many he touches": this refers to the number of Brāhmaṇas whom a Śūdra—acting as the officiant or instructor for a *pākayajña* and other such rites—touches with his limbs while they are seated on prepared seats strewn with sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Because of the prohibition against touching them individually, the fruit of the meal does not accrue to those whose number he equals by sitting in their row; that is to say, it is the fruit of feeding one who officiates for a Śūdra. For this very reason, it should be understood that there is a prohibition even for one listed among the groups forbidden from the head of the row. (3.178)
Even a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, having accepted a gift from him out of greed, goes quickly to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water. (3.179)

Even a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, having accepted gifts such as alms from the presence of one who officiates for a Śūdra out of greed, quickly meets destruction like water in an unbaked earthen vessel. This, though not the primary subject, has been mentioned here incidentally for the sake of brevity; otherwise, had it been treated elsewhere, the mention of "one who officiates for a Śūdra" would have had to be made separately. (3.179)
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood; what is given to a temple-attendant is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no foundation. (3.180)

"Regarding the seller of Soma": that which is given to a seller of Soma turns into dung for the sake of the giver's own food; and by eating that dung, the result would be rebirth in the animal realm—it is in this manner that it is stated. In the same way, pus and blood are also to be explained. "Lost" means it has come to destruction, and therefore it does not produce a fruit. "Unestablished" means it has found no footing, and therefore, due to having no basis, it is incapable of yielding a fruit. (3.180)
That which is given to a trader brings no fruit either in this world or the next;
likewise, a gift to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman is like an oblation poured into ashes.

Regarding the word "that": what is given to a merchant is not proclaimed here [as meritorious], nor does it bear fruit in the next world. And what is given to the son of a remarried woman (punarbhū) is fruitless, like an oblation poured into ashes; that gift should be known as such.
But regarding other unworthy persons who have been specified as those unfit for company (apaṅktya), the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone. (3.182)

Regarding the phrase "to others": the wise know that food given to those others—those from whom no fruit has been mentioned and who are outside the company of the *paṅkti*—becomes fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone. Alternatively, this should be explained as being like the statement, "for the seller of Soma, [the gift becomes] excrement. (3.182)

Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify the assembly when it has been defiled by one unworthy of the company—those best of the twice-born who are the sanctifiers of the row. (3.183)

Regarding the phrase "defiled by those unworthy of the company" (*apāṅktyopahatā*): listen in full to those Brāhmaṇas who purify the company that has been defiled by thieves and others seated at the line (*paṅkti*). Although this statement concerning the "purifiers of the company" (*paṅktipāvana*) might seem redundant—since it is impossible for thieves and the like to receive a *śrāddha* offering due to their exclusion from the company—it nevertheless serves a purpose: even when an examination has been conducted, there remains the possibility of a fault arising from secret knowledge; this [statement] is intended to prevent that. (3.183)
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions,
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

Regarding the term *agryāḥ*: among all the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, those who are foremost (*agre bhavāḥ*)—meaning that even while having mastered the Vedas, they perceive the Veda as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand—are called *agryāḥ*; these are to be understood as the sanctifiers of the company (*paṅktipāvanāḥ*). Likewise, it is said that the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgāni*) are "proclamations" (*pravacanāni*) because by means of them the meaning of the Vedas is proclaimed; among these, as before, those who are foremost—even in the absence of knowledge of the Veda itself—are sanctifiers of the company. Similarly, those whose lineage possesses the uninterrupted Veda are sanctifiers of the company. Previously, in the verse "he whose father is not learned in the Vedas" (1.136), the fitness for being fed was stated based on the father’s possession of Vedic learning; here, however, one is called a sanctifier of the company by virtue of the uninterrupted Veda throughout the entire lineage. (3.184)

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the Veda was given as a dowry, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman. || 3.185 ||

"Triṇāciketa": a Brāhmaṇa is also called *triṇāciketa* because of the quality of having performed the Vedic vow known as the *triṇāciketa-ādhvaryava*. "Pañcāgni" has already been explained. "Trisuparṇa" is so called because of his connection with the Vedic vow of the *Ṛgveda* known as the *trisuparṇa*, as before. He who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), such as grammar and the rest—by the phrase "in all the expositions" (*sarvapravacaneṣu*), the student of the auxiliaries was mentioned; by this [term], however, one who knows the auxiliaries is meant. "Jyeṣṭhasāmaga": the offspring of a wife married according to the *brāhma* rite, because of his connection with the vow of the Sāmavedic chant known as the *jyeṣṭhasāman*. (3.185)

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder of them, a student of sacred knowledge, one who gives a thousand [cows], and one who lives for a hundred years—these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly. (3.186)

"One who knows the meaning of the Veda" (*vedārthavit*): even without [the study of] the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), he who through his wisdom understands the meaning of the Veda—whether as a reciter, a teacher, or an expounder—and who is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) for the sake of dharma and the meaning of the Veda; and because of the Vedic vision that "cows are indeed the mothers of sacrifice," one who here also gives a thousand cows because of the Veda being the root, and who is a giver of much; likewise, one who is a hundred years old—these Brāhmaṇas are to be understood as "purifiers of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*) when they possess these qualities, according to the rule: "Gifts are to be given only to a *śrotriya*. (3.186)
On the day before or on the very day when the Śrāddha rite is to take place,
he should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities previously described.

"On the previous day": when the rite of *śrāddha* is to be performed, if there is a concern regarding the employment of women, one should invite on the day preceding the *śrāddha* day—or, if that is not possible, on the following day—the aforementioned Brahmins with humility; provided they are not fewer than three (though not necessarily exactly three), since it has been stated that even a single person may perform each of the rites. || 3.187 ||
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedic hymns, and that [rite] shall be his śrāddha. (3.188)

"Being invited": A Brāhmaṇa who has been invited to a *śrāddha* and who observes the restraints and observances regarding the cessation of sexual intercourse with women should remain so from the time of the invitation until the day and night of the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, he should not study the Vedas, except for those recitations that are mandatory. And the performer of the *śrāddha* should likewise observe these same rules. (3.188)
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit.

"Those who have been invited": the ancestors approach those various twice-born men who have been invited, coming into their presence in an invisible form; they follow them as they move, like the vital breaths; and when the Brahmins are seated, they sit down near them. Therefore, one who has been invited must remain self-controlled. This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the preceding injunction. 3.189.
But when the best of the twice-born has been duly invited for the offerings to the gods or the ancestors, that sinner who somehow neglects them shall go to the state of a pig. (3.190)

Regarding the term *ketita*: a Brāhmaṇa who has been invited for offerings to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*) in accordance with the boundaries of the scriptures, having accepted the invitation, becomes guilty of transgressing those rules if he does not eat by any means; such a person goes to the state of a pig in another birth. In the reading *pāpaśūkaraḥ*, it means a "sinful pig," that is, a village pig. (3.190)
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a Śūdra woman, incurs all whatever evil deed the giver has committed. (3.191)

Regarding the term "invited" (*āmantrita*): this is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Gautama, which states, "On that day, he should observe celibacy. As for the phrase "even a *vṛṣalī*, when desiring him, causes the husband to waver," here the word *vṛṣalī* refers even to a Brāhmaṇa woman. This is merely an exposition on the arising of sin, stating that if one, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, indulges with her according to the sexual union of man and woman, he incurs all the sin of the donor. Otherwise, if the donor were sinless, there would be no connection to the evil deed. In that case, this [penance] is not enjoined as an expiation for the donor by which he might be released from the evil deed. (3.191)
Free from anger, devoted to purity, always practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons— these highly fortunate ancestors are the ancient deities.

"Free from anger" means those devoid of wrath, who are devoted to purity through gentle speech and other such virtues, who always abstain from sexual union with women, who have laid down their weapons, who are great-souled, and who are the ancestors (pitṛs) whose nature is that of primordial deities; therefore, the Brahmins at a *śrāddha* ceremony should be free from anger and similar vices. 3.192.
Since the origin of all these [deities] is entirely from these [five elements], learn now those rules by which they are to be worshipped. (3.193)

Regarding the phrase "because": listen to from whom these ancestors originated; who the ancestors are; by which [classes], such as Brāhmaṇas and others; and by what sacrifices and observances—that is, by the ritual acts prescribed in the scriptures—they exist as they do. 3.193.
The sons of all those sages, beginning with Marīci, who were the offspring of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha, are recorded as the groups of Pitṛs.

Regarding the word "of Manu": those sons of Manu, the offspring of Hiraṇyagarbha, such as Marīci and the others—as stated in the passage beginning, "Marīci, Atri, Āṅgirasa," and so forth—it is recorded by Manu and the others that these foremost ancestors, beginning with Somapa, belong to all those sages, Marīci and the rest. (3.194)
The sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are the ancestors of the gods, the offspring of Marīci.

Regarding the phrase "the sons of Virāṭ": the sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are the Pitṛs of the Sādhyas; they are the gods called Agniṣvāttas, the sons of Marīci, renowned in the world. (3.195)
The Barhiṣads, sons of Atri, are remembered as the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.

Regarding the phrase "of the Daityas, Dānavas, and Yakṣas": the ancestors known as the Barhiṣads, sons of Atri, are recorded as the ancestors of the Daityas and others whose divisions were described in the first chapter. (3.196)
Among the Brahmins they are named Somapas; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaiśyas, Ājyāpas; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins. (3.197)
Regarding the name "Somapas": the ancestors of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are, respectively, named Somapas, Havirbhujs, Ājyapas, and Sukālins. (3.197)
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha. (3.198)

"Drinkers of Soma": the ancestors of the Brāhmaṇa are the Soma-drinkers, the sons of Kavi Bhr̥gu. The ancestors of the Kṣatriya are the Havis-eaters (Havirbhujas), the possessors of oblations (Haviṣmantas), the sons of Aṅgiras. The ancestors of the Vaiśya are the Ghee-drinkers (Ājyapas), the sons of Pulastya. The ancestors of the Śūdra are the Sukālins, the sons of Vasiṣṭha. (3.198)
One should designate the *anagnidagdhas*, the *agnidagdhas*, the *kāvyas*, the *barhiṣads*, as well as the *agniṣvāttas* and the *saumyas*, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins. (3.199)

"Those not burnt by fire": one should know that the *anagnidagdha*, the *agnidagdha*, the *kāvyabarhiṣad*, and those known as the *agniṣvātta* and *saumya* are other types of ancestors (*pitṛ*) belonging exclusively to the Brahmins. Such names for the ancestors are well-known in the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
Regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed,
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite.

Regarding the word "ya" (those): those groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa) mentioned here, beginning with the Soma-drinkers, who constitute the primary [ancestors], are to be understood in this context of saṃsāra as being the very fathers who are the sons and grandsons [of others]. (3.200)
From the sages the ancestors were born; from the ancestors, gods and humans; and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—was produced in due order. (3.201)

"From the sages [come] the ancestors. This means that from those named Marīci and the others, there arose those known as the Somapās and so forth; and from them, the gods and Dānavas were born. From the gods, the entire world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, was produced in due order. Thus, because the ancestors—such as the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—are born from the aforementioned [sages], it should be understood that the mention of the groups of ancestors beginning with the Somapās is intended to demonstrate that when they are honored, those [ancestors] are also honored, and thereby to praise the worship of the ancestors under discussion. (3.201)
Even water given with faith in silver vessels, or in those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible results for them. (3.202)

Regarding the phrase "with silver [vessels]": even water given with devotion using silver vessels or vessels containing silver for those ancestors becomes a cause for inexhaustible happiness. How much more so, then, excellent meat and the like, or ghee and the like? This is the specific fruit resulting from the excellence of the recipient of the gift. 3.202.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitr-karya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daiva-karya);
for it is traditionally taught that the rite for the gods is the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors. (3.203)

Regarding the phrase "on account of rites for the gods": it is taught that the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*) must be performed especially by the twice-born on account of the divine (*daiva*), that is, from the perspective of the divine rite. For that [divine rite] is primary; since the divine rite is traditionally held to precede the rite for the ancestors and to complete it, it thus possesses the status of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the ancestral rite, just as the latter completes it. (3.203)
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the *rakṣas* plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection. (3.204)

Regarding the word "of them": it serves as a protection for the ancestors. According to the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, one should first invite a Brāhmaṇa with reference to the Viśvedevas. For the Rākṣasas snatch away a Śrāddha that is shown [only] to the Rākṣasas; since the divine rite for the ancestors is a protection for the ancestral rite, therefore [one should invite first]. (3.204)
One should seek that which begins and ends with the divine; it should not begin and end with the ancestors.
For one who seeks that which begins and ends with the ancestors perishes quickly, along with his lineage. (3.205)

Regarding the phrase "beginning and ending with the gods": one who attempts [the rite] beginning and ending with the ancestors (pitr) perishes quickly along with his lineage. Therefore, one should perform the Śrāddha beginning with the gods and ending with the gods; for by performing it beginning and ending with the ancestors—starting and concluding with the ancestors—one is destroyed swiftly together with one's progeny. (3.205)
One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung, and one should carefully ensure that it slopes toward the south. || 3.206 ||

"Pure" means: one should smear with cow dung a place that is undisturbed and not crowded by people. Alternatively, if it is not naturally sloping toward the south, one should then make it so through deliberate effort. (3.206)
In open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and indeed in secluded places, the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered. (3.207)

Regarding the phrase "in open spaces": the ancestors are always satisfied by a *śrāddha* or similar offering given in places that are pure by nature, such as the sandy banks of rivers and the like, and in secluded regions; and [they are satisfied] in that very place. (3.207)
When separate seats provided with sacrificial grass have been prepared, he should cause those Brahmins, who have duly sipped water, to sit down upon them. (3.208)

Regarding the phrase "on seats": once individual seats have been arranged separately on the ground, he should cause those previously invited—who have properly performed their ritual bathing and sipping of water—to sit down. 3.208.
Having seated those irreproachable Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the deities.

"Having seated them": having seated those blameless Brahmins upon their seats, he should thereafter worship them, beginning with the gods and the Brahmins, with fragrant substances such as saffron, garlands, incense, and so forth. || 3.209 ||
Having brought water for them, along with sesame seeds and purifiers (pavitra), the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the rite in the fire. (3.210)

Regarding the word "of them": having given water mixed with *darbha* grass and sesame seeds to those Brahmins, and being permitted by them according to the form prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*—namely, when they say, "I shall perform the fire-rite (*agnau karavāṇi*)," and [he asks], "I will do so," and they reply, "Do it"—being thus authorized by the Brahmins, he should perform the oblation (*homa*) in the fire as will be described hereafter. The mention of "Brahmins" is for the purpose of indicating the twice-born (*dvija*), since all three [classes] are under discussion in this context.
Having first performed the *āyana* (invocation) for Agni, Soma,
and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors according to the rule by the offering of oblations.

Regarding the word "of Agni": although Soma and Yama are mentioned as a dual compound (*dvandva*), because Agni is not mentioned [in that specific context], there are two deities. Thus, having first performed the satiation of Agni and the others through the offering of oblations according to the rules—such as *agnaye svāhā*, *somāya svāhā*, and *yamāya svāhā*—along with the ritual sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should afterwards proceed with the feeding of Brahmins and other rites. (3.211)
But in the absence of fire, one should place the offering directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras. (3.212)
