Regarding the phrase "in the absence of fire": since it is prescribed that for one who lacks a sacred fire—such as one who has not been initiated, one who has been initiated but has not yet returned home from study, one who has not taken a wife, or one whose wife has died—the śrāddha on the anniversary of death and other such occasions should be performed with the hand of a Brāhmaṇa in the absence of the *aupāsana* fire; for those Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas declare, "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the very same as the fire. (3.212)
The ancients speak of these best of the twice-born as gods at the *śrāddha* ceremony—those who are free from anger, easily propitiated, and devoted to the nourishment of the world. (3.213)

Regarding the phrase "free from anger": Manu and others speak of these Brāhmaṇas—who are free from anger, devoid of wrath, and who perform their own worship and other duties—as the recipients of the Śrāddha offering, because they serve as the means for the prosperity of the world according to the maxim, "The oblation cast into the fire [reaches the gods]. Therefore, because they are equal to deities, the aforementioned explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the ritual rule applies to their hands. 3.213.

Having performed the entire circumambulation with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apassavya) around the fire, he should pour water upon the ground with his hand in the apassavya manner. 3.214.

"Apasavyam" means as follows: whatever sequence of duties must be performed at the fire—such as sprinkling water around it, spreading the sacrificial grass, and offering oblations—all that should be done with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), following the procedure for rites for the ancestors (pitṛ-karman), and directed toward the south. Having thus performed these acts directed toward the north, he should pour water with his right hand in the *apasavya* position, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, upon the ground that serves as the support for the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). 3.214.
Then, having formed three balls from that remainder of the sacrificial food, he, being composed,
should offer them facing south according to the very same rite prescribed for the water libation.

"Three. Therefore, having offered the oblation intended for the fire-offerings (agnyādi-homa), one should form three balls from the remnants of what was offered. Then, according to the water-rite (audaka-vidhi), with the right hand, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors), with an undistracted mind and facing south, one should offer them upon those *darbha* grasses—since it is observed in the scripture that "one should wipe that hand [on the grasses]" (*taṃ hastaṃ nimṛjyāt*)—one should place them on the *darbha* grasses. For this very reason, one should also offer the water on the same *darbha* grasses as were previously mentioned as the support for the balls. 3.125.

Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) there according to the rule with self-restraint, he should wipe that hand upon those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāginaḥ).

He should offer those balls of rice upon the other balls, preceded by the rites prescribed by the author of the Sūtras, such as the offering of collyrium, ointment, and clothing; having done so, he should then perform the rubbing of the hands upon the Darbha grass that served as the base for those balls, because of the Vaiṣṇava tradition which states: "Upon the roots of the Darbha grass, he should apply that hand [to the remnants] for the satisfaction of the three ancestors preceding the great-grandfather, who partake of the scrapings and receive the portions of food adhering to the hand. (3.216)
Having sipped water, turned toward the north, and slowly restrained his breath three times, he should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras. (3.217)

"Having sipped water and turned away from the water": having touched that [water] again after sipping, and having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to his ability while facing north, he should pay homage to the six seasons with the formula "Salutation to Spring" (*vasantāya namaḥ*). Then, having performed the rites for the ancestors with the mantras beginning with "Salutation to you, O ancestors" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*), he should turn around and, facing south—according to the *Gṛhya* tradition which states "having turned around"—he should pay homage. (MDh 3.217)
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the rice-balls;
then, with a concentrated mind, he should smell those rice-balls in the order they were placed. (3.218)

"Water": he should again pour out the water remaining from the darbha-grass used as a support for the *piṇḍas* near the *piṇḍas*, reciting the [appropriate] verse. And he should smell those *piṇḍas* with an undistracted mind, in the very same order in which they were offered. 3.218.
Having taken very small portions from each of the balls of food in successive order,
he should first cause those seated brahmins to eat according to the prescribed rule.

"From the rice-balls (piṇḍas)": having taken a very small portion from the rice-balls according to the sequence of the ancestral rice-balls, he should lead those same Brahmins—who were seated for the sake of the ancestors and others—in accordance with the rule. At the time of eating, he should feed them in the proper order, before [they eat] from any other vessel. (3.219)
While his father is still living, however, he should offer the oblation to his ancestors alone;
or else, like a Brahmin, he may cause his own father to partake in that Śrāddha.

Regarding the term "while he is living": as long as the father is alive, one should perform the *śrāddha* for the three ancestors beginning with the grandfather, but not for the father. Alternatively, in the place of the father, one should feed that very person—one's own father—at the *śrāddha*, and one should feed two Brahmins for the grandfather and great-grandfather and offer the two funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*). (3.220)
But he whose father is deceased while his grandfather is still living should, having pronounced his father’s name, pronounce the name of his great-grandfather. (3.221)

"But whose father has passed away" (*pitā yasya tu vṛttaḥ*): the word "or" (*vā*) refers to the alternative case where the father is still living. However, for one whose father is deceased but whose grandfather is living, he should mention the name of his father when performing the feeding of Brahmins, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and so forth; he should then perform the *śrāddha* for both of them—namely, for the great-grandfather and for the father. As Viṣṇu says: "He whose father is deceased, having placed the rice-ball for his father, should give [rice-balls] to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather. (3.221)
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
"or, being duly permitted, he himself may perform it at his will. (3.222)

Regarding the term *pitāmaha*: in place of the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*), one may instead feed the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*). One should perform the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) and the feeding of Brahmins for both the father and the paternal grandfather. Alternatively, if the father or the paternal grandfather is living, one should be permitted by them with the words, "I shall not eat; do as you wish," and then proceed oneself according to one's preference. An alternative to the aforementioned positions is stated in the *Gṛhyasūtra*: "For one whose father is living, there is no commencement of the rites; [the rite] ends with the oblation (*homa*). (3.222)
Having placed the *tilodaka* together with the *pavitra* grass into their hands, he should offer them the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them. (3.223)

"Of them" means: having given water with sesame seeds and darbha grass into the hands of those Brahmins, he should offer the "fore-portion of the pinda," as indicated by the phrase "a very small portion from the pindas," saying in due order: "May this svadhā be for the father," and so forth. (3.223)
Having himself taken the increased portion of food with both hands, he should slowly place it near the Brahmins while mentally offering it to the ancestors. (3.224)
"With both hands" means: having taken the vessel full of food with both hands and remembering the ancestors, one should place it slowly near the Brahmins for the purpose of serving. || 3.224 ||
The food that is brought forth, released from both hands—that the Asuras, with their evil minds, suddenly snatch away. (3.225)

Regarding the phrase "by both": when food that has not been grasped with both hands is brought near a Brāhmaṇa or offered to him, the Asuras—the enemies of the gods who possess wicked intentions—seize it. Therefore, one should not bring or serve food with only one hand. (3.225)
Being self-restrained and composed, he should first place upon the ground itself the various condiments such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey. (3.226)

Regarding "the condiments": one should place the side dishes such as soups, and the pourings such as milk and so forth, separately according to their primary nature and as instructed, being restrained, pure, composed, and single-minded; one should set them down on the ground itself and nowhere else, so that they do not become scattered. 3.226.
Various kinds of food and edibles, roots and fruits, as well as savory meats and fragrant drinks. || 3.227 ||

Various kinds of food to be chewed and food to be swallowed, as well as delicious fruits; likewise, food to be chewed that is crisp and hard such as sweetmeats (modaka), and food to be swallowed such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and other varieties, as well as roots, fruits, meats dear to the heart, and fragrant drinks and the like—these should be placed upon the ground itself. (3.227)
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great composure, being purified and extolling all its qualities. (3.228)

"Having brought all this near": having brought all this—food and so forth—into the presence of the Brāhmaṇas, he should announce all its qualities, such as sweetness and smoothness, saying, "This is sweet," "This is smooth," and so on; with a focused mind, he should serve it slowly over a long time according to what is appropriate, but he should not serve everything all at once. (3.228)
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it. (3.229)

"Without tears": one should not weep, nor express anger, nor speak untruths, nor touch the food with the foot; nor should one discard it by repeatedly tossing it up. One should not speak falsehood out of anger, because both anger and falsehood are contrary to human goals and are prohibited; their instruction here is for the purpose of making them auxiliary elements of the *śrāddha* rite. (3.229)
Tears send the hungry ghosts (preta) away; anger, enemies; falsehood, dogs; the touch of one's feet, the rākṣasa demons; and shaking [the feet], evildoers. (3.230)

"It causes tears to go to the *pretas*. This means that anger causes the tears shed during the performance of a *śrāddha* to reach the *pretas*, who are a specific class of beings; falsehood [reaches] dogs; touching with the foot [reaches] *rakṣases*; and shaking [the head] [reaches] evildoers. Therefore, one should not do these things. (3.230)
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without stinginess; and he should engage in discourses on the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors. (3.231)

Regarding the word "yad" (whatever): and as for "brahmodyāś ca" (and Vedic riddles), whatever food, condiments, and so forth there may be, he should offer each of those while remaining free from fault. Likewise, he should perform the description of the Supreme Self, meritorious narratives, and hymns—whatever is intended for the ancestors. 3.231.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause the Vedic study, the treatises on Dharma, as well as narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and supplementary texts to be recited. (3.232)

"One should cause the Veda to be recited at a rite for the ancestors (pitrya). This means that at a *śrāddha*, one should cause the Brahmins to hear the Vedas, the *Mānava-dharma-śāstra* and other legal treatises (*śāstras*), the narrative legends (*ākhyānas*) such as those concerning Suparṇa and Mitrāvaruṇa which are separately proclaimed in the Vedas, the *Mahābhārata* and other works spoken by Vāyu and others, and the *Śivasaṃkalpa* and similar hymns. (3.232)
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and by praising their virtues. (3.233)

Being joyful, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them food slowly; he should repeatedly encourage them with food and by praising its qualities. Having become joyful through various pleasant words and the like, he should satisfy the Brahmins and feed them without haste with milk-rice, cakes filled with ghee, and other such foods; he should repeatedly prompt them, saying, "Please accept this. (3.233)
One should diligently feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.

"Even a daughter's son who is observing a vow": one should always diligently feed a daughter's son at a *śrāddha*, even if he is a student (*brahmacārin*). Since the daughter's son is already prescribed among the secondary options (*anukalpa*), this statement regarding "diligence" indicates that he must not be excluded from among those secondary options (it clarifies his essential status). One should provide a well-prepared and beautiful seat; it is not the daughter's son alone to whom one should give it, but rather to all the Brahmins, according to such statements as, "There are three purifiers at a *śrāddha*" (3.235). And one should scatter sesame seeds upon the ground. (3.234)
At a Śrāddha, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a blanket made of goat’s hair, and sesame seeds.
And in this regard, they praise three other qualities: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste. (3.235)

Because it says "three": the three [relatives] beginning with the daughter's son are pure for the *śrāddha*, and there are indeed three other things—namely, purity, freedom from anger, and trust—which they especially desire at the *śrāddha*. (3.235)
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent;
nor should the twice-born speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering when questioned by the giver.

"Excessively hot": one should offer hot food with faith to the foremost of the twice-born, except for fruits, roots, drinks, and curds; for such is the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha, and thus one should give everything else while it is hot. And the Brāhmaṇas should eat with their speech restrained. Even when asked by the donor about the qualities of the food—whether it is "delicious" or "not delicious"—they should not speak of them, not even by means of gestures, because the restraint of speech has been prescribed (and because the praise of fire has also been mentioned). 3.236.
As long as there is steam from the food, as long as they eat with speech restrained, so long do the ancestors eat—until the qualities of the sacrificial offering have been mentioned. (3.237)

As long as there is heat in the food—so long as warmth remains in the food, O wise ones—and as long as they eat in silence and do not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering, so long do the ancestors consume that food through the mouth of the Brahmin. (3.237)
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats wearing shoes—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.238)

Regarding the word "yad" (which): if a Brāhmaṇa eats food while his head is covered with a turban or the like, or likewise if he faces south, or has his feet shod with sandals, the Rākṣasas consume that food, not the ancestors. Therefore, this must be avoided.
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog, a woman in her menses, and a eunuch—these must not look at twice-born men while they are eating. (3.239)

And the action should be such that even a Caṇḍāla, a boar, and a cock [are excluded]; for at the time of feeding the twice-born, one should remove from there a Caṇḍāla, a boar, a village pig, a cock, a woman in her courses, and eunuchs. (3.239)
Whatever is looked upon by these at the giving of a house, at a meal, or at an offering to the gods or the ancestors, that goes astray from its proper course. (3.240)

Regarding the phrase "because [it is] a *homa*": in the case of a *homa* such as the *agnihotra*, in giving, in feeding Brāhmaṇas for the sake of merit (*dharma*), and in offerings to gods (*havya*) and ancestors (*kavya*), whatever rite is observed by Caṇḍālas and others—that which is performed for whatever purpose—does not accomplish that purpose. (3.240)
The pig destroys [the merit] by its smell, the cock by the wind from its wings, the dog by the casting of its gaze, and one born of a low caste by touch. (3.241)

"By means of the nose": having smelled that food and so forth, the pig renders that act fruitless. The cock [renders it fruitless] by the wind from its wings; the dog also [renders it fruitless] by the gaze of its eyes. An "avaravarṇaja" is one born of a low caste (*avaravarṇa*), namely a *śūdra*, to a Brāhmaṇa woman—a *caṇḍāla*. This [prohibition] applies to one who performs a *śrāddha* on a riverbank and such places, because of the suspicion of impurity arising there from contact with wind. It does not refer to the giver, nor is it concerned with the touching of the food and so forth, for if it were, the mention of food would be redundant, since the prohibition of a *caṇḍāla*'s touch is already established by general rule. Since such a suspicion of redundancy exists, those who say that this [mention of food] is intended to prohibit the touch of a *śūdra* are incorrect; for it is meaningful according to the reasoning already stated. Furthermore, the *śūdra* is not denoted by the word "avaraja. Moreover, this is a restatement of the natural disposition of the pig and others, mentioned here as a specific detail of the subject at hand, and not because they are defiled apart from this particular action. (3.241)
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the donor, or one with deficient or redundant limbs—one should remove him as well. (3.242)

"Regarding the term *khañja*: a *khañja* is one deficient in a foot; a *kāṇa* is one deficient in an eye. Or, the *sāsa* of a giver refers to a Śūdra, because of his status as a servant. By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that any other Śūdra, or one who has deformed nails, is a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍaka*), and so forth—he too should be driven away from that place. (3.242)
When a Brahmin or even a mendicant has approached for the sake of food, he should, with the permission of the Brahmins, honor him according to his ability. (3.243)

"A Brahmin or a mendicant" (3.243): A donor, having been permitted by the Brahmins invited to the *śrāddha*, should honor with a gift of food according to his capacity any Brahmin appearing in the form of a guest or any other mendicant who has arrived at that time for the purpose of eating.
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have finished eating.

Regarding the term *sārvavarṇika*: having gathered together all kinds of food and drink and moistened them with water, one should cast them upon the ground in front of the Brāhmaṇas who have finished eating; for, according to the indicative mark (liṅga) of what will be stated later—“and that scattering which [is done] on the *darbha* grass”—one should discard them upon *darbha* grass. (3.244)

The food-remnants and whatever scattering of grains occurs during the rites shall be the portion for those who have died an untimely death, for those who have perished without performing the sacraments, and for women who have left their families. (3.245)

Regarding the phrase "for those who have died without the funeral rites" (*asaṃskṛtapramītānām*): for deceased women of noble family whose cremation rites have been prohibited by such injunctions as, "The rite of cremation with fire shall not be performed for her" (GDh 5.69), and for those who have left their families, the portion shall be that which is scattered upon the *darbha* grass—the leavings contained in the vessel. The specific mention of "women of noble family" (*kulayoṣitām*) is used here just as in the expression "prepared alms" (*saṃskṛtaṃ bhaikṣam*). 3.245.
They declare that the food remaining on the ground after the meal belongs as its share to the group of servants who are straightforward and free from deceit during the ancestral rite.
Regarding "the remnants": Manu and others declare that whatever leavings have fallen upon the ground constitute the allotted share for a group of servants who are neither crooked nor lazy. (3.246)
Until the rite of sapindikarana for a deceased member of the twice-born caste has been performed,
one should offer a śrāddha meal without an invitation to the gods and present a single pinda.

"Until the *āsapiṇḍakriyā* rite": for a twice-born person who has recently died, the basis for the *āsapiṇḍakriyā* must be performed on the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha*) and so forth. It is not to be done like the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), where the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is made together with the ancestors of the previous generations. What then? One should feed a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the *śrāddha*, providing food devoid of the *vaiśvadeva* offerings and the feeding of Brāhmaṇas [for other purposes]. One should give a single *piṇḍa* to that very person. Therefore, one should continue feeding Brāhmaṇas until that point. This has been established in detail in the *Smṛtimañjarī* and the *Ṛjupañjikā*; however, for fear of making this book too voluminous, it is not elaborated upon here. (3.247)
But once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the Dharma, the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) using this very same procedure. (3.248)

Regarding the phrase "also in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*": because of the inclusion of the word "his" (*asya*), it refers to the deceased who has recently died and is the recipient of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed according to the established rules of the scriptures, it is as stated by Yājñavalkya (1.253):
"One should prepare four vessels joined with fragrant water and sesame seeds;
for the sake of the *argha* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*)."
With the two verses beginning "ye samānā," one should perform the remainder as previously described;
and as stated by Uśanas:
"One should always perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha according to the Pārvaṇa rite."
"And one should perform another [rite] separately according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
Likewise, it has been stated by Śātātapa:
"One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha preceded by the [deities of the] *daiva* rite."
"One should invoke the ancestors there and likewise designate the deceased (preta).
And so it is stated in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"Having offered the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the ancestors, one should afterwards offer [one] to the deceased at the side."
"Having divided that ball of rice into three parts in the proper sequence, one should place them upon the three balls; this is the rule for the sweeping."

The vessel for the *preta* should not be poured entirely into the vessels for the ancestors; rather, because of the specific instruction regarding the *preta*-brāhmaṇa, some [water] must be left there for the sake of his *arghya*. This is because it is common property, like the use of undivided wealth among brothers; therefore, the *arghya* must be offered. Thus, as for what has been stated by some—that in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite there is a feeding of five brāhmaṇas, that the *arghya*-vessel belonging to the great-grandfather and the father is used, and that the *piṇḍa* is divided threefold—that is incorrect, precisely because it contradicts the stated scriptural texts. When this has been performed according to the scriptures, the sons must perform this same procedure every year on the anniversary of death in the absence [of the father].

Objection: Since a pronoun refers to what is proximate, it is logical that the extension (*atideśa*) from the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite applies here by the phrase "by this very [rite]. Reply: It is not so; for by specifying a distinction in this way, one would not be providing an instruction based on the sacred scripture (*śāstra*). This rule applies to the *asapiṇḍa-kriyā* (the rite before the sapinda-connection); however, once the *sahapiṇḍa-kriyā* has been performed, this [other] rule applies. Therefore, it is logical that this is an instruction regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsya*). Thus it is stated in the *Smṛtimañjarī* concerning the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) following the sapinda-connection. This is investigated in detail in the *Ṛjupañjikā*. (3.248)
That fool who, having eaten at a śrāddha feast, gives the leavings to a Śūdra,
goes headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell.

Regarding the term *śrāddha*: that fool who gives the remnants of food from a *śrāddha* meal to a Śūdra goes headfirst into the hell named Kālasūtra. This prohibition is established because, although it might otherwise follow that food remnants should be given due to his being a virtuous (*sat*) Śūdra who has sought refuge [with the donor], this specific restriction is made. (3.249)
If one who has partaken of a funeral feast approaches the bed of a low-caste woman on that same day, his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement. (3.250)

Regarding the phrase "one who eats at a *śrāddha*": for one who has been invited to a *śrāddha*, celibacy (*brahmacarya*) was previously prescribed prior to the meal; by this [verse], however, that same requirement is stated for the period following the meal, lasting for a day and night (*ahorātra*). And the term *vṛṣalī* has already been explained. For him who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, engages in sexual union with a woman during that day and night, his ancestors remain in her excrement for a month. Therefore, such is the nature of his connection to this transgression. (3.250)
Having asked, "Was it well-tasted?", he should then have those who are satisfied rinse their mouths; once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you be happy on all sides."

Having asked those Brāhmaṇas who are satisfied, "Was it well-savored?"—that is, having thus asked them with a blessing for prosperity—he should then cause them to sip water. And once they have performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should dismiss them with the words, "Stay here" or "Stay at your own home. || 3.251 ||
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhā astu.
For in all rites for the ancestors, the utterance of "svadhā" is indeed the supreme blessing.

"They should utter the word 'svadhā'": immediately after granting permission, the Brāhmaṇas should say "svadhā" to the giver; for in all ancestral rites—whether involving prepared food, unprepared food, śrāddha, or water libations—the utterance of the word *svadhā* is the supreme blessing. (3.252)
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food;
he should act according to what they say, having been authorized by the twice-born. (3.253)

"Then," [it is said]: after the Brahmins who have eaten together have uttered the word *svadhā*, he should offer the remaining food according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Having been granted permission by those twice-born ones with the words, "Let this be done with this food," he should employ it exactly as they have directed. (3.253)
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "it is well-savored" (svaditam); at a rite for cattle, "it is well-cooked" (suśṛtam);
at a rite for prosperity, "it is excellent" (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods, "it is pleasing" (rucitam).

At a rite for the ancestors (pitrya), one should say "it is well-tasted" (svaditam); in a cow-pen, "it is cooked" (śṛtam). Even by another person who has arrived at the time of the śrāddha, one should say "it is well-tasted" in the midst of the herd of cows, and "it is cooked" or "it is prepared. At weddings and other such occasions, for the sake of the deities, one should say "it is pleasing" (rocitam). 3.254.
The afternoon, as well as darbha grass, the preparation of the site, sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent brahmins—these are the perfections in rites for the ancestors. (3.255)

"The afternoon, as well as the *darbha* grasses," and so forth. "The afternoon" is for the purpose of the *viṣṭara* (seat); "the *darbha* grasses" are for the preparation of the site; "the cleansing of the house" refers to the purification of the dwelling with lime, cow dung, and so on; "sesame seeds" are for scattering on the ground and other such purposes; "liberality" (*sṛṣṭi*) is the distribution of food without miserliness; "refinement" (*mṛṣṭi*) is the preparation of the food; and "eminent Brahmins"—these are the excellences (*sampadaḥ*) in a *śrāddha*. This statement is intended to indicate their superior quality over other constituent elements. (3.255)

Darbha grass, the strainer, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial foods (haviṣya), as well as whatever else was previously mentioned as pure—these should be understood as the requisites for the oblation. 3.256.

Regarding "darbhas": *darbhas* are for the purpose of the seat (*viṣṭara*) and so forth; the *darbha* used as a purifier (*pavitra*) is taught separately because of its preeminence. The morning time, sacrificial foods such as the grains of sages (*munyanna*), and all that was previously mentioned as purifying acts pertaining to the site—this much alone constitutes the accomplishment of the ritual action (*arthakarman*). (3.256)
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is unseasoned, and salt that is not alkaline—these are by their very nature called sacrificial oblations (havis). (3.257)

Regarding the phrase "foods of sages": forest food, milk, Soma, and meat that is not too pungent—provided it is salt free from additives such as *biḍa* salt—and rock salt (*saindhava*), are declared by Manu and others to be sacrificial oblations (*havis*) by their very nature. (3.257)
Having dismissed those Brahmins according to the prescribed rules with self-restraint, he should, looking toward the southern direction, entreat these boons from the ancestors: || 3.258 ||

"Having dismissed them": having dismissed those Brahmins, being pure and single-minded, looking toward the southern direction, he should pray to the ancestors for these desired objects which are about to be mentioned. || 3.258 ||
"May our donors increase, as well as our Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (3.259)

"May we be givers"—meaning, "may faith not depart from us, and may there be much for us to give"; "may many in our family be of a generous disposition"; "may the Vedas increase through the forms of study, teaching, comprehension, and sacrifice"; "may progeny, such as sons and so forth, increase"; "may our faith regarding the offerings to gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*) not depart"; and "may there be much for us to give"—meaning, "may there be abundant wealth for us for the purpose of giving. (3.259)

Having thus performed the offering of the water libations, he should immediately thereafter cause those rice-balls to be eaten by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire, or else he should cast them into the water. (3.260)

"Thus. Having thus performed the offering of the *piṇḍas* according to the procedure beginning with "But three from that remnant of the sacrificial food" (3.215), one should immediately thereafter—following the request for the boon—cause one of the cows, Brahmins, or birds to eat those *piṇḍas*, or else cast them into fire or water. (3.260)
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes only afterwards; others feed them to birds, or cast them into water or fire. (3.261)

Regarding the "offering of the rice-ball" (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*): some teachers perform the giving of the rice-ball before the feeding of the Brahmins; others have it eaten by birds. This is an optional alternative for the preliminary procedure. Furthermore, others maintain that the throwing into fire or water and the eating by birds are themselves optional alternatives. (3.261)
Then, a devoted wife who is the lawful partner, intent upon the worship of her ancestors and desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*. (3.262)

Regarding the term *pativratā dharmapatnī*: she whose vow (*vrata*) is that "in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, my husband alone is to be served by me through the actions of mind, speech, and body" is a *pativratā*, a lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). She must be the first-married wife, of the same caste (*savarṇā*), endowed with faith (*śraddhāvatī*), and desiring sons. From among those rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), he should eat the middle rice-ball (*madhyama-piṇḍa*) properly, using the mantra prescribed by the author of the Sūtras beginning with "O ancestors, place the embryo" (*ādhatta pitaro garbham*). (3.262)
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence, wealthy, possessed of progeny, virtuous, and likewise righteous. (3.263)

"O Long-lived One! [Thus addressed, she] gives birth to a son endowed with such qualities as these: one who delights in the practice of dharma, possesses the quality called *sattva* which will be described in the twelfth chapter, is long-lived, renowned, possessed of the memory of past events, endowed with wealth such as gold and other riches, and having a continuous lineage. 3.263.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide for his kinsmen;
having given what is respectful to his kinsmen, he should also honor the Brāhmaṇas. (3.264)

"Having washed his hands, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Having given honored food to his kinsmen, he should also honor the Brāhmaṇas. Following that, having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water, he gives [food] to his kinsmen on the paternal side; thus he should make the food primarily for his kinsmen. Having given to them preceded by honor, he should also give with full honor to those on the maternal side and others. (3.264)
That remnant of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the law is established. (3.265)

Regarding the term "remnant" (*uccheṣaṇa*): that leavings of the Brāhmaṇas should not be wiped away until the Brāhmaṇas have departed. Once the *śrāddha* is completed, one should perform the daily rites such as the *vaiśvadeva* in their entirety. As stated by Vyāsa:
"When a man desires to give a *śrāddha* to the ancestors, he should then perform the *vaiśvadeva* once the *śrāddha* rite has been concluded."
Thus is the law established. 3.265.
I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for a long night and even for eternity. (3.266)

Regarding the verse beginning "The oblation which [is for] long-lasting satisfaction": whatever *havya* and *kavya* food has been given to the ancestors so that it may properly result in long-term satiation—that food which leads to their satisfaction, I shall describe that in its entirety. (3.266)
By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits, the ancestors of virtuous men are satisfied for a month when given according to the prescribed rule. (3.267)
For two months with fish-meat, for three months with the meat of the deer,
for four months with the meat of the sheep, and for five months indeed with the meat of the porcupine.
For six months with the meat of a goat, and indeed for seven with that of the spotted deer;
for eight with the meat of the black antelope, and for nine with that of the Ruru deer. (3.269)

"By sesame seeds," "for two months by the flesh of fish," and "for six months by the flesh of goats. By offering sesame, grain, barley, beans, water, roots, and fruits at a *śrāddha*, the ancestors of men are satisfied for one month; for two months by the flesh of fish such as the *pāṭhīna*; for three months by the flesh of deer; for four months by the flesh of sheep; for five months by that which comes from edible birds; for six months by goat's flesh; for seven months by the flesh of the spotted antelope (*citramṛga*); for eight months by the flesh of the *sāraṅga* (spotted deer); and for nine months by the flesh of the deer called *śambara*. (3.267–269)
They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boar and buffalo;
however, by the flesh of rabbit and tortoise, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
"For ten months they are satisfied. For ten months they are satisfied by the meat of wild boar and buffalo; for eleven months by the meat of rabbit and tortoise. 3.270.
But with cow’s milk and milk-rice, and with the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa, there is satisfaction for twelve years. (3.271)

"But for a year with beef"—that is, furthermore, for a year with beef or with the milk of a *vārdhrīṇasa*. They call that white, aged goat, which drinks three times [a day] and has its virility exhausted, a *vārdhrīṇasa*; so say the ritualists in the rites for the ancestors.

Thus, according to what is recited in the Nigama, satisfaction lasting for twelve years is obtained through meat. He whose water touches his ear and tongue as he drinks is called a *tripiba*, like one who drinks from three [sources]. 3.271.
Black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and red deer, honey, and all kinds of food fit for sages are ordained for the sake of infinite results. (3.272)

"Kālaśāka and mahāśalka": *kālaśāka* is the vegetable known as *kālaśāka*, and *mahāśalka* is a species of fish known as *śakalīcitacima*, as well as others well-known in the Āyurveda. *Khaḍga* is the rhinoceros; *loha* is the red goat. The flesh (*āmiṣa*) of these two, honey (*madhu*), which is *mākṣika* honey, and all forest-grown grains (*munyanna*)—all these together serve to produce infinite satisfaction. (3.272)
Whatever one might give mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.

"Whatever is mixed with honey": whatever is not otherwise forbidden, when mixed with honey, should be offered as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey in that spot where, during the rainy season on the thirteenth day of the month of *Maghā*, the shadow associated with the elephant moves toward the eastern direction; one should give it there in that shadow. (3.273)
"May there be born in our family one who would offer us milk-rice with honey and ghee on the thirteenth lunar day, during the time when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east. (3.274)
Moreover: Whatever one gives according to the rule and correctly, endowed with faith, that becomes for the ancestors in the next world infinite and inexhaustible. (3.275)

Whatever one gives according to the rule, correctly and endowed with faith, that becomes for the ancestors in the hereafter an infinite and imperishable [reward]. Whatever is not forbidden, one should give it properly, endowed with form and faith, according to the scriptures; in this regard, food becomes for the ancestors in the other world at all times without depletion, just as there is satisfaction lasting from two months up to an infinite limit. By performing this monthly by month, as enjoined by the scriptural injunction, and because this matter is the exclusive domain of the scriptures, one must certainly perform this every month, since the capacity of the *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) to satisfy them is withdrawn once they are already satisfied. 3.275.
In the dark fortnight, beginning from the tenth day and excluding the fourteenth, these lunar days are recommended for the Śrāddha rite; other days are not so. (3.276)

Regarding the "dark fortnight" (kṛṣṇapakṣa): from the tenth day onwards in the dark fortnight, excluding the fourteenth day, the other days are thus praised for the śrāddha; they are appropriate, yield great fruit, are pure, and are commended, whereas the others are not so. (3.276)
By performing [the rites] on even lunar days and under even asterisms, one enjoys all desires;
but by performing them on odd days and under odd asterisms, one obtains abundant progeny for all the ancestors.

"Yukṣu" means: by worshipping the ancestors on even lunar days—such as the second, fourth, and so forth—and under even asterisms—such as Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and so forth—at Śrāddha rites, one obtains a lineage nourished with sacred learning, wealth, and other virtues. (3.277)
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight, so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for a *śrāddha* ceremony. || 3.278 ||

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): according to the observation of the *jyotiḥśāstra* (astronomy/astronomical science) that "the months begin with the bright fortnight of Caitra," the latter fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) yields more distinguished results than the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) for a *śrāddha*. Likewise, the afternoon portion (*aparāhṇabhāga*) connected to the *śrāddha* yields more distinguished results than the forenoon portion (*pūrvāhṇabhāga*). From the statement "it is distinguished" (*viśiṣyate*), it is understood that occasionally the *śrāddha* may even be performed in the forenoon. Furthermore, the establishment of the example must be understood through the very impossibility [of the argument] otherwise; for an unestablished thing cannot logically function as an example. (3.278)
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, properly turning from left to right, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion.

"With the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (prācīnāvītī): with all [the aforementioned requirements], being one who wears the *prācīnāvīta* thread, possessing non-laxity, with *darbha* grass blades in hand, using the *apasavya* (left-hand) path for the ancestors, the ancestral rite (*pitrya-karman*) must be performed correctly according to the scriptures throughout one's life. 3.279.
One should not perform a śrāddha at night, for it is declared to be demonic;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen.

Regarding the phrase "at night": one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night because it shares the common characteristic of being destructive, and it has been described by Manu and others as being demonic (*rākṣasī*). Likewise, by prescribing the prohibition for the beginning of the night in the context of the two twilights with the words "when the sun has not long risen," he indicates that the *śrāddha* exists even outside of the afternoon, in view of requirements such as the interruption of a lunar day (*tithiccheda*), since monthly and other periodic *śrāddhas* would otherwise be impossible. (3.280)
By this procedure, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the Pāñcayajñika rite every day.

"By this" means: by this aforementioned method, one should perform the *śrāddha* three times within the year—during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons; furthermore, that which occurs between the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña-mahāyajña*) should be performed every day. (3.281)
The oblation pertaining to the sacrifice for the ancestors is not prescribed to be performed in a common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha rite without the Darśa sacrifice for a twice-born man who has consecrated the sacred fires. (3.282)

"The oblation belonging to the ancestral sacrifice (paitryajñika) is not [performed] in the common fire. This means that the oblation which is an integral part of the ancestral sacrifice—performed with the formula "O Agni, together with Soma and Yama"—is not enjoined by the scripture to be offered in the *laukika* fire, that is, in a fire distinct from those used for Śrauta and Smārta rites. Furthermore, for a twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), a *śrāddha* on the tenth day and other dates of the dark fortnight is not prescribed except as part of the New Moon (*amāvāsya*) ritual. However, there is no prohibition regarding the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) and so forth, because that is enjoined as a mandatory (*naiyamika*) duty. (3.282)
When that best of the twice-born, having bathed, gratifies the ancestors with water, he thereby obtains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña). (3.283)

"In the event that the previously mentioned *pañcayajña* *śrāddha* is impossible" means as follows: by performing the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) for the ancestors after bathing, a Brāhmaṇa obtains the entire fruit of performing the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*). The mention of the "best of the twice-born" is for the sake of illustration, since all three [classes] are the subject under discussion. (3.283)
They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.

Regarding the word "Vasūs": Manu and others state that these ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—are the deities known as the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas. For there is this beginningless Vedic revelation: "The fathers and so forth are the Vasus and so forth. This statement praising the ancestors by superimposing the status of deities upon them is intended for one who, out of hatred for the ancestors or due to atheism, would not otherwise engage in ancestral rites (*pitṛkarman*). || 3.284 ||
One should always be an eater of *vighasa*, and always an eater of *amṛta*.
*Vighasa* is the remains of what has been eaten, while *amṛta* is likewise the remains of a sacrifice. (3.285)

"Subsisting on *vighasa*" means that he should always eat *vighasa*; this is stated again for the sake of praise by establishing his equality with one who eats the remnants of a sacrifice. And he should always subsist on *amṛta*. Since these two terms are not commonly known, he defines them: the remainder of what has been eaten by guests and others is called *vighasa*, while the remnants of a sacrifice, such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, are called *amṛta*. (3.285)
"All this rule for the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now hear the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born. (3.286)

"Regarding this": all this performance arising from the five sacrifices has been declared to you. The conclusion of the interrupted treatment immediately following the rite for the ancestors is for the sake of auspiciousness. Now, let the performance of the means of livelihood associated with the Brāhmaṇa—such as subsistence on nectar and so forth—be heard. (3.287)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Rules for Śrāddha," in the commentary on Manu composed by Govindarāja, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mādhava, which follows the teachings of Manu.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, a twice-born man should dwell in his house, having taken a wife, during the second quarter of his life. (4.1)

In order to establish that for one who has entered the householder stage following the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), the modes of conduct to be described hereafter apply, and to restate the period of studentship as well as the period of householdership which is about to be described, the author says "the fourth. A Brāhmaṇa who adheres to the view of the sequential performance of all stages of life (*āśrama-samuccaya*)—having spent the first quarter of his life in the teacher’s family, observing the specific injunctions such as "sixty-four years" even if the time is shorter or longer—should then, during the second quarter of his life, having taken a wife, practice the householder stage, observing the specific injunctions to be described later, such as "when the householder sees his skin wrinkled... (6.2), even if the time is shorter or longer. Nor is it appropriate to regard this [mention of the fourth part] as merely intended to assign a fixed duration, because the length of life is indefinite and thus inherently expectant [of qualification]. 4.1.
A Brahmin should live in times of no distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury. (4.2)

"Without injury" means: among the modes of livelihood to be described hereafter, he should live as a Brāhmaṇa by depending on that subsistence which involves no oppression of living beings—such as gleaning ears of grain (*śila-uccha*)—or, in its absence, by that which involves only slight oppression, such as begging, provided that the maintenance of his wife and others and the fulfillment of daily obligatory rites are thereby secured. Nor is there here permission for even a slight desire to kill, because violence is prohibited. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of excluding the Kṣatriya and others. Nevertheless, he should live [in this manner]. (4.2)
For the sake of accomplishing the mere necessities of life, one should accumulate wealth through one’s own irreproachable occupations, without causing distress to the body. (4.3)

"For the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence" means that one should accumulate wealth only to the extent necessary for the maintenance of life—preceded by the constant support of one's wife and the performance of obligatory duties—by means of blameless activities prescribed in the scriptures, such as those to be described beginning with "truth" (*ṛta*) and so forth, while avoiding bodily affliction; the rule is that one should not accumulate more than this. 4.3.
One should live by means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and the *pramṛta*, or even by the *satya* and the *anṛta*; but never by the "dog's way of life" (*śvavṛtti*).

To the question "By what actions [does he live]?", he says: "By the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*. He should live by means of the *ṛta* and so forth except in times of distress; however, he should never practice them even in times of distress. (4.4)
Gleaning ears of grain is to be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
Begging for alms is called *mṛta*, while agriculture is traditionally known as *pramṛta*. (4.5)
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one must subsist by it; service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it. (4.6)

"Truth" (*ṛta*) means: the collection of grains and the like, and the piling up of stones, should be called "truth" because their fruit is equal to that of truth. That which comes unasked is "ambrosia" (*amṛta*), because it is a cause of happiness like ambrosia. On the other hand, begged food is "death" (*mṛta*), because one experiences suffering comparable to death. And agriculture is "extreme death" (*parkarṣeṇa mṛtam*), because it is a cause of death for many, according to the saying: "The ploughshare, with its iron mouth, destroys both the earth and those who dwell within the earth. Trade is "truth-and-untruth" (*satyānṛta*), because it is accomplished through dealings involving both truth and falsehood; furthermore, by the traditional teaching of Gautama—"Agriculture and trade [are permissible] when not performed by oneself, as well as usury"—one lives by what is not done by oneself. And service is said to be the "dog's way of life" (*śvavṛtti*) because it consists of looking with a wretched gaze and so forth; therefore, the Brahmin under discussion should abandon that. (4.5–6)
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or enough for a single jar;
he may have enough for three days, or he may not even have provisions for tomorrow. || 4.7 ||

And that Brāhmaṇa, depending on the degree of his contraction of purificatory practices (*śauca-saṃkoca*), may be one who possesses a granary of grain (*kusūladhānyaka*); that is, he may have a store of grain and so forth in the measure of a storehouse (*koṣṭhaka*), or he may possess wealth sufficient for only twelve days. Or he may have a collection of grain and so forth in the measure of a leather bag (*uṣṭrikā*), possessing wealth sufficient for only six days. Or he may be one whose grain and so forth exist only for three days, being acquired through effort (*īhā*) or exertion (*ceṣṭā*). Or he may be one whose grain and so forth exist only for the morrow, being for today or for tomorrow (*nādyāhnika-śvastana*). Thus, this is an exception (*apavāda*) based on the relative degree of contraction of the constant store of possessions, intended solely for the accomplishment of subsistence (*yātrā*). 4.7.
And among these four twice-born householders,
each subsequent one is to be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds.

Regarding the phrase "of the four": among these four types of householders, beginning with those who possess grain in a granary (*kusūladhānyaka*) and so forth, it should be understood that whichever is mentioned later is more praiseworthy than the preceding one. This is because, through the excellence of his self-restraint (*saṃyama*) and the restriction of his livelihood (*vṛttisaṃkoca*), he becomes a conqueror of worlds such as heaven. || 4.8 ||
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmasattra).

Regarding the "six duties" (*ṣaṭkarma*): among these householders, a certain householder, depending on the abundance of his possessions and other factors, engages in the ordinary rites such as the *ṛta* and so forth. Another, however, because officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, proceeds to live by these three; yet another, because it will be stated that receiving gifts is the lowest of those, abandons that and proceeds to live by the two [remaining], officiating at sacrifices and teaching. And compared to the aforementioned three, the fourth lives by teaching alone. (4.9)

Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the *agnihotra*, he should always perform only those sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices. (4.10)

"Subsisting," it is said: living by means of gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains, and when other occupations are impossible, being devoted to the morning and evening fire-oblations, he should perform at all times the New and Full Moon sacrifices, known as the *pārvaṇa* rites, exclusively. 4.10.
One should never engage in worldly conduct for the sake of a livelihood; one should live the life of a Brahmin, straightforward and free from deceit. 4.11

"One should not follow worldly conduct. For the sake of a livelihood, one should never engage in various jests and the like; rather, one should practice the Brahminical way of life, which is self-impelled, free from evil, endowed with faith, and devoid of deceit and other pretenses. (4.11)
Relying upon supreme contentment, one who seeks happiness should become self-restrained;
for happiness has contentment as its root, while the opposite is the root of suffering. (4.12)

Regarding "contentment": he who is equanimous, seeking the happiness of seen and unseen rewards such as heaven, yet free from longing for specific personal gains, and who possesses only that accumulation of wealth sufficient for the constant maintenance of himself and his family—having resorted to the highest renunciation regarding wealth, he should undertake its acquisition and accumulation; for all happiness, both seen and unseen, such as heaven and the like, originates from contentment. Conversely, discontent is the root of both seen and unseen suffering. (4.12)
But a twice-born Snātaka, living by any one of these modes of livelihood, should observe these vows which lead to heaven, long life, and fame: 4.13.

Regarding the word *ataḥ*: because it has been stated that "among these [means of livelihood], such as the dead [animals] and so forth, he shall subsist by one or another of these modes alone" (*ṣaṭkarmaiko bhavaty eṣām*), a *snātaka* Brāhmaṇa living by means other than those [six] must always maintain these vows—which will be described below and which consist of specific mental resolutions of the form "this must be done by me, this must not"—for the sake of heaven, long life, and renown. Nor does the fact that their fruits are mentioned imply that they are non-obligatory (*anitya*), for they are enjoined as obligatory (*nitya*) in the Vedic text: "By this much he becomes freed from sin. (4.13)
One should perform one's own duty as declared in the Veda constantly and without laziness;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. (4.14)

"Revealed in the Vedas" means that which is declared in the Śruti; and that which is declared in the Smṛti is also "spoken in the Vedas" because it is rooted in the Veda. Whatever one's own obligatory duty (*nitya-karma*) has been enjoined—not a desire-driven act (*kāmya*)—that he should perform without laziness. For, by performing his obligatory duties according to his capacity, through the destruction of past sins and the non-origination of new ones, and by not performing desire-driven acts, there being an absence of the merit (*dharma*) that causes fruits, and consequently an absence of both auspicious and inauspicious effects, he attains liberation. (4.14)
One should not pursue wealth through excessive attachment, nor by contrary actions; one should not seek it even when objects are available, nor from here and there even in times of distress. (4.15)

"Not when objects are being conceptualized" means that one should not acquire wealth through singing and the like, nor by officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate, and so forth. Nor [should one accept gifts] when there is wealth sufficient for what must necessarily be done. Furthermore, even if the maintenance of oneself and one's family is at risk, if another means is available, one should not accept gifts from those defiled by birth or action; however, he will state later (4.15) that in times of distress, when no other means exist, one may accept gifts from such persons.
One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire;
one should also restrain the mind from excessive attachment to them. 4.16

Regarding the phrase "in the objects of the senses": one should not form an attachment toward any of the objects such as forms and so forth, which are perceivable by the eyes and other senses, for the sake of enjoyment. Furthermore, even regarding those things that are not prohibited—such as approaching one's own wife—one should properly turn the mind away from excessive indulgence by considering the possibility of faults such as instability. 4.16
One should abandon all worldly pursuits that obstruct one's Vedic study; by sustaining oneself in whatever manner possible, that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of one's purpose. 4.17

"Regarding the word 'all': 'maintaining yourself in whatever way possible' means that by whatever means one sustains oneself and so forth, one should abandon those objects such as the enjoyment of sense-pleasures—even if they are not prohibited—provided they are contrary to the study of the Veda; for that is the fulfillment of duty for a Brahmin, namely, being devoted to one's own sacred recitation (svādhyāya). 4.17.
One should conduct oneself here by practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. (4.18)

"According to one's stage of life": one should conduct oneself in the world by adopting dress, speech, and mental disposition in accordance with one’s age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. For example, the performance of bathing, wearing garlands, and applying ointments, as well as speech and thought, should follow the three stages of life; this same principle should be applied to actions and other matters as well. (4.18)
One should constantly study the scriptures that increase the intellect, which are auspicious and beneficial, as well as the Vedic Nigamas. (4.19)

Regarding the phrase "those which increase the intellect": he should constantly study treatises on logic (*nyāya-śāstra*) and so forth that do not contradict the Vedas, as they quickly produce mental acuity; those such as the works of Uśanas intended for wealth; beneficial works such as those providing visible benefits like medicine (*āyurveda*); and the texts known as *Nigamas*, which explain the meaning of the Vedas by stating synonyms for words whose meanings were previously unknown. 4.19.
For in whatever measure a person masters a treatise, in that same measure he understands it, and his specialized knowledge finds delight in it. 4.20

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): because as long as a person thoroughly discriminates a treatise, he comes to know its specific details, and his knowledge even regarding the subject matter of other treatises becomes radiant. 4.20.

One should never neglect the sacrifice to the sages, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to the ancestors, according to one's ability. (4.21)

Regarding the phrase "the sacrifice of the sages" (ṛṣiyajña): this designation of the five sacrifices already mentioned is intended to state that one should not abandon the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) and the rest according to one's ability, and to explain that they are to be accomplished by means of the senses as will be described hereafter. (4.21)
Some people, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from desire.

Regarding the phrase "these": certain persons who know the scriptures that teach external and internal sacrifices, by the power of knowledge, having ceased all efforts toward wealth for the sake of constant performance, accomplish these great sacrifices within the senses themselves at all times. They contemplate the senses as being the form of the fires, guests, and so forth, or as the restraint [of the senses] in the form of speech, arms, and so on; thus they accomplish these. (4.22)

Some say that one should always invoke the vital breath into speech and speech into the vital breath, perceiving within both speech and the vital breath the inexhaustible accomplishment of the sacrifice. (4.23)

Regarding the phrase "in speech": others, however, considering that the perfection of sacrifice—which yields inexhaustible fruit—resides in speech and in the vital air called *prāṇa*, offer the oblation of speech into the fire of speech (*vāg-agni*) through mere silence, and they offer the oblation of breath into the fire of breath (*prāṇa-agni*). Thus they remain, constantly cultivating this state. And so says the Kauṣītaki Rahasya Brāhmaṇa: "As long as a person speaks, he is not able to breathe; at that time, he offers his breath into speech. As long as a person breathes, he is not able to speak; at that time, he offers his speech into breath. These two infinite, immortal oblations he offers continually, whether waking or sleeping. Now, other oblations involving food are indeed made of action (*karma-mayyaḥ*); thus, in former times, the wise offered the Agnihotra for him in this manner. (4.23)
Other brahmins always perform those sacrifices with knowledge alone,
perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "by knowledge": other learned Brahmins, perceiving through the eye of knowledge—that is, through the scripture—that the performance [of these sacrifices] must be based on such understanding as "the knower performs these sacrifices" and "the knower causes them to be performed," accomplish these sacrifices throughout their lives solely by the power of discernment (vijñāna), which is the correct comprehension of their subject matter. And thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "For he who, being a twice-born, performs this rite in this manner, and he who indeed knows it thus. (4.24)
One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night,
as well as with the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and with the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice likewise.

And as for the *agnihotra*: in the case of the *uditahoma* (offering after sunrise) view, one should perform the oblation at the beginning of the day and at the end of the day; likewise, in the case of the *anuditahoma* (offering before sunrise) view, one should perform the oblation at the beginning of the night and at the end of the night. Furthermore, at the end of the dark fortnight, one should sacrifice with the rite called *darśa*, and at the end of the bright fortnight, with the sacrifice called *paurṇamāsa*. 4.25.
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the seasonal sacrifices;
at the end of the sun's course, he should offer an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

"At the end of the grain": when one has become satisfied for the year due to the exhaustion of previously gathered rice and other grains, according to the statement of the author of the Sūtras, "Then one should sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa [offering] in autumn upon new grain. Even one who possesses existing grain should sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa. According to the view that "the season is a year," one should sacrifice at the end of each of the four-month periods with the seasonal sacrifices known as the Cāturmāsya rites. One should sacrifice with the rite called Paśubandha at the beginning of the northern and southern solstices, and at the end of the year with the Soma sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma. || 4.26 ||

A twice-born man who desires to live a long life must not eat new grain or meat without having first performed the sacrifice of the new harvest (navasasyeṣṭi) and the animal sacrifice (paśubandha). 4.27.

"No," [it is said]. A twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires, desiring long life, shall not eat new grain or meat without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice or the animal sacrifice. 4.27.
For when the sacred fires are not honored with new grain and animal offerings, they, greedy for fresh food and meat, desire to consume his very life-breaths. (4.28)

Regarding the word "with new [grain]": because the sacred fires (*agni*) of this *āhitāgni*—having not yet been propitiated with the sacrifice of new grain or the animal sacrifice (*paśuyajña*)—desire fresh food and meat and thus wish to consume his very life-breaths (*prāṇa*), therefore the *Āgrayaṇa* and the animal sacrifice must be performed. 4.28.
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of his ability, whether with seats, food, beds, water, or roots and fruits. (4.29)

Regarding the phrase "with seats, food, and beds": having stated that one should honor a guest according to one's ability with such things as seating and food, this restatement concerning the guest is intended for the purpose of prohibiting heretics (*pākhaṇḍin*) and others, as will be explained in connection with the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*). (4.29)
One should not honor, even with a mere word, heretics, those who follow improper occupations, those who act like cats, deceivers, rationalists, and those who live like herons. 4.30

And thus he says, "those who follow heretical paths" (pākhaṇḍinaḥ). One should not honor—even with mere words—those who wear the marks of red garments and the like, who live by the livelihoods of others, who follow the "cat-like" or "heron-like" modes of conduct whose characteristics will be described below, who are deceitful, faithless, and practitioners of logic outside the Vedas. This is a prohibition against giving food and other gifts preceded by such honor; however, he will later state that one should give gifts according to one's ability to those who do not cook for themselves. 4.30.

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those who are householders, learned in the Vedas, purified by their vows, and well-versed in sacred knowledge; but one should avoid those who are the opposite.

Regarding the phrase *vedavidyāvratasnātān*: by the expression *vedavidyāvratasnātān*, all three types of *snātakas*—the *veda-snātaka*, the *vratasnātaka*, and the *vidyāvratasnātaka*—are included. As Hārīta states: "He who bathes after completing the Veda but not the vows is a *veda-snātaka*; he who bathes after completing the vows but not the Veda is a *vratasnātaka*; he who bathes after completing both is a *vidyāvratasnātaka*. One should honor with offerings to gods (*havya*) and ancestors (*kavya*) those *śrotriyas* (Vedic scholars) and householders who are thus included under the term *snātaka*, yet are mentioned separately because of their preeminence. Conversely, one should avoid those who are the opposite of this. This serves to strengthen the prohibition against heretics (*pākhaṇḍins*) and others; the mention of *śrotriyas* and so forth again indicates that food and other gifts should not be given to heretics and the like, even at the end of a meal, except as preceded by formal honor. (4.31)
A householder should give according to his ability to those who do not cook for themselves, and he should share with all living beings without causing hardship to his own household. 4.32

"Furthermore, one who is able should give food alone": a householder should give food according to his ability to those such as heretics (pāṣaṇḍins) who lack cooked food; he should perform a distribution of shares by giving milk and other gifts even to those as far as the trees, provided it does not cause hardship to his own family. 4.32.
A Snātaka who is perishing from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; but not from anyone else—this is the settled rule. 4.33.

"From a king": A *snātaka*, even when suffering from hunger, should first seek wealth from a king who follows the scriptures, or from his own sacrificer (*yājya*) or pupil, even if accepting gifts from other castes is possible; he should not seek it from any other twice-born person. If those are unavailable, he may accept from another twice-born person. Furthermore, the author will later state the rule for times of distress (*āpad-dharma*): "If the aforementioned means prescribed for non-distress are unavailable, one may accept gifts from anyone. Because a king possesses great wealth, and because a sacrificer and a resident pupil benefit him through their own meritorious deeds, this rule restricts the acceptance of wealth to these three first. Thus, this statement serves to prohibit the acceptance of wealth from anyone other than a king, a sacrificer, or a pupil during non-distress. For this very reason it is said, "but not from another. As for the claim that this rule pertains only to times of distress based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the word "suffering" (*saṃsīdan*), that is incorrect, because it does not fall within the context of such a discussion. Moreover, "distress" (*āpad*) is not defined merely as a lack of wealth; rather, it refers to the exhaustion of the prescribed means available when wealth is lacking. Otherwise, the rules for times of distress—such as immediate cleansing—would become applicable even in ordinary circumstances. Furthermore, if this were restricted to times of distress, the phrase "but not from another" would contradict the subsequent injunction, "one may accept from anyone. As for the statement that "the lord of the earth should be petitioned by those suffering or desiring base metals (*kupya*) or wealth," that refers to a Kṣatriya king, as indicated by the context of accepting gifts from a ruler. For that reason, the term "lord of the earth" (*pṛthivīpati*) is used there, whereas here the term "king" (*rājan*) is used. (4.33)
A learned Snātaka shall not at any time suffer from hunger if he has the means;
nor, while possessing wealth, shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (4.34)

"No," [it is said]. A *snātaka* Brāhmaṇa, being learned, is capable of receiving gifts; therefore, when wealth from kings and others is available, he should never fall into exhaustion through hunger, nor should he wear worn-out or dirty clothes when such resources exist. 4.34.
Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure, he should be constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas and in what is beneficial for the self. (4.35)

"Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard": one whose hair, nails, and beard have been clipped should be tranquil, dressed in white garments, endowed with both external and internal purity, habituated to the study of the Vedas, and devoted to the administration of medicinal herbs and the like. 4.35.
He should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water;
he should wear the sacred thread, the Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings.

Regarding the phrase "made of bamboo": he should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot accompanied by water, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a handful of *darbha* grass, and two beautiful golden earrings. Although the possession of the sacred thread and water-pot is already established for householders and others by the rule "kindling the fire, wandering for alms" (2.108), they are mentioned again here for the purpose of defining the specific observances (*vrata*) of a *snātaka*. In the same way, one should understand that other rules such as "he should not go anywhere while impure from food remnants" (4.37) are also restated for this specific context. 4.36.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting; not when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky. (4.37)
"No," [he said]. One should not look at the sun at any time—whether it is rising, setting, eclipsed by Rāhu, reflected in water, or positioned at midday. 4.37.
One should not leap over a calf’s tethering rope, nor run while it is raining, nor look at one's own reflection in water; such is the rule. 4.38.

"One should not leap" means one should not leap over the rope to which a calf is tied; while it rains, one should not run; and in water, one should not look at one's own reflection—such is the settled rule. 4.38.
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known lordly trees. (4.39)

"Clay," he says. Having set out, he should, by way of his right hand, pass those who stand before him, as well as excavated clay, cow-dung, stones, and so forth; and deities, Brahmins, clarified butter, honey, crossroads, the *aśvattha* tree, and trees worshipped with offerings. 4.39.
Even if he is impassioned, he should not approach a woman during her menstrual period;
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed. 4.40
"One should not approach" means that even if afflicted by desire, one should not go to a woman in her courses, nor should one lie down on the same bed with her. (4.40)
For when a man approaches a woman who is overwhelmed by her menses, his wisdom, vitality, strength, sight, and even his lifespan are diminished. (4.41)
Regarding the phrase "with the menses": since the wisdom, virility, and other qualities of a man who approaches a woman during her menstrual period are destroyed, he should not approach her. (4.41)
For him who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by the menses, wisdom, splendor, strength, sight, and even life itself increase. (4.42)
Regarding the word "her": if one does not approach her while she is in her menses, wisdom and other virtues increase; therefore, one should not go to her.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating, sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease. 4.43.

"He shall not eat" means he should not eat together with his wife. As for the statement, "The mouth of women is always pure" (5.130), that refers specifically to the time of sexual union, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "And women [are pure] during the context of sexual pleasure. Furthermore, he should not look at her while she is eating, or when she is sneezing, or when she is opening her mouth due to wind, or when she is in an unrestrained state such as having her feet extended, and so forth. (4.43)

A twice-born man who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is naked, nor one who is giving birth. (4.44)

One should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her eyes, nor at one who is naked—except during sexual intercourse, according to the Smṛti of Āpastamba which states, "A woman is naked nowhere except during sexual intercourse"—nor at one anointed with oil. Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa desiring virility should not look at a woman giving birth to offspring. (4.44)
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked.
One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen. (4.45)

"Not food": he should not eat while wearing only a single garment, nor should he bathe without at least a loincloth to cover him. He should not void urine or excrement on a path, in ashes, or in a cow-pen. (4.45)
Neither on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain; neither in a ruined temple, nor ever upon an anthill. (4.46)
"Not on ploughed land": likewise, one should never perform [the rite] on ploughed land, in water, on a site built with bricks, on a mountain, in a temple, on an anthill, or on a mound of earth. 4.46.
Neither in pits inhabited by living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing;
neither having reached a riverbank, nor on the summit of a mountain. (4.47)

"Not among those with living beings" means that one should not perform [the ritual] in holes containing creatures; nor should one perform it while walking or standing, nor by resorting to a riverbank or a mountain peak. Although the prohibition of the mountain summit is already established by the mention of "mountain" itself, the repetition is for the sake of providing an option regarding the mountain other than the peak. Nor is this an equal option, because such [locations as riverbanks and peaks] are established by one's own whim, which would render a general prohibition useless.
