Therefore, this option is settled such that there is no fault on a mountain in the case of one who is extremely distressed, but otherwise there is a fault. 4.47.
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows, one should never discharge feces or urine. (4.48)

"Wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun"—one should never perform the voiding of urine or feces while looking at wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or the quarters; and "looking at the wind" means facing toward it. (4.48)
Having set aside wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, and the like, he should pass by them, restraining his speech, being pure, with his limbs covered and his head veiled. (4.49)

"Having covered," etc. [means]: having concealed the ground with wood, leaves, clods of earth, or grass, remaining silent, free from the need for penance regarding contact with those who have eaten leftovers (ucchiṣṭa) or with *caṇḍālas* and the like, with his body covered and his head veiled, he shall void urine and feces. 4.49.
One should discharge urine and feces facing north during the day;
at night one should face south; and during the two twilights, one should face as one does during the day. (4.50)
"Regarding the voiding of urine and excrement": one should discharge urine and feces facing north during the day and at the two twilights, and facing south at night. (4.50)
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purificatory acts] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as also when there is fear of danger to life. (4.51)

"In the shade" means: whether at night or during the day, in the shade; or at night in the darkness, or during the day in the darkness caused by mist and the like—in these cases, when there is confusion regarding the directions, and likewise when there is a danger to life caused by wind and so forth, one may void urine or excrement with the face turned as one pleases. 4.51.
The wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or twice-born brahmins, or facing a cow or the wind, is destroyed. (4.52)

Regarding the phrase "toward the fire": for one who voids urine or excrement facing the fire, the sun, the moon, water, a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, or the wind, wisdom perishes; therefore, that must not be done. This is the statement of the consequence for the verse beginning with "the wind, fire, and a Brāhmaṇa," as well as for facing a boundary; thus, the prohibition is established, since this was not mentioned previously. (4.52)
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it. (4.53)

"Not fire": one should not blow on a fire with the breath from the mouth. One should not look at another's wife while she is naked, according to the Smṛti of Gautama. One should not cast urine or other such things into the fire, nor should one warm one's feet there. 4.53.
One should not place it underneath, nor should one step over it; one should not treat it as if it were beneath one's feet, nor should one cause any injury to living beings. (4.54)

"Below" means: one should not place it [the fire] at the feet, nor should one practice the killing of living beings. Likewise, one should not place the fire beneath beds and such, nor should one step over it. One should not place it at the region of the feet, nor should one perform any act that causes pain to living creatures. (4.54)
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should one travel, nor should one lie down to sleep;
nor indeed should one scratch the ground, nor should one remove one's own garland.

"One should not eat": at the time of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), one should not engage in eating, walking, or sleeping; one should never scratch the ground with one's nails or similar objects; and one should not remove a garland from one's own head. || 4.55 ||
One should not discharge urine, feces, or spittle into water; nor any other impure substance, blood, or poisons. (4.56)
"Not in water": one should not throw urine, feces, phlegm, impure substances, blood, or poisons into water. (4.56)
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person; one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice uninvited. (4.57)

"One should not sleep alone": one should not sleep by oneself in an uninhabited house; one should not wake someone who is sleeping with wealth or other valuables in excess; one should not converse with a woman in her menses; and a priest should not go to a sacrifice for which he has not been formally chosen. Regarding this, Gautama says: "But he may go at will for the purpose of seeing [the performance]. (4.57)
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.

"In the fire-sanctuary": in the fire-hall, in a cow-pen, in one's dwelling, in the presence of a Brāhmaṇa, and during the times of Vedic study and eating, one should lift up the right hand as far as the forearm or the edge of the garment. 4.58.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling her calf, nor should one inform anyone of it;
likewise, a wise man, having seen a rainbow in the sky, should not point it out to anyone. 4.59

"One should not restrain" means one should not turn back a cow while it is drinking. Nor should one inform anyone else that another's cow is drinking milk or other liquids. Furthermore, having seen a rainbow in the sky, one who knows the scriptures should not point it out to another. (4.59)
One should not dwell in an unrighteous village, nor in one where disease is rampant;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one reside for long on a mountain. (4.60)

"Not unrighteous" means that one should not dwell for too long in villages or similar places where the people are largely unrighteous or where diseases are exceedingly prevalent. One should not travel alone on a journey, nor should one remain for a long time on a mountain. (4.60)
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people; nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes. (4.61)

"Not in a kingdom of Śūdras": he should not dwell in a country ruled by a Śūdra king, where the people are unrighteous, which is surrounded by foreigners, brought under control by those who wear external marks such as the sacred thread despite being outside the Vedic tradition, and which is harassed by Caṇḍālas and other outcasts. 4.61.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice excessive gluttony;
one should not eat too early, nor too late, nor at evening after having already eaten in the morning. (4.62)

"He does not eat": he should not eat oil-cakes and the like from which the oil has been extracted; nor should he seek satiety. He should not eat too early in the morning or at the end of the day; nor should he be fully satiated both in the evening and in the morning. Rather, being satisfied at one mealtime, he should eat with a sense of expectation at the other.
One should not engage in vain exertion, nor drink water with cupped hands; one should not eat food in one's lap, nor ever be a seeker of idle curiosity. (4.63)

"One should not do" means one should not perform any activity that yields results visible or invisible. One should not drink water with the hollowed palms. One should not eat sweets by placing them upon the thighs. And one should never be intent on curiosity, wondering, "What might this be for? without a purpose. (4.63)
He should not dance, nor should he sing, nor should he play musical instruments; he should not clap his hands, nor shout, nor, being impassioned, raise a clamor. 4.64

"He shall not dance" means he shall not perform unscriptural dancing, singing, or instrumental music. He shall not strike his arm with his hand. Even when joyful, he shall not make indistinct dental sounds, nor shall he make harsh cries. (4.64)
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal; nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its nature. 4.65

"Not with the feet": one should never wash one's feet in a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*). This is because of the traditional teaching of Paiṭhīnasi: "Copper, silver, and gold—whether broken or unbroken. Apart from those, one should not eat from a broken vessel, nor from one that causes mental distress. 4.65.
One should not wear shoes, clothing, a sacred thread, ornaments, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others. (4.66)
"Sandals," etc.: one should not wear sandals, garments, the sacrificial thread, ornaments, garlands, or a water-pot that have been used by another. 4.66.
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are deformed. 4.67.

"Not with the undisciplined" means: one should not travel with horses, bulls, and so forth—those yoked to pull carts and other vehicles—who are untamed, afflicted by hunger or disease, have broken horns, eyes, or hooves, or whose tails have been cut off. (4.67)
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks, and perfect in color and form, without excessively prodding them with the goad. (4.68)

"By those who are well-trained": he should proceed with horses that are well-disciplined, swift-moving, endowed with auspicious marks such as the *devamaṇi* and *āvarta*, free from defects such as the *kakuda*, possessed of excellent colors like *śoṇa*, and of beautiful form; and he should travel without excessively paining them with the goad. (4.68)
The morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat should be avoided;
one should not cut one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.

Regarding "the heat of the early sun": this refers to the heat of the sun when it has first risen. One should avoid sitting on stools and such that have been broken by the smoke from a corpse. One should not cut one's own nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with one's teeth. (4.69)
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless labor, nor any action that results in future suffering. (4.70)

“Not a clod of earth,” [as stated in the verse]. According to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: “One should not pick up a clod of earth or cut grass without a purpose. One should not take up a clod of earth without a cause, nor should one cut grass with one's fingernails. For since no visible or invisible fruit arises from one’s own action, one should not perform that which brings about unhappiness in the future. (4.70)
The man who crushes clods of earth, tears up grass, or bites his nails, as well as the slanderer and the impure person, quickly goes to destruction. (4.71)

"Regarding 'the crusher of clods': a man who crushes clods, cuts grass, bites his nails, acts as a spy, or is impure, quickly goes to destruction. Therefore, these things must not be done; for this very reason, both eating [clods] and impurity are prohibited. (4.71)
One should not engage in contentious debate, nor should one wear garlands on the outside;
riding on the backs of cows is in every way censured. (4.72)

"Nor should one engage in dispute" means that one should not carry on a conversation with dogmatic attachment, nor should one wear outer garments or garlands. Traveling by riding on the back of a cow—whether by way of wandering, obstruction, or other such means—destroys one's dharma. 4.72.
One should not enter an enclosed village or house except through the gate; and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar. (4.73)

"By a non-gate": one should not enter a village or a house enclosed by a wall or similar structure by a place other than the gate. Furthermore, one should avoid staying at the foot of a tree at night from afar. 4.73.
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.

"Not with dice" means that one should not play even for the sake of sport with dice and such things. Furthermore, one should not hold shoes in one's own hands except when they are on the feet. Nor should one eat while seated upon a bedstead. Nor should one eat food with the hand not separated by a vessel, nor should one eat while placing the vessel directly upon the seat. 4.74.
And when the sun has set, he should not eat anything mixed with sesame;
nor should he sleep here naked, nor should he go anywhere while still impure from food.

"Everything": whatever is mixed with sesame, such as *kṛsara* and the like, that he shall not eat when the sun has set; nor shall he sleep in this world without the covering of a loincloth; and he shall never go anywhere while still impure from food remnants. (4.75)
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one shall attain a long life. (4.76)

Regarding "with wet feet": one should begin the meal with feet moistened by water; furthermore, one should not sleep with wet feet. This statement regarding the result—that one who eats with wet feet shall attain a long life—is intended as a commendation. Nor does this lead to the fallacy of non-eternality [of the rule]. One should eat while possessing five things that are wet, facing the east and observing silence.
One should not revile those from whom the food was given, nor should one disparage its flavor.
Thus, because of the constant recollection [of this] by Vyāsa. 4.76.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.

"Regarding 'beyond the range of sight': he should never go to a place that is difficult of access and is not within the range of his vision. He should not look at urine or excrement. He should not cross a river or similar body of water using only his arms. (4.77)
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds; nor should one step upon cotton seeds or husks. (4.78)
"One should not step upon them": one who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, ashes, bones, potsherds, cotton seeds, or husks. 4.78.

One should not dwell with paternal kinsmen, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas; nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with those of the lowest castes, nor with those who live by the occupations of the lowest castes. (4.79)

"He should not dwell [with them]" means that he should not sit even for a moment in one place with outcasts (patita), Cāṇḍālas, Pulkasas, those of small intellect, those who are despised, or Antyāvasāyins, even if they reside in another village, for the sake of performing his duties. This is distinct from such rules as "he should not dwell in an unrighteous village" (MDh 4.60). The outcasts and others will be described in the tenth and eleventh chapters. (4.79)
One should not give advice to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared for a sacrifice; one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him. (4.80)

"Not for a Śūdra. In this context, "instruction" refers to *dharma*, because it is taught separately [from other matters], or because of its association with the *ucchiṣṭa* (remnants), the *haviskṛt* (oblation-preparer), and so forth; thus, one should not provide instruction on what is beneficial for a Śūdra regarding matters of visible utility. Furthermore, "remnants" (*ucchiṣṭa*) should not be given to a slave or a Śūdra, since it will be stated later that "in the case of a slave, food consisting of remnants should be given. As for the statement, "the meal [consists of] the remnants of the twice-born," this is an instruction for the eater and not for the giver. Likewise, regarding the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings intended for the *havis* (sacrificial oblation), after stating the prohibition—"the food of the gods and the *havis* [are forbidden]"—it will be stated that "whatever remains of the *havis*" may be eaten by the twice-born; therefore, that which has become a remnant of the *havis* must not be given to a Śūdra. Similarly, one should not instruct a Śūdra in *dharma* such as, "this and that, which is for the sake of invisible merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), must be performed by you. Nor should one directly instruct him in a religious vow (*vrata*) or an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). And thus, regarding even highly virtuous Śūdras, Aṅgiras says:
"Likewise, having approached a Śūdra, one should always place Dharma at the forefront;
having interposed a Brāhmaṇa, one should prescribe the penance.
This [verse] states that the granting of penance is done through the medium of a Brāhmaṇa's instruction, not directly. (4.80)
For he who explains this doctrine to him and likewise instructs him in the vow sinks into the darkness called "the unrestrained" along with him alone. (4.81)

Regarding the word "yaḥ": because that Brāhmaṇa who instructs a Śūdra in his religious duties and observances enters, along with that very Śūdra—who has become the cause for the production of sin—into a darkness called *asaṃvṛta* (uncovered), which is of extreme magnitude. Although five [categories] were under discussion, the mention of the results for two of them is for the purpose of emphasizing the gravity of the expiation. (4.81)
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without using water. 4.82.

"Not with both hands joined together": one should not scratch one's own head with two hands pressed against each other. Because of the mention of "joined," there is no prohibition regarding hands that are not joined. In this manner, it should be understood that [the rule] is to be applied by excluding [the specific cases] everywhere. One should not touch the head with anything, even with a hand that is impure (ucchiṣṭa) or otherwise. Furthermore, one should not perform the obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) ritual bathing without using the head. However, there is no prohibition when it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), because this is syntactically connected as a single statement with the injunction for bathing. (4.82)
One should avoid seizing others by the hair and striking them on the head;
and having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil. (4.83)

"Regarding 'seizing by the hair': one should not, out of anger, seize the hair or strike another on the head. Having bathed with the head still wet, one should not touch even a small part of the body with oil. (4.83)
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess a slaughterhouse, a wheel, or a banner, nor from those who live by prostitution. (4.84)

"Not from a king": according to the rule "the term for a caste is used [here] to denote the offspring of a king," a *rājanya* refers specifically to a Kṣatriya. His lineage or offspring—due to this specific designation—is the progeny of a Kṣatriya; that which is not the progeny of a Kṣatriya is "non-Kṣatriya progeny. Therefore, one should not accept gifts from such a non-Kṣatriya king except in times of distress, as indicated by the context. Likewise, one should not accept gifts from those who live by the trade of butchers, oil-pressers, liquor-sellers, or prostitutes. (4.84)
A slaughterhouse is equal to ten [other] slaughterhouses; a banner is equal to ten banners;
a prostitute is equal to ten prostitutes; and a king is equal to ten prostitutes. (4.85)

"Equal to ten slaughterhouses": a prostitute is equal to ten taverns; a king is equal to ten prostitutes. A *sūnā* is a place of execution; whatever fault belongs to a butcher at ten slaughterhouses, that same fault belongs to an oil-presser who is a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). Whatever fault belongs to ten oil-pressers, that same fault belongs to a tavern-owner who sells liquor. Whatever fault belongs to ten tavern-owners, that same fault belongs to one who maintains a brothel. Whatever fault belongs to ten brothel-keepers, that same fault belongs to a king. Thus, by observing this progressive increase in censure, when there is a choice between a previous donor and a subsequent one in times of distress, the latter should be avoided. (4.85)
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, the acceptance of gifts from him is terrible. (4.86)

And thus, according to the calculation stated: "Ten thousand slaughterhouses"—a king is declared by Manu and others to be equal to a butcher who employs ten thousand slaughterhouses for his own ends. Therefore, accepting gifts from such a person is to be feared, as it is a cause for falling into hell. (4.86)
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall, in due course, go to these twenty-one hells. (4.87)

Regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): he who accepts gifts from even a Kṣatriya king who is miserly and acts in transgression of the scriptures, he shall successively attain these hells—places of torment—which are about to be described. (4.87)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka. 4.88
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana, Saṃghāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pūtimṛttika.
The Iron Spike, the Residue, the Path, the Śālmalī River,
the Forest of Sword-leaves, and indeed the Iron Bar.

*Tāmisra*, *Saṃjīvana*, *Lohaśaṅku*, and *Ṛjīṣa*—the word "one goes to" (*yāti*) is understood to follow here. Among these, *Tāmisra* consists of darkness; *Andhatāmisra* consists of dense, blinding darkness; *Mahāraurava* and *Raurava* consist of great clamor and shrieking; and the hell called *Kālasūtra* is where there is great suffering of every kind. *Saṃjīvana* is where beings are repeatedly revived and then killed. *Mahāvīci* is where one is carried away by great waves. *Tapana* consists of the heat of fire and so forth. *Saṃpratāpana* is the boiling in cauldrons (*kumbhīpāka*). *Saṃghāta* is the dwelling of many in an extremely confined space. *Kākola* is where one is devoured by crows. *Kuḍmala* is where one is tormented with ropes. *Pūtimṛttika* is earth smelling of excrement. *Lohaśaṅku* is where one is pierced by needles. *Ṛjīṣa* is where one is thrown into the dregs used for baking flour. *Panthā* is where one is made to wander on a path. *Śālmala* is where one is pierced by thorns of the silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*). *Nadī* is where one is swept away by a river. *Asipatravana* is where one is torn apart by saws. *Lohadāraka* is where one is bound in iron fetters. (4.88–90)
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king. (4.91)

Knowing this fruit of accepting gifts from a king, those Brahmins who are learned in the scriptures and devoted to the study of the Vedas, desiring the absence of suffering in the next world, do not accept the wealth of a king. || 4.91 ||
One should wake during the *brāhma* hour and reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as the physical austerities rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas. (4.92)

Regarding the word "brāhma": he should wake up during the final *muhūrta* of the night. Then, for the sake of acquiring [wealth], he should deliberate upon dharma and artha so that they do not conflict with one another. Likewise, he should reflect: "To this extent of physical hardship and to this extent of temporal exertion, such-and-such dharma (or artha) shall be acquired. He should also reflect upon what the ultimate meaning of the Veda might be. (4.92)
Having risen and performed the necessary duties, having purified himself and being composed,
he should stand for a long time chanting the morning twilight prayer at its proper time, and likewise the evening prayer.

"Having risen": then, having risen from bed at the time of dawn, and having performed urination and other such acts if necessary, and having completed the purification to be described below with a restrained mind, one should perform the *japa* at the stated times of the morning and evening twilights—even after the sun has risen—and maintain the practice of the "sunrise sacrifice" (*uditahoma*). Even for one who performs the "pre-sunrise sacrifice" (*anuditahoma*), he should sit after having performed the oblation. This repetition of the mention of the twilights is for the purpose of enjoining the long-term fruits of the twilights, such as longevity and so forth. (4.93)
By virtue of their long twilight devotions, the seers attained long life, as well as wisdom, glory, fame, and spiritual luster. (4.94)

And so it is said: "The sages," and "wisdom. Because the sages, through the performance of the long twilight devotions (*dīrghasaṃdhyā*), attained long life, wisdom, fame, the heavenly realm, renown, and the perfection of Vedic study and other virtues, therefore one who desires these should perform the long twilight devotions. (4.94)

Having performed the ritual commencement (upākarma) according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin should diligently study the Vedas for four and a half months. 4.95.

"On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa" means that, having performed the rite called *upākarma* on the full moon of either Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, a Brāhmaṇa should then diligently study the Vedas for four and a half months. (4.95)
Under the Puṣya asterism, a twice-born man should perform the external dismissal of the Vedic hymns (chandas),
or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon.

The twice-born man who has performed the *upākarma* on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa should, after five and a half months have passed, go outside the village during the month of Pauṣa under the Puṣya asterism and perform the rite called the *utsarga* of the Vedas as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras. He who has performed it on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada should perform it when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha arrives, either in the forenoon or at that time.
Having thus performed the ritual dismissal of the Vedic meters outside according to the scriptures, one should cease [recitation] for the intervening night and that very same day and night. (4.97)

"According to the scriptures" means that, without transgressing the rules thus stated in the scriptures, one should perform the rite called *utsarga* for the Vedic meters outside the village; thereafter, for that single day and night—the middle night of which has two sides like wings—one should observe non-study (*anadhyāya*). (4.97)
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and one should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.

Regarding the word "ataḥ" (therefore): after the period of suspension for study has passed, one who possesses self-restraint should study the Vedas during the bright fortnights; however, during the dark fortnights, he should recite the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, such as grammar and the rest, according to the prescribed rules. 4.98.
One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night while exhausted, one should not sleep again.

"Not indistinctly": one should never recite that which is indistinct or unclear. Likewise, one should not study in the presence of Śūdras. Similarly, having risen from sleep, one should not go back to sleep at night after becoming exhausted from studying the Vedas during the latter part of the night. (4.98)
A twice-born man who is disciplined should always recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule, provided there is no time of distress. 4.100

Regarding the phrase "as previously stated": if the teacher is occupied with other duties and the student himself is unable to hear much, then in the absence of that [teacher], the twice-born man, being diligent, should always recite the *brahman* known as the *ṛk* and *sāman*, which are joined with meters such as the *gāyatrī*. Likewise, he should recite the *brahman* known as the *brāhmaṇa*—that is, the *yajurveda* interspersed with mantras joined with meters such as the *gāyatrī*. This separate mention is made because of the distinction between the *mantra* and the *brāhmaṇa*, owing to their being recited in a mixed manner. (4.100)
One who is studying should always avoid these occasions of non-recitation, as should one who is teaching students according to the prescribed rule. (4.101)

"These" refers to the following: while studying according to the previously mentioned rule and teaching his pupils, he should always avoid the occasions for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) that are about to be described. (4.101)
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, or when it stirs up clouds of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.

Regarding the term *karṇaśrava*: since hearing occurs through the ears alone, the expression *karṇaśrava* is used with the intention of emphasizing its intensity. Therefore, when the wind blows at night with excessive noise, or during the day when it is capable of sweeping up dust, those who know the rules for study declare these two times to be periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*) lasting as long as those conditions persist. 4.102.
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when great meteors fall, there shall be an interruption of Vedic study for the remainder of the day. 4.103.

Regarding the phrase "during lightning, thunder, and rain": when lightning, thunder, and rain occur simultaneously, and when there is a fall [of a celestial body] due to a great divine light or from its station, Manu declares that during such rains, there shall be no study for as long as that same period lasts, beginning from the time of these omens until the following day. (4.103)
One should know that when these [phenomena] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should know it to be a time unfit for study; likewise, so too when clouds are seen out of season.

"Regarding these": when one recognizes that these [phenomena], such as lightning and the rest, have arisen from the fires manifested by the desire to sacrifice during times characterized by the twilights, then one should observe a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). This does not apply at all times during the rainy season; rather, there is a suspension of study only upon such an omen, and likewise elsewhere than in the rains when clouds are seen. (4.104)

In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly bodies, one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study until the same time the following day, even during the proper season. 4.105.

Regarding the term "nirghāta" (thunderclap): when there is a portentous sound in the atmosphere, an earthquake, or a halo around the sun and other celestial bodies—whether it occurs outside the rainy season or even during the rains—one should know that these are occasions for non-study (*anadhyāya*) until the same time the next day; this is understood from the word "api" (even), which implies that this applies at other times as well. || 4.105 ||

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; for the remainder of the night, it is as [regulated] as during the day.

Regarding the phrase "when [the fires] have been made manifest": when the fires have been revealed by the removal of their ashes at the time of twilight, if there is only the sound of lightning and thunder and no rain, then the suspension of study lasts only as long as the light persists; this is not an "untimely" (*ākālika*) suspension. During the day, this refers to the light of the sun; at night, to the stars. Therefore, if this portent occurs during the morning twilight, the suspension of study is only for the day; if it occurs during the evening twilight, it is only for the night. Furthermore, regarding the remaining cases—specifically when the third type, known as rain, has arisen—the statement that "as it is by day, so it is by night" is a restatement of what has already been taught. (4.106)
For those who desire proficiency in dharma, there shall be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, and in all cases where there is a foul odor. (4.107)

"Permanent suspension of study (*nityānadhyāya*). For those seeking excellence in *dharma*, there should always be a suspension of study in villages and towns. Furthermore, when a foul odor is perceived everywhere, there is a suspension of study. In this section on suspensions of study, because terms such as "permanent" (*nitya*) are absent in some instances [but present in others], their permanence applies in those specific cases, while elsewhere there is an option. This [distinction] is to be understood as being established according to the difference between those desiring excellence in *dharma* and those desiring excellence in knowledge (*vidyā*). For students are of two kinds: those desiring excellence in *dharma* and those desiring excellence in knowledge. Among them, those who have already mastered the Vedas and seek only the transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭātiśaya*) arising from the performance of observances are those desiring excellence in *dharma*; for them, there is respect for all [types of] suspensions of study. On the other hand, there are beginners; they are seekers of excellence in knowledge. For them, there is no respect for suspensions of study other than those indicated by the term "permanent. (4.107)
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a low-caste man (vṛṣala), nor while one is weeping, nor in a crowd of people. 4.108.

"Regarding the phrase *antargataśava* (a corpse inside)": when a corpse is present, or in the vicinity of a *vṛṣala* (a low-caste person) or an unrighteous person—since the term *śūdra* was mentioned in the rule "not in the vicinity of a Śūdra person"—and also during weeping; furthermore, when people have gathered together for some business, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). 4.108.

While in water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine, while impure from food, or after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony—one should not entertain even a thought in one's mind [of reciting the Veda]. (4.109)

Regarding the term "udaka" (water): during the two middle watches known as the "great night"—for it is recorded by Devala that "the great night should be understood as the two middle watches"—and during the time of voiding urine or excrement, one remains impure until after performing *ācamana*. Furthermore, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, from the moment of invitation until the conclusion of the *śrāddha* meal, one must not even mentally recite the Veda for a full day and night. (4.109)
Having accepted an invitation to an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days during the impurity caused by a king or by Rāhu (an eclipse).

"Having accepted," [it means]: a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures, having accepted an invitation to a *navaśrāddha* (a funeral rite for a recently deceased person), or at the birth of a king's son, or when there is an eclipse of the sun or moon by Rāhu, he shall not study the Veda for three days. (4.110)
As long as the fragrance and the smear of a single funeral offering remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should one not recite the Veda. 4.111

Or even after three days; "as long as" means: as long as the garland, sandalwood paste, and other fragrant ointments belonging to the Śrāddha remain on the body of a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures who has been invited for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, so long he shall not study the Veda. (4.111)
One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food provided by one in a state of birth-impurity. 4.112.

"Regarding the term 'lying down': one should not study while lying on a bed with limbs stretched out or feet crossed at the ankles, nor having assumed the *paryastikā* posture, nor after eating meat or food that is impure due to ritual defilement. (4.112)
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the new moon day, the fourteenth day, and on the full moon and eighth days; 4.113.

One should not study during a haze, when there is the sound of an arrow, at the two twilights, nor on the new moon day, the fourteenth, the full moon, or the eighth days; for since the *aṣṭakās* are mentioned later, the mention of *aṣṭakā* here—due to its association with the new moon and other such times—is intended to signify the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*). (4.113)
The new moon day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the disciple;
and the Brahma-aṣṭakā and the full moon day [destroy both]. Therefore, one should avoid those days.

Because it is said, "The new moon (amāvāsyā) kills the teacher, the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) kills the pupil, and the eighth and full moon days (aṣṭamī-paurṇamāsī) cause one to forget the Veda"; therefore, one should always avoid study on these days. (4.114)
A twice-born man should not recite while there is a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, and camels are barking in a row.

Regarding "a shower of dust": when there is a rain of dust and a conflagration of the quarters, by which the directions appear as if ablaze; and during the howling of jackals, dogs, and donkeys—if they sit down in a row—the twice-born man shall not recite [the Veda]. (4.115)

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting a gift related to a funeral rite (śrāddha). 4.116

"One should not study" means: according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba, "One should not study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw on all sides of a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*)," one should likewise not study while near such a cremation ground or a cow-pen; nor should one study while wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor having accepted clothing for the purpose of a funeral rite (*śrāddha*) or food and other items intended for a funeral feast. (4.116)

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha ceremony, there is a suspension of study even upon touching it; for the twice-born is traditionally declared to have his hand as his mouth. (4.117)

Upon touching anything whatsoever—be it cattle, gold, or other items—for the sake of a *śrāddha* rite, there is a suspension of Vedic study; how much more so after actually accepting them? For the Brāhmaṇa has his hand as his mouth, since his hand is indeed his mouth. (4.117)
When a village is beset by thieves, during a panic caused by fire, and during all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is no study for the duration of the day. (4.118)

"By thieves," etc.: one should know that there is no study for the remainder of the day when a village is plundered by thieves, when there is danger caused by fire, or when portents occur—whether divine, atmospheric, or terrestrial—in the form of miracles such as the raining of blood and so forth. (4.118)
At the Upakarman and the Utsarga ceremonies, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
on the Aṣṭakās, however, it lasts for a day and a night, as does the suspension on the nights at the end of the seasons.

Regarding the phrase "on the *upākarma*": when the two rites called *upākarma* and *utsarga*, as prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, have been performed, a three-night suspension of study is traditionally ordained. In that context, regarding the *utsarga*, there is an option between this [three-night period] and the "bird-day" (*pakṣiṇī*) consisting of the aforementioned two days and one night. After the full moon of *Āgrahāyaṇī*, on the eighth days of the dark fortnights—whether there be three or four such days—there is a suspension of study for one day and night. Furthermore, the mention of "on the eighth days" is for the purpose of indicating that the suspension lasts as long as those eighth days endure; thus it has been stated there: "One should not study on the *aṣṭakās*. As for the fact that this is repeated here as "but on the *aṣṭakās* for a day and night," some say it is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*), but that is incorrect, because its obligatory nature is already established there by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "The new moon (*amāvāsyā*) destroys the teacher. Moreover, during other seasons as well, there is a suspension of study for a day and night. (4.119)

One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle. 4.120.

"One should not study": one who is mounted on a horse, a tree, an elephant, a donkey, or a camel; likewise, one standing in a saline or barren region (ūṣara); and one traveling by means of a vehicle such as a cart—these should not study. 4.120.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle; not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when there is acidity. 4.121.

"Nor during a dispute": when verbal abuse has begun, or when a physical fight has broken out; or when one is stationed with an army that has not yet engaged in battle, or while it is already engaged in combat; and immediately after eating, as long as the hands are still moist, according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha. Furthermore, on the following day, if there is indigestion, or after vomiting food, or if there is a sour eructation, one should not study.
Nor having failed to take leave of a guest, nor while a strong wind is blowing, nor when blood flows from the body, nor when one is wounded by a weapon. (4.122)

Regarding the term "guest" (*atithi*): one should not study as long as a guest has not been granted permission with the words "Please study," nor when the wind is excessively agitated by the fatigue of recitation, nor when blood flows from the nose, nor even when blood has been drawn by a weapon and a wound has arisen. (4.122)

One should never recite the *Ṛg* and *Yajur* Vedas while the sound of the *Sāman* is heard; likewise, one should not do so after having completed the study of the Veda, nor after having studied the *Āraṇyaka*. (4.123)

Regarding the phrase "when the sound of the Sāman": while the sound of the Sāman is being heard, one should never engage in the recitation of the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda. Likewise, having completed the Veda and having studied that portion of the Veda known as the Āraṇyaka, one should not study anything else during that day and night. (4.123)
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda, however, belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure. (4.124)

Regarding the term *ṛgveda*: that which has the gods as its deity is the *ṛgveda*, called "having the gods as its divinity" (*devadaivatya*). Because it has humans as its deities, the *yajurveda* is "human" (*mānuṣa*). The *sāmaveda* is traditionally held to have the ancestors as its deity (*pitṛdevatāka*). Having performed a rite for the ancestors, one sips water for purification; therefore, the implication is that it is impure. Consequently, while that [Sāmaveda] is being heard, the *ṛc*s and *yajus* formulas should not be studied; this is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding injunction. (4.124)
Knowing this, the learned daily practice the essence of the three Vedas in sequence first, and afterwards they study the Veda itself. (4.125)

Knowing this divinity inherent in gods, ancestors, humans, and so forth, those who know the three Vedas and are conversant with various scriptures first practice daily—according to the sequence stated in the second chapter—the essence of the triple Veda consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, namely that which is called the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*. Only after practicing the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* should they study the Veda. Just as there is no study during periods when study is forbidden (*anadhyāya*), so too one must not study without first practicing the *praṇava* and the others; this is what is restated here. (4.125)

If a domestic animal, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat passes between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is a suspension of study for a day and a night. (4.126)

"By cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, mongooses, and mice": when a student and a teacher who are studying have a cow or other animal, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a mouse pass between them, one should know that there is a suspension of study for a day and a night. (4.126)
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study: an impure place for Vedic recitation and an impure self. (4.127)

With reference to one who desires proficiency in knowledge, he says "two" in order to set forth an alternative regarding the previously mentioned occasions for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). With respect to the impurity of the place of study and the impurity of oneself, there are two occasions for the suspension of study. A twice-born man should always avoid those two with special effort. Even other than those two, wherever the word "always" (*nitya*) occurs, or where there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) such as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that points to its being obligatory, he should likewise avoid them at all times; but in other cases, there is an option. (4.127)
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born Snātaka must always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.

“On the new moon day”: on the new moon day and other such occasions, a twice-born man who has completed his studentship (*snātaka*) should never approach his wife, even during her fertile period (*ṛtu*). The charge of redundancy with the rule “he may approach her except on the sacred days (*parvan*)” has already been addressed in that very context. This [present rule] is stated here as a subsidiary part of the penance for violating the *snātaka* vows. (4.128)
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor with many garments, nor constantly, nor in an unknown body of water. (4.129)

"Not bathing": having eaten, one should not perform an occasional bath at will; however, a bath on account of a specific occasion (*naimittika*) is not prohibited, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "Even for a moment, when capable, one should not be negligent. Likewise, one who is ill should not perform even an occasional bath, but rather should perform substitutes for bathing as far as possible—such as sprinkling with water from a golden vessel while reciting mantras, touching a cow, and changing one's garment—as well as the *paṭaparivartana* (changing clothes). The "great night" (*mahāniśā*) should be understood as the two middle watches of the night.
One should not perform a bath in that [river] except for rites performed for specific desires or occasional observances.

Because of this traditional teaching of Devala, one should not bathe there. Furthermore, one who wears many garments should never bathe; however, there is no prohibition against it in the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*). Nor should one bathe in a body of water that is unknown for being infested with deep or shallow crocodiles and the like. (4.129)

One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, of one's teacher, of a king, of a *snātaka*, of an *ācārya*, of a tawny person (*babhru*), or of one who has been initiated for a sacrifice. (4.130)

"Of the deities": one should not intentionally step on the shadow of deities represented in paintings or books, nor that of a guru, one's father and so forth, a king, a *snātaka*, or a teacher—Kapila being mentioned separately from the [general category of] gurus because of his preeminence—and one who has been initiated for the sake of a sacrifice. 4.130.
At midday and at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
Regarding the term "madhyandine": having eaten at a *śrāddha* ceremony held at midday, midnight, or during the twilights, one should not remain for long at a crossroads. (4.131)
One should not intentionally step upon a body-scrub, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit. (4.132)

Regarding "avoiding stepping over": one should not intentionally step over bath water, urine, feces, blood, phlegm, or vomit; nor should one step over chewed betel and the like, even though they have the form of phlegm. (4.132)
One should not serve an enemy, nor a companion who is an enemy, nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another. (4.133)

Regarding the term "enemy" (*vairiṇam*): one should not serve an enemy, nor one who is excessively attached to friends, nor one who is unrighteous, nor one who is lacking in character, nor one who is devoted to the wives of others. The unrighteous person is mentioned separately from the thief because of the latter's extreme contemptibility. Furthermore, although the fault in serving an enemy and the like is indeed visible in this world, it is nevertheless determined that an invisible (karmic) fault also arises by virtue of the prohibition in the scriptures. This should be understood in other cases as well. (4.133)
For there is nothing in this world so detrimental to long life as a man’s pursuit of another's wife in this world. (4.134)

"Indeed, there is nothing like this," because in this world there is nothing else that causes such a depletion of a man's lifespan as approaching another's wife; therefore, this must not be done. (4.134)
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak. 4.135

"And likewise a Kṣatriya" means that one who is habitually inclined toward arrogance should never, even at times when they are weak, show contempt for Kṣatriyas, serpents, or learned Brāhmaṇas. || 4.135 ||
For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt. (4.136)

"These three": because these three, when treated with contempt, destroy a man—the Kṣatriya and the serpent by their manifest power, but the Brāhmaṇa through malevolent spells and the like—therefore, one of refined intellect should never disregard these three. (4.136)
One should not despise oneself because of former failures; until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable. (4.137)

"Nor [should he despise] himself": one should not despise oneself on account of initial failures; rather, one should exert effort for the sake of prosperity until death, and should not think that prosperity is difficult to attain. (4.137)
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant; nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma. (4.138)

"Truth. When questioned by anyone, one should speak only the truth. One should speak what is both true and pleasant even without being asked, such as the birth of a son and the like. However, one should not speak what is unpleasant though true, such as the separation from a kinsman; rather, when there is an alternative, one should remain silent. Furthermore, one should not utter that which is pleasant but untrue. This is the eternal law (dharma). 4.138.
One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (well-being, well-being), or simply say "bhadram" (well-being); one should not engage in dry enmity or dispute with anyone. 4.139.

"‘Bhadram’ (auspicious): Because of the traditional teaching of Gautama that ‘what is inauspicious is auspicious,’ this term is employed here for the sake of the meter. In this context, it should be explained by supplying the missing words: one should say of that which is of an inauspicious nature, ‘This is auspicious, this is welfare, this is the highest good,’ and so forth; for the particle *iti* has the sense of ‘in this manner. By the word *bhadram* itself, or by the word *evam* (thus), [one expresses this]. One should never engage in disputes or quarrels caused by arguments, even with an inferior person. (4.139)
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not go with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcasts.

"Not too early" means that one should not travel on a road at dawn, at twilight, or at midday with an unknown person or with Śūdras. Although it was already stated [in verse 4.60], "One should not set out on a journey alone," the repetition of the word "alone" here is for the purpose of prescribing a specific penance. 4.140.
One should not despise those who have missing limbs or extra limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth. (4.141)

"Those with deficient limbs": one should not mock those with deficient or extra limbs, the foolish, the very old, the deformed, the poor, widows, and so forth, by calling them names such as "one-eyed" or by using other forms of derision. 4.141.
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire;
nor, while remaining in his natural state, should he look at the hosts of luminaries in the sky while he is impure.

"Should not touch": a Brāhmaṇa who is fit for ritual sipping (ācamana) and other rites should not touch cows, Brāhmaṇas, or fires. Likewise, being impure and not being ill, he should not even look at the collection of lights such as the sun located in the heavenly world. 4.142.
Having touched these while being impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water, as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand. (4.143)

Regarding the word "having touched": being impure, having touched cows and the like, one should touch with water the seats of the vital breaths—the eyes and so forth—and all the limbs. The penance prescribed in the context of the section, namely, "one should touch the navel with water using the middle of the hand," is mentioned here for the sake of brevity; for if that were performed there, it would have to be done whenever touching cows and the like occurs. (4.143)
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own bodily orifices without a reason; he should avoid touching all the hairs on his private parts as well. (4.144)
"Unafflicted" means that, being healthy, one should not, without cause, touch one's own orifices or the hairs located in the anus and genitals. 4.144.
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should constantly recite prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness. (4.145)

"Endowed with auspicious conduct" (*maṅgalācārayukta*) means that, because it is the cause of auspiciousness in the form of the accomplishment of one's intended aims, one should be diligent in auspicious things such as yellow pigment (*gorocana*) and sandalwood, and in conduct such as rising to greet others; being pure in soul and having mastered the tongue and other senses, one should, while remaining free from laziness, constantly perform recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*). Here, although conduct and the rest have already been mentioned, they are stated again with the intention of ensuring the cessation of misfortune. (4.145)
For those who are devoted to auspicious conduct, who are ever self-restrained,
and who engage in recitation and burnt offerings, no downfall exists.

And as it has been said: "For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct"—that is, for those whose habit is the performance of auspicious rites and the like, who are pure, and devoted to recitation and fire-offerings—no affliction caused by fate or by human agency exists. (4.146)
One should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without weariness; for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty. 4.147

"One should constantly recite the Veda"—at whatever time there is an obstruction to ritual acts with visible results, at that time one should, being free from laziness, constantly recite the Veda alone; for Manu and others declare this to be the supreme duty of a Brahmin, while any other is said by them to be a secondary duty. (4.147)
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. (4.148)

He states the purpose for which the practice of the Vedas, though already mentioned, is restated: "By the study of the Vedas... [4.148] "Through constant study of the Vedas, purity, austerity, and non-violence, one remembers one's previous birth."
Remembering his former birth, the twice-born man practices the Brahman;
and through the constant practice of the Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss. (4.149)

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "paurvikīm" (his former birth). Recalling his own previous birth, thinking, "Such is this practice of the Vedas by which another birth is remembered," he constantly engages in the very practice of the Vedas. And as a result of that constant practice, when the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas arises, he attains Brahman—that is, the imperishable bliss consisting of the nature of the Supreme Self. || 4.149 ||
He should constantly perform oblations for Savitṛ and propitiatory offerings on the festival days (parvan);
and he should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days. (4.150)

Regarding the phrase "sāvitrān" (related to Savitṛ): at the junctions of the fortnights and on the new moon days and so forth, one should always perform the oblations dedicated to the deity Savitṛ and those intended for the removal of misfortune with clarified butter (*ājya*), according to the traditional teaching of the Sūtra-author: "Clarified butter is the sacrificial offering that must not be withheld. Likewise, one should satiate the deceased ancestors, such as the father and others, by means of the rite called Aṣṭakā and by the rite called Anvaṣṭakā performed on the ninth lunar days following the Aṣṭakās. || 4.150 ||
One should discharge urine far from one's dwelling, far away from where one has washed one's feet, and likewise, one should dispose of the remains of food far from the house. (4.151)

"From afar": according to the traditional teaching of the Purāṇas, "having gone quickly a distance equal to the flight of an arrow," one should discharge urine, feces, water used for washing the feet, water from rinsing the mouth, and so forth, from such a distance away from the house. (4.151)
One should perform the preparation of unguents, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and the worship of the deities during the forenoon alone. (4.152)

Regarding the term *maitra*: because it is heard in the praise of the limbs of a sacrificial animal that "the anus is Mitra," here too the anus is called *maitra* by way of figurative identification (*abhedopacāra*). That which pertains to it—namely, purification upon evacuation, as well as body-consecrations such as anointing, daily bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and worshipping the gods—one should perform during the forenoon alone. (4.152)
On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and most excellent brahmins, the Lord for the sake of protection, and his teachers. 4.153.

"He should visit the deities" means that he should go to see the deities made of gold, gems, and so forth; Brahmins who are preeminent in dharma; kings and others capable of providing protection for the sake of his own security; and his elders, such as his father and others, on the new moon day and other junctions of the fortnights. (4.153)
He should salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
with palms joined in reverence, he should receive [their instructions] and follow behind them as they depart. (4.154)

"One should salute" means that one should salute those elders who have come to one's house and offer them a seat for the purpose of sitting; furthermore, one should remain near them with palms joined in reverence. When they depart, one should follow behind them. Although this matter of salutation and so forth has already been mentioned, it is stated again here with the intention of describing the results that will be explained later. (4.154)
One should, unwearied, always practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma, properly established in one's own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti. (4.155)

"Proclaimed by Śruti and Smṛti": being untiring, he should constantly practice that virtuous conduct which is the root of Dharma, which is correctly declared by the Śruti and Smṛti, and which is connected as an auxiliary to his own duties such as Vedic study and sacrifice. (4.155)
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. (4.156)

He states the purpose for which conduct (*ācāra*) is mentioned again with the words "from conduct" (*ācārāt*). Through conduct—that is, through its performance—one obtains long life, desired offspring, the non-destruction of wealth, and so forth. Furthermore, conduct renders fruitless the appearance of moles and other marks that indicate the destruction of a beloved wife; this is the statement regarding the fruits of conduct. Nor does this entail the charge of inconsistency, because its permanence has been established by such statements as, "even one whose essence consists merely of the *Sāvitrī*" (2.118). 4.156.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly partakes of suffering, being diseased and short-lived. (4.157)
Regarding "of bad conduct": because a person of bad conduct is censured in the world and is always miserable, diseased, and short-lived, one should therefore be possessed of good conduct. 4.157.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct, is full of faith, and is free from envy, lives for a hundred years. (4.158)

"Devoid of all auspicious marks": one who possesses correct conduct, is faithful, and is not a reviler lives for a hundred years even if he is devoid of all the praiseworthy marks such as having arms reaching to his knees. In the first chapter, the praise of conduct was for the purpose of praising the scripture; here, however, it is for the purpose of establishing the fruit of conduct. (4.158)
Whatever action depends on another, that one should avoid with effort;
but whatever depends on oneself, that one should practice with diligence. (4.159)

"Whatever is dependent on others": whatever action depends on others, such as giving special gifts through gains obtained unasked and so forth—that one should avoid with effort. On the other hand, whatever is under one's own control, even by means of a small portion of one's own wealth, such as through one's own gain or benefiting others—that one should practice with diligence. (4.159)
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering. (4.160)

Regarding the phrase "because everything": that which is to be accomplished through the entreaties of others and so forth is entirely a cause of suffering; whereas that which is accomplished by oneself alone is entirely a source of happiness—one should understand this, in brief, as the definition of happiness and suffering. (4.160)
Whatever action one performs that brings satisfaction to one's inner self, that one should perform with diligence; but one should avoid the opposite. (4.161)

Whether it be unenjoined, unprohibited, or optional—that action which brings internal satisfaction to the person performing it, that one should perform with effort; however, one should avoid that which causes dissatisfaction to oneself. (4.161)
One must not harm one's teacher, one's expounder of the Veda, one's father, one's mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever. (4.162)

"And the teacher" means: one should not harm the teacher—that is, the instructor who merely performs the initiation (*upanayana*)—nor the father, mother, or guru in the worldly sense, nor those devoted to cows, Brahmins, or asceticism, even if they are assassins (*ātatāyin*). Otherwise, since the general prohibition against harming exists, this specific statement would be redundant. (4.162)
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities; one should also avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, anger, and harshness. (4.163)

Regarding "atheism": one should avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, anger, and harshness. Atheism is the conviction that the unseen world (adṛṣṭa) does not exist; one should avoid reviling the Vedas and the deities, as well as envy, lack of humility, conceit, anger, and cruelty. (4.163)
One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down—with the exception of a son or a pupil; these two may be struck for the purpose of discipline. 4.164.

"Of another" means that one who is angry should not raise a staff or other weapon against another; however, having excluded those about to be mentioned—namely one's own son, pupil, wife, younger brother, uterine brother, and slave—one should not strike them with a blow. But for the purpose of instruction, one may strike them with a rope or a split bamboo cane, and so forth. (4.164)
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him wanders for a hundred years in the Tāmisra hell. (4.165)

Regarding the phrase "to a Brahmin": even a twice-born man, by merely raising a staff or similar weapon with the intent to kill a Brahmin, wanders for a hundred years in the hell named Tāmisra. 4.165.
Having intentionally struck [another] even with a blade of grass out of anger, one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in states of woe. (4.166)

"Having struck," etc.: having intentionally struck [another] even with a blade of grass out of anger, one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in the wombs of dogs and other such animals caused by that sin. In the word *ājātīḥ*, the prefix *ā-* is used for the sake of completing the meter. (4.166)
A man who, through lack of wisdom, causes blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting, undergoes very great suffering after death. (4.167)

Regarding the phrase "of one not fighting": without engaging in battle, a man who causes blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin out of foolishness will experience great suffering in the next world. (4.167)
As many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth, for that many years shall the shedder of that blood be devoured by others in the next world. (4.168)

Regarding "blood": for as many particles of dust as the blood produced from a slain Brāhmaṇa solidifies upon the surface of the earth, for that many years shall the one who caused that blood to flow be devoured by dogs and other beasts in the next world. 4.168.
Therefore, a learned man should never revile a twice-born man;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body. (4.169)

"Never indeed. Since [the sin] arises in this way through threatening a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, therefore one learned in the scriptures should never raise a staff or the like against a Brāhmaṇa; nor should he strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body. (4.169)
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood, and who is constantly devoted to violence—does not find happiness in this world. (4.170)

"Unrighteous" means this: because a man whose nature is to practice unrighteousness, or one for whom wealth is merely false and who is primarily intent on litigation, is always devoted to violence—he does not increase in happiness even in this world. Therefore, this must not be done. (4.170)
Even if he should suffer for it, he must not, by means of righteousness, turn his mind toward unrighteousness;
for he quickly perceives the reversal of fortune that befalls those who are unrighteous and sinful. (4.171)

"Not desponding" means as follows: just as the word *dharma* is seen to be used in reference to sacrifices and the like, as well as the self-purification (*ātmasaṃskāra*) produced by them, so too the word *adharma* is seen to be used in reference to violence and the like, as well as the self-purification produced by them. Therefore, it is explained as "of the unrighteous, the sinful. For one who observes the harassment by kings in this world for those whose character is to practice unrighteousness such as violence—who are possessed of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) called sin produced by that—and who, by the vision of the scriptures, perceives hell in the next world, should not apply the mind to unrighteousness even while falling into despondency, provided there is an excellence of self-restraint through the performance of dharma. (4.171)
Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow;
but turning back slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer. (4.172)

"Not unrighteousness" means: just as a cow yields fruit immediately in this world through its use for riding, milking, and so forth, so too unrighteousness, when practiced, does not bear fruit immediately. What then? Gradually, over the course of time, it becomes intent on yielding its fruit and cuts away the very roots of the doer. Like a tree whose roots have been severed, it destroys the doer utterly, leaving no lineage behind. || 4.172 ||
If [the merit] does not accrue to oneself, it goes to one's sons; if not to the sons, then to one's grandsons; but a dharma that has been performed never becomes fruitless for the doer. 4.173

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if unrighteousness (*adharma*) does not bear fruit by way of producing disease in one's own body, then it bears fruit through the manifestation of diseases and so forth in one's sons and grandsons. However, that which has been committed never becomes fruitless for the doer; rather, those who are destined to be afflicted by disease and the like due to their own misdeeds, are born as such sons and grandsons—either in this life or in another birth—by the power of the doer’s own evil karma, in order that they may experience the suffering of witnessing his own ruin and other calamities. (4.173)
By unrighteousness one prospers for a while, then one sees auspicious things;
thereafter one conquers one's rivals, but finally one perishes root and branch. (4.174)

"By unrighteousness" means that through unrighteous acts such as seizing the property of others, one becomes possessed of wealth and so forth in the present life. Immediately thereafter, one experiences pleasures by way of enjoying that wealth and other possessions; and because of that experience, one overcomes enemies by virtue of being happy and so on. Then, in this very life, one perishes with total destruction, or having died, one goes to hell from which there is no return. (4.174)
He should always take delight in truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and he should instruct his pupils in accordance with dharma, restraining his speech, his arms, and his belly.

Since this is so, therefore [the verse says] "toward truth, dharma, and noble conduct. One should always cultivate delight in truth, dharma, virtuous behavior, and purity. Furthermore, regarding those who are to be instructed, such as one's wife and others, it has been stated that one should restrain them—using speech, arms, and the belly—in accordance with the limits of the scriptures, beginning with the rule: "But behind the back of the body," and so forth. This repetition is for the purpose of strengthening the resolve of those who are undisciplined. (4.175)
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness, and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future suffering and is censured by the world. (4.176)

"One should abandon" means that even though the three aims of life (*trivarga*) are declared to be goals for man, one should nevertheless abandon them. One should not practice a *dharma* that results in unhappiness or is censured by the world; nor should one pursue wealth and pleasure that contradict *dharma*; nor should one perform a *dharma* such as intense asceticism when one lacks the capacity for it, or a *dharma* that provokes public reproach, such as the slaughter of cows during the *madhuparka* ceremony. (4.176)
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor crooked; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others. (4.177)

"Not fickle with hands or feet" means that one should not perform purposeless activities of the hands, feet, eyes, or speech; nor should one be dishonest, cruel, harmful to others, or possessed of improper intellect. The repetition [of this injunction] serves the purpose already stated. (4.177)
By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that way, he does not come to harm. (4.178)

When two interpretations of a statement appear, or regarding optional matters, one should follow that very path which has been pursued by one's father, grandfather, and so forth, and perform exactly what they have performed; by following that very same virtuous path and acting accordingly, one is not harmed by violating dharma. 4.178.

With officiating priests, family chaplains, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with children, the elderly, and the sick; and with physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends. (4.179)
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants. (4.180)

Regarding the terms "officiant" (*ṛtvij*), "parents," and so forth: one should not engage in verbal quarrels with officiants and the others. A *purohita* is one who performs rites for peace and other such purposes. "Dependents" (*saṃśritāḥ*) are those who live off one's support. An "afflicted person" (*āturaḥ*) is one suffering from disease. "Kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) are those related through the father’s side. "In-laws" (*vaivāhyāḥ*) are relatives through the mother’s side, such as sisters, sisters-in-law, daughters-in-law, and so on. The "group of servants" (*dāsavargaḥ*) is the assembly of slaves. (4.179–180)
By renouncing disputes through these [means], one is liberated from all sins;
and having conquered by means of these, the householder conquers all these worlds. (4.181)

"By these": having abandoned disputes with these [persons], he is liberated from all sins, which have become exceedingly attenuated. Likewise, by setting aside these disputes, the householder takes possession of all these worlds that are about to be described. 4.181.

The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati; the guest is the lord of Indra’s world; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods. (4.182)

Regarding the word "teacher" (*ācārya*): since teachers and others are, by virtue of their vision and power, the source of the worlds of Brahmā, Prajāpati, Indra, and the gods, they declare these worlds to belong to the householder who has abandoned disputes concerning them. By abandoning such disputes, the world of Brahmā and the others are attained; this is precisely what is stated here through this figurative expression. It should be understood that the same applies in subsequent passages as well. 4.182.

Sisters-in-law are the kinsmen of the Apsarases in their world; maternal uncles and mothers are the relatives of the Viśvedevas in their world; and paternal uncles and mothers are the kinsmen of the Waters in their world and of the Earth in hers. (4.183)

Regarding the term "jāmayah": sisters-in-law (jāmayah) have power in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen (bāndhavāḥ) in the world of the Viśvedevas; and maternal uncles and mothers in the world of mortals. 4.183.
Children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as lords of the sky;
an elder brother is equal to a father, and one's wife and son are one's own body. (4.184)

Regarding the phrase "lords of the sky": children, the elderly, dependents, and the sick exercise authority in the intermediate realm (*antarikṣaloka*). An elder brother is equal to a father; therefore, he too is a lord in the world of Prajāpati. As for the wife and son, according to the Vedic revelation: "The wife is indeed half of one's own self, and the son is called the very self" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.51), they are one's own body. Therefore, how could one dispute with them as if they were separate from oneself? 4.184.
One's shadow, one's circle of servants, and one's daughter are the utmost objects of pity; therefore, when reviled by these, one should always endure it without distress. (4.185)

"Shadow": one's own group of servants, because they follow closely behind like one's own shadow; therefore, they are not an object of dispute. And a daughter is pitiable, an object of compassion; thus, when reviled by these, he should always forgive without being distressed. (4.185)
Even though he may be capable of receiving gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, his spiritual luster (brāhmaṃ tejaḥ) is quickly extinguished. (4.186)

"Capable of receiving gifts": even though one is capable of receiving gifts through learning, study, and so forth, one should avoid engaging in them again. For by receiving gifts, the power resulting from the causes of study and the like is quickly destroyed. Although this was already stated in the verse beginning with "for the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence," it is stated again here for the purpose of explaining that its fruit is the quenching of one's vital energy (*tejas*). 4.186.
Without knowing the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of material gifts, a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger. (4.187)
