"Not of material things" means that a wise man, even if he is suffering from the exhaustion of hunger, should not accept gifts without understanding the rules for acceptance—such as the specific mantras, materials, and deities—which are inseparable from dharma; how much less so when there is no distress? (4.187)
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood. (4.188)
"Gold": one who is devoid of sacred learning and Vedic study, by accepting gold and other such things, is reduced to ashes through contact with fire, just like wood. 4.188.
Gold [prolongs] life and food; land and a cow nourish the body;
a horse [prolongs] sight, clothing the skin, ghee brilliance, and sesame seeds progeny. (4.189)

And so it is said: "Gold, life-span, food, land, and a cow consume the body. When gold and food are accepted, they burn the life-span of one who lacks knowledge; and the cow and land burn his body. Horses, clothing, ghee, and sesame seeds, respectively, burn his sight, skin, vital energy, and offspring. It is not only through acceptance that the ignorant man is always consumed by these; rather— 4.189. Not only is the ignorant man burned by accepting gifts, but he is also burned while giving them away. Just as fire burns wood when it is both received and given, so do these things burn the ignorant man whether he accepts or bestows them. Therefore, the wise man should never accept or give gold, food, land, a cow, horses, clothing, ghee, or sesame seeds. For the ignorant man is burned by these very things, whether he receives them or gives them. Thus, the wise man should avoid accepting or giving these eight items. Furthermore, the ignorant man is burned by accepting or giving other things as well, such as elephants, horses, chariots, beds, seats, slaves, slave-girls, garments, grain, houses, and the like. Therefore, the wise man should avoid accepting or giving all such things. Moreover, the ignorant man is burned by accepting or giving even small things, such as flowers, fruits, water, roots, and vegetables. But a twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study the Vedas, and who delights in accepting gifts, sinks along with that very recipient, like one in water using a stone as a raft. (4.190)

"But one who is without austerity is unlearned. This refers to one who, being devoid of austerity and Vedic study, is desirous of receiving gifts; then, as if crossing water in a boat made of stone, he sinks into hell along with the giver who is joined by the sin of giving to an unworthy recipient. For in this context, because of the connection with the act of receiving, the phrase "by him" (tena) refers to both the ignorant giver and the receiver, according to the view that will be stated later. (4.190)
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear whatever gift he might receive; for even by means of a very small thing, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud. (4.191)

"Therefore" means: since even when accepting insubstantial things, the ignorant man sinks into hell like a cow in the mud, therefore the unwise man should fear the acceptance of anything whatsoever, even that which is distinct from gold and such [valuables]. 4.191.
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat, nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas. (4.192)

"Not to a woman. It is said that water indeed may be given to everyone; however, one who knows the Dharma should not give even that to those who follow the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratika) and the like. By this hyperbolic statement (*atiśayokti*), the giving of other substances is prohibited, but not the gift of water. Furthermore, the prohibition against giving to heretics (*pākhaṇḍin*) and others—even though such people are well known in the world—as being "those who follow the cat-vow," is stated here again with the intention of defining their characteristics. Moreover, the prohibition against giving to the ignorant is intended to prevent gifts from being made to the ignorant when a learned person is available. And thus, the rule "gifts should be given only to a *śrotriya*" is to be understood as applying when a learned *śrotriya* is unavailable. (4.192)
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, when given to these three types of persons, results in misfortune for the giver and likewise for the recipient in the next world. (4.193)

Regarding the word "in three": wealth acquired by righteous means, when given to these three types of people—beginning with those who observe the "cat-vow"—results in misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world, as it causes their downfall into hell. (4.193)
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks beneath it, so do the ignorant donor and recipient sink to the bottom. (4.194)

"Yathā" means: just as two Brahmins—one a donor and the other a recipient—plunging into a boat made of stone while attempting to cross the water, perish together with it in that very water [in hell], so too do the donor and the recipient go to hell if they are ignorant of the rules governing acceptance (*pratigraha*) and perform the giving and receiving of gifts from one unworthy. The donor, indeed, desiring to reach the further shore of the ocean of *saṃsāra* by means of the recipient’s boat, if out of foolishness takes hold of a recipient who resembles a mere floating log, then on the contrary, he sinks even deeper along with him, experiencing the sensation of vanishing within the bottomless sea; thus, the meaning of the simile is that this results in a greater misfortune than any other. The statement "But one who is without austerity and unlearned... was spoken with reference to the recipient (*pratigrahītṛ*), whereas this [present verse] is spoken with reference to the donor (*dātṛ*). Thus, there is no redundancy. This is intended to ensure the diligent avoidance of what is prohibited, lest it be confused with what is merely unknown. (4.194)

One who carries the banner of the Dharma while being always greedy, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world; one who is violent and a subverter of all—such a person should be known as a "cat-vowed" hypocrite (baiḍālavratika). || 4.195 ||

He describes the characteristics of those who follow the "cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratika*) and so forth with the words "one who makes a banner of righteousness" (*dharmadhvajī*). One who makes a banner of righteousness is so called because he covers his private parts for the sake of public reputation, making his religious practice a mere outward sign. He is greedy, miserly, hypocritical, a hidden sinner, a deceiver of the world, and a trickster. He is violent by nature, intent on injury, and a detractor of all; because he cannot tolerate the virtues of others, he is a reviler of everyone. Such a person, who conducts himself according to the cat-vow, is to be known as a *baiḍālavratika* Brāhmaṇa. (4.195)
With downward gaze, treacherous, intent on accomplishing all his own ends, deceitful, and falsely humble—such is the twice-born who practices the "heron-vow. (4.196)

"One with downward gaze, deceitful" (adhodṛṣṭir naiṣkṛtikaḥ): "With downward gaze" means for the sake of appearing disciplined; he looks only downward. "Deceitful" (naiṣkṛtikaḥ) refers to one who conducts himself with cruelty, who is intent on achieving his own ends, devoted to securing his own interests, crafty, indifferent to the food of others, falsely disciplined, and full of hypocrisy; such a person acts with the behavior of a crane, and thus he is a Brahmin who bears the vow of a crane (bakavrata). 4.196.
Those Brahmins who observe the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful action.
"Those who"—namely, those Brahmins who bear the marks of the crane-vow and the cat-vow—by that sinful cause of action, fall into the hell named Andhatāmisra. (4.197)
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing a sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras. (4.198)

"Nor [for the sake] of dharma": having committed a sin, one should not perform an expiation while concealing that sin under the pretext of a religious vow, thereby deluding the ignorant world of Śūdras and others by making it appear, "This man is righteous. (4.198)
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda;
and a vow practiced through deceit goes to the Rākṣasas.

Regarding the word "pretya" (after death): such Brahmins, both while living and when dead, are censured by those intent on defining the true nature of the Self. And that hypocritical conduct leads them to the state of demons. (4.199)

He who, though not a bearer of the [ascetic] marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing those marks, takes upon himself the sin of the true mark-bearers and is born among the animal species. (4.200)

"Without the marks" (aliṅgī) means one who, though not a celibate student, lives by the livelihood of a celibate student or others while wearing their dress; he takes upon himself the sin of those celibate students and others, and is born in the wombs of dogs and other such creatures. Therefore, this must not be done. (4.200)
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the person who constructed the reservoir. (4.201)

Regarding the phrase "at water-reservoirs belonging to others": one should never bathe in ponds and such belonging to others. By bathing there, the sin that the perpetrator incurs in those ponds and such is connected with the fourth part [of the penance] which is about to be described. Even for righteous people, misdeeds committed in previous lives and accumulated remain; therefore, it does not follow that there is an absence of sin simply by bathing at the reservoirs of the righteous. (4.201)
One who makes use of another's vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given shall incur a fourth part of the sin. (4.202)

Regarding "vehicles, beds, and seats": one who makes use of vehicles, beds, seats—such as chariots, couches, and stools—as well as wells, gardens, and houses belonging to another without they being given, incurs a fourth part of that sin. And here, because of the inclusion of the terms "belonging to another" and "without being given," there is no fault in bathing when it has been permitted as part of a general relinquishment of property. (4.202)
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs. (4.203)

Regarding the phrase "in rivers": one should always perform bathing in rivers, in natural (unartificial) ponds and large lakes, and in reservoirs of water that have leaky currents. Since the exclusion of others' watering-troughs (*nipāna*) is already established by this very [rule], the separate mention is for the purpose of permitting bathing in those belonging to oneself, as well as in abandoned or permitted waters. Even there, because of the inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*), one should first strive to bathe in rivers and the like; only in their absence may one bathe in those belonging to oneself and so forth. (4.203)

The wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not the observances (niyamas) exclusively; for by failing to practice the restraints while devoting oneself solely to the observances, one falls. (4.204)

Regarding the term *yamān*: the *yamas* are those things to be avoided, such as violence and the like; the *niyamas* consist of duties to be performed, such as the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth. In this regard, one who understands the relative weight and gravity of these rules should always practice the *yamas*, even at the risk of violating the *niyamas*. For if one should practice the *niyamas* alone by abandoning the *yamas*—that is, by failing to avoid prohibited acts such as the killing of a Brahmin—one falls [from one's status] and becomes disqualified even from the performance of the *niyamas*. As Gautama has stated: "Falling away from the duties of the twice-born constitutes a loss of caste. This statement is made for the purpose of emphasizing the importance of the *yamas*, not for the purpose of prohibiting the *niyamas*, since the latter are enjoined by scripture as duties to be performed. (4.204)
A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one performed by a priest for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch. (4.205)

"Not from one who is not a Śrotriya": when a sacrifice has been commenced by one who has not studied the Vedas, a Brāhmaṇa should not eat even after the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice. This is because the prohibition for such a person is already established by the rule, "The food of an initiated miser" (4.210). The author of the Sūtras has stated that the food of an initiated person is unfit to be eaten until the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice; therefore, the prohibition "the food of an initiated miser" applies only up to that point. Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa should never eat in a house where the Vaiśvadeva and other oblations have been performed by a priest who always officiates for many people, or by a woman, or by a eunuch. (4.205)
This is offensive to the virtuous; there they offer oblations.
This is contrary to the will of the gods; therefore, one should avoid it. (4.206)

"Indecent": that place where those previously mentioned perform a fire sacrifice is considered indecent and improper by the learned, and is offensive to the gods; therefore, one should not cause these [persons] to perform a fire sacrifice. 4.206.

One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease; nor food into which hair or insects have fallen, nor that which has been intentionally touched with the foot. (4.207)

"Of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted": one should not eat the food of a eunuch, an angry person, or one who is diseased, nor that which is defiled by contact with hair and all twelve kinds of insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched with the foot. (4.207)
That which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog; 4.208.

"Regarding 'that which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo' (bhrūṇaghnāvekṣitam)": one should not eat food that has been looked upon by those fallen from their caste, such as a slayer of a Brahmin; that which has been touched by those who are untouchable, such as a woman in her menses; that which has been tasted by a bird, such as a crow; or that which has been touched by a dog. (4.208)

Food smelled by a cow, and especially food announced [for all], food belonging to a group, food belonging to a courtesan, and that which is despised by a learned man—[these should be avoided]. (4.209)

"From a cow": that which is smelled by a cow; that which is given after having been proclaimed, "Who will eat?"; and likewise the food of a community such as a monastery or Brahmins, as well as the food of a courtesan—all this, which has been declared contemptible by those who know the scriptures, he shall not eat, especially so for the sake of specific penance. (4.209)
The food of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer, one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, a miser, and one who is bound in fetters [is forbidden]. (4.210)

"Of the thief and the singer": one should not eat the food of a thief, a professional singer, a snake-charmer, or one who lives off usury. [Nor should one eat] the food of one consecrated for a sacrifice before the Agniṣomīya offering, or of one who is bound—whether bound with fetters other than those born of the womb (i.e., natural) or shackled by them—or even when no such bond exists. 4.210.
The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as sour gruel, stale food, and the leavings of a Śūdra—[these must not be eaten]. (4.211)

"Of one who is accused": of one who has incurred an accusation on account of being a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*); one should not eat the food of a *napuṃsaka* (eunuch), even if his guilt is unproven; nor that of a *puṃścalī* (unchaste woman), a *vyabhicāriṇī* (adulteress), or a *gaṇikā* (prostitute); nor that of a *dāmbhika* (hypocrite), one who practices a semblance of righteousness. Likewise, one should not eat what is *śukta*—that which was originally a fresh juice but becomes sour over time through contact with water or other substances—and what is *paryuṣita* (stale), having been kept overnight; nor the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) of a Śūdra. The prohibition against eating *śukta* and *paryuṣita* will be stated in the fifth chapter; here, however, it is mentioned because they constitute observances (*vrata*) for a *snātaka*. (4.211)
The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats leavings;
the food of a fierce man, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and that which has been tasted by another before being served; the food of one within ten days of death; 4.212.

"Of the physician" means of a doctor who lives by practicing medicine. Likewise, one should not eat the food of hunters, those of dishonest nature, those who eat the leavings of others, and so forth; nor that which is prepared for an *ugra*—one born of a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother—at the direction of a woman recently delivered (*sūtikā*), even if it is prepared by those who are otherwise not subject to ritual impurity (*anāśaucin*), nor that in which the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) has been omitted; nor food from a woman recently delivered before ten days have passed, since the food of the deceased (*pretānna*) will be discussed later. Others, however, say that "the *ugra*" refers to a king; but that is incorrect, because Yājñavalkya mentions both [meanings]. (4.212)

One should not eat meat that has not been honored, meat obtained for no purpose, the food of a woman who has no hero (husband), the food of an enemy, the food of a city, the food of an outcast, or food that has been sneezed upon. (4.213)

"Unhonored" (anarcita) means that which is given to one who is worthy of honor without having been honored; that which is given to guests and others for a month without having performed worship to the gods and so forth, because it will be stated later [in verse 4.215] that "one should eat after having honored the gods and the ancestors," one should not eat such food. 4.213.
The food of a slanderer and a liar, of one who sells the results of sacrifices, of an actor and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person—[these should not be eaten]. (4.214)

"And [the food] of the slanderer and the liar. One should not eat the food of a barker, a speaker of untruth, a seller of sacrifices or merit, a dancer, a tailor, or those who have done one a favor or an injury. (4.214)
Of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player, a goldsmith, a basket-maker, and likewise a seller of weapons; 4.215.

"Of the blacksmith," etc.: one should not eat the food of a blacksmith, nor of a Niṣāda or a Veṇa—both of whom will be mentioned in the tenth chapter—nor of anyone else who lives by entering the stage (other than an actor or a singer), nor of a goldsmith or a seller of weapons. (4.215)
[One should not eat the food] of dog-keepers, of liquor-sellers, of a washerman, of a dyer, of a cruel man, or of one in whose house a paramour resides. (4.216)

One should not eat the food of those who keep dogs for sport, those who sell liquor, washermen, dyers of cloth, or those who are cruel, nor of one in whose house the paramour of his wife remains unknown. (4.216)

Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely dominated by women, and food from a deceased person within ten days of death, as well as food that causes dissatisfaction—[these one should avoid]. (4.217)

"Those who endure"—meaning those who tolerate a paramour of their wife; the food of such persons is indeed unfit to be eaten. Furthermore, this prohibition applies even when the adulterous woman has left the house and has been neglected. Regarding all ritual acts dependent upon women, one should not eat the food of those in a state of impurity following a death (*mṛtaka-anna*), nor that which is disagreeable. 4.217.
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster; the food of a goldsmith, one's longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame. (4.218)

"Kingly food": kingly food destroys one's *tejas* (vital energy); for this very reason, the prohibition against such food should be understood. He will later state the prohibition against the food of a Śūdra in the verse, "One should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra," or that of a friend of a low-born family; therefore, that food takes away the *tejas* caused by study and other [virtues]. Regarding the food of a goldsmith and a leather-cutter, it is said that they take away longevity and fame; this is a statement of the consequences of transgression. (4.218)
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny; that of a washerman, one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the worlds. (4.219)

"Food of artisans" (*kārukānna*) refers to the food of cooks and the like; it destroys one's offspring. For this reason as well, there is a prohibition against it. Furthermore, the mention of the food of leather-workers and others should be understood according to the maxim of "the cow and the ox" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). This should be understood everywhere in this treatise in the same way. And the food of a washerman (*nirṇejaka*) snatches away from one the worlds of heaven and so forth earned through other meritorious deeds. (4.219)
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; the food of a seller of weapons is filth. (4.220)

"Pus" means that by eating the food of a physician, one is born into such a state where one becomes a consumer of pus. Likewise, the food of an unchaste woman becomes semen; the food of a usurer becomes feces; and the food of a seller of weapons becomes urine and other impurities, excluding semen and excrement. (4.220)
Regarding those others who have been successively proclaimed as persons whose food should not be eaten, the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair. (4.221)

Regarding the word "ya" (those): those others who have been described as food to be consumed in sequence, distinct from the fruits explicitly mentioned [in the preceding verses], it is said by those of excellent intellect that the food associated with them consists of skin, bone, and hair. (4.221)
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance. (4.222)

Regarding the word "having eaten" (*bhuktvā*): having unknowingly eaten food belonging to any one of these [outcastes], one should fast for three days; however, having eaten it intentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. Furthermore, having unintentionally consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* according to the tradition of Gautama. Thus he says: "In the case of drinking liquor unintentionally, [one should consume] milk, clarified butter, water, or air, each heated, for three days; that is the *taptakṛcchra*, after which there is the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). The same applies to the consumption of urine, feces, and semen. Although the phrase "any one of these" (*anyatamasya*) is heard here, nevertheless—

One should always avoid food that is spoiled by its inherent nature, the passage of time, contact with impure things, or the process of fermentation, as well as that which is contaminated by the person who provided it.

Thus, this very same expiation applies even to the seven types of defilement not mentioned here, because they are taught within the same section (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, since no other expiations for these are prescribed in this section, some say that even *śukta* (fermented) and *paryuṣita* (stale), whose prohibitions will be stated in the fifth chapter, are mentioned here solely for the sake of specifying their particular expiations. That is incorrect; for if that were intended, the author would have said, "any one of these [seven] defilements. In non-human (Vedic) texts, even a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) serves as a basis for determination, since the intention of the speaker is inferred from that alone. Moreover, the teaching within this single section is for the purpose of establishing that these are the observances (*vrata*) of a *snātaka*. Even though no expiations are explicitly recited here for them, the expiations for these will be those stated in the eleventh chapter. And the mention of *śukta* and *paryuṣita* here is solely for the purpose of classifying them as *snātaka*-observances. Therefore, one should accept exactly what is heard in the text: therein, *svabhāvaduṣṭa* (defiled by nature) refers to urine and the like; *kāladuṣṭa* (defiled by time) refers to stale food and the like; *saṃsargaduṣṭa* (defiled by contact) refers to food from a defiled person and the like; *pariṇāmaduṣṭa* (defiled by transformation) refers to fermented liquids and the like; *bhāvaduṣṭa* (defiled by intention) refers to grape juice pressed on the same day and the like; and *āśrayaduṣṭa* (defiled by source) refers to that which belongs to an intoxicated person and so forth. Furthermore, the instruction on expiation outside of a specific context is for the sake of brevity; for if it were performed there [in the specific context], it would be necessary to include the recitation of mantras and other such details. (4.222)

A learned twice-born man shall not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra who does not perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha); however, in the absence of other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for one night. 4.223.

"He shall not eat" means that a twice-born man learned in the scriptures must not consume cooked food from a virtuous Śūdra who is devoid of rites such as the *śrāddha*. However, in the absence of other food, he may accept raw grain (*āmam*) alone—not cooked food—and only an amount sufficient for one day and night, no more than that.
Having deliberated upon both the learned man who is miserly and the usurer who is generous, the gods ordained that their food be equal. (4.224)

Regarding the phrase "of the *śrotriya*": one is a wretched man who has merely studied the Veda, while the other is noble or lives by lending at interest; having considered both qualities of these two, the gods determined that the food for both was equal, because both possess [the quality of being learned]. (4.224)
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal!
That which is purified by faith belongs to the generous man; the other is struck down by lack of faith. (4.225)

Regarding the word "those": Brahmā approached those gods and declared that which was uneven to be even. Because the food of the generous becomes purified through faith, whereas the food of the miser is defiled by a lack of faith; thus, even though both [types of food] are prohibited, this [verse] serves as a counter-exception for the food of usurers who possess faith. 4.225.

One should always perform what is desired and pure with faith, remaining unwearied; for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired through righteous means, those two acts become inexhaustible.
Since it is thus, therefore [it is said]: "with faith. (4.226)

One should constantly practice the duty of giving—both that which pertains to sacrifices and that which pertains to public works—with a state of complete contentment, whenever a worthy recipient is found, according to one's ability. (4.227)

Regarding the "duty of giving" (dānadharmam): whatever duty is called "giving," whether it pertains to what is within the Veda or outside the Veda, one should always perform it according to one's ability by means of the mental state known as "satisfaction," having encountered a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with all virtues such as learning and study. (4.227)
Whatever may be given when asked by one free from malice, for there will arise a worthy recipient who delivers one from all [suffering]. (4.228)

"Whatever it may be": even a small amount should be given as far as possible by one who has been requested and does not investigate for faults; because for one who is constantly engaged in giving, a worthy recipient will inevitably at some point arrive—one who liberates from both seen and unseen faults. (4.228)
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, excellent vision. (4.229)

Regarding the phrase "vārida" (giver of water): the giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, infinite happiness; the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, eyes unafflicted by darkness and other such impairments. || 4.229 ||
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty. (4.230)

Regarding "the giver of land": the giver of land obtains lordship over land; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a house, excellent houses; and the giver of silver, obtains an exquisite form. (4.230)
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun.

Regarding the phrase "vāsodaḥ": the giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon—that is, the lunar world; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins; the giver of a bull attains great prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the world of the Sun. (4.231)

The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty; the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman. (4.232)

"Bestower of vehicles and beds": one who gives beds and the like [attains these]; one who protects those in distress [attains] a wife; one who bestows sovereignty [attains] power; a giver of grain [attains] perpetual happiness; and a giver of the Vedas attains a state equal to that of the Supreme Brahman. In all these cases, one should understand the gradation of smallness and greatness, as well as the duration of time and so forth, based on the relative smallness or greatness of the quality of the substance given, even when the visible fruit is small. (4.232)
Of all gifts whatsoever—water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter—the gift of the Veda is preeminent. (4.233)
"Of all"—that is, among all gifts such as water, food, cows, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, and so forth, the gift of the Veda is distinguished by its superior fruit. (4.233)
With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift, one receives that very same thing, honored by that same disposition. (4.234)

"By which" means: by whatever mental state—whether rajasic, sattvic, or tamasic, pure, middling, or impure—with whatever substance one gives, that very substance, by way of its fruit, is obtained in another birth when one is honored, precisely according to that state of the mind at the time of giving and in accordance with the nature of that disposition, whether it be happiness, middling, or accompanied by suffering. (4.234)
He who accepts what has been honored, or he who gives what has been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell. (4.235)

Therefore, it should be given with a hand that has been honored; for it is said: "As long as both the giver and the receiver perform the acts of giving and receiving preceded by such honor, both go to heaven. But with an unhonored hand, they both go to hell. Even though the act of receiving is for the sake of livelihood and thus has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the attainment of heaven is not improper because of the scriptural injunction regarding the invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction: "I must accept only what is honored, and not otherwise. (4.235)

One should not take pride in one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice; even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift. (4.236)

"He should not be proud" means that even when great asceticism such as the *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* has been performed, he should not harbor pride, thinking, "How much asceticism I have accomplished! Furthermore, having performed a sacrifice, he should not speak untruth. Although the prohibition of falsehood exists as a general rule for human conduct (*puruṣārtha*), this instruction is given again so that it may serve as an integral part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. Likewise, even when oppressed, he should not revile Brahmins. Having given a gift, he should not say, "This was given by me. (4.236)
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; life perishes through reviling Brahmins; and a gift perishes through boasting of it. (4.237)

"Because [it is called] sacrifice": because sacrifices and other rites, when performed with falsehoods and the like, become equivalent to those not performed at all; therefore, this [falsehood] must not be committed. (4.237)
One should gradually accumulate merit, like termites building an anthill, for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings. (4.238)

"Dharma slowly": one should avoid causing pain to any living being; for the sake of benefiting the next world, one should acquire dharma little by little, just as ants collect a heap of earth. (4.238)
For in the next world, neither father nor mother remain for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsmen remain—dharma alone remains. (4.239)

"Not in the next world. Because in the other world, neither mother, father, son, wife, nor kinsmen remain for the sake of accomplishing one's supportive tasks; rather, it is Dharma alone that remains for the purpose of assistance. Therefore, one should not abandon Dharma out of regard for one's mother or others. (4.239)
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds. (4.240)

"Alone" means that a living being is born alone, not together with kinsmen; alone he dies; and alone he experiences the fruits of his good and evil deeds. Therefore, since parents and others do not share in the experience of the suffering caused by one's birth, death, or misdeeds, one should not abandon dharma out of consideration for them. (4.240)
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; only Dharma follows him. (4.241)

"Regarding the dead": having cast away the body of the deceased upon the ground with contempt like a piece of wood, the kinsmen turn their faces away and depart; they do not remain to accompany him. But Dharma follows after him as he goes to the next world. (4.241)
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate Dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with Dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse. 4.242

"Therefore" means: since one crosses over the difficult-to-traverse suffering of the hells and other realms by means of Dharma as a companion, therefore one should always gradually conquer Dharma for the sake of a companion. (4.242)
The radiant one, whose body is ethereal, swiftly leads that person who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity to the next world.

"Preeminence of Dharma": When a righteous man has committed some transgression through negligence, his sin is removed by penance; blazing with a mass of his own spiritual luster, he moves about like Brahman, being essentially of the nature of space. Such a person, being thus established in Dharma, is swiftly led to the next world by that very Dharma. Therefore, one should gradually accumulate Dharma. (4.243)
One who desires to lead one's family to eminence should always form connections with the most excellent people; one should avoid those who are base. (4.244)

"With the best, with the best": one who desires to lead his family to excellence should constantly form connections—such as giving a daughter in marriage—with those who are superior in learning, lineage, and other such qualities; he should avoid inferior persons in such relations. This separate statement, following the rule regarding the "best," is for the purpose of ensuring the avoidance of unrighteousness; it also serves to permit marriage with equals in the absence of superiors. (4.244)
By approaching only the most excellent and avoiding those who are inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; by the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra. (4.245)

"Going only to the highest, and avoiding the lowly"—by following the highest among those connected with the highest and by avoiding the base, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; but by the opposite course, since his caste does not thereby disappear, he reaches a state equal to that of a Śūdra. (4.245)
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not dwelling with those of cruel conduct,
one who is non-violent and observes such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and generosity.

"Acting with firmness" means possessing the power to complete what has been undertaken; being free from cruelty toward cold, heat, and so forth; being patient with the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*); and being non-violent even while living among those of merciless conduct—such a person, through self-restraint (*niyama*) consisting of gentleness, tranquility, and the gift known as control of the senses, shall attain heaven. (4.246)
One may accept from anyone fuel for the fire, water, roots, fruits, food that has been offered, honey, and the gift of safety. (4.247)

"Water from a single source": one may accept from all sources wood, water, fruits, roots, honey, and food that has been offered unasked, provided it is not obtained through improper means—excluding, however, those who are outcastes and others who are utterly contemptible due to their condition. Likewise, considering safety as a protection for oneself and as something exceedingly pleasing, one should accept from everyone—even from a *caṇḍāla* or similar person—that which is equal to a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) and capable of protecting one from personal danger. (4.247)
Prajāpati considered alms brought forward and offered spontaneously, even if not previously solicited, as acceptable even from one of evil deeds. (4.248)

Regarding the phrase "brought and offered": Hiraṇyagarbha considered that even for one who has committed evil deeds, alms such as cattle, gold, and so forth—which have been brought to the place of the recipient, which are urged upon the giver with the thought "I shall give this to you," and which were not previously mentioned [as being given]—are to be accepted, provided they are not from those who are fallen (patita) or otherwise extremely despicable, since this falls under the section concerning non-calamities. 4.248.
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, if he treats her with contempt. (4.249)

"They do not eat": for fifteen years the ancestors do not consume his *kavya*, and Agni does not deliver his *havya*—such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—to the gods, if he rejects that alms-offering. (4.249)
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or vegetables. (4.250)

"Bedding and a house": one should not refuse bedding, a house, *darbha* grass, water, flowers, gems, curd, a vessel, fish, milk, meat, vegetables, or fragrant substances such as camphor and the like, when they are offered unasked. The repetition of the word "water"—which was already mentioned in the verse concerning fuel and so forth—is for the purpose of making it known that the refusal of these items is equal whether they are mentioned in two separate verses or together. Thus Gautama read them together in a single sūtra: "Fuel and the rest, along with the bed and the rest. (4.250)
Desiring to support his teachers and servants, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself must not be satisfied by that alone. (4.251)

"Teachers and dependents": desiring to rescue from exhaustion due to hunger his teachers—such as mother, father, and so forth—and his dependents—such as wife, sons, and others who must necessarily be supported—as well as intending to honor deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources, excluding those who are outcastes (*patita*) and other such utterly contemptible persons, since this pertains to a time of distress (*anāpad*). He should not, however, satisfy his own needs with that wealth if other means are available; for the author will later describe the conduct for times of distress (*āpaddharma*) as being for one who is "wasting away due to lack of livelihood" when primary means have been exhausted. (4.251)
But when his teachers have passed away, or when he lives at home without them, seeking his own livelihood, he should always receive it from a virtuous person. (4.252)

Regarding the phrase "toward gurus": when his mother and others have passed away, or if he is living in the house without them, seeking his own livelihood, he should always accept gifts only from virtuous people, except in times of distress. (4.252)
A partner in a business venture, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [to the Brāhmaṇa]. (4.253)

Regarding the term "ardhika": among Śūdras, those who are cultivators, family friends, cowherds, slaves, and barbers are permitted to have their food eaten by [twice-born men]. Furthermore, it will be stated that a Śūdra may live by the work of a barber or other such crafts, or by the labor of artisans, provided he offers himself [to the higher castes] saying, "I am dependent upon you. (4.253)
Whatever his nature may be, whatever he intends to do, and how he would treat him, in that manner one should present oneself. (4.254)

He states how the self-offering should be performed by saying "of what kind" (*yādṛśa*). Of what kind his self may be—by way of lineage, character, and so forth—and what kind of service he desires to perform for the sake of visible ends or for the sake of transcendental excellence; or in whatever manner he would serve a Brahmin for the purpose of fetching water, earth, and so on—in this manner he should offer himself. (4.254)
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is when among others is the greatest evildoer in the world; he is a thief who robs his own self. (4.255)

Regarding the phrase "he who": whoever else, even though different from the aforementioned Śūdra by virtue of his lineage and other such factors, falsely represents himself as being otherwise—saying "I am thus"—and speaks deceptively about himself, he is a thief in the world and an exceeding evildoer, precisely because of his denial of the true nature of the self (*ātman*), since he has stolen away that which is the most preeminent of all things. (4.255)
All expressible objects are fixed; they are rooted in speech and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals that speech is a thief of everything. (4.256)

"Meanings are to be expressed": all meanings are connected to words because the relationship between word and meaning is fixed; furthermore, since meanings are rooted in words and are understood from words, and since the comprehension of worldly usage regarding meanings is preceded by the comprehension of words, meanings are strictly determined by words. Therefore, one who would steal that speech—by saying one thing while performing another—becomes a man who steals all things. (4.256)

Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule, and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live established in equanimity. (4.257)

Regarding the phrase "of the great seers, ancestors, and gods": having purified his debts toward the great seers, ancestors, and gods by accomplishing the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), the procreation of offspring (*prajā*), and the performance of sacrifices (*yajña*) according to the scriptures, and then having entrusted the entire burden of the household to his son, he may dwell for some time in the home itself—engaging in the acquisition of wealth, giving gifts, and supporting the needy—while performing the great sacrifices and other rites through the power of knowledge (*jñāna-bala*) in accordance with the principle stated in 4.23: "Some offer the vital breath in speech," and so forth. 4.257.
One should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself;
for by reflecting alone, one attains the supreme good. (4.258)

And thus, "dwelling alone": being alone in a secluded place, reflecting upon his own welfare through the investigation of the nature of the Supreme Self by means of the meditations taught in the Upaniṣads, he attains the highest good known as liberation. || 4.258 ||
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for the Brahmin householder,
as well as the auspicious ritual of the Snātaka vows, which increases one's inner essence.

"This" refers to this livelihood beginning with *ṛta* and so forth, which is declared for the Brāhmaṇa householder as being permanent because it is prescribed even for the temporary state of misfortune. Likewise, the rule for the vows of a *snātaka*, which increases the quality known as *sattva*, is declared only for one who is already praiseworthy. (4.259)
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from sin and is glorified in the world of Brahma.

"By this" means: by means of this aforementioned conduct prescribed in the scriptures, a Brāhmaṇa who knows the meaning of the Vedas, having his sins exhausted through the performance of obligatory duties, enjoys greatness in the world of Brahman. 4.260.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the eternal conduct of the householder, in the commentary titled *Manvāśayasāriṇī*, composed by Govindarāja, the son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Mādhava.
Fifth Chapter.

"Having heard these... means: having heard these aforementioned duties of a *snātaka*, the sages spoke this which is about to be told to the highly fortunate Bhṛgu, who was born from Agni and is a benefactor of others. In the first chapter, Bhṛgu’s origin from Manu was stated; here, however, his origin from Agni is stated from the perspective of a Vedic explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For there it is heard: "Of that [Agni's] semen, that which first shone forth became yonder sun; that which was second was Bhṛgu. Therefore, because he was produced from fallen semen (*bhraṣṭa-retas*), he is called "Bhṛgu. And thus, since there is one cause for him in one birth and another in another, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. (5.1)
O Lord, how does death prevail over those brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duty and are learned in the Vedas and the scriptures? (5.2)

"Thus. In this way, for those Brāhmaṇas who know the Vedic scriptures and practice their own duty as prescribed by the Teacher even when it has passed away, how should they fare? For there is an absence of the loss of dharma and other such causes that lead to the exhaustion of life. (5.2)
The righteous Bhṛgu, son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen to the fault by which death seeks to slay the Brahmins. (5.3)
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the avoidance of proper conduct, laziness, and the defects of food, Death seeks to slay the Brahmins. (5.4)

He said to them: "By lack of practice. Lack of Vedic study, neglect of conduct, laziness, and defects in food are known as the causes of the exhaustion of life. Thus, even when the study of the Vedas, the performance of conduct, and the absence of laziness—these being the subjects taught in the aforementioned scriptures—have been carried out, if the defect of food to be described hereafter is not avoided, then by that cause, untimely death seeks to slay the Brahmins.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms, as well as those things produced from impure substances, are not to be eaten by the twice-born. (5.5)

Anticipating the question, "What, then, is this defect of food? he states: "Garlic," and so forth. These are the leaf-vegetables known as garlic (*laśuna*), *gṛñjana*, and onion (*palāṇḍu*). *Kavaka* is a specific type of mushroom; *khukam* is synonymous with *khaṇḍakam*, as is well-known in the *Āyurveda*. Furthermore, those things produced from impurity—namely, those originating solely from impure matter because they emerge from the excrement of humans and other creatures who have eaten them, those grown in places of feces, and those like *taṇḍulīyaka* that arise through contact with impurity—are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born (*dvijāti*). The mention of "twice-born" is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra; however, the section on forbidden foods (*abhakṣya*) applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa, since the section begins with "In a sacrifice not performed by one learned in the Vedas... (4.205) and concludes with "A Brāhmaṇa may eat [only] occasionally" (4.213). For this very reason, there is a distinction between the sections. (5.5)
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions, and the *śelu* fruit, along with cow’s milk that has not yet turned to curd (*peyūṣa*). 5.6.

"Red" refers to those [exudations] which, distinct from flowers and the like, emerge from trees by way of oozing; likewise, [the red sap] arising from the *gunda* region of a tree, and the *śelu*, which is the *śleṣmātaka* tree, as established in the medical treatises (*āyurveda*) and lexicons such as the statement, "The *śelu* is known as the *śleṣmātaka*. It does not refer to the cream of milk (*kṣīrasṛt-kṣīrasantānikā*), as explained by others, because that is not established [as the intended meaning]. And [it includes] the *pīyūṣa* (colostrum) related to a cow. One should carefully avoid that milk of a cow recently calved which becomes solidified through contact with fire. This is prohibited even if it should occasionally occur after ten days have passed; for that which occurs within ten days is already prohibited by the rule: "The milk of a cow that has not yet passed ten days. (5.7)
One should not eat kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, or cakes in vain, nor meat that has not been consecrated, nor the food of the gods, nor sacrificial oblations.

"Vainly prepared *kṛsara* and *saṃyāva*": *Kṛsara* is rice cooked with sesame and mung beans; *saṃyāva* is what is commonly known as *puṣkarikā*, made with ghee, molasses, milk, and so forth; and *pāyasa* (milk-rice) and *apūpa* (cakes)—these, when prepared without being dedicated to specific deities in sacrifices such as the *vāstuyajña*. One should not eat even that for which the daily *vaiśvadeva* rite has been performed. Likewise, one should not consume the meat of cows, sheep, or goats—which are fit for the specific Vedic consecration called *upākaraṇa*—if they have not been formally consecrated (*anupākṛta*). Regarding the meat of guests and others, however, having stated "meat not offered [to a guest] is vain meat," one should avoid the food of the gods, such as offerings (*naivedya*) and oblations (*havīṃṣi*), prior to the fire-offering (*homa*). For he will later state that the remnant of an oblation is indeed fit to be eaten. (5.7)

The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of a one-hoofed animal, that of a sheep, the milk of a *sandhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died—[these are forbidden]. (5.8)

Regarding the phrase *anirdaśāyāś ca*: one should avoid the milk belonging to a cow that has recently calved and is within the ten-day period (*anirdaśā*); likewise, the milk of camels, and that of single-hoofed animals such as horses and goats; and also the milk of a *sandhinī* cow—even if she is not currently being milked—since the *Trikāṇḍābhidhāna* states, "A *sandhinī* is defined by the wise as one who is in heat at the time of milking"; and furthermore, the milk of a cow whose calf has died. By the specific mention of the "calf" (*vatsa*), it is indicated that when a cow is mentioned, it refers only to a cow and not to a goat or a buffalo. Here, although the subject under discussion is "milk," the repetition of the words "milk" (*kṣīra*) and "payas" (in the phrase *sandhinīkṣīraṃ vivatsāyāś ca goḥ payaḥ*) serves to prohibit specifically the milk of the *sandhinī* and the *vivatsā* cow, and not their derivatives. However, some say this is incorrect, because it is improper to permit the use of derivatives from substances that are inherently impure, just as we see prohibitions regarding those [impure] fires. And Śaṅkha says:
"A wise man, being composed and diligent, should perform a seven-night vow when consuming the products of those [animals] whose milk is forbidden to be eaten.

Because the derivative suffix has been applied to "sandhinī" (a cow in heat), the inclusion of the word "milk" (*kṣīra*) is necessary [to form the compound *sandhinīkṣīra*]; furthermore, since the word "milk" occurs within the compound *sandhinīkṣīra*, the specific mention of "cow's milk" (*goḥ payaḥ*) is required. (5.8)
And among all wild animals, except for the buffalo, as well as the milk of females and all fermented acids, these indeed are to be avoided. (5.9)

"Of wild animals": one should avoid the milk of all wild animals—elephants and so forth—with the exception of the buffalo, as well as the milk of females. Likewise, one should avoid all fermented acids (*śukta*), which are substances that have acquired their own natural flavor and become sour through the passage of time and by being steeped in water or other liquids. 5.9.
Curd is fit for consumption during the Śukta days, as is everything produced from curd,
and those [liquids] which are distilled from auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits.

Regarding this, he states an exception: "But curd is to be eaten among sour things, as is everything produced from curd. Among sour things (*śukta*), curd is edible, as is everything derived from it, such as whey (*udaśvit*) and the like. Furthermore, those substances which are mixed with water and flowers or other ingredients for the sake of purification are fit for consumption. Since customary practice (*ācāra*) serves as the basis for interpreting the statements of the *smṛti*, it is logical to assume the meaning of the *smṛti* in accordance with what does not contradict established custom. Therefore, one should understand that the inclusion of flowers and other items, as well as the presentation of other substances, occurs without transgressing the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Moreover, because there is an exception made here for fermented sour liquids (*abhiṣuta-śukta*), the general prohibition "all sour things" must also refer specifically to fermented liquids. Consequently, some maintain that naturally sour fruits such as the *āmalaka* are not prohibited; however, this is incorrect, because the exception "but curd is to be eaten" applies even to non-fermented sour substances. Nor does it follow that *āmalaka* and similar fruits become inedible, for the word *śukta*—which is a synonym for "sour"—refers precisely to the meaning already stated. (5.10)
One should avoid all carnivorous birds, as well as those that dwell in villages, those not specifically mentioned, those that feed on raw flesh, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird. (5.11)

"Regarding the phrase 'all carnivorous birds': one should avoid all such birds, including the hawk and others, that feed exclusively on raw flesh. Thus, there is no prohibition against those that eat both [raw and cooked meat], such as the peacock and others. And so Śaṅkha says:
'The partridge, the peacock, the quail, the francolin, the rhinoceros-bird, and the bustard—Yama declares these to be edible for the virtuous.'"

One should avoid village-dwelling birds such as pigeons and the like. Likewise, according to the Śruti, regarding those animals that are not specifically mentioned as fit for consumption—such as the injunction, "One should sacrifice a camel or a mule and eat its meat"—one should avoid those single-hoofed animals that have not been so specified. However, one may eat those that are specifically mentioned in a particular context, because the scriptural injunction prescribes their consumption only in that specific context as an integral part of the sacrifice, and not elsewhere. Furthermore, one should avoid the bird known as the *ṭittibha*. (5.11)
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the domestic cock, the sārasa, the rajjuvāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina. 5.12.

Regarding the term *kalaviṅka*: the *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow (*grāmacaṭaka*), according to its mention in the *Nigamas*. Since it dwells in both places during the rainy season—living in the forest [by nature] while residing in the village [during that time]—there is a prohibition against its dwelling in the village. This statement is made because of the possibility of it being raised for the sake of livelihood. Likewise, one should avoid the *plava* bird known as *saṃkaṭavila*, as well as the swan (*haṃsa*), the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), the village cock (*grāmakukkuṭa*), the parrot (*śuka*), and the maina (*śārikā*). The mention of the "village cock" is for the purpose of permitting the wild variety; for although the prohibition is already established by the fact that it dwells in the village, there might be a suspicion that the wild variety is permitted because it belongs to the same species. To prevent that, this statement is made. Now, one might ask: since the prohibition is established simply by its dwelling in the village, why is the mention of the "village cock" not explained as being intended to allow for other village-dwelling birds besides these, rather than being solely for the purpose of permitting the wild variety? It is not so; for when a purpose exists within the meaning of its own word, it is improper to assume that the intent lies in determining a specific distinction from another sentence. One should avoid the *sārasa* bird known as *lakṣmaṇa*, the *rajjuvāla* known as *pāyika*, and the *dātyūha* commonly known by the terms *cakravāka* and *jalakukkuṭa*.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, claw-scratching birds, and those that dive to eat fish; likewise, meat from a slaughterhouse and dried meat. (5.13)

Regarding the term *pratuda* ("pecking birds"): one should avoid the meat of those such as woodpeckers (*dārvāghāṭa*) and others who eat by pecking with their beaks; those such as the *koyaṣṭi* and the bird called *dhūsarika*, who eat by scratching with their claws; and those such as the *cakora*, *kakubha*, and *gī*—excluding the wild cock permitted by faith—as well as those such as the *madgu* who eat fish by diving. According to the lexicographical tradition stating that *sūnā* means "a place of slaughter," one should avoid meat from a slaughterhouse, as well as dried meat (*vallūra*), even if it is otherwise edible. Since the prohibition of the *plava*, *haṃsa*, and *cakravāka* is already established by the fact that they are web-footed (*jālapāda*), their separate mention is for the purpose of making known the option (*vikalpa*) regarding other web-footed birds such as the *māyā*. This option is to be understood as being regulated such that these are edible in times of distress (*āpad*) but not in times of non-distress. For from this work composed by an author acting intentionally, the Master’s intention is inferred as follows: surely there would be no confidence in the general prohibition of web-footed birds if he had prohibited specific web-footed birds like the *haṃsa* by their own names. Nor is there absolute lack of confidence; for if that were the case, the general prohibition of web-footed birds would be redundant. Therefore, a distinction is inferred: in a certain state, the eating of *madgu*s and others is intended, while in another, there is simply a prohibition. Thus, in times of distress there is permission to eat, but in times of non-distress there is a prohibition, because the purpose of the prohibition is to preclude [eating at all]. If, on the other hand, there were an equal option (whereby they could be eaten or not at any time), then the prohibition of web-footed birds would be entirely useless. Even without that statement, such an option—namely, that they are edible sometimes and not at others—would be established by worldly custom itself, since eating is determined by desire or lack of desire. Therefore, it is concluded that this option is fixed precisely by the explicit mention of the prohibition of web-footed birds. (5.13)
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, those that eat fish, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; 5.14.

"And the crane," etc. One should avoid the crane (*baka*), the heron (*balāka*), the raven (*kākola*)—for the *Trikāṇḍa* lexicon states, "the raven is cited as the *droṇakāka*"—and the bird called the *kañjarīṭa*; one should also avoid fish-eaters, even those that are not birds such as crocodiles and the like, village pigs, and all kinds of fish. (5.14)
Whoever eats the flesh of another is called an eater of that being's flesh; since an eater of fish is an eater of all flesh, one should therefore avoid fish. (5.15)

The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for this is: "He who eats the flesh of another... This is stated for the purpose of censure: he who eats meat belonging to a particular being is considered a "meat-eater" of that very being. One who eats fish does not incur the same degree of defilement as one who eats other meats; however, it is appropriate to designate him as a "consumer of all meats. Therefore, one should avoid those fish. (5.15)
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are the first two prescribed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*);
likewise, all *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *saśalka* fish are permitted. (5.16)

Now, by relying on specific species and specific actions, he states the exception regarding fish in the verse beginning with *pāṭhīnarohitau*. *Pāṭhīna* is a particular kind of fish, the *candrakāraṇya*; *rohit* is also known as the *rohitamatsya*. These two are fit for consumption when employed in rites for the gods (*daiva*) or the ancestors (*pitrya*), but not at other times. Furthermore, *rājīvas* are a specific class of fish with the color of a lotus. Likewise, those called *siṃhamukhas* (lion-faced) and *saśalkas* (scaled), known in the *Āyurveda* by the terms *śakalī* and *cilicima*, are fit for eating at all times, even apart from offerings to the gods and ancestors. (5.16)
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown, nor any five-toed creatures, even if they are among those designated as edible. (5.17)

"One shall not eat" refers to those such as snakes that generally wander alone; likewise, those wild animals and birds which cannot be identified by name or species even by experts—since there is no specific prohibition against them, they fall into the category of edible animals and are thus designated as fit for consumption—one must not eat any five-toed creatures, such as humans, cats, and the like.

The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—these they say are edible among five-toed animals, as are those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel. (5.18)

Regarding this, he states an exception: "The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and likewise the hare. Manu and others declare that among five-toed animals, these—the porcupine (known as *sedhā*), the hedgehog (*śalyaka*), the monitor lizard (*godhā*), the rhinoceros (*khaḍga*), the tortoise (*kūrma*), and the hare (*śaśa*)—are fit for consumption. Likewise, among those possessing a row of single tusks, all except the camel, such as goats and so forth, are fit; this is the sense. (5.18)
Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, village pigs, garlic, village cocks, onions, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]. (5.19)

Regarding the term *chatrāka*: if a twice-born man intentionally and repeatedly eats any one of the following—mushrooms, *kavaka* fungi, village pigs, garlic, and so forth—he falls from his status. "Falling" (*patana*) means the loss of the rights and duties of the twice-born. Consequently, there is no penance for him. As the author will state later: "Eating forbidden food and [forbidden] gifts are six acts equal to drinking liquor" (11.56). || 5.19 ||
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.

"Thinking these to be unfit for consumption": having intentionally eaten each of these six, beginning with mushrooms (*chatrāka*), one shall perform the *sāntapana* penance or the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*, whose nature will be described in the eleventh chapter. Regarding other items such as red exudations (*lohitaniryāsa*) and the like, if one eats any of them individually, one should fast for a day and a night. The "excessive extension" (*prakarṣotkarṣa*) of the penance is intended to show respect for the avoidance of garlic (*laśuna*) and similar substances. The rule "one should fast for a day regarding the remainder" is stated again for the sake of brevity; for if that were not done, it would have been necessary to specifically mention the red exudations and so forth. (5.20)

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for a year for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; but for that which is known, it must be done with special care. (5.21)

"Even for a single [day] of the year": within the course of a year, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the *prājāpatya* penance—since it is mentioned first among the *kṛcchras*—even for the sake of expiating the unintentional consumption of the resin of red trees and other such things just discussed, according to the rule: "In the remaining cases, he should fast for a day. However, if the consumption is intentional, one should specifically perform whatever particular penance has been prescribed for that act. From this very fact, it is understood that sin and its corresponding penance exist even when a transgression is committed unintentionally. Thus, the verse: "The gods ordained three purifiers for Brāhmaṇas: that which is unseen [unintentional], that which is washed with water, and that which is purified by fire," applies to matters distinct from these specific penances. And so it was stated by Ārya in the section on the purification of substances: "The mention of 'Brāhmaṇa' is intended to indicate the twice-born in general, because all three [classes] are under discussion, and because of the concluding summary: 'This has been declared for the twice-born. (5.21)
"Commendable wild animals and birds may be slain by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice, as well as for the sustenance of their dependents; for so did Agastya act in former times. (5.22)

The statement that "those beasts and birds which are prescribed in the Veda as commendable for sacrifices performed by Brāhmaṇas and others are to be killed" is a restatement of what is declared in the Śruti. Furthermore, the phrase "and likewise of dependents" is intended to be enjoined: they may be killed for the sake of maintaining dependents—such as one's parents and others who must necessarily be supported—in order to prevent their falling into distress. This is also because of the concluding remark that Agastya acted in this very manner in former times. (5.22)
For in ancient times, during the sacrifices of the seers and the rites of the Brahmins and Kshatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) were made from the meat of wild animals and birds. (5.23)

"They became [meat]," it is said. Because even in ancient sacrifices involving relatives, and in the sacrifices of Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) were made from the flesh of edible deer and birds; therefore, they may be killed even for the sake of sacrifice. 5.23.
Whatever food, whether hard or soft, is mixed with oil or fat and is not otherwise censured, that may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, as may whatever remains from an oblation.

Now, he says "whatever" (*yat kiṃcit*) for the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding stale food. Whatever is edible (*bhakṣya*), such as sweets (*modaka*) and the like, which is solid and fit for consumption; and whatever is soft food (*bhojya*), such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like, provided it is free from other forms of spoilage—that, having been mixed with fats such as curd or ghee, may be eaten even if it has become stale, meaning it has been left overnight. This is to be explained by transposing the word *tat* (in the verse). For if one were to apply the text literally, since the mixing of fat is inevitable when there is a sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) on the oblation (*havis*), the remaining portion of the oblation would already be established by the phrase "whatever is mixed with fat"; thus, its further mention would be redundant. Furthermore, that which remains after the offering (*hutaśiṣṭa*), such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), if it should become stale, may be used for eating at the time of the meal even if it is devoid of any mixture with fat. 5.24.
Even if it has been stored for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be consumed by the twice-born even if they are not mixed with oil. (5.25)

Regarding the phrase "long-standing": all products derived from barley, wheat, and milk may be eaten by the twice-born and others even if they have not been kept for one night, provided they have not been deprived of the sprinkling of oil. 5.25.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what is fit and unfit to be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat. (5.26)

This has been stated in its entirety regarding what may and may not be eaten by the twice-born; hereafter, I shall declare the rule and the injunction concerning the eating and the avoidance of meat. (5.26)
One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is engaged in a rite according to the rules, or only when there is danger to one's life. (5.27)

"Prokṣita" (consecrated). The Vedic injunction is: "One should eat the meat of a cow, sheep, or goat that has been consecrated by the Vedic purificatory rite known as *prokṣaṇa*. This is a restatement of the rule for eating as part of a ritual (*karma*), intended to establish its equivalence with the rules for eating based on the desire of a Brāhmaṇa and other such causes. As for those who claim this is for the purpose of a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding what is *prokṣita*, that is incorrect; for the statement "meats not offered [in sacrifice]" serves to prohibit meat that is not *prokṣita*. The phrase "and of Brāhmaṇas" means that one may eat even meat that is explicitly forbidden, provided it is requested by Brāhmaṇas, while remaining under the observances of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. Likewise, at a *śrāddha* or a *madhuparka* ceremony, the rite must be performed with that meat; for even a non-Brāhmaṇa, when appointed by one enjoined by the Smṛti and Gṛhya scriptures stating "the *madhuparka* shall not be without meat," must eat it according to the rule. Furthermore, the author will later state the fault of transgression regarding one who is so appointed. Even in a life-threatening situation, or when the eyesight is impaired, or due to illness, one who has renounced meat may still eat it while remaining under the observances of celibacy and so forth. (5.27)
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa); both the stationary and the moving—all is the sustenance of the vital breath. 5.28.

Regarding the phrase "of the vital breath" (*prāṇasya*): for the sake of the body's maintenance, Prajāpati fashioned all this as food for the internal wind (*koṣṭhya-vāyu*). What is that? To this he says: everything moving, such as cattle and so forth, and everything stationary, such as roots and fruits, is the food of the vital breath. Therefore, the statement that "meat is to be eaten when life is at stake" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the eating of meat in cases of mortal danger to life. 5.28.
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs; the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave. (5.29)

Regarding the phrase "of those that move": for mobile beings (*jaṅgama*), immobile beings (*sthāvara*) are food; for fanged creatures such as tigers, toothless ones such as snakes are food; for clawed creatures such as cats, handless ones such as fish are food; and for the brave such as lions, the timid such as elephants are food. This is an elaboration of the preceding verse, explaining what constitutes "food without a [specific] cause. 5.29.
The eater is not defiled by eating the creatures that are his food, even day after day; for both the eaters and the creatures to be eaten were created by the Creator himself. (5.30)

Thus, when the conception of Prajāpati is accepted, the eater does not incur sin. Even though one eats—that is, consumes—beings fit for eating day after day, the consumer does not fall into fault, because it was by Prajāpati himself that those fit for eating and the eaters were created. This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended to strengthen the rule regarding the consumption of meat in cases where life is at risk; it is not a logical reason [for the absence of sin], since there is an instruction prohibiting the harming of living beings. (5.30)
"Eating meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance; but engaging in it otherwise is called the demonic ordinance. (5.31)

"Regarding the phrase *yajñāya* (for the sake of sacrifice): meat-eating that constitutes a subsidiary part of the sacrifice for the purpose of its successful completion is an observance appropriate for the gods; therefore, it must be performed with great care. On the other hand, engaging in meat-eating in a manner other than this is said by Manu and others to be conduct appropriate for Rākṣasas. Consequently, [the rule] "this should not be done" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the injunction regarding the eating of consecrated meat. (5.31)
Having purchased it oneself, or produced it oneself, or even received it as a gift from another, one does not incur sin by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors. (5.32)

"Having purchased" means having bought it oneself or produced it; as it has been stated: "and for the sake of the livelihood of servants. And that which has been brought by another is as described: "grains, fish, milk, meat," and so forth. Eating such meat after offering it to the gods and ancestors, one incurs no sin. This refers specifically to the meat of hares and other animals unfit for ritual slaughter (*upākaraṇa*). It does not apply to the meat of cows, goats, or sheep, which are fit for ritual slaughter, when they have not been slaughtered for that purpose but are remnants of an offering to the gods and others, because of the prohibition: "meat and so forth that has not been ritually slaughtered" (*anupākṛtamāṃsādi*). (5.32)
A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when he is not in distress;
for by eating meat contrary to the rule, he becomes a ghost and is helplessly devoured by those very creatures. (5.33)

"From a river," etc. A twice-born man who knows the rules regarding the consumption of meat should not eat meat outside of times of distress unless it is for the purpose of worshipping the gods and others according to the prescribed injunctions; for he who eats meat without such an injunction, having died, is eaten in the next world by those very creatures over whom he had power, under the thought that "this is the meat which was fitly consumed by him"—this is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) on the preceding matter. (5.33)
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as that which belongs to one who eats meat in vain after death. (5.34)

"‘Not such [is the sin]’: for one who kills deer for the sake of wealth—distinct from those such as Śabala, who live by hunting deer—the sin is not of such a kind as that which befalls in the next world one who eats without having performed worship of the gods and so forth; this is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda) of the preceding matter. (5.34)
But that man who, when duly appointed, does not eat meat, goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births. (5.35)

"But the man who, being duly appointed, does not eat meat"—meaning, a person who, having been appointed according to the scriptural rules for the *śrāddha* and *madhuparka* rites, does not eat meat, shall upon death attain the state of an animal for twenty-one births. Thus, the phrase "but he who is duly appointed according to the rule" is a statement regarding the fruit of violating that injunction. (5.35)
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated with mantras. (5.36)

"Unprepared" (asaṃskṛtān) means that a Brahmin or others should never eat animals such as cows, sheep, or goats that are devoid of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) enjoined by mantras for animal sacrifices and the like. What then? Relying upon the occasional Vedic injunction for animal sacrifice and so forth, one should eat only those animals that have been consecrated by mantras. This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to define what constitutes "unslaughtered meat" (*anupākṛta-māṃsa*), [and it serves as a restatement for the purpose of rejecting meat]. 5.36.
In times of distress, one may perform a sacrifice with clarified butter as the victim, or likewise with a victim made of flour;
however, one should never desire to slaughter an animal in vain.
