"One should perform [this]" means that when there is exhaustion of the body and so forth due to the defect of possession by spirits and the like, one may offer an animal made of ghee for the purpose of destroying that [affliction]; however, one should never desire to kill an animal even once without it being for the sake of a deity or similar purpose.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body, so many times does the one who kills an animal in vain undergo death hereafter, birth after birth.

"Because for as many hairs as there are on the animal..."—this means that he who kills an animal in vain, without a [proper] purpose, shall, upon his own death, undergo slaughter birth after birth for as many times as there are hairs on that slain animal. Therefore, one should not kill an animal in vain. The word *ha* indicates that this is based on traditional scripture (*āgama*). (5.38)

Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice; since the prosperity of the entire universe depends upon sacrifice, therefore killing in a sacrifice is not killing. (5.39)

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of sacrifice": for the purpose of accomplishing sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) himself created animals with great care. And sacrifice, according to the principle that "what is cast into the fire [rises up]," is for the sake of the prosperity and growth of this world; therefore, the killing that occurs in sacrifice is indeed non-killing (*avadha*), because it lacks the effect of killing known as unrighteousness (*adharma*). 5.39.
Herbs, animals, trees, quadrupeds, and likewise birds, having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states once again. (5.40)

Regarding the term "herbs" (oṣadhyaḥ): these are plants such as *darbha* grass and the like. "Beasts" (paśavaḥ) refers to goats and so forth. "Trees" (vṛkṣāḥ) refers to *plakṣa* trees and the like. "Crawling creatures" (tiryañcaḥ) refers to tortoises and the like. "Birds" (pakṣiṇaḥ) refers to *kapiñjala* partridges and so forth. Having met their destruction for the sake of sacrifice, they abandon that state of degradation acquired through unrighteousness and, by obtaining a body qualified for the knowledge of the Self, they attain states of excellence once again. 5.40.
"Manu has declared that animals may be slain only in the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), in sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods; nowhere else. (5.41)

"And at the honey-mixture (madhuparka)": Manu has declared that animals are to be slaughtered only at the honey-mixture as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras for kings, officiating priests, snātakas, and others; at sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; and at rites pertaining to the ancestors or the gods, but not elsewhere. (5.41)
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, when killing animals for these purposes, leads both himself and the animal to the highest state. (5.42)

Regarding the phrase "in these": a twice-born man who knows the ultimate meaning of the Veda, while performing acts such as the *madhuparka* offering among these [rituals], causes both himself and those animals to attain the highest state—a connection with various bodies in heaven and other realms. Nor should it be objected: "How can one person obtain the fruit of an action belonging to another? For the object is determined by the authority of the Word (*śabda-pramāṇaka*); whatever the Word makes known must be accepted exactly so. Otherwise, what confidence could there be in obtaining the fruits of dharma and wealth when they are based on the authority of the Word? In the midst of the mantras for the immolation of the animal, the Veda records: "Truly, you do not die here; you do not suffer harm. You go to the gods by easy paths. Indeed, the Hotṛ priest says this to the animal: "Verily, you do not die, nor are you harmed or injured. What then? By easy paths—those devoid of the intervention of inferior births—you go to the gods; the meaning is that you attain heaven. And thus, in other cases as well, there is no lack of benefit to oneself or others. (5.42)
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress. (5.43)

And thus, because it serves the welfare of oneself and others in other respects, it is called "home. A twice-born man who has cultivated his self through the stages of householder, forest-dweller, student, and mendicant should not, even in times of distress, practice violence that is contrary to the scriptures. (5.43)
One should know that the violence ordained by the Veda, which is restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings, is indeed non-violence; for from the Veda, dharma has shone forth.

But how is it that, while the destruction of living beings is equal [in both cases], there is unrighteousness (*adharma*) in the worldly case and righteousness (*dharma*) in the scriptural case? To this he says: "That which... For one should know that injury (*hiṃsā*) enjoined by the scriptures—though occurring in this world of moving and stationary beings—is indeed non-injury (*ahiṃsā*), because it lacks the actual effect of injury due to its beginningless continuity. Therefore, dharma has no other source of authority; it shone forth and became manifest from the Veda alone. And thus, the speculations of sophists do not encroach upon this matter. (5.44)
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead. (5.45)

Regarding the phrase "those who do not harm": he who harms harmless living beings, such as deer and the like, out of a desire for his own pleasure, will never increase in happiness in this world or the next. (5.45)
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage or death, seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness. (5.46)

"Who [avoids] bondage, killing, and afflictions": he who does not wish to inflict upon living beings bondage, killing, fear, and so forth, being characterized by the desire to bring about the welfare of all, attains infinite happiness. (5.46)
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherever one fixes one's delight—that one attains without effort, provided that one harms nothing at all. (5.47)

Regarding the phrase "that which he meditates upon": whatever he contemplates—such as the propitiation of the Lord God—or whatever he performs—such as prostrating at the feet of Hari and Hara—or in whatever he fixes his delight, such as in the cultivation of devotion to Bhava—he attains all that effortlessly, provided he does not harm even living beings such as snakes. (5.47)
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat. (5.48)

Having thus described the merits and faults associated with the practice of eating meat, he now says "not having done" (*nākṛtvā*) in order to follow the subject at hand: Meat is never produced without the injury of living beings; and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven, but rather is a cause for hell and other such states. Therefore, one should avoid the consumption of meat that is not according to the prescribed rule. (5.48)
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from the consumption of all meat. (5.49)

And regarding its origin: one should reflect that [the body] originates from semen and blood—the very first things produced by physicians—and that at the time of death, it faces execution and imprisonment, which are the foremost of all cruel deeds; having considered this, one should desist even from the eating of meat that has been prepared for oneself. 5.49.
He who does not eat meat, even while disregarding the rules like a flesh-eating demon (piśāca), becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases. (5.50)

"How much more so from eating meat that is not prescribed?"—with this in mind, he says "he does not eat" in order to censure the consumption of meat not sanctioned by rule. He who, having abandoned the injunctions for the worship of the gods and other such rites, does not eat meat like a *piśāca*, becomes beloved by all the world and is not afflicted by diseases. (5.50)
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the one who buys or sells, the one who prepares, the one who serves, and the one who eats—all these are slayers. (5.51)

The "consenter" (*anumantṛ*) is one who, having observed another being killed, approves of it, thinking, "Well done, this killer is doing [his work]. The "dismemberer" (*viśasitṛ*) is the one who divides the limbs; he is not the "killer" (*nihantṛ*) or the "slayer" (*vadhaka*). The "buyer and seller" is one who buys and then sells. The "preparer" (*saṃskartṛ*) is the cook. The "server" (*upahartṛ*) is the waiter. The "eater" (*khādaka*) is the consumer. These are called "killers. In this context, with the exception of the actual slayer, the statement that the others are killers is intended to show that even acts such as consenting to the killing of animals—which are not themselves sanctioned by scripture—should not be performed. It is not, however, for the purpose of establishing their status as "killers," because this scripture is devoted to defining what ought and ought not to be done, and because distinct penances are seen to be prescribed for the slayer, the eater, and the rest. (5.51)
There is no doer of greater demerit than he who, without having honored the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another. (5.52)

"His own flesh": he who desires to increase his own body's flesh by means of the flesh of another—which has not been used for the worship of the gods—is no greater sinner than that; this is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda) intended to condemn the consumption of meat obtained through improper means. 5.52.
He who should perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years, and he who should not eat meat—the merit and fruit of these two are equal. (5.53)

Now, in order to demonstrate that abstaining from meat that is neither prescribed nor prohibited leads to spiritual merit (*dharma*), he says: "Year by year. One should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) every year; likewise, for one who does not eat meat for as long as they live—the fruit of heaven and so forth belonging to the merit produced by the abandonment of the horse-sacrifice and the abandonment of meat is equal for those two. (5.53)
One does not obtain that fruit by eating pure fruits and roots or by consuming the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat. (5.54)

Regarding the phrase "by eating fruits and roots": one does not obtain such a result merely by consuming pure fruits and roots, nor by eating the forest-grown foods associated with sages, such as *nīvāra* grain and the like. (5.54)
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'meat-ness' (māṃsatva) of meat. (5.55)
"He will devour me," [he thought]. || 5.55 ||
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; these are the natural inclinations of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit. (5.56)

"There is no fault in eating meat. There is no fault whatsoever in the consumption of meat, the drinking of liquor, or the practice of sexual intercourse when these are not prohibited by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), because for beings whose nature is mobile, this activity consisting of eating, drinking, and sexual intercourse is natural; indeed, abstaining from them yields great fruit. Thus, in the context of discussing the fruits of abstaining from meat, this verse is intended to state the fruits of desisting from liquor, sexual intercourse, and so forth, which are not prohibited by the learned. (5.56)
I shall now declare the purification for the deceased, as well as the purification of objects, for all four castes, duly and in their proper order. (5.57)

Regarding the phrase "purification after a death": I shall fully declare the purification of objects such as those made of metal, as well as the purification of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective order starting with the Brāhmaṇa. (5.57)

When a child has teethed, when it has grown its secondary teeth, and when the tonsure ceremony has been performed, all the relatives remain impure upon its death; the same is likewise declared regarding birth-impurity.

"Upon the eruption of teeth and after the eruption of teeth": this means when a tooth has erupted and when one is born after that; and "after the eruption of teeth" refers to one younger than a child who has had his *cūḍākaraṇa* performed. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that upon the death of one for whom the *upanayana* has been performed, all kinsmen—both *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*—are impure; likewise, it is stated that they are equally impure during a birth. Regarding the term "one for whom the *cūḍā* has been performed," the state of having had the *cūḍā* performed is intended as an indicator of the age generally prescribed by the *Gṛhya-sūtras* for the *cūḍā* ceremony, namely the third year. The phrase "by nights equal to the months" refers to the period starting from conception. Since an increase in the duration of impurity is observed based on the majority of cases, and since here too the commencement is made through the gateway of age in the phrases "upon the eruption of teeth" and "after the eruption of teeth," even in the case of the ten-day impurity, the [period] characterized by the primary time for *upanayana* should be understood. However, because there is no requirement for one initiated at five years of age, the full period of impurity occurs immediately at that time. (5.58)
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapindas;
it may last for three days or even one day until the collection of the bones has taken place. (5.59)

"Ten days": regarding the death of a *sapiṇḍa*, impurity (*āśauca*) caused by a corpse is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa as lasting ten days and nights. Since that for Kṣatriyas and others will be stated later, [this refers to the Brāhmaṇa]. Alternatively, it lasts until the collection of bones (*asthisañcayana*); for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the collection occurs on the fourth day, because the *Gṛhya-sūtra* prescribes the rite of collection on the fourth day. In this section on impurity, the mention of "days" (*ahaḥ*) and "nights" (*rātri*) everywhere is intended to indicate a full day and night (*ahorātra*). This option depends upon one's conduct, Vedic study, and so forth; therein, these options depend on the relative degree of distress regarding study, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and receiving gifts. One should adopt whichever alternative is appropriate according to the circumstances. Thus says Parāśara:
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the Vedas is purified in one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas in three days; but one devoid of virtues is purified in ten days.

Thus, he states that the variety of purity depends precisely upon conduct (*vṛtta*) and other such factors. Even when the contraction of purity and impurity depends on conduct and the like, one must observe the statements of Gautama and others—such as "for the sake of not interrupting the Brāhmaṇa’s private Vedic study"—which indicate that the purpose of the contraction of impurity is merely to perform that much of the rite from which a person suffers distress during the midst of study and so forth, and not for any other activity. Furthermore, this contraction of impurity applies only to that person who suffers distress regarding their private study and the like; it does not apply to another person, as seen in the statements of Śaṅkha and others: "If one bathes and touches water for the sake of the *agnihotra*, at that time the father is pure," and so forth. Such being the case, once the contraction of purity is established for situations involving distress, in all other instances outside of that, food from the family must not be eaten by either party for ten days.

"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended"—this statement indeed holds true. Even in the subsequent cases, the options are to be understood only with reference to one's livelihood and other such factors. (5.59)
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka (distant relative) persists as long as there is knowledge of the birth or the name.

Because the nature of the *sapiṇḍa* relationship is not known from common worldly experience, he states its definition: "The state of being a *sapiṇḍa*... Having passed beyond six persons—namely the father, grandfather, and so forth—and upon reaching the seventh, the status of *sapiṇḍa* ceases. This should be understood to apply equally to sons, grandsons, and others. Furthermore, the status of being a *samānodaka* (one who shares the same water) ceases when there is no longer knowledge of both the birth and the name, such that one can no longer recognize [the other] as: "He was born in our family, has such-and-such a name, and is a descendant of our lineage from such-and-such an ancestor. (5.60)
Just as this impurity on account of death is prescribed for the sapinda relatives, so too should it be in the case of birth for those who desire complete purification. (5.61)
For all others there is impurity due to death (śāva), but for the mother and father there is birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution. (5.62)

Regarding the term "birth": "of all" means that just as there are four alternative views concerning the ten-day period of impurity (*śāva-āśauca*) for *sapiṇḍas*, the same applies to birth (*janana*) among *sapiṇḍas*. However, the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is again [defined] by the capacity for touch; it belongs only to the mother and father, not to the *sapiṇḍas*. Moreover, that [impurity] belongs to the father alone: "When a son is born, bathing with one's clothes on (*sacaila*) is prescribed for the father;
the mother becomes pure in ten days, but the father may touch her after bathing."

Thus, by performing the ritual bath and libations according to the *Saṃvarta* [Smṛti], the father becomes pure. As for what is extended here regarding these ten days, they say: "No other procedures are extended; otherwise, in the case of a total extension, it would contradict established custom (*ācāra*) even for the mother, resulting in the application of the one-day period and so forth. That is incorrect, because since the one-day period and so on are desired for the sake of study and other such purposes, how could there be any application of it to the mother? (5.61–62)
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.

Regarding the phrase "having cast off," since bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse (*maithuna*) according to the rule, "Bathing is ordained for one who has had sexual union," a man becomes pure simply by touching water (*upaspṛśya*) when semen is emitted unintentionally other than during sexual intercourse. Thus Āpastamba stated that purification occurs upon the emission of semen just as with urine; this he mentions here incidentally. However, where there is a connection based solely on the cause of the seed—as in the case of giving birth to a child by a wife who previously belonged to another—where it is not so ordained by scripture, there the three-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) continues. And so Viṣṇu says: "In the case of wives who have previously belonged to another, when they have given birth, [the impurity lasts] for three nights. (5.63)
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or even in three periods of three nights; those who offer water for the dead are purified after three days. (5.64)

Regarding the phrase "in one day": by means of one day and night, and nine days—thus, by ten days as specified according to the nature of their conduct—at the price of a Brāhmaṇa (meaning at the cost of a Brāhmaṇa's wealth), those Brāhmaṇas who perform the bathing, decorating, and carrying out [the corpse] become pure, provided they are distinct from the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*. This applies when the carrying out is done out of affection; for the author will later state: "A deceased twice-born man who is not a *sapiṇḍa*... Furthermore, there is no impurity at all for those carrying out [the body] for the sake of dharma, because of the Vedic revelation: "This indeed is the supreme austerity, that they lead the deceased to the forest."
For those who have committed no impurity or evil through unwholesome deeds,
immediate purification is ordained by immersion in water.

And because of this traditional teaching of Parāśara, one should likewise maintain this regarding the Veda and the matter of its price: "Those who offer water [become pure] by mere water; those who are *samānodaka* relations become pure after three nights. (5.64)
A disciple who performs the funeral rites for his deceased teacher becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse. (5.65)

"Of the guru": having performed the funeral rites for a deceased teacher (guru) such as an Ācārya who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, the disciple becomes pure after ten nights, in the same manner as those previously mentioned who carry out the corpse. 5.65.
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified after as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
when her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who is menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath. (5.66)
For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is prescribed as lasting one night;
but for those whose heads have been shorn, purification is held to occur after three nights.
Regarding the phrase "by nights":
in the ninth or even the tenth [month], impelled by powerful birth-pains,
he is expelled like an arrow through the aperture of a machine, accompanied by feverish distress.

Thus, because Yājñavalkya records the time of birth as nine months, if a miscarriage occurs before the ninth month, one is purified by as many nights as there were months of gestation. However, where a child born prematurely somehow survives, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is indeed complete; for the relationship between a word and its meaning is manifested through the usage of elders, and such a case is not designated by the term "miscarriage" (*garbhaprasrāva*). Furthermore, a menstruating woman becomes fit for rites intended for both seen and unseen purposes upon bathing once her menstrual flow has ceased. Yet, according to the *smṛti* of Vasiṣṭha—which states that a menstruating woman remains impure for three nights—she becomes pure only after bathing on the fourth day, at which point she is fit to be touched.
Until birth, impurity is said to last for an immediate period;
until the tonsure ceremony, it lasts one night; until the initiation into vows, it lasts three nights; and beyond that, it lasts ten nights.

According to this recollection by Yājñavalkya, for men who die after the eruption of teeth but before the time of the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), purification among *sapiṇḍa* relatives occurs in one day and night; for those who die after the time of the tonsure ceremony but before the time of initiation (*upanayana*), purification is prescribed to occur in three nights. (5.66–67)
Relatives should place a deceased child less than two years old outside, having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones. (5.68)

"Less than two years old": having adorned a deceased child who is less than two years of age—measuring exactly one month [or more]—the relatives should cast it outside the village upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones which occurs at a later time. (5.68)
For him, no cremation with fire should be performed, nor should the water-libation rite be performed;
having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, one should simply pass three days [in mourning]. 5.69.

"Of this one" means that for this deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age, the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskāra*) must not be performed, nor should water be poured out even once while restraining the speech, mentioning his name and lineage. Thus, none of the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*), such as the offering of water, prescribed by Yājñavalkya and others, should be performed. What then? Having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, independent of the rite of cremation, one should not perform the ritual acts prescribed by the scriptures until the three-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) has passed. And this option of three days applies specifically to one whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, since the three-day rule was already stated regarding those for whom the tonsure has been performed. It has been said that this [option] would otherwise be purposeless, and that the choice depends on the conduct and other circumstances of the deceased. (5.69)
The ritual offering of water should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it once a tooth has emerged or when the naming ceremony has been completed. (5.70)

"Nor for one less than three years old. This is a restatement of the preceding rule for the purpose of intending to state the subsequent rule: for one whose third year has not yet passed, the water-rite (*udaka-kriyā*), the fire-consecration (*agni-saṃskāra*), and other funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) should not be performed. Furthermore, because of the observation in the *Gṛhya* texts that "having presented [the child] on the tenth day, the father gives him a name," and from this statement, it follows that [the rites] should be performed after [the naming]. If, when the option of non-performance is possible, one were to insist on the option of performance, it would entail hardship; thus, since both options are traditionally taught, it is concluded that by performing [the rites] for a named child, there is benefit for the deceased (*preta*), whereas by not performing them, there is no sin (*pratyavāya*). 5.70.
For a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin), purification is prescribed after one day has passed;
however, for those who share the same ancestry (ekodaka), purity is held to be attained after three nights. (5.71)

Regarding the phrase "a fellow student": when a co-student has died, there is one day of impurity; however, for those who share the same water (sapindas), purification is held to occur after three nights once a birth takes place. As for the rule "after three days for those who offer water," that refers to the first case mentioned. (5.71)
But for female relatives who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen are purified after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) are purified in the time already prescribed.

Regarding the phrase "of women": for those who have been verbally betrothed but not yet married, the husband and others become pure after three days; however, for women whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, the brothers and others become pure according to the rule already stated. (5.72)
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days;
they should abstain from eating meat and sleep separately on the ground. (5.73)

"Those who eat food without pungent salt or salt": they should eat food that is free from pungent salts such as *viḍalavaṇa* and other alkaline substances. They should perform their ablutions in rivers and the like, avoiding clay. This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "And food without meat until purification. As long as the period of impurity lasts, they shall not eat [at night] and shall sleep alone on the ground. (5.73)
This rule for impurity caused by death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure for relatives and kinsmen is to be understood as applying when one is absent. (5.74)

"In his presence" (saṃnidhau) means this: when there is no knowledge of the deceased's location at the time of cremation, this aforementioned rule for impurity due to death (śāvāśauca) is proclaimed; however, in the case of ignorance because he was staying in another country, this rule which is about to be stated must be understood by the sapindas and samānodakas. || 5.74 ||
But he who hears that one residing in a foreign land has died within ten days shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights. || 5.75 ||

"But when it has passed" means: "the remainder of that ten-night period shall apply. Having heard that someone residing in another country has died or been born, if the ten-day period and so forth have not yet elapsed, one remains impure only for as long as remains of that ten-night period; one does not observe a ten-day impurity starting from the time of learning the news. (5.75)
When ten days have passed, one remains impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.

"Passed over": when the period of impurity has elapsed, upon learning of a birth or death among the sapinda relatives, one becomes subject to three nights of impurity; but if a full year has passed, one becomes pure simply by bathing after learning of it. (5.76)
Upon hearing of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed, a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes. || 5.77 ||

"Regarding 'the death of a kinsman beyond ten days': having heard of the death of a sapinda relative after the ten-day period has elapsed, or having heard of the birth of a son, a man becomes pure simply by bathing with his clothes on; this is according to what was stated previously. In the case of a *sahasya* (winter) month, there is an option of a three-night period. (5.77)
If a child, one residing in another country, or a person of a different lineage has died, one becomes pure immediately by plunging into water along with one's clothes. 5.78.

Regarding the term "child" (*bāla*): [this refers] to a child who has not yet developed teeth, even if he is in another country; or to a child who is in another country, provided he is neither a *sapiṇḍa* nor a *samānodaka*. As for the phrase "in another country": having bathed with one's clothes on when such a person has died, one becomes pure immediately. Regarding the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa* residing in another country, purification by the remainder of that period has been stated; and regarding *samānodakas*, purification after three days has been stated. This present rule of immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) is declared as an alternative to those [other periods]. (5.78)
If death or birth should occur again within ten days, the Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period has not yet reached its ten-day conclusion. (5.79)

Regarding the phrase "within ten days": a Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period has not yet passed ten days. If, in the midst of those ten days or more, there occurs another birth or death—meaning a death within a period of death, or a birth within a period of birth—the word "again" (punaḥ) implies: "Even if a birth should somehow occur again during a period of birth, purification shall occur by the remainder of that very period; likewise, if a death occurs during a period of death."

This is because of the traditional teaching of Aṅgiras. Furthermore, for a Brāhmaṇa and others, the impurity (āśauca) would last only for that duration until the previously arisen impurity has passed; once that has elapsed, the ten-day period and so forth begins. In that case as well, the specific rule of Gautama should be observed: "If there is one night remaining, [the purification is] by two days; if it is dawn, by three days. (5.79)
When an Ācārya has passed away, they say that impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it is established that it lasts for one day and night. (5.80)

"Regarding 'three nights': when the teacher has died, they say the period of impurity lasts three nights, and for his son and wife it lasts one day and night; such is the boundary of the scriptures. (5.80)

Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has arrived as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights; likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, the impurity lasts for a night with its two flanking days.

Regarding the term "śrotriya": when a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) who is a reciter of the Veda (*vedādhyāyin*) dies due to any cause such as friendship and so forth, even if he is nearby, one becomes subject to impurity for three nights. In the case of a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, a sister’s son, and others, [the impurity lasts] two days on both sides, like two fortnights. The specific mention of the maternal uncle—despite his being included among kinsmen (*bāndhava*)—is for the purpose of providing an option regarding his sons and other descendants. (5.81)
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun] lasts;
but if the king is not learned in the Vedas, the impurity lasts for a full day, as does it when a teacher who has not mastered the Veda has died.

"When the king in whose territory [one resides] has died, [the impurity lasts] as long as the light": when the king in whose domain a Brāhmaṇa or other [person] resides has passed away, the impurity lasts "as long as the light"—that is, together with the sun during the day and with the stars at night. Thus, if the death occurs during the day, the impurity lasts only for the day; if it occurs at night, it lasts only for the night. It has been stated that "if a Śrotriya who is a relative dies, it is for three days"; however, if one who is not a Śrotriya but a relative dies, it is for the full day, but not for the night. If the death occurs at night, it lasts only for the night and not for the day—just as in the case of a limb [of the body], etc.—and the same applies to a Guru who possesses such a nature, whether [the cause of death] be small or great. (5.82)
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month. (5.83)

"May he be purified": having stated that "I shall describe the purification for the dead of the four castes in due order," the rule of ten days was previously established. This very rule—that "a Brāhmaṇa is purified by ten days"—which was prescribed specifically for the case of a Brāhmaṇa, is here restated with the intention of prescribing the rules for the others regarding impurity caused by birth and death: "A Kṣatriya is purified in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra in a month. (5.83)
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed in the sacred fires; furthermore, even a kinsman performing that rite does not thereby become impure. (5.84)

"He shall not extend [the period]" means that for one for whom a contraction of the impurity has been prescribed—such as "until the collection of the bones" in relation to the *agnihotra* and other rites—he should observe that period of impurity only for the sake of those specific rituals, and not with the intention of remaining at ease without performing them. He should extend the days associated with impurity; he should not rely on the ten-day period for that particular rite. Furthermore, even while the fires are present, one should not abandon the *hotrā* and other rituals, nor does one become impure by performing those *śrauta* rites—even a *sapiṇḍa* relative; how much more so anyone else? Therefore, one should have another perform them. As it is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "The obligatory rites are suspended; however, some say that those performed in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*)—excluding those for hire—should be performed by others. (5.84)
Having touched a divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing. (5.85)

Regarding the term *divākīrti*: having touched a Caṇḍāla, a menstruating woman, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, or one who has touched them, one becomes pure by bathing. Others, however, maintain that the same rule (*tatspṛṣṭinyāya*) applies even to the touch of those who have touched a Caṇḍāla and so forth. Nevertheless, there is this statement of Yājñavalkya: "One should bathe when touched by a menstruating woman or impure persons; if touched by those, one should merely sip water. Thus, even regarding the meaning of the Smṛti, established custom (*samācāra*) must be investigated. (5.85)
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability. (5.86)

"Having sipped water": upon seeing an impure object such as a *caṇḍāla* or the like, which was previously mentioned, one is purified by always sipping water. He should, according to his ability, mutter mantras dedicated to Sūrya and the *Pāvamānī* verses beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā," etc., to the best of his capacity. 5.86.
Having touched a human bone that still has marrow, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is bone without marrow, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun. (5.87)

Regarding the phrase "not a man" (nāram): having touched human bone that is still moist with fat, a Brāhmaṇa or others become pure by bathing; however, having touched it when devoid of fat, one becomes pure by sipping water (ācamana) and then performing either the touching of a cow or the gazing at the sun. (5.87)
One who has been initiated for a vow shall not offer water libations until the completion of that vow;
but once it is completed, having offered the water libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone. (5.88)

"One who has been instructed [in the Veda] does not offer water. Because of his connection with the instruction in the vows (*vrata*), the student (*brahmacārin*) is "one who has been instructed"; for there is a traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha stating: "For a student, there is an exemption from the vows regarding funeral rites, except in the case of his mother and father. Therefore, he should not perform the offering of water or the *samāvartana* ceremony for sapindas and others other than his mother and father. However, when his period of studentship is completed, having offered the water libation to them, he becomes pure after only three nights. (5.88)
The water-libation rite shall be withheld from those born of illicit unions, those who persist in false ascetic orders, and those who commit suicide. (5.89)

Regarding the phrase "of those born in vain or through intermixture": it refers to those born in vain who for the most part have abandoned their own dharma, or to those born from intermixture such as the *niyuktāsuta* (son of an appointed woman) and others; and because of their association with transgression, it also refers to those who abide in vows outside the Veda, such as the red-robed ones (*raktapaṭa*) and so forth. (5.89)

And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor—[for these, there is no atonement]. || 5.90 ||

Regarding the term *pākhaṇḍa* (heretic): just as there is a prohibition against those who follow the Vedic and Brāhma vows, so too for unchaste women, those who kill their embryos or their husbands, those who drink liquor, and those who act in violation of prohibitions like twice-born men; with reference to the wife of a twice-born man, [the text] states respectively: "She should avoid such forbidden things as liquor, garlic, onions, and *gṛñjanaka*; for such a woman, the water-libations and other funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*), as well as the period of impurity (*āśauca*), shall cease. (5.90)
Having carried out the funeral rites for his own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or preceptor, one who is under a vow is not deprived of his vow by that act. (5.91)

Regarding the word "ācāryam": according to the principle that "one should not perform the duties toward one's own teacher when the Guru is present," even by carrying out the funeral rites for an *ācārya*—that is, for a mother, father, or *upādhyāya*, or any such person who is a Guru "whether [the instruction received from him was] little or much"—the religious student (*brahmacārī*) does not become one whose vows are broken. It is understood that he remains so by carrying out the rites in this manner. (5.91)
One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern city gate;
however, for the twice-born, one should do so through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate.

"By the southern [gate]" means that one should carry out a dead Śūdra by way of the city gate situated in the southern direction. One should carry out Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas respectively by way of the city gates situated in the western, northern, and eastern directions. Because they are inauspicious, the exposition of the rule here follows the sequence beginning with the Śūdra. (5.92)
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions;
for they always abide in the station of Indra, having become one with Brahman.

"Not for kings" means that since kings occupy the sovereign position of Indra’s station, and since *brahmacārins* are engaged in vows such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*, and since *sattrins* are established in rites such as the *gavāmayana* and are intent on attaining the status of *brahman*, therefore no defect known as impurity (*āśauca*) occurs for them in their own respective duties. And so Viṣṇu says: "Not for kings in royal affairs, not for those under a vow during the vow, nor for *sattrins* during the *sattra*. And thus [it is said]. (5.93)
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his position of high dignity;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], intended for the protection of his subjects. (5.94)

Regarding the word "of the king": for a king who occupies that station called "kingdom," wherein the nature of the self is great, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed. And in this case of immediate purification, the reason is the king's remaining in his position for the sake of protecting the subjects through rites of pacification (*śānti*), fire-oblations (*homa*), the distribution of food during famine, and so forth. (5.94)
And for those killed in a riot or in battle, by lightning or by a sovereign, or for the sake of cows and Brahmins, or for whomever the king so desires. || 5.95 ||

Regarding the phrase "of those killed in a riot" (ḍimbāhavahatānām): for those killed in a *ḍimba*—meaning in a crush of a crowd or in a weaponless scuffle—as well as those killed by a thunderbolt in battle, or even those killed by a king in battle for the sake of protecting cows or Brahmins; and also those killed even outside of battle by tigers and the like for the sake of protecting cows or Brahmins; and furthermore, for whomever the lord of the earth desires [to kill] for the purpose of thwarting his own interests—even such a person’s purification is immediate. (5.95)
The king bears the body of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, Appati, and Yama. (5.96)

"Of Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, and Indra"—that is, the terrestrial [king] sustains the splendor belonging to these world-protectors: Candra (the Moon), Agni (Fire), Āditya (the Sun), Vāyu (Wind), Indra, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa the Lord of Wealth, and Varuṇa the Lord of Waters. (5.96)
The king is empowered by Lokeśa; no impurity is prescribed for him.
For purity and impurity belong to mortals, whereas he has originated from Lokeśa. (5.97)

"Presided over by Lokeśa": according to the principle thus stated, because the king is presided over by Lokeśvara, impurity is prescribed for others while he is instructed in his own duty. Since whatever purity or impurity belongs to human beings originates from and departs with the Lokeśas, how could there be any impurity for the king himself—he who possesses the form of Lokeśa, capable of producing and receiving the purity and impurity of others? This is a praise of the subject at hand. (5.97)
For one slain in battle with uplifted weapons according to the duty of a Kshatriya, the sacrifice is immediately completed and so too is the impurity; such is the established rule. (5.98)

Regarding the phrase "by those who have raised [their weapons]": for one who has been killed by swords and other weapons raised in battle, being endowed with the dharma of a Kṣatriya such as not turning his back [to the enemy], the completion of the sacrifice occurs at that very moment, because he attains the fruit of the sacrifice at that very time; likewise, the period of impurity (āśauca) also reaches its end at that very moment—such is the established limit of the scriptures. (5.98)
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, by touching his mount or weapon;
a Vaiśya, by touching his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, by touching a staff.

Regarding the term "vipra": at the end of the period of impurity, a Brāhmaṇa who has performed the śrāddha and other rites becomes pure by touching water with his hand according to propriety; a Kṣatriya by touching a sword or similar weapon; a Vaiśya by touching the goad of a bull or the iron-tipped rein or the tethering rope of a horse and so forth; and a Śūdra by touching a staff. (5.99)
This purity regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you, O best of the twice-born;
now learn the purification for the dead among all those who are not sapindas.

"Regarding this": "O Brahmins! That which was stated by you concerning the impurity for those who have died among sapinda relatives has now been explained; now listen to the purification for the dead regarding all those who are not sapindas," thus Bhṛgu spoke to the great sages. (5.100)
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the kinsmen on his mother’s side. (5.101)

"Non-sapiṇḍa": having carried out a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is not a *sapiṇḍa* with the affection due to a kinsman, and having carried out the mother's close relatives such as maternal uncles (*mātula*) and others, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after three nights. (5.101)
If he eats their food, however, he is purified in ten days;
but if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if that carrier eats food belonging to those who are in a state of impurity (*āśauca*), then he becomes pure after ten days, not after three nights. Furthermore, if he does not eat that food and does not reside in the house belonging to them, then he becomes pure after only one day and night, not after three nights or ten nights. Thus, for the carrier who neither resides nor eats there, it is one day and night; for one who resides there but does not eat, it is three nights; and for one who both resides and eats, it is the aforementioned ten days. (5.102)
If one follows out of desire a deceased person, whether a kinsman or a stranger, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. 5.103.
"Having followed"—that is, having intentionally followed a kinsman or another deceased person, one becomes pure after bathing, then touching fire, and subsequently consuming clarified butter. (5.103)
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that offering, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven. (5.104)

"No," [says the author]. When a Brāhmaṇa has died, his son or other relatives must not have him carried out by a Śūdra while members of their own caste are present and available. This is because that bodily oblation, being defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would certainly not serve as a means for the deceased to attain the heavenly world. And since this fault is thus specified, the phrase "while those of one's own [caste] are present" is intended to be emphasized. 5.104.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with clay], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents that purify embodied beings. (5.105)

Now, for the sake of a concise understanding, he says "jñānam" (knowledge) in order to mention incidentally some means of purification established by other statements, and to prescribe incidentally some others that have not yet been mentioned. Knowledge is the purifier of the intellect (*buddhi*), as he will say: "The intellect is purified by knowledge. The mind (*manas*) is the agent of volition, while the intellect is the faculty of determination; this is the distinction between the intellect and the mind. Likewise, austerity (*tapas*) is the purifier for those who know the Vedas, as he will state: "By austerity, those most excellent in Vedic knowledge [are purified]. Fire is the purifier, as he will say: "An earthen vessel [is purified] by being fired again. Food is the purifier, as he will declare: "[One should eat] sacrificial food or barley-gruel. Earth and water are the purifiers, as he will speak: "Earth and water are to be used as long as the purpose [of purification] is served. The mind is the purifier, as he will explain: "The mind should always be pure. Smearing and plastering are the purifiers, as he will say: "[By] sweeping and smearing. In this treatise, no specific purifier for air is indicated; however, regarding its purification when touched by outcasts, crows, or the like, as well as for earth, leaves, grass, and wood, the action of cleansing by means of washing and so forth has been stated, such as: "[Purification occurs] by the rays of the moon, the sun, and the wind," and as he will proclaim: "Or one should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). The sun is the purifier, as it is said: "Having touched a cow or looked at the sun. Time is the purifier, as it is said: "A Brahmin is purified in ten days. Thus, knowledge and the rest are the agents of purification for humans, both directly and through the medium of substances useful for them. (5.105)
Of all forms of purity, purity in wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water. (5.106)

"Of all"—among all [purifications] such as those by clay, water, the senses, and the mind, the purification of wealth (*artha-śauca*) is declared by the seers to be the most excellent for the purpose of avoiding desire for the property of others. For he who is pure regarding wealth should be understood as truly pure; whereas one who is purified by clay and water but is impure regarding wealth is indeed impure. (5.106)
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts, by charity;
those whose sins are concealed, by the recitation of prayers; and those most learned in the Vedas, by austerity. (5.107)

Regarding the word *kṣāntyā* (by forbearance): those who are learned in the scriptures are purified by forbearing offenses against others. As he will say (11.245): "The performance of the great sacrifices and forbearance destroy sins. Those who have committed improper acts [are purified] by giving gifts. As he will say: "Or one's entire property to a knower of the Veda. Those whose sins are not publicly known [are purified] by the recitation of prayers (*japa*). As he will say: "The *Taratsamandīya* hymn is supreme. And those who know the true meaning of the Vedas [are purified] by the methods of expiation such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa*, which will be described hereafter. 5.107.
That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.

Regarding the phrase "by earth and water": that which requires purification is purified by earth and water, according to the manner that will be described later. A river, when its sandy banks have been damaged during the summer and the like due to having very little flow, becomes pure; it becomes pure when the force of the water produced by the rains has washed away its opposite banks. A woman who has somehow formed a mental intention toward another man becomes pure through her menses. And Brāhmaṇas become pure through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), as will be described in the sixth chapter. (5.108)
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. 5.109

"By waters": the limbs, when afflicted by sweat and the like, are purified by water. And the mind, when somehow afflicted by improper volitions (*asat-saṃkalpa*), is purified by the utterance of truth. Furthermore, the ultimate Self—which, like a silkworm in its cocoon, is bound by the web of impurities such as passion—is itself the Supreme Self; through the knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads and other texts, and through austerity, it sheds all impurity and remains established in its very nature as Brahman. Likewise, the intellect, which perceives objects erroneously and is thereby impure, is purified by the realization (*vijñāna*) that grasps things as they truly are. 5.109.
This decision regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the determination concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.

"Regarding this": this discussion concerning the purification of those connected to the body has been stated for you. Now, listen to the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of substances. (5.110)
For luminous gems, for all things made of stone, and for metal objects,
purification has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.

Regarding the phrase "of metallic objects" (*taijasānām*): those things which become liquefied by the heat of fire are "metallic," such as gold and the like. Because this is well-known, Manu and other learned authorities have declared that for all such gems and for everything made of stone—as well as, due to the word "and" (*ca*), for earth and so forth—the purification is to be performed by either water or ash, since they share the single common purpose of removing stains and odors; thus, it is an option chosen by the wise. This rule applies to cases of minor defilement involving contact with food-leavings of the same kind, or with impure substances. Accordingly, other methods of purification are seen for more serious defilements. For instance, Baudhāyana and others prescribe re-melting for metallic objects that have been thoroughly saturated by urine, feces, semen, blood, or corpses; scraping for brief contact; and wiping twenty-one times for defilement by mere touch. Re-melting (*āvartanam*) means making anew; scraping (*parilekhanam*) means planing. (5.111)
An unblemished golden vessel, as well as one made of lotus-fiber, stone, or silver that has not been chemically treated, is purified by water alone. 5.112

"Untainted" (nirlepa) means that a golden vessel or a silver lotus-vessel, which has been defiled by contact with food remnants and the like, or by drinking water and so forth, is purified by water alone, and not by water mixed with earth or ashes. (5.112)
From the conjunction of water and fire, silver emerged from heat;
therefore, its purification by means of its own source is more effective. (5.113)

Regarding the word "of waters" (*apām*): it is heard in the Veda, beginning with, “Agni, indeed, desired the waters of Varuṇa. In that context, it is heard that gold is the *indriya* (vital essence) of Agni, while silver belongs to Varuṇa and the others. Thus, since gold and silver have arisen from the union of fire and water, their purification by means of their own respective causes—namely, that which is called water for the former, and likewise by ash, which shares a single cause [with fire] for the latter—is most highly commended. In this way, ash is superior to earth for the purification of gold and silver. 5.113.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin, and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.

Regarding the phrase "of copper, iron, bronze, and brass": for copper, iron, bronze, bell-metal (*pittala*), tin, and lead, purification must be performed by means of ash, water, alkaline solutions (*lāñjika*), and so forth, without exceeding the removal of impurities. And this [rule] applies to those cases where earth and ash are incapable of removing the impurities of food-leavings and the like, because of the statement "as is appropriate" (5.126). 5.114.
The purification of all liquid substances is declared to be straining;
for solid objects it is sprinkling, and for wooden items it is planing.

Regarding the term "of liquids": for liquids such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like—measured at one *prastha* according to Baudhāyana and others—which have been defiled by the leavings of dogs, crows, and so forth, or contaminated by contact with impure substances, or struck by insects and the like, or touched by objects that have come into contact with impurities, purification is achieved by sprinkling them with water using the hymn beginning, "Pavamāna, the purifier, [is] the source of heaven" (*Ṛgveda* 9.1.6–7), up to the point of adding curd and milk as prescribed in other Smṛtis; or alternatively, the consumption of another substance of the same kind is ordained. Furthermore, for solid objects such as beds and the like, which have been defiled by leavings and so forth, purification consists in sprinkling them after one part has been washed; and for wooden objects defiled by the smearings of leavings and the like, purification is by planing. (5.115)
In the performance of a sacrifice, the cleansing of the sacrificial vessels is done with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* cups and the *graha* ladles is by means of washing.

Regarding "cleansing" (mārjana): it refers to the wiping with the hand of sacrificial vessels, such as the *juhū* and the *ājyadhānī*, by virtue of their being constituent parts (*karmāṅga*) of the sacrificial rite; and the purification of the *camasa* cups—which are specific types of sacrificial vessels—by washing, likewise by virtue of their being constituent parts of the rite. (5.116)

The purification of the *caru* vessels and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is by means of hot water; likewise for the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the cart (*śakaṭa*), and the pestle and mortar (*musala-ulkhala*). (5.117)

Regarding the phrase "of the *carus*": the purification of the specific vessels such as the *caru*-pots and winnowing baskets—which are constituent parts of the sacrifice—by means of hot water is due to their being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of that rite. (5.117)
The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling with water;
however, for small quantities, purification is prescribed by washing them with water. (5.118)

Regarding the phrase "with water": since Bodhāyana and others state that "wood and stone [objects] that cannot be removed [should be cleaned] like the ground," and because we observe that other substances situated on the ground require only slight purification, and because of the absence of a person [to carry them away], there is merely sprinkling with water for grains, clothes, and so forth when defiled by a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste. For those same items, however, when they are small in quantity, washing with water is prescribed. (5.118)
The purification of skins is like that of cloth, and the same applies to articles made of split cane;
however, the purification of vegetables, roots, and fruits is held to be like that of grain. 5.119.

"Like cloth" means that the purification of touchable skins and of woven articles made from tree bark and the like is to be performed as with cloth. Furthermore, regarding vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is prescribed according to the distinction between cooked and uncooked, and according to whether they are threshed or unthreshed—just like grain that is pure or impure. Although the rule "like cloth" would have sufficed, the author begins again with "like grain" [to indicate specific exceptions]. (5.119)
Silk and woolen cloths [are purified] with salt; blankets (*kutapa*) with *ariṣṭaka* fruits; fine cotton cloth (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) with bilva fruits; and linen with white mustard seeds. (5.120)

Regarding the phrase "with alkaline salts (*ūṣa*) for *kauśeya* and *āvikā*": for a specific kind of silk cloth (*paṭṭa*) produced from cocoons and for that made of wool, purification is prescribed with alkaline salts (*ūṣa*)—specific types of earth—accompanied by water, according to the views of Yājñavalkya and others in the rule "with alkaline salts, water, and cow's urine" (YDh 1.186). Likewise, for *kutapa* cloths made from the hair of goats, purification is desired with the powder of *ariṣṭaka* along with water; for *aṃśu-paṭṭas*—cloths made from the thin bark of trees—with the powder of *bilva* along with water; and for those made from *kṣumā* (flax) and similar fibers, with the powder of white mustard seeds along with water. || 5.120 ||
For objects made of conch, horn, bone, or ivory, as well as for linen, purification should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow's urine or water. (5.121)

"Like linen": for conch shells, horns, unclean bones, teeth, and impurities, purification should be performed with white mustard powder mixed with water or cow's urine, according to the specific nature of the stain, just as in the case of linen cloth. (5.121)
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again. (5.122)
An earthen vessel that has come into contact with intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, or blood is not purified even by baking it again. (5.123)

Regarding the phrase "by sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇāt*): "The house [is purified] by sweeping and scraping. Grass, wood, and straw that have become defiled through contact with *caṇḍālas* and the like are purified by sprinkling. Because of its association with grass and straw, "wood" here should be understood as wood other than that used for household vessels. In that regard, there is the rule: "Water [is for purification] of wooden objects, and sprinkling [for others]," and so forth. Furthermore, when a house is defiled by the entry of a corpse, a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), and so on, or when impurities are removed, it is defiled by the entry of *caṇḍālas* and the like; such a house, being defiled by a corpse and so forth, is purified by smearing with lime, cow dung, and the like. As for earthenware touched by substances defiled by food leavings and the like, it is purified by re-firing—the word "firing" (*pāka*) here implying the restoration of newness; however, in the case of that which is excessively defiled, there is simply abandonment. And as Vasiṣṭha says:
"An earthen vessel that has been touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus, or blood is not purified even by baking it again. (5.122)
The ground is purified by these five means: by sweeping, by burning, by sprinkling, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows. (5.124)

"By sweeping and by burning," etc.: the ground is purified by these five methods—either individually or collectively—namely, cleaning away refuse, smearing with cow-dung, sprinkling with milk-water or cow-urine, scraping, and letting many cows stay there for at least one day and night, depending on the specific degree of defilement caused by food-leavings, urine, excrement, *caṇḍālas*, cemeteries, and so forth. (5.124)
Food that has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed over,
and that which is defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.

Regarding the phrase "defiled by birds": food that is not excessively damaged, even if it is the leavings of birds such as parrots, or smelled by a cow, or shaken (avadhūta)—meaning it has been shaken over [the vessel] where it was stored—or if it is affected by sneezing, or struck by hair, or defiled by crawling through impure matter or by insects, such food, according to the word *jagdha* ("eaten"), is purified by the scattering of earth. 5.125.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from an object smeared with it, so long must earth and water be applied in all cases of purifying substances. (5.126)

"As long as the odor and the stain caused by it do not depart from an object smeared with impurity"—this refers to the specific rules for purification regarding objects smeared with impurities, whether those rules have been explicitly stated or not, meaning that in all cases of purifying substances, earth and water must be employed as long as the odor and stain associated with the feces or other such matter do not disappear. (5.126)
The gods have ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word. (5.127)

"Three": those things whose connection with any kind of defilement has not been determined by any means of knowledge, and those things suspected of being defiled by contact with a mass [of impurity], are purified by water. Thus says Hārīta: "Whatever may be subject to doubt becomes pure through contact with water. And when there is a suspicion of defilement, that which cannot withstand washing is purified by the word of a Brāhmaṇa, [uttered] as "May it be pure! These three purifiers were ordained for Brāhmaṇas by the gods. (5.127)
Water on the ground is pure if it quenches the thirst of a cow, provided it has not been contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste. (5.128)

Regarding the word "water": if water in such quantities as would satisfy a cow's thirst is not pervaded by impure substances—given that it possesses fragrance, color, and taste—then it is pure even when located on the ground and so forth, despite the possibility of doubt regarding its being unfit for ritual use (*aprayata*). This mention of "ground" is not intended to exclude the purity of water in the atmosphere. (5.128)
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the established rule. (5.129)

Regarding the word "always" (*nityam*): even when a craftsman performs cooking for gods or Brahmins and the like, his hand is pure through its own inherent purity, even if he does not perform specific purifications regarding the substances or the purpose of the food; for there is a traditional teaching of Viṣṇu stating, "In the case of craftsmen, [the hand is pure] during their craft. His hand is pure in the mere act of his own work, and the mention of the "hand" is used because such activities are primarily performed by the hand. Likewise, food that is to be sold and is displayed spread out on a market stall is pure—even though it has been handled by the hands of many common buyers—because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "One should not eat food from a market stall. With the exception of prepared food, alms obtained while observing celibacy and other vows are pure; and food given by a woman who has not rinsed her mouth is always pure, even if she has stepped upon a chariot or similar objects—such is the established limit of the scriptures. (5.129)
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game. (5.130)

Regarding the word "constantly" (*nityam*): according to the traditional teaching of Gautama, "He [the husband] moves in association with women," at that time the mouth of women is always pure. Likewise, fruit fallen from the beaks of birds such as crows after they have completely pecked at it is pure. And the face of a calf is pure at the time of milking when the milk flows forth. And a dog is pure in its activity when it seizes deer or other prey in order to kill them. (5.130)
Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by its own kind is pure, as is that of one killed by carnivorous beasts, or by others such as Caṇḍālas and robbers. (5.131)

Therefore, it is said: "by dogs" (5.131). Manu has declared that the flesh of deer and other animals killed by dogs, as well as by carnivorous beasts (*kravyād*), by others such as *cāṇḍālas* and the like, or by robbers (*dasyu*), is pure; likewise [he declared the flesh pure] of those killed by others who eat raw meat, such as hawks and the like, or by *cāṇḍālas*, *pulindas*, and others who live by killing deer and such creatures. 5.131.
All those apertures that are above the navel are pure in every respect;
those that are below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body. (5.132)

"Upwards" means that those sense organs which are above the navel are all pure; thus, when there is contact with what is free from impurity, they do not become impure. However, those which are below the navel are impure; "those which are below" refers to the apertures in relation to the navel—the plural number is used because there are many such openings. Likewise, the impurities to be described later are impure once they have fallen from their natural locations within the body. (5.132)
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun, dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch. 5.133.

Regarding "flies": flies, even though they touch impure things, are pure when free from their secretions; likewise are drops of water, which are inferred to be pure by the mere fact of contact; and the shadow belonging to a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, as well as that of a cow, except for its mouth. Thus Baudhāyana says: "Goats and horses are pure from the mouth; cows are pure except for the mouth;
cats and mongooses are pure upon contact, as are auspicious wild animals and birds."

Thus, one should know that horses, the rays of the sun, dust stirred by the wind, and even those touched by outcastes (cāṇḍāla) and the like, become pure merely by passing over them, as well as through contact with wind, fire, and so forth. 5.133.
Earth and water should be taken purposefully for the sake of purification after the voiding of feces and urine, as well as for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities. (5.134)

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of purification after voiding feces and urine": earth and water should be taken—that is, they must be used—for the purpose of purifying the feet and other items with which one voids feces and urine, extending as far as the removal of odors and stains; likewise, for the purification related to the bodily impurities to be described hereafter, earth and water should be taken throughout all ten types of purification, extending as far as the removal of stains and the like. On this point, some say:
"One should take earth and water for purification during the first six [purifications];
however, in the latter six, one becomes pure by means of water alone."

Based on this observation from another *smṛti*, one might think that for the subsequent [excretions] such as earwax and so forth, earth should never be applied. That is incorrect; for here there is an injunction stating, "even in all twelve. Therefore, regarding the subsequent ones, there is an option (*vikalpa*). And that is a regulated option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) depending on place, time, and other factors, as Baudhāyana says:
"Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the occasion, and the state, one should perform purification."

Therefore, one who has engaged in rituals for invisible purposes such as those for the gods or ancestors may take [wealth] even from those of higher status, but not otherwise. The justification is that the person—whether he be endowed with excellence in Vedic learning and conduct or otherwise—is capable of providing wealth, whether small or great, for the purpose of purification through rites of impurity and expiation, serving both visible and invisible ends; thus there is the acquisition of purifying substances according to his condition and physical capacity. (5.134)
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, nasal mucus, earwax, excrement, phlegm, tears, and rheum from the eyes—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. (5.135)

"Fat" (vasā) is the oil of the body; "semen" (śukra) is the reproductive fluid; "blood" (asṛk) is blood; "marrow" (majjā) is the fat located in the head; and urine, feces, earwax, phlegm, tears, eye-secretions, and sweat—these are the impurities of men. These are the impurities of animals such as humans that are not to be eaten, following the discharge of urine and feces. (5.135)
One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand, and seven on both hands by one who desires purification. (5.136)

"One" means: for one who desires purity, a single amount of clay mixed with water—sufficient for its purpose—should be applied to the *liṅga*. Three [applications] should be used for the anus. Likewise, the knower of Dharma should not apply the right hand below while cleansing the left hand;
similarly, he should not cleanse above the navel using the left hand.

Thus, according to the view of Devala, ten [applications] of that same purificatory rite should be made there; seven are to be made on both hands. However, when the removal of odor and smear does not occur by the stated number, then—according to the statement, "As long as the impurity does not depart from that which is smeared with it"—purification must be performed until its removal, even if it exceeds the stated number. Even if the smear and so forth are removed before the number is completed, the number must indeed be fulfilled, because of the force of the scriptural injunction establishing the number. (5.136)
This is the standard of purity for householders; it is double for students, triple for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics. (5.137)

Regarding this: that which was stated as "one [application] on the penis" and so forth constitutes the purification prescribed for householders; for students, forest-dwellers, and mendicants, this very same purification is to be performed two, three, and four times respectively. (5.137)
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise always when about to study the Veda or while eating food. (5.138)

"Having done so": having voided urine or feces and performed the aforementioned purification, and having eaten food, he should touch the apertures of the sense organs beginning with the head—that is, the eyes and so forth. The term "ācamana" (sipping water) is used here for the sake of the meter; this will be specified further in the following verse: "One desiring to study the Veda and one eating food should sip water throughout life. Both of these [rules] were stated in the second chapter—"one about to study should have sipped water" and "having offered [the food] to the teacher, he should eat and sip water"—for the purpose of being ancillary to the vow (*vrata*); however, here they are stated as being ancillary to purification (*śauca*). (5.138)
One desiring bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do this once each. (5.139)

And thus it says, "three times": one desiring purification of the body should first sip water three times; then, for two rounds, he should wipe the mouth at the region of the lips. But a woman or a Śūdra should consume water for the purpose of sipping only once.
Śūdras who live according to the law must have their hair shaved every month;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born. (5.140)

Regarding the phrase "of the Śūdras": for those Śūdras who abide by the boundaries of the scriptures and depend upon the twice-born, there shall be a monthly tonsure; and like the Vaiśyas, they must perform the rules of purification beginning with "one [cut] on the penis" and ending with the sipping of water (ācamana). Since the context concerns the eating of the remnants of the twice-born, [the food] should be given when it relates to oneself. 5.140.
The principal [limbs] do not become defiled by drops that fall upon the body;
nor are the beard hairs considered part of the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth. (5.141)

Regarding the phrase "not rendered impure by remnants" (*nocchiṣṭam*): droplets that have issued from the mouth fall as detached particles; therefore, they do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa*. Consequently, beard hairs resting in the mouth, or fragments of food and the like stuck between the teeth—some say that what adheres to the teeth is treated like the teeth themselves until it falls off before being touched by the tongue—do not render one impure. According to the system of Gautama, which states, "One should know that when [particles] have fallen, it is like [the case of] hearing [the Veda]; one becomes pure simply by spitting them out," such [particles] do not make one *ucchiṣṭa*. (5.141)
The drops that touch the feet of one who is rinsing the mouth for others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. 5.142

"Those that touch... means: those [drops] should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. When others are giving water for sipping (ācamana), those drops which touch only the feet and not the shanks or other parts, are to be known as equal to pure water-drops situated on swept ground; therefore, one does not require sipping because of them. (5.142)
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled, he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down. 5.143.

Regarding the phrase "by what is left over" (ucchiṣṭena): if one who is holding a substance becomes touched by something left over from a meal, then, having set that substance down and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he attains purity. || 5.143 ||
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
