one who has eaten food should simply perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.

Regarding the term "vomited": according to the view of Āyurveda, "one who has performed emesis [should do] ten [purgations], but one who is free from passion [should do] double that. Thus, one who is free from passion after ten purgations should bathe and perform the consumption of ghee (*ghṛtaprāśana*). However, if one vomits immediately after eating food, one should simply perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*); one need not perform bathing or the consumption of ghee. Furthermore, for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse, bathing is prescribed by tradition. (5.144)

Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, and having spoken untruths; and after drinking water or when about to study, one should sip water (ācamana) even if one is already pure. 5.145.

Regarding the phrase "having slept": even if one is already pure, having performed sleeping, eating after hunger, expectoration of phlegm, speaking untruths, drinking water, and likewise commencing Vedic study, one should sip water (ācamana). In that regard, although the sipping of water after eating was mentioned in the second chapter in the rule, "And having eaten, one should properly touch [water]," for the purpose of being an ancillary part of a vow (*vrata*), it is stated here for the purpose of purification. Similarly, regarding the study of the Veda at the proper time, even though the two rules—"one who has sipped water" and "one about to study the Veda"—are distinct, they are explained here together with their respective purposes according to the other regulations. 5.145.
This entire rule of purification, as well as the purification of objects, has been declared for all social classes; now learn the duties of women. 5.146.

"This," [he says]. This entire rule regarding purification after birth and so forth, as well as the complete purification of metallic substances, pertaining to all castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, has been declared to you; now, however, listen to those duties which are to be performed by women. 5.146.
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman, a female should not perform any action independently, even within her own home. (5.147)
Regarding the word *bālā*: even in her state of childhood, youth, or old age, a woman must not perform even the slightest domestic task according to her own will. (5.147)

In childhood she should remain under the control of her father, in youth under the control of her husband; when her husband has died, she should remain under the control of her sons. A woman must never enjoy independence. 5.148.

What then is meant by "childhood"? When her husband has died, a woman must not exercise independence. In childhood, youth, or when the husband is deceased, she remains dependent upon her father, her husband, or her son; and in their absence, she shall be dependent upon her kinsmen or the king. She must never resort to independence. (5.148)
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or even her sons; for by being separated from these, she brings reproach upon both families. (5.149)

"By her father," etc.: she should never be left by her father, husband, sons, or all [these] together, as far as possible, nor even by herself; for through separation from them, an unchaste woman brings reproach upon both her husband’s family and her father’s family. (5.149)
She should always be cheerful and skillful in her domestic duties; she should keep the household utensils well-maintained and be not wasteful in her expenditures. (5.150)

"Always": even when her husband is angry, she should always maintain a pleasant countenance; she should be skillful in household duties; she should keep the pots, pans, and other vessels well-polished; and she should be frugal in expenditure. (5.150)
To whomsoever her father or her brother— by the father’s consent— may give her,
she should serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him.

"To whomsoever she may give" means: she should serve him to whom her father, or with the father's consent her brother, gives her while he is alive; and when he is dead, she must not transgress against him through misconduct. (5.151)
For the sake of auspiciousness, a rite for well-being, and sacrifice to Prajāpati are performed at their weddings; the giving away [of the bride] is the cause of his ownership. (5.152)

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of auspiciousness' (maṅgalārtham): that which is performed at weddings for these women—the recitation of mantras for well-being, peace, and so forth, as well as the sacrifice to Prajāpati—is for the sake of auspiciousness, for the fulfillment of desired goals, and for the attainment of prosperity; it is not, however, for the purpose of establishing the husband's ownership over them. This is because the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) that occurs prior to the wedding does not itself generate the husband's ownership. Thus, their dependence on the husband begins from the moment of the verbal betrothal, not from the wedding. (5.152)

A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with mantras, whether out of season or during the fertile period, is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife both in this world and in the next. (5.153)

Regarding the phrase "at the improper time": the husband who performs the marriage is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife both in this world and at other times, as well as during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), in accordance with the view of Gautama that "or [he may approach her] everywhere except when she is devoid of affection. Furthermore, by means of propitiating him alone, she attains worlds such as heaven; thus, he is the bestower of happiness in the next world as well. (5.153)
Whether he is devoid of virtue, given over to lust, or even destitute of all good qualities, a husband must always be served by a virtuous wife like a god. (5.154)

"Unvirtuous" means one who is of bad conduct, or addicted to another wife, or devoid of the practice of sacred learning and so forth; nevertheless, a husband must always be propitiated like a god by a virtuous woman. (5.154)
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is exalted in heaven. (5.155)

Just as there is the performance of sacrifice by a wife by relying on another husband, there is no such sacrifice for women without a husband; nor is there any fasting, such as the *kṛcchra* penance, permitted for those [women] who have not been authorized by him. What then? By serving her husband, she attains greatness in heaven. Therefore, because of this state which serves as the means for reaching the next world... (5.155)
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should never do anything displeasing to him who took her hand, whether he be living or dead. (5.156)

Regarding the phrase "of the one who took her hand": a virtuous woman, desiring to attain the realms of heaven and other worlds by practicing dharma together with her husband, should never perform anything displeasing to her husband—such as infidelity—whether he is living or dead; and this remains true even when her means of livelihood are unavailable. (5.156)
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died. (5.157)
"Granted," he said: "One may rather let the body waste away on pure flowers, roots, and fruits than, for the sake of a livelihood, utter even the name of another with a mind of transgression. (5.157)
"Until death, let her remain patient, self-controlled, and chaste, longing for that unsurpassed dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband. (5.158)

And thus it was: she who desires that dharma of women with a single husband—which is the most excellent of all dharmas—should endure the pain of hunger until death, remain indifferent to other thoughts, and avoid sexual union with a man; nor, even for the sake of offspring, should she abide in a state of passion. (5.158)
Many thousands of brahmins who had practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to the divine state without producing offspring for their lineage. (5.159)

"Many indeed" means that even from their childhood, the Vālakhilyas—Brahmins described in the Purāṇas who remained celibate and did not take wives—went to heaven without producing offspring, despite there being many thousands of them, for the sake of increasing their lineage by eighty-eight families. (5.159)
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong students of sacred knowledge. || 5.160 ||

"Regarding the word 'dead': a virtuous wife, upon the death of her husband, even if she has not performed the ritual union with another man and is without a son, attains heaven—just as those Vālakhilyas and others who were celibate attained it—even by virtue of having rendered visible service. (5.160)
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband, incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world. (5.161)

"Out of greed for offspring": a woman who, out of excessive greed for offspring, behaves improperly toward her husband—that is, commits adultery—incurs reproach in this world and does not attain the heavenly worlds and other realms earned together with her husband. Furthermore, even that offspring does not belong to her. (5.161)
No offspring born here belongs to anyone else, nor does it fall under the guardianship of another;
for virtuous women, a second husband is never prescribed anywhere. (5.162)

"Nor is she born of another. This means that in this scripture, offspring are not produced as something distinct from the husband; therefore, even through the application of rites such as the *paunarbhava* sacrament, she must not resort to another husband. 5.162.
She who, abandoning her own husband though he be inferior, resorts to one who is superior, becomes contemptible in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband. (5.163)

"Her husband": a woman of the Kṣatriya or other castes who, having abandoned her own husband, resorts to a superior man such as a Brāhmaṇa, becomes censurable in the world precisely because of her service to a superior. She is called "one whose former [husband] was another" (*parapūrvā*) in the world, meaning she has had a previous husband other than the present one. (5.163)
But by being unfaithful to her husband, a woman incurs infamy in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. (5.164)

But through association with another man, a woman incurs reproach in this world and attains the womb of a jackal in another birth; she is also tormented by extremely cruel diseases such as leprosy. (5.164)
She who does not act treacherously toward her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the world of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous. (5.165)

She who, being endowed with mind, speech, and body, does not violate her husband through those very means of speech, mind, and body, attains the worlds such as heaven earned by her husband and is called a "virtuous woman" (sādhvī) in this world; thus, this statement is repeated to exclude [the possibility of transgression] by speech or mind alone. 5.165.
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech, and body attains supreme fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter. (5.166)

"By this": by means of this aforementioned conduct consisting of restraint of mind, speech, and body, the noble woman attains the highest renown in this world and the world of her husband in the next world; this is for the purpose of a concluding summary. 5.166.

A twice-born man who knows the law should cause his wife—who is of the same caste, of virtuous conduct, and who dies before him—to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial implements. (5.167)

Thus it is said: A twice-born man who knows the Dharma should cremate the deceased wife of the same caste, who has followed the prescribed conduct, using the Śrauta and Smārta fires along with the sacrificial implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. (5.167)
Having given the sacred fires to a wife who has died before him during the funeral rites, he may again perform the marriage ceremony and likewise the re-establishment of the fires. (5.168)

"Of the wife": having performed the funeral rites and cremation for a wife who has died previously, and having offered the sacred fires, he may—out of a desire to fulfill the single stage of life of the householder, due to the absence of a son, or for some other reason such as having reached the end of his allotted lifespan—resort to another stage of life, such as that of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and thereby perform a remarriage and the formal adoption of the sacred fires again. 5.168.
By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life. (5.169)

"By this": following the procedure prescribed in the third chapter, and not abandoning the five great sacrifices and so forth, he should perform the second stage of life, having taken a wife, by observing the householder's stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama). 5.169.

Thus ends the section on the determination of permitted and forbidden foods, the purification of substances, and the duties of women, in this commentary on Manu composed by Govindarāja, the son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Mādhava, which follows the intended meaning of Manu.
The Fifth Chapter named [so-and-so].
The Sixth Chapter:
Having thus remained in the householder stage of life, a twice-born man who has performed the ritual bath according to the rules—
He should dwell in the forest, self-restrained, according to the rule, with his senses conquered.

"Thus": having performed the rite of returning home (*samāvartana*), the twice-born man, following the prescribed procedure according to the scriptures, should practice the householder stage of life; thereafter, being self-restrained, firm in resolve, and especially controlling his senses, he should practice the forest-dweller stage of life (*vānaprasthāśrama*) in the manner that will be described, as is appropriate for him. 6.1.
But when a householder perceives his own wrinkles and gray hair, and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest. (6.2)

Regarding the householder: when a householder perceives the flaccidity of his own skin, the graying of his hair, and the birth of grandsons, he should then resort to the forest for the sake of the forest-dweller's stage of life. 6.2.
Having abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest either alone or together with her.

"Having renounced" means: having abandoned the eating of food grown in villages, as well as cattle, horses, and all such things, and having entrusted [his responsibilities] to his wife and sons, he should go to the forest either alone or with her. 6.3.
Taking with him the *agnihotra* fire and the implements for the domestic fire, he should depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained. (6.4)

Regarding the *agnihotra*: having taken up the Vedic fires (*śrauta-agni*), the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*), and the sacrificial implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he should depart from the village and dwell outside, with his senses subdued. 6.4.
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
"By the food of sages": by other pure foods of sages, or by vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should perform these very aforementioned great sacrifices according to the scriptures. 6.5.
He should wear either a skin or a bark garment; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always maintain his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails.

(6.6) "He should wear a skin, a bark garment, a deerskin, or even a tree-bark garment. He should clothe himself in the skin of a deer or similar animal, or in a piece of cloth, or in the inner bark of a tree. He should bathe in the evening and in the morning. And he should always keep his beard, body hair, and nails [untrimmed]. (6.6)
Whatever he may eat, from that he should offer the bali-oblation and alms according to his ability;
he should honor one who has come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, or alms-food. (6.7)

Regarding the phrase "whatever he eats": whatever food he may eat, from that he should offer the *bali* and alms as previously described. Furthermore, he should honor those who have come to his hermitage by giving them water, roots, fruits, and alms. (6.7)
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the scriptures, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
one should always be a giver, never a taker, and compassionate toward all living beings. (6.8)
One should be constantly devoted to the study of the scriptures, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
having abandoned the pairs of opposites, one should be a constant giver, compassionate toward all living beings.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas, enduring the dualities such as cold and heat, he should be habitually inclined toward helping all beings and restrained in his pride. 6.8
He should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the rules,
performing the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices at their proper times without missing the appointed days.

Regarding the term *vaitānika*: on the two festival days (*parvan*) of the new moon and the full moon, one should not neglect the *darśa* sacrifice; rather, one should perform the Vedic *agnihotra* according to the scriptures, even in the case where the wife has been entrusted [to others], and for the sake of obtaining ritual materials as prescribed by the texts. (6.9)
One should perform the Darśeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsyas,
as well as the Turāyaṇa and the Dākṣāyaṇa, in their proper sequence.
He should likewise perform the Nakṣatreṣṭi sacrifice, as well as the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices,
in succession during both the northern and southern solstices.

One should perform, in due order, the *nakṣatreṣṭi* (star-sacrifice) whose nature is described by the author of the Sūtras, its specific rites, as well as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the northern and southern solstices (*uttarāyaṇa* and *dakṣiṇāyaṇa*), and other such Śrauta particulars. As for what has been said by some—that all this is Smārta ritual mentioned under the names of *darśapūrṇamāsa* and so on merely for the sake of praise; that because the Śrauta *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others are enjoined by Vedic revelation (*śruti*) as being accomplished with village-grown rice, meat, and fine sacrificial cakes (*caru-puroḍāśa*), the Smārta grains like rice and so on cannot be substituted by force—it is incorrect. It is replied: since it is not right to abandon the literal meaning of words when there is no other way to attain the goal, how could these [Śrauta rites] not be performed by means of wild-grown rice and the like? For what is impossible? Indeed, the author himself will state in the following verse: "with pure forest foods" (*munyannair medhyaiḥ*). That which is fit for sacrifice is *medhya*. 6.10.
With pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons,
he should separately offer oblations of meat and sacrificial porridge according to the prescribed rule.

"By means of those belonging to spring and autumn" means: one should offer sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and oblations of boiled rice (caru), consisting of forest-grains produced in spring, fit for sacrifice, and brought by oneself, according to the scripture and for each respective rite. || 6.11 ||
Having offered that to the deities, he should employ the remainder for himself as forest-grown food, which is a most pure oblation; and he may also use salt prepared by himself.

"And for the deities": having offered that forest-grown product—which has been prepared as an oblation and is thus especially worthy of sacrifice—to the deities enjoined by the scriptures, he should apply the remainder to himself; and likewise, the salt, ornaments, unguents, and so forth, which have been prepared by himself. 6.12.
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits produced from pure trees, along with oils derived from fruits.

Regarding "vegetables grown on land and in water": one should eat vegetables produced on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits growing in the forest or from sacrificial trees. One may also consume oils derived from fruits such as *iṅguda*, even though they do not originate from the forest. (6.13)
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the ground,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard the food of sages previously stored, as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits. (6.15)

"One should avoid" means: honey, meat, mushrooms grown on the ground—whether they be umbrella-shaped (*chatrāka*) or not even those growing on trees; *bhūstṛṇa* (also known as *bhūtṛṇa*), which is well-known in the Mālava country; by association with that, *śigruka*, which is of the same grass-like kind and well-known in the Vāhīka country; and the fruits of the *śleṣmātaka* tree—one should discard worn-out clothes in the month of Āśvayuja. (6.14–15)
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plowshare, even if it has been discarded by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat roots and fruits grown within a village.

"Not from what is ploughed": even when distressed, he should not eat flowers and fruits grown in a village. Nor should he eat even wild [plants] that have grown in a ploughed area, even if they were neglected by their owner. Likewise, he should not eat flowers, roots, or fruits grown somehow in a village—even those from the forest that are not cultivated—though he may be tormented by hunger. (6.16)
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar. (6.17)

"Regarding the phrase 'one who eats food cooked by fire': he should eat forest-grown food that has been cooked by fire, or fruit and the like ripened by time. Therefore, having thus threshed that food—such as *nīvāra* grain—with a stone, he should consume only that food; for him, his own teeth shall serve the function of a mortar in the process of removing the husks. (6.17)
He may be one who washes [his bowl] immediately after a meal, or one who stores food for a month;
he may be one who accumulates food for six months, or even one who accumulates it for a year. (6.18)

Regarding the term "one who washes [the dishes] immediately": he may store food for six months, or even for a year; or he may collect food only for a single day; or he may store enough for a month, or enough for six months, or enough to last a year. (6.18)
One should eat food at night or by day, having gathered it according to one's ability; or one may eat only every fourth mealtime, or even every eighth mealtime. (6.19)

Regarding the term *naktam*: having brought food according to his capacity, he should eat at the very onset of night; or he may be one who eats only at the fourth meal-time. Since the rule "eating in the evening and morning is the meal ordained for humans by the gods" is already established, he should fast on one day and eat in the evening on the following day; or, being one who eats at the eighth meal-time, he should fast for three days and eat in the evening on the fourth day. (6.19)
Or he should pass the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he should eat a single meal of boiled barley gruel.

"By means of the Cāndrāyaṇa rules": he should subsist according to the Cāndrāyaṇa rules for the bright and dark fortnights, which will be described as consisting of the gradual increase and decrease of food morsels; or else, on the full moon and new moon days, he should eat once a day a decoction of barley flour and other such substances. 6.20.
Or he may always subsist solely on flowers, roots,
and fruits that have ripened in their own time and fallen of themselves, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas.

"By means of flowers, roots, and fruits": one should eat only roots and fruits that have ripened in their own time, not those cooked by fire, but those naturally ripened. Abiding by the doctrine of the forest-dweller known as the *Vaikhānasa*, one should also perform whatever else is prescribed therein. (6.21)
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for the day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the three ritual libations.

"Upon the ground": he should either roll about on the ground or perform repeated movements back and forth; or he should stand on the tips of his toes for a day, remaining standing for some time. And while remaining seated for some time, he should bathe during the *savanas*—at dawn, at midday, and in the evening. The option provided by the phrase "likewise at dawn" is intended for one who requires an even greater degree of discipline. (6.22)

In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky; and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity. (6.23)

Regarding the term "summer": for the sake of gradually increasing his ascetic heat, he should subject himself to the heat in summer by means of the four quarters [of the fire] placed around him and the sun above. During the rainy season, he should bear on his head the falling water—that which flows down from streams. In winter, he should wear wet clothes. This statement refers to the entire year, based on the view that a year consists of three seasons. 6.23.
Performing ablutions at the three times of day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing most rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.

"Touching water" means that he should emaciate his body by performing the three daily ablutions (triṣavaṇa) as prescribed for morning, evening, and midday; by performing the libations to the gods and ancestors (devapitṛtarpaṇa); and by practicing intense austerity (tapaḥ) as taught in the Vaikhānasa scriptures. 6.24.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should become a sage without fire and without a fixed dwelling, subsisting on roots and fruits.

"And the sacred fires" (agnīṃś ceti). After six months, according to the view of Vasiṣṭha—"without fire, without a dwelling"—one should, after that time, internally deposit the Śrauta fires by means of the Vaikhānasa scriptures through the consumption of ashes and other such methods. Thereafter, being devoid of worldly fire, leaf-huts, and houses, the sage should remain with speech restrained, subsisting solely on roots and fruits. 6.25.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, he is a celibate student who sleeps upon the ground;
having no sense of "mine" regarding shelters, his dwelling is at the foot of a tree. (6.26)

"Without effort" means: he should be free from exertion regarding the pursuit of pleasures such as the avoidance of cold and heat; he should be devoid of sexual union with women; he should sleep on a small mound or a bare patch of ground; he should dwell in hermitages or at the roots of trees; and he should live in a tree-hut, being entirely free from the sense of "mine" or personal ownership regarding things like "this is mine. || 6.26 ||
He should obtain alms for his sustenance from ascetic Brahmins alone, or from other twice-born householders who dwell in the forest. (6.27)

"But in the absence of fruits and roots, [he may seek alms] among ascetics"; that is, he should obtain alms for the sole purpose of sustaining life from Brāhmaṇas who are forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) and from others who likewise dwell in the forest. (6.27)
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from the village, receiving them either in the hollow of his hands, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd. (6.28)

But in the absence of that, [the rule is] "from the village. Having brought food from the village, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) should eat eight mouthfuls of the village's food, having received it either in a leaf-cup, with his hand, or in a fragment of a bowl or similar vessel. 6.28.
Living as a forest-dweller, a Brahmin should practice these and other initiations, as well as various Upanishadic scriptures, for the sake of the perfection of the self. (6.29)

"Regarding these": the Brahmin practicing the forest-dweller's life (vānaprastha) should practice these and other rules prescribed in the Vaikhānasa scriptures; and for the sake of attaining the state of a tree for himself, he should practice in various ways the scriptural teachings (śrutis) declared in the Upaniṣads according to their meaning. 6.29.
These have been practiced by sages and brahmins, as well as by householders, for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity and for the purification of the body. (6.30)

"Because these were practiced by the sages"—that is, by the sages such as Aṅgiras and others, as well as by other Brāhmaṇas, both forest-dwellers and householders, for the sake of increasing their knowledge; and because they practiced initiations with diligence for the sake of increasing their austerity and for the destruction of the body's impurities; therefore, "these were practiced"—this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning a past event (purākalpa) which supplements the preceding injunction. 6.30.
Or, having taken his stand upon the Aparājitā [direction],
he should proceed straight ahead until the fall of his body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air.

When an incurable disease has arisen, or when undesirable sights appear, one should resort to the Aparājitā [direction]—that is, the north-eastern direction—or, being established in non-crooked yoga and subsisting on water, one should go until the dissolution of the body. There is no contradiction with the Vedic injunction that "one who desires his own [will] should not depart before the end of his lifespan," because from the word *svakāmin* (desiring his own), it is understood that what is prohibited here is death contrary to rule (*avidhi-maraṇa*), and not that which is enjoined by the scriptures. 6.31.
Having cast off the body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

"Of these": from among these aforementioned practices, by means of any one practice, having abandoned the body, free from distress and devoid of fear, the Brahmin receives honor in the world of Brahmā, provided he has performed death as it was correctly described. 6.32.
Having thus spent the third part of his life wandering in the forests, he should renounce all attachments and go forth as a wandering mendicant during the fourth part of his life. (6.33)

Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests, he should wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life, having abandoned all attachments. In the manner described, having dwelt in the forest for the third part of his life for the sake of practicing the *vānaprastha* stage, he should then, during the fourth part of his life, abandon passion and other defects even more thoroughly than in his previous state and practice the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*), according to the view that the stages of life are to be followed cumulatively as will be explained hereafter. (6.33)
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations and conquered his senses,
one who has grown weary of begging and making offerings prospers after death by embracing the life of a wandering mendicant.

Regarding the phrase "from the hermitages" (āśramāt): having practiced each preceding hermitage in succession among those previously mentioned, and having performed the fire-sacrifices as far as possible within those stages, one who has conquered the senses and is weary from the giving of alms and offerings, while practicing renunciation, prospers in the next world. By attaining liberation, he becomes filled with bliss—namely, Brahman—and thus becomes endowed with such preeminent excellence. || 6.34 ||
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward. (6.35)

Thus, when the position of the combination of all stages of life (*āśrama-samuccaya*) is accepted, it is said: "Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation. Having cleared the three debts that are to be mentioned in the following verse, one should then apply the mind toward liberation by means of renunciation (*pravrajyā*). However, if one practices renunciation without having cleared them, this person incurs censure and goes to hell. (6.35)
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation.

He indicates those debts with the words "having studied," etc. One should say: "A man is born burdened by three debts: to the gods by sacrifice, to the ancestors by progeny, and to the seers by the study of the Veda" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10.5). Having studied the Vedas according to the scriptures, having procreated offspring through the duty of approaching one's wife during the proper seasons—avoiding intercourse at forbidden times or out of mere lust—and having performed sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma according to one's capacity, one should thereafter apply the mind to renunciation, which is called the means to liberation. (6.36)
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated offspring, and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward. (6.37)

"Without having studied the Veda, and likewise without having procreated a son... [Thus it is said: Desiring liberation without having performed the study of the Veda, the procreation of offspring, and the performance of sacrifices, one goes to hell. (6.37)
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa should renounce his home and go forth.

"Regarding the *prājāpatyā* [sacrifice]: having performed the sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati—which is described in the texts known as the *Yajurveda-pūrva*—and for which the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one's entire wealth, and having then, according to the very procedure prescribed therein, deposited the fires by means of drinking the ashes and so forth, a Brāhmaṇa should practice renunciation (*pravrajyā*) immediately thereafter, without even entering the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), but directly from the householder stage itself. Thus, the position of the sequential combination (*samuccaya*) of the stages of life is shown by this; and all positions regarding the optional combinations of three or four stages, as enjoined by the Śruti, remain established. And so it is stated in the Jābāla-Śruti: "Having completed the student stage (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce. Or, if he should do otherwise, he may renounce directly from the student stage, or from the house, or from the forest. (6.38)
He who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, goes forth from his home, for him, as a teacher of Brahman, the worlds consist of splendor. 6.39

"Of him"—of that teacher of Brahman who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, renounces from his very home, there are worlds of light; for him who is devoted to the Upanishads and other scriptures intended to define the nature of Brahman, there are eternally luminous worlds. 6.39.
Since not even the slightest fear arises for the twice-born from living beings, there is no fear whatsoever for him once he is liberated from the body. (6.40)

Regarding the phrase "yasmāt": for that twice-born man from whose presence not even the slightest fear arises for living beings, there shall be no fear whatsoever after the fall of his present body. (6.40)
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by his observances, should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him. 6.41

"From the home": having departed from his house, equipped with pure items such as *darbha* grass, an antelope skin, a staff, and a water-pot, with his speech restrained, he should go forth, free from longing even for sweet food and other things brought to him by someone else. (6.41)
Wandering always alone, without a companion, for the sake of perfection;
seeing that perfection belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons nor is abandoned. (6.42)

"Alone" means that liberation is attained by one who exists as a single entity. Knowing this, he remains alone—not with another renunciant, without a companion, and free from servants and the like—by the renunciation of others, so say some. For Baudhāyana has stated, "And for some, [renunciation] also for women," thus declaring renunciation even for women. Acting in this way, he abandons nothing, nor is he abandoned by anyone; he does not experience the suffering of separation, nor is it experienced by another. Because of the absence of the nature of close attachment, there is the unimpeded attainment of the means to liberation. (6.42)
He should be without fire and without a fixed abode; he may resort to a village only for the sake of food.
Indifferent, free from agitation, the sage should be fully concentrated in his being. (6.43)

"Without fire": the sage is one who does not look about, who is not fickle, and whose mind is concentrated on the true nature of reality (*bhāva*). Because it is stated in the scriptures that fire is to be superimposed [upon the self], he is devoid of worldly fire; he is "without a wife" (*agṛhyaka*) and indifferent even toward his own body because of the arising of disease and other afflictions. As Śaṅkha says: "One should perform medical treatment for oneself, nor cause it to be performed by others. [The term] *anumānya* (? means "not having obtained permission. "Not fickle" (*asaṃkusuka*) means one whose intellect is restrained; he should be restrained in mind and should go to the village for the sake of alms. (6.43)
A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.

"A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, and being without companions"—a tattered cloth for the purpose of begging, the roots of trees as a dwelling, ragged clothing such as a patched garment for the sake of dress, delighting in solitude for the sake of abandoning attachment, and equanimity toward enemy and friend: because these are the means to liberation, they are the marks of one who is liberated. 6.44.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the time, just as a servant awaits his instructions. 6.45

"One should not rejoice" means that one should desire neither death nor life; rather, just as a laborer awaits the time for his wages, so too should one await that time of death when it arrives of its own accord. || 6.45 ||
One should step with the eye as one's purifier; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure. (6.46)

"Pure by sight": one should step with feet purified by the eyes for the sake of avoiding injury to living beings; and one should drink water purified by a cloth for the sake of avoiding minute aquatic creatures; and one should speak words consecrated by truth. Thus, through silence, the mind should always be purified by the abandonment of frivolous speech and false intentions. (6.46)
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone. (6.47)

"Regarding 'excessive words' (ativādān): one should endure even insulting speech and should not despise anyone at all. Nor, relying upon this body—which is the locus of disease and as perishable as a flash of lightning—should one, for its sake, engage in even a moment’s quarrel with anyone; for such conduct is an obstacle to heaven and liberation. (6.47)
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates. 6.48

"Even toward one who is angry": one should not become angry in return toward someone who has become enraged. Even when reviled, one should speak kindly to the reviler. Regarding these seven occasions for the utterance of speech—namely, dharma, artha, kāma; dharma and artha; artha and kāma; dharma, kāma, and artha; and all three together—one should not speak words that are scattered or distracted among them, nor words concerning those objects that are false in meaning, characterized by divisiveness or lack of well-being; rather, one should speak only that which is grounded in liberation (mokṣa). || 6.48 ||
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent, and free from worldly desires, one who seeks happiness should wander here with the self alone as his companion. (6.49)

"Delighting in the inner self": being one whose activity is directed toward the inner self through the Upaniṣads and so forth, free from any particular regard for such things as the staff and water-pot, desireless, and without companion, he moves about happily in this cycle of existence. (6.49)
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor through instructions or discourses. (6.50)

And not even this: by explaining the results of omens such as earthquakes, portents, and the throbbing of the eyes; by means of the science of the body parts of the constellations (*nakṣatrāṅgavidyā*), such as "today is Āśvinī" or "this is the mark of the hand, nail, or ear"; and by speaking on the meaning of the scriptures through instruction that "he who desires this path of policy should not act otherwise"—[the mendicant] should never desire to obtain alms [by such means]. 6.50.
One should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants. (6.51)
"No," [he says]. He should not enter a house for the sake of alms that is crowded with forest-dwelling brahmins, birds, dogs, or others who are habituated to wandering for alms. 6.51.
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, not causing pain to any living beings.

"Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard"—meaning one whose hair, nails, and beard have been clipped—carrying an alms-bowl and a staff with a skull-topped finial, not causing pain to any living beings, self-restrained and wise, he should always wander about. (6.52)
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as for the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.

"Non-metallic" means they should be made of materials other than gold, iron, and so forth; the begging bowls for eating should be without holes and free from blemishes. And their purification is by water alone, just as that of the *camasa* cups in a sacrifice. 6.53.
A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for ascetics. (6.54)
"Or a gourd, or a wooden bowl. Manu, the Self-Existent, has declared that bowls made of gourd, wood, clay, or bamboo bark belong to those who have gone forth. (6.54)
One should go for alms at a single time and not become attached to abundance;
for a mendicant who is addicted to alms becomes attached even to sense-objects. (6.55)

"At one time" means that he should go for alms only once, solely for the purpose of sustaining his life for a single day; he should not even go for alms at both times [morning and evening], lest he fall into the trap of excessive wandering for food. For, through an excess of eating alms-food, an ascetic becomes intoxicated by the abundance of food and becomes attached even to other sense-objects. (6.55)

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has taken place—at these times the ascetic should always go for alms. (6.56)

"Smokeless," etc.: when the time is smokeless, when the pounding with pestles has ceased, when the flames of cooking have subsided, and when the people down to the householders have finished their meals and discarded the bowls of leavings—at such a time the ascetic should always go for alms.

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice in its presence; one should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, being free from attachment to material requisites. (6.57)

“He should be neither lustful nor despondent, and gain should not cause him joy. Thus, he should not indulge in joy or despondency regarding gain and loss. He should eat food merely for the nourishment of life. Regarding the mere possession of a staff, a water-pot, and so forth, he should not form an attachment by thinking, “This is my purification” or “This is not. (6.57)
One should utterly loathe gains obtained through honor;
for even a mendicant who is already liberated becomes bound by gains obtained through honor. (6.58)

“One should diligently avoid alms obtained through excessive honor; for by the greed for excessively honored gains, even a liberated ascetic is bound. (6.58) One should always censure and therefore avoid the acquisition of alms preceded by honor. For, because the gain of honor arises simultaneously [with the attachment], an ascetic seeking liberation nevertheless falls into saṃsāra.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude, one should turn back the senses when they are being carried away by sense-objects. 6.59

"By the consumption of little food": one should withdraw the senses from their objects by means of eating little food and sitting in a secluded place, so that the senses, which are being led away by objects such as forms for the sake of enjoyment, are turned back. 6.59.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred, and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality. 6.60
Because of the words "of the senses": one who has conquered the senses and is free from passion, hatred, and so forth, becomes fit for liberation through non-violence and avoidance [of harm]. 6.60.
One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions, as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama. (6.61)

Now, as a means for conquering the senses, he teaches the avoidance of worldly existence with the words "one should observe. One should, by means of the vision of the scriptures, contemplate the attainments of bodies such as those of snakes, chameleons, and worms for the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) arising from the sins produced by failing to perform what is prescribed and engaging in what is forbidden; as well as the falling into hells within the abode of Yama and the tortures consisting of being torn apart by extremely sharp saws. 6.61.
Separation from what is dear, union with what is unpleasant, being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases. (6.62)

Regarding "separation": one should reflect upon the afflictions born from separation from the beloved and union with the disliked, as well as the torments of old age, disease, and birth, which arise from the defects of karma. 6.62.
The departure from this body, the subsequent birth in a womb, and the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of wombs—[all these he beheld]. (6.63)

"From the body," etc.: he should contemplate the departure of this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) from this body—a process harsh due to the entry into densest darkness following the violent dislocation of joints difficult to endure—and furthermore, his birth in a womb abundant with the sufferings of food, drink, and so forth, produced by cold, heat, bitter, pungent, and other [sensations], as well as his migrations into the wombs of base species such as jackals and the like, all arising from the defects of karma. || 6.63 ||
And the connection with suffering for embodied beings arises from unrighteousness, while the inexhaustible union with happiness arises from righteousness and purpose. (6.64)

"Arising from unrighteousness": one should observe that for embodied knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), there is a connection with suffering caused by unrighteousness (*adharma*), and a connection with well-being and happiness caused by the purpose of righteousness (*dharma*). Therefore, having reflected in this manner, one should strive for the conquest of the senses, which is the means to liberation. 6.64.
And by means of yoga, one should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.

"Subtlety": one should perceive the subtlety of the Supreme Self through the steadiness of the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), based on the Vedic scripture which says, "He who is within the heart, more minute than an atom. Alternatively, when the designation of "subtlety" is established by relying on its being distinct from gross objects such as the body, one should perceive that subtlety. Likewise, one should perceive its sovereignty over superior and inferior bodies for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions. (6.65)
Even if adorned, one should practice the Dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life one finds pleasure in;
being equal toward all beings, outward appearance is not the cause of righteousness.

“Even though adorned, one should practice the Dharma, dwelling in whatever stage of life (āśrama). This means that regardless of which stage of life one occupies, being impartial toward all beings, one should observe the entire collection of restraints (yama) prescribed for that stage—even while discarding the external marks and ornaments of that stage and instead adopting dress and adornments contrary to it. For the carrying of the staff, water-pot, and so forth is not the cause of Dharma; rather, it is the performance of the restraints and observances (yama-niyama). This statement of censure regarding the external marks is intended to proclaim the primacy of the performance of the restraints and observances as the essential action, not to advocate the abandonment of the marks, since they have been prescribed [by rule]. 6.66.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water, the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (6.67)

Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "fruit" (phalam). Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree produces clarity in turbid water, the water does not become clear merely by the utterance of its name; rather, it requires the act of casting the fruit [into the water]. Likewise, the elevation of Dharma does not occur through the mere wearing of the insignia (*liṅga*), but requires actual practice (*anuṣṭhāna*). || 6.67 ||
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day, he should always walk upon the earth after carefully scanning it, even when his body is in distress. (6.68)

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of protection': because it is said that 'even when there is bodily suffering, one should walk upon the earth after having observed this,' its expiation is stated here even though it does not belong to the immediate context, for the sake of showing due respect. (6.68)
Whatever living beings an ascetic injures unintentionally by day or by night,
for the sake of their purification he should bathe and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).

Regarding the word "ahni": if an ascetic kills living beings that were not intended to be killed during the day or night, for the purpose of removing the sin of that killing, he should bathe and recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining his breath;
that is called Prāṇāyāma.

Thus, according to the definition established by Vasiṣṭha, one should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). The increase in the number of these through an intensification of the expiation is for the sake of showing respect. It is determined from the statement "even in the case of a transgression in conduct that has not been accumulated, sin arises from this [ignorance]" that sin indeed occurs even when the act is committed unintentionally. (6.69)
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa,
joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the supreme austerity.

Regarding the statement "because [they are] breath-restraints" (prāṇāyāmāḥ): when the breath-restraints are performed according to the rules of retention (kumbhaka), inhalation (pūraka), and exhalation (recaka), joined with these sacred utterances (vyāhṛti)—bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ—and the syllable Om (oṃkāra), they should be understood as the supreme austerity of a Brahmin. In that context, the restraint of the entry and exit of the external and internal air into the body is retention (kumbhaka); the continuous expulsion of the air being exhaled is exhalation (recaka). (6.70)
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burned away when they are being smelted, so too are the defects of the senses burned away through the restraint of the vital breath. (6.71)

"They are burned" means: just as substances such as gold and other minerals are burned when they are smelted in the midst of fire along with clay and the like, so too, those defects such as passion (rāga) that arise through the engagement of the senses with their objects are [extinguished] by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). By the restraint of the vital breath, there is the non-contemplation of sense-objects; from that, there is the turning away from passion and the rest. This is what is expressed by this [verse]. 6.71.

One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā); one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). 6.72.

And this being so, regarding the phrase "by means of breath-restraints" (*prāṇāyāmaiḥ*): according to the method just described, one should burn away passion and the like by means of breath-restraints. Regarding the definition of *dhāraṇā* as "the binding of the mind to a place," one should burn away impurity—that is, protect oneself from sin—by means of fixing the mind, which is otherwise unsteady and without a fixed support, upon locations such as the heart. And by means of *pratyāhāra*, through the withdrawal of the mind from sense objects, one should burn away—that is, protect oneself from—the attachments that consist of contact with the objects of the senses and which are the causes for the perception of those objects. By means of *dhyāna*, defined in the Yoga scriptures as "meditation consisting of the one-pointedness of thought," and by means of meditation in the form of self-realization untainted by heterogeneous perceptions, one should burn away the qualities of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and powerlessness—specifically the forms of virtue, knowledge, and power that are contrary to the pure, eternal [Sāttvika] nature—as described in the Sāṃkhya system. (6.72)
Through the yoga of meditation, one may perceive the course of this inner self within beings of high and low station— a course that is difficult for those of unrefined soul to understand.

Regarding the phrase "among high and low": this *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) undergoes attainment among beings ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—both superior and inferior. Those whose selves are unrefined, acting contrary to the scriptures, bring about this state for him; thus, by this cause, he enters various transmigrations, such as that of a twice-born or others. (6.73)
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of vision enters the cycle of transmigration. (6.74)

Because it is said "correctly": one who is endowed with correct knowledge regarding the Self is not bound by actions—just as seeds fried in oil are incapable of producing an effect when self-knowledge exists—and thus does not undergo rebirth in saṃsāra; however, one devoid of self-knowledge returns again to saṃsāra. (6.74)
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rituals,
and the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state in this world.

Regarding the word "non-violence" (*ahiṃsayā*): by practicing non-scriptural non-violence, by avoiding attachment of the senses to their objects, by means of the obligatory Vedic rites, and by performing sacred penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, one attains the station characterized by the realization of Brahman in this world of transmigration. With these two verses, he declares the fruit of the combination of knowledge and action. (6.75)
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement. (6.76)
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is assailed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place of disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent. (6.77)

Now he describes the nature of the body, which is the object for the arising of detachment—the means to liberation—stating: "having bones for its pillars, bound together by tendons," and "assailed by old age and grief. One should abandon this house, the body, which is a modification of the elements such as earth and consists of flesh and other [tissues]. By means of a metaphorical description, he shows its nature as a house: it has bones for its pillars because they support it; it is bound together by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, and filled with urine and excrement. For this reason, it is overcome by foul odors and old age, serves as the abode of diseases, is afflicted, distressed by hunger, thirst, and the like, is predominantly *rājasa*, and is perishable. (6.76–77)
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree, so too, by abandoning this body, one is released from the crocodile of suffering. 6.78

To demonstrate the two types of abandonment based on the difference between the knower and the non-knower, he says: "Like the riverbank. First, one who is devoted to the practice of self-knowledge, yet has not—due to the exhaustion of karma—attained the reality of the Self, should regard the falling of the body as something dependent on external causes, like a tree on a riverbank. On the other hand, one who has realized the distinct light of the Self may abandon the body even intentionally, like birds leaving a tree, by means of the support of *utkrānti* (the upward departure of the soul). Thus, abandoning this body, he is liberated from *saṃsāra*, which is the root of suffering, just as one is freed from aquatic creatures. The view of the knowers of Yoga is that for one devoted to the practice of self-knowledge, even if the body should somehow fall prematurely, liberation (*apavarga*) is certain once the remaining portion of self-knowledge is completed through another body; therefore, even for such a person, the statement that "abandoning this body in that manner, he is released from the crocodile of hardship" is appropriate. (6.78)
Having cast off his good deeds toward those he loves and his evil deeds toward those he dislikes, through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman. (6.79)

Regarding the phrase "in regard to dear things": when those things agreeable to one's own duty are brought about by someone else, this does not happen for anyone without the merit (*sukṛta*) accumulated in a previous birth. Therefore, thinking, "This person is merely a doer of what is dear to me; rather, it is my own previously performed merit [that is the cause]," he—by means of the mental exercise of meditation—attributes his own merit as the agent. Likewise, even when disagreeable things are done by someone, he postulates his own previously accumulated demerit (*duṣkṛta*) as the cause, and by conceiving the person who accomplished them as the instrument, he remains free from attachment and aversion toward that person. Thus, he constantly approaches Brahman; that is, he attains its state. (6.79)
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition, then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death. (6.80)

Regarding the phrase "when": when one becomes free from desire for all things by means of the mind's ultimate nature (*pāramārthika-cetodharma*), then, after the fall of the body, one attains eternal bliss of liberation (*apavarga-sukha*) in this world, even while the performer of a hundred sacrifices (*śatamakha*) has passed away. || 6.80 ||
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments, one who is completely freed from all dualities abides in Brahman alone. (6.81)

"By this": by means of this method consisting of the investigation into the true nature of saṃsāra, having gradually abandoned all contacts with sense objects, he then remains established in Brahman, which is the perfected state, being completely freed from all dualities such as hunger and satiety. || 6.81 ||
All this that has been described is indeed meditative;
for no one who is not a knower of the inner self enjoys the fruit of ritual action.

"Relating to meditation" (dhyānika): This teaching which has been stated is "relating to meditation"; it yields a superior fruit only when there is meditation—that is, when there is contemplation of the Supreme Self. For he who does not know the true nature of the Self obtains an incomplete result from his practice, as stated in the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇa*: "O Gārgī, for one who, having understood this Imperishable, performs oblations, sacrifices, or practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years, his [merit] is indeed finite. (6.82)
One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, as well as that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and whatever is declared in the Vedāntas. (6.83)

Regarding the term *adhiyajñam*: one should constantly recite that which pertains to sacrifice—that is, the Veda known as the Brāhmaṇa; that which pertains to the deities—that is, the texts dedicated to the manifestation of the deities such as "Agni is the head" (*agnir mūrdhā*); and that which pertains to the Self—that is, the Puruṣasūkta and so forth—as well as what is declared in the Upaniṣads. (6.83)
This is the refuge for those who understand, this very thing for those who discern;
this for those seeking heaven, and this for those seeking the infinite. (6.84)

"This" means that for those ignorant of the meaning of the scriptures, Brahman alone—known as the Veda—is the refuge, because it is the cause for attaining excellence and avoiding decline. Likewise, this very [Veda] is the refuge for those possessed of knowledge who desire heaven and liberation.
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant by means of this sequential yoga,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.

"By this"—that is, by the aforementioned connection with the stages of life (āśrama)—the twice-born who takes recourse to renunciation (pravrajyā) burns away his impurity in this very world and, through its destruction, attains the supreme Brahman-nature. 6.85.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action for those who have renounced the Vedas.

"This" refers to this dharma pertaining to those of self-restraint which has been declared to you by one of them. Now, listen to how the bondage of karma is removed for those who have abandoned the Agnihotra and other rites prescribed by the Vedas, yet accomplish those very rites through the power of knowledge in the manner described by the verse beginning, "Some perform these great sacrifices. Nor should it be asked how there can be a renunciation of the Agnihotra and other rites enjoined by the Śruti on the basis of Smṛti; for even this practice is Vedic, according to the scriptural method shown in the fourth chapter beginning with, "As long as a man speaks," and so forth. Although the Veda-renouncer (*vedasaṃnyāsika*) is indeed a specific type of householder, the mention of him immediately after the duties of the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*) is intended to indicate that being a renouncer (*saṃnyāsika*) is an alternative to the life of a wandering mendicant. Furthermore, since the Veda-renouncer is included within the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) by virtue of being a householder of the Veda, [the author] first states what is desired to demonstrate the various positions regarding the combination, option, or sublation of the four, three, or two stages of life. (6.86)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder. (6.87)

Regarding the term *brahmacārī*: those stages of life (*āśramiṇaḥ*) such as the student (*brahmacarya*) and others who have been mentioned separately are born from the householder. Thus, for those known to have transgressed the scriptures by means of stages of life other than that of the householder, there is no entitlement to the stage of the student and the others.
All these, when practiced in succession according to the scriptures, lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal. (6.88)

"All [of them] as well" (*sarve ’pi*). "All" means even all four; by the word "as well," it is implied that three, two, or even one alone—provided they are practiced without transgressing the teachings stated here—lead the practitioner of what has been taught to the goal characterized by the attainment of the state of a *vipra* or *brahman*. Thus, the scriptural basis for the positions of combination (*samuccaya*), option (*vikalpa*), and sublation (*bādha*) regarding celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth has been shown. Even in the case of the position of sublation, the scriptural basis is found in such texts as: "This sacrificial session (*sattra*) consists of old age: namely, that one offers the *agnihotra*, that one sacrifices with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s," and so on. And thus, since all these positions—combination, option, and sublation—are rooted in scripture, the practice of any one of them according to one's preference demonstrates that the status of a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) is also rooted in scripture. Consequently, the claim made by some—that because the status of a lifelong student and the like are based on *smṛti*, they are sublated by the Vedic (*śrauta*) householder stage, and that the householder stage itself applies only to those like the blind who are ineligible for other stages—is incorrect; for it has been demonstrated that all of these are rooted in direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). (6.88)
And among all these, according to the injunctions of Vedic revelation,
the householder is declared to be the best, for he indeed supports these other three.

Regarding the word "of all": among all [the stages of life], beginning with the student (brahmacārin), the householder is declared by Manu and others to be the best because, due to the predominance of householders, the performance of rituals is directly enjoined for them by Vedic texts. Furthermore, he is the best because he sustains the students, ascetics, and renunciants through alms and other means, as it is said: "Day after day, by knowledge and by food"; and since [it is stated] that "they are supported by the householders alone," therefore he is the most excellent. (6.89)
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean, even so do all those in the various stages of life find their support in the householder. 6.90

"Yathā" (as): Just as all rivers and streams, such as the Gaṅgā and others, reach their place of abiding in the ocean, even so all those in the stages of life, beginning with the religious student (*brahmacārin*), reach their station within the domain of the householder for the sake of obtaining food and other necessities. 6.90
Moreover, by these four classes of twice-born men belonging to the various stages of life, the tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort. (6.91)

By these four classes of twice-born men belonging to the stages of life, beginning with the student (brahmacārin), the dharma consisting of the ten causes to be described hereafter should be practiced with diligence. (6.91)
Fortitude, forbearance, self-control, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, wisdom, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma. 6.92

Regarding "fortitude" (dhṛti): contentment, endurance of offenses, tolerance of the dualities such as cold and heat, refraining from taking the property of others, purity through soft water and so forth, mastery over the senses, unimpaired intellect, knowledge of the Self, speaking only what has been perceived, and the non-arising of anger—this tenfold measure is the characteristic of dharma. Although all of this has already been mentioned scattered throughout this treatise, it is stated here again because dharma generally consists of just this much; it is stated in brief for the sake of awakening those who are confused. (6.92)
Those brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma, and having studied them, live in accordance with them, go to the supreme goal. (6.93)

"Ten characteristics": those Brahmins who recite these ten characteristics and, having recited them, practice accordingly, attain the supreme station, the world of Brahmā, or, if they possess knowledge, liberation. 6.93.
Practicing the Dharma characterized by the ten marks with a concentrated mind, and having heard the Vedānta according to the injunctions, the twice-born man, free from debt, should renounce. (6.94)

"Consisting of ten characteristics": thus, having practiced the Dharma described as having ten characteristics with a self-controlled mind, and having correctly understood the Upaniṣads, a twice-born man of the three castes who has performed the prescribed rites—being "indebted by three debts"—should practice the state of renunciation of the Vedas as it has been taught. 6.94.
Having renounced all actions and cast off the defects of action, he should dwell happily under the sovereignty of his sons, self-restrained and devoted to the study of the Veda. (6.95)

He should renounce. Having abandoned all ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* and so forth, and performing them through the power of knowledge in the manner described by such passages as "other Brahmins [attain liberation] by knowledge alone," he should, by means of renunciation itself, destroy the accumulated sins that were previously committed unconsciously—as will be stated in the following verse. Having thus formed his resolve, he should dwell happily, studying the Veda both in its textual form and its meaning, supported by his son who provides him with food, clothing, and shelter through the prosperity belonging to the son. 6.95.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from desire, he destroys sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal. (6.96)

"Thus": according to the principle stated thus, having abandoned ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* and making the knowledge of the Self his primary duty, he becomes free from desire; by means of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), he removes the unperceived evil that has arisen, and upon attaining knowledge, he reaches the world of Brahman or liberation. 6.96.
This fourfold dharma of the Brahmin, which is meritorious and yields inexhaustible fruit after death, has been declared to you; now learn the dharma of kings.

"This" refers to this fourfold dharma pertaining to the Brāhmaṇas—consisting of the stages of the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the renunciant—which has been declared to you as meritorious because it is a cause of merit, and as having imperishable fruit in the next world because its result is the world of Brahmā and final liberation (*apavarga*). Furthermore, from this mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" and from the Vedic text stating, "A Brāhmaṇa should renounce his home," it is determined that the qualification for renunciation belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone, and not to the twice-born in general. Now, listen to the dharma pertaining to the Kṣatriya. (6.97)
Thus ends the sixth chapter on the duties of ascetics in this commentary on Manu, composed by Govindarāja, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mādhava.
The Seventh Chapter:
On the Duties of Kings. I shall proclaim how a king should conduct himself, how his origin came about, and how he may attain supreme success. 7.1.

Regarding "the duties of kings": I shall explain how a ruler ought to conduct himself, having observed those actions that bear fruit both in this world and the next; likewise, I shall describe the manner of a king’s origin and how he may achieve the excellence of attaining results in both the visible and invisible realms. 7.1.
A Kṣatriya who has received the Vedic consecration according to the rule must provide protection for all this [world] in accordance with justice. (7.2)

Regarding the term "brahmic": Having undergone the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) according to the scriptures—from the initiation (*upanayana*) for the purpose of mastering the Vedas up to the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)—the Kṣatriya must, as a rule, protect this entire world without transgressing the boundaries of the scriptures. Even though [protection] may serve as his means of livelihood (*vṛtti*), protection is taught as having an unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) as well, in accordance with the statement: "Austerity is the protection of the Kṣatriya.
For when this world was without a king and everyone fled in fear from every side, the Lord created a king for the protection of all this. (7.3)

Regarding the phrase "without a king": because in this world, which was previously without a king, all things were trembling on every side out of fear, Hiraṇyagarbha created a king for the sake of protecting this world; therefore, protection must be performed by him. 7.3.
Having extracted the eternal portions from Indra, Anila, Yama, Arka, Agni, Varuṇa, Candra, and Vitteśa, [he created Brahmā]. (7.4)

He explains how he created him: "Of Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka. Having extracted the essential portions—the constituent parts—belonging to Indra, Vāyu, Yama, Āditya, Agni, Varuṇa, Candra, and Vaiśravaṇa, he created the king. (7.4)
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods, he therefore overcomes all beings with his splendor. (7.5)
Regarding the phrase "because": since the king was fashioned from portions belonging to those lords of the quarters, Indra and the others, therefore he surpasses living beings in prowess. (7.5)
Like the sun, he scorches both eyes and minds;
no one at all on earth is able even to look upon him. (7.6)

"He scorches": this king, by his own prowess, heats both eyes and minds of those who behold him like the sun; yet, due to his possession of such extraordinary valor, no one on earth is able to look directly at this king. This is for the purpose of stating that he is born from a portion of a portion of Indra. (7.6)
By his power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma; he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra. || 7.7 ||

"He" refers to what will be stated later, such as "one endowed with majesty is radiant. Because he performs activities equal to those of the sun, through his possession of supramundane power, the king becomes equal to Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Candra, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, Varuṇa, and Indra in those actions. (7.7)
A king must not be despised even if he is a child, for thinking "he is merely a human being";
for he is a great deity dwelling in human form. (7.8)

"Even a child": even a king, though a child, is not to be despised with the notion that he is merely a human being; because, due to his origin from a portion of a god, he is a great deity dwelling in human form. (7.8)
Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the king’s fire, like the fire of destruction, consumes the entire family along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.

"Only one": ordinary fire burns only a single person who approaches it without precaution; but the king’s fire destroys not only the offender but also his entire circle of kinsmen along with their herds and wealth. Therefore, this [king] must not be disregarded, for he is destructive like the king’s fire; nor should he be comforted by the display of excessive affection, because— || 7.9 ||
Having truly considered the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.

Regarding the task at hand: having deliberated upon the purpose and having properly considered his own power, as well as the place and time, that king—acting appropriately for the sake of affection or enmity and for the fulfillment of the prescriptions of the treatises—constantly assumes various diverse forms according to whether he is dealing with a friend, an enemy, or a neutral party. (7.10)
In whose favor dwells the lotus-goddess Śrī, in whose prowess lies victory,
and in whose anger resides death— for he is composed of all splendor.

Regarding the phrase "of whom": because he arises from portions of Agni and the other deities, he is endowed with all the splendors of Agni and the rest; therefore, when he is in a state of clarity, great prosperity (*śrī*) dwells within him. Thus, one who desires prosperity should worship him at that time, for he is then possessed of heroic power (*vīrya*). || 7.11 ||
But whoever hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind quickly upon that person's destruction. (7.12)
