"Towards him"—that is, disregarding the instruction as it was given, because he repeatedly exerts himself, one should not hate him, nor [hate] that by which there is a failure regarding the goal. But another person, when being hated, might perhaps endure it through the power of examining the Dharma; however, for a king who endures [such hatred], there is an independent contradiction [to his authority], since he is unable to carry out punishment. Therefore, he should always be followed by virtuous people free from afflictions. (7.12)

Therefore, that lord of men should determine what is right for those he holds dear; and as for what is wrong for those he holds unloved, he should not deviate from that principle of righteousness. (7.13)

Since this is so, therefore, O lord of men, one should apply the Dharma toward those who are dear. Thus, a ruler of men should determine that toward those who are beloved, he must act in accordance with the established order—even if it involves worldly matters—that is not contrary to the scriptures. Likewise, even toward those who are unpleasant, he should not transgress the established order regarding such things as their expulsion, provided it is not contrary to the scriptures. (7.13)
For its sake, the Lord first created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.

"For that purpose" means for the sake of accomplishing the king's objective of protecting his subjects, and as the protector of all living beings through protection from the disturbances of thieves and the like; because of the proper execution of duties, Prajāpati first created the *daṇḍa* (the rod of punishment)—which is produced from the body of the King and fashioned from the *tejas* (fiery energy) of Brahman—since kingship is impossible without it. (7.14)
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, provide for his enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties.

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): since it has been stated that even stationary beings possess consciousness in the passage, “These possess internal consciousness,” even stationary entities such as trees, out of fear of being cut down or punished, act for the sake of enjoyment by means of fruits, flowers, and so forth; they do not overstep the fixed order of providing flowers and the like at their appointed times—how much more so, then, for mobile beings? (7.16)
Having truly considered the place, the time, the power, and the knowledge [of those involved],
he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly.

"Therefore, that" means: having carefully considered the place and time of the punishment, as well as the capacity of the offender's body and wealth—such as his Vedic study and so forth—taking into account whether the offense was committed by a person from a village or a forest, during the day or at night, and so on, the king should inflict upon men who have acted unjustly a punishment corresponding to their crime. This refers to the ministers and other officials acting as judges, because it will be stated later [in 8.126]: "having fully understood the consequences. || 7.16 ||
That king is the man who wields the rod; he is the leader and the punisher.
He is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.

"He" refers to the one who is the cause of punishment (*daṇḍa-hetu*). Because of that [cause], he is the very person who commits the offense; by this same logic, he is the leader, the commander of the army and so forth; he is the instructor, the magistrate charged with dharma, the king’s deputy; and he is remembered as being like a guarantor for the performance of dharma in all four stages of life (*āśrama*), such as studentship (*brahmacarya*), because he causes them to be practiced. (7.17)
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be Dharma itself. (7.18)

Since this is so, therefore it is called "the rod" (*daṇḍa*). It is only through fear of the rod that the commands of kings and others are carried out by the subjects. Thus, it is established that the rod alone is what must be applied to all subjects in their duties. Neither the king nor the scripture [is the primary agent]; rather, the rod alone protects the virtuous from the wicked. Even when other protectors are asleep, the rod alone remains awake; for it is only through fear of it that thieves and the like do not act. Because the practice of righteousness (*dharma*) occurs only through fear of temporal and otherworldly punishment, those who speak of righteousness consider the rod itself to be righteousness. (7.18)
When properly supported after due deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when applied without due deliberation, he destroys them on every side. (7.19)

"Having deliberated": that punishment, when properly applied after considering the place, time, and other factors, and being executed with the complete abandonment of greed and the like, makes all subjects full of affection. However, if it is applied without such deliberation, it destroys the perpetrator in both visible and invisible ways. (7.19)
If the king did not tirelessly inflict punishment upon those deserving of it, the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit. (7.20)

"If"—that is to say, if the king, having become indolent, were not to inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment, then, just as fish on a spit are roasted by fearless hunters such as Niṣādas, so too would those possessed of superior strength roast the weak. (7.21)
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake, and a dog might lick the oblation; there would be no ownership over anything, and the low would prevail over the high. (7.21)

"He would eat": if there were no punishment, then even an utterly base crow would eat the sacrificial oblation called *puroḍāśa* offered to the gods; likewise, even a most lowly dog would lick the sacrificial offering such as barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), and ownership over anything would not belong to anyone. Furthermore, the inversion of superiority and inferiority among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others would prevail.
The whole world is kept in check by punishment, for a pure man is hard to find;
indeed, through fear of punishment, the entire world is fit for enjoyment.

"Everyone": some person or other in the world is established on the path of righteousness by means of punishment; therefore, a man who is pure by nature is found with great difficulty. Likewise, this entire world proceeds toward necessary acts of service out of fear of punishment.
Even gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when they are oppressed by punishment alone. (7.23)

"Gods, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas. The gods and so forth are the categories mentioned in the first chapter; and the winged creatures (pataṅgas), birds, and serpents (uragas)—those too, being tormented by fear related to the Lord who is the cause of the instruction on the origin of the entire world, do not perform the service of bestowing rain and so forth. Thus says the *Adhvaryava* Śruti:
"Out of fear of him the fire burns; out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra, Vāyu, and Death run as the fifth. (7.23)
All social classes would become corrupt, all moral boundaries would be shattered, and there would be universal upheaval in the world through the failure of punishment. (7.24)

"Lest they should become corrupted": because of the failure to inflict punishment or its infliction through injustice, all the social classes (*varṇas*), beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, would become intermingled by sexual intercourse with one another's women; and all the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the boundaries established by the scriptures, would perish. In this way, the [injunction] beginning with "the fire is to be maintained" proceeds for the sake of mutual assistance. (7.24)
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punisher stalks about, destroying evil, there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly. (7.25)

Regarding the phrase "wherein": in that kingdom where the rod of punishment—dark-complexioned and red-eyed, appearing thus as the presiding deity whose authority is derived from the scriptures, and which destroys evildoers—pervades, there the subjects do not become agitated, provided that the king or whoever administers the rod of punishment deliberates correctly. (7.25)

They say that the king who is a speaker of truth, who acts with due deliberation, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who should be appointed as its administrator. (7.26)

Regarding the phrase "of him they say": Manu and others have declared that the one who is the author of that rod [of punishment] is a Kṣatriya endowed with consecration and other [qualifications], who speaks according to what he has perceived, who acts with deliberation, who is capable of reasoning and refutation, who is possessed of wisdom, and who is skilled in the mutual application of dharma, artha, and kāma. (7.26)
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
but one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by that very punishment.

"Regarding that": by administering that punishment correctly, a king prospers in virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*). However, a king who is dominated by passion, prone to anger, deceitful, or hateful, perishes—either through excessive wrath or through unrighteousness—even when he has administered punishment correctly. (7.27)
For punishment is a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.

Regarding the term *daṇḍa*: that which is that very great splendor (*tejas*) is the rod (*daṇḍa*). Because it is naturally devoid of discipline, it is difficult for those who act unjustly to wield; it utterly destroys even a king, together with his sons and kinsmen. (7.28)
Then he would afflict the fortress, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately after the destruction of the king along with his kinsmen, that army would afflict the country—consisting of desert forts and other such strongholds—as well as the realm, the earthly world including all moving and stationary beings, and the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), because they subsist on what is offered from here. (7.29)
Thus, he could not be led by right means by that companion who was foolish, greedy, of unformed intellect, and attached to sensual pleasures. (7.30)

"By one who is without allies and is foolish": that punishment cannot be administered according to the standards of the treatises by a king who is devoid of allies such as ministers, who is foolish, greedy, lacking the refinement of scriptural training (or, being devoid of scriptural refinement, having an untrained intellect), and who is addicted to the objects of sense-pleasure such as gambling. (7.30)
Punishment can be administered by one who is pure, true to his word, acting in accordance with the scriptures, possessed of good assistants, and wise. (7.31)

"By one who is pure," etc. By a king who is endowed with purity regarding wealth and other matters, who has conquered his senses, who is true to his promise, who acts without transgressing the scriptures, and who is possessed of wisdom—thus, by a king endowed with these qualities which serve as the antidotes to the previously mentioned defects, punishment can be properly administered. (7.31)
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies, straightforward with friends, and full of forbearance toward Brahmins. (7.32)

"In one's own kingdom, one should act with justice": he should conduct himself within his own realm according to the boundaries of the scriptures. Furthermore, toward the territory of the enemy, he should be severe in punishment. Toward affectionate friends and allies acting for his sake, he should be straightforward. And toward Brahmins who have intentionally committed minor offenses, he should be endowed with forgiveness. (7.32)
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water.
"Thus it is. Thus, even though King Ācāra’s treasury was exhausted, his fame spread throughout the world like the spreading of drops of oil upon water. (7.33)
Let it be so for the king who acts perversely and has not conquered his own self;
his fame is diminished in the world like a drop of clarified butter upon water.
"Therefore" means: from conduct contrary to this [proper] conduct, the reputation of a king who has conquered his senses shrinks away like a drop of ghee in water. (7.34)
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, each established in their respective duties according to their order. (7.35)

"Each his own"—thus [the Lord] spoke for the purpose of what was to follow. By Brahmā, a king was created as the protector of all the social classes (*varṇas*), beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who are devoted to their respective duties (*svadharma*) in due order, as well as of the stages of life (*āśramas*), beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*). (7.35)
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his retinue,
all that I shall declare to you correctly and in due order.
"By that," [he means]: "I shall relate to you in due order everything that was to be done by that king while protecting his subjects, together with his ministers. (7.36)
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon the Brahmins—those learned men who are advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas—and he should abide by their instruction. (7.37)

"Brāhmaṇas": rising every morning day after day, he should serve learned Brāhmaṇas—who have mastered the meaning of the texts of the three branches of knowledge known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma, and who are experts in the sciences of logic (*vīkṣikī*) and statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*) to be described below—and he should carry out their instructions. (7.37)
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the aged is honored even by the Rākṣasas. (7.38)

Regarding the word "elders": he should constantly serve those Brahmins who are advanced in age, pure in their knowledge of the Vedas and their meaning, and so forth, for the purpose of generating trustworthiness. For he who serves the elderly is honored even by Rākṣasas who are utterly distrustful; he becomes trustworthy even to them, let alone to human beings. (7.38)
From them, even one who is already self-disciplined should constantly learn the principles of discipline;
for a king who is self-disciplined never comes to ruin. (7.39)

"From them": even if he is already highly disciplined due to his mastery of the sciences that are difficult to master, or by virtue of innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*), nevertheless, for the sake of excellence, he should constantly learn the path of policy (*nīti-mārga*) from those Brahmins; for a king who prioritizes policy shall never perish. (7.39)
"Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those living in the forest have obtained kingdoms through discipline. (7.40)

"Many," it is said: many kings, though possessed of the concealments of elephants, horses, treasuries, and so forth, have perished due to lack of discipline; others, however, living in the forest without such retinues, have obtained kingdoms through discipline. (7.40)
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (7.41)
And so it was with Vena; both Vena and Nahuṣa, as well as Nimi—the son of Pijavana and Sudāsa—were ruined through their lack of discipline. (7.41)
Through discipline, Pṛthu obtained his kingdom, as did Manu;
Kubera attained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi attained the status of a Brahmin.

"Pṛthu," it is said; Pṛthu and Anu obtained their kingdoms through discipline. Vaiśravaṇa, too, attained wealth and sovereignty while possessing discipline. And Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, though being a Kṣatriya, attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa—so difficult to reach—through his body alone by means of the practice of discipline. Therefore, one should acquire discipline from the elders. (7.42)

From those learned in the three Vedas, he learned the triple knowledge, the eternal science of government, the science of inquiry, the science of the self, and the methods for undertaking economic pursuits from the world.

"From those learned in the three Vedas": from those who have studied the triad of sciences known as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, he should study the triple science (*trayī-vidyā*) consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, but he should not teach it himself. Since the king’s authority over the kingdom belongs to one who has returned home from his teacher (the *samāvṛtta*), he should acquire it only in the fourth stage of life (*turīyāvasthā*). Furthermore, he should learn the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*)—the treatise on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*)—which is eternal, having come down through an unbroken tradition since time immemorial, and which is useful for the acquisition and preservation of wealth, from those very same persons. Likewise, he should learn the science of logic (*tarka-vidyā*) and the spiritual sciences such as Sāṃkhya, which are useful for diplomatic correspondence with foreign realms and for the composition of official dispatches, and which prevent the arising of joy or despondency during times of prosperity or calamity. Similarly, a Kṣatriya should learn from the world—that is, from farmers and others like them—the various occupations (*vārtā*) such as agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing, as well as the undertakings and activities based upon them that serve as the means for the accumulation of wealth. || 7.43 ||
One should practice the discipline of mastering the senses day and night;
for one who has conquered the senses is able to keep the subjects under control. (7.44)

Regarding the phrase "of the senses": one should constantly apply effort toward the withdrawal of the power of the objects of the senses, such as the eye and so forth. He who has conquered his senses is able to bring subjects under his control. (7.44)
One should diligently avoid these ten calamities arising from desire, as well as the eight born of anger, which have miserable endings. (7.45)

"Ten" refers to the ten types of amorous gestures (*kāmodbhava*) that will be described as constant manifestations; one should diligently avoid the eight types born of anger (*krodhaja*), which end in suffering. (7.45)
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived even of his own self.
A lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of anger is deprived of his very self. (7.46)
Hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and music], and idle wandering—this is the tenfold group born of desire. (7.47)

"Hunting" refers to all activities for the sake of sport, such as killing deer or playing with dice; furthermore, daytime sleep, speaking of the faults of others, women, intoxication caused by drinking liquor, the triad of musical instruments—namely dancing, singing, and instrumental music—and following after [women] without cause: this group of ten vices arises from specific desires. (7.47)
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault with others' merits, and the corruption of wealth, along with verbal and physical harshness—this is the eightfold group born of anger. (7.48)

"Slander" means the disclosure of faults that have not been recognized. "Violence" is the infliction of base treatment upon a virtuous person or their imprisonment. "Malice" is killing by means of deceit. "Envy" is the inability to endure another's equality with oneself in qualities. "Rancor" is the intolerance of praise for another's virtues. "Destruction of property" is the non-payment or the seizure of wealth that has been obtained. "Harshness of speech" refers to abuse and the like. "Harshness of punishment" refers to beating and the like. Thus, this group of eight vices arises from anger. (7.48)
One should strive to conquer that greed which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these two groups arise from it.

"Of the two": all authors of treatises on the compendium of mindfulness consider greed (*lobha*) to be the cause of both these categories—the group of sensual vices and the group of higher-world vices. One should therefore strive to avoid that greed, because this pair of groups arises from it; for greed is the root of all, since activity [in these realms] proceeds either from a desire for wealth or from a craving for bodily pleasure. (7.49)
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—in this sequence, one should know this tetrad to be the most grievous among the group of vices born of desire. (7.50)

Regarding "drinking": one should understand that this group of vices associated with desire—drinking to the point of intoxication, gambling, sexual indulgence, and hunting—which are listed in this sequence, constitutes a quartet among the vices dependent on honey-wine that is an extreme cause of suffering, because it is the cause of the greatest amount of suffering. (7.50)
One should know that these three—inflicting punishment, verbal abuse, and the embezzlement of wealth—are always difficult to overcome, even within the group born of anger. (7.51)

Regarding the phrase "of punishment": one should always recognize the cause of harm within the triad consisting of verbal abuse, physical assault, and the spoiling of property—which belongs among the vices born of anger—whenever there is an abundance of fault. (7.51)
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices, which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the next. (7.52)

"Of this group of seven": a person of refined character should understand that among this entire collection of vices—consisting of drinking, inflicting punishment, and so forth, arising from desire and anger, numbering seven in total, and generally prevalent throughout the whole circle of kings—whichever vice was mentioned earlier is more wicked than the one following it. Drinking is more wicked than gambling; for while the faults mentioned in the treatises on statecraft (nītiśāstra), such as the loss of consciousness and the like, apply there, in gambling there is also the possibility of gaining wealth. Gambling is more wicked than addiction to women; for while the faults mentioned in the treatises on statecraft, such as enmity and the like, apply there, in addiction to women there is also the occurrence of the merit of producing offspring and forming virtuous alliances. Furthermore, in hunting, there is even the acquisition of merit through physical exercise and the like. Thus, within the four vices born of desire, each preceding one is more evil. Among those born of anger as well, physical assault is more wicked than verbal abuse, because [the latter] can be remedied by gifts and honors, whereas physical assault involving the amputation of limbs and so forth cannot be easily countered. Verbal abuse is more wicked than the misappropriation of wealth, because the burning pain caused by cutting to the quick and insults is difficult to endure; however, the misappropriation of wealth can be rectified by the giving of even greater wealth. Thus, within the triad of vices born of anger as well, each preceding one is more evil. Therefore, one should avoid whichever vice is more wicked—that is, the more harmful addiction. (7.52)
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
the man of calamity sinks lower and lower, while the man free from calamity goes to heaven when he dies. (7.53)

Regarding the phrase "of vice" (*vyasanasya*): between death and vice, vice is the more wicked, because as long as a person addicted to vice lives—even for a very long time—he falls into a deeper hell due to his increasing transgression of the meaning of the scriptures. On the other hand, one free from vice, upon dying, goes to heaven by virtue of his practice of the scriptures. (7.53)
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested. (7.54)

"Hereditary" (maulān) means those who have descended through a lineage beginning with his father; he should appoint seven or eight ministers as assistants for counsel and other matters—men who, out of excessive affection, are non-deviant; who know the scriptures concerning visible and invisible goals, so that they do not transgress the bounds of the seen and the unseen; who are valiant, so that they may perform the duties of a master regardless of their own bodies; who have again performed royal service, so that there is no confusion regarding the successful completion of tasks; who are of noble birth, so that they remain non-deviant due to their sense of family pride; and who have been tested through the employment of spies and other means regarding the domains of dharma, artha, and kāma, and are thus proven pure. || 7.54 ||
Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so the highly exalted sovereignty, especially when undertaken without assistance? (7.55)

"Because even [of that which is difficult]" means: how much more so, then, a kingdom of great prosperity without an assistant? Whatever action can be performed, even that becomes difficult for one person alone to accomplish; especially so a kingdom, which yields great fruit—how could that be performed by one without assistance? (7.55)
Together with them, he should constantly deliberate upon common matters: peace and war, stability, acquisition, security, and the consolidation of what has been gained. (7.56)

"By them": he should deliberate together with those ministers on all matters that are always highly secret, such as peace and war which will be discussed hereafter. Likewise, he should consider "sthāna"—that by which one stands; this refers to the army (*daṇḍa*), the treasury (*kośa*), the city (*pura*), and the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). Among these, the army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and its maintenance and so forth must be considered. The treasury is the accumulation of wealth, and its expenditure and so forth must be considered. Regarding the city, the author will state that it should be "well-supplied with weapons. As for the kingdom, it is the country; one must consider whether its inhabitants, livestock, and other resources are capable of enduring hardship. Likewise, "samudaya" means that from which wealth arises; he should consider the sources of grain, gold, and so forth, such as agriculture. He should attend to "gupti," or protection, both pertaining to himself—he should eat food that has been thoroughly inspected—as the author will state in the verse beginning with "And women who have been tested" (7.219); and that pertaining to the kingdom, as he will declare in the verse beginning with "Constantly in the administration of the kingdom" (7.212); and the measures for pacifying what has been acquired, as he will say in the verse beginning with "Having conquered, he should worship the gods" (7.201). (7.56)
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions,
he should act for his own benefit in matters concerning all of them collectively.

Regarding the phrase "of them": having ascertained the individual opinions of those ministers on matters of state through their more frequent private deliberations, and having understood the collective intention of all of them simultaneously due to their proficiency in assemblies, he should do that which is beneficial to himself. (7.57)
But with a distinguished, wise Brāhmaṇa,
the king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel endowed with the sixfold policy.

"Of all these": from among all these very ones, with whichever one is most distinguished by excellence, being an exceedingly learned Brāhmaṇa, the king should deliberate upon the excellent counsel—consisting of peace, war, and so forth, endowed with the six qualities to be described hereafter. (7.58)
Always placing full confidence in him, one should entrust all affairs to him;
having reached a decision together with him, one should then commence the work. (7.59)

"Always": having become completely free from doubt and having gained full confidence in that Brāhmaṇa, one should always entrust all tasks to him. Even if one performs them oneself, one should do so only after reaching a decision together with him and then carry it out. (7.59)
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, stable, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.

"Others" means that he should also appoint other servants who are pure in their motives and so forth, wise, and whose integrity regarding wealth and other matters has been tested through their conduct as stable attendants and the like; who are habituated to properly generating revenue from the various sources, and who have already attained wealth [through such service].
He should appoint as many diligent, capable, and discerning men as are required for his duties. (7.61)
"Let it cease": he should appoint as many diligent and clever men, knowledgeable in those duties, as are required to accomplish the multitude of tasks that must be performed by this king. (7.61)

He should employ them according to their aptitude: the brave, the skillful, and those of noble birth at the mines and in industrial works; the pure in the management of the interior of the palace; and the timid within the inner apartments.

"Of them": among those, he should employ the brave ones in the treasury; at the mines where gold and other minerals are produced, and at places such as the presses for sugarcane and grain, he should appoint those endowed with integrity regarding wealth. And within the inner apartments, such as the dining hall and the harem, he should employ the timid. (7.62)
And he should appoint as his envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures, who understands gestures, facial expressions, and conduct, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth. (7.63)

Regarding the envoy: he should appoint as an envoy one who has mastered the meaning of the treatises concerning both visible and invisible matters, who understands the specific verbal and physical activities that indicate intention, as well as bodily distortions and gestures—such as those involving armor, weapons, or food—that reveal intent; and who is endowed with integrity, purity, and other such virtues, and is of noble birth. (7.63)
Devoted, pure, skillful, mindful, and knowing place and time; handsome, fearless, and eloquent—a messenger such as this is praised by kings. (7.64)

Because he is "devoted" (anurakta): one who possesses devotion; who is clever for the purpose of avoiding matters that are entangled with wealth, women, or impurity; who remembers [his instructions] so as not to transgress the four [proper] times; who knows place and time for the purpose of conveying the entire message; who is eloquent for the purpose of acting appropriately; who is of pleasing appearance and whose speech is persuasive for the sake of the truth of the matter; who speaks in refined and varied language for the purpose of communicating the king's message to other men; and who possesses the skill for dialogue and retort—it is such a messenger as this that a king highly desires. (7.64)
Punishment depends upon the minister; the administration of discipline depends upon punishment; the treasury and the kingdom depend upon the king; and peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy.

Regarding the minister (*amātya*): the army (*daṇḍa*), consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, is dependent upon the commander-in-chief; its increase depends on his will, and the application of policy (*nīti*) toward that army of elephants and so forth is also dependent upon him, for in his absence there is an absence of policy. Furthermore, the treasury (*artha*) and the fort (*gāra*) are dependent upon the king, because their growth or decline arises through his will. Finally, peace and war (*saṃdhivigraha*) are dependent upon the envoy (*dūta*), because they proceed according to his will. (7.65)
For it is the messenger alone who unites those who are divided and indeed breaks apart those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are divided. (7.66)

Regarding the word "messenger" (*dūta*): a messenger performs that action by which men are divided. Since it is the messenger alone who is capable of establishing peace among those who are divided, as well as causing dissension among those who are united, and since he operates in a foreign kingdom in such a way that the united are split apart, [the author] states this for the purpose of defining that peace and its opposite depend upon the messenger. (7.66)
He should discern, through secret gestures and movements during his duties, the master's facial expression, his inner intent, his conduct, and what he desires to accomplish among his servants. (7.67)

"He should know" means that the charioteer (sūta) should recognize, through his own unmanifest facial expressions and gestures, the outward signs of another king—such as the expansion or pallor of the face—which indicate joy or dejection; he should recognize the physical movements consisting of twitching, perspiration, trembling, and horripilation that signal the intent regarding the fivefold policy of peace and war; and he should recognize the actions of preparing vehicles and weapons or remaining indifferent, which indicate resolve. Furthermore, he should know when a desired objective has not been neglected, and among the tasks at hand, he should effect the gathering of those servants who are angry, greedy, fearful, or insulted. (7.67)
Having understood in its true essence everything intended by the enemy king,
one should apply such effort as will not cause oneself to suffer.

"Having understood" means: having known in its ultimate sense the entire desired harm pertaining to another king, the messenger should strive in such a way that his own destruction does not occur through the destruction of his master. (7.68)

One should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and providing a means of livelihood. (7.69)
"Jāṅgala is abundant in crops, inhabited mostly by Āryas, and free from disturbances.
That region which has little water and grass, is windy, and has much sunshine, should be known as Jāṅgala.

Thus, the king should establish his residence by taking recourse to such a region—one abundant in grain and other resources, populated by many righteous people, untroubled by diseases, gadflies, and other afflictions, endowed with orchards, flowers, gardens, and the like, inhabited by forest-dwellers and neighboring chieftains, and easily accessible for the livelihood of farmers and others. (7.69)
Having taken refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, a forest fort, a human fort, or a mountain fort, he should dwell in a city. (7.70)

Regarding the "fortress of the desert" (*dhanvadurga*): a desert fortress is one surrounded on all sides by a waterless wasteland extending for five *yojanas*. The "earth fortress" (*mahīdurga*) is a solid rampart equipped with a defensive wall (*vaprāpanihita*), twelve *hasta* high and twice its width, topped with windows and other structures for the purpose of combat. The "water fortress" (*ambudurga*) is surrounded on the outside by deep, unfathomable water that cannot be crossed. The "tree fortress" (*vṛkṣadurga*) extends for a *yojana* all around the exterior and is filled with dense, massive trees. The "human fortress" (*manuṣyadurga*) is provided on all sides with stationed elephants, horses, and infantry, as well as men skilled in weaponry. The "mountain fortress" (*giridurga*) is a mountain ridge that is extremely difficult to ascend or is accessible only via very narrow paths, and is supplied with water from internal rivers and springs. Having taken refuge in any one of these fortresses, one should build the city. (7.70)
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for, by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress excels all others.

"But with every effort" means that since, among these types of fortresses, the mountain fortress (giridurga) is praised for its abundance of qualities, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress with all possible effort. (7.71)
Of these, the first three are inhabited respectively by wild beasts, by those dwelling in pits, and by apsarases; the latter three are inhabited respectively by monkeys, humans, and gods. (7.72)

The first three among these [forts] were formerly inhabited by wild animals, pits, and trees; the middle three, consisting of earth, water, and mountain forts, were inhabited by wild animals and the like. Among them, the earth fort was inhabited by wild animals; the pit fort by mongooses and others who live in holes; the water fort by aquatic creatures such as tortoises; and the final three—tree, man, and mountain forts—were inhabited respectively by monkeys, humans, and gods. Among those, the tree fort was inhabited by monkeys; the man fort by humans; and the mountain fort by the gods. (7.72)
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a stronghold, so too do foes not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress. (7.73)

"Yathā" means: just as hunters and others do not harm these deer and other animals dwelling in difficult terrain because they lack the power [to do so], even so, enemies do not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress. 7.73.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is established. (7.74)

Regarding the word "one": because a single archer standing upon a rampart is able to fight a hundred enemies belonging to the opposing side, for that reason the construction of a fortress is taught as something that ought to be done. (7.74)
That city shall be well-provided with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
with Brahmins, artisans, and machines; and with fodder and water. (7.75)
Therefore: That fort should be made abundant in weapons such as swords, wealth, grain, mounts such as horses, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, artisans, machines, fodder, and water. (7.75)
In the center of that [site], he should have his own house constructed—spacious, well-protected, beautiful in all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees. (7.76)

Regarding the phrase "of that": in the center of that fortress, he should have a house built for himself—one that is well-proportioned and spacious, equipped with separate halls for weapons and other necessities, protected by ramparts and moats, suitable for all seasons through its provision of fruits, flowers, and the like, whitewashed with lime, supplied with long ponds and water, and surrounded by trees. (7.76)
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks, born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue. (7.77)

"Regarding that": having established himself in that house, he should marry a wife of the same caste, endowed with auspicious marks such as fine lines and *tilakas*, born of a noble family, beautiful, well-proportioned, and perfected in conduct and other virtues. (7.77)
He should appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests; they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires. (7.78)

Regarding the domestic priest: he should appoint a domestic priest who is knowledgeable in the Atharva-veda rites, and he should select officiating priests according to the procedure prescribed by the authors of the Sūtras. They, in turn, shall perform for this king the domestic and Śrauta rituals as they have been taught. 7.78.
The king should sacrifice with various kinds of rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the brahmins. (7.79)

"He shall sacrifice": he should perform various kinds of sacrifices, such as the Aśvamedha and Puṇḍarīka, accompanied by sufficient sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). For the sake of dharma, he should give to Brāhmaṇas his own enjoyments, such as houses and beds, as well as wealth such as gold; this is stated as the additional duty of giving and sacrificing that must necessarily be performed by the king. (7.79)
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy men;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects as toward his own father.

"Annual": from the kingdom, he should cause to be brought the annual supply of grain and other goods to be described hereafter, by means of trustworthy ministers who act for his benefit and possess the qualities already mentioned. Furthermore, he should be preeminent in the application of the treatises regarding taxes, duties, and so forth in the world, and he should behave toward the subjects like a father, through affection and similar sentiments. (7.80)
He should appoint various learned supervisors in each respective place;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men as they carry out their work.

"Regarding the supervisors": he should oversee their duties while they are performing the tasks of men. In various places—such as the stables for elephants and horses, armories, and treasuries—he should appoint various learned officials who are skilled in those respective works, assigning them individually. Furthermore, in those places such as the stables for elephants and horses where no negligence occurs, he should oversee all the affairs of the men performing the work appropriate to those locations, so that every task is properly executed. (7.81)
He should be a worshiper of those brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house;
for this is declared to be the imperishable brahminical treasure of kings. (7.82)

"Of those who have returned": this imperishable treasure of the Brahmanas is ordained for kings. Since he must invariably perform worship by the gift of wealth to the Brahmanas who have completed their residence in the teacher's household, this is taught in the scripture as a "treasure"—like a hoard—deposited among the Brahmanas; whereas other treasures consisting of wealth and the like are perishable for kings. That which is called a Brahmana remains well-deposited even in another birth. (7.82)
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brahmins. (7.83)

"No," [it is said]. Neither thieves nor enemies carry off that treasure of Brahman. Unlike other treasures, it does not perish through contact with the earth or similar causes. Therefore, this imperishable treasure called "Brahman" should be deposited by the king among the Brāhmaṇas for the sake of attaining the highest ultimate fruit in another birth, just as wealth and other assets are deposited. (7.83)
It does not overflow, it does not fall away, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices. (7.84)

"It does not spill" means that, it is said, the oblations of the *agnihotra* and other rites suffer from defects such as leaking, spilling, or destruction; consequently, there is a deficiency in the ritual efficacy (*karmavaiguṇya*). However, what is offered here into the fire of the Brāhmaṇa’s mouth—that which is given to a Brāhmaṇa—does not leak, does not spill, nor is it ever destroyed by burning or other such means. Therefore, because these defects are impossible here, this is superior to the *agnihotra* and other rites; this statement is intended as praise for the gift under discussion. (7.84)
A gift given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa yields equal merit; to one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa, it yields double;
to a teacher, a hundred-thousandfold; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it is infinite. (7.85)

"Equal" means: [the fruit is] a thousandfold for a teacher, and infinite for one who has mastered the Vedas. Regarding the case of those other than Brāhmaṇas, since there is no formal giving or receiving of gifts in the form of providing assistance, it is understood that the fruit of whatever gift is heard to have is not superior to that [act of assistance]. Thus, for a Brāhmaṇa who lives by his caste alone, the fruit is double compared to the former; for one engaged in the study of the Vedas, the fruit is a hundred-thousandfold; and for one who studies all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*), the fruit is infinite. (7.85)
Indeed, depending especially on the recipient and by virtue of one's own faith, one enjoys the fruit of a gift—whether small or great—after death. (7.86)

Indeed, depending on the excellence of the recipient, as well as the degree of one's faith, whether small or great, the fruit of giving is obtained after death. Having regard for the gradations of worthiness—such as being endowed with study, specialized knowledge, and austerity—and the gradations of faith, the fruit of giving, whether small or great, is attained in the other world. (7.86)
When challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, a king protecting his subjects must not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya. (7.87)

"By those who are equal, superior, or inferior": when summoned for battle by kings of equal, greater, or lesser strength, one who is intent on protecting the subjects and who regards the duty of a Kṣatriya—namely, that "one must certainly fight when summoned"—should not retreat from the fray. (7.87)
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects, and service toward the brahmins—this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings. (7.88)
"Regarding 'in battles'": not turning one's back in wars, protecting the subjects, and serving the Brahmins—this is the preeminent means for kings to attain heaven and other such goals. (7.88)
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another and who fight with their utmost strength, never turning their backs, go to heaven. (7.89)
And so, "in battles": rivaling one another, kings who desire to slay each other in combats, fighting face-to-face with preeminent power, go to heaven. (7.89)
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons, nor with barbed ones, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose tips are blazing with fire. (7.90)

"Not with deceptive weapons" means: not with those having the shape of ears, nor with burnt ones, nor with blades set ablaze by fire. While engaging in battle in combat, even when being struck by enemies with deceptive weapons and the like—such as blades fashioned in the form of ears, or those smeared with poison, or those with blades ignited by fire—he does not strike back. (7.90)
One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in supplication;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

"And not" means: one should not strike a eunuch who has abandoned the battlefield and ascended to high ground, who stands with palms joined in reverence, who sits with disheveled hair, and who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

One must not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another. (7.92)

"Not while asleep": one should not strike those who are asleep—meaning those whose alertness has vanished and who are without armor—nor those who are not wearing their garments, nor spectators of the battle with weapons, nor others who are already engaged in fighting. 7.92.

Remembering the dharma of the virtuous, he did not strike one who was suffering from a weapon-wound, nor one who was distressed, nor one who was severely mangled, nor one who was terrified, nor one who had turned away. (7.93)

"Nor one who has met with the calamity of weapons": remembering the conduct of the virtuous, one should not strike one whose weapon is broken, one whose son or others have been killed, one who is struck by a blow, one who is terrified, or one who has retreated from battle. (7.93)
But he who, being afraid, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies, incurs all whatever misdeed his master has committed. (7.94)

Regarding the verse beginning with *yas tu*: if one who is terrified turns his back in battle and is slain by the enemies, even then he incurs whatever sin belongs to his lord; this much is intended here—that the sin becomes his. Alternatively, it says something else: since there would be the consequence of the absence of sin if the lord were sinless, the expiation for that belongs to the lord alone, and by that he is released from the evil deed. Because of the mention of the "master" (*bhartṛ*), the fault of turning away and so forth applies to the minister as well, not only to the king who is the subject under discussion. (7.94)
Moreover, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter, the master seizes it all from him who is killed while turning back. (7.95)
Regarding the word "yat" (whatever): whatever merit for the sake of the next world has been acquired by this man slain while facing away, all of that belongs to his master. 7.95.
Chariots, horses, elephants, parasols, wealth, grain, livestock, women, all kinds of goods, and base metals—whatever one conquers belongs to him. (7.96)

"Chariots and horses," etc. Chariots, horses, elephants, banners, gold, grain, cattle, and female slaves—these constitute [the spoils]; as well as all base metals such as molasses and salt, and metals such as copper and iron; whatever one seizes after defeating the enemy belongs to that person alone, not to the king. (7.96)
"And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually. (7.97)

And regarding the king: although it is logical that whatever one wins belongs to him, nevertheless, whatever is most excellent therein, the servants should give that to the king. There is Vedic revelation on this point, such as: "Having slain Vṛtra, they extracted the extraction for Mahendra. Furthermore, that which was won without individual distinction must be given by the king to all the warriors. (7.97)
This eternal warrior code has been declared as unadorned;
a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma.
"This" refers to this blameless warrior-dharma handed down through beginningless tradition; therefore, O Kṣatriya, while slaying enemies in battle, you must not abandon this dharma. (7.98)

One should seek to obtain what has not yet been obtained, protect with effort what has been obtained, increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.99)

"Unobtained" means that one should exert effort to win over land, silver, gold, and so forth that have not yet been won; and what has been won, one should protect with effort; and what has been protected, one should cause to increase. In this way, because he possesses great wealth, there will be no humiliation from himself or others. And what has been increased, he should give to worthy recipients (*pātra*). When it is thus, his prosperity in the next world will also come to pass. (7.99)
One should know that this fourfold [duty] is the means for achieving the goals of human life;
one should perform its constant practice correctly and without sloth. (7.100)

"Regarding this": one should understand that the purpose of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) consists of these four types—acquisition, preservation, increase, and distribution. Therefore, one who is not indolent should always exert effort in their performance. (7.100)

One should seek what is not yet obtained by means of force; protect what has been obtained with vigilance; increase what has been protected through growth; and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.101)

"Unobtained" means that one should desire to conquer by means of an army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. What has been conquered should be protected through supervision as prescribed in the treatises. What has been protected should be increased by means of methods for growth, such as land-based trade and so forth. And what has been increased, whatever is in excess, one should give to worthy recipients for the sake of the next world. (7.101)
He should always have his rod of punishment uplifted, always display his manly prowess, always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy. (7.102)

"Constantly": he should be one whose army—consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—is perpetually ready, and who has practiced the art of warfare and other skills with his disciples. And he should be one whose manly prowess (*pauruṣa*) is constantly displayed (*vivṛta*), made manifest through the raising of weapons in regions such as borders and forests, and through the slaughter of armed men. He should be one whose secret deliberations, undertakings, and mobilizations are always kept concealed (*saṃvṛta*), guarded, and restricted. And at all times, he should be intent on searching for the enemy's vulnerabilities by observing their calamities and corrupting their affairs. (7.102)
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds up the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod alone. (7.103)
"Of one whose rod is always raised": because the entire world trembles before one whose rod is always raised, therefore he should bring all beings under control by means of the rod alone. (7.103)
One should always conduct oneself with absolute sincerity and never with deceit; remaining ever well-guarded, one should also recognize the guile employed by the enemy.

Being well-guarded, he should always remain alert for the deceptions employed by his enemies; as long as the enemy employs stratagems such as sowing dissension among his subjects, he should deal with them through stratagem alone, but never initiate a stratagem first. Having clearly defined his own position and protected it, he should constantly observe through spies and other means any stratagem used by the enemy, such as the incitement of discord among his subjects.
An enemy should not discover one's own vulnerability, but one should discover the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own weak point. 7.105.

"Of him not"—he should strive in such a way that the enemy does not discover his vulnerabilities, such as dissension among his constituent elements (*prakṛti*) and so forth; conversely, he himself should diligently seek out the enemy's vulnerabilities, such as dissension among his elements and so forth. Furthermore, like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, he should protect the constituents of the kingdom, beginning with the constituent elements, by means of battle and other measures. And whenever any vulnerability of his own arises, such as dissension among his elements, he should apply diligent effort toward its rectification. (7.105)
One should contemplate one's goals like a crane, exert prowess like a lion, snatch away like a wolf, and flee like a hare. (7.106)

One should contemplate one's goals like a crane, flee like a hare, seize like a wolf, and exert prowess like a lion. Just as a crane, while moving about in difficult terrain, contemplates even its own nature with undistracted and tireless internal focus due to its intent upon seizing fish and meat, so too should one contemplate matters such as the enemy’s kingdom and its connections when the enemy is well-guarded. Just as a hare, even when within the range of a hunter, escapes to another region by means of its extremely swift and zigzagging gait, so too should one who finds himself in the midst of an enemy surrounded by all his vassals—having somehow induced confusion in the enemy—move away from that place to seek refuge with another king of superior quality. And just as a wolf destroys even animals that have been protected, provided they fall into some negligence during the effort to seize them, so too should one, having found some lapse in the enemy despite the latter being stationed in a fortress or similar stronghold, seize him by some means. And just as a lion, through the application of the power of enthusiasm (*utsāha-śakti*), attacks and slays even an elephant shaped like the peak of a great mountain, so too should one, though possessing little strength, attack to destroy the enemy by relying on one's entire force, provided there is no other means such as seeking refuge when overwhelmed by a stronger power. 7.106.
Thus, while he is victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation.

"Thus": in the manner described above, the king who has set out to conquer should bring under his control all those who are adverse to his victory by means of the expedients of conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force. 7.107.
If, however, they do not abide by these through the first three expedients, one should gradually bring them under control by force alone with the rod. (7.108)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if those adversaries do not come under control through the initial means of conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension, then one should bring them under control by force alone—gradually, according to whatever sequence of punishment is appropriate—by means of military force, such as the suppression of the country's borders and so forth. || 7.108 ||
Regarding the four means of policy, conciliation and the others, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom. (7.109)

Regarding the phrase "of conciliation and the others": among the four means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), the wise always consider conciliation (*sāma*) and force (*daṇḍa*) to be praised for the purpose of increasing the kingdom. This is because in the case of conciliation, there is an absence of depletion and expenditure, while in the case of force, there is an excellence of success even when evils such as war arise. (7.109)
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain, so should the king protect his realm and slay those who stand as obstacles. 7.110

Regarding the phrase "just as he weeds": just as one who clears away the weeds from a field destroys the weeds and protects the grain, so too should the king protect those subjects who are well-disposed and destroy those who are hostile. (7.110)
The king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, oppresses his own kingdom, shall soon be deprived both of his realm and his life, along with his kinsmen. (7.111)

"Out of delusion": that king who, through a lack of discrimination between what is beneficial and harmful, oppresses his subjects, quickly perishes from his kingdom and from life, along with his kinsmen, due to the loss of his constituents and the abundance of unrighteousness; this happens before long. (7.111)
Just as the vital breaths of living beings are diminished by the emaciation of the body, so too are the vital breaths of kings diminished by the emaciation of the kingdom. 7.112

"Because of the emaciation of the body": just as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of living beings are exhausted by long journeys and the like, so too the vital breaths of kings go to their destruction when the subjects are provoked to anger by the oppression of the realm. (7.112)
One should always practice this method for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness. (7.113)

And wishing to avoid this fault, he says "of the kingdom. One should always employ the means that will be described for the protection of the kingdom; for a king whose kingdom is well protected prospers through effort. (7.113)
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) among two, three, or five [villages], and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom. (7.114)

"Of two" means: between two villages, or among three, five, or many hundreds of villages, he should establish a station (*sthānaka*)—supervised by trustworthy men (*āptapuruṣa*) and serving as a protection—taking into account the place, time, and other factors; this is for the purpose of perceiving the faults of the villages and so forth, and for the purpose of collecting taxes and the like. (7.114)
One should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
Regarding the phrase "of the village": he should appoint a supervisor for one village and for ten villages. (7.115)
The village headman shall himself gradually report any faults that have arisen in the village to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten shall report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, in turn, should report it himself to the lord of a thousand.

"Regarding the faults of the village": as for the "lord of twenty. When faults such as theft have arisen in a village, the village headman, being unable to manage the command himself without agitation, should report it to the lord of ten villages. The lord of ten should report it to the master of twenty; the lord of twenty to the lord of a hundred; and the lord of a hundred to the lord of a thousand. (7.116–117)
Whatever items are to be paid daily by the village dwellers to the king—such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth—the village headman shall receive those. (7.118)
Regarding the word "those which": whatever food, drink, and so forth are to be given by the village dwellers to the master, those the lord of the village shall take. (7.118)
The collector of ten should enjoy one family, and the collector of twenty, five families;
the superintendent of a hundred villages [should enjoy] a village, and the lord of a thousand [should enjoy] a city.
It is said: "The plough of Dharma has eight oxen for those seeking a livelihood, six oxen for householders,
and two oxen for those who have slain a Brahmin."

Thus says Hārīta: A plough with six oxen is considered medium; twice that is considered a *kula*. The lord of ten should enjoy for the sake of his servants the produce of as much land as can be cultivated by two such medium ploughs. Likewise, the lord of twenty [should enjoy] five *kulas*, the lord of a hundred a medium village, and the lord of a thousand a medium city. (7.119)
Indeed, another affectionate minister of the king, remaining vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their private matters. (7.120)

"Of these": thus, the king's appointed official, being diligent, should oversee the affairs of village-dwellers belonging to the village headmen and others—those matters which are difficult for them to manage individually, as well as whatever else, whether done or left undone, pertains to them. (7.120)
In every city, he should appoint one overseer of all affairs,
stationed in a high place and possessing a formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.

Regarding the term "city": in every city, one should appoint a lord of the city who occupies a preeminent position, is of noble lineage, possesses a formidable appearance, is accompanied by a complete array of forces such as students, ornaments, elephants, and horses, has a terrifying form, and stands in the center like the sun within a planet. (7.121)
He himself should always inspect them all one by one;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through his spies.

"Regarding 'he' (sa): that *nāgarika* (city magistrate), from the position of head of a single village upwards, shall always personally follow behind [the army] whenever there is a need to fill out the ranks. The king should learn through spies stationed in the territories what is practiced among those [officials] down to the *nāgarikas*, so that he may understand their conduct. (7.122)
For the king's protectors are generally deceitful servants who seize the property of others; therefore, he should guard these subjects from them. (7.123)

"Of the king": because the king's servants who are appointed to guard [the people] are for the most part by nature prone to seizing the property of others and are deceivers, therefore the king must protect his own subjects from them. 7.123.
Those of evil intent who seize wealth solely from litigants, the king shall confiscate their entire property and carry out their banishment. (7.124)

"Those who": those officials appointed by the king who, with evil intent, might seize wealth from litigants in the form of taking what belongs to others; of them, the king shall confiscate all property and carry out their banishment from the country. 7.124.
For women and servants engaged in the king's service, he shall provide daily maintenance according to their rank and their work. (7.125)

"In royal affairs" means: for women employed in services useful to the king, such as female slaves and the like, and for groups of male slaves, he shall grant daily maintenance according to their respective high or low status and in accordance with their specific work. (7.125)
A paṇa shall be given as the fee for the lowest laborer, and six for the highest;
likewise, clothing every six months and one droṇa of grain every month. (7.126)

He demonstrates that very point: "One paṇa is to be given to the lowliest laborer, six to the highest, and [provisions for] food. A *paṇa* is what will be described later; it must be given daily for the sake of food to the lowest hired servant (*jaghanya-bhṛtaka*). Furthermore, he should be provided with clothing every six months—a pair of garments—and a *droṇa* of grain monthly, along with five hundred and twelve *palas* [of salt or other condiments]. To the highest, however, six *paṇas* are to be given for the sake of food. According to this same calculation, six pairs of garments are to be given every six months. Following this same principle, three *paṇas* every six months and three pairs of garments, as well as three *droṇas* of grain monthly, are to be given to the middling one. (7.126)

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of the goods, the king should cause the merchants to pay taxes.

Regarding "buying and selling": having considered how much was purchased, for how much it is sold, from what distance it was brought, how much was spent by the merchant on food, broth, and so forth while coming from another country, and how much was spent on security against robbers and other dangers in forests and similar places, the king shall cause taxes to be paid by the merchants. (7.127)
Just as the king and the doer of actions are joined with their fruit,
so should the king, having considered this, always apportion taxes within his realm.

"Yathā" means: having reflected upon how the connection with the fruit of action occurs for a king as well as for laborers such as merchants and farmers, the king should always determine taxes within his realm accordingly. 7.128.
Just as water, fire, a calf, and a bee take only a little at a time of what they consume, so should the king take only a small annual tax from his realm. (7.129)

Regarding the phrase "little by little," he provides an illustration here: just as leeches, calves, and bees consume their food—blood, milk, and nectar—very gradually and in small amounts, so too should a king, without cutting off the root [of his subjects], collect an annual tax that is very small and very small. (7.129)
The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
an eighth part of grain, or a sixth, or even a twelfth. (7.130)

"An fiftieth part" means that for cattle and gold exceeding the original value, a fiftieth part shall be taken by the king. Likewise, in the case of grain, a sixth, eighth, or twelfth part shall be taken, depending on the degree of hardship endured by the cultivator. (7.130)
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
Of leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and split-bamboo vessels; of earthenware pots and of everything made of stone.

"He should take," [it is said], "one-sixth of grasses, hides, and bamboo. Thus, he should take one-sixth of trees, meat, honey, clarified butter, camphor, and other fragrant substances; of medicinal herbs such as *guḍūcī*; of liquids such as salt; and of flowers, roots, fruits, leaves, vegetables, grass, hides, articles made of bamboo, earthenware, stone vessels, and so forth. (7.131–132)
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling in his realm perish from hunger. (7.133)

Regarding the phrase "even when dying": a learned man (*śrotriya*) living in the king's realm should not fall into despair. Even if his treasury is utterly exhausted, a king should not take taxes from Brahmins who are devoted to the study of the Vedas; nor should a learned man living in that country fall into despair.
In whosever king’s realm a learned Vedic scholar perishes from hunger, his kingdom likewise perishes from that hunger before long. (7.134)
"Because of whose"—meaning, in the territory of whichever king a learned *śrotriya* falls into distress from hunger, that king's kingdom also soon falls into the distress of famine. (7.134)
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son. (7.135)

Since this is so, therefore [the verse says]: "In learning and conduct... He should likewise protect him from dangers, as a father protects his own biological son. Having understood his application of knowledge, he should provide for him a livelihood that conforms to it and does not deviate from dharma; and he should be protected from dangers such as thieves and adulterers, just as a father protects his son. (7.135)
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king, by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase. (7.136)
Regarding the phrase "being protected": that Brāhmaṇa, being protected by the king, performs his duty day after day; by that, the king's lifespan increases, and the realms flourish. 7.137.
Whatever little the king may cause to be paid by commoners in his realm who live by trade, designated as "tax" (kara), [that shall be one-sixteenth of a year's yield]. 7.137.

"Whatever it may be": whatever means of livelihood exists in that kingdom, such as the sale and purchase of goods by bakers and others, even from lowly people—if it is "whatever," meaning even a very small amount, the king shall cause that which is called tax (*kara*) to be paid for the year. (7.137)
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month. (7.138)

"Artisans" (kārukān): he shall cause artisans such as cooks and the like, craftsmen such as leather-workers and the like, and Śūdras who live by manual labor, such as porters and so forth, to perform work for one day and night every month. (7.138)
One should not, out of excessive greed, cut off one's own root nor that of others;
for by cutting off one's own root, one afflicts both oneself and them. (7.139)

"One should not cut off," it says; "cutting off one's own root. When a king, out of excessive affection, refrains from collecting taxes and the like, he would cause the destruction of his own root—namely, the ruin of his kingdom—due to the depletion of his treasury. Likewise, being excessively greedy, he should not cause the destruction of the root of these subjects either. Therefore, by cutting off his own root through the imposition of taxes, the king would afflict both himself and his subjects. (7.139)
A lord of the earth should be both harsh and mild after considering the task at hand;
indeed, a king who is both harsh and mild becomes esteemed.

"A king should be neither harsh nor mild, having considered the task at hand. Depending on the requirements of the task, the king may be either harsh or mild; a king who adheres exclusively to either harshness or mildness does not become beloved by his subjects. (7.140)
When weary from overseeing the affairs of men, he should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth. (7.141)

Regarding the phrase "the chief minister": when the king is weary from overseeing state affairs concerning his servants, he should appoint a principal minister—one who knows the law, is wise, has controlled his senses, and is of noble birth—to that position of overseeing affairs. (7.141)
Having thus performed all these duties incumbent upon himself, he should protect these subjects with diligence and vigilance. (7.142)
"Thus": having accomplished his entire range of duties in the manner described above, he should, being diligent and with an unerring intellect, protect his own subjects. (7.143)
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while they cry out for help—even as he looks on, along with his servants—he is dead and does not truly live. (7.143)

"Those who cry out": when the subjects of a king, along with his servants, are being carried off from the kingdom by enemies and others while he looks on, they cry out because they have no hope for their own lives; such a king is as good as dead, he does not truly live. (7.143)
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed fruits of his office is joined with righteousness. (7.144)

Regarding the Kṣatriya: among the various duties of a Kṣatriya, the protection of subjects alone is the preeminent duty; since [the king] is the enjoyer of the fruits because of this protection, the king is connected with dharma. (7.144)
Having risen during the final watch of the night, purified and composed,
having offered oblations into the fire and honored the brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.

"Having risen": when only a short while of the night remains, he should rise, perform the necessary purification, restrain his mind, and having performed the *agnihotra* sacrifice and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the assembly hall endowed with the characteristics of a dwelling site—the chamber for seeing his ministers and others. (7.145)
Staying there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects after greeting them;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.

Regarding the word "therein": having remained in that assembly hall and having gratified all the subjects who have come to the assembly for the purpose of an audience by means of speech, sight, and so forth, he should dismiss them. Having dismissed them, he should deliberate upon peace, war, and other matters together with his ministers. (7.146)
Having ascended a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place, or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate unobserved. (7.147)

"Upon the mountain ridge": having ascended a mountain peak or a white palace, or staying in a secluded place in the forest that is free of grass and the like, and devoid of the fear of the disclosure of mantras, this is the means for commencing the ritual actions of the five-limbed mantra: one should reflect in this manner upon the excellence of personnel and materials, the distinction of place and time, the remedy for misfortunes, and the accomplishment of the task. (7.147)
That king who, even if devoid of treasure, enjoys the entire earth, while ordinary people do not know his secret counsel when they have come together. (7.148)

Regarding the phrase "of whom": that king, even if his treasury is depleted, enjoys the entire earth, provided that people other than his ministers do not know his counsel by gathering together and deliberating. (7.148)

At the time of reciting the mantra, one should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf; animals; those who have passed old age; women; barbarians; the diseased; and the deformed. (7.149)

"One should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf; likewise those deficient in intellect, speech, sight, or hearing; as well as cattle, deer, parrots, elderly women, barbarians, the sick, and those with missing limbs—at the time of reciting the mantra. (7.149)
Those who are despised, as well as animals, and women especially, betray a secret; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard. (7.150)

"Those who break [the mantra]" means that those who are dull-witted and so forth, being possessed of defects such as stupidity, break the mantra through their lack of respect. Likewise, even those born of animal wombs break the mantra upon hearing it while walking on the earth and so forth. And especially women, due to their excessive fickleness; therefore, one should be diligent in avoiding them. 7.150.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue, he should contemplate the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, either together with them or alone. (7.151)

"At midday": free from mental fatigue and with physical exhaustion gone, at noon or at midnight, he should reflect together with his ministers or alone upon the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, thinking: "How should I cultivate Dharma, Kāma, or Artha? (7.151)
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons. || 7.152 ||

Regarding the phrase "of those that are mutually contradictory": when those [three goals]—dharma, pleasure, and wealth—manifest in mutual conflict, one should contemplate the means for achieving their non-conflict. One should consider the giving away of daughters as having the fruit of the successful accomplishment of one's own purpose. And one should consider the correction of the undisciplined behavior of sons and princes as having the fruit of winning over the lowly. (7.152)
The dispatching of messengers, as well as the remaining tasks,
