the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the spies.

Regarding "the dispatching of envoys": he should consider the dispatching of envoys to foreign kingdoms according to whether they are entrusted with full powers, limited powers, or are merely bearers of letters. Likewise, he should consider the completion of the remaining tasks of undertakings already begun. He should consider the activities of the women of the harem for the sake of his own self-protection and to ensure their lack of transgression, given that they are governed by an extremely fickle and treacherous conduct. And he should ascertain the activities of spies through other spies. (7.153)
He [should know] in truth the entire eightfold business and the five classes,
as well as affection and enmity, and the conduct of the circle of states.
Regarding the term "entirety": Uśanas has stated that there are eight kinds of royal duties:
in taking and in giving, as well as in commanding and forbidding, in the fifth, in speaking for the sake of purpose, and in the supervision of legal proceedings.
Constantly engaged in the purification of punishment, the king who possesses these eightfold qualities and performs the eight duties goes to heaven, honored by Śakra.

In this context, he should contemplate these eightfold duties: (1) *ādāna*, which is the collection of taxes and so forth; (2) *visarga*, the distribution of wealth to servants; (3) *praiṣa*, the dismissal of the wicked; (4) the prohibition of arbitrary conduct among those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramiṇaḥ*) and providing authoritative instruction when they have doubts regarding their own duties; (5) the supervision of legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) when subjects encounter disputes over property and the like; (6) the punishment of those who are defeated; and (7-8) the purification through penance (*prāyaścitta*) for lapses due to negligence. Likewise, he should appropriately manage a group of spies (*cāravarga*) consisting of five types: the *kārpaṭika* (a wandering mendicant), the *udāsthita* (a fallen ascetic), the *gṛhapati* (a householder), the *vaidehika* (a merchant), and the *tāpasa* (an ascetic). Among them, the *kārpaṭika* is one who knows the secrets of others and has been tested. The king should recognize him as a spy, win him over with wealth and honor, and treat him as before. In private, the king should say to him: "If you see such-and-such, you must report it immediately. The *udāsthita* is one who has fallen from his ascetic vows. Recognizing him as a spy seeking a livelihood and devoted to the purity of his subjects, the king should say to him in secret: "You shall perform the work of a student (*antevāsika*) in a kitchen capable of producing all kinds of food. Then, provide me with food, clothing, and other necessities as you wish, from the land belonging to yourself, others, and those ascetics employed by us who deal in our interests. The *gṛhapati* is a farmer whose livelihood is exhausted but who possesses wisdom and purity. Having addressed him as before, the king should have him cultivate the aforementioned land. The rest is as previously described. The *tāpasa* is one who is shaven-headed or wears matted hair and desires a livelihood. Having addressed him as before, the king should have him perform the work of a merchant on that land. Or, a shaven-headed or matted-haired man desiring a livelihood, acting as a *tāpasa* spy by royal command, should establish a monastery near the city, filled with many shaven-headed and matted-haired men under the guise of disciples. Publicly, he should eat a handful of *iguda* or *badara* fruits every month or two months; in secret, however, he should eat whatever food he desires provided by the king. And his disciples should proclaim to the world that he knows the past and future. Likewise, he should predict the gain, honor, or danger from thieves for the people. Those agents of the state acting in disguise should fulfill these predictions to create an impression of truthfulness. Thus, when all the people have gained confidence in him, everyone—desiring to know the success of their various undertakings—approaches him and asks about what should and should not be done. They maintain their discourse with the desire to please him. In this way, he should contemplate the fivefold group in its true nature. Having thus established the fivefold group, he should then, through that very group, ascertain the loyalty or disloyalty of the ministers and others of the enemy king, as well as his own. Having understood the movements of the circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) to be described hereafter—who seeks peace, and so forth—he should deliberate accordingly. (7.154)
He should diligently investigate the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the one seeking conquest, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy. (7.155)

Regarding "of the middle king": one should consider the conduct of a middle king who is situated at a distance of one intervening territory from both the enemy and the conqueror (*vijigīṣu*), and who is either incapable of exertion when they are united, or equal to them when they are united in war. Likewise, one should consider the actions of the conqueror—who is endowed with wisdom, energy, and natural virtues—to determine what he intends to do. Furthermore, regarding the enemy, the conqueror, and the middle king, one should consider the conduct of the neutral king (*udāsīna*)—who is capable of favoring those who are united and suppressing those who are not—and one should especially consider with diligence the conduct of the three types of artificial neighbors situated immediately adjacent to the enemy. (7.155)
In brief, these constituents are the root of the circle;
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve. (7.156)

"These" refers to these four primary powers (prakṛtis), beginning with the middling one; in brief, they are the root of the circle (*maṇḍala*), for since all other powers are produced from them, they are called the "root. Furthermore, eight others are enumerated. Namely: in front [of the central power] are the ally (*mitra*), the enemy (*amitra*), the ally-of-the-ally (*mitramitra*), and the enemy-of-the-enemy (*arimitra*). Thus there are another four. Behind [the central power] are the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), the rear-enemy's ally (*ākranda*), the rear-enemy's rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāhāsāra*), and the rear-enemy's ally's ally (*ākrandāsāra*); thus there are exactly four. Together with the four primary powers, these are recorded as the twelve powers. || 7.156 ||
The five others are known as ministers, the realm, fortresses, wealth, and the army;
each of these has been described in brief, totaling seventy-two.

"Minister, kingdom, enemy, and army. For each of these four primary constituents (*mūlaprakṛti*) and the aforementioned secondary constituents (*śākhāprakṛti*), there are five material constituents (*dravyaprakṛti*) known as minister, territory, fort, treasury, and army. Thus, the four primary constituents, the eight secondary constituents, and the sixty material constituents—briefly stated, seventy-two are thus enumerated. (7.157)
Immediately after [the conqueror] one should know the enemy, and likewise the one who serves the enemy; next to the enemy is the friend, and beyond those two is the neutral party. (7.158)

"Immediately thereafter, one should know the enemy, and likewise the one who serves the enemy. One should recognize those surrounding the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) as enemies when they form a circle and are adjacent to his territory; likewise, one should know the one who serves that enemy as indeed an enemy. Furthermore, one should know those separated by one territory from the enemy as being of the nature of a friend to the seeker of victory. One should know the state beyond both that enemy and that friend to be that of a neutral power (*udāsīna*). It is by distinguishing between these very powers—whether they are in front or behind—that the various designations such as "enemy," "one who attacks the rear" (*pārṣṇigrāha*), and so forth, are established. (7.158)
He should win over all of them by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation—both individually and collectively—and through personal prowess and statesmanship. (7.159)

"One should direct all of them toward this end. One should bring all these subjects under control—whether by means of conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, or force, used individually or collectively as appropriate, or by human effort alone, or by force alone, or by policy alone, or by conciliation alone. (7.159)
He should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge. (7.160)

Regarding "alliance" (*saṃdhi*): one should always contemplate the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), which consists of alliance, internal dissension (*dvaidhībhāva*), and seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*). Among these, *saṃdhi* is an agreement that brings mutual benefit; *vigraha* (war) is an act of injury; *yāna* (marching) is advancing when there is a prospect of success; *āsana* (sitting encamped) is remaining neutral or waiting; *dvaidhībhāva* (double-dealing) is making peace with one while waging war against another; and *saṃśraya* (seeking refuge) is surrendering oneself to a superior power. One should always contemplate these six measures, which are conducive to prosperity. By resorting to these six measures, one's own advancement occurs and the decline of the enemy follows; therefore, one should abide by those very measures. (7.160)
Having carefully considered the task at hand, he should employ sitting encampment, marching, alliance, and war, as well as the double policy and seeking protection. (7.161)

"Waiting, marching, making peace, and likewise waging war"—having examined the task at hand, such as one's own advancement or the enemy's decline, one should, after deliberating, practice waiting or marching, or adopt a double policy, or seek refuge. In that regard, when there is a suspicion of equality with the enemy in the present or the future, one should conclude a peace treaty and remain stationary. But when, even in the absence of such equality, one considers that one's own constituents (*prakṛtis*) are not wavering and that the enemy's constituents are susceptible to intrigue (*upajāpa*), then one should resort to war and remain firm. Furthermore, when one has risen against the enemy and has thus consolidated one's own kingdom, one should march forth having declared war; or, in the absence of grounds for marching after declaring war, one should march after concluding a treaty with a rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*). Likewise, depending on the requirements of the task, one should employ a double policy by making peace with one and waging war with another. But when, being weak, one is attacked by a powerful foe, then one should seek refuge with another who possesses superior strength. (7.161)
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds; likewise, marching and sitting encamped are both twofold, and seeking refuge is recorded as being of two types. (7.162)

Regarding the term "alliance" (*saṃdhi*): the answer is that the king should know all the factors such as alliance and war (*saṃdhivigraha*) in their two respective varieties; this is for the sake of [understanding] the opposing side. (7.163)

A peace treaty should be known as having two characteristics: one where the parties undertake the same mission, and likewise one that is contrary to it; it is joined with both immediate and future consequences. (7.163)

Regarding "an expedition with equal effort" (*samānayānakarma*): when an expedition is undertaken against another king by means of a present benefit and supported by a future benefit, that is a treaty involving an expedition with equal effort (*samānayānakarmā saṃdhi*). That which is performed with the thought, "I shall follow after you," for the sake of a present benefit, is [a treaty] involving an expedition with unequal effort (*asamānayānakarmā saṃdhi*). Thus, this treaty should be understood as being of two kinds. (7.163)

War is declared to be of two kinds: that undertaken by oneself for the sake of a specific objective, either out of season or at the proper time, and that waged against a friend who has committed an injury. || 7.164 ||

"Self-inflicted": War is recorded as being of two kinds. One is "self-inflicted," which occurs either at a time other than the periods such as Mārgaśīrṣa that will be described, or at that very same time when required by the nature of the task. The second is when an injury is inflicted by an ally of the enemy—who is himself a friend of the conqueror—while the enemy is in a state of calamity. Thus, war is recorded as being of these two kinds. (7.164)
When an urgent matter has arisen by chance, marching alone or in conjunction with an ally is said to be the two-fold way of marching. (7.165)

Regarding the term "alone" (*ekākina*): when an enemy’s calamity or similar crisis arises, and a swift remedy is required, marching (*yāna*) is said to be of two kinds: that of one who is capable and alone, and that of one who is incapable and accompanied by allies. (7.165)
Sitting is traditionally said to be of two kinds: that undertaken when one's resources are exhausted due to fate or past deeds, and that undertaken out of deference to a friend. (7.166)

"Of one who is diminished": this refers to two types of sitting postures (*āsana*) as traditionally taught: first, for one whose land and other assets have gradually been depleted due to the force of karma accumulated in previous lives or through negligence in this life; and second, for one who possesses all prosperity but sits out of deference to friends or for the sake of protecting their interests. // 7.166 //
The dual state of both the army and the lord for the sake of accomplishing the objective is proclaimed as "duplicity" (dvaidha) by those who know the qualities of the six measures of policy. (7.167)

Regarding the term *bala* (force): for the sake of accomplishing a task, the stationing of the army—consisting of elephants and so forth, commanded by generals and others—in one place is one [form of] action; and the stationing of the king himself, accompanied by a portion of his force, within a fort is the other. Thus, by those who know the benefits of the six political measures (*ṣāḍguṇya*) such as peace (*saṃdhi*) and the rest, this twofold division (*dvaidha*) is proclaimed. Furthermore, there is a twofold sub-division of this *dvaidha*: making peace with one [party] while waging war with another, which constitutes its existence in two distinct forms. (7.167)
Seeking refuge is recorded as being of two kinds: for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose when oppressed by enemies, and for the sake of gaining a reputation among the virtuous. (7.168)

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of accomplishing an objective': taking refuge with a virtuous king is recorded in tradition as being of two kinds: first, for the sake of accomplishing a purpose known as the removal of fear for one who is being overwhelmed by enemies; and second, even when there is no actual defeat at that moment, for the sake of making a declaration such as 'this person has taken refuge with [such-and-such a king]' out of apprehension of a future defeat. (7.168)
When one perceives that there will certainly be a great advantage for oneself in the future, and only a slight suffering in the present, then one should resort to peace. (7.169)

When one should perceive that in the future there will certainly be a greater [gain] for oneself—when one considers that in the time to come there will definitely be a superior result for oneself, while the present loss is small—then, accepting that loss, one should resort to a superior treaty. (7.169)
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly joyful and himself likewise highly exalted, then he should wage war. (7.170)

Regarding the phrase "when": when he considers all his subjects, such as the ministers and others, to be thoroughly satisfied by means of gifts, honors, and so forth, and when he considers himself elevated by abundant power of counsel (*mantra*), energy (*utsāha*), and strength (*śakti*), then he should resolve upon war. (7.170)
When he perceives his own force to be joyful and robust in spirit, and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe. (7.171)

"When he should think" means: when he knows his own army, consisting of ministers and others, to be fully satisfied and nourished with wealth and other resources for the sake of the supreme goal, while that of the enemy is the opposite, then he should march against him. || 7.171 ||
But when he is depleted of both mounts and troops, then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies. (7.172)

"But when," [it says]. When, moreover, one is utterly exhausted by elephants and other such assets as well as wealth, then, gradually pacifying the enemies through conciliation, gifts, and so forth, one should with effort resort to a state of waiting, avoiding excessive elevation. || 7.172 ||
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then,
having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose.

"One should consider" means: when one considers an enemy to be superior in every respect and exceedingly powerful such that his defeat is impossible to achieve, then, accompanied by a portion of one's own army, one should take refuge in a fortress while another portion of the army carries out the attack against him; thus, having divided the force into two parts, one should accomplish one's own purpose through the gathering of allies. (7.173)
But when he becomes most vulnerable to attack by the forces of his enemies, then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king. (7.174)

Regarding the phrase "when": when one becomes subject to attack due to the excessive provocation of the subjects and so forth by the forces of the enemy, then one should immediately seek refuge with a righteous king who is capable of providing protection. 7.174.
One should always serve with every effort that man who effects the suppression of both the subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one would a teacher. (7.175)

Regarding "subjugation" (nigraha): he should always serve like a teacher with all his forces that king who, having conquered both those two—namely, those constituent elements (prakṛtis) which have become subject to him due to the faults of their own associates, and the enemy force by which he himself has become powerful—should exercise subjugation over them. (7.175)
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from the act of seeking refuge, he should nevertheless engage in fair combat there as well, free from hesitation. (7.176)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): even in that case, one should engage in a fair fight without hesitation. For seeking refuge is indeed a desperate resort; yet, if one perceives that there is a fault inherent in seeking such refuge, then, becoming free from doubt, one should at that time engage in a righteous battle alone. This is because even a weak man may see victory over the strong, and because one who is slain attains heaven. (7.176)
A king who understands policy should employ every means such that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him. (7.177)

"By all means": a king skilled in policy should strive by all means, such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest, so that his friends, neutrals, enemies, and middling powers do not become superior. For if they become superior, he becomes exceedingly vulnerable to agitation; for through the pride of wealth, a friend may fall into enmity. (7.177)
One should examine the future of all undertakings as well as their present state, and one should also truly investigate the merits and faults of all past actions. (7.178)

"Regarding the future": one should thus deliberate upon the merits and defects of all undertakings, even the smallest, with respect to their consequences in the time to come; and regarding the present, for the sake of swift accomplishment, one should deliberate upon the merits and defects of all tasks, considering how much has been done, how much has been deliberated, and what remains to be done. (7.178)
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present, and who understands the remaining tasks of the past, is not overcome by enemies. (7.179)

"Regarding 'protracted' (*āyata*): he who, knowing the defects of future times among his undertakings, initiates a meritorious task and avoids one that is defective; and he who, in the present time, performs a task that must be decided upon quickly and does not procrastinate regarding the work; and he who knows the remainder of a task—he obtains the fruit of that task upon its completion. Therefore, because of such attentiveness toward the three times, he is never overcome by enemies. (7.179)
He should arrange everything in such a way that friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.
"Yathā" means: he should carry out every arrangement in such a way that those mentioned, such as friends and others, would not deceive this king; such is the concise method of policy (*nīti*). 7.180.
But when the lord intends to set out toward the enemy's kingdom, he should then proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this following method. (7.181)

Regarding the phrase "yadā" (when): when he, being capable, should undertake an expedition against the enemy's kingdom, then he should proceed to the enemy's territory without haste in the manner that will be described hereafter. (7.181)
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition,
or else toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra, according to his strength.

Regarding the month of Mārgaśīrṣa: a lord of the earth who possesses a fourfold army should set out on his expedition in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, provided there is abundant fodder and the region is endowed with grain, chariots, and horses; he should march when the time is favorable, for a long duration, and when the crops are near ripeness. On the other hand, one whose strength consists primarily of cavalry should go to a region where spring crops predominate; since his expedition is of short duration, he should march in Phālguna or Caitra. Thus, he should march without transgressing the time appropriate for his own forces. (7.182)
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory, he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for his enemy. (7.183)

Regarding the phrase "in other [times]": even at times distinct from those already mentioned, when he anticipates a certain victory for himself—then, being primarily possessed of elephant forces during the rainy season and primarily possessed of horse forces during the summer—he should undertake a military expedition only after declaring war. Furthermore, when the enemy has fallen into misfortune such as the provocation of his own subjects, he should march even at a time other than those previously specified. (7.183)
Having performed the ritual arrangements at the base according to the rules, as well as the preparations for the journey, and having secured his residence and properly stationed his spies; 7.183.
Having cleared the threefold path and his own sixfold power,
he should advance slowly toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a protracted campaign.

"Having done so" means: having performed the preliminary measures such as securing alliances with rear-enemy states (*pārṣṇigrāha*), protecting the countryside, forts, and the class of the angry and so forth; having arranged the foundations consisting of his own fort and kingdom; having prepared, according to the scriptures, the necessary vehicles, weapons, armor, and secret mantras (*mantra*); having seized the stronghold where the enemy's army is stationed within the enemy circle (*paramaṇḍala*); having brought under his control the factions of that enemy's servants; having properly established his own spies and others, as well as intelligence regarding the enemy's territory, for the purpose of battle; having cleared the three types of roads—namely those through arid lands (*jāṅgala*), marshy lands (*anūpa*), and forested regions (*āṭavika*)—by cutting down obstructing thickets and leveling depressions and elevations, digging wells, and so forth; and likewise having refreshed his own sixfold army—consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, commanders, and laborers—with appropriate food, medicine, hospitality, and rewards—he should advance toward the enemy's country at a steady pace according to the rules of warfare.
One should be especially vigilant regarding a hidden enemy who has become a friend, as well as one who has gone away and returned; for such a person is indeed the most dangerous foe.

Regarding "one who serves the enemy": both of these are indeed most difficult enemies—the one who, having made a secret friend of someone, serves the enemy, and the servant or similar person who, having previously departed due to resentment, returns later. One must be vigilant toward them, for they are exceedingly difficult enemies. (7.186)
He should proceed along that path in the staff-array, or the wagon-array, or the boar or crocodile-arrays, or the needle-array, or the garuḍa-array. (7.187)

"By means of the *daṇḍavyūha* (staff-array). An array (*vyūha*) is the arrangement of troops in the form of a staff; likewise, there are also arrays in the shape of a cart (*śakaṭa*) and so forth. In that [staff-array], the commander-in-chief is at the front, the king is in the middle, the general is in the rear, elephants are on the flanks, horses are near them, and then the infantry. Thus arranged, long and with a symmetrical deployment on all sides, is the *daṇḍavyūha*; by means of it, one should march along the path to be traversed when there is danger from all directions. A cart-array has a needle-like point at the front and is broad in the rear; by means of it, one should advance when there is danger from the flanks. A crocodile-array (*makaravyūha*) is the reverse of a boar-array; by means of it, one should go when there is danger in the front and the rear. Where the soldiers are stationed in a long line, like a row of ants, without being compact, having a human face [at the front], that is the needle-array (*sūcīvyūha*); by means of it, one should march when there is danger in the front. (7.187)
From whichever direction he suspects danger, there he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up position in the lotus formation.

Regarding the phrase "from which": in whichever direction danger from an enemy might be anticipated, one should extend the army precisely there. Finally, having emerged from the city in the *padmavyūha* (lotus formation) with the circumference expanded and the seeker of victory seated in the center, he should always remain well-secured in this manner himself. 7.188.
The commander-in-chief and the chief of the forces should station them in all directions;
and whichever direction he suspects danger from, that he should designate as the east.

Regarding the "commander-in-chief and the general": a single leader should be appointed for each of the ten constituent parts consisting of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry; he is called a *pattika* (infantry commander). A single leader of ten *pattikas* is a *senāpati* (army commander). A single leader of ten of those is a *nāyaka* (leader). He alone is also the *balādhyakṣa* (supreme commander of forces). When there is a plurality of principal leaders in all directions, he should employ them for the purpose of a contest of forces. And in whichever direction he should suspect danger, he should place that as the front line. (7.189)
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides—men who are skilled in both their positions and in battle, fearless and steadfast. (7.190)

"Regarding 'ambushes' (gulmān): he should station ambushes—consisting of men occupying strategic positions, equipped with signals such as conch shells, kettledrums, and tabors for withdrawing from a position or engaging in battle, arranged according to forest terrain, fearless, and infallible—on all sides.
One should make a few soldiers fight in a compact formation, but one may extend many as desired;
having arrayed them in the *sūcī* (needle) or *vajra* (thunderbolt) battle arrays, one should cause them to fight.

"Consolidated" means: having made a small number of warriors consolidated, one should make them fight against many; then, one may spread them out again as desired. Having arranged the army in the previously mentioned needle formation (*sūcī*) or the formation called the thunderbolt (*vajra*), with the forces stationed in three divisions, one should cause the battle to be fought.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy terrain;
with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other weapons on firm ground.

"By means of chariots and horses" means that one should fight with chariots and horses on level ground, because of the efficacy of the chariot there; likewise, [one should fight] with boats and elephants in water that has followed [the terrain], with bows in places overgrown with trees and shrubs, and with weapons known as swords and shields in places free from stones, thorns, pits, and the like. (7.192)
He should station men from Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena, as well as those who are tall and agile, at the vanguard of the ranks. (7.193)

Regarding the "Kaurukṣetras": one should station at the front of the army the Matsyas born in Kurukṣetra, the inhabitants of the Virāṭa country, the Pāñcālas, the Kānyakubjas, and the Śūrasenas—these being large-bodied men, generally so because they possess a pride in their physical stature, strength, and valor; likewise, one should employ others who are tall as well as those who are short-statured. (7.193)
He should gladden his army, properly inspect its divisions, and discern the movements even of the enemies as they fight. (7.194)

"He should gladden them" means he should recognize the gestures of the enemies as they fight. Having arrayed his forces, he should encourage them for the sake of battle with such words as: "In victory there is dharma and wealth; in defeat, heaven and fame. He should observe and examine those warriors, noting who rejoices or becomes angry when addressed in this way. Likewise, he should discern the gestures of the warriors, even when they are not fighting the enemy, such as their behavior during a deceptive battle or similar maneuvers. (7.194)
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain there and afflict his kingdom;
he should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel. (7.195)

"Having besieged" means that one should surround even an enemy who has taken refuge in a fortress and is fighting by encircling him through the gates of the fort; and at night, one should harass him outside the fortress by plundering and other such means. One should also always spoil his fodder, food, water, and fuel by mixing them with harmful substances and so forth. (7.195)
He should break down the tanks as well as the walls and moats; he should launch a surprise attack upon him at night and likewise cause him terror. (7.196)

"He should break" means that he should destroy by breaking open the tanks and other waterworks upon which the fort depends; likewise, he should breach the walls of the fort and fill up its moats, or render them waterless by creating breaches. In this way, he may properly launch a surprise attack while the enemy is unawares; he should fall upon him by night or by day, or terrify him with jackals, crows, and the like. And now, repeatedly... (7.196)
One should instigate those who can be sown with discord and remain ever vigilant regarding their actions;
when fate is favorable, one who desires victory should fight, free from fear. (7.197)

"Those to be instigated" means: he should instigate those connected with him who seek the kingdom, as well as angry servants who are susceptible to instigation. And he should ascertain what task has been accomplished by them. When the divine conditions—such as the positions of the planets and the lunar mansions—are favorable, one desiring victory and free from fear should go forth to battle. (7.197)
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension—either collectively or individually—and never by means of war. (7.198)

"By conciliation": one should strive to conquer enemies never by means of war. One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation—which consists of affection, the presentation of boons, and the speaking of beneficial advice—and through gifts such as gold, and through sowing dissension among their subjects and their kinsmen; thus, by these means either individually or collectively, according to what is appropriate, one should strive to conquer enemies, but never, however, by means of war. (7.198)
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two who fight, and defeat likewise occurs in battle, one should therefore avoid war. (7.199)

"Uncertain": because, when two parties are fighting, victory and defeat are seen to occur unpredictably depending solely on whether one side is stronger or weaker; therefore, when other means are available, one should avoid war. (7.199)
When even the three previously mentioned expedients are unavailable, one who is well-prepared should fight in such a way that he conquers his enemies. (7.200)

"When the three previously mentioned means have been exhausted, he should then fight with full resolve. This means that when the previously mentioned means—conciliation and the rest—have failed to achieve their purpose, and victory or defeat remains in doubt, he should fight with such vigilance that he may conquer his enemies. If he does not conquer them, then, since his own death in heaven is certain, he should effect an escape from defeat, as it will be said: "He should protect himself in every way. (7.200)
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety. (7.201)

"Having conquered," etc. Having conquered a foreign kingdom, he should honor the local deities and the *brāhmaṇas* preeminent in righteousness with gifts, honors, and the like. Likewise, regarding the obligatory gifts due to those such as *śrotriyas*, he should grant exemptions by saying, "This has been permitted by me. Furthermore, out of devotion to his masters, he should proclaim safety (*abhaya*) by saying, "Whatever wrong was done to us by those [people], that has been forgiven by me; now, being reassured, let them attend to their own duties. (7.201)
But having understood the intended purpose of all these [kings] in brief, he should install a member of their lineage there and establish a covenant. (7.202)

"Of all"—having briefly ascertained the desire of all those subjects belonging to others, he should consecrate one who has conquered his passions to that conquered kingdom. Furthermore, he should issue instructions to him and his ministers and so forth, saying, "This must be done by you in the kingdom, and this must not. (7.202)
And one should establish for them the righteous laws as they have been declared;
and one should honor him with jewels, together with the leading men.

"Regarding the authorities": one should take as authoritative those practices belonging to others which do not deviate from the Dharma, which are recognized by the scriptures as local customs (*deśadharma*), and which are accepted by the treatises. And thus, having been consecrated, one should diligently honor him together with the ministers and others by means of gifts such as jewels. (7.203)
Taking what is not given causes displeasure, while giving what is desired causes pleasure;
at the proper time, acting in accordance with desired objects is praised. (7.204)

Regarding "taking": the seizure of desired objects is unpleasant, whereas giving them away produces pleasure; this is the general rule. Furthermore, giving is also praised when governed by the proper time; therefore, one should honor him at that time. (7.204)
All this action depends upon both divine and human destiny;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists the possibility of action.

"Everything": whatever is to be accomplished—that is, both the auspicious and inauspicious karma from previous births as well as that performed in this life—is dependent upon human effort. Among those two, fate cannot be deliberated upon; however, regarding human effort, there is room for reflection, and one should strive for the successful completion of one's task through this means, remaining free from attachment. (7.205)
Or, being disciplined, he may even march together after having diligently made a treaty, perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of an ally, gold, or land. (7.206)

"Or he may march together with him"—thus, if one must wage war against an enemy, one should do so provided that the enemy himself becomes an ally, or gold is given by him, or a portion of his territory is surrendered; having thus considered the fruit of the expedition, one should make peace with him and march forth with diligence. (7.206)

Having carefully observed the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*) as well as the ally-in-distress (*ākranda*) within the circle of states, one may obtain the fruit of an expedition from either a friend or even an enemy. (7.207)

Regarding the term *pārṣṇigrāha*: for one who has set out against an enemy with the desire for victory, he who attacks his rear is the *pārṣṇigrāha*. For such a rear-attacker, there is one who acts as a check; that is the *ākranda*. Taking into account that *ākranda*, one should secure results from the one to be attacked (*yātavya*), whether from a friend or an enemy. If one takes [the result] without regard for him, one may at some point become joined with the fault arising from that [negligence]. (7.207)
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend, even if that friend is weak, provided he is capable of enduring for the future. (7.208)

Regarding the phrase "by the acquisition of gold and land": a king does not increase as much by the gain of gold and land as he increases now by obtaining a steady friend, even if that friend is currently weak, provided that friend is endowed with future growth and prosperity. (7.208)
One who knows the Dharma, is grateful, and acts with contentment;
who is devoted, steadfast in his undertakings, and light—such a person is praised as a true friend. (7.209)

"Knowing the Dharma": one who knows the Dharma, who is skillful in providing assistance, whose ministers are devoted, who is full of affection, and whose actions are steadfast—such a person is desired as a friend with excellence. (7.209)
The wise say it is difficult to find an enemy who is intelligent, of noble birth, heroic, skillful, generous, grateful, and steadfast. (7.210)

"Regarding the term 'wise' (prājña): they say that a wise man is one of noble lineage, valiant, endowed with energy, magnanimous, a protector of favors, impartial toward profit and loss, difficult for an enemy to destroy, and learned. Therefore, one should diligently form an alliance with such a person. (7.210)
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and compassion; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of one who remains equanimous. (7.211)

Nobility is defined as excellence, the capacity to discern the specific qualities of men, valor, compassion, constant generosity with wealth, and subtle insight regarding matters of state. Such a person is always characterized by a complete set of neutral qualities; therefore, one should rely upon such a neutral party and wage war even against an enemy who possesses the aforementioned characteristics. (7.211)
A king should, without hesitation, abandon even land that is secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of livestock, for his own sake. (7.212)

"Secure," [it is said]. A king, keeping his own welfare in mind, should abandon territory even if it is capable of defense, provided by rivers, always yielding truth, and productive of an increase in livestock due to its abundance of grass, leaves, and so forth. A king, having no other recourse, may abandon such land for the sake of protecting himself. (7.212)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune, and protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (7.213)

For this duty is recorded as applicable to all men: that wealth must be preserved for the sake of misfortune; wives must be protected even at the expense of wealth; and the self, moreover, must be protected even by the relinquishment of everything, including wealth and wives. As for the claim that it is right for one to sacrifice oneself for the sake of another’s wife when no king is present—that is incorrect. Since "one should protect oneself from all things" is established, death not sanctioned by scripture is forbidden; nor should one suddenly abandon wealth and wife. (7.213)
Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen together, the wise should employ every means, both those joined with others and those acting alone. (7.214)

Because of the phrase "together with" (saha): having recognized that all calamities—such as rebellion against one's nature, internal strife, depletion of resources, and the misfortune of allies—have arisen simultaneously and to an extreme degree, a wise person should not fall into delusion; rather, he should employ all the means, such as conciliation and the rest, whether individually or collectively, in every way possible. (7.214)
Relying upon these three—the practitioner, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety—one should strive for the accomplishment of the purpose. (7.215)

"Regarding the 'approacher' (upetāram)": relying upon these three, one should strive for the realization of the Self. The "approacher" is the self; the "goal" is that which is to be attained; and the "means" are all [the qualities] beginning with conciliation (sāma), which are here complete. Thus, when this triad is fully present, one should exert oneself for the sake of realizing the Self—this is the summary. 7.215.
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
after exercising and bathing at midday, shall enter the inner apartments to eat.

"Thus. Having deliberated on everything according to the method thus stated, together with his ministers, and having thereafter performed physical exercise with the bow and other such activities and bathed, the king shall enter the inner apartments at the time of midday to eat. (7.216)

There, having thoroughly examined the food and other provisions with attendants who are like his own self, skilled in the arts of time, incorruptible, and who employ mantras that neutralize poison, he should eat. (7.217)

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): there, in the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*), one should eat food that has been prepared by cooks and others who are like oneself, who know the proper time for meals, and who are unassailable; and which has been thoroughly examined through the casting of fire and the observation of *cakora* birds and the like—for when poisoned food is cast into the fire, it crackles (*catacaṭāyate*), and the eyes of the *cakora* bird turn red—and so forth; and which has been consecrated with mantras that remove poison. (7.217)
One should purify all his belongings with water that destroys poison;
and, being self-restrained, he should always wear gems that counteract poison. (7.218)

Regarding the phrase "with poison-destroyers": one should examine all substances, such as articles of enjoyment and food, by means of the application of poison-destroying medicinal herbs. Furthermore, being diligent, one should always wear poison-destroying gems, such as the *nāga-maṇi* vomited forth by Garuḍa and others. (7.218)
And women who have been thoroughly examined, purified by their dress and ornaments, and composed in mind, should touch him with fans, water, and incense. (7.219)

"Having been tested": female attendants who have undergone testing regarding matters of dharma, artha, kāma, and both combined—by means such as employing them as spies—and whose dress and ornaments are pure due to the suspicion that they might carry concealed weapons or wear poison-smeared jewelry, should serve this king with single-minded devotion using yak-tail whisks, bathing waters, and perfumed fumes. (7.219)
In this manner, one should exert effort regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food; likewise, in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment. (7.220)
"Thus": one should apply such efforts as examination and so forth regarding vehicles, beds, seats, food, bathing, anointing, and all matters pertaining to ornaments. (7.220)
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again attend to his duties. (7.221)

"Having eaten" means that, having finished his meal, he should sport with his wives in that very inner apartment. And when the time has passed, having enjoyed himself there during the seventh part of the day, he should again attend to his duties during the eighth part. (7.221)
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the military personnel again, as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments. (7.222)

"Being adorned": having become adorned, he should further observe the people who live by arms, as well as all the vehicles such as horses, and the weapons such as swords, along with their ornaments. 7.222.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should, bearing his weapon, listen within his inner apartments to the activities of those who report secrets and of his secret agents.

"Regarding the twilight [devotions]: having then performed the twilight worship, he should listen to the report on his own activities from those who communicate secrets while holding weapons within the interior of the house. (7.223)
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people, he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating. 7.224.

"Having gone," etc.: having gone from that place to another secluded spot, and having observed the guards, he should enter the inner apartments again to eat, surrounded by female attendants and others. || 7.224 ||
Having eaten there a little more, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments, he should go to rest at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled. (7.225)

Having eaten there a little more, amidst the joyful sounds of musical instruments, he should go to rest at the proper time and rise free from fatigue. There in the inner apartments, having eaten while not yet fully satiated by the sounds of musical instruments that are pleasant to the ear, he should sleep when the night has passed its half-watch; and having slept, he should rise during the final watch.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
but when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants. (7.226)

"Regarding this: when healthy, the king himself should carry out all this without neglecting the protection of his subjects; but when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his ministers. (7.226)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Duties of Kings," in the Commentary on Manu composed by Govindarāja, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mādhava, which follows the teachings of Manu. || 6 ||
Chapter Eight:
Desiring to inspect legal proceedings, the king, modestly attired, shall enter the court together with Brāhmaṇas and ministers who are experts in counsel. 8.1.

"A king shall examine legal cases" means that a king, desiring to inspect the matters of dispute between plaintiff and defendant—cases concerning the non-payment of debts and so forth, which consist of mutual conflicting claims—should enter the court to be described hereafter, accompanied by ministers possessing the characteristics to be mentioned and who are conversant with the five-limbed counsel previously described, and himself free from fickleness and other such defects. (8.1)
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and being modest in dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.

"In that regard": in that assembly, having sat down with respect for the weightiness of the matter and rising otherwise [when it is concluded], and having uncovered his right arm from his garment, with his dress and ornaments not ostentatious, he shall invariably deliberate upon the legal proceedings of those who have come seeking justice. (8.2)
Day by day, through reasons observed in the world and observed in the scriptures, [these matters] were recorded separately in eighteen different categories. (8.3)

"Daily" means that those legal proceedings—which are established separately within the eighteen titles of law to be described hereafter, beginning with non-payment of debt—must indeed be examined every day by means of a system consistent with local custom for merchants, farmers, and others, as well as by a system derived from the scriptures, consisting of witnesses, oaths, inference, and so forth. (8.3)
Of these, the first is non-payment of debt; then deposit, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given. (8.4)
The non-payment of wages, the breach of an agreement, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and his herdsman; 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault, theft, violence, and the abduction of women; 8.6.
The duties of women and men, partition of inheritance, gambling, and betting—these eighteen are the titles of law established here in this world. (8.7)

Regarding the phrase "of these": [the topics are] wages, boundary disputes, the law concerning women and men, and so forth. Among these eighteen, first is considered here the non-payment of a debt incurred through unlawful means. Following that, in sequence: deposits; sale and other transactions made by one who is not the owner; the desire to acquire wealth by joining together; the non-delivery of what was given or promised for the sake of a sacrifice or similar purpose when the sacrifice is not performed; non-payment of wages; violation of established agreements regarding villages and the like; regret after having purchased or sold; disputes between owners and herdsmen; settlement of disputes over boundaries of villages and the like; verbal abuse, physical assault, and so forth; theft; robbery involving force such as plundering; sexual intercourse with women, both mutual and with another's wife; the legal arrangement regarding a husband accompanied by his wife; the partition of paternal and other types of property; the regulation of games such as dice; and the pitting of animals, birds, and the like against one another—these eighteen are the bases for the arising of legal proceedings in the world. (8.4–7)
In these matters, for men who are mostly engaged in disputes,
one should determine the outcome of the case by resorting to the eternal dharma.

"In these" means: in these eighteen titles of law (*sthāna*), which are established bases for human beings who frequently engage in disputes, one should carry out the determination of legal proceedings by relying on the established rules handed down through beginningless tradition. Because of the use of the word "mostly" (*bhūyiṣṭha*), there are others as well. As stated by Nārada:
"A further subdivision of these alone is recorded as being one hundred and eight. (NSM 1.8)
But when the king himself does not personally attend to the inspection of legal affairs,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to inspect those affairs.

Regarding the phrase "yadā" (when): when, due to being preoccupied with other affairs, the king himself does not attend to legal proceedings, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the administration of justice. (8.9)
Surrounded by three members of the assembly, he should examine his legal cases, having entered the foremost hall, either seated or standing. (8.10)

"He" refers to that Brāhmaṇa who, joined by virtuous and righteous Brāhmaṇas in the assembly, having entered that very excellent royal court, whether seated or standing, shall examine the legal cases to be seen by this king. 8.10.
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together, along with a learned man appointed by the king, they know that assembly as a *brahma-sabhā*. (8.11)

"In which"—in that place where three Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as a learned man appointed by the king, reside, they regard that assembly hall as being like Hiraṇyagarbha himself. 8.11.
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly, and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (8.12)

When a judge, though not oppressed by an unjust decision according to the established rules of the Dharmaśāstra, sits upon the bench, and the members of the court—being Brahmins—do not extract the dart known as unrighteousness (adharma) which is like a thorn lodged there, then those members of the court are pierced by that dart of unrighteousness. (8.12)
One should either not enter the assembly or speak what is correct;
for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner. (8.13)

"Or one should not enter the assembly": for the purpose of witnessing legal proceedings, one should not enter the court; but if one has entered, then one must speak the truth. Alternatively, by remaining silent or speaking falsely, the member of the court itself becomes guilty of sin. (8.13)
For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members of the assembly look on, they too are slain. (8.14)

"In which [assembly]" means: in whatever assembly the dharma of the plaintiff or the defendant is subverted while the judges and others seated in that assembly look on; and where truth is subverted by falsehood by the witnesses—in such cases, those judges and members of the assembly are struck down by sin. Therefore, even the transgression committed by the defendant against the witnesses must not be tolerated. (8.14)
Dharma alone, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma slay us. (8.15)

Regarding "Dharma": therefore, it is Dharma alone that, when transgressed, destroys both visible and invisible [merits], and not the plaintiff, the defendant, or others. And it is that very same Dharma which, by not being transgressed, protects them. Therefore, Dharma must not be overstepped, lest Dharma, being transgressed, cause the destruction of our visible and invisible interests while we are associated with you. Thus, the members of the court (sabhyas) should admonish the judge (prāḍvivāka) who has engaged in improper conduct. (8.15)
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed the Bull (vṛṣa); those who act against him, the gods know as a Vṛṣala (outcaste). Therefore, one should not destroy Dharma. 8.16.

Regarding the word *vṛṣa*: therefore, among all those whose desires have been fulfilled (*kāmavarṇa*), the word *vṛṣa* denotes *dharma*. He performs the utterance of that [word]. The gods consider him a *vṛṣala*, not a *vṛṣala* by birth; thus, the term *vṛṣala* is used for the purpose of avoiding the transgression of *dharma*, so that one should not destroy *dharma*. (8.16)
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for everything else indeed perishes along with the body. (8.17)

"Alone": therefore, everything else—wife, sons, friends, and so forth—perishes along with the body itself; nothing follows after one for the sake of protection as dharma does. Therefore, one should not abandon dharma, which is a true friend. (8.17)
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness, one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king. (8.18)

Regarding the word "pāda" (quarter): this is intended to demonstrate that, according to worldly convention, one quarter of the demerit associated with the case goes to either the plaintiff or the defendant as they proceed in the lawsuit; another quarter goes to the witness who speaks untruthfully; and yet another quarter goes to the king, bypassing all the other members of the court as they look on. Thus, there is a connection with demerit for everyone. (8.18)
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the assembly are released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (8.19)

Regarding the word "king": furthermore, in a court where either the plaintiff or the defendant is censured for speaking falsely because of their lack of right vision, the king becomes sinless and the members of the assembly are not connected with the sin; rather, it goes only to the one who committed the offense regarding the matter and so forth. 8.19.
One who merely lives by his birth may, if he so desires, be called a "pseudo-Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva);
however, a Śūdra can never be a proclaimer of dharma to the king. (8.20)

"One who lives by his birth alone" means one who possesses nothing but the mere status of the Brāhmaṇa caste; such a person, following the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, would be the authorized proclaimer of Dharma for this king in the absence of learned Brāhmaṇas, but never a Śūdra. Since the prohibition of a Śūdra is already established by the rule "then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa," the repetition here serves to exclude the appointment of a Śūdra specifically, as opposed to the appointment of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. (8.20)
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow sinking in the mud while he looks on. (8.21)
"Because of whom, and for whom": when a Śūdra performs the deliberation of dharma for a king, that kingdom sinks away even as he looks on, like a cow in the mud. 8.21.
That kingdom, abounding in Śūdras, overrun by atheists, and devoid of the twice-born, will quickly perish in its entirety, afflicted by famine and disease. (8.22)

Regarding the word "that": that kingdom which is populated mostly by Śūdras, overrun by those who look only to the world beyond, and devoid of twice-born men—all of it, having become afflicted by famine and disease, perishes. This is because of the absence of the [Vedic] verse beginning with *agnau prāsta* (when cast into the fire), and due to the lack of sacrifices and other rites intended for peace. 8.22.
Having occupied the Dharma-seat, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should perform the judicial investigation after bowing to the guardians of the world.

Regarding the "seat of dharma": having bowed to the guardians of the world, he should conduct the examination of legal cases. For the purpose of administering justice, having sat upon his seat with his body covered and his mind undistracted, and having paid homage to the guardians of the world, the king should thereafter attend to the investigation of lawsuits. (8.23)
Having understood both profit and loss, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes. (8.24)

"Regarding 'gain and loss'": having observed such worldly conditions consisting of the natural pacification or provocation [of subjects], and having looked solely at merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) for the sake of the next world, he should oversee all legal proceedings in such a way that there is no loss of merit and no arising of demerit or loss. Furthermore, in an assembly of social classes (*varṇas*), he should preside according to the order beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. (8.24)
One should discern the internal state of men by external signs: through their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, gaze, and movements. (8.25)

"By external [signs]" means: by means of external indicators—such as stammering and other vocal qualities, paleness of complexion and other colors, trembling, horripilation, and other gestures; discoloration and other facial expressions; downward glancing and other such forms; and specific movements like the clenching of hands in the four directions—the practitioner, having perceived through these inherently indicative natures the hidden intention of worldly people, whether it be real or unreal, reaches a certainty. 8.25.
By means of outward forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived. (8.26)

For even in the world, it is said: "The internal mind is known through facial expressions and distortions of the eyes. By means of the aforementioned expressions and so forth, as well as by a gait characterized by stumbling, one's hidden true nature is recognized. (8.26)
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his childhood. (8.27)

Regarding the phrase "the property of a child heir" (*bāladāyādika*): the king shall protect the wealth belonging to a child who is without a guardian, until that child has returned from the teacher’s house or until his childhood has passed. This rule is stated in this legal proceeding for the purpose of protecting the property from those—such as paternal uncles—who seek to seize it under the pretext of asserting their own ownership; for the king's duty of protection, which pertains to general matters, extends to all subjects. (8.27)

The same protection should be afforded to women who have sons by a eunuch, to those whose families have perished, to women devoted to their husbands, and to widows who are afflicted by illness. (8.28)

Regarding the phrase "of the sons of barren women": just as the king must protect the property of a child, so too must there be protection for women who are barren, those who have no offspring even though their husband is alive, those of undivided lineage, unmarried girls, those whose husbands are dead or absent, virtuous wives, and those afflicted by disease; here, multiple terms are employed according to the maxim of "the cow and the ox" (to include all such cases). 8.28.
But those kinsmen who might seize the property of these women while they are still alive, the righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves. 8.29.
"Of those who are living": by means of such pretexts as future ownership or dependence on them, those kinsmen might seize the wealth of those women while they are still alive. (8.29)
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in custody for three years;
within three years the owner may reclaim it, but after that period the king may take it for himself. (8.30)

"Property whose owner has disappeared": the king, having announced by means of a drum or other such means—"Whose property is this? What has been lost?"—should keep wealth whose owner is unknown at the city gates and other such places for three years. If the owner arrives within three years, he may take it; but after that, the king shall take it. He may seize it as long as the owner does not come. Thus, because it would be unjust to deprive another of his property even after hundreds of years, [the term] "lost" refers to the period prior to that. (8.30)
He who says, "This is mine," shall be questioned according to the rule;
having verified the form, number, and other details, the owner deserves that property. (8.31)

Regarding the phrase "this is mine": he who says, "This wealth belongs to me," must be interrogated according to such rules as, "What is its substance? What is its quantity? Where was it lost? and so forth. Thereafter, if he declares the appearance, the number, and other details truthfully, he is entitled to take that wealth. (8.31)
One who does not truly report the place, the time, the color, the appearance, and the size of what has been lost deserves a fine equal to the value of that object. (8.32)

"Without declaring" means that for one who does not correctly know the place and time of the lost property as far as possible, its color, price, and so forth, its appearance, such as whether it has a handle, and its size, the punishment shall be equal to that [of a thief]. (8.32)
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth part, or even a tenth or a twelfth, of goods lost and then found. (8.33)

"Furthermore, in the case of agreement regarding the number and other details, he should take [a portion]"—meaning that when the king recovers what was lost, after verifying the number and other particulars belonging to the owner, he should take a sixth, tenth, or twelfth part out of regard for the trouble of guarding it; this is the duty of righteous men, and thus the king should take it, while returning the remainder to the owner. (8.33)
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves the king may catch therein, he should cause to be executed by means of an elephant.

"Regarding 'what is recovered from what was lost': when a certain person's property has been lost and subsequently found by royal officers, the king should protect it. Having appointed someone to guard it, the king should maintain it; and regarding that property, since it is seen [in the law] that for those thieves whom the king may seize, there shall be death if the value exceeds one hundred [gold pieces], he should have them executed by an elephant in the case of theft involving a value of one hundred gold pieces or more. (8.34)
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth part of it, or even a twelfth. (8.35)

"This is mine"—if a person should speak thus regarding a treasure, asserting that "this hoard belongs to me" or that it belongs to someone else, provided his claim is true through corroboration by witnesses or by agreement with prior declarations, the king shall take a sixth or even a twelfth part of that treasure from him, having regard for the place, time, caste, and other factors, and he shall leave the remainder to him. (8.35)
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth, or a smaller fraction of the value of that very treasure. (8.36)

"Regarding 'untruth': those who, having been questioned, speak falsely while claiming it to be the truth, shall be fined one-eighth of their own property. Or, if he [the finder] calculates an extremely small portion of that very treasure such that he does not fall into despair and accepts the legal settlement, he shall be fined; there is an option [regarding the amount] depending on whether the person is virtuous or lacking in virtue. (8.36)
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited, may take it entirely, for he is the lord of all. (8.37)

Regarding the term "learned" (*vidvān*): a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the scriptures, upon seeing a treasure deposited by his ancestors or others, shall not give a share to the king; he should take the whole of it. The statement that "the Brāhmaṇa is the master of every kind of wealth" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of taking the entirety. And as for the phrase "this is mine": this refers to the case of an unlearned Brāhmaṇa and to the case of Kṣatriyas and others. (8.37)
But whatever ancient treasure a king may discover buried in the earth, he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury. (8.38)

Regarding the word "yam" (which): furthermore, if one should find a treasure buried in the earth whose owner is long deceased, he shall give half of it to Brahmins and deposit the other half in his own treasury.
For regarding ancient treasures and minerals in the earth, the king is entitled to a half-share because of his protection; indeed, he is the lord of the land. (8.38–39)

Regarding the phrase "of treasures": since the king takes half of ancient treasures that have no owner, which have been found by another and lie buried in the earth—because he protects them, he is the lord of the soil. (8.39)
Let this wealth stolen by thieves from all castes be given back by the king;
for the king who makes use of it incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.40)

"It must be given. Whatever wealth of the people has been stolen by thieves, that wealth, once recovered from the thieves by the king, must be returned to them; for if the king were to keep it for himself, he incurs as much sin as the thief. (8.40)
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should establish the specific duty for each individual. 8.41

"Regarding the customs of castes and regions": having ascertained the customs of castes—such as Vedic study and the like—and the customs of regions, which are established practices of specific localities, provided they are not contradictory; likewise, having ascertained the guild customs pertaining to merchants, farmers, and so forth, and the family customs established within specific families, he should establish each person's own duty (*svadharma*) accordingly. Furthermore, for those who engage in conduct contrary to these, he should restrain the litigant. (8.41)
Even when they are far away, those men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world. (8.42)

Because they are their own: even while performing the duties of their caste, family, and locality, and remaining close to those who lack discernment and affection, men established in their own respective works become dear to the next world through their actions toward others. (8.42)
The king himself should not initiate a legal matter against anyone else, nor should he ever seize for himself a case brought by another. (8.43)

Having thus explained the matter concerning wealth through a series of related topics, he now states the general rule: "The king himself shall not initiate a lawsuit, nor that of anyone else. Although it has been stated that "he should examine the cases of the litigants," nevertheless, by way of an implied restriction, the king himself must not, through instigation, initiate lawsuits regarding matters such as the non-payment of debts and so forth—excluding those duties incumbent upon the king, such as the punishment of crimes (*sāhasa*) and protection. Nor should an official appointed by the king initiate one on his own; the same should be understood to apply to the defendants as well. He must not, for any reason such as passion or hatred, remain indifferent toward the purpose of the case. (8.43)
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference. 8.44

"Yathā" means: just as a hunter tracks the path of a wounded deer whose tracks have vanished by observing drops of blood flowing from its wound, so should the king determine the course of justice through the means of inference (*anumāna*). He should establish the legal standard for regions, families, and castes based on that which has been practiced by learned twice-born men who prioritize dharma and is not contrary to the scriptures. This is for the purpose of making an effort to grasp the internal disposition of litigants by means of their speech and other signs. 8.44.
Abiding by the rules of legal procedure, one should examine the truth, the matter at hand, oneself as the witness, the place, the appearance, and the time. (8.45)

"Truth," [it is said]. A king engaged in the business of worldly affairs should perceive truth as the cause of both seeing and not seeing; he should perceive wealth according to its essence or lack thereof; himself by means of his good or evil deeds; the territory by its immediate neighboring kings; his pleasure-park; time in relation to his life-span; and this physical form as being subject to disease, old age, and consumption, so that he may not stumble through greed and other vices. (8.45)
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, that one should establish for countries, families, and castes, provided it is not contradictory [to sacred law]. 8.46

Regarding the phrase "by the virtuous": this [rule] would apply to a litigant in cases of conflicting practices; however, because the expression "practiced by the virtuous" is employed here, this refers to the domain of the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*), whereas [the previous rule concerning] caste, local custom, and so forth, refers to a domain of dharma distinct from the conduct of the virtuous. || 846 ||
When urged by the creditor for the purpose of fulfilling the debtor's obligation, the king shall cause the debtor to pay the proven amount to the creditor. (8.47)

Having thus stated the general technical terminology common to all legal procedures, he now speaks concerning the non-payment of debts and other matters, beginning with the words "for the sake of establishing the claim of the debtor" (*adhamarṇārthasiddhyartham*). "He shall cause the debtor to pay the wealth of the creditor that has been proved by the debtor. Being informed by the owner of the wealth for the purpose of recovering what was taken by the debtor—the creditor—the king, having been made aware [of the case], shall cause the debtor to pay to the owner of the wealth the amount established by means of the documents and other proofs to be described hereafter. This is a general indication of the detailed exposition that follows. (8.47)
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth, by those very means he should constrain the debtor and compel him to pay. 8.48.
"By whatever means" (yair yair iti): By whichever means a creditor obtains his own wealth, by those very means he should restrain the debtor and compel him to pay that debt. (8.48)
One should recover a debt through legal process, through trickery, through customary practice, and by the application of force as the fifth means. (8.49)

By what means, then, are these [debts] to be recovered? To this he says: "by lawful means" (*dharmeṇa*). That wealth which has been lent by the creditor to the debtor is to be recovered from the creditor by means of *dharma*—that is, by legal procedure (*nīti*), by judicial process (*vyavahāra*), by the methods to be described hereafter, by trickery (*chala*) such as taking collateral under a pretext, by customary practice (*ācarita*) such as the seizure of goods, by fasting and other such acts, by force (*bala*) such as confinement in the house, and fifthly, by the aforementioned [means]. || 8.49 ||
A creditor who recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own. (8.50)

"By himself" means that a creditor, without resorting to legal proceedings, may recover his own wealth from a debtor through means such as moral pressure (*dharma*) or by employing men, independently of the king. The king must not be reproached thus: "You have imprisoned him and so forth without my permission while he was recovering his own property. (8.50)
But if the debtor denies the debt when it has been made manifest by means of evidence,
the king shall compel him to pay the creditor's due and a small fine according to his ability.

"But if he denies the matter, one should establish it by means of evidence. If the debtor disputes the debt, saying "I will not pay this to him," the king should cause the creditor to receive his money once the debtor has been proven by evidence consisting of written documents, witnesses, or other means. (8.51)
When a debtor, being summoned in court by a creditor who says "Pay!", denies the debt, the judge shall cause him to point out a surety or state another valid reason for his denial. (8.52)

Regarding "denial" (apahnava): When the plaintiff points out the place [of the transaction] or cites another witness, and when the defendant—having been addressed by the judge in court with the words "Give! to the debtor or "The wealth! to the creditor—denies it by saying "I do not owe," he should declare the evidence (*karaṇa*) because of his denial of the place of the accusation, the anger, the seizure, and the presentation of witnesses present there. (8.52)

He who gives false testimony, he who, having testified, retracts his statement, and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows—[these are also untrustworthy]. (8.53)
Furthermore, he who, having stated and restated his case, then evades it;
or who, when questioned, does not accept a matter that has been correctly established. (8.54)
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer a question being put to him, or he who runs away; 8.55.
When told "Speak," he does not speak; and what has been said, he does not clarify.
He does not understand the sequence of what precedes and follows; therefore, he fails in his case. (8.56)

He who points out an improper place, and having pointed it out, denies it; he who, having pointed it out, says "I did not point it out"; he who says "Speak" [to the witnesses] when he ought not to speak; he who, being the plaintiff, fails to point out the place as prescribed; therein, he who as the claimant (*arthin*) points out such an improper place where neither the giving nor the receiving is possible, or where the debtor’s presence there at that time is impossible; he who, having pointed out an improper place and so forth, subsequently disclaims it, saying "This was not pointed out by me"; he who does not understand the mutually contradictory matters stated earlier and later; he who, having pointed out that "Gold was taken from my hand by him," then withdraws by saying "It was received by him through a document" and so forth; he who, when questioned properly by the judge during the expansion of the plaint, conceals the matter that was presented at the time of the formal plea—asking "Why was the giving or receiving done in such a way at night or at such a time?"; he who converses with witnesses in a place unfit for conversation, such as a secluded grove; he who does not attend while the questioning of witnesses is being conducted; or he who, having leaped up from his seat due to agitation caused by the presence of the defendant, departs from the court; he who, when told "What do you say regarding this plaint? fails to give an answer; or he who cannot substantiate his claim through witnesses, or who previously did not know what was recorded in the witness-declaration; and he who, though the sequence of his own statements is clear, fails to clarify them—he is defeated in that legal proceeding. (8.53–56)
