If one says, "I have witnesses," but when told "Produce them," he does not produce them, the judge shall declare him to be defeated on these grounds. (8.57)

Regarding the term "witnesses": when one has said, "I have witnesses here," and is told, "Name them," if he should not name them, the judge (prādvivāka) engaged in the determination of justice shall declare of him, "He is defeated" by these aforementioned grounds for defeat.
If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall be punished with death according to the law;
if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated.

Regarding the term "plaintiff" (*abhiyoktṛ*): if one who is the claimant (*arthin*) does not state his case immediately, then, depending on the degree of his transgression against the law (*dharma*), he should be liable to corporal punishment and be fined. Furthermore, if one who has been summoned (*ākṣipta*) does not speak within three fortnights, then he is defeated in matters of law because of his unrighteous conduct and lack of virtue. (8.58)
Whatever amount of wealth one may conceal, or whatever amount one may falsely state, those two—being ignorant of dharma—must be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount. (8.59)

Regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): whichever defendant denies a certain amount of wealth, or whichever plaintiff falsely states a certain amount of wealth during an act of unrighteousness (*adharmapravṛtti*), he should be made to pay double that denied or falsely stated amount as a fine. Because of the expression "ignorant of dharma," this refers to cases involving extreme obstinacy and the like. However, in the case of denial due to mere obstinacy, the author will later state that the fine shall be ten percent, even though it is double that [two-fold] amount. (8.59)

But one who, having been questioned, denies [the claim] while being established in his position by a creditor seeking wealth, shall be judged by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas. 8.60.

"Being questioned": when the defendant, having suffered humiliation such as being dragged away by royal officers at the hands of the creditor seeking his wealth, denies the claim before the judge by saying "I do not know," then he must be made to prove his case there by three witnesses who are not excessively inferior [in status] to him, in the presence of the king's appointed Brahmins. (8.60)
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be appointed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them. (8.61)

Regarding the word "which": I shall describe the kinds of witnesses who are to be employed by creditors and others in legal proceedings such as the non-payment of debts; and I shall also explain the manner in which they must speak the truth. (8.61)

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, are worthy of being called as witnesses when summoned for a legal matter, but not just anyone, except in times of emergency. (8.62)

Regarding the term "householders" (*gṛhinaḥ*): householders who have sons, who are natives of that same region, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, when designated as suitors, are fit to serve as witnesses. They too do not speak falsely out of fear of being deprived of their homes and other possessions. [Objection: But in certain legal proceedings—such as those concerning the non-payment of debts, or cases involving verbal and physical assault—is it not the case that even persons other than those mentioned, such as householders and so forth, may also be witnesses? 8.62.

Trustworthy persons from all castes should be made witnesses in legal matters, provided they are knowledgeable in all dharmas and free from greed; however, one should avoid those who are the opposite.

"Trustworthy persons" means that witnesses should be appointed from among all castes who do not contradict one another in their dealings, who are learned in all the treatises on dharma, and who are free from greed; the meaning is that one should avoid those who are the opposite of this. The mention of "established" (siddha) is for the purpose of imposing a fine.

One should not employ those who have a financial interest, nor those who are unreliable, nor companions, nor enemies; nor those whose faults are evident, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt. (8.64)

"No," [it is said]. Witnesses should not be appointed when there is a suspicion of unjust testimony due to fear, greed, passion, hatred, loss of memory, or similar causes. Those who have a financial relationship with the creditor or debtor, those who are friends or enemies, those who have committed perjury, those afflicted by disease, fainting, or chronic illness, and those who are corrupt—these should not be made witnesses. (8.64)
The king must not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments. (8.65)

"Not as a witness" means that because he is the king's minister, because he has observed the legal proceedings, and because it is impossible to question him according to the rules of the sacred law (*śāstradharma*), he should not be made a witness. Cooks, actors, and others who have renounced the Vedas while remaining householders—these, though devoted to dharma, should not be made witnesses; for actors and the like are generally intent on wealth, are consumed by their own occupations, and are distracted, so they should not be made witnesses. Nor should those established in the outward marks (*liṅga*)—Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), celibate students (*brahmacārin*), ascetics (*tāpasa*), and mendicants (*bhikṣu*)—who are free from attachment, be made witnesses. By the mention of "Vedic scholar," there is no prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa who lacks study and ritual performance. (8.65)

Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts; neither an elderly man, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties. (8.66)

"Not dependent" (*nādhyadhīna*): a "dependent slave" (*adhyadhīna-garbhadāsa*) is not to be employed because of his extreme subservience. One who is "blameworthy" (*garhaṇīya*) due to the faults of all his actions—meaning one who is called a "thief" (*dasyu*), a "hireling" (*bhṛtaka*), or a "false witness" (*asatyudāsa*) precisely because of his contemptible speech and so forth, according to the etymologists (*nairukta*) regarding such activities—he too is not to be employed because of his dependence on others. Likewise, a "thief" (*taskara*) will be described later; he is excluded because he performs prohibited acts and is untrustworthy. An "old man" (*vṛddha*) is excluded because his capacity for legal transactions has passed. A "child" (*śiśu*) is excluded because he lacks the capacity for legal transactions. Even a single person is not permitted, due to the suspicion of loss or flight; since the prohibition by the phrase "by at least three" (*tryavaraiḥ*) is already established, this statement is intended to permit two persons under certain circumstances. An "outcaste" (*antyaja*), such as a *caṇḍāla* and so forth, is excluded because of his ignorance of the Dharma. One with "deficient senses" (*vikalendriya*) is excluded because of the impairment of his perception. (8.66)
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane; neither one oppressed by hunger and thirst, nor afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by passion, nor angry, nor even a thief. (8.67)

"Not distressed" means: one who is distressed by the loss of relatives and so forth; intoxicated by liquor and the like; insane, being possessed by spirits and the like; overcome by hunger or thirst; exhausted, being weary from traveling on foot and so forth; overcome by passion; and thieves, because of their lack of righteousness, are not [suitable witnesses] due to their extreme impairment of the intellect through anger. (8.67)
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men; virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of the lowest birth for those of the lowest castes. (8.68)

Regarding the phrase "of women": since women serve as witnesses for women, this rule concerns matters pertaining to women's affairs that are generally secret and outside the sphere of others. In such cases, if a man were to act as a witness, there might arise a constant suspicion as to why he is not within the scope [of secrecy]. In other legal proceedings, such as those concerning the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth, they have the same witnesses as previously stated; this same principle should be understood to apply to rules such as "of the twice-born" (*dvijānām*) and the like. For the twice-born—the Brāhmaṇas and others—there are twice-born men of equal caste and qualities; for Śūdras, there are virtuous Śūdras; and for Caṇḍālas and the like, there are only those of their own kind. (8.68)
But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants in a private house, in a forest, or even in a matter involving the loss of life; 8.69.

"Anubhāvī" (an eyewitness): whoever has personally witnessed [an event]—whether it be a disturbance caused by thieves such as the theft of jewels and other goods within the house, or physical injury inflicted by assassins and the like, or [any matter] for the sake of one's own business such as the non-payment of debts—and who is capable of producing the aforementioned witnesses, becomes a witness for the litigants. (8.69)
In the absence of a woman, the duty may be performed by a child, an elderly person, a disciple, a relative, or even a slave or a hired servant. (8.70)
"Regarding women": when there are no men present in the inner apartments and similar locations, even women, children, the elderly, pupils, kinsmen, slaves, and laborers may serve as witnesses. (8.70)
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick who speak falsely in witness-depositions is unstable, as is the speech of those with agitated minds. (8.71)

Now, one might object: "Since the testimony of women and others is forbidden when instability of intellect and similar causes are known, how can a determination be reached here [in this case] based on their words? To this he says: "Of children, the aged, and the sick... Children, the elderly, the diseased, those of unsteady mind, and those such as the intoxicated or insane, speak falsely; therefore, one should recognize them in testimony through inference, thinking, "One should discern [them] by external signs" (8.71).
In all cases of violence, in theft and adultery, and in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely. (8.72)

Regarding the phrase "in cases of violence" (*sahaseṣu*): in all acts of violence, such as tearing clothes or setting fire [to property], as well as in theft, adultery, verbal abuse, and physical assault, one should not examine witnesses based on their status as householders, their sons, their wealth, and so forth. However, for children, matters involving property, and the like, examination by means of inference is not prohibited. If that were the case, would it not result in a state of uncertainty? For it has been stated [elsewhere] regarding children, the elderly, and the sick, etc. (YDh 8.72).

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, O lord of men, the king should accept the majority; but if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict even among those distinguished by virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.

Where there are claimants, defendants, and witnesses, there [the rule of] plurality applies. Among all witnesses, when those who have been examined provide mutually contradictory statements, the judge should accept as the basis for the decision that which was stated by the majority. But if the number of witnesses is equal on both sides, he should rely upon those who possess superior qualities. In the case of a disagreement among those of superior qualities, he should rely upon Brāhmaṇas who possess superior qualities on both sides. (8.73)
Testimony is established by seeing or hearing in person;
in such a case, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from merit or wealth. (8.74)

"Because of seeing in person": when [the matter] is perceivable by the eye, it is established as evidence through direct observation; and when it is perceivable by the ear, testimony is established through direct [hearing]. In such cases, a witness who speaks the truth is not deprived of dharma and artha, because by producing the merit of truthful speech, there is an absence of punishment. (8.74)
A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men concerning anything other than what was seen or heard goes headfirst to hell after death and is deprived of heaven. (8.75)

Regarding the term "witness": a witness who, in an assembly of Brahmins, speaks falsely—contrary to what was seen or heard—and in contradiction [to the truth], goes headfirst into hell. In the next world, when there is an obstruction of that sin by means of heaven and the like produced from other meritorious deeds, he is diminished [of his merit]. (8.75)
Even where one has not been formally appointed, if one should see or hear anything at all, one should report that matter there as well, exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard. (8.76)

"In which case": even though he has been bound by the agreement, "May you be my witness," if he should see anything there such as a debt-transaction or hear anything such as verbal abuse, then, being questioned, he must not fail to declare what he has perceived as a witness. (8.76)

A single person who is greedy shall not be a witness, nor shall women, even if they are pure; this is because the intellect of women is unstable, and others who are tainted by faults should also be excluded. (8.77)

"One who is greedy is not a witness at all. Thus, even one who is not greedy but possesses extreme vices may, under certain circumstances, become a single witness. Furthermore, women—due to their instability and fickleness—are never witnesses, even if they are numerous or endowed with integrity and purity, in a lawsuit concerning the non-payment of debt or similar matters where the parties are otherwise sound. However, it has been stated that "in the absence of others, women may also be made witnesses" in cases of extreme necessity. Likewise, those who are tainted by other defects such as impurity and so forth would also not be witnesses in a lawsuit involving sound parties. (8.77)
Whatever they may say by their very nature, that should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is meaningless. (8.78)

"By their own nature" means that non-witnesses should speak the truth according to their natural disposition. Since the purpose [of testimony] is the determination of legal proceedings, whatever they might say that is contradictory—spoken for some other motive rather than out of their natural disposition—is useless and therefore not to be accepted. (8.78)
When the witnesses have arrived in the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, the judge shall question them, consoling them with this following procedure: (8.79)

"In the midst of the assembly" (sabhāntare): the king or his appointed Brahmin official, acting with kindness, should question the witnesses who have arrived in the middle of the assembly in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, in the manner that is about to be described. (8.79)
"Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for you possess the status of witnesses here. (8.80)

"Regarding that which: indeed, whatever has transpired between these two parties—the plaintiff and the defendant—concerning an improper matter, tell all of it with truth; for that must be seen by you here directly. (8.80)
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains irreproachable worlds;
moreover, he gains unsurpassed fame in this world—for such speech is honored by Brahmā.

"Truth. By speaking the truth in the matter of giving testimony, one attains the most excellent worlds such as Brahmaloka, and in this world as well, one gains preeminent renown; for this speech, which consists of truth, was honored by Prajāpati. (8.81)
Speaking falsely when giving testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred lifetimes, rendered powerless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony. 8.82.

Regarding the term "testimony": because one who gives false testimony in a judicial proceeding is bound for a hundred births by the nooses of Varuṇa—serpentine cords over which he has no control—one should therefore speak only the truth in testimony. (8.82)
By truth a witness is purified; by truth dharma increases.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes. 8.83

"By truth": because by means of truth a witness is released even from other sinful acts, and his merit increases through the speaking of truth; therefore, witnesses must speak the truth regarding all social classes. 8.83.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self. Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men. 8.84

Regarding the word "self" (*ātman*): since for a self engaged in auspicious or inauspicious actions, the self alone is the witness and the self alone is the refuge of the self, therefore you should know this very self of yours to be the supreme witness among men. Do not deceive it by speaking untruth, having formed the thought, "By whom was this seen of mine?"—because here, the self exists as your all-seeing, most excellent witness. The designation of the self as both the agent and the object of action is intended solely for the purpose of preventing falsehood. (8.84)
Evil-doers indeed think, "No one sees us"; yet the gods see them, as does their own inner self (antarapūruṣa). 8.85.

"They think, 'We are alone. Yet the gods behold them, as does their own inner person (antarapūruṣa). They perceive themselves in their sinful conduct, thinking, 'No one sees us,' but they do not realize that the aforementioned gods see them, and their own inner self also sees them. (8.85)
The sky, the earth, the waters, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, and the wind;
night, the two twilights, and Dharma—these are the knowers of the conduct of all embodied beings. (8.86)

Regarding the word "dyaiḥ": in the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), because of the perspective found in the *itihāsas* and other texts, there exists for the earth, water, moon, sun, fire, wind, night, the twilights, and dharma a form possessed of a physical body (*vigrahavat*). These, as well as the Self (*ātman*) residing in the heart and Yama, know the conduct of all embodied beings.

In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either the north or the east. (8.87)

"In the presence of gods and Brahmins": when the presence of the aforementioned deities has been established through paintings and the like, and in the presence of Brahmins and members of the court, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born witnesses—who have attained the nature of truth through their diligent performance [of the ordeal]—in the forenoon, while they are facing north or east. (8.87)
One should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak"; the King, "Speak the truth"; the Vaiśya, with [threats of] cattle, seed, and gold; and the Śūdra, with all [the aforementioned] sins. 8.88.

"Speak!"—thus he should address a Brāhmaṇa; a Kṣatriya, after saying "Truth"; a Vaiśya, with the words, "Whatever sin there is in the theft of cattle, seed, or gold would be yours if you speak falsely"; and a Śūdra, with the words set forth hereafter that describe various sins. (8.88)
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the murderer of women and children,
and for the betrayer of friends and the ungrateful— those shall be the lot of one who speaks falsely.

"The worlds ordained for killers of Brahmins, and those for killers of women and children"—those hells and other realms ordained by the sages for those who harm Brahmins, women, and children, as well as for those who do harm here and those who have committed evil deeds—those shall be yours if you speak falsely. (8.89)
"O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—all of that shall go to a dog if you speak otherwise. (8.90)

"From birth onwards," etc.: O auspicious boy, whatever merit has been performed from birth onwards—all that shall belong to you; [the priest] would say it yields fruit for the dog if you speak untruth. (8.90)
O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, "I am alone," this sage who observes merit and demerit is ever present within your heart. (8.91)

"Regarding the word 'one': O noble one, do not think thus of yourself—that you are 'one' alone, or that you are the very self consisting of the body merely. For [the Self] who is the witness of merits and sins, whose nature is that of a sage, and whose form is absolutely pure, is eternally established within your heart. (8.91)
The god Yama, son of Vivasvat, who dwells here within your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the land of the Kurus.

"Yama": This deity named Yama, who consists of all beings, is the son of Vivasvat, the Sun; because he has come within the range of your hearing, he flashes forth in your heart. Since there is no dispute with him—because you have not committed any unrighteous acts (*adharma*) with him—at that time, for the sake of purifying your sins, do not go to the Gaṅgā or Kurukṣetra. || 9.92 ||
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty, and blind—such shall he be who goes to an enemy’s house as a beggar for alms if he speaks false testimony. (8.93)

"Regarding the word 'naked': 'The blind man should go to the enemy's house' means that he who gives false testimony shall go naked—having his hair shorn as a mark of humiliation—to the enemy's house like a blind man, afflicted by hunger and thirst, clad in a rag, for the sake of alms. This is stated as applying specifically to witnesses; it is not intended as a question regarding Śūdras, because of the use of the second-person pronoun (*madhyama-puruṣa*). These were thus established as oaths. (8.93)
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell, he who, when questioned regarding the determination of dharma, speaks falsely. (8.94)

"Downward" (avāk): he who, when questioned for the sake of determining the Dharma, speaks falsely in response to the inquiry—that sinner shall fall headlong into a hell of exceedingly dense darkness. 8.94.
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man. (8.95)

"Blind" refers to one who, having entered an assembly, speaks what he has not seen due to the delusion of a forged document; such a person, like a blind man eating fish with thorns, acquires only excessive suffering while acting for the sake of pleasure. (8.95)
For the gods know no other man in this world to be more excellent than that learned man whose speech the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) does not distrust. 8.96

Regarding the phrase "of whom": the meaning is that the gods do not consider any other person more praiseworthy than that man from whom one has no apprehension when speaking—thinking, "Does he speak truth or falsehood?"—but who speaks the truth with absolute certainty, being entirely free from doubt. 8.96.
Listen, gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony, in that very order, according to their count. (8.97)

Regarding the phrase "as many as": listen to the number of friends and other relatives whom one who speaks falsely in a legal proceeding concerning an animal or similar object will be joined with in hell, according to that same number, in due order, as I shall now state. From this it follows that by performing an act that causes another to fall into hell, that person also goes to hell; in that case, the relatives of the false witness go to hell as a result of their own accumulated karma. As for the objection regarding the arrival of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) or the loss of what was done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*): just as in some cases a person kills someone else by means of poison or the like, yet that victim dies in such a way due to the power of karma acquired in a previous birth, so too does this [false witness] incur [the result] by becoming the instrumental cause. Furthermore, in this matter, it is logical that the statement [of the result] should be understood as a meaningful explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) without a literal basis, as it serves to instill heedfulness (*apramāda*). (8.97)
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men. (8.98)
"Five": regarding a falsehood concerning livestock, one binds five kinsmen to hell; ten, regarding cattle; a hundred, regarding horses; and a thousand, regarding human beings. (8.98)
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak a lie concerning land. (8.99)

"He destroys" means: by speaking a falsehood regarding gold, one causes one's ancestors, such as one's father, and one's descendants, such as one's son, who are born after them, to be driven into hell because of one's own untruthfulness. And by speaking a falsehood regarding land, one joins the entire multitude of living beings [to that fate]; therefore, one should not speak a falsehood regarding land. (8.99)
Regarding women’s enjoyment and sexual intercourse, as well as all gems produced from water and those made of stone, they say: "It is like [the nature of] the earth in the waters. (8.100)

Regarding the verse beginning with "apsu": they say that in the case of water, in falsehoods concerning women, in their enjoyments, and regarding things born in water such as rubies and other gemstones made of stone—including all varieties of lapis lazuli and the like—a falsehood carries the same fault as [lying about] land; it destroys everything. (8.100)
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and as it was seen, straightforwardly.
"Regarding these": having recognized all these faults in speaking untruth, speak all this in accordance with reality, without overstepping what has been seen or heard. (8.101)
One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers as Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas. (8.102)

"Those who tend cattle," etc.: one should question Brahmins who subsist by tending cattle, trading, cooking, or other crafts, or by servitude, or by forbidden means of livelihood, in the same manner as Śūdras when they are questioned as witnesses. (8.102)
Speaking thus according to dharma regarding his purposes, even if he acts otherwise, a man does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods. (8.103)

"Speaking thus": even though a person knows this testimony to be otherwise, if he speaks falsely in legal proceedings out of a sense of duty (*dharma*)—that is, out of compassion (*dayā*) as the motive, being free from any ulterior motive—he does not fall from the heavenly world; for Manu and others declare that this specific kind of untruthful statement is made for the sake of these particular circumstances, referring to speech connected with the divine. Others, however, explain this as referring to the judge: when a judge questions a *śūdra* who is honest among Brahmins such as cowherds and the like, he incurs no loss of merit. (8.103)
Where the death penalty would fall upon a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa, there one should speak an untruth; for that is superior to the truth. (8.104)

But where, then, should that falsehood be spoken? To this he says: "In the case of Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas, where death would otherwise occur. This refers to cases where life is preserved; and this applies to persons who are extremely righteous but have stumbled through negligence, not to those who are utterly unrighteous. Thus, in such matters as Gautama’s statement—"There is no fault in speaking a falsehood if one's life depends upon it, but not if the life of a Pāyīyasa depends upon it"—the king should reach a decision by other means of proof, not by witnesses, nor by other proofs, nor even by inference and the like, so as to avoid completely defiling the witnesses. One should not fear how the killing of a Brāhmaṇa might occur, given the scriptural injunction "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa"; for since the punishment has already been inflicted by the king, a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) may arise from the possibility of such talk, and in other similar cases as well, a falsehood is desired because actual killing is inauspicious. Therefore, the enumeration is given in the order of Śūdra and the others. (8.104)
And they should sacrifice with oblations of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to Vāk as the deity, thereby performing the supreme atonement for that sin of untruth against Sarasvatī. (8.105)

"By means of those whose deity is Speech" (vāgdaivatyaiḥ): Since the Veda states, "Speech indeed is Sarasvatī," there is an identity between Speech and Sarasvatī; therefore, by means of *caru* offerings dedicated to the goddess of Speech, the witnesses—who have spoken falsely—should perform sacrifices for the sake of that untruth, effecting the full accomplishment of its sin. On this point, some say that even though there are multiple witnesses, they should offer three *carus*, according to the rule regarding the *kapiñjala* birds; but that is incorrect, because [the text says] "if the god rains, many Brāhmaṇas should sacrifice. This expiation involves the plural number "by means of *carus*" in view of the plurality of performers, just as in the case of the *vrātyastoma*. These sacrifices are established here for them to be performed. Here, the displacement of the expiation from its original context is for the sake of brevity; for if it were performed there [in the section on ordeals], it would follow that this should be done whenever a witness speaks the truth among the Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas. (8.105)
Or he should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses dedicated to the Waters.

Regarding the phrase "with the Kūṣmāṇḍas": one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the rules for the *paristaraṇa* and other oblations, using these mantras addressed to their respective deities beginning with *yad devā devaheḍanam*. One should offer with the verse addressed to Varuṇa, *ud uttamam*, and with this mantra addressed to the Waters, *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. || 8.106 ||
A man who, being free from illness, gives testimony regarding debts and other matters after three fortnights have passed,
shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth on the whole amount.

"Three fortnights": if a witness who is not ill does not give testimony in legal proceedings such as the non-payment of debts within three fortnights, then he shall pay even the entire debt that is the subject of that dispute to the creditor; and from that entire debt, he shall pay a tenth part to the king as a fine. (8.107)
If, within seven days of the witness having given his testimony, disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall him, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine. (8.108)

"Of whom": if, within seven days of the witness having given testimony as stated, any one of the following occurs—namely, disease, fire, the death of a kinsman, or a burning affliction—even in the absence of any other cause, then because he has always established his falsehood, he shall be made to pay that same fine and the debt. (8.108)
But in matters where there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot discover the truth in its true nature, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.

Regarding the phrase "in cases without witnesses": when two litigants are disputing with one another and no witnesses are present, the judge, failing to ascertain the truth of the matter, shall extract the truth by means of an oath to be described hereafter. (8.109)
Oaths have been taken for the sake of a purpose by great seers and by gods;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before King Praijavana.

"By the great seers": oaths were taken by the great seers, such as Agastya and others, and by the gods, such as Candra and others, for the purpose of deciding doubtful matters. Vasiṣṭha also, having been provoked by Viśvāmitra with the words "Your hundred sons have been devoured," took an oath before King Sudās, the descendant of Pijavana, for the sake of proving his wife's purity. He did not take an oath in vain. (8.110)
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, he perishes both in this world and after death. (8.111)
"No. Even in a very small matter, a wise man should not take a false oath. By taking a false oath, he incurs ill repute in this world and the next, and perishes by falling into hell. (8.111)
In matters concerning women, marriages, the fodder for cows, as well as fuel, in assisting a Brāhmaṇa, and in taking an oath, there is no sin. (8.112)

Regarding the phrase "among women": for one who has many wives, there is no sin in a false oath made in such matters as—"I desire no other woman; you alone are the mistress of my life"—or "you must not marry another," or when stealing fodder for the sake of cattle, or when stealing cooked grain for the sake of the fire-sacrifice ordained by scripture, or in the protection of a Brāhmaṇa involving the giving of wealth and so forth. In these cases, there is no transgression. (8.112)
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by [the truth of] the Vedas, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins. (8.113)

"By truth": one should cause a Brāhmaṇa who speaks to swear by the utterance of the word "truth"; a Kṣatriya by saying, "May your vehicle and weapons become useless"; a Vaiśya by saying, "May your cattle, seed, gold, and so forth become fruitless"; and a Śūdra one should cause to swear by saying, "May all your sins fall upon you. (8.113)
One should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or else, one should have him touch the heads of his son and wife separately. (8.114)

And with regard to the gravity of the matter, [one may test him] by means of fire. Following the procedure prescribed by Yājñavalkya and others, one should cause a Śūdra—holding a lump of gold the color of fire in his hand covered by aśvattha leaves—to step seven paces. Or, having taken [the gold] into water, he should enter into the water; according to this very procedure, one should cause him to submerge. Alternatively, one should touch the heads of each of his sons and wives individually, saying, "This is his thorn. (8.114)
He whom kindled fire does not burn, whom water does not cause to float, and who quickly meets no misfortune—he should be known as pure in his oath. 8.115.

Regarding the word "yam": he whom a blazing fire does not burn, whom water does not wash away, and who does not immediately fall into a causeless state of unconsciousness—he is to be known as an elder among those subject to curses. (8.115)
For in the past, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother, the fire did not burn even a single hair of him who touched the world with truth. (8.116)

Therefore, he tells a narrative of past events regarding Vatsa: because in former times, when his period of studentship had been completed, a Brahmin was addressed as "you are a Śūdra" by his younger half-brother, and having entered the fire for the sake of an oath, saying "it is not so," the Fire—being the witness to all the world in matters of what is good and evil—did not burn him even by a hair's breadth, on account of his truthfulness. (8.116)
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; what has been done shall be as if undone. (8.117)

"In which [case]" means: in whatever legal proceeding false testimony has been given by witnesses, the judge shall set aside that very matter as if it were unperformed; even that which has already reached the point of punishment, he shall examine again. (8.117)
"Through greed, delusion, fear, friendship, desire, and likewise anger, as well as through ignorance and childishness, a witness gives false testimony. (8.118)

"Out of greed," etc. This presentation is intended to show the variety of punishments: false testimony is spoken out of greed, perverted knowledge, fear, friendship, lust, anger, ignorance, folly, or from a childish disposition. || 8.118 ||
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for anyone who gives false testimony in any one of these cases. (8.119)
Regarding the word "of these": when any one of these motives, such as greed and so forth, exists, I shall describe in order the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony. 8.119.
Out of greed, the fine is one thousand; out of delusion, it is the first *sāhasa*; out of fear, it is two middle *daṇḍas*; and out of friendship, it is four times the first. (8.120)

"Out of greed": when one speaks falsely out of greed, he shall be fined one thousand of the *paṇas* to be mentioned later. Out of delusion (*moha*), the first amercement (*prathamasāhasa*) to be mentioned; out of fear, the two amercements to be mentioned; out of friendship (*maitryāt*), four times the first amercement. (8.120)
Ten times more [severe] than desire is the former [retribution], but three times more than anger is the latter;
from ignorance there are two full hundreds, but from childishness there are exactly one hundred.

"Out of desire": one who speaks a falsehood out of desire shall be fined ten times the first amercement. Out of anger, he shall be fined three times the highest amercement which is about to be described. Out of ignorance, he shall be fined two full hundred *paṇas*, and by mistake, only one hundred. (8.121)
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony to be for the purpose of ensuring that justice does not fail and for the restraint of unrighteousness. (8.122)

Regarding the phrase "these": Manu and others have declared these punishments, which were proclaimed by ancient scholars concerning false witnesses, for the purpose of preventing the subversion of the legal system established by the scriptures and for the purpose of warding off the arising of lawlessness; and this applies to a single judicial proceeding (8.122).
A righteous king, having punished them, shall banish members of the three castes who give false testimony; however, he shall only exile a Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding "false testimony": having punished the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya who have given false testimony with the previously mentioned penalty, the king, whose primary concern is dharma, shall banish them from the kingdom; but a Brāhmaṇa, after being punished, he shall cause to be stripped naked. 8.123.
Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, has declared ten places for punishment;
in these cases involving the three social orders, a Brāhmaṇa may depart unhurt. (8.124)

"Tenfold," etc.: Manu, the son of Hiranyagarbha, has declared ten types of punishment for those belonging to the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya; however, as for a Brāhmaṇa, even in the case of a great offense, one should banish him from the country with his body unharmed. (8.124)
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body. (8.125)

"Upastha" (the private parts). Because of this indicative mark (*liṅga*), these are the locations for punishment; therefore, when there is an offense against a limb, that specific punishment must be carried out according to the gravity of the offense against that particular limb. However, in the case of a minor offense, a monetary fine shall be imposed. || 8.125 ||

Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature, and having considered both the essential strength and the offense, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. (8.126)

"Regarding the consequence": having repeatedly observed the cause of the offense according to his own inclination, having carefully considered the place of the offense such as a village or forest, the time of the offense such as day or night, the strength of the offender consisting of wealth, body, and so forth, and having weighed the gravity or lightness of the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it; this [verse] constitutes the supplement to the punishments already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned. 8.126.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys one's reputation and ruins one's fame; it also prevents access to heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it. 8.127.

Regarding "unrighteous punishment": because punishment inflicted here in this world without regard for the consequences and other factors leads to the destruction of fame and reputation for living, and because falsehood in the next world results in immediate downfall—which obstructs the attainment of heaven earned through other meritorious deeds—one should therefore avoid it. (8.127)
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it, incurs great infamy and shall go to hell. (8.128)
"Those who should not be punished": by punishing those unworthy of punishment and by neglecting those worthy of punishment, a king incurs great infamy and goes to hell. (8.128)
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal death. (8.129)

Regarding "verbal punishment": one should administer verbal censure through such words as "You have not acted rightly; do not do so again," directed at a person of good character for an offense of unrighteousness committed through his actions. If, however, he does not thus become pacified, then one should address him with "Fie on you, you fool! or "May you suffer defeat! or "May you incur theft," and so forth. If even then he does not desist from that path, then one should impose the third punishment, which is the fine of wealth. If he still does not abide by it, then beyond this, one should inflict upon him punishments consisting of corporal assault, flogging, amputation of limbs, and the like. (8.129)
But when he is unable to restrain them even by execution, then he may employ all these four measures against them. (8.130)

"By execution": furthermore, when one is unable to subdue them even by means of cutting off their limbs and so forth, then against these offenders one may employ all four of these punishments, beginning with verbal censure (*dhig-daṇḍa*). (8.130)
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold that are renowned on earth for the purpose of worldly calculation and transaction.

"For the sake of worldly transaction" means that I shall specifically designate names such as *paṇa* for copper, silver, and gold on this earth for the purpose of worldly dealings in buying and selling, and for the practical application of punishments and so forth. (8.131)
That subtle particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is declared to be the first among all measurements, the *trasareṇu*. (8.132)
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in measurement;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*. (8.133)
Six mustard seeds make one medium barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*. (8.134)
Four *suvarṇas* are one *pala*; ten *palas* are one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one *rūpyamāṣaka*. (8.135)
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* shall be one *purāṇa*; furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, or a *paṇa*. (8.136)
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* should be known by its measure as consisting of four *sauvarṇikas*. 8.137.

"Through the lattice," "motes of dust," "mustard seeds," "a *pala*," "those [weights]," and "dharaṇas. The dust that is seen in sunbeams entering through a window or similar opening is a *trasareṇu*. Eight of those should be known as one *likṣā* (nit) by measure; three of those *likṣās* are a royal mustard seed (*rājasarṣapa*); three of those are a white mustard seed (*gaurasarṣapa*). Six of those are a medium-sized barley grain (*yava*), neither too thick nor too thin; three barley grains make a *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇalas* make a *māṣa*; sixteen *māṣas* make a *suvarṇa*; four *suvarṇas* make a *pala*. Ten *paṇas* are a *dharaṇa*. It should be understood that silver weighing two *kṛṣṇalas* on a scale is a silver *māṣaka*. Sixteen silver *māṣakas* are called a silver *dharaṇa* or a *purāṇa*. A copper coin of the weight of a *karṣa* made of silver-related metal is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*. One hundred silver *dharaṇas* should be understood as a *rūpyaśatamāna*. By measure, four *suvarṇas* are known as a *niṣka*. (8.132–137)
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement; five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest. (8.138)

Regarding "of paṇas": two hundred and fifty paṇas was declared by Manu and others to be the first amercement (sāhasa); five hundred paṇas is to be known as the middle; and one thousand paṇas is likewise the highest, which is exactly one thousand. 8.138.
When a debt is admitted as due, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent; if it is denied, that fine shall be double. This is the ordinance of Manu. (8.139)

Regarding the word "debt" (*ṛṇa*): when the debtor has declared in court, "I must pay this debt to the creditor," that debtor deserves a fine of five *paṇas* for every hundred *paṇas*. But if he denies it, saying, "I owe him nothing at all," he deserves a fine of ten percent of a hundred. This is the punishment prescribed by Manu. (8.139)
One should employ the rate of interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
a moneylender may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month. (8.140)

"Prescribed by Vasiṣṭha" means that one who lives by lending money may produce interest for the increase of wealth as stated by Vasiṣṭha, because it is lawful. He states this in full: "the eightieth part. When a hundred has been lent and a month has passed, he should take the eightieth part of that hundred for the sake of interest. (8.140)
Remembering the duty of the virtuous, he may take two per cent;
for by taking two per cent, he does not become a sinner regarding wealth. (8.141)

"Two per cent": thinking that for the virtuous it is a matter of wealth and dharma, not adharma, one may take two paṇas per month from a hundred paṇas as interest, living by the previously mentioned rate of interest; for by taking two per cent on a hundred, one does not become joined with the sin of seizing the property of others. (8.141)
One may take interest at the rate of two, three, four, five, or ten percent per month, according to the order of the social classes. (8.142)

"Two per cent," etc.: for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, he may take interest on money related to a month in the order of two, three, four, and five percent respectively—equal, neither less nor more. (8.142)
But one shall not obtain interest on a secured loan through negligence;
nor, due to the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge. (8.143)

"But not so," it says. When a pledge has been given for the purpose of food, the creditor does not receive the interest that was previously mentioned as accruing after the principal has ceased to be lent. Furthermore, there is no rule regarding a pledge given for interest remaining in force beyond the time when the debt has doubled; otherwise, the pledge would serve as wages for the use of the property. Nor can there be a sale, because the pledge is redeemed once the debt has doubled. Thus, the pledge is simply enjoyed [by the creditor], for otherwise there would be no recovery of the principal. (8.143)
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge. (8.144)

"Regarding the phrase 'it must not be used': if, disregarding the master's command 'do not use it,' one fails to enjoy the wealth due to some lack of means, then even while using it, one shall not incur interest. However, if through such use the pledge has been exhausted, then one should satisfy the owner of the pledge with the price equivalent to the undiminished value of the pledge; otherwise, one would be a thief of the pledge. (8.144)
Both a pledge and a deposit do not suffer from the lapse of time; yet both become liable to forfeiture if they remain for an excessively long period. 8.145.

Regarding the term *ādhi*: both a pledge (*bandha*) and an object for friendly enjoyment (*prītibhogya*) ought not to suffer the lapse of time; rather, they must be reclaimed by the owner when the proper time arrives. Therefore, because they remain in the hands of another for a long duration, they could be lost due to the absence of witnesses and other evidence—this being the case for both a pledge (*ādhi*) and a deposit (*upanidhi*). Thus, this [rule] is intended merely as friendly advice, for it will be stated later that "the pledge is lost" (*ādhiḥ sīmeti*) refers to its forfeiture. (8.145)
Things enjoyed with mutual affection never perish:
a cow, a camel, a draft horse, and whatever animal is employed for training. (8.146)

Regarding the term *saṃprītyā* (with mutual affection): a milch cow, a camel that carries loads, and a horse—these, when enjoyed by one another with mutual affection, are never taken away from their owner. The payment given for the taming of horses and other animals is for the purpose of breaking them in; thus, "being enjoyed with mutual affection" is a specific statement following a general introduction. (8.146)
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while remaining silent in its presence, he does not deserve to recover it. (8.147)

"Whatever" means: if any kind of property is being enjoyed by others openly for ten years, and the owner of the property remains silent and does not object—saying "What is this? or "Do not enjoy it thus"—he is no longer entitled to reclaim it through legal means. (8.147)
If the owner is not an idiot and not a minor, and the property is enjoyed by another in his presence, that possession is subverted by the legal proceeding; the enjoyer deserves that wealth. (8.148)

Regarding the term "non-dull-witted" (*ajaḍa*): if the owner of the treasure is neither mentally incapacitated nor a child, and while he remains in that very place, his property is enjoyed by another, that wealth is lost through legal process; there can be no dispute for the owner in that case. Since the enjoyer alone deserves that wealth. Because of the expression "lost through legal process," it follows that according to *dharma*, it always belongs to the owner himself. And thus, this is a verse supplementary to the preceding one (8.148).
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of one learned in the Vedas do not perish through adverse possession. (8.149)

"Security" (ādhi) refers to a pledge, land, villages, and the like; boundaries; the property of a minor; a deposit; that which is to be enjoyed through affection; female slaves; and the property of the king or a Śrotriya. Because of the previously mentioned rule regarding possession for ten years, the owner cannot be deprived of these; and since this [rule] is an exception to property to be enjoyed for ten years, there is no room for doubt that pledges and the like—which are enjoyed for short periods—would not fall under its scope. The separate mention of "those enjoyed through affection" is made because they are enjoyed out of friendship. (8.149)
If a prudent person enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner, he must pay half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment. (8.150)

"Who" refers to that fool who, without the permission of the owner, enjoys in secret wealth given as interest in a manner that does not destroy its principal form; according to the rule ending with "he must be made to enjoy by force until the force ceases," half of the interest must be relinquished for the sake of his purification. (8.150)
Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double the principal;
for grain, fruit, wool, and beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.

Regarding "interest on loans": the interest pertaining to wealth lent for the sake of profit, which is collected from the debtor all at once after a very long time has passed—whether taken gradually or month by month—does not exceed doubling; it becomes exactly double the principal and no more than that may be obtained. However, in the case of grain lent for interest, or sesame, or tree fruits, or wool, or draft animals such as oxen, when lent out and a long time has elapsed, even if collected all at once from the debtor, it does not exceed fivefold when combined with the original grain or other goods. (8.151)
An interest rate higher than the established rate is not permitted;
they call that the way of usury, for it is held that five percent is the maximum one may receive. (8.152)

Regarding the phrase "due to a stipulated increase": when the creditor, having recognized a specific degree of need on the part of the debtor, sets forth an increased rate of interest that exceeds what has been prescribed, that interest is outside the scope of the scriptures and is not valid. For the learned indeed say that this refers to those who follow prohibited methods of interest. At most, however, that creditor may take from a twice-born man (dvija) the five percent per month which has been prescribed for the case of a Śūdra; he may likewise take it from a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya. (8.152)
One should not collect interest exceeding that of a year, nor that which is not sanctioned; [namely] compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, and bodily interest. (8.153)

"Not exceeding a year": if one does not take coins for two or three years, then one gives them. One should not take that interest which has exceeded a year. When there is the employment of vehicles such as carts and the like, the interest [accruing] is "wheel-interest" (*cakravṛddhi*). That may even be greater than the previously mentioned interest; thus it is not permitted, yet it is favored by the Teacher because of its primary mention. Because of the absence of connection [to the previous context], and because it will be stated later that "one mounted on wheel-interest," for this very reason, here the interest upon interest—beginning with "wheel-interest"—is expressed by the term *cakravṛddhi*. Furthermore, regarding that which is based on a contract, it is "periodic" (*kālikā*), for tradition records: "Periodic means month by month. Therefore, it should be taken monthly. Interest arising from a mutual agreement among merchants and others may be higher than the legal rate; however, for others, it is said to be higher than the "following the flow" (*anusārataḥ*) rate. "Bodily" (*kāyikā*) refers to what is denoted by the number of bodily actions. (8.153)
He who is unable to pay a debt and wishes to enter into a new transaction shall, after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond. 8.154.

Regarding "debt": if a debtor, due to an inability to pay the principal, should wish to perform the transaction thinking that [the debt] has been brought [to settlement], he shall, after paying the interest that has accrued, execute the instrument—such as a written document—once again. (8.154)
Without having shown the gold there, one may exchange it; one ought to pay back as much interest as has accrued. (8.155)

"Without having shown it," etc.: even if interest and principal have not been paid due to poverty, if the document and so forth are executed again in that very same place, he should cause that [debt] to be entered therein. || 8.155 ||
Having ascended to the increase of the wheel and being established according to place and time, one who transgresses the proper place and time will not obtain that fruit. (8.156)

Regarding "increase of the vehicle": by means of lending carts and the like on the basis of a rental fee, the creditor, having established the terms regarding place and time, fails to obtain the profit from transporting that cart once those specific places and times have passed, even though he has fulfilled the requirements of what was to be given and received. (8.156)
Those skilled in sea voyages, who perceive the proper place, time, and purpose, establish whatever profit there may be; that indeed constitutes the attainment in that case. (8.157)

"Skilled in sea-voyages" means that merchants and others who are experts in traveling by water, who determine the profit to be gained when gold and other goods are transported in a particular place, at a particular time, and for a particular purpose—such as "this is the gain"—that rate of interest which they establish in such circumstances is to be understood there as the definitive rule. (8.157)
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance, failing to produce him, he shall pay the debt from his own property. 8.158.

Regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): if a surety (*pratibhū*) at the time of the loan agreement stipulates, "I must produce this person," and he stands as a surety for a debtor (*adharmarṇa*) to a creditor (*uttamarṇa*)—whether at the time of the transaction or at another time—he shall, at that time, failing to produce that debtor to the creditor, endeavor to pay the debt from his own property. (8.158)
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a gift made in vain, what is owed for gambling or liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax. (8.159)

Regarding "suretyship" (*prātibhāvya*): that which is to be paid by a surety; a gratuitous gift such as a reward or honorarium which was accepted by the father as a debt; what was won by the father through gambling or prize-fighting; the price of liquor consumed by the father; and the remainder of a fine or the remainder of a toll related to the father—all these the son does not have to pay after the father has died. (8.159)
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
if the surety for payment has died, the court shall cause even his heirs to pay. 8.160.

Regarding "surety for appearance": the rule previously stated—that one who is a surety is not liable to pay [the debt] if he is not the son—should be understood to apply to the act of being a surety for appearance on behalf of the father. However, as for the purpose of payment, if a surety stands as such and dies, one should cause even his heirs to pay, let alone his sons. (8.160)
But when the debtor has not paid, and the guarantor—who was known for his character—is subsequently deceased, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt? (8.161)

Regarding the term *adātari* (in the case of one who does not pay): if a surety has stood as such based on a prior agreement to receive the money, and having thus provided suretyship, that surety for appearance dies, by what reason would the creditor desire to obtain the debt from the son of the surety? Is there a basis for his recovery, or not? Since he is not the son of a surety for payment (*dānapratibhū*), there is no expectation of recovery. However, because his father previously stood as a surety for appearance (*adarśanapratibhū*) regarding the receipt of the money, there is an expectation of recovery from his son. (8.161)
But if the surety has been designated as having sufficient wealth, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one who has been designated. (8.162)

Having thus raised a doubt, he says "one whose wealth has been assigned" (*nirādiṣṭadhana*). If that surety—whether a surety for appearance (*darśanapratibhū*) or a surety for confidence (*pratyayapratibhū*)—has had his wealth assigned, meaning he has received the money with the instruction, "This is your wealth for the sake of trust," and the amount is equal to the extent for which that surety stood, then that wealth has been placed in his hand; in such a case, the established rule of the scriptures is that the son of the one whose wealth was assigned must pay that debt to the creditor from his own property. (8.162)
A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent, or by a child, or by an elderly person, or one that is otherwise invalid, is not established. (8.163)

"By those who are intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent" means that a transaction such as the payment of a debt or the like, which is entered into by one whose mind is impaired by intoxication, insanity, disease, or the like; by a slave, a child, or the very aged; or by one who is incompetent—provided it is not with a father, a brother, or another authorized person—is not valid. (8.163)
A speech does not become true even if it is well-established, if it speaks of phenomena that are external to the fixed, conventional [truth]. (8.164)

Speech does not become true. Even if a convention—such as "this must be performed by you"—is established through a written contract or similar means, nevertheless, if it appears outside of the dharma that exists within the worldly and scriptural practices handed down through beginningless tradition, and if it is determined to be contrary to that [dharma], then it is not true; its purpose is not to be carried out. (8.164)
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given, or received through fraud, or where one perceives deceit, all that he shall annul. (8.165)

"Regarding 'what is mortgaged, sold, or given through fraud' (yogādhamanavikrītam): whatever mortgages, sales, gifts, or acceptances are made under a fraudulent pretext (upādhi)—but not those involving [legitimate] receipt and so forth—the king shall annul them; he shall treat what has been done as undone. Likewise, in other cases such as deposits and the like, wherever he knows the transaction was made for deceptive purposes and that the deposit or other act was not performed in reality, he shall annul it. (8.165)
If the borrower should perish after having incurred an expenditure for the sake of the family,
that debt must be paid by his kinsmen from their own property, even if they have already divided the inheritance.

"Having borrowed": whether undivided or divided, having taken a loan for the sake of the expenses of the family held in common with brothers and others, or for the sake of the expenses of the family of a divided brother, and having died or become incapacitated while incurring those family expenses, that debt must then be paid from his own property by the heirs—whether they be undivided or divided. (8.166)
Whatever legal transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family, whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not annul it. (8.167)

"Regarding 'for the sake of the family': even if he is wealthy, one should examine a man who, while conducting business for the sake of his family, has gone to or is returning from his own country or a foreign land. (8.167)
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even caused to be written by force—Manu has declared all such matters effected by force to be as if not done at all. (8.168)

"By force": Manu has declared that all matters performed by force are to be annulled—such as a daughter or similar person given by force, a field or similar property enjoyed by force, and a document or similar instrument written by force. (8.168)
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a guarantor, and a family;
whereas four prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.

"Three": witnesses, sureties, and judges—these three suffer, that is, they undergo distress. Indeed, these [three] must be made to act as witnesses and so forth by force. "Four," on the other hand—the Brāhmaṇa, the creditor, the merchant, and the king—attain an increase of wealth while assisting others in their efforts to produce the fruit of giving, through the transactions of depositing, selling, and dealing with money. Therefore, in transactions involving lending and borrowing, such as forced seizure, non-granting, or buying, these four should not be engaged in the legal proceedings. 8.169.
Even when impoverished, a king should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor, even when prosperous, should he relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be. (8.170)

"Regarding 'that which is not to be accepted': even a king whose treasury is exhausted should not seize what is forbidden to take; likewise, even when prosperous, he should not abandon a small amount of wealth that is rightfully due. (8.170)
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death. (8.171)

Regarding the phrase "of that which should not be taken": because he seizes what should not be seized and abandons what should be seized, he employs the powerless in unjust punishment; yet toward the powerful, out of cowardice, he even neglects his primary duty. In this way, the king's weakness is made manifest by the citizens. Furthermore, through the taking of what should not be taken, he incurs the wrath of his subjects by violating his own dharma; and through the avoidance of what should be taken, his treasury becomes depleted. Thus, due to the destruction of the kingdom, he perishes both in this world and the next. (8.171)
From the enjoyment [of taxes], from the blending of castes, and from the protection of women, the strength of a king is born; he prospers both in this world and after death. (8.172)

"Because of his taking [what is due]... means: A king is proclaimed as "strong" because he takes lawful wealth from the castes, because of his alliances with women of equal caste, and because he protects the weak from the powerful; thus the king is called "the strong one" in the world. And for this reason, he prospers both in this world and in the next. (8.172)
Therefore, like Yama, a master should conduct himself with the impartiality of Yama, abandoning his own likes and dislikes, having conquered anger and subdued his senses. (8.173)

"Because of that, therefore... means: Therefore, like Yama, the king—who has brought under control his anger and senses—should avoid both what is pleasant and unpleasant to himself and conduct himself with equanimity toward enemy and friend through actions characteristic of Yama. || 8.173 ||
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, conducts affairs according to unrighteousness—his enemies will soon bring him under their control. (8.174)

Regarding the word "yaḥ": furthermore, whatever king, through delusion caused by greed and other vices, performs his duties—such as presiding over legal proceedings—in an unrighteous manner, his enemies will swiftly overcome him because he has made unrighteousness his very nature. (8.174)
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives matters according to righteousness—toward him the subjects turn, as rivers flow toward the ocean. (8.175)

"Regarding 'lust and anger': when a king, having abandoned hatred, settles legal cases according to dharma, his subjects resort to him as rivers flow to the ocean, and they become devoted to his mind. (8.175)

If one should report to the king that a creditor is recovering his debt by his own will, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of that amount to the king, and the creditor's debt shall be paid by him. 8.176.

"Whoever"—meaning that debtor who, out of pride in his favor with the king, reports to the monarch the creditor who is attempting to recover the debt through conciliation and other means—that person shall be made by the king to pay a fourth part of the debt as a fine for that wealth. (8.176)

A debtor should repay the creditor in equal value even by means of labor; one of lower caste who is equal [in status] should pay immediately, but one of superior caste should pay that gradually. (8.177)

Regarding the phrase "by work": when a debtor of equal or lower caste lacks wealth, he should indeed be made to perform work appropriate to his own caste; however, he should pay that debt slowly, as far as possible. (8.177)
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of resolution the legal matters of men disputing with one another, as established by the evidence of witnesses. 8.178

"By this [means]" means that the king should settle the legal cases of two litigants, plaintiff and defendant, who are disputing with one another, in the manner described above—cases determined by witnesses or determined through conviction by means of inference, oaths, and so forth—in accordance with the resolution of the disagreement between the plaintiff and the defendant. (8.178)
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, devoted to righteousness, truthful, possessed of a great following, wealthy, and honorable. (8.179)

Regarding the phrase "one born of a noble family": this is advice from a friend with a visible purpose, stating that one should deposit (place) a trust with a person who belongs to the great community, who follows established conduct, knows the Dharma, speaks the truth, has many friends and virtuous kinsmen, is wealthy, and is upright by nature—because such a person is free from deviation. 8.179.
Whatever object a person deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the receipt. (8.180)

"Who" means: whatever person, in whatever manner, for whatever purpose, and into whose hand deposits gold or other property—whether with witnesses or without witnesses—that object must be received by that depositor in that very same manner; because it is only right that the receipt should be in the same manner as the delivery. One who acts otherwise shall be punished. (8.180)
He who, when asked for a deposit, does not return it to the depositor, shall be summoned by the judge in the absence of that depositor. (8.181)
If he should act in accordance with what was entrusted and as it was performed, there would be nothing therein by which he could be accused by others. (8.182)
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the rule, he shall be seized and compelled to pay both; such is the settled law. 8.183.
In the absence of witnesses, having truly deposited gold with him through spies endowed with youth and beauty, and by means of pretexts; 8.184.

Regarding the phrase "who [says] 'this is a deposit,'" "he," "of them," and "in the absence of witnesses": when one who is being petitioned with the words, "Give me back the gold and other items deposited by you," does not return them due to the absence of witnesses, the judge, acting on behalf of the depositor while that depositor is absent, should have some secret agents—men of pleasing appearance, gentle mien, and those who can feign threats from the king—deposit gold with him under the pretext of a real transaction, in such a way that no suspicion arises in him. Then, at a later time, while the original depositor is still absent, the judge should have that man petitioned by those same agents with the words, "Give us back our deposited gold. If that holder of the deposit returns it exactly as it was deposited—with or without a seal, and in its original form, such as the shape of a bracelet or a string—and says, "It was received by all of you in this manner," then nothing further need be known regarding what was previously alleged by the other depositors (the plaintiffs) who informed the judge: "This belongs to us, and it is in his hand. However, if he does not return that deposited gold to those secret agents exactly as it was placed, then, having seized both deposits—the one belonging to the plaintiff and the one belonging to the agent—he should be compelled to pay. Such is the determination of the law (*dharmaniścaya*). Thus ends these four verses (8.181–184).
A sealed deposit (*nikṣepa*) and an open deposit (*upanidhi*) must never be handed over to a close relative;
they are lost if [the original depositor] perishes, but not lost if he does not perish. (8.185)

Regarding "deposits and sealed deposits": these two perish upon the death [of the owner], but they do not perish if he does not die. While the depositor and the person holding the sealed deposit are alive, they remain as objects of affection and enjoyment for them. It is said that these two should never be given away even to one's sons, brothers, or others by way of half-share, because if those sons and others were to perish, what need is there to mention that the deposit and sealed deposit would then belong to the rightful owner when he makes a claim? Furthermore, if the sons and others do not perish, it is possible that the two might never be lost [to the original owner]. (8.185)
But if one should himself deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased, he must not be prosecuted by the king nor by the kinsmen of the depositor. (8.186)

"By himself" means: he who, upon the death of the depositor, gives that which was deposited without [the depositor's] knowledge to the son or other heirs who are entitled to that wealth, and not by the king being directed by the depositor’s sons or other kinsmen. (8.186)
One should seek that object with sincerity and with affection;
having examined his conduct, one should settle the matter through conciliation alone. (8.187)

Now, if he should have some doubt regarding that [deposit], then [the judge] should act "without guile. Having deliberated, he should give it back to him by means of conciliation (*sāman*) alone, satisfying him. He should determine [the matter] with affection, avoiding verbal deception (*vākchala*) and the like—which consist in the existence of other wealth—by means of indirect methods such as divine ordeals (*divya*). Or, having observed the character of that depositary and knowing him to be righteous, he should settle it through the application of conciliation and so forth, rather than by punishment or divine ordeals. (8.187)
In all these cases of deposits, the rule for recovery shall be as follows:
if the depositary does not withdraw it from the sea, he shall not receive anything at all. (8.188)

Regarding the phrase "in deposits": for all types of deposits, there would be the rule that witnesses are required for their recovery, and so forth; however, in the case of a sealed deposit, the holder of the deposit shall incur no fault whatsoever if he does not take anything from it, provided that nothing has leaked out from below or been removed by means of a counter-seal or similar methods. (8.188)
If it has been stolen by thieves, swept away by water, or consumed by fire, he need not give it back, provided that he does not take anything from that [remaining property]. (8.189)

"By thieves," etc.: the holder of a deposit need not pay if it has been stolen by thieves, carried away to another country by water, or consumed by fire, provided that he has not in fact misappropriated anything from the deposit. (8.189)
One should investigate the one who misappropriates a deposit and the one who did not entrust it by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths. (8.190)

Regarding the deposit: the king shall determine the identity of the misappropriator of a deposit by all possible means—conciliation and the like—and by Vedic ordeals such as carrying fire and so forth, as prescribed by all the sages who perceive the truth. By using the term "one who has not deposited," he indicates that this applies to the depositor as well. (8.190)

He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands it without having made a deposit—both of them should be punished like thieves, or compelled to pay a fine equal to the value of the object. (8.191)

Regarding "deposit": he who does not return a deposit and he who demands it without having made a deposit—these two, when a great offense has been committed, shall be punished like thieves with the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa) or the like; or, if the offense is small, they shall be fined an amount equal to that deposit. (8.191)
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates an open deposit, without distinction.

Regarding the phrase "of the deposit": the statement that one who misappropriates a deposit should be punished with a fine equal to its value is a restatement of what was already established; it is repeated for the purpose of specifying that even in the case of a first offense, if the amount is large, he should be treated like a thief. As for those who claim this repetition is intended to preclude the punishment of limb-mutilation and the like for a Brāhmaṇa thief—that is incorrect, because it will be stated later that "one must never kill a Brāhmaṇa" and so forth. Likewise, one who misappropriates property held in trust or for enjoyment should be made to restore all of it without distinction, regardless of his caste. (8.192)
Any man who, by means of fraudulent tests, should seize the property of another, shall be put to death publicly with various modes of execution, together with his accomplices. (8.193)

"But regarding 'whatever [is taken] by means of fraudulent tests': a man who, with an accomplice, should take another's property, having been cut into pieces by various means of execution such as the amputation of hands and feet, must be put to death by the king on the public highway or similar place. (8.193)
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses, it must be understood to be exactly that much; he who declares otherwise deserves punishment. 8.194.
