Regarding "deposit" (*niṣepa*): whatever kind of substance and quantity of goods was deposited in the presence of witnesses, that same substance and quantity must be understood through the testimony of the witnesses and not by other means of proof; no further examination should be conducted therein. And in that case, the depositor who speaks falsely deserves the punishment declared by Viṣṇu. (8.194)
If a gift was made in secret, or received in secret, it must be returned in secret; as the giving was, so must be the taking back. (8.195)

"Secretly" (*mithaḥ*) means mutually. A deposit that was made in private by one person and received in private by the holder of the deposit must be returned in private alone. It is not for the claimant to depend upon witnesses and the like; for in whatever manner the giving was done, in that very same manner the returning occurs. Thus, the phrase "it should be given back" is intended to establish a rule for the holder of the deposit, while the phrase "in whatever way one deposits an object" is intended to establish a rule for the depositor. As for the interpretation that this verse serves as a specific remedy when there is an excess of what was taken or heard, that general explanation—or rather, the view of some—should be examined by those learned in the tradition. (8.195)
In this manner, the king shall make a decision regarding both deposited wealth and that which has been entrusted out of friendship, without causing loss to the holder of the deposit.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has been deposited": one should reach a decision in this manner concerning the property deposited—which was entrusted for the sake of enjoyment at the present time with affection, without causing distress to the holder of the deposit. (8.196)
One who sells another's property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner—one who is a thief yet considers himself no thief—should not be made a witness. (8.197)

"Let him sell. This means that if one who is not the owner sells another's property without the permission of the owner, the judge shall not cause such a person—who is not a thief but is a thief by reputation—to undergo an ordeal with witnesses; this prohibition of the witness-ordeal is intended to demonstrate his untrustworthiness, thereby establishing his unsuitability for other judicial actions as well. (8.197)
He shall be liable for restitution along with his family and a fine of six hundred panas;
if he has no family ties and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief. 8.198.

Regarding the term "to be confiscated": if this seller of another's property is recognized by the owner as being his son or some other relative, he should be made to pay six hundred *paṇas* as a fine. However, if he is not authorized by the owner and has no valid excuse—provided that the property was not entrusted to him by the owner’s son or other relative due to some business transaction or similar reason—then he incurs the guilt associated with a thief. Even when the designation is that of one who associates with sinners, there is an extension of the punishment. (8.198)
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings. (8.199)
"By one who is not the owner": that which is sold or given away by one who is not the owner must be understood as if it were not done at all; such is the established rule of legal procedure. 8.199.
Where enjoyment is perceived but no scripture is seen anywhere, there the scripture is the cause and not the enjoyment; such is the established rule. (8.200)

Regarding "enjoyment" (saṃbhoga): when enjoyment is observed with respect to a certain object, yet there is no traditional title (āgama)—such as [the right to] cultivation or other such acts—then in that case, the title is not the cause; rather, it is enjoyment. Therefore, even by ten years of enjoyment, the accomplishment of the legal effect follows for one who possesses a pure title. || 8.200 ||
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family, he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified. (8.201)

Regarding the phrase "from one who sells": it should be understood that whatever is given on the marketplace floor must be done in the presence of the merchant. If someone were to take something for a small price, he would be considered unfit for public dealings; for his wealth is purified by the lawful process established in the marketplace through the proximity of reputable merchants and prices, and he does not receive from their hands anything exceeding the value of the goods. (8.201)

Now, if the root [of the sale] cannot be produced, but the purchase was proven by witnesses, the seller is not to be punished by the king and is released; the original owner recovers his property. 8.202.

Now, regarding the phrase "the root [price] being irrecoverable, [the sale] is cleared by an open purchase": if, having gone to another country, it is impossible for him to recover the price of the goods purchased, then—having cleared the matter by means of an open purchase according to the principle of the preceding verse—the purchaser must be punished by the king; and the owner recovers from the hand of the purchaser that property which was sold by one who was not its owner. (8.202)
An item whose form is mixed with another does not deserve to be sold;
nor one that is defective, nor one that is deficient, nor one that is far away, nor one that is concealed. (8.203)

"No," [it is replied]. "It is not blameworthy. Substances such as saffron and the like may be mixed with substances such as safflower under the pretext that they are the same for the purpose of sale. However, it must not be possessed of defects such as internal impurities or flaws that would affect its value, nor should it be fixed by means of a scale or other devices so as to have its true nature concealed by passion and the like; otherwise, in this case, there would be a punishment equivalent to that for selling what does not belong to oneself (asvāmivikraya). || 8.203 ||
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the groom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for the price of a single bride-price.

"Another" refers to a maiden who is to be given for a bride-price (*śulka*). If, at the time when the bride-price is to be increased, one displays a faultless girl but then gives a faulty one to the groom, then he may take both girls with that single payment of the bride-price. This is mentioned here because it shares the same nature as a sale. (8.204)
A giver does not deserve punishment if he has first declared the defects [of the girl], provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not already had sexual intercourse. 8.205.

"No. Even in the case of a girl who is insane, or afflicted with leprosy, or one who has already experienced sexual intercourse—even when giving her in a Brāhma or other form of marriage—the giver deserves punishment if he reveals the defects of insanity and so forth to the bridegroom before giving the girl away. And it will be stated later that the punishment applies to the one who gives a defective girl. (8.205)
If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty,
a share proportionate to his work must be given to him by the other performers together.

And he states that the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is one who acts collectively. If the principal priest, having performed his duties through the performance of *śrauta* rites such as the *homa* in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, should abandon his work due to illness, then the fees (*dakṣiṇā*) corresponding to the portion of the work already performed by him must be paid to him by the *mitrāvaruṇa* and others who have been requested to take over. (8.206)
If, after the sacrificial fees have been distributed, one abandons his own work, he shall receive his entire share even if he causes it to be performed by another. (8.207)

Regarding the phrase "at the sacrificial fees" (dakṣiṇāsu): when the sacrificial fees have been given at the time for the fees—such as during the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) when they lead the fees forward—if, by fate, he abandons the rite he was performing, this appointed priest shall have another perform the entire remainder of the ritual involving the sacrificial fees. 8.207.
In whatever rite specific fees for individual components have been prescribed, he alone shall take them; or alternatively, all [the officiants] may share them together. (8.208)

Regarding the phrase "in which": in whatever ritual act, within the fire of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), specific parts (*aṅga*) may have been prescribed as fees—for instance, the primary fees such as cows to be given to the *adhvaryu* and others as they were undertaken—one who is explicitly mentioned by name should accept that very portion because it was so ordained in the scripture. Now, this is raised as a point of doubt: since the act of acceptance is performed through the mediation of the assembly (*parṣad*), just as in the case of a representative, does it follow that everyone present is considered to have been mentioned? [This is the objection. (8.208)
The Adhvaryu priest shall take the chariot at the establishment of the sacred fires, and the Brahman priest the horse;
or the Hotṛ may take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma]. (8.209)

Regarding this, the author states the final decision by adopting the view that [the items] are for the sake of those [officiants], because it is so heard in scripture: "The chariot" (verse 8.209). Since the chariot is heard in scripture as being given to the *adhvaryu*, he alone should take possession of it; likewise, since it is heard in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) that "a horse is to be given to the *brahman*," the *hotṛ* should also take the horse and make it his own; and the *udgātṛ* should take the cart used at the purchase of the *soma*.

Of all [the heirs], the primary ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that; those entitled to a third receive one-third shares, and those entitled to a fourth receive one-fourth shares. (8.210)

Now he states the rule for the principal sacrificial fee (*pradhānadakṣiṇā*) with the words "of all" (*sarveṣām*). It is heard in the scripture: "He initiates him with a hundred. In that context, among all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those who are the primary priests—the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Udgātṛ—are the "half-takers" (*ardhahara*); they alone receive forty-eight cows. In this way, the enumeration of their respective shares to be mentioned hereafter becomes consistent. And Kātyāyana says: "Twelve each for the first [set]. He further says: "With half of those forty-eight, namely twenty-four, for the second [set]. For the third-positioned ones—the Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Agnīdh, and Pratihartṛ—they receive sixteen cows, which is one-third of forty-eight. And Kātyāyana says: "Four each for the third [set]. Those established as the fourth share—the Subrahmaṇya, Grāvastut, and Unnetṛ—receive twelve cows, which is one-fourth of forty-eight. And Kātyāyana says: "Three each for the others. Therefore, he says [verse 8.210]: The primary priests take half; the next group takes a third; the others take a quarter. The remaining four take three each. (8.210) The meaning is as follows: from the total of forty-eight cows, the primary priests take half, which is twenty-four. From the remainder, the second group takes a third, which is sixteen. From what remains, the third group takes a quarter, which is twelve. From what is left, the other four priests take three cows each. Thus, the distribution is complete. Alternatively, one may interpret the verse by dividing the forty-eight into three parts of sixteen each, and distributing them according to the respective shares. Or, one may divide the forty-eight into four parts of twelve each and distribute them accordingly. Or, one may divide the forty-eight into five parts of nine and a third each and distribute them. However, the first interpretation is preferable because it conforms to the scriptural statement: "He initiates him with a hundred. Furthermore, the distribution of the cows must be equal; otherwise, there would be no basis for the rule that "one should give the same number of cows to all. Moreover, the rule regarding the distribution of the *dakṣiṇā* applies to the principal fee, not to the various minor fees (*parikraya*). This is because the distribution of the principal fee is based on the specific roles of the priests, whereas the distribution of the minor fees is based on the general status of being an officiant. Therefore, the distribution of the principal fee is determined by the aforementioned method. As for the minor fees, however, since they are given equally to all, the distribution is equal. Thus, the distribution of the principal fee is established. Alternatively, one might argue that the distribution of the principal fee should also be equal, because the scriptural injunction "he initiates him with a hundred" does not specify unequal portions. To this we reply: it is not so, because the distribution is based on the specific roles of the priests. Since the roles differ, the distribution cannot be equal. Furthermore, the scriptural statement "he initiates him with a hundred" is intended to indicate the total amount of the fee, not to prescribe an equal division. Therefore, the distribution is as stated above. Moreover, the rule that "one should give the same number of cows to all" applies to the minor fees, not to the principal fee. Consequently, the distribution of the principal fee is as described. Thus, the rule for the principal sacrificial fee is established. When men here perform their respective duties in combination, the apportionment of their shares must be determined by this application of the rule. (8.211)

Regarding the word *saṃbhūya*: having come together, while performing their respective tasks such as building a house with men such as architects, carpenters, and master builders, a distribution of shares must be made according to the various types of labor, based on the aforementioned rules and depending on the application of their specialized knowledge. 8.211.
If wealth has been given by someone to another who asks for it for the sake of dharma, and that wealth subsequently does not serve that purpose, it should not have been given to him. (8.212)

"Regarding 'for the sake of dharma' (dharmārtham)": if wealth has been given or promised to someone who is begging for the purpose of performing sacrifices and the like, but later he does not employ that wealth for the sake of sacrifice in an amount equal to what was given, then what was promised to him should not be given, or what has already been given should be taken back. (8.212)
If, however, he should recover it out of pride or greed, he must be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king; that shall be the expiation for his theft. (8.213)

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): if the recipient, out of pride or greed, does not relinquish that promised wealth—whether it be equal to the value received or something he himself has produced—on the path [of restitution], then he must be punished by the king for the sake of purifying the sin of theft. It is understood from this statement regarding atonement (*niṣkṛti*) that even for one punished by force, the removal of sin occurs through that punishment. (8.213)
Thus has been declared the lawful manner of non-repayment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.

Regarding the word "dattasya" (of what is given): this presentation of it is not devoid of Dharma; that reality has been stated. Therefore, immediately after this, I shall explain another presentation as well. (8.214)
If one who has been hired, though not in distress, should out of pride fail to perform the work as prescribed, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* and his wages shall not be paid. (8.215)

"Regarding the term 'hired' (bhṛta): if one who has been hired for wages, or purchased by another, or afflicted by disease and the like, should out of egoism fail to perform the work as stipulated, he, while performing it [negligently], shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* of gold or similar precious metal as prescribed in the rules on legal proceedings; furthermore, his wages shall not be paid from the portion of the work performed. (8.215)
But one who, having been distressed, performs the work once he has recovered his health, shall receive that wage exactly as stated from the beginning, even after a long period of time. (8.216)

Regarding the term "afflicted": when, however, one does not perform the ritual due to pain or other such reasons, then, being healthy, one should perform it exactly as previously described; and one must certainly obtain that entitlement even after the lapse of the entire [prescribed] time. 8.216.
As it has been said: "Whether he be distressed or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be performed, his wages must not be paid, even for work that is only slightly incomplete. (8.217)
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate an agreement. 8.218

As it has been stated: "This is the law," or "This is the settled rule. Thus, the entire procedure regarding the work known as the payment of wages has been declared. Immediately following this, I shall explain the rules concerning punishments and other matters for those who violate their agreements. (8.218)
A man who, having made a covenant in truth with villages, districts, or assemblies, should break that covenant out of greed—him the king shall banish from the realm. (8.219)

"Whoever"—meaning any man among the villagers, local inhabitants, merchants, and so forth—who, having made a secret agreement such as "this must be done by us" or "this must be avoided," should speak [of it], the king shall banish him from the kingdom. (8.219)
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the agreement to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one silver śatamāna. (8.220)

"Having seized," [it means]: whoever should thus violate this agreement, he shall be fined four *niṣkas* of four *suvarṇas* each, of the form described above—and not the *niṣkas* consisting of one hundred and fifty *suvarṇas* mentioned in other treatises—along with a silver *śatamāna*. (8.220)
In this manner, a righteous lord of the earth should administer the rule of punishment against one who violates the compact within villages, castes, or assemblies. (8.221)
"Thus [is] the rule for punishment": a king who prioritizes dharma should apply this ordinance of punishment to those among the Brāhmaṇas and others in the villages who have transgressed. (8.221)
If, after having bought or sold anything, one should have cause for regret in this matter, he may return that object or take it back within ten days. 8.222.

"Regarding 'krītvā' (having bought): Having sold some substance that is impermanent in nature, or having sold it for the sake of something stable, if out of greed one later feels regret, thinking "I have not done well," then within ten days he may take back what was sold. 8.222.
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause [the object] to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred by the king. (8.223)
"By another": one should not cause [an item] purchased after ten days to be returned. (8.223)
But for him who gives away a maiden who has defects without disclosing them, the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas. (8.224)
But if a man, out of malice, should declare that a maiden is not a virgin when she is one, he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for failing to demonstrate her fault. (8.225)

"But he who... || "Not a maiden" means: if a man, out of malice, should declare of a maiden, "This is no maiden; her virginity is impaired," yet fails to prove that defect in her, he shall incur a fine of one hundred *paṇas*. This is a punishment for violating what has been stated [in the law]. (8.225)
The mantras of marriage are established for maidens alone;
they are never for women who are not maidens, for such women have lost the performance of religious rites. (8.226)
Because they are called "pertaining to the taking of a living being": "Aryaman indeed must be given; the maiden has worshipped Agni"—these and others are the marriage mantras of human beings. (8.226)
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step. (8.227)

"The marriage mantras are definitive" means that the wedding mantras are the certain cause for the status of wife; by their employment, one becomes a wife. Furthermore, regarding those mantras, when the seventh step has been taken by the girl with the mantra "May you be my companion at the seventh step," experts in the scriptures must understand that the rite is completed. Moreover, if before the seventh step there is a realization that she is not a maiden and a subsequent regret arises, he may abandon her; but not after that. For in the case of those born as *kānīna*, *sahoḍha*, or *gūḍhotpanna* sons, the scripture shows them to be the son of the husband. (8.227)
Whatever offense has been committed by anyone, and whatever remorse he may feel regarding it, one should establish him on the path of righteousness according to this procedure. 8.228

Regarding the phrase "in which": not only in the case of buying and selling, but even in whatever matter such as a formal agreement (*saṃvit*) or a transaction, if a person should later feel regret in this world, the king shall establish him on the path that does not deviate from *dharma* by means of the procedures for giving away a son and so forth. (8.228)
I shall now fully declare, according to the true nature of the law, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock. 8.229

Regarding the phrase "in the case of cattle": having exhaustively dealt with the disputes between owners and their herdsmen arising from faults related to cattle, he will state the definitive legal settlement. (8.229)
During the day, the responsibility for what happens rests with the keeper; at night, it rests with the owner if the animal is in his house.
Otherwise, if the security of the property is otherwise maintained, the keeper shall incur the responsibility. (8.230)

Regarding the word "by day": when cattle placed under the care of a keeper suffer harm by day, the fault lies with the keeper; however, at night, the fault lies with the owners who seek to recover their property from the keeper. But where the cattle remain in the keeper's charge even at night, the fault is stated to belong to him alone; he would incur the blame, just as the term *yogakṣema* (security and acquisition) implies both components. (8.230)
A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be the wages for the herdsman if he is not otherwise paid. (8.231)

Regarding the "cowherd" (gopa): that servant known as a cowherd who is paid with milk rather than with food and other provisions may, with the permission of his master, milk one superior cow from among ten for his own maintenance. That [milk] would indeed suffice for a herdsman supported by food and other means; furthermore, he should tend ten cows with the milk of this one alone. (8.231)
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place,
or if it perishes through a lack of human effort, the keeper alone shall be held liable.

"Lost": the herdsman himself shall restore to the owner that which was lost—meaning that which, being devoid of the direct human effort required for its protection by the herdsman, has passed beyond the range of sight, been devoured by worms, or died in a pit or similar place. (8.232)
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the keeper is not liable to pay, provided he informs the owner himself at the proper place and time. (8.233)

Regarding the term *vighuṣya*: if it has been stolen by thieves after they have again sounded the drum and other instruments, the keeper is not liable to pay; provided that the theft occurs in that very same place and is reported to his own master immediately after the lapse of time. (8.233)
One should give the ears, hide, tail-hair, bladder, sinews, and bile to the owners of the animals; when they have died, one should also show them the various parts. (8.234)

"Both the ears and the hair"—he should give these to the owners of the animals; and when they have died, he should show the specific parts. When animals die of their own accord, he should give to the owner the ears, the hide, the hair, the bladder (the organ for storing urine), the sinews, and the gallstone (*gorocanā*), because these are useful. By mentioning the marks such as the ears, skin, and so forth, he should provide evidence for identification. (9.234)
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid, whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman. (8.235)

Regarding the phrase "among goats and sheep": when goats or rams are attacked by jackals and the like, if the herdsman does not return and a wolf kills them after overpowering them, that shall be the fault of the herdsman. The mention of goats and the like is made because, due to their great number, it would be impossible for a single wolf to attack them all. (8.235)
If, among those cows grazing together in the forest, a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter. (8.236)

Regarding the word "tāsām" (of them): if, while those goats and sheep are being herded by their keeper, followed by a dog, and moving together in a herd through the forest, some predator such as a jackal should spring out from somewhere—such as the woods—and kill one of them, the keeper is not at fault in that case. (8.236)
The common land surrounding a village shall be one hundred bows on all sides, or else three throws of a wooden pin; for a city, it shall be three times that amount. 8.237.

"A hundred bows" means as follows: a bow is four cubits long; a *śamyā* is a wooden staff, and its "fall" is the distance at which it lands when thrown. Near a village, a protection zone for the sowing of crops—measuring four hundred cubits or three throws of the staff in all directions—must be maintained for the grazing of cattle. However, near a city, this area must be made three times as large. (8.237)
If cattle should graze upon unenclosed grain there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the cattle. (8.238)

"In that regard": if anyone should sow grain in that place of common usage (*vyavahārasthāna*), and if cattle should eat it while the [right of] use has not been granted, then the king shall not inflict punishment upon the herdsmen there. (8.238)
One should construct a fence there such that even a camel cannot look over it, and one must block every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass. (8.239)

"An enclosure" (vṛtim): at that site for the disposal [of waste], one should construct a strong enclosure made of thorns and other materials, shaped like a wall, on the left side and the opposite side, such that even a camel cannot look over it. And in that enclosure, they should cover up every single gap, even one large enough for the snout of a dog or a pig to enter. (8.239)

On a path, in an unfenced field, or again at the edge of a village, the owner of the cattle is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for letting them stray; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are unattended. (8.240)

"Path" means: if, however, when [the cattle] have gone near a path or near a village, they are not protected by a herdsman who has been assigned to them by their owner because he failed to provide an enclosure (*vṛti*), then the keeper is to be fined one hundred *paṇas*, since it is impossible to fine the animal itself; therefore, the keeper alone is to be fined. Furthermore, the owner of the field should restrain an animal that has proceeded to graze there without a keeper. (8.240)
But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
however, in all cases, a sixth part must be given to the owner of the field—this is the settled rule. (8.241)

Regarding the phrase "in fields": it should be understood that in all cases [the following applies]. In fields other than those on the road or at the edge of a village, an animal that grazes there deserves a fine of one and a quarter *paṇas*; the implication is that the keeper alone is liable. Furthermore, in every field, the owner of the field must have the value of the crop eaten by the animal paid by either the keeper or the owner of the animal, according to the offense; this is the settled rule. (8.241)

Manu has declared that a cow that has recently calved within ten days, as well as bulls and animals dedicated to the gods, are not subject to punishment, whether they are accompanied by their keepers or are without keepers. 8.242.

"Within ten days": Manu has declared that a cow that has recently calved within ten days, as well as goats, bulls, and other such animals received for breeding, or domestic animals tied up month by month, or those kept for protection or left unattended, are not subject to punishment if they eat standing crops. The meaning is that the punishment falls on the owner, not on the keeper. Since the negligence of the protectors—the very nature of divine beings—is beyond human control, one should not raise the objection that the punishment for crop-eating applies to livestock that is without a keeper or is of a divine nature. (8.242)

In the event of a transgression by the landowner, the fine shall be ten times his share; however, if it occurs through the negligence of the servants, the fine for the landowner shall be half of that. 8.243.

Regarding the farmer: if the owner of the field commits an offense such as allowing his own cattle to eat the crop, or failing to sow at the proper time, or stealing it, he shall be fined ten times the amount of the king’s share that was lost. Furthermore, if servants commit such acts without the knowledge of the field-owner, they shall be fined half of the tenfold amount. However, if they do so intentionally, the fine for them shall be tenfold. This is the rule concerning the injury of fields. (8.243)
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule in cases of transgression involving owners of cattle, the animals themselves, and their keepers. (8.244)

Regarding this: when cattle commit an offense against owners or herdsmen by eating crops—such as when they eat the crops of gods, cattle-pens, and so forth—the king, who is preeminent in righteousness (*dharma*), should carry out what has been previously stated. (8.244)
When a dispute has arisen regarding a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.

Regarding the boundary: when a dispute has arisen concerning the limits between two villages, the king should determine the boundary during the month of Jyeṣṭha in summer, when the boundary markers have become visible because the grass has been withered by the heat. Having observed that people in the world are always confused about the knowledge of boundaries, he should cause the following boundary signs—both those already mentioned and those yet to be described—to be established. (8.245)
And he should establish boundary trees—*nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees, as well as *śālmalī*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and other milky-sap trees. (8.246)

"Boundary trees": he should cause to be planted long-lasting specific types of trees that serve as boundary markers, such as the *nyagrodha* and other trees, as well as milky-sap trees such as the *udumbara*. (8.246)
The boundary is not lost even when various thickets, bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and grassy plots, as well as reeds and kubjaka shrubs, have perished. (8.247)

Regarding the word *gulmān*: they are recorded as being "without trunks" (*aprakāṇḍa*), because of the mention of "trunks" (*kāṇḍa*) [in the preceding verse]. Thus, one should avoid various *gulmas* (shrubs), trees, and bamboos—such as the *veṇu*, *kīcaka-veṇu*, and others of diverse kinds—as well as those called *śamī*, the variegated *mallikā* and so forth, and sown plots of land, and the *gulmas* belonging to the *kubjaka* tree; for these have not been long used and are therefore distinctively situated. (8.247)
Ponds, wells, large tanks, and springs, as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries. (8.248)

Regarding "tanks" (taḍāgāni): tanks, wells, lotus-pools, water-channels, and temples should be constructed at the boundaries—in the junctions between two villages—and in places where people congregate for the purpose of seeking water, so that witnesses may be available. (8.248)
And he should cause other boundary markers to be made concealed, having observed that in the world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries. (8.249)

Regarding the phrase "concealed": having observed that people in the world are always confused regarding the lack of knowledge about boundaries, one should have the faultless, secret boundary markers described below constructed. 8.249.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand— (8.250)
And whatever objects of this kind the earth would not consume due to their age, those he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at the junctions of the boundary. (8.251)

"Stones," "and those which": stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, baked bricks, charcoal, fragments of rock, sand, and other such items as these—such as *khadira* wood, *sārika* wood, black collyrium, and so forth—he should place them hidden at the boundaries of villages. (8.250–251)
By these signs, the king should determine the boundary between two disputing parties, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water. (8.252)

"By these": by means of these aforementioned marks, the king should determine the boundary between two contending villages, whether they are deserted or inhabited. Furthermore, in the case of being inhabited, [the boundary is determined] by prior possession (*pūrvabhukti*); for it has been stated that "in the case of desertion, the boundary is the boundary-mark (*ādhi*). And regarding the flow of water, which is caused by something else, there is the desertion of the dwelling due to the conditions prevailing at the time of the villages' settlement. (8.252)
If there were doubt even when the marks are visible, the determination of the boundary dispute would depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses. (8.253)

Regarding the word "yadi": even when there are signs [of boundary marks] visible, if there should still be even a slight doubt concerning the boundary on both sides, then the determination of a boundary dispute shall be based upon the testimony of witnesses. (8.253)
In the presence of the village communities and the two litigants themselves, witnesses concerning the boundary markers must be questioned at the border. (8.254)

"Of the village families" means: the witnesses who are direct observers of the boundary marks must be questioned by the two litigants, or by the villagers, regarding the communities of village folk and those appointed by the village. || 8.254 ||
Once they have been questioned, he should establish the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, and he should record the names of all of them. (8.255)

"Regarding the phrase 'as they, when questioned, should unanimously declare a decision on the boundary': once those witnesses have been questioned, in whatever manner they may all unanimously and without disagreement declare a certain determination concerning the boundary, in that same manner the boundary should be recorded in a document for the sake of memory, and all those witnesses should be written down according to their individual names. (8.255)
Or, having taken him by the head, wearing garlands and clad in red garments,
and being sworn by their own good deeds, they shall lead him in accordance with justice.

"By their heads": those witnesses, having put on garlands and red garments and having taken a clod of earth upon their heads, being sworn by such good deeds as "May whatever merit we have become fruitless," shall all together determine the boundary, having made it not deviate from the truth. (8.256)
Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it otherwise shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.

"According to what has been stated": those witnesses who prioritize the truth, determining matters in the manner prescribed by the scriptures and being bound by the rule of speaking the truth, all become pure. However, if they determine them falsely, each shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred paṇas. (8.257)
In the absence of witnesses, however, four inhabitants living on the outskirts of the village boundary shall, being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king. (8.258)

"But in the absence of witnesses, four villagers living on the boundary," [so it is said]. In the absence of witnesses belonging to the two villages that are the subject of the dispute, four villagers living on the boundary in the four directions shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king according to the rules for witnesses. (8.258)
But in the absence of neighboring witnesses within the boundary of the primary witnesses, one should also interrogate these men who frequent the forest. 8.259.

But in the absence of neighboring villagers who are original boundary-witnesses, he should also question other men who frequent the forest. From the time of the village's settlement, if there are no original boundary-witnesses residing on the edge of that village, he should interrogate other men, namely those who dwell in the forest, as will be described hereafter. (8.259)
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers. (8.260)

"Regarding 'hunters' (vyādhān)": one should question hunters who live by killing birds, cowherds whose livelihood consists of digging ponds and the like, those who produce roots for trees and such, snake-catchers, those who live by gleaning ears of grain and single grains, and others who frequent the forest for the sake of fruits, flowers, firewood, and so forth. One should ask them: "Do they ever enter the middle of the village from here for the sake of some business, or do they go to the forest? (8.260)
Whatever marks they may describe when questioned regarding the boundaries and junctions, the king shall establish those exactly so for the two villages in accordance with dharma. (8.261)

Regarding the word "ta" (them): having been questioned, those hunters and others should provide an indication of the boundary-junction according to the location and in whatever manner it may be known; the king, in that same form and avoiding partiality, shall establish the boundary between the two villages.
The determination of boundaries and landmarks for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be known as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors. (8.262)
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary, they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement. (8.263)

Regarding "of fields, wells, and tanks," and "neighbors": if, when men are disputing over a boundary marker, the neighbors living near the boundary should speak falsely, then the king shall fine each of them individually with the middle amercement. And thus, for those who are neighbors, the previously mentioned fine of two hundred [paṇas] is to be understood as the penalty. (8.262–263)
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred. (8.264)

"House": one who takes away any one of the house, a pond, or a garden after first threatening with death, imprisonment, or fear, shall be fined five hundred paṇas; however, if he takes it by mistake, he shall be fined two hundred paṇas. (8.264)
If the boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, knowing the law, shall assign land to them for their benefit; such is the settled rule. (8.265)

Regarding the phrase "at the boundary": when a boundary is impossible to determine due to the absence of boundary markers, witnesses, and so forth, the king who knows the Dharma, acting without partiality, shall establish the limit as follows: the land situated between two villages belongs to those villagers alone for whom that land provides benefit. (8.265)
This law concerning the determination of boundaries has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse. (8.266)

"This" refers to this aforementioned determination of boundaries (*sīmāvinirṇaya*), which is not devoid of dharma, having been stated in its entirety. Immediately following, I shall explain in detail the determination regarding the subject of harsh speech (*paruṣabhāṣaṇa*); for verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) is generally more intolerable than physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). First, the investigation of verbal abuse follows the sequence [of the table of contents]. Furthermore, although the term *daṇḍa* (punishment) is mentioned first in the verse because of the meter—reading "punishment for verbal abuse" (*pāruṣye daṇḍaḥ vācike*)—the discussion proceeds accordingly. 8.266.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya deserves two hundred or fifty; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. (8.267)

"Regarding 'one hundred'": since it will be stated later that this applies "in disputes," [the rule is as follows]: having reviled a Brāhmaṇa man—excluding his mother, sister, or a woman who has committed a heinous sin or an act causing loss of caste—a Kṣatriya shall pay one hundred *paṇas*, a Vaiśya one hundred and fifty or two hundred, but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. Furthermore, depending on the specific nature of the insult, he may deserve such things as beating or the cutting off of the tongue. (8.267)
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for violating a Kṣatriya woman;
for a Vaiśya woman, the fine shall be forty-five; and for a Śūdra woman, the punishment is twelve. 8.268.

"Forty-five" means: with respect to the aforementioned [offenses], a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra are to be fined fifty, twenty-five, twenty, and twelve and a half paṇas respectively. (8.268)
In the case of an offense committed by twice-born men against one of equal caste, the fine shall be exactly twelve;
in disputes that are not fit for verbal discussion, that same fine shall be doubled.

Regarding the phrase "of equal caste": when an insult of the aforementioned kind is uttered by members of the twice-born against one of their own caste, and a transgression has occurred, the offender shall be fined exactly twelve *paṇas*. However, in the case of unspeakable disputes—such as those involving abusive language directed at a mother, a sister, and so forth—the fine becomes double that which was prescribed for insulting a Brāhmaṇa, such as in the rule stating "one who insults a Brāhmaṇa [shall pay] a hundred," and so on. (8.269)
But one of low birth who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of inferior origin. (8.270)

"Regarding 'of one birth': a Śūdra, having insulted twice-born men with speech such as 'slayer' and so forth, or by saying 'these [men] are low-born like feet,' shall undergo the cutting off of his tongue. (8.270)
But for one who utters their names or castes with malice, a glowing iron spike ten finger-breadths long shall be thrust into his mouth. (8.271)

"Regarding 'the utterance of name and caste': for a Śūdra who, with the intent to insult these twice-born men, utters their names and proclaims their castes, an iron nail ten fingers in length, blazing with fire, shall be thrust into his mouth. (8.271)
If he should out of pride give instruction in the Dharma to Brahmins, the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears. (8.272)

Regarding "instruction in the Dharma": if a Śūdra, having perceived some slight trace of dharma practiced by someone through deceit, should with pride instruct Brāhmaṇas, saying, "This is your own duty," the king shall cause burning oil to be poured into that person's mouth and both ears.
If one speaks falsely out of pride regarding another's learning, country, caste, or even their physical body, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. (8.273)

"Regarding the word 'heard': if one says to someone of the same caste, 'This has not been heard by you,' 'You were not born in this country,' 'This is not your birth-status,' or 'The rites for purifying the body, such as initiation (*upanayana*), have not been performed by you'—if he speaks such falsehoods, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred *paṇas*. However, a Śūdra is not subject to this rule when speaking to the twice-born, because of the lightness of the punishment in his case. (8.273)
Whether speaking of one who is one-eyed, or lame, or otherwise similarly deformed, even if speaking the truth, he shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa. (8.274)

"Regarding 'one-eyed' (kāṇaṃ)": if one speaks—even truthfully—of another who is one-eyed, or lame in a foot, or otherwise deficient in a limb such as being blind, using words like "one-eyed" and so forth, he shall be made to pay the lowest fine of one *kārṣāpaṇa*. (8.274)
One who defames his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; likewise, one who does not yield the path to his teacher. 8.275.

Regarding the word "mother": according to the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana*, it is stated that those who are accused by the virtuous are classified as either "defamed" (*kṣārita*) or "not defamed" (*akṣārita*). Therefore, one who brings a charge of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) against a mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher, or who does not yield the path to a teacher, shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. Here, the establishment of unequal boundaries for the punishment of the mother, wife, and others—whether based on repetition or non-repetition of the defamation—must be avoided. (8.275)
But a wise king should inflict punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (8.276)

"By a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya": when mutual insults involving grounds for loss of caste have been uttered by a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya toward one another, this punishment must be inflicted upon them according to their learning, lineage, country, caste, and so forth. When an insult is made against a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya, a first amercement (prathamasāhasa) shall be imposed on the Brāhmaṇa; when an insult is made against a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa, a middle amercement (madhyamasāhasa) shall be imposed on the Kṣatriya. (8.276)
In the case of Vaiśyas and Śūdras toward their own respective castes, the rule is certain: the infliction of punishment is exactly as prescribed, with the exception of mutilation. 8.277.

Regarding the verse beginning with *viṭśūdrayoḥ*: when a Vaiśya or a Śūdra utters an insulting word that causes loss of caste (*patanīya*) against each other, the punishment shall be carried out exactly as in the case of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya—consisting of the first and middle amercements—but excluding the cutting off of the tongue. And this applies to one instance of insulting a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya; thus, for a Śūdra, the cutting off of the tongue remains the final penalty. (8.277)
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to its true nature;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault. 8.278

"Regarding this": this refers to the aforementioned type of punishment for verbal abuse, which immediately precedes [the discussion of] physical assault involving hands, sticks, weapons, and so forth; following this, I shall declare the determination of punishment for the infliction of pain through beating, injury, and the like, which are the causes of physical assault. (8.278)
If an outcaste should injure any part of the body of a superior, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu. (8.279)

Regarding the word "yeneti" (by which): if an outcaste, that is, a Śūdra, should strike a twice-born man with anything whatsoever—whether by hand, foot, or the like, either directly or indirectly through an instrument such as a staff—the very limb by which he struck him must be cut off. This is the instruction connected to Manu; the mention of Manu is for the sake of showing respect, and the following [verse] is likewise [for that purpose]. 8.279.
Raising his hand or a staff, he deserves the cutting off of his hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of his foot. (8.280)

"Raising the hand" means that by threatening with the hand or a staff, one becomes liable to have one's hand cut off; by striking with the foot out of anger, one becomes liable to have one's foot cut off. (8.280)
One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of superior caste shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be gashed. (8.281)

"Regarding 'sharing a seat': a Śūdra of inferior birth who sits upon the same seat as a Brāhmaṇa, having a permanent mark made of heated iron on his hip, shall be banished from the country; or else, one shall have the flesh cut from the region known as the buttocks. (8.281)

The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of pride to be cut off; likewise, he shall have the penis of one who urinates upon him cut off, and the anus of one who passes wind against him. (8.282)

"Regarding 'on account of spitting': if one causes a Śūdra to vomit phlegm by means of forcibly inducing him to spit, one should cut off both his lips; likewise, if he insults [the teacher] with urine, one should cut off his penis, and if he insults him with the sound of his lower parts, one should cut off his anus. (8.282)
If someone seizes him by the hair, he should cut off the hand without hesitation; the same applies if they seize him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles. (8.283)

Regarding the phrase "in the hair": if a Śūdra pulls a Brāhmaṇa by the hair, or by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles, the king shall cause his hand to be cut off while it is still hanging down. 8.283.
One who cuts the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished. 8.284.

Regarding the phrase "one who pierces the skin": one of the same caste who merely pierces the hide, but is not a Śūdra, shall be fined one hundred paṇas for a Brāhmaṇa, because of the lightness of the punishment. Likewise, one who causes blood to flow shall be fined exactly one hundred; one who pierces the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas; and one who breaks a bone shall be banished from the country. (8.284)
According as the utility of all forest trees is [utilized], so must punishment be inflicted for injury; such is the settled rule. 8.285.

"Regarding the enjoyment of all forest trees, according to the manner [in which it occurs]": the inferior form of enjoyment consists in providing shade; the middling form of enjoyment for all forest trees consists in the taking of flowers; and the superior form consists in the taking of fruit. In consideration of these, punishment for cutting them down should be imposed. For one who enjoys merely the shade, there is a small fine at the outset; for one who enjoys the flowers, such as jasmine and the like, the fine is middling; and for one who enjoys the fruit, such as the mango and the like, it is severe. (8.285)
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the sake of causing pain, one should inflict a punishment that corresponds exactly to the magnitude of that suffering. (8.286)

"Of men" means that when a blow is struck for the purpose of causing pain to humans or animals, to the extent that great pain arises—whether from tearing the skin or by piercing the vital organs (*marmans*) and so forth—to that same extent, the one who caused the tearing of the skin shall be punished; thus, one should impose a punishment even greater than the initial [prescribed] amount. (8.286)
In cases of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of [injuring] vital breath or blood, he shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery or even the full fine. (8.287)

In cases of injury to a limb, or likewise to vital breath (*prāṇa*) or blood, the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery or even the full penalty. When injuries are inflicted upon limbs such as the belly, arms, and so forth by means of binding with clothes or similar objects, or when injuries are inflicted upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*, i.e., wind) by means of its obstruction and the like, or when injuries are inflicted upon the blood—even those that do not cause it to flow externally—by means of grasping with a tight fist, a rope, or other such means; the offender must be made by the king to pay the expenses for medicines and the like required to restore the body to its former condition. If he does not pay his own share of the penalty along with the expenses for recovery, then both that expense and the penalty must be made to be paid by him to the king for the purpose of the fine. (8.287)
If one should damage the property of another, whether intentionally or even unintentionally, he shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king. (8.288)

"Goods" (dravyāṇi): he who, whether by force or through negligence, destroys those goods belonging to another—such as leather, leatherwork, and so forth, which will be mentioned later, as well as surplus items such as bracelets, armlets, and the like—should satisfy the owner by repairing them or other means, and he should pay the king a fine equal to the value of the destroyed goods. (8.288)
For leather and leatherwork, as well as for articles made of wood or clay, and for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value. (8.289)

Regarding the phrase "in leather and leather-worker's vessels": in the case of leathers, and in vessels made of leather, wood, or clay, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits belonging to others, there is no fine of five times their value to be paid by the king; rather, the satisfaction of the owner must be secured. (8.289)
They say there are ten exceptions regarding the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in all other cases, punishment is ordained. (8.290)

Regarding the phrase "of the vehicle" (*yānasya*): for the vehicle—such as a cart—and the driver—such as the charioteer—and the owner of the vehicle, those [faults] pertaining to them, such as having a broken nose or mouth which will be described below, exist beyond the causes and so forth; that is, they occur even when transgressing the prescribed rules. When these [faults] exist, even if injury to living beings or destruction of property has been caused by the vehicle, Manu and others have declared that there is no punishment for the driver and the rest of those connected to the vehicle, provided that the owner of the vehicle and the others have issued a verbal command [to proceed], such as "drive on. However, that is not correct; for in cases other than those specific causes, punishment is indeed imposed. (8.290)
He first states those cases where there is no fault:
"When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction, and likewise when the axle of the vehicle breaks or the wheel breaks. (8.291)
In the case of breaking a machine, as well as a yoke or a rein, and also when one cries out "Go away!", Manu has declared that there is no punishment. (8.292)

Regarding the terms *chinnanāsya* ("with a cut nose-rope"), *chedana* ("cutting"), and so forth: when the rope attached to the nose of a bullock is severed; when the wooden yoke (*yugma*) of a cart or similar vehicle is broken; when the vehicle, such as a cart, moves sideways or backwards due to uneven ground or other causes; when a pin or similar part fails to enter the axle of the vehicle and breaks; when the leather straps that bind the mechanical parts are torn; when the rope on the neck of an animal called a *yoktra* is severed; and when there is a call from the charioteer or others saying "Move aside! Move aside!"—in these cases, Manu states that there is no punishment for the charioteer or others for injury to living beings or destruction of property caused by the vehicle. (8.291–92)
If a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for any injury and shall be fined two hundred panas.

Regarding the phrase "where the pair turns back": furthermore, where the vehicle proceeds otherwise due to the driver's lack of skill, in that case of injury, the owner of the vehicle must be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] for employing an unskilled driver. And regarding the driver, even though there is the killing of a person, the driver to be mentioned later is defined by his being "not slow," meaning he is "swift. Thus, some say that the mention of "two hundred" here and the mention of "one hundred" in the subsequent verse are intended to be significant; however, that is incorrect, because the Sage’s intention was to express the necessity of vigilance (apramāda). (8.293)
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred. (8.294)

Regarding the term *prājaka*: if, however, the charioteer (*sārathi*) is skilled, then the charioteer alone deserves the punishment to be described later for the killing of a human, and not the owner [the fine of] two hundred. If the charioteer is unskilled, then all others besides the owner who are riding in the vehicle must each be fined one hundred for mounting a vehicle with an unskilled charioteer; as for the charioteer, he remains subject to the penalty for the killing of a human and so forth. (8.294)
But if, while obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot, he should cause the death of living beings, the punishment there is not to be deliberated upon. (8.295)

Regarding the word "he": if that charioteer, his vehicle obstructed by oxen and other animals blocked by another vehicle coming from the opposite direction, or if, due to an unevenness in the ground, he moves backward and—out of inexperience—should cause a living being to be crushed by the chariot, the punishment for this has been deliberated upon by Manu and others. (8.295)
In the case of killing a human being, one quickly incurs guilt like that of a thief; likewise for taking the property of living beings such as cows, camels, horses, and the like. (8.296)

Regarding "the killing of a human": even when a human is killed through the driver's lack of skill, there is only a delay [in punishment] for him; like a thief, he receives the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*), but not the corporal punishment or other penalties of a thief. Since half [of the fine] is seen for large living beings, it should be according to power in the case of large animals such as cows and so forth, and according to size. (When snakes or buffaloes are killed,) the fine shall be five hundred of the highest amercement. (8.296)
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.

Regarding "small animals": since goats and sheep will be mentioned later, for the killing of small-sized animals such as calves, foals, and the like, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed. Furthermore, for the killing of wild animals and birds, such as boars and so forth, the fine shall be fifty paṇas. (8.298)
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa. (8.298)

Regarding the phrase "of donkeys, goats, and sheep": for the killing of donkeys, goats, and other such animals, the fine shall be the measure of one silver *māṣaka*. This is because we observe that the prescribed fines decrease progressively; furthermore, the mention of the *māṣaka* here refers to silver (*ahairaṇya*), since it would otherwise not be less than the previous fines, nor does it refer to copper, as that would result in an excessively low penalty even for the killing of dogs and pigs. (8.298)
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—when they have committed an offense, they may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane. (8.299)

"A wife, a pupil, a slave, a son, and a uterine brother—these, beginning with the wife, when they have committed an offense, may be punished with a rope or a bamboo strip; this refers to the punishment for injury. They shall be punished according to their means. (8.299)
But one must strike on the back of the body and never on the head;
for striking otherwise, one incurs the guilt of a thief. (8.300)

"Behind" means that they should be struck on the back part of the body, but never on the head or the chest; having struck him otherwise than in the manner described, or by means of a staff, he shall incur the punishment for a thief, which consists of verbal reprimand. (8.300)
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
"This" refers to the verbal punishment for harshness just mentioned, which has been fully explained. Hereafter, I shall state the rules for the determination of punishments for theft. (8.301)
The king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase. (8.302)

"Supreme" means that the king should apply the most rigorous prosecution in the case of the regulation regarding thieves; because through their suppression, the king's subjects become free from calamity, and the country prospers through an abundance of people and wealth. (8.302)
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of worship;
indeed, his sacrificial session, even when lacking ritual fees, is ever-increasing.

Regarding the phrase "of the fearless": by suppressing the wickedness of thieves, he grants fearlessness to the virtuous; thus, he is always worthy of worship by everyone. For the suppression of thieves constitutes a *sattra* (sacrificial session) that is like a specific ritual (*ṛtu*). This [suppression], known as the "suppression of thieves," is accomplished for him with a pre-eminence distinct from other *sattras*. Indeed, another *sattra* has a fixed duration, whereas this one exists at all times; furthermore, another *sattra* involves sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), whereas this one has "fearlessness" as its fee—that is, it is one where fearlessness is the sacrificial fee. (8.303)
A sixth part of all merit belongs to the king who protects;
indeed, a sixth part of even demerit belongs to him who does not protect. (8.304)

"From all sides" means that, in addition to the payment of wages, a sixth part of the merit (*dharma*) belonging to learned *śrotriyas* and other virtuous persons accrues to the king by virtue of protecting his subjects. Conversely, for one who fails to protect them, a sixth part of the demerit (*adharma*) arising from theft in the world also accrues to him; therefore, he should diligently protect the subjects by suppressing thieves. Nor is it improper for the king to acquire merit simply because he has been hired for his livelihood, since, just like the hiring for a livelihood, the hiring for a share of merit is also sanctioned by the scriptures. (8.304)
Whatever he studies, whatever he sacrifices, whatever he gives, and whatever he worships—the king becomes a sharer in a sixth part of that by virtue of protecting him properly. (8.305)

Regarding the phrase "whatever has been studied": whatever fruit results from study, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, worshipping deities, and so forth—a sixth part of that fruit is obtained by the king through his proper protection of the subjects. (8.305)
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices day after day with fees of hundreds and thousands. (8.306)

"Protecting by means of righteousness" (dharmeṇa): By protecting all beings, both stationary and moving, according to the established rules of the scriptures, and by executing those deserving of death—such as thieves and others—in accordance with the scriptures, the king daily acquires the fruit associated with sacrifices (*yajña*) that require a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of one hundred thousand. In this regard, it might be objected: "How can the fruit associated with actions involving great effort be obtained from an action involving little effort? If that were so, who indeed would engage in strenuous efforts? This objection is valid, for a distinction does exist regarding the brevity or length of the time of enjoying the fruit. Thus, it should be understood in other cases as well. (8.306)
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls, shares of produce, and fines, shall immediately go to hell. (8.307)

"He who does not protect" and "the enjoyment of prosperity": that king who, failing to protect his subjects, collects taxes such as the one-sixth share of grain and so forth, or levies fees from forest guards, slaves, and others who travel by land routes and so on for the sake of profit—the enjoyment of prosperity, the fruit consisting of fruits, flowers, and the like, or the means thereof, namely tolls and fines in legal disputes and the like—he goes to hell itself at the end of his life. (8.307)
They say that one who does not protect, but consumes [the people] while taking a sixth part as tax, is the remover of all the impurities of the entire world. (8.308)

"An unprotecting [king]" means: Manu and others have declared that a king who does not protect and yet takes a sixth part of the produce as tax in the form of tribute is one who appropriates all the sins belonging to the entire world. (8.308)
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect and instead devours his subjects, is destined for a downward path.

"Disregarding the bounds of propriety" means that one should know a king who has transgressed the bounds of scriptural conduct and custom, who holds the view that there is no world beyond, who inflicts unjust punishments and confiscates wealth, and who collects taxes such as the *karabali* [or *balī*], to be one destined for hell. (8.309)
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment. (8.310)

"Unrighteous" means that one should diligently restrain an unrighteous thief according to his offense by three methods of restraint: by confining him in a prison, by binding him with fetters and the like, and by various forms of corporal punishment such as cutting off his hands or feet. (8.310)
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous, kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrificial rites. 8.311

Regarding the phrase "by means of suppression": since kings become purified at all times—just as the twice-born are purified by great sacrifices and other rites—through the suppression of those who commit evil deeds and the favoring of those of virtuous conduct, they should therefore suppress the unrighteous. 8.311.
A lord should always be patient with men who come before him with petitions, as well as with children, the elderly, and the sick, while acting for his own welfare. (8.312)

"One must practice forbearance. Forbearance should always be exercised by a king toward children, the elderly, and the sick who act for their own benefit; toward those occupied with business; toward those who revile while being robbed or whose kinsmen have been slain; and toward children, the elderly, and the diseased who revile out of distress, desiring the assistance that will be described for themselves. (8.312)
He who endures being reviled by those in distress is exalted in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not endure it, goes to hell because of that. (8.313)

Regarding the statement "that he endures when insulted": because he forgives those who revile him with harsh words, he is exalted in the heavenly world; he partakes in greatness. But because he does not tolerate [insults] out of pride in his power, he goes to hell. (8.313)
The wise thief should go to the king with disheveled hair, confessing that theft: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me. (8.314)
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood, or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron mace. (8.315)

"By the king," "on the shoulder," and so forth—this is what is being restated in these two verses within this section on punishments (*daṇḍaprakaraṇa*), for the purpose of instructing the king in his duty known as punishment regarding the theft of gold, which will be explained in the section on penances (*prāyaścittaprakaraṇa*) starting with the words "A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold. The thief of a Brahmin’s gold must go before the king carrying on his shoulder a weapon called a *muśala* (a pestle), or a club made of *khadira* wood, or a weapon called a *śakti* (a spear), or an iron staff with sharp points at both ends; he should do so while proclaiming that theft by saying with urgency, "This gold of a Brahmin has been stolen by me! and with his hair disheveled. Having arrived, he must say to the king: "I am the thief of a Brahmin’s gold; kill me with this pestle or other weapon. (8.314–315)
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.316)

"By the command" means "command him yourself. By killing or abandoning one who belongs to the king, that thief is released from that sin. However, since it will be stated later, "One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa thief, even if he is guilty of every crime," the king who kills one who merely threatens a Brāhmaṇa incurs the sin belonging to that [Brāhmaṇa]; therefore, such a person must be killed by the king. It is with this intent that all this has been stated here. (8.316)
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief to the king. (8.317)

Because it is said, "he who eats his food": he who is a Brāhmaṇa eats the food related to that [person]; he purifies his own sin pertaining to that object, and thus the sin becomes his—this is precisely what is intended here. It is not, however, with the thought that this is an expiation for the murder of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*). Likewise, when a husband forgives an unfaithful wife, he takes on her sin. And a disciple, when his teacher endures the non-performance of restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*), transfers the sin born thereof to him. And a patron (*yājya*), when performing a sacrifice otherwise than prescribed, casts his sin upon the officiating priest (*yājaka*) if the latter forgives him. And a thief, when the king forgives him, [the sin remains]; therefore, the king must speak [of the punishment]. (8.317)
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds. (8.318)

"By kings": having committed sins in former births, those [thieves] who have been extracted [from their guilt] by kings, having likewise performed excellent sacrifices, go to heaven as sinless ones, like the learned (śiṣṭa) who perform auspicious deeds. Regarding those who receive punishment from the king on account of that sin, because of the plural "sins" (*pāpāni*) here, it is understood that the thief of gold alone is subject to punishment; it is not merely a removal of the specific act, but rather the entire transgression is determined within his own domain. Furthermore, the removal of sin through punishment is to be understood as applying only to one who has come forward of his own accord, and not in the case of one punished by force. For even in the case of one punished by force, if he should subsequently establish [his innocence], a removal of sin through penance such as entering fire is shown; otherwise, how could there be a removal of sin for one who is under the power of another through the torments of Yama? (8.318)
But he who draws a rope or a jar from a well, or who breaks a water-shed, shall incur a fine of one māṣa, and he must restore that [damage] to it. (8.319)

"Whoever" means: whoever should take away a rope or a jar from a well, or whoever should destroy (or tear open) a water-distribution house, or [steal] gold with silver weighing a *māṣa*, he shall receive a punishment from the king according to the circumstances, such as the total loss of his property; and in that case, the rope and so forth must be restored to that well. (8.319)
For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
for any lesser amount, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value, and that property shall be returned to its owner. (8.320)

Regarding "grain": two *palas* make a hundred [units], twenty *droṇas* make one *kumbha*. For one who steals grain exceeding ten *kumbhas*, the king shall impose a corporal punishment consisting of flogging, mutilation of limbs, or execution, depending on the status of the thief and the circumstances of the time, such as whether it is a time of plenty or famine. Furthermore, for the amount stolen up to ten *kumbhas*, he should be made to pay a fine eleven times the value of what was taken. He must also be made to restore that property to its owner; and in all cases, the following [punishment] shall be imposed upon the owner. (8.320)
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, or for the finest garments, there is the death penalty when the amount exceeds one hundred. (8.321)

"So be it. Regarding gold, silver, and the like, as well as highly valuable garments: not only in the case of grain, as previously stated, but even when superior items such as gold, silver, coral, and so forth, as well as excellent garments such as fine silk (*antaḥpaṭṭa*) and the like, have been stolen in an amount exceeding one *chatā*, the death penalty must be imposed. Furthermore, in this matter, the equalization of unequal [values] must be avoided by taking into account the place, time, the nature of the stolen object, and the caste and qualities of the owner. Otherwise, there would result an identical punishment for both high-value and low-value items; it should be understood in this manner. (8.321)
But for an amount exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value. 8.322.

"Of fifty": for stealing more than these fifty previously mentioned items, up to one hundred, this amputation of the hand is prescribed by Manu and others. For every fifty items stolen, the king shall impose a fine eleven times the value of that property. (8.322)
One who steals men of noble birth, and especially women, as well as the finest of gems, deserves the death penalty. (8.323)

Regarding "of men": for stealing from persons of noble lineage—especially women born of noble families—and for stealing principal gems such as diamonds (*vajra*) and lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), one deserves execution consisting of flogging and the amputation of limbs, depending on the place, time, the thief, the owner, the species [of the object], and so forth. (8.323)
In the case of the theft of large animals, weapons, or medicine, the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the circumstances of the act. (8.324)

Regarding "of large animals": having carefully considered the seizure of large animals such as elephants, horses, cows, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as the purpose of the theft—such as swords and the like, or fine ghee and so on—and the resulting consequences, namely war, famine, or personal ruin, as well as the forms of the offense such as gambling, enmity, or the failure of a rope, the king shall determine a punishment that is neither too light nor too heavy. Having fully understood the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*), this is stated not for the sake of leniency, but rather for the sake of showing due regard; for in cases such as the theft of weapons, medicine, or tools of the hand, there arises a grave calamity leading to war and other disasters. (8.324)
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for piercing their noses,
and likewise for the theft of animals, one must immediately undergo the penance of standing on one foot for half a day.

"Regarding cows belonging to Brahmins and the piercing of the nose": upon the theft of cows related to Brahmins, as well as upon the piercing of the nose of a barren cow for the purpose of using it for transport, and upon the theft of animals such as sheep intended for sacrifices and other rites—because the punishment for these is more severe—one must immediately inflict a penalty consisting of the cutting off of a foot or half a foot. (8.325)
Of thread, cotton, and fermenting agents; of cow dung and molasses; of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass. || 8.326 ||
For the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, as well as salts, and likewise for the theft of earthenware, earth, or ashes; (8.327)
Of fish and birds, of oil and ghee, of meat and honey, and whatever else originates from animals. (8.328)
For other such items as these, for raw grain, for cooked rice, and for all kinds of prepared food, the fine shall be double their value. (8.329)
