Regarding "cotton, thread, and fermenting agents," and "bamboo and split-bamboo vessels": for the theft of wool and other fibers, of that substance called *kiṇva* (fermenting agent), of buttermilk, of cow's milk, of vessels made from the bark of bamboo and similar materials, of salts such as rock salt (*saindhava*) and black salt (*biḍalavaṇa*), of honey (*mākṣika*), of even the smallest products derived from animals such as horns and teeth, as well as other such solid substances like realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and vermilion (*sindūra*), of cooked rice, of flour-meals (*saktu*) and the like, of prepared foods such as cakes (*apūpa*) and sweetmeats (*modaka*), and of all well-known items such as cotton—twice the value shall be imposed as a fine for their theft. (8.326–329)
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other such things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas*.

Regarding the phrase "in flowers": in the case of fields of indigo, grain, shrubs, creepers, or trees that are densely populated by men—as indicated by the verse to be cited later—and because of the possibility of sowing [seeds] there, as well as in the case of grain that has been stored in a threshing floor and stolen, the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas* of gold or silver, depending on the place and the time. (8.330)

When grain, vegetables, roots, and fruits have been winnowed, the fine shall be one hundred panas for stealing them without prior connection [to the owner], and fifty panas if there was a prior connection. (8.331)

Regarding the phrase "when [the goods] have been cleared": when the remaining vegetables and such have been winnowed and then stolen, the fine for theft is one hundred *paṇas* when there is a struggle with the owner; however, if they were already gathered together, the fine is fifty *paṇas*. (8.331)

An act committed by force with a connection [to the owner] would be *sāhasa* (violence); that which is done without such connection, as well as what is taken and then denied, constitutes *steya* (theft). 8.332.

It may be argued that this refers to *sāhasa* (violence). That act which is committed by force (*prasahya*) in the very presence of the owner of the property—such as the theft of grain or other goods—is *sāhasa*; therefore, the punishment for theft should not be applied there. It is for this purpose that the specific type of theft is taught here. On the other hand, that which is committed in the owner's absence (*parokṣa*) constitutes *steya* (theft). And even if, after having stolen, one denies it, that too is indeed *steya*. (8.332)
The king should inflict the same punishment on a man who steals these prepared materials as he would on one who steals the sacrificial fire from the house. (8.333)

"Whoever [steals] these," etc.: whoever a man should steal these substances—thread and so forth—which have been prepared for the purpose of use, and whoever should even steal common fire, the king shall punish him with the first amercement. Since the valuation of fire is not established through commercial practice, the fine of double its value would be impossible; therefore, it is mentioned separately from thread and the other items. (8.333)
With whichever specific limb a thief acts against men, that very limb the king shall take away as a deterrent. (8.334)

"By whatever [means]" means: whichever limb—such as a hand or a foot—and by whatever method—such as cutting a knot or climbing a ladder—a thief seeks to commit an act hostile toward men, such as the theft of wealth, the king shall have that very limb cut off once he has engaged in such practice, in order to eliminate that offense. (8.334)
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—there is no one who, failing to abide by his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king. (8.335)

"Father and teacher": among father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, and domestic priest, he who does not proceed according to his own duty is not one who "cannot be punished" by the king; rather, even he may be punished. This statement is made because of the fear that fathers, mothers, and others might escape punishment due to pride or affection. (8.335)
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, the king should be fined one thousand; this is the established rule. (8.336)

Regarding the term "kārṣāpaṇa": the settled rule is that for whatever offense an ordinary person other than the king would be fined one *paṇa*, for that same offense the king shall be fined one thousand *paṇas*. As for the phrase "having cast that fine into the waters," etc., the punishment consisting of the king's own person is to be thrown away or given to a Brāhmaṇa, as will be explained hereafter. (8.336)
But for a Śūdra, the guilt incurred in theft becomes eightfold;
for a Vaiśya, it is sixteenfold, and for a Kṣatriya, thirty-twofold. (8.337)
For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even a full hundred;
or it may be double that sixty-four, for he indeed knows both their faults and virtues. (8.338)

"Eightfold," [it is said]. "Of a Brāhmaṇa. Whatever punishment has been declared for a theft, that same punishment is incurred eightfold by a Śūdra who knows the merits and defects [of the act]; it should be made eight times greater on account of his qualities. For a learned Vaiśya, it is sixteenfold; for a Kṣatriya versed in the scriptures, thirty-twofold; for a Brāhmaṇa, sixty-fourfold, or seventy-twofold, or even a full hundredfold, depending on the excellence of his qualities, since this Brāhmaṇa knows both the merits and the defects regarding theft. (8.337–338)
Manu has declared that wood from trees, roots and fruits, as well as wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, are not subject to the law of theft. (8.339)

Regarding the phrase "products of trees": based on the Smṛti of Gautama, "the flowers and fruits of trees that have not been cultivated," one should understand that roots and fruits belonging to uncultivated trees and the like are not subject to theft; likewise, wood for the purpose of providing fodder for cows or for maintaining the sacred fire (as seen in the context of the cow and the fire) is not theft, as it serves a visible purpose and is for the sake of the fire prescribed by the scriptures. Furthermore, in the absence of any other recourse, Manu has declared that even grass belonging to another, taken for the sake of feeding a cow, is not theft; therefore, there is no punishment or penalty in these cases. (8.339)
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching—is exactly like a thief. (8.340)

Regarding the word "he": even a Brāhmaṇa who, like a thief, takes what has not been given—even if he acquires another's wealth, however small, through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or receiving gifts—he too should be recognized as a thief; therefore, he is to be punished like a thief. (8.340)
A twice-born man traveling on a road whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished. (8.341)
Regarding the term "dvija": a twice-born man who is a traveler with exhausted provisions, taking two sugarcane stalks and two radishes from another's field, is not liable to pay a fine. (8.341)
One who binds those who are unbound, releases those who are bound, and seizes the slaves, horses, and chariots, shall incur the guilt of a thief. (8.342)

"Of those not tied up": one who, out of arrogance, ties up the untethered horses and other animals belonging to others, or releases those that are tied up, or steals chariots from stables and the like, or whoever carries off slaves, horses, and chariots, shall receive the punishment for a thief.
By carrying out the suppression of thieves according to this rule, a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. (8.343)
"By this": by means of this aforementioned method, a king who effects the restraint of thieves shall obtain fame in this world and supreme happiness in the next. (8.343)
A king who desires to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, undecaying glory should not overlook a reckless man even for a moment. (8.344)

Now he speaks of rashness: "Aindra," etc. Desiring the station characterized by universal sovereignty—which is indestructible, undiminishing, and renowned—the king, even by means of rashness or through the force of his power, must not neglect for even a moment a person who commits acts such as arson or the tearing of clothes. (8.344)
A man who commits violence through harsh speech, theft, or indeed by means of physical punishment, should be known as the worst among evildoers. (8.345)

Regarding the phrase "than one who is verbally wicked": it should be understood that a person who commits violence is an even greater evildoer than those who commit verbal abuse, theft, or capital offenses. (8.345)
But that king who tolerates one who persists in violence quickly goes to destruction and incurs hatred. (8.346)
Regarding "violence": he who forgives one engaged in violence is very quickly destroyed by those violent doers due to excessive attachment, and he incurs hatred in the world. (8.346)
Neither for the sake of a friend nor from the acquisition of vast wealth should a king release those who act with violence, for they bring fear to all living beings. (8.347)

"No," [says the author]. A king should not abandon even those who act with reckless violence and cause fear to all living beings, whether through the word of a friend or through the acquisition of great wealth. 8.347.
The twice-born should accept the sacred teaching when their dharma is obstructed, and when there is a disruption among the twice-born and the social orders caused by the force of time. (8.348)
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in order to protect a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma. (8.349)

Regarding the term *śāstra* (weapon) and *ātman* (self): Brāhmaṇas and others may take up weapons such as swords and the like. At a time when members of the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) are not permitted to perform their religious duties (*dharma*) due to thieves and other obstacles, and when there is a confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) among the twice-born Brāhmaṇas and others caused by the absence of a king, foreign invasions, or internal disturbances; and likewise, for the sake of protecting one’s own person, inheritance, and property, or in a battle connected with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or in a war caused by robbery, or for the protection of women and Brāhmaṇas—one who, being without other recourse, slays enemies according to the law (*dharma*) through treacherous combat (*kūṭayuddha*) with that weapon, does not incur sin. Furthermore, in such a case, the punishment for violence (*sāhasadaṇḍa*) shall not be imposed. (8.348–349)
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin, one should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation. (8.350)
Regarding the term "guru": an incendiary, a poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, a robber of wealth, and a stealer of land or wife— these six are *ātatāyin*s (aggressors).

Thus, as stated by Vasiṣṭha and others, one should indeed kill without hesitation even any one of the following—whether a teacher, a child, an elder, or a Brāhmaṇa—if they approach as an *ātatāyin* (an assailant) intent upon acts such as killing. How much more so for anyone else? For even in the case of teachers, expounders, and the like, there is no censure for the killing of such harmful persons, as indicated by the passage beginning with "and the teacher who expounds [the Veda]. (8.350)
No fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an assassin, whether done openly or in secret; it is fury that meets that fury. (8.351)

"No," [it is said]. In the case of open combat, or in secret [acts] such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) or the killing of an assailant (*ātatāyin*), no fault whatsoever—known as either a low penalty or a penance (*prāyaścitta*)—accrues to the killer. This is because the deity who presides over wrath (*manyu*) and anger, being created by the killer, turns back that wrath residing in the victim; this is the meaning of the first half-verse, similar to the statement "desire may be for the sake of desire. Furthermore, in cases of violence (*sāhasa*), punishments such as mutilation of limbs, banishment, or others—whether first, middle, or highest degrees—must be inflicted according to the nature of the offense. (8.351)
The lord of the earth should brand those men who are intent on violating another's wife with marks that cause terror, and then banish them. 8.352.

Now he speaks of adultery (*strīsaṃgrahaṇa*). Regarding "in cases of violating another's wife": having branded those men who have repeatedly engaged in sexual intercourse with another's wife with painful punishments, such as cutting off the nose or lips, the king shall banish them from the country. (8.352)
For from that arises the confusion of castes among the world, by which unrighteousness, destroying the very root, leads to total destruction. (8.353)

Regarding the phrase "arising from that": because from sexual union with another's wife there arises for the world a confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), and through that confusion of castes, due to the absence of qualified sacrificers (*yajamāna*) for sacrifices and other rites, the verse beginning with "what is placed in the fire" (*agnau prāsta*) being absent, a dharma characterized by lack of rain—which is the root cause of the destruction of the world—arises, leading to total ruin through the severing of its very roots. (8.353)
A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife, having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement. (8.354)

If a man should engage in conversation with another's wife, saying "let us [go together]," he who has already been accused of the prior offenses of approaching another's wife shall converse with that other's wife; he shall incur the first amercement as punishment. (8.354)
But he who, having not been previously accused, speaks for a valid reason, shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part. (8.355)

Regarding the word "yaḥ": furthermore, if someone should address another in the presence of people due to some cause of prior enmity, he shall not incur punishment, because there is no offense whatsoever. (8.355)
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, or even in a forest, or at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery. (8.356)

"Another's wife" (*parastriyam*): When emerging from water, or in a secluded place outside a village, or in a region overgrown with trees, shrubs, and creepers, or at the confluence of rivers—if one should converse with another’s wife, even if previously unaccused, on account of some prior cause, he shall incur the offense described below. That by which she is properly grasped—that is, known—"this is her connection"—is *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse). [8.356]
The playful act of attending upon her, the touching of her ornaments and garments, and even sitting together on the same bed—all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery). 8.357.

"Acts of service" refers to play; "sitting on the same bed" refers to the performance of services such as anointing the limbs and so forth, which is a form of sport, as well as touching ornaments and garments. Sitting on the same bed and traveling in the same vehicle—all this is recorded by Manu and others as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery). 8.357.

If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he allows himself to be touched by her when she desires it, it is all recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse), provided there is mutual consent. 8.358.

Regarding the phrase "a woman": if a man touches her on a limb in an improper place or in a secluded spot, or if he is touched by her on a limb such as the hip in an improper place or in a secluded spot, and they remain silent—this constitutes *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) when there is mutual consent, as recorded by Manu and others. In this case, even if no actual union has occurred, a punishment less than that for a verbal proposal (*mukhopagama*) must be prescribed for mere *saṃgrahaṇa*, because it has been stated that "one must take full account of the attendant circumstances. (8.358)
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes are declared to be most worthy of protection. (8.359)

"Regarding the term 'non-Brahmin': the wives of all four castes are traditionally held to be most worthy of protection. Because of the severity of the punishment, a non-Brahmin Śūdra deserves the penalty for sexual intercourse with an unwilling Brāhmaṇī woman. Among the wealth, sons, and other possessions of all four castes, the wife is to be protected with the greatest care. Therefore, women must be guarded by their respective castes even from being approached by those of superior status. (8.359)
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans may converse with women without being hindered. (8.360)

"Regarding the term *bhikṣukas*: those who live by begging, panegyrists, cooks, and others who have undergone initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the sake of a sacrifice may engage in conversation with women in the house for the purpose of obtaining alms and so forth without being prohibited at all. There is no prohibition against them precisely because there is no act of sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*). (8.360)
One who has been forbidden shall not engage in conversation with women; but he who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa. (8.361)

"Regarding 'he shall not converse with women': being forbidden by his master, he must not engage in conversation with women. But if he converses despite being forbidden, he shall pay a fine of one suvarṇa to the king. (8.361)
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own labor;
for they procreate women and keep them hidden away. (8.362)

"Not this one": the injunction prohibiting conversation, such as "he who addresses another's wife," does not apply to the wives of actors, singers, and the like, nor to the wives of those who live by the brothel (*veśajīvī*). For the *cāraṇas* (wandering performers) and those who subsist on their own means unite their own wives with other men; and having become concealed, they indicate [the availability of] their brothel-work by saying, "This has certainly not been done by us for a hundred [pieces]. Therefore, because their maintenance is of the nature of a brothel, there is no prohibition against conversing with them. (8.362)
But he who engages in conversation with them, or with female slaves who eat alone, or with women living in seclusion, or with female ascetics, shall be made to pay a small fine. (8.363)

But he who engages in conversation with them should be made to pay a small fine; that is, one who holds secret or private conversations with women who subsist by their own wits as performers (cāraṇas) should be compelled to pay a very slight punishment. One who converses with female slaves, concubines, Buddhist nuns, or women observing religious vows should be made to pay some measure of fine. (8.363)
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution; but a man who violates one who is willing, being equal to her in desire, shall not suffer death. (8.364)

"He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution. He of equal caste who violates—that is, has sexual intercourse with—an unwilling maiden deserves, at that very moment, execution such as the cutting off of the genitals and so forth, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa. One of equal status who violates a willing maiden shall not suffer execution. (8.364)

One should not cause a maiden who is consorting with a superior man to pay anything at all; however, one who is consorting with an inferior man should be made to live restrainedly in the house. (8.365)

Regarding the maiden: if a maiden is found serving a man of superior status, the king shall not inflict any punishment upon her at all. However, if she serves one of lower caste, he should have her protected and kept in her father’s house; as long as her desire has not ceased—due to her association with a man of low livelihood or kin—he should keep her there for the rest of her life. (8.365)
But a man of lower caste who courts a woman of higher caste deserves punishment;
if her father consents, he may be made to pay a bride-price for courting a woman of equal status. (8.366)

"An 'excellent' [woman]": if a man of lower caste approaches a maiden of higher caste who desires him, he deserves death consisting of mutilation of limbs or execution, depending on the caste. However, if he approaches a maiden of equal caste who desires him, and if her father so wishes, then he should pay the father an appropriate bride-price (*śulka*) as in the Āsura form of marriage; he is not to be fined. But if the father does not wish it, then he must be made to pay the amount of the bride-price by the king. (8.366)
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force, his fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. (8.367)

"By force": if a man, out of arrogance, forcibly causes a woman of equal status—that is, of the same caste—to abandon her journey by merely thrusting out his finger, he shall have two fingers cut off immediately and shall be made to pay a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. || 8.367 ||
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who cuts off her finger;
rather, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] to prevent the recurrence of such an offense. (8.368)

"Regarding 'with her consent': if a man of the same caste causes the ruin of a willing maiden merely by the insertion of a finger, he shall not suffer the amputation of his finger; however, in order that he may not repeat this act out of habit, he shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (8.368)
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod. (8.369)

Regarding the maiden: she who, while still a maiden, should ruin another maiden by the insertion of a finger shall receive a fine of two hundred [paṇas], shall pay the bride-price to the father of that maiden, and shall also receive ten lashes with a whip. (8.369)
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head, or else the cutting off of two fingers, and likewise being led away on a donkey. (8.370)

Furthermore, a woman who causes the ruin of a maiden deserves, at that very moment, the amputation of two fingers instead of shaving the head, as well as being paraded on a donkey along the royal highway; and this [punishment] is to be combined with the two alternatives previously mentioned. (8.370)
But that woman who, arrogant on account of her kin or her virtues, should transgress against her husband,
the king shall have her torn by dogs in a public place crowded with many people.

Regarding the word "husband": if a woman, out of pride in her powerful and wealthy father or other kinsmen, or because she is filled with self-conceit due to her beauty, cleverness, and multitude of virtues, should transgress against her husband by taking another man, the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a place crowded with many people. (8.371)
One should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they shall pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire. (8.372)

"He should cause that arrogant adulterer to be burned. The king should cause that evildoer to be burned upon an iron bed set ablaze with fire; they should throw on logs until that evildoer has been consumed by the flames. (8.372)
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine is double;
likewise, for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī*, the fine is exactly that much.

"Regarding the phrase 'one accused after a year has passed': for a man who has been punished for the offense of approaching another's wife, if he is accused again of that same act after a year has elapsed, a double fine shall be imposed according to the instruction; such is the prescribed penalty. And here, because of the mention alongside a *caṇḍālī* woman, and based on the rule "but a thousand for women of the lowest castes," this same double fine must be applied to one who approaches that very same *vrātyā* woman after a year has passed, as it is equal to the offense of approaching a *caṇḍālī*. (8.373)

A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes, whether she be guarded or unguarded, shall have all his limbs cut off if she was unguarded; if she was guarded, he is deprived of everything. (8.374)

Regarding the term "Śūdra": if a Śūdra should approach again a woman protected by her husband or one who is unprotected—whether he approaches her while she is protected or unprotected—he should be subjected to the cutting off of his organ and the confiscation of all his property. If he approaches one who is unprotected, a corporal and monetary fine must be imposed. The severity or mildness of the punishment should be determined in consideration of the specific circumstances of the case. (8.374)
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.

Regarding the Vaiśya: A Vaiśya who has sexual intercourse with a protected Brāhmaṇa woman shall be placed in confinement for one year and fined his entire property. Regarding intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman—if a Vaiśya has intercourse with a protected Kṣatriya woman, as he will state later; and a Kṣatriya who has intercourse with a protected Brāhmaṇa woman shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]. His head shall be shaved and he shall be sprinkled with donkey urine. (8.375)
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman,
the king should fine the Vaiśya five hundred and the Kṣatriya one thousand.

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇī": if a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī who is unprotected, then the Vaiśya is to be fined five hundred [paṇas]. As for the Kṣatriya, however, because he has failed to provide protection, he must be subjected to a heavier fine than the Vaiśya, consisting of one thousand [paṇas]. (8.376)
But both of them, having violated a protected Brahmin woman, shall be punished like Śūdras or burned in a fire of straw. (8.377)

"Both"—that is, both those two, the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, having committed sexual intercourse with a protected Brāhmaṇa woman, are to be punished like a Śūdra: they are to be fined everything, or they are to be burned entirely by fire; thus they are subject to the ultimate penalty, because the severity of the punishment applies to the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman who possesses the qualities of a learned Śrotriya's wife. "The Vaiśya shall be fined his entire property, and the Kṣatriya likewise one thousand [paṇas]. (8.377)
A Brahmin who approaches a guarded Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]; he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred. (8.378)

"A thousand," it is said: a Brāhmaṇa who approaches a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]; but if she consents, he shall be fined five hundred for sexual intercourse with her. (8.378)
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the other castes, the punishment may be one that ends in death. (8.379)

"Shaving the head": for a Brāhmaṇa, shaving the head is prescribed by the scriptures in place of the punishment of death; however, for Kṣatriyas and others, the aforementioned punishment of death applies. (8.379)
One must never kill a Brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of sin; one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and unhurt. (8.380)

"Never," it is said: one must never at any time kill even a Brahmin who has committed every possible sin; rather, even if he possesses all wealth, one should banish him from the kingdom with his body unharmed. (8.380)
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind. (8.381)

"Not from the killing of a Brahmin": there is no other unrighteousness on earth greater than the killing of a Brahmin; even if a Brahmin has committed every possible sin, the king should not kill him even in thought. (8.381)
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a guarded Vaiśya woman, both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman. (8.382)

Regarding the term "vaiśya": if a Vaiśya should approach a protected Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya should approach a Vaiśya woman, then they shall receive the same punishment as that prescribed for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya for approaching an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman—namely, a fine of five hundred for the Vaiśya and one thousand for the Kṣatriya. Thus, these two, the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, deserve such punishment. Consequently, for a Vaiśya approaching a Kṣatriya woman there is a fine of five hundred, while for a Kṣatriya approaching a Vaiśya woman there is a fine of one thousand due to the superior quality [of the offense] resulting from his duty to provide protection. (8.382)
A Brahmin should be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas] for approaching those two when they are protected;
for approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya shall indeed be one thousand.

"A thousand": if a Brāhmaṇa approaches a protected Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman, he shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]. If two [men], a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, approach a protected Śūdra woman, the fine shall be one thousand in measure. (8.383)
If a Kṣatriya has intercourse with an unprotected Vaiśya woman, his fine shall be five hundred;
he shall undergo tonsure with urine, or else pay a fine. (8.384)

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall be fined one thousand.

"Regarding a Kṣatriya woman": "Regarding one who is unprotected. A Brāhmaṇa approaching a protected Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]. Furthermore, approaching a woman of the Cāṇḍāla or other such castes, he shall be fined one thousand. (8.384–385)
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with impunity, shares in the world of Śakra.

"Of whom": that king in whose realm there are no thieves, adulterers, those who commit verbal abuse, those who commit physical assault, arsonists, or other perpetrators of violent crimes (*sāhasa*), that king shall go to heaven. (8.386)
The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings him imperial power over his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world. (8.387)

"Of these" refers to these [offenders], such as thieves and others; the king's suppression of them within his own realm produces kingship among those of the same class and generates renown in the world. (8.387)

If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—provided both are capable of the rite and free from fault—the punishment for each of them shall be one hundred [paṇas]. (8.388)

Regarding the term "officiating priest" (ṛtvij): if a patron (*yājya*) abandons an officiating priest who has been passed down through tradition, who is capable of performing the ritual acts, who is free from defects such as excessive muttering [of mantras], and who is blameless—then, as a corollary, it is stated that a fine of one hundred [paṇas] each should be imposed upon both of them. (8.388)
Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned. He who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their status, shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.389)

"Not [considered] a mother": one does not incur the sin of abandoning a mother, father, wife, or son by failing to provide for them through maintenance, service, and so forth. Therefore, even when abandoning these persons though they have become outcasts (patita), one should be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king for mutual abandonment. (8.389)

When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties, a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to act righteously should not pronounce a legal judgment for himself. (8.390)

Regarding the phrase "in the hermitages": when twice-born householders are disputing among themselves as to whether or not this is the meaning of the scripture concerning the stages of life (āśrama), the king—desiring to secure his own welfare, both seen and unseen—should declare, "This is not the meaning of the scripture," by means of a particularly grand seat. (8.390)
Having honored these men as is appropriate, the king, together with the Brahmins,
should first pacify them with gentle words and then establish them in their own duty.

"What then? According to merit. Having honored each person with such worship as they deserve, and having first removed their anger from them along with other brahmins, the king should then instruct them in their own respective duties. (8.391)
If a Brahmin fails to feed his immediate neighbor and next-door neighbor at a festive meal for twenty twice-born men when they are worthy, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka.

Regarding the terms "neighboring" (*prātiveśya*) and "adjacent neighbor" (*anuveśya*): when there are more than twenty other people to be fed at a festival, if a Brāhmaṇa or similar person fails to feed two suitable individuals living behind his house from the front of that residence, he deserves a fine of one *māṣaka* here, since gold is prescribed as the penalty in subsequent cases. (8.392)
If a learned Vedic scholar does not feed another virtuous learned scholar during rites for prosperity, he shall be made to pay double the value of that food and a masha of gold. (8.393)

One who is blind, mentally deficient, a cripple who moves about on a board, or one who is seventy years old and infirm, as well as one who provides service to those learned in the Vedas, shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone. (8.394)

Regarding the "Vedic scholar" (*śrotriya*): the blind, the deaf, the lame, and those who are aged from seventy years onwards—when performing services such as attendance for Vedic scholars, they shall not be made to pay even a sixteenth part of the grain or any royal dues, such as the *gulma*-tax, by a king, even if his treasury is depleted. (8.393–394)
The king should always honor one learned in the Vedas, those afflicted by illness or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous. (8.395)

"And one who is learned in the Vedas and afflicted by disease. The king should always honor with gifts, marks of respect, and kind deeds a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to study and religious observances, as well as those who are sick, overwhelmed by separation from loved ones, children, the elderly, the poor, those born of noble families, and those endowed with uprightness. (8.395)
On a smooth board of *śālmalī* wood, the washerman shall wash the garments slowly;
he shall not rub one garment against another, nor shall he let them dry together. (8.396)

Regarding the phrase "on a board of *śālmalī* wood": on a board made from the *śālmalī* or similar trees, which is smooth, the laundryman shall wash the garments very slowly. He must not wrap the clothes and such items with the cloths belonging to others and give them back outside, nor shall he give them for the purpose of covering someone else. If he should act in this manner, he would be subject to punishment. (8.396)
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread increased by one pala;
if he acts otherwise, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve paṇas. (8.397)

Regarding the weaver: if a weaver cuts a thread of ten palas or more, he shall take it, cast it into a pit of flour, and provide a garment weighing eleven palas; whatever remains beyond that, for that he shall be fined twelve times its value. (8.397)
Those skilled in customs offices and expert in evaluating all merchandise should determine the value of the goods;
from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax.

"Regarding 'at the toll-stations' (śulkasthāneṣu)": At marketplaces and other such places, those who are unable to determine the fixed tolls to be collected by the king from traders, and who are capable of discerning the quality—whether high or low—of the merchandise, shall fix a price for each article as appropriate; from the resulting profit, the king shall cause a twentieth part to be paid as toll. (8.398)
If one, out of greed, exports those articles which are the king’s famous treasures or those that have been prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property. (8.399)

Regarding the phrase "of the king": whatever gems, pearls, and so forth originate in that [king's] territory, as well as those which have been prohibited by the king—such as grain, which during a famine must not be taken to another country—if one carries such items to another country out of greed, the king shall confiscate everything. (8.399)

One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time, or one who gives false accounts in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty. (8.400)

Regarding the term "customs station" (śulkasthāna): one who, desiring to avoid what has been prescribed, travels by a wrong path or at an improper time, or who states the actual value of his goods for purchase, sale, or customs duty as being of only a small amount—he shall be made to pay eight times that which is due to the king as a fine. (8.400)
Having investigated the importation, exportation, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he shall regulate their purchase and sale. (8.401)

Regarding the term "source" (*āgama*): having investigated the place of origin of a commodity from another region—considering from what distance it was brought—and having examined its departure from one's own country—considering for how long it has been on the market—one should oversee the purchase and sale in such a way that no harm is done to either the goods or the merchant-owners, taking into account the merchant’s profit or loss, as well as the cost of food, clothing, and laborers. (8.401)
Every five nights, or else at the passing of every fortnight, the king should perform the formal offering of the guest-water (argha) in their presence. (8.402)

Regarding the phrase "every five nights": because the application of traditional rules (*āgama*) and so forth regarding these commodities of unstable value is not fixed, the king himself should, every five nights, personally verify the fixing of prices for those [goods], and every fortnight for those whose value is relatively stable. (8.402)
All weights, measures, and standards should be well-marked;
they must be re-examined every six months. (8.403)

Regarding "weights and measures": scales, as well as measures made of wood and other materials—such as the *droṇa*, *kuḍava*, and *prastha*—and the balances used for weighing gold and other substances; all of these must be marked with the royal seal. Every six months, all of them must be inspected again and again by trustworthy officials. (8.403)
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
cattle and women, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half of that quarter. 8.404.

Regarding the term *paṇa*: since he will later state that it refers to those [vehicles] which are full of goods, the king shall cause the empty carriage and other such items to pay a fine of one *paṇa*. Likewise, a load carried by a man shall be made to pay half a *paṇa*. A beast of burden such as a cow, as well as a woman, shall be made to pay a quarter *paṇa*; a man without goods shall be made to pay an eighth of a *paṇa*. (8.404)
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they can. (8.405)

"Filled with goods" (*bhāṇḍapūrṇāni*): Carts and other such vehicles returning empty should be made to pay a ferry-toll in proportion to the excellence or deficiency of the goods they carried, and their relative weight or lightness. Men who have come without luggage—such as merchants and others who are not entitled to full equipment—should be made to pay whatever little [is required]. It has been stated that for another man, the person traveling empty-handed pays nothing; this is because it is impossible to establish a fixed rule in such a case. This much alone is for the sake of instruction: chests and other such containers returning empty of goods should be made to pay whatever little [is appropriate] themselves. (8.405)
On a long journey, one should know that crossing occurs according to the place and according to the time; this applies to riverbanks, but there is no such fixed characteristic for the ocean.

Regarding "a long journey": what was previously stated for the purpose of crossing from one shore to the other applies here as well; however, in the case of a distant journey by way of a river via boat or similar means, the ferry fare should be determined with respect to the distance to be traversed—considering whether the terrain consists of slippery ground, stones, and so forth—and with respect to the time, such as summer or winter. This is to be understood as applying to rivers; in the case of the ocean, however, because one may be carried by the force of the wind into the underworld (pātāla) and the like, there is no fixed length [of distance], and thus it serves to indicate specific variations in ferry fare. Furthermore, since a river has no fixed measure such as *yojana*s, only the appropriate toll should be taken in that case. (8.406)
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a renunciant, a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing. (8.407)

"Regarding the term 'pregnant woman': a woman who has conceived a fetus after two months have passed shall not be made to pay the penalty for unchastity to those [students] observing celibacy. (8.407)
Whatever may be lost on a ship due to the fault of the boatmen, that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together from their own respective shares. (8.408)

Regarding the word "yat" (whatever): whatever property, by whatever amount, should perish through the fault of the boatman, that must be paid by those on board collectively from their own respective shares. (8.408)
This has been declared as the decision regarding legal disputes involving those traveling by boat;
in the event of an accident on the water caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment for a divine (act of God).

"Regarding this [verse]: whatever was said [to be lost] due to the fault of the boatmen must all be paid by the boatmen. Thus has been declared the legal decision regarding those traveling by boat; however, in the case of a calamity caused by fate—such as a sudden storm or the breaking of the boat—there is no legal proceeding involving punishment or imprisonment for the boatmen. (8.409)
He should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and he should cause the Śūdra to perform service for the twice-born. (8.410)

Regarding "commerce": the king shall cause the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform, as a rule, trade, the investment of capital, agriculture, and the tending of cattle—since these are the visible duties of the Vaiśya—and the service of the twice-born, for the Śūdra; those who do not perform these shall be punished by the king, according to the instruction given here. (8.410)
A Brahmin should support with compassion both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.

Regarding the term "Kṣatriya": when a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is distressed due to a lack of livelihood, a Brāhmaṇa may cause them to perform his own tasks, such as protection or agriculture; he must indeed support them with food, clothing, and so forth. And if a wealthy Brāhmaṇa does not do so, he is to be punished by the king according to the law. This concludes the section [on this matter]. 8.411.
But a Brāhmaṇa who, out of greed, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will by virtue of his superior power, shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.412)

"He who says 'I will serve'": if a Brāhmaṇa, out of greed, causes initiated twice-born men to perform servile work such as washing his feet at that time, he shall be fined six hundred paṇas by the king. (8.412)
One may cause a Śūdra to perform service, whether he has been purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa. (8.413)

"Regarding the Śūdra": furthermore, one may compel a Śūdra—whether maintained with food and other provisions or not—to perform servitude, because he was created by Prajāpati specifically for the purpose of being the servant of a Brāhmaṇa (or a Brāhmaṇī). 8.413.
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that [status] is innate to him, so who can remove it from him? (8.414)

"Not by the master" means that even though he has been released by the one to whom he became a slave because it was prescribed for his own caste, the Śūdra is not freed from servitude. Therefore, since servitude is innate to the Śūdra—just as one speaks of his "Śūdra-ness"—who can remove that servitude from the Śūdra, even for a visible worldly purpose? This statement, "servitude must not be performed," is intended for others; otherwise, it would apply to those counted among the classes born into a state of servitude. (8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one inherited, one enslaved by way of a fine, and one inherited from an ancestor—these seven are the sources of slavery. (8.415)

Regarding the term *dhvajāhṛta* ("acquired by the banner"): in battle, one who is won from the treasury by a master; a hired servant; the son of a female slave; one purchased from another; one given by another; one who has come down through a lineage beginning with his father; or one who, due to poverty, enters into slavery for the sake of purification when there is no other means of clearing a fine—these are the "seven banners," which are the seven grounds for the status of slavery and so forth. (8.415)
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. 8.416

Regarding the word "wife" (*bhāryā*): for this reason as well, one who is destitute is so designated by Manu and others, because they acquire that wealth for him whose wife and other dependents they are; thus, that wealth belongs to him. Or rather, it is said of him that he possesses such dependence on them. (8.416)
A Brahmin may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has nothing that is his own, as his wealth is to be taken by his master. 8.417

"Confidently" means that the Brāhmaṇa is entirely free from doubt, as he is not [legally] joined with the status of an ordinary slave or Śūdra. Therefore, that slave or Śūdra possesses no property of his own from which the wealth of his master could be taken away. And thus, if a Brāhmaṇa takes property confidently from a slave, he is certainly not to be punished; this is what is stated by the phrase "in all cases.
One should cause the Vaiśyas and Śūdras to perform their own duties with diligence; for if they fall away from their respective duties, they would throw this world into disorder. (8.418)

"Regarding the Vaiśyas and Śūdras": the king should cause the Vaiśyas and Śūdras to perform their own duties, such as agriculture and servitude. For if the Vaiśya does not engage in agriculture, trade, and so forth, and the Śūdra does not perform servitude and the like, the world would fall into disorder due to the decline of dharma. Furthermore, if a Śūdra, failing to understand his own low status and not performing servitude, should at some time engage in the work of the twice-born, he would become a source of affliction through famine, hell, and other calamities. (8.418)
Day by day he should inspect his undertakings and his vehicles, as well as his fixed income and expenditure, his mines, and his treasury. (8.419)

"Day by day" (ahanīti): he should attend daily to the completion of his duties, such as agriculture and the collection of taxes, and remain vigilant regarding the accumulation of wealth for the sake of security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*). This is stated again so that even one unable to oversee legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) shall not abandon his royal duties. 8.419.
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king, having cast off all evil, attains the supreme goal. || 8.420 ||

"Thus": by casting off all impurity, he attains the supreme goal. According to the principle thus stated, the king—who brings these legal proceedings, beginning with the non-payment of debts, to their conclusion through adjudication—by observing lawsuits without partiality and through the power of bestowing the scriptures, dispels the accumulated sin born of negligence and attains the world of Brahmā. This description of the reward is intended to refer to the conclusion of the principal dispute, even though not all legal matters have been finalized. (8.420)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of All Legal Proceedings," in this work following the Intent of Manu, composed by Govindarāja, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mādhava.
The Ninth Chapter:
I shall declare the eternal laws concerning the union and separation of a man and a woman who abide in the path of righteousness. 9.1.

Regarding the phrase "of the man": I shall declare the eternal duties of husband and wife when they abide by the path characterized by mutual non-deviation, whether they are united or separated. When there is a mutual disagreement between husband and wife, if a report is somehow made to the king, the king must ensure their adherence to that path through this legal arrangement—even by means of punishment and so forth. Since the king incurs fault by failing to act, the duties of husband and wife are stated here among the royal duties within the context of judicial procedure. (9.1)
Women must be kept under control by their own men day and night; even when they are attached to sensual pleasures, they must be established under one's own authority. (9.2)

"Without independence" means that women must always be kept dependent by their husbands and others, and even when forbidden from objects such as sound and the like, they must be led away from excessive attachment to them so that they remain devoted to their own [spiritual] selves. (9.2)
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth; in old age, the sons protect her. A woman does not deserve independence. 9.3

"By the father": before marriage, the father protects the woman; thereafter, the husband; and in his absence, the sons. Therefore, she must never be made independent by these [relatives]. The mention of the husband’s youth and old age is for the sake of establishing the order of protection; however, this is merely a restatement of what is already established by propriety. (9.3)

A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable; and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable. (9.4)

Regarding "time": there is the traditional teaching of Gautama, "The giving [of a daughter] is [proper] after the period of menstruation. At this time, a father who does not give away his daughter is censurable; a husband who does not approach her during the period of menstruation is blameworthy; and furthermore, when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is to be reproached. (9.4)
Women must be guarded especially against even the slightest of attachments; for if they are not protected, they will bring grief upon two families. 9.5

"From even the slightest" means that they must be protected with extreme care from even minor associations that lead to immoral conduct; how much more so from great ones? For if left unprotected, they would immediately cause distress to both families—those of their fathers and their husbands—through the occurrence of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). || 9.5 ||
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes, husbands—even those who are weak—strive to protect their wives. (9.6)

Regarding the word *imām*: since the protection of the wives of all castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, is superior to all other duties according to the principle set forth in the verse to be cited hereafter, therefore husbands—even if they are weak—should make an effort to protect their wives. For it has already been stated [in verse 9.5] that "women must be protected. 9.6.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he indeed protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (9.7)

"His own": by protecting his wife with effort, he protects his own progeny by preventing the production of mixed-caste offspring (*saṅkara*). And by remaining committed to the protection of his wife, he preserves proper conduct (*samācāra*). He protects the lineage of his father, grandfather, and so forth, as well as himself, by performing the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) without falling into confusion. He protects his own duty (*dharma*), because one whose wife is pure possesses the qualification for procreation and other such rites. (9.7)
The husband, having entered his wife, becomes an embryo and is born here; for that is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her. 9.8.

"Regarding the term *pati*: having entered his wife, the husband becomes an embryo and is born here [again]. Thus, one may also state that there is a commonality of syllables and phonemes [between *pati* and *jāyā*]; for that reason, she is called the *jāyā* (wife) of the husband, and furthermore, she is to be protected by him in the form of a son—for this purpose is the etymological definition of the name. (9.8)
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should protect women with great effort.

"Of what kind" means this: because a woman who serves a man of such a sort—whether he be her husband as prescribed by law, or one forbidden by the scriptures—begets a son of that very same kind as described in the scriptures; namely, one who is exalted by following the prescribed rules, or degraded by serving those who are forbidden. Therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, she should protect her husband with great effort. (9.9)
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded by the application of these means. 9.10

When it has been taught that they must be protected in this way, [the author asks] how they are to be protected; to this he says: "No one... No one is able to protect women by force, such as through confinement and so forth, because when these two [senses] are subject to mental transgression, they cannot be guarded [in that manner]. However, they can be protected by means of the methods of protection to be described hereafter. (9.10)
He should employ her in the collection of wealth and in its expenditure, as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils. (9.11)

He states those means for the sake of wealth: "In the preservation and expenditure of riches, as well as in the purification of property and body, in ritual purity, in dharma, and in attending to beds, seats, and so forth—thus, with her mind occupied by these tasks, she sleeps without fatigue and does not remember sexual union. (9.11)
Those women who are confined at home and guarded by trustworthy men, yet protect themselves by their own efforts—they are truly well-protected. (9.12)

"Unprotected" means that even those [women] are indeed unprotected because of the possibility of mental transgression. However, for those who protect themselves by themselves through reliance on self-restraint—that is, those who are well-established in conduct and the application of restraint—an effort must be made. Thus is the instruction on the primary means of protection. 9.12
Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping, and dwelling in another's house—these are the six things that corrupt women. 9.13.

"Drink" refers as follows: drinking intoxicants, association with wicked people, living together with an ignoble man, separation from her husband, and dwelling in another's house—these six things are the causes of corruption for women, producing the fault known as infidelity even in a woman of virtuous nature; therefore, they must be protected from these. 9.13.
They do not examine beauty, nor do they take into account age; whether handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply as a man. (9.14)

"Not these" means that they do not discriminate between the handsome and the ugly. For they do not find a man dear on account of his youth; rather, whether he be handsome or deformed, they enjoy a man simply by virtue of him being a male. Moreover, because their virtue wavers at the mere sight of a man, they are unchaste women. 9.14.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle minds, and their natural lack of affection, these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world. (9.15)

Regarding the phrase "due to unchastity": because of the fickle-mindedness of an unchaste woman and because of the absence of affection by her very nature, these women—even when guarded with great effort—undergo a transformation toward their husbands by resorting to falsehood and malevolent spells. 9.15.
Having thus understood their nature, which arises from the creation of Prajāpati, a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection. (9.16)

"Thus. In this way, having understood that the nature of these [women]—as described in the two verses concerning their immorality and fickle-mindedness—was produced at the time of Hiraṇyagarbha’s creation, a man must exert effort in guarding them.
Manu did not attribute to women the desire for beds and seats, ornaments, lust, anger, dishonesty, malice, or misconduct. (9.17)

"Sleeping, sitting, ornamentation, lust, anger, and dishonesty"—at the beginning of creation, Manu ordained these—sleep, sitting, ornamentation, gems, lust, anger, greed, deviation from the path, and ignoble conduct—for women. Therefore, one must exert effort in protecting them. (9.17)
"It is established in the Dharma that women have no ritual efficacy through mantras;
for women are without sensory power and devoid of mantras, and are falsehood—such is the settled rule. (9.18)

"There is no ritual for women with mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma. This means that according to the boundaries of the scriptures, women do not have ritual ceremonies such as the *jātakarman* (birth rite) performed with mantras. Thus, due to the absence of such rites as the *jātakarman*—which are accompanied by mantras—and because they are naturally devoid of spiritual power (*vīrya*), and further because of their lack of Vedic study, women are without mantras. Since they lack mantras, they lack knowledge of the Dharma; and even if they were to practice [ritual purity], they would proceed toward impurity because of the absence of fear and other [restraints]. Therefore, it is the established rule of the scriptures that "women are impure. (9.18)
And likewise, many scriptural verses have been sung even in the Vedas;
listen now to their expiations for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics. 9.19.

"So be it. Indeed, there are many scriptural passages in the Vedas, such as "And we do not know whether [he is] a Brāhmaṇa," which serve as indicators that the nature of [certain acts] is characterized by deviation from the norm; these have been recited from the Śruti. Now, listen to a scriptural passage among those very texts concerning expiation (prāyaścitta). 9.19.
"Whatever my mother lusted for while wandering unfaithful to her husband, may my father take that seed of mine"—this is the illustration of that [Vedic verse]. (9.20)

Regarding the mantra *yan ma*: "My mother was devoted to the waters (*aptyaparāyaṇā*), yet she became possessed of desire for another man. My father, having informed me that my mother’s menstrual flow (*mātṛrajaḥ*) was defiled by the intention toward another man—that this is the sign of her being of an adulterous nature—remained established in his purpose through this mantra. They say that the application of this mantra occurs in the context of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices and the *Aṣṭakā*, during the consecration of the water for washing the feet (*pādya-anumantraṇa*). || 9.20 ||
Whatever undesirable thing she meditates upon in her mind for the sake of her husband, this is correctly called the concealment of that transgression. (9.21)

"She meditates" means that she mentally contemplates any act of approaching another man that is not desired by her husband; by this, it is stated that her mental infidelity is fully understood. This does not concern speech or physical action, because her nature consists of such mental infidelity; therefore, these women must be guarded with effort. Since she is referred to as "mother," this expiation applies only to the son, not to the mother. (9.21)
With whatever qualities a husband honors his wife according to the prescribed rule, she comes to possess those same qualities, just as a river does by the ocean. 9.22

"Of whatever quality" means: by whatever kind—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—a man enters into union with women according to the prescribed rule, she becomes of that same kind through association with him, whether her conduct is excellent or her character is corrupt. Just as even the Gaṅgā, when joined with the ocean, becomes salty water despite its own sweet water, this [verse] is intended to teach another means of protecting women, known as self-restraint. 9.22.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained a state of venerability through her union with Vasiṣṭha;
and Sāraṅgī reached the same honor by being united with Mandapāla.

Therefore, he provides an illustration with the words "akṣamālā" and "śārṅgī. Akṣamālā, known as Caṇḍālī, was married by Vasiṣṭha, and Śārṅgī, a forest-dweller, was married by the one named Mandapāla; yet both attained a state of purification. 9.23.
These and other women in this world, though born of lowly origin, have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives. (9.24)

"These women"—thinking that these women have attained excellence through their own respective auspicious qualities of their husbands, the author uses the plural "these" (*etāḥ*) for the sake of illustration regarding these two [virtues], even though they are singular; for even those women from lowly families and the like, whose husbands are inferior, attain eminence in this world through their husband. Therefore, for the sake of protecting one's wife, self-restraint must be resorted to by me. (9.24)
Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women in this world, which yields happy results both in this life and after death; now learn the duties regarding progeny.

"This," he says: "This entire auspicious decision regarding husband and wife, which follows worldly custom, has been declared to you; now listen to these duties of subjects—such as those who are miserable, those who live by trade, and those who live by their sons—which are the causes of happiness for both. (9.25)
For the sake of progeny, these highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) in households, there is no distinction whatsoever. (9.26)

"‘For the sake of progeny’—thus, even though they possess these faults, because they are capable of being remedied, women are worthy of being provided for with gifts such as garlands, garments, and ornaments. These women are the very beauty of the home; indeed, Fortune (*śrī*) and women are identical in form within households. A house devoid of Fortune does not shine, nor does a house without a woman. Thus, even great wealth exists for the sake of progeny; therefore, in these three verses, it is *bhūti* (prosperity) that pertains to women. (9.26)
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born, and the daily conduct of worldly life—woman is visibly the foundation for all this. (9.27)

Regarding "procreation": for the sake of pleasure, the daily dependence on a woman, the procreation of offspring, the protection of those already born, and the enjoyment of friends and kinsmen—each of these is a single virtue of worldly conduct. (9.27)
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme delight—these depend upon the wife; likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent on her. (9.28)

"Regarding offspring: heaven for the ancestors and one's own self always depend upon the wife. The procreation of children, the maintenance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, service to the body, pleasure, and play—for the ancestors and for oneself—result in heaven through the birth of offspring and so forth; all this is always dependent upon the wife. (9.28)
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous. (9.29)

Regarding the word "husband": she who, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, does not prove unfaithful to her husband in thought, word, or deed, attains the heavenly worlds acquired by her husband; she is called a virtuous wife (*sādhvī*). (9.29)
But by being unfaithful to her husband, a woman incurs infamy in this world; she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. (9.30)

"Because of infidelity": through association with wicked people, a woman incurs reproach in this world and attains the womb of a jackal in another birth; furthermore, her inner self is tormented by diseases and other afflictions like axes. Since there is a danger that women might develop excessive pride due to their great utility, it is stated here once again for the purpose of preventing that. (9.30)
This meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, has been spoken by the virtuous and by the great seers of old; listen to it. (9.31)

"Regarding that which has been declared: listen now to this supreme teaching, which is being proclaimed by the learned Manu and others, as well as by other great seers of former times—a work for the benefit of all people and a source of auspiciousness. (9.31)

They recognize the son as belonging to the husband, yet there is a conflict in the sacred scriptures regarding the husband; some say he is the progenitor, while others know him to be the owner of the field.

Regarding the word "bhartuḥ" (of the husband): he who is the husband is one from whom a son has been directly begotten; that he is not considered such is not a point of dispute here. However, where the begetter is the one who wedded [the woman], there the tradition is of two kinds. Some say that even one who is the begetter but not the wedder makes himself possessed of a son by means of that son. Others, however, say that the owner of the field (the wedder) becomes possessed of a son even by a son begotten by another. (9.32)
Woman is considered to be the field, and man is considered to be the seed; from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings. 9.33

"Being like a field" means it is remembered by the seers as being similar to the place where rice and other crops grow; and man is remembered as being similar to the seed of rice and so forth, because the birth of all living beings results from the conjunction of field and seed. And thus, since the causality of both is equally prominent, the dispute is justified: does the offspring belong to him whose field it is, or to the owner of the seed? (9.33)
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the female womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised. (9.34)

"Superior" means: in some cases the seed is primary, where, according to the principle "those born of an unauthorized woman," the woman was obtained through a fee; in other cases the field is primary, where, according to the principle "that which is born from the bed of one who has died," she was obtained [as a wife]; but where both the seed and the womb—the mother and the father—are equally the progenitors, that offspring is most excellent. (9.34)
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the procreation of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed. 9.35

Regarding that, he states the position of primacy with the words "of the seed" (*bījasya*). Between the seed and the field, the seed is said to be primary, because the production of all things is seen to be characterized by the signs of the color, form, and so forth residing in the seed. (9.35)
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, such a crop grows from it, manifested by its own inherent qualities. (9.36)

And so it is said, "of whatever kind": whatever kind of substance, such as rice and the like, is sown in the field at the proper time—such as the *saṅgava* period—by means of plowing and other preparations, that very same kind of seed, characterized by its own specific marks, grows in that field. (9.36)
For this ground is called the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth. (9.37)

Having thus demonstrated the predominance of the seed by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he says "this" in order to establish it through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "Since this earth is called by all people the 'womb' (*yoni*) or 'field' (*kṣetra*) for living beings such as shrubs and creepers, yet no quality of the womb known as 'earth'—such as being composed of clay and so forth—is present in the seed of the shrub and the like during its own internal stages of sprout and stalk; therefore, the seed is the primary factor, following the qualities of the womb. (9.37)
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers arise here in various forms according to their own nature. (9.38)

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "on the earth" (bhūmau): even in a single field on the earth, when farmers have sown various seeds such as rice and mung beans at the time of proper sowing, they arise according to the inherent nature of each seed and become manifold forms upon the earth. || 9.38 ||
Rice, śāli grain, mung beans, sesame, masha beans, as well as barley, garlic, and sugarcane—these all sprout according to their respective seeds. (9.39)

Regarding the term "vrīhayaḥ": among the awned grains (*śūkadhānya*), those with short awns are *vrīhayaḥ*; those with long awns are *ṣaṣṭika* and so forth; and those such as red rice (*raktaśāli*) are *śālayaḥ*. Likewise, *mudga* and other legumes arise in various forms without ever deviating from their inherent nature as seeds. (9.39)
That one thing is sown and another grows—this is not tenable;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth. (9.40)

This being the case, the notion that "it is something else"—namely, that sesame seeds sown would produce mung beans and so forth—is not possible. For the seed alone is what is sown; as with rice and other grains, so too among humans, the seed is the primary factor. (9.40)
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another. 9.41

Now he speaks of the preeminence of the field with the word "that" (*tat*). That seed should never be sown in the wife of another by one who possesses wisdom, who is endowed with moral conduct, and who knows the worldly scriptures and social conventions—since it has been stated that such an act shortens life—and because it is fruitless. As he will say later (9.43): "In the same way, that seed cast upon what belongs to another perishes. || 9.41 ||
Regarding this, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Therefore, a man must not sow seed in what belongs to another. (9.42)

Regarding this: in this matter, those who know the proper time for policy recite verses proclaimed by Vāyu—sentences composed in specific meters—such as: "A man must not sow his seed in another's wife. (9.42)
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sight of one who continues to shoot at the mark it has already pierced, so too does a seed sown in another's possession quickly perish. 9.43

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Just as an arrow shot [at a moving target] perishes. Just as when one person has pierced a deer through a certain opening, another arrow released later through that same opening becomes fruitless, because the share of the deer belongs solely to the first shooter; likewise, what is sown in the wife of another quickly becomes fruitless. It is said that the fruit belongs to the owner of the field immediately upon the conception of the embryo. (9.43)
Those who know the past recognize this earth as the wife even of Pṛthu;
they call her a field for the destruction of those who stand upon it, like a deer pierced by a poisoned arrow.

Regarding the word "of Pṛthu": because even this earth is reckoned as belonging to one who has not paid taxes, just as that very field which was protected by uprooting Sthāṇu is called the "demonstrated field," so too they say the deer belongs to the original appropriator due to his ownership; it becomes the offspring of him alone, and not of the biological father. (9.44)
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have said; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman. (9.45)

"Of such extent" means that it is not merely the man alone, but rather the wife, the body, and the offspring—this very transformation [is the man]. And thus, the offspring produced in her belongs to the husband alone, because of the oneness of the couple. || 9.45 ||
A wife is not released from her husband by means of sale or abandonment;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati. (9.46)

"No," [he replied]. "We understand the law to have been thus established by Prajāpati from the beginning: that a woman does not cease to be her husband's wife through sale, bondage, or abandonment, for such was the tradition of Prajāpati; it was impossible even previously to make a woman one's own. (9.46)
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once among the virtuous.

"Once" (sakṛt): "I give," he says once; these three things happen only once for the virtuous. At the time of partition, the division of ancestral wealth and so forth falls only once; one does not become a sharer again through a subsequent arrangement of the share of dharma. A daughter, too, is to be given away only once; even for a girl who has been verbally betrothed, obtained through a bride-price, or even conceived by the seed [of another], she does not become the offspring of that progenitor. Likewise, in the case of cows and other animals besides daughters, these three acts—such as the branding of the ear and so forth—occur only once for the righteous. There is no repeating of them; "I give," he says only once. (9.47)
Just as one who does not beget offspring upon cows, mares, female camels, slave-girls, buffaloes, goats, or sheep does not share in their progeny, so it is likewise with the wives of others. 9.48
Those who possess seeds but have no field, who sow them in another's field, never obtain any fruit when the crop has grown. (9.49)

"Yathā" (as): "yaḥ" (who). Those who are not owners of the field, but merely owners of the seed—when their seed has been sown in another's field, they never receive any share of the fruit produced from that field, such as grain and so forth; this is the illustration for the subject at hand. 9.48–49.
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain. (9.50)

Regarding the word "yat" (which): concerning the phrase "of the owners"—if a bull belonging to another were to sire even a hundred calves upon cows belonging to others, then all those calves belong to the owners of the cows alone; not even a single one belongs to the owner of the seed, for the semen related to the bull is entirely fruitless for the owner of the bull. (9.50)
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit. (9.51)

"So be it. Just as in the case of cattle, so too those who, lacking ownership of women themselves, sow their seed in the wife of another, do not obtain the fruit known as offspring—the characteristic result of progeny—which belongs solely to the owners of the field. (9.51)
But when no fruit is intended for either the owner of the field or the sower, the benefit belongs clearly to the owner of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed. (9.52)

Regarding the term "fruit": "That which is produced here is the offspring of both [parents]. Thus, where there is no connection between the owner of the field and the sower of the seed, it is undoubtedly the offspring of the owner of the field, according to the principle stated that the field is stronger than the seed. (9.52)
But when this [land] is given for the purpose of seed because of an agreement to perform the labor, both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in the crop. (9.53)

"Because of the acceptance of the act": when there is an agreement between both of us that "the offspring shall belong to both," then this fruit of the sower—which was previously [stated] by the owner of the field for the purpose of sowing the seed—[applies here as well]. 9.53.
If seed carried by the force of a flood sprouts in someone’s field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit. (9.54)
