"Carried away by the flood-wind": in this case, the owner of the field does not obtain the fruit from that seed. If seed brought from another's field by water and wind belongs to the owner of the field where it falls, that seed belongs to him, but he who sowed the seed does not obtain its fruit. By this very nature of things, even in the case of approaching the wife of another—even if she has had two previous husbands—it is indicated by this that the offspring belongs only to the owner of the "field. (9.54)
This law regarding the offspring of cattle, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood. (9.55)

Regarding the word "this": this rule is to be understood as applying specifically to the offspring of cows, horses, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes. That is to say, the ownership of the offspring such as the cows belongs to the owner of the field alone, and not to the owner of the bull and so forth; however, because they were conceived through union, the ownership of those offspring belongs to both.
Thus has been proclaimed to you the essential and the worthless nature of seed and womb;
hereafter, I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress. 9.56
"Regarding this": this essential and non-essential nature of the seed and the womb has been told to you. Immediately after this, I shall declare what must be done when women lack offspring. (9.56)
The wife of an elder brother is the wife of a guru for the younger;
however, the wife of the younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law of the elder. (9.57)

Regarding the brother: "The wife of the younger brother is declared to be the daughter-in-law of the elder. The wife of the elder brother is equal to the wife of a guru for the younger; furthermore, the wife of the younger is called the daughter-in-law of the elder. (9.57) "If the elder approaches the wife of the younger, or the younger the wife of the elder—even if they are authorized [to do so]—they both become outcasts, unless there is a state of distress. (9.58)

Regarding the word "eldest": if the eldest brother goes to the wife of the younger brother, or the younger brother goes to the wife of the eldest—even if they have been authorized by their father as will be described later—they both become outcasts (*patita*). (9.58)
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring. (9.59)

"By the king of the gods": in the absence of a husband, a woman—being authorized by her father-in-law or others, or by her husband himself if he is ill, because of the injunction for the procreation of a son—must, being thus appointed, procure through her husband’s brother or, in his absence, through one of his *sapiṇḍas*, the desired offspring characterized as sons, since she lacks a son [of her own]. (9.59)
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and restrained in speech, shall procreate only one son at night; by no means a second. (9.60)

Regarding the term "widow": based on the observation that "he who is born on the bed of one who has died or whose husband is away," a man authorized by his elders in the case of a wife who is barren or diseased—having been anointed with ghee and observing silence—may procreate one son during the night, but not a second. (9.60)
Some who know the truth consider procreation with women to be the second [duty], seeing that the purpose of the appointment between those two has not yet been fulfilled according to dharma. (9.61)

Regarding the phrase "a second": certain teachers who are experts in the rules for sons, considering that "an only son is equal to having no son at all," believe that when an only son has been produced, the purpose of the *niyoga* (authorization for procreation) remains unfulfilled according to the law; thus, they maintain that a second son should be produced through women. 9.61.
When the purpose of the appointment with the widow has been accomplished according to the rule,
the two should behave toward each other as a teacher and a daughter-in-law.

Regarding the verse beginning with "vidhavāyām": when the purpose of *niyoga*—namely, the act of union—has been performed by a widow or similar woman in accordance with the scriptures, the elder brother and his brother's wife should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law. (9.62)

If those two, having been appointed, should act according to their own desires by abandoning the prescribed rule, both would become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher. 9.63.

Regarding the phrase "if they are appointed": if the elder and younger brothers, having been so appointed, should act according to their own will while disregarding the injunctions such as being anointed with clarified butter and so forth, both of them would become guilty of violating the bed of a daughter-in-law or a teacher. (9.63)
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal dharma. (9.64)

Having thus stated the injunction, he speaks in order to refute it: "A widow shall never be appointed to another man. A widow shall not be joined with another, such as a brother-in-law or the like; for those who would join her with a brother-in-law or others would destroy the beginningless dharma—the vow of devotion to a single husband. (9.64)
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* (appointment) mentioned;
nor, furthermore, is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies. (9.65)

"No," [he says]. For among the mantras used for the purposes of marriage, there is "Aryaman, the god... nor is the remarriage of a widow with another man mentioned in the treatises on marriage (vivāha-śāstra). 9.65.
For this practice of animal sacrifice was condemned by learned brahmins even for men, though it was prescribed when [Manu] was ruling the kingdom. (9.66)

Regarding the word "this": because this practice associated with cattle, being utterly contemptible when performed under King Vena, was declared to be something distinct [from the Vedic], therefore it does not exist in the Śruti; this is the reason for what was stated previously by Manu and others. (9.66)
In former times, while ruling over the entire earth, that most excellent of royal sages,
his mind struck down by passion, brought about the intermixture of the social orders.

"He" refers to that Vena; while previously he was protecting the entire earth, he was merely the best among royal sages (*rājarṣi*) but not truly righteous. Consequently, with the permission of the Brahmins, he engaged in this confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) characterized by approaching the wives of his own brothers. 9.67.
From that time forward, virtuous men censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring. (9.68)

"From that time onwards" means: since this practice is so recent, from the time of Vena onwards, there has been a hearing of censure regarding those who appoint a woman whose husband is deceased to *niyoga*—an act which is thus both prescribed and prohibited by the scriptures—and this is heard among the duties of women. (9.68)
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this procedure.

Because it concerns the mode of appointment (niyoga), this [verse] states "of her" regarding the girl; if the husband of a girl who has been betrothed should die, her uterine brother shall marry her according to this rule. (9.69)

Having approached her according to the prescribed rule—she who is clad in white garments and pure in her vows—he and she should unite with one another once in each fertile season until conception occurs. (9.70)

"Accordingly": that brother-in-law, having taken her according to the marriage rite—she being dressed in white garments and restrained in speech and body—in secret, from the time of conception onwards, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the sacramental rite, she becomes the wife of that brother-in-law; and thus, the offspring belongs to the owner of the field alone. (9.70)
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her once and then bestowing her again, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being. 9.71
"No," [says the opponent]. One who knows the sacred law should not give his daughter to another after she has been given to one [already]. (9.71)

[From verse seventy-two through the end of the chapter, the commentary composed by Govindarāja is not seen in the extant manuscripts; only the root verses remain. Therefore, those verses have not been included in this work.
**The tenth chapter. The commentary on verses 72–336 is not found in the available manuscripts. The tenth chapter.**

The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study; however, it is the settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound [the Veda], and not the other two. 10.1.

Oṃ Siddhiḥ! Since the origin of the mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇavarṇa*) can only be described by first stating the origin of the [four] castes (*varṇotpatti*), and because it is impossible to explain that origin without a formal statement, the author says "they should study" (*adhīyīran*) in order to introduce the study of the Veda—the primary duty of the three twice-born classes—which was established in the second chapter. In connection with this restatement of the duty of study, he states the rule for the Brāhmaṇa’s teaching: "But a Brāhmaṇa should teach them. Although the exclusion of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya from teaching is already established by this very statement, the explicit prohibition using his own words is intended to prescribe a specific penance for performing what is forbidden. (10.1)
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule;
he should proclaim them to the others and himself likewise abide by them. (10.2)

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of all": a Brāhmaṇa should know, according to the scriptures, the means for the maintenance of himself and his family for all [classes] up to the Śūdras; likewise, he should instruct them in those matters and personally observe the rules of conduct. 10.2.
Due to his distinction, the excellence of his origin, his observance of the rules, and the particularity of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes. 10.3.

Regarding this, there is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*): "Because of his preeminence" (10.3). Due to the excellence of his birth, his origin from the mouth [of Brahmā], and being produced from the most excellent causes; because of his performance of the vows of a *snātaka*; and because the sacrament known as initiation (*upanayana*) is prescribed for him while he is still a child—on account of these distinctions, the Brāhmaṇa alone possesses authority over the conduct, livelihood, and instruction of the social classes (*varṇas*).
The Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth, however, is once-born, the Śūdra; there is no fifth. (10.4)

Regarding the term *brāhmaṇa*: the three castes (*varṇas*)—the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya—are the twice-born (*dvija*), because for them the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is prescribed. The Śūdra, however, is the fourth caste; he is "single-born" (*ekavarṇa* or *ekajāti*) because of the absence of initiation. Furthermore, there is no fifth caste, because those born from intermediate unions possess a caste distinct from the castes of their mother and father, and thus this [Śūdra] is exactly like the others. Moreover, this teaching of his status as a caste in the scripture is for the sake of conventional usage. Since the single-born nature of the Śūdra is established precisely by the lack of instruction regarding initiation, the statement "the fourth is single-born" is made so that those who know the true nature of things may understand through this mantra that, unlike other purificatory rites such as the shaving of the hair, there is no initiation for him. (10.4)
Among wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity, those born in the direct order [of castes] are to be known as belonging to that same caste. (10.5)

"Among all castes (*sarvavarṣeṣu*). Those born in the direct order (*ānulomyena*) should be known as belonging to the same caste as their parents. Even among the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, those born in the direct order—such as a Brāhmaṇa from a Brāhmaṇī woman, a Kṣatriya from a Kṣatriyā woman, and so forth—in women of the same caste who have not lost their virginity and have been wedded according to the scriptures, must be understood to belong to the very caste of their parents. The inclusion of the phrase "among all castes" is for the purpose of removing the doubt that they might be equal merely by virtue of being members of a caste; hence the mention of "in the direct order. This indeed is the definition of caste for the entire lineage of mother and father, because this cycle of rebirth is beginningless and pervasive. Furthermore, in this entire section, the discussion on the definition of caste is for the sake of fully understanding the castes that result from scriptural practice, such as "cow" and "horse," since no specific physical form that distinguishes the castes of Brāhmaṇas and others is perceived, as is the case with cows and horses. And thus, because of the requirement of taking a wife (*patnī*), those born of women who are not wives do not belong to that caste at all. As Devala says:
But he who is begotten by the second [class] upon a wife of the same caste is known as an Adhareṣṭa; by birth, he follows the dharma of a Śūdra.
Those sons who, though born of women of the same caste, are produced by one who has failed in his vows and lacks the purificatory rites,
are excluded as *vrātyas*.
Thus he says. Likewise:
"From those of the same caste, in women of the same caste, children are born belonging to their own caste.

This statement of Yājñavalkya also refers specifically to wives (*patnī*), because it forms a single syntactical unit with the *Mānava* [Smṛti] and because of the concluding summary: "This rule is recorded as applying to wedded wives (*vinnāsu*). Vyāsa says the same.
"Those born of women wedded to their own [caste] are equal; otherwise, they would be of mixed caste (saṃkara).
So he said. And Baudhāyana says: "They declare these or other forms of marriage; those born of women consecrated by these [rites] become of that same caste, but not otherwise. And Bṛhaspati says:
"Those born in the reverse order (prātilomya), and those born through *niyoga* without [proper authorization]..."
Those born from women who have fallen from the Sāvitrī are three types of mixed castes.
Thus he said. But others [say]:

Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jābālā, saying, “Mother, I wish to live the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*). Of what lineage (*gotra*) am I? She said to him, “I do not know this, my son, of what lineage you are. In my youth, while I was serving many people, I conceived you. Therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. But I am Jābālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. So, simply say that you are Satyakāma Jābāla. He went to Hāridrumata Gautama and said, “I shall live the life of a religious student with your reverence; I would approach your reverence as a pupil. He said to him, “Of what lineage are you, my dear? He replied, “I do not know this, sir, of what lineage I am. I asked my mother, and she answered me: ‘In my youth, while I was serving many people, I conceived you. Therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. But I am Jābālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. So, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla. He said to him, “A non-Brahmin would not be able to speak thus. Fetch a sacrificial fuel-stick, my dear; I will initiate you.”

Thus, because of the observation of the Jābāla Śruti and because of the observation of the prohibition of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* from performing the *śrāddha*, it follows that even among these, there is one who possesses the same caste as his father. And since there is no certainty on the part of the mother—due to [her union] with another man and her thought "I have known this"—[as expressed in the text], "this person is not a Brāhmaṇa fit to speak," it is possible for him to arise even from the father; therefore, this [prohibition] must be intended for that case. As for the observation of the prohibition of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* from the *śrāddha*, that was stated for the purpose of removing the suspicion of Brāhmaṇahood based on a confusion regarding the Vedic revelation, and not to cause the loss of Brāhmaṇahood by its very nature. (10.5)
Sons begotten by twice-born men upon women born immediately after them in the social order are said to be equal [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers. (10.6)

Regarding the phrase "among women": those sons who are procreated by the twice-born among wives of the immediately following caste—such as a Brāhmaṇa with a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣatriya with a Vaiśya woman, and a Vaiśya with a Śūdra woman—are censured because their mothers belong to a lower caste. However, Manu and others have stated that these sons are similar to their fathers; furthermore, Yājñavalkya and others have specified their names according to the father's caste, namely *mūrdhāvasikta*, *māhiṣya*, and *karaṇa*. Moreover, their livelihoods have been pointed out by Uśanas:

Training in elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the wielding of weapons, is for the *mūrdhāvasiktas*; living by means of song, dance, and astrology, as well as the protection of crops, is for the *mahiṣīs*; service to their own kind, supervision of grain, service to the king, and the guarding of forts and the inner apartments are for the *pāraśavas* and *ugrakaraṇas*.
Thus [ends the section]. 10.6.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower. (10.7)

"Regarding the phrase 'in the immediate [castes]': this is the eternal rule stated for those born of wives of the immediately following caste—those separated by one or two [castes], such as from a Brāhmaṇa with a Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya with a Śūdra woman, or a Brāhmaṇa with a Śūdra woman. One should know this designation of names to be free from unrighteousness, as it will be described hereafter. (10.7)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from the daughter of a Śūdra is born a Niṣāda, who is called a Pāraśava. (10.8)

Regarding the phrase "from a Brāhmaṇa": based on the view of Yājñavalkya, who states that "this rule is prescribed for [daughters] born of wives," when a daughter of a Vaiśya is married by a Brāhmaṇa, an Ambaṣṭha is born; when a daughter of a Śūdra is married by him, a Niṣāda is produced. This same person is referred to by another name, Pāraśava, in other treatises. The mention of this alternative name is for the purpose of dispelling the confusion that might arise regarding the Niṣāda who follows the occupation of a fisherman, who is a different kind of Pratiloma. (10.8)
From a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother is born a creature named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel. (10.9)

"From a Kṣatriya": when a Śūdra maiden is wed by a Kṣatriya, a man is born who possesses cruel conduct, a sinful nature, and a body produced from the union of a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra; he is called an Ugrākha. His livelihood has been shown in the preceding verse as stated by Uśanas.
These six are remembered as the base-born (apasada): those born from a Brahmin in the three [lower] castes, from a Kshatriya in two castes, and from a Vaishya in one caste. 10.10.

Regarding the word "of the Brāhmaṇa": among the wives of the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—namely, the Kṣatriya’s wives belonging to the two castes beginning with the Vaiśya, and the Vaiśya’s wife belonging to the caste called Śūdra—these aforementioned sons are known as *apasadas*. This is because, in comparison to sons of equal caste (*savarṇa*), they have fallen away from the duties of a son; thus, these are remembered as *apasadas*.

From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a Sūta is born by birth; from a Vaiśya [and the daughters of a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa], a Māgadha and a Vaideha are born as the sons of a king and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.

Having thus stated the [castes] in direct order (*anuloma*), he speaks of those in reverse order (*pratiloma*) with the words "from a Kṣatriya. In this verse, the first half is easy to understand; the second half has been explained. Here, because marriage is impossible [in the case of the latter], the mention of "maiden" (*kanyā*) is intended to indicate women in general. From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, sons known respectively as Māgadhas and Vaidehas are born. Their occupations have been specified in this very treatise. As for those whose occupations are not specified, they are described by us in another treatise and will be pointed out when the occasion arises. (10.11)

From a Śūdra [beget upon women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes] are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—these being the offspring of the intermixture of the castes. || 10.12 ||

"From a Śūdra": when there is sexual union (saṃkara) with women of the twice-born castes, mixed castes (varṇasaṃkara) are born from a Śūdra. From a Śūdra, an Āyogava is born of a Vaiśya woman, a Kṣattṛ of a Kṣatriya woman, and a Cāṇḍāla—the lowest of men—of a Brāhmaṇa woman. (10.12)
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are traditionally declared to arise from a one-intervening [generation] through natural order (ānulomya),
so too do the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka arise from birth in the inverse order (prātilomya).

Regarding the term "separated by one" (*ekāntara*): Just as the *ambaṣṭha* born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother, and the *ugra* born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother—produced in the direct order (*anuloma*) with the intervening caste separated by one—are worthy of physical contact and other such interactions, so too the *kṣatriya* and the *vaidehaka*, though born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), should be understood as being fit for physical contact and the like. Since the permission for physical contact and so forth is granted to those born separated by one, it follows by implication that the *sūta*, *māgadha*, and *āyogava*, who are born separated by two castes, are also established as being fit for physical contact and the like. Thus, in this context, the *caṇḍāla* alone is excluded. (10.13)
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [the wife] in order have been mentioned;
however, they are designated by the name "immediate" (anantara) due to the defect of their mothers. 10.14.

Regarding the term "sons": those sons who have been mentioned in sequence as being born from women of the next lower, one degree lower, or two degrees lower castes among the twice-born—because they possess mothers of a lower caste, they are designated by the caste of their mother. Since these sons belong to a caste distinct from that of their mother’s father, this statement is intended to ensure that they receive the religious rites (*saṃskāra*) and other duties pertaining to the mother’s caste; for the reason is stated to be "due to the defect of the mother," the mention of the "next" (lower) caste is for the purpose of illustrating the case of the one-degree-lower caste. (10.14)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra; but from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa. (10.15)

"From a Brāhmaṇa": [this refers to] the Ugrī, born of a Kṣatriya from a Śūdra woman; from her, one born of a Brāhmaṇa is produced by name as an Āvṛta. The Ambaṣṭha is born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman; from her, one born of a Brāhmaṇa is produced as one called an Ābhīra. Regarding these two, the duties of the Āvṛtas—such as the management of elephants and so forth—and the duties of the Ābhīras—the protection of cattle, goats, and sheep—are stated in the *Auśanasa* [treatise]. The Āyogavī is born of a Śūdra from a Vaiśya woman; from her, one born of a Brāhmaṇa is produced as one called an Ābhīra. (10.15)
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—these three base-born (apasada) sons are born from a Śūdra in the reverse order of castes. 10.16.

Regarding the Āyogava: the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—these three, born in the reverse order from a Śūdra upon women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes respectively, are known as base-born sons (apasada) because they are excluded from the duties of a son. 10.16.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, the Sūta alone is born.
These others are also three base-born (apasada) castes who are produced in the inverse order.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pulkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka. || 10.18 ||

"From a Vaiśya... [it is said]. Born from a Niṣāda woman... he is known as a Kukkuṭaka. Because the male progenitor belongs to a *pratiloma* (inverse) caste, the Niṣāda here is not the *pāraśava*; for regarding the *pratiloma* status of the father, Vyāsa says: "Born from the union of an Ugra and a Māgadha woman, one is called a Kuntalaka;
he is declared to be a barber (*nāpita*), performing the rites of shaving."
From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother is born a Māgadha, who lives by his speech;
from a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya mother, due to the transgression of the order, is born a Niṣāda, a killer of fish.

Thus, one who is born from this Niṣāda by a Śūdra woman is a Pulkasa by birth. Furthermore, one who is born from a Śūdra by a Niṣāda woman of such a kind is known as a Kukkuṭa; and for those Kukkuṭas, Śaṅkha has declared their livelihood to consist of the work of striking with clubs, *cakras*, *tomaras*, *bhiṇḍipālas*, spears, swords, axes, bludgeons, iron nets, and weapons that destroy living beings. (10.17–18)
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
one begotten by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhī woman is called a Veṇa.

Regarding the word *kṣattuḥ*: one born from a *kṣattṛ* father and a mother of the *śūdra*-Kṣatriya caste is called a *śvapāka*. One born from a *vaidehaka* father—that is, from a Vaiśya and a Brāhmaṇa woman—and a mother of the *ambaṣṭha* caste—that is, from a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya woman—is called a *vena*. (10.19)
Those sons whom twice-born men beget on wives of equal caste, but who are devoid of the sacred observances, one should designate as *vrātyas*, fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*. (10.20)

Now, in order to establish that even those born of *vrātyas*—though not born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*)—are eligible for sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), he says "the twice-born" (*dvijātayaḥ*) to restate the definition of a *vrātya* previously stated in the passage beginning with "these three also. If the sons whom one begets upon women of the twice-born castes lack the vow known as initiation (*upanayana*), then one should designate those who have not received initiation by the other name of *vrātyas*. (10.20)
From a Vrātya Brāhmaṇa is born the evil-natured Bhūrjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.

“From a *vrātya* Brahmin is born the evil-natured *bhūrjakaṇṭaka*. From a *vrātya* possessing the characteristics already described—who has returned [to the fold] among women of his own caste—the one born of a Brāhmaṇī woman from that sinful man is born with a corrupted body, known by the name *bhṛjjakaṇṭaka*. Likewise, those known as *vāṭadhāna*, *puṣpadha*, and *śaikha* are born; these are the names of this very same person, well-known in different regions. Similarly, later on Gautama states that the one born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is the *bhṛjjakaṇṭaka*; and because he is born in the natural order (*anuloma*), he is characterized as being "sinless. Regarding their occupations, it is stated in the *Auśanasa*: “The practice of the *bhṛjjakaṇṭakas* consists of sorcery, root-work, and the use of spells and herbs for the purpose of subjugating or destroying enemies. Having conquered their own armies along with the *āvantyas* and *vāṭadhānas*, they live by this. By other *vrātya*-born men, the knowledge of the treasury, counsel, and conduct of foreign kingdoms, as well as the status of friends and enemies, is to be understood. (10.21)
From the *rājanya* *vrātya* come the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Nicchivi;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Draviḍa. (10.22)

"Jhalla and Malla. From a Kṣatriya father and a Vratya mother of the same caste (savarṇā), there are born those known as Jhallas, Mallas, Nichchavis, Naṭas, Karaṇas, Khasas, and Draviḍas. Now, regarding their occupations, that which was stated by Uśanas is as follows: because of their occupation as spies, the fetching of water and the providing of water-stalls (prapā) and houses belong to the Naṭas and Karaṇas; and for the Khasas and Draviḍas, [the occupations] such as being begotten by other Vratyas have been shown in the preceding verse. 10.22.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.

Regarding the phrase "from a Vaiśya": from a *vrātya* Vaiśya are born those known as Sudhanvans, Ācāryas, Kārūṣas, Vijanmans, Maitras, and Sātvatas. Their livelihoods have also been described by Auśanasa; it is observed that the worship of the gods is performed by the Sātvata teachers for the initiated, while it is performed by other *vrātya*-born individuals for others, and so forth. (10.23)
Through adultery, through marrying outside one's own Veda, and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises. (10.24)

Regarding the phrase "by transgression": when members of the castes, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, engage in sexual intercourse with women of other [castes], and by marrying those who are not to be married due to being of the same lineage (*gotra*) and so forth, and by abandoning their own duties known as initiation (*upanayana*), that which arises is called "the confusion of castes" (*varṇasaṃkara*). Therefore, it is appropriate that the offspring born of *vrātyas* are mentioned in this section. 10.24.
But those of mixed origin who are born from inverse and natural orders,
and those who are mutually intermingled— I shall describe them in their entirety.

Regarding the phrase "those of mixed origin": those who have mixed origins are born from women of the inverse order (*pratiloma*) by men of the inverse or the natural order (*anuloma*), and those born from women of the natural order by men of the natural or the inverse order. I shall explain all of them, thus interconnected with one another, in their entirety. (10.25)
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men;
as well as the Māgadha, the Kṣattṛ caste, and likewise the Āyogava. || 10.26 ||
Regarding the word "sūta": those such as the *sūta* whose characteristics have been previously described are mentioned here for the sake of what follows. 10.26.
These six produce offspring of similar caste within their own wombs;
they also procreate in wombs of superior castes that are born from the mother's caste. (10.27)

"Regarding these": these six, beginning with the Sūta, are born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). When they procreate upon women of their own kind—such as a Sūta procreating upon a Sūta—he begets one who is of the very same caste; thus, because they originate from a [specific] caste, they produce offspring belonging to that caste. However, those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) produce offspring similar to themselves when procreating upon women of their own kind or upon women of the mother’s caste. For example: an Ambaṣṭha procreates an Ambaṣṭha upon a Vaiśya woman or upon an Ambaṣṭha woman. As for those of mixed origin who are born both in the inverse and direct orders—since those born in the direct order have already been introduced, and since it is impossible for those born in the inverse order to produce offspring similar [to the father] when procreating upon a woman of the mother’s caste—the second half of the verse is explained as referring specifically to the irregularity of the *anuloma* births. (10.27)
Just as for the three castes, a son is born from two [members] of one's own self,
so too, by immediate succession, is it among the outsiders according to their respective orders.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): "The sequence is the same for those born outside [the caste system] as it is for their own [caste] origins. Just as among the three castes—Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—when one approaches two of the castes, namely the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, a twice-born man is produced through *ānulomya* (natural order), and a twice-born man is likewise born from a woman of his own kind; so too, when children are born to a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya from women of the Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa castes respectively, there is a transgression of the natural order (*vyutkrama*). This praise of those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) from twice-born parents is made in comparison with those born in the inverse order from a Śūdra mother. As for the claim that "this statement establishing their status as twice-born is intended for the purpose of initiation (*upanayana*)," that is incorrect, because Gautama’s code prohibits the sacramental rites for those born in the inverse order, stating: "But those born in the inverse order are devoid of dharma. (MDh 10.28)
And they also procreate upon the wives of others many outsiders, even more corrupted than themselves, who are held in contempt by one another. (10.29)

"Those" refers to these six, beginning with the Āyogava, who beget upon wives of their own respective inverse castes many sons who are even more wicked than themselves and are censured. This is to be understood as follows: the Āyogava begets upon a Kṣatriya woman a son inferior to himself, and the Kṣattṛ begets upon an Āyogava woman one even more inferior; the same should be seen for the other inverse castes as well. (10.29)
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcast child upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, so does an outcast beget an even more outcast child within the fourfold caste system. 10.30

"Just so" means: in that same way, a caste even more outside than the outside is produced from the outside. Just as a Śūdra begets upon a Brāhmaṇī woman a degraded creature called a Caṇḍāla, so too from those who are outside, such as Caṇḍālas and others, one even more degraded than the Caṇḍālas and others is born among all four castes, including the Brāhmaṇas and the rest. (10.30)
Acting in opposition [to their own kind], those who are outsiders beget yet more outsiders;
being inferior, they give birth to fifteen even more inferior castes.

He elaborates on this very point with the words "contrary" (*pratikūlam*). Outsiders to the fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*)—namely, the Caṇḍālas, Kṣattṛs, and Āyogavas, who are the three offspring of Śūdras—intermarry within the fourfold caste system and produce for themselves fifteen castes that are lower than themselves, yet superior to one another through mutual comparison. This is as follows: a Caṇḍāla begets upon a Śūdra woman a son lower than himself, but superior to those born of Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa women. From him, moreover, an Apasada begets four sons each upon the four women of the fourfold caste system. Thus, twelve distinct divisions arise from these Caṇḍāla, Kṣattṛ, and Āyogava offspring of Śūdras. Together with the three original types—the Caṇḍāla, Kṣattṛ, and Āyogava—they constitute fifteen castes originating from Śūdras. Likewise, there are fifteen originating from Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas. Thus, there are sixty castes; together with the fourfold caste system itself, there are sixty-four clearly defined divisions. Yet, through intermarriage among these, they produce endless offspring. (10.31)

From a Dasyu and an Āyogava woman is born a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply cosmetics and personal adornments, yet though not a slave, he lives the life of a servant, or one who subsists by means of snares.

"One who knows the art of decoration and service, yet is not a slave, but lives as a slave"—because he is a Śūdra equal to a slave in his capacity for the services of decorating the hair and limbs and massaging, he lives by the work of a slave such as decoration; and because he lives by killing deer and other animals through the binding of nooses, he is called a *sairandhra*. As will be stated later, this *dasyu* begets [an offspring] upon an *Āyogavī*, born of a Śūdra woman. For him, the killing of deer and other animals may be permitted for Āryas when they have reached a state of extreme distress regarding themselves, their children, or their wives, for the sake of the gods, the ancestors, or medicine. In this same way, it should be understood that for others who generally live by killing, [the same applies]. (10.32)
The Vaideha, however, procreates the Maitreyaka, who praises men incessantly and strikes a bell at the break of dawn. (10.33)

Regarding the term *maitreyaka*: a Vaideha—a son born to a Brāhmaṇī woman from a Vaiśya father—begets upon a Prakṛtā Āyogavī woman a son called a Maitreyaka, who is sweet-spoken; he is one who, having struck a bell at dawn, praises kings and others for the sake of uninterrupted prosperity. (10.33)
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by the work of boats;
those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.

"A Niṣāda [begets] a Māgadha. Because this occurs in the section concerning inverse (pratiloma) unions, the Niṣāda mentioned by Vyāsa—the one previously described—begets upon an Āyogavī woman a Māgadha, also known as a Dāsa, who lives by working on boats; him those dwelling in Āryāvarta call by the term "Kaivarta" (fisherman). 10.34.
Among the Āyogavīs—who wear the clothes of the dead, are ignoble, and eat despised food—these three base-born castes arise separately. (10.35)

"Among those who wear the clothes of the dead and are ignoble"—these three, namely the Sairandhra, the Maitreya, and the Magadha, belong to low castes; they are born from fathers of different lineages into women of the Yogī class who wear the shrouds of the deceased, are cruel, and subsist on food such as leavings. (10.35)
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born, who is a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehika are born the Andhra and Meda, whose dwellings are outside the village.

Regarding the term *kārāvara*: because of the restriction to be stated later—that [the *māgadha*] "is born only from a *vaidehī*"—this restriction implies that the *vaidehī* status applies even in the preceding case; thus, although not explicitly mentioned here, the *vaidehī* is indicated by implication. Since the *niṣāda* belongs to the category of those born of inverse (*pratiloma*) unions, he is described here as such. Therefore, from a *niṣāda* father and a *vaidehī* mother, one known as a *kārāvara* is born. From the observation of the *Purāṇas*, the *kārāvaras* have the occupation of cutting and sewing leather. From a *vaidehika* father, two types called *andhra* and *meda* are born, who dwell in the forest, as indicated by other scriptural references. Furthermore, the production of distinct castes from a *vaidehī* would occur; however, due to the proximity of the *kārāvara* and *niṣāda* castes in this verse, it is understood that [the offspring] is born specifically from a *kārāvara* or *niṣāda* woman. (10.36)
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. (10.37)

"From a Caṇḍāla": from a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born one called Pāṇḍusopāka, who lives by the trade of reed-work. And from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī is born one called Āhituṇḍika; his livelihood is stated in the Auśanasa [treatise] to be the external guarding of prisons for snake-charmers. 10.37.
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pulkasī woman, is born the sinful Sopāka, who subsists by the occupation of root-thievery and is always censured by virtuous people. (10.38)

"And by a Caṇḍāla": a sinful man, always censured by the virtuous, is born from a Pulkasī woman. One born from a Caṇḍāla and a Pulkasī—who is said to be the offspring of a Niṣāda and a Śūdra woman—is known as a Sopāka; he is a sinful soul, forever despised by the righteous, and by royal decree, his livelihood consists in executing those condemned to death. 10.38.
But from a Caṇḍāla, a Niṣāda woman bears a son called an Antyāvasāyin, who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system. (10.39)

Regarding the phrase "the Niṣāda woman": a Niṣāda woman born of inverse order (pratiloma) bears to a Caṇḍāla a son known as an Atyantāvasāyin, who is more wicked than the Caṇḍālas and others, and dwells in cremation grounds. || 10.39 ||
These castes resulting from intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own actions. (10.40)

Regarding the term *saṃkara*: in the context of the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), these castes have been demonstrated by first stating their paternal and maternal origins—such as "this is his mother," "this is his father," and "he is of such a lineage. Furthermore, whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be recognized by observing the performance of the duties prescribed for those respective castes. (10.40)

Six sons born of women of the same caste or of those immediately following in rank possess the dharma of the twice-born; however, all those born of women further removed are recorded as being of degraded status (apadhvaṃsaja) for Śūdras.

"Born of their own caste and born of the next lower caste": those born of wives of the same caste as the twice-born, as well as those born of women one degree lower—namely, from a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya woman, and from a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya woman—these six sons possess the status of the twice-born and must be initiated (*upanetavya*). Regarding the phrase "but they are named after the next lower [caste]," someone might mistakenly think that this specification of names is for the sake of social convention and not for the sake of the sacramental rite; therefore, this statement is made for the purpose of their initiation. As for others who are born of mixed unions, such as the Sūtas and so forth, they are all of equal form, and there is no initiation for them, even though they were born of twice-born men. (10.41)
But by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age.
"By the power of the seed of austerity, they go from age to age. This means they are born of their own kind; by the cause that is the power of austerity, they proceed according to their birth. 10.42.
But through the gradual neglect of sacred rites and by the absence of Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya lineages have attained the status of Śūdras in this world. (10.43)

And so he said, "Gradually": these Kṣatriya castes about to be described have, through the omission of rites such as the initiation (upanayana), and because they were not seen [to perform] the sacrifices, teaching, and penances of Brāhmaṇas, gradually attained the status of Śūdras in the world. (10.43)
The Puṇḍrakas, the Auḍras, the Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Cīnas, the Kirātas, the Daradas, and the Khaśas. (10.44)
Regarding the Pauṇḍrakas: the Pauṇḍrakas and others, though being Kṣatriyas by birth, fell into the status of Śūdras due to the neglect of ritual duties and other causes. (10.44)
Those castes in the world who are outside those born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—whether they speak the speech of barbarians or the speech of the Aryas—are all remembered as Dasyus. 10.45.

Regarding the phrase "from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet": those castes among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are excluded from [the fourfold system] due to the neglect of rites and so forth—whether they possess Mleccha speech or Ārya speech, such as the Barbaras, Kālas, and others—all of them are traditionally designated by the term *dasyu*.
Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions, shall subsist by means of those despised occupations of the twice-born themselves. (10.46)

"Those who" refers to those born through the inverse order (prātilomya) among the twice-born, and those born in the natural order (ānulomya) from twice-born men upon a Śūdra woman; these should subsist by means of blameless occupations that are beneficial to the twice-born. (10.46)
The management of horses and charioteering for the Sūtas; medical practice for the Ambaṣṭhas; service to women for the Vaidehakas; and the trade of merchants for the Māgadhas. (10.47)

Regarding the phrase "of the Sūtas": the duty of the Vaidehakas is the service of women; that of the Māgadhas is trade on the roads; that of the Sūtas is the training and yoking of horses; that of the Ambaṣṭhas is the medical treatment of wounds and the like; that of the Vaidehakas is the protection of the inner apartments and so forth; and that of the Māgadhas is commerce by land and water routes. Here, the Ambaṣṭha should be understood as being born from a Śūdra woman by a man of lower caste (avadya), according to the view of Baudhāyana, and not one born of a Vaiśya woman by a Brāhmaṇa, because this treatise has introduced the subject with the statement: "Those who are the base-born (apasada) sons of the twice-born, and those sons born of a violation of the order (apadhvaṃsaja), they should subsist by means of despised occupations. (10.47)
The killing of fish is the occupation of the Niṣādas, while carpentry is that of the Āyogava;
the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus have the slaughter of wild animals as their livelihood.

Regarding "matsyaghāta" (fisherman): it refers to the killing of wild animals by the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus; and for the Āyogava, it refers to carpentry and the killing of wild animals by the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus. The Māgadhas and Kṣattṛs are the Cuñcus and Madgus. As Yama says:
"From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother is born one named Cuñcu;
from a Śūdra father [and a Kṣatriya mother] is born a Madgu, where the Kṣatriya woman is deluded."
For the Kṣattrus, Ugras, and Pulkasas, however, there shall be dwelling in holes and the killing and binding of animals;
for the Dhigvaṇas, the work of leather-tanners; and for the Veṇas, the playing of drums.

Regarding the phrase "of the Kṣattrus, Ugras, and Pukkasas": for the Kṣattras and others, their livelihood consists of killing and binding animals such as dogs and iguanas. Furthermore, the *Ugra*—mentioned here because of its designation as a lowly occupation—should be understood as a certain *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) caste; however, the *Nartaka* (dancer), who is an *anuloma* (direct-caste), has his livelihood specified by Auśanas as "service to the twice-born, supervision of [state] treasuries," and so forth. For the *Dhigvaṇas*, the livelihood consists of working with leather and selling its products, as seen in Auśanas’ statement: "Working with leather and living by its sale is the livelihood of the Dhigvaṇas. Therefore, distinct from these are the two types of livelihoods for the *Kārāvaras* and the *Veṇas*: the former [the Kārāvaras] play bamboo flutes (*veṇu*) and other musical instruments made of bamboo, while the latter [the Veṇas] play drums and other percussion instruments. (10.49)
These learned men, subsisting by their own prescribed duties, should dwell at sacred shrines, near trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves. || 10.50 ||

"Near shrines, trees, and cremation grounds" (caityadrumaśmaśāneṣu). A well-known tree near a village or similar place is a shrine (caitya); at its base, or in the vicinity of cremation grounds, mountains, and forests, these [ascetics], being publicly known, may live by their own occupations. || 10.50 ||
The dwellings of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village;
they must be provided with outcast vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their garments shall be the clothes of the dead; their food shall be from broken vessels;
their ornament shall be iron; and they must maintain a state of perpetual wandering.

"Of the Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas... and "garments... [refer to the following]: The Caṇḍālas and Śvapākas should dwell outside the village; they must be excluded from using vessels, for it has been said: "A vessel made of iron and other metals is not purified even by ritual consecration. Their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys and nothing else, and their garments shall be the clothes of the dead. They shall eat from broken bowls and the like, and their ornaments shall be of iron. They must never remain in one place. (10.51–52)
A man practicing the Dharma should not seek association with them; their mutual dealings consist of marriage with their own equals. (10.53)

"Not with them" means that a righteous man should not engage in worldly transactions such as social intercourse with Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas. Their transactions, such as the giving and receiving of gifts, and their marriages should be conducted mutually among those of their own kind. 10.53.
Their food should be given by others in a broken vessel;
they must not wander at night through villages or cities.

"Regarding food": their food must be dependent on others and not prepared by themselves. Furthermore, it should be given to them in separate vessels. And they must not wander through villages or cities at night. || 10.54 ||
They should move about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they should carry out a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the established rule.

"By day," [means]: during the daytime in villages and such places, they should wander about for a purpose, marked with signs such as the king’s command or a razor; they should carry out a corpse without a protector from the village—this is the standard of the virtuous. 10.55.
They shall constantly execute those condemned to death according to the scriptures and by the king's command;
they shall also take the garments, beds, and ornaments of the executed.

"Those deserving of death"—by the king's command and in accordance with the scriptures, they shall always execute those who deserve execution by means such as pure killing or impalement on a stake, and they shall seize their clothes, beds, and ornaments. (10.56)
One should discern by their own actions a man who is devoid of proper caste, unrecognizable, born of a defiled womb, and though appearing noble in form, is actually ignoble. (10.57)

"Devoid of caste" means one who has fallen from the state of being a member of the [four] castes—a human being born of mixed parentage (*saṃkara*) who is thus unknown to the world, appearing outwardly like an Ārya but in reality non-Āryan, born of a defiled womb. One should ascertain such a person by their appropriate actions; and having ascertained this, one should avoid them. (10.57)
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a disposition toward inaction reveal in this world that a man is born from a defiled womb. 10.58
Regarding "un-Aryan-ness": cruelty, harsh speech, violence, and the habit of performing what is enjoined and avoiding what is prohibited reveal a man of mixed birth in this world. 10.58.
He inherits the character of his father, or of his mother, or indeed of both;
for one born of a low womb cannot, by any means, suppress his own innate nature. (10.59)

Because it is said to be "paternal": due to the wicked nature of his parents, he is born of a corrupt womb; thus he partakes in the state of wickedness associated with the father, or that which pertains to both the mother and the father. Furthermore, he is never able to conceal his own origin. 10.59
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth, that man will surely adopt the conduct of that [family], whether it be little or much. (10.60)

Regarding the word "family": even for one born of a great family, if there is a secret confusion of lineage, that person will surely exhibit the disposition inherited from his own father, whether to a small or a great extent. (10.60)
But where these corrupters of the social orders arise, causing total upheaval along with the subjects of the realm, that kingdom perishes very quickly. (10.61)

"In which [land]" means: that kingdom in which these outcasts born of mixed castes (saṃkaraja), who are defilers of the social orders (varṇa), are produced, quickly goes to destruction along with its inhabitants. Therefore, the king must protect against the mixing of the castes. 10.61.
The self-sacrifice of one's body, unconditionally offered for the sake of a Brahmin or a cow, and for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those of foreign lands. (10.62)

"For the sake of a Brahmin" means: assisting women and children is a cause of success for outsiders; the sacrifice of one's life, regardless of visible motives, for the purpose of protecting cows, Brahmins, women, and children, or for the sake of those born in the inverse order of castes (*pratiloma*), is a cause for attaining heaven. (10.62)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—Manu declared this to be the summary of dharma for the four castes. (10.63)

"Non-violence," [and so forth]. Manu has declared this summary of dharma to be practiced by the four castes: performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), hospitality toward guests, giving gifts, freedom from anger, uprightness, procreation with one's own wives, and likewise freedom from envy; as well as the avoidance of violence, the taking of another's property only as it is found, purification with earth and water, and restraint of the senses. And because of the force of the context, since the mention of "the four castes" is intended to include those born of intermediate unions (*antaraprabhava*), this statement applies to that subject matter as well. (10.63)
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with someone of superior status, he attains the higher caste by the seventh generation. (10.64)

Now, in order to demonstrate that one may be a Brāhmaṇa even outside of the aforementioned definition—namely, "among all castes who are equal"—he says, "In a Śūdra woman. A caste born from a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman is called a Pāraśava, characterized by female descent. If she, having been married by an outsider, gives birth and produces a daughter, and she too, having been married by another Brāhmaṇa, produces only a daughter, and she likewise does the same—in this manner, that person called a Pāraśava, due to the predominance of the seed, attains the Brāhmaṇa caste in the seventh generation. One born in the seventh [generation] becomes a Brāhmaṇa. (10.64)
A Śūdra attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise descends to the state of a Śūdra; one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. 10.65.

Regarding the term "Śūdra": according to the principle thus stated, a Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa. However, if a male is born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, he produces only a Śūdra through marriage with a Śūdra woman; and he too, by marrying only a Śūdra woman, produces only a male. Then, having reached the seventh generation, that Brāhmaṇa gradually attains the status of a pure Śūdra due to the extraction of his seed (bīja-niṣkarṣāt), and the one born as the seventh becomes a Śūdra. In this same manner, one should understand the rise and fall for those born from a Śūdra through Kṣatriya or Vaiśya fathers. Nevertheless, they explain that due to the gradation of castes, the rise and fall for a Kṣatriya occurs at the fifth birth, while for a Vaiśya it occurs at the third. Likewise, by this very logic, the rise and fall for one born from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother occurs at the fifth birth, for one born from a Kṣatriya father at the third, and for one born from a Vaiśya father [and a Kṣatriya mother] also at the third. (10.65)
If it should be asked: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father to a non-noble mother, and one born from a non-noble father to a Brāhmaṇī mother? (10.66)

Regarding the phrase "in a non-noble woman": if you should have a doubt as to which of these two is more praiseworthy—one born of a Brāhmaṇa from an unmarried Śūdra woman, and one born of a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra—then, while Bhṛgu has presented excellence based on the predominance of the seed, [the sages] might wonder why excellence might not also arise through the predominance of the field (*kṣetra*), since the world has both the field and the seed as its causes. Anticipating this confusion among the sages, he says to them: 10.66.
One born of a noble father to a non-noble mother may become noble through his qualities; but one born of a non-noble father to a noble mother is certainly non-noble—this is the settled rule. (10.67)

Regarding this, he states the definitive conclusion with the words "one born [to a Śūdra woman]": one born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman becomes praiseworthy when performing the *pākayajña* and other rites permitted by the Smṛtis; however, one born even to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra man is not praiseworthy because, being born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), he lacks the entitlement even to the duties of a Śūdra. This is the certainty, since in this matter authority rests solely upon the explicit statement and not upon inference. (10.67)
The law is established that both of these are ineligible for sacramental rites:
the former because of the deficiency of his birth, and the latter because he was born in the inverse order. (10.68)

"Those two" refers to both the Pāraśava and the Caṇḍāla; it is the established limit of the scriptures that both are ineligible for initiation (*anupaneya*). This is because the Pāraśava, being born from a Śūdra woman, suffers from a deficiency of caste (*jāti-vaiguṇya*), while the Caṇḍāla has been produced through the reverse order of castes (*prātilomya*). (10.68)
Just as good seed sown in a fertile field comes to fruition, so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement. 10.69

"Good seed": just as a good seed grown in a fertile field becomes abundant, so too one born from a twice-born man by a twice-born woman through natural order (*ānulomya*)—whether born of the same caste, the next lower caste, or one caste below—is entitled to all the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), both revealed (*śrauta*) and traditional (*smārta*), and not to the status of a *pāraśava* or a *caṇḍāla*. This is stated for the purpose of reinforcing what was previously mentioned. 10.69.
Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established principle is as follows: || 10.70 ||

Having set aside other views for the sake of establishing the true meaning, he says, "the seed. Some praise the seed, because we see that those such as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, who were born from yakṣas and the like, attained the status of seers (*ṛṣi*). Others, however, these wise ones, praise the field, because we observe prosperity [resulting from it]. Since there is thus a disagreement among them, this following systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is to be understood.
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
and even a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground. (10.71)

Regarding the term "non-field": a seed sown in a saline wasteland perishes without even yielding fruit. Likewise, even an excellent field, if devoid of seed, would be nothing more than a bare, cleared plot, resulting in the non-production of crops. Therefore, it is logical that both are essential.
Since sages born of animal species became honored and praised through the power of their seed, therefore the seed is praised. 10.72.

Regarding the position that the seed is primary, he provides an illustration with the words "tasyād" (from that). Because, through the power of the seed, even those born of animal species or of lowly mothers—such as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and others—became accomplished, worthy of worship through honors such as saluting their feet, and were praised as children; therefore, the seed is extolled by some. This makes it known that the seed is indeed predominant. Thus, between the seed and the womb, the caste produced from a superior seed is what is praised. || 10.72 ||
Having deliberated upon one who is ignoble yet performs noble deeds, and one who is noble yet performs ignoble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal. (10.73)

Regarding the term "un-Aryan": Prajāpati, having considered a Śūdra who performs the duties of the twice-born and a twice-born who performs the duties of a Śūdra, declared, "These two are neither equal nor unequal. For a Śūdra performing the duties of the twice-born is not equal to a twice-born, because even though he has access to the duties of the twice-born, he lacks their excellence and incurs sin through the performance of prohibited acts; likewise, a twice-born person performing the duties of a Śūdra is not equal to a Śūdra, yet he is not unequal either, for despite his service to the prohibited, he remains superior due to his great fortune, though both fall by the performance of what is forbidden. Therefore, one must perform that which is prescribed for oneself; such is the instruction regarding the castes, extending even to those of mixed origin. (10.73)
Those Brahmins who abide in the womb of Brahman and remain established in their own duty should properly subsist by means of the six duties in their proper order.

Now, with the intention of explaining the duties in times of distress (*āpaddharma*), he says "the Brāhmaṇas. Those Brāhmaṇas who are established in the practice of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) as the means for attaining Brahman should properly perform the six duties. And those who are devoted to the performance of their own specific duties should, being established in the practice of self-knowledge which will be described, properly perform those six duties. (10.74)
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts—these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa). 10.75.

"Teaching": the six duties beginning with teaching are to be performed by the Brāhmaṇa; namely, studying and teaching the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (sāṅga), reciting it to disciples, sacrificing for oneself and officiating as a priest for others—these are the six duties. (10.75)
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts. (10.76)

"Of the six": among these six occupations, beginning with teaching, from which sacrificing and teaching are the most praiseworthy for the twice-born in their respective duties, a Brāhmaṇa may subsist; and according to the view of Gautama, "he may accept gifts," meaning he may receive gifts from a righteous twice-born person—these three occupations are for the sake of livelihood. (10.76)
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts. (10.77)

"Three": with respect to Brāhmaṇas, three occupations—namely teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts—which serve as the means of livelihood for a Kṣatriya, are prohibited. This being the case, [for him] there remain the acts of studying, sacrificing, and giving. 10.77.
It is the established rule that these [duties] should likewise cease with respect to the Vaiśya;
Manu Prajāpati did not prescribe those beneficial duties for them. (10.78)

"Regarding the Vaiśya": Just as teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are excluded for the Kṣatriya, so too are they excluded for the Vaiśya; such is the established rule of the scriptures. For Manu Prajāpati has recorded these duties as those to be performed by way of livelihood for both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. And thus, for the Vaiśya as well, there exist the duties of study, sacrifice, and giving. (10.78)
Bearing weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya. But the duty [of all] is giving, study, and sacrifice. (10.79)

Regarding "the bearing of weapons and missiles": for the sake of livelihood and for the purpose of protection, the Kṣatriya bears swords and other weapons, as well as incantations. For the Vaiśya, trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are for the purpose of subsistence; furthermore, for both of these [castes], giving, study, and sacrifice are for the sake of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). 10.79.
The study of the Vedas for the Brāhmaṇa, protection for the Kṣatriya, and the occupation of trade for the Vaiśya are the most distinguished among their respective duties. 10.80.

Regarding the phrase "the study of the Vedas": because it is taught together with [the duties] for the sake of livelihood, and because study is common [to all], the study of the Vedas is the duty of the Brāhmaṇa; the protection of the world is that of the Kṣatriya; and agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are those of the Vaiśya. Although these serve as means of livelihood, they are praised among their respective duties because they produce unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). 10.80.
But if he cannot subsist by his own prescribed duty as a Brahmin, he may live by the dharma of a Kshatriya, for that is the next best [duty] for him. 10.81.

Having thus described their natural duty (*svadharma*), he now states the duty in times of distress (*apaddharma*) with the words "if not living" (*ajīvan*). If, while maintaining his own station through the aforementioned activities such as teaching and so forth—preceded by the performance of the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) for the sustenance of a Brāhmaṇa household—he is unable to subsist, he may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, such as protecting villages, cities, and the like; for since that [occupation] is enjoined for a varṇa immediately following his own, it is the most proximate means of livelihood (*vṛtti*). (10.81)
But if he should find it impossible to subsist by either of these two, how should he live?
He may indeed live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing. (10.82)

Regarding the phrase "by both": if a doubt should arise as to how a Brāhmaṇa should conduct himself if he cannot subsist even by the occupations of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, then he should resort to agriculture and cattle-rearing and follow the occupation of a Vaiśya. The mention of agriculture and cattle-rearing is intended to indicate trade as well; for the author will later specify which goods may and may not be sold. Furthermore, this practice of agriculture and so forth for a Brāhmaṇa in times of distress is said to be performed by himself, whereas in other times of distress, non-self-performed work is permitted by such injunctions as, "He may live by ṛta and amṛta," and so on. (10.82)
Even if he must live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which is characterized by violence and dependent upon others. 10.83.

Now he declares the relative strength and weakness of agriculture and other occupations under the heading of the Vaiśya’s livelihood. A Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya may also live by the occupation of a Vaiśya. However, one should carefully avoid agriculture—which is full of violence according to the principle that "he who takes the earth [for his own] destroys those who dwell upon it" (as will be stated later)—since it depends on oxen and other such animals. From this, it is understood that in the absence of cattle-rearing, this [agriculture] may be performed. Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the phrase "the Kṣatriya also," it is understood that even for a Kṣatriya, the occupation of a Vaiśya exists when his own specific duty is unavailable. (10.83)
They consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is despised by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it. (10.84)

"Is agriculture good?"—some consider that agriculture is appropriate; however, that livelihood is censured by the virtuous because the wooden plough, mattock, and other iron-tipped tools kill living beings dwelling within the earth. (10.84)

But this [wealth], for one who abandons skill in the Dharma due to a deficiency in livelihood, is a merit like that of a courtesan—its essence extracted, it is for sale to increase one's riches. (10.85)

"Regarding this": for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who, unable to subsist by his own occupation due to a lack of wealth, abandons his proficiency in dharma, he may sell that which is fit to be sold by a Vaiśya, excluding what is forbidden as mentioned below, provided it increases his wealth. 10.85.
One should avoid all prepared liquids and cooked food along with sesame seeds, as well as stones and salt, for those people who witness [the funeral rites]. (10.86)

They say that all these should be avoided. One should not purchase any of the flavors, such as sugar-candy and the like, nor cooked food, sesame, stone, livestock, salt, or human beings. Although salt is already included by the word "flavors" (*rasa*), its separate mention is for the purpose of indicating a specific fault [in its sale]. By this, the explanation for other items mentioned separately is also elucidated. (10.86)
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as garments made of hemp, linen, and wool—even if they should be undyed—as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs. (10.87)

"All" means that one should avoid anything made from all types of threads, such as dyed silk cloths (*paṭṭa*) or large woolen blankets (*bṛhatikā*), even if they are not red; likewise, one should avoid those made of linen or woolen threads if they are non-red. Similarly, one should avoid fruits, roots, substances, and medicinal herbs.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and perfumes of all kinds; milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass. (10.88)

Regarding the word "apa" (water): one should avoid water, weapons, poison, meat, *soma*, milk, curd, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), oil, molasses, and *darbha* grass; likewise, all fragrant substances such as camphor and the like, honey (*kṣaudra*), *mākṣika* honey, *madhu* honey, and beeswax (*madhūcciṣṭa*, *sikthaka*). As Yājñavalkya has stated: "Weapons, fermented liquors (*āsava*), and beeswax. || 10.88 ||
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
likewise, indigo, lac, and all one-hoofed animals. (10.89)

"Regarding 'wild animals' (āraṇyān)": one should not sell any wild animals, such as elephants and the like; all fanged beasts, such as lions and the like; single-hoofed animals, such as horses and the like; nor birds, including peacocks, parrots, and the like. || 10.89 ||
Having generated a desire for cultivation, a farmer himself may sell pure sesame seeds that have not been kept long, for the sake of dharma.

Regarding the word *kāmaṃ* (at will): "One may sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept long. This means that a farmer, having himself produced the sesame seeds through cultivation, may sell them—unmixed with other substances—at the very time of their production for the purpose of dharma, if he so desires. This is an exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibition found in the rule: "And [cooked food] along with sesame seeds" (MDh 10.94). 10.90.
If one performs with sesame seeds any act other than giving them as food or as an ointment, he becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks there together with his ancestors. (10.91)

"From food and ointment": apart from the giving of food and ointment, if one engages in the sale of sesame seeds or similar acts through association, then, having attained the state of a worm together with his ancestors, he sinks into dog-dung; this is the statement of the result following the sequence of previous manifestations. (10.91)
One falls immediately from one's status by selling meat, lac, or salt;
by selling milk, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days.

Regarding the word "sadyas" (immediately): A Brāhmaṇa who sells meat, lac, or salt becomes an outcast (*patita*) at that very moment; this is for the purpose of proclaiming the gravity of the offense. This is because there is a restrictive rule regarding outcasting specifically for the five great sins (*mahāpātaka*), and because the penance for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) is seen to be lighter in the case of selling these [substances] or other commodities. By this, the statement that "one attains the status of a Śūdra by selling milk for three days" is also explained, as well as the subsequent mention of "attaining the state of a Vaiśya.
But by intentionally selling other commodities here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.

"Of others": by selling for seven nights other forbidden commodities—besides meat and the like already mentioned—which are mixed with other substances, and which he sells out of desire rather than through negligence, a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya. (10.93)
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for other flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal. (10.94)

Regarding "flavors" (*rasā*): flavors such as molasses and the like may be exchanged for other flavors such as clarified butter and the like; however, salt must not be exchanged for another flavor. Cooked food may be exchanged for uncooked food. Sesame seeds and grain are to be bartered in such a manner that a *prastha* is exchanged for a *prastha*. || 10.94 ||
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all of this;
yet he must never at any time take pride in a higher mode of livelihood.

"He may live": when a Kṣatriya has fallen into distress, he may subsist by selling all these things, such as liquids and so forth, even by the sale of [forbidden] goods; however, he must never resort to the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa. (10.95)
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed, the king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately. 10.96.

"Whoever"—meaning one of low birth—who, out of greed, seeks a livelihood through actions forbidden by those of superior birth, the king shall confiscate his entire property and banish him from the country at that very moment. (10.96)
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another;
for by living according to the duty of another, one falls immediately from one's caste.

"Better," [he says]. It is right to perform even one's own duty imperfectly, but not another's duty even if it is complete. For one who lives by performing the work of another without being prompted by him falls from his caste at that very moment; this extreme censure is intended for the purpose of avoidance. 10.97.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts and, being capable, he desists from such conduct.

Regarding the term "vaiśya": a vaiśya living by his own occupation may also live by the occupation of a śūdra through service to the twice-born, provided he does not perform forbidden acts such as eating the remnants of food; once he has survived the time of distress, he should desist from the occupation of a śūdra. (10.98)
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having fallen into distress regarding the livelihood of his sons and wife, may live by the work of artisans. (10.99)
"Being unable [to subsist]" means: a Śūdra who cannot live by serving the twice-born and whose wife and himself are perishing from hunger may live by the work of a cook. 10.99.
Those various crafts and diverse arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are the works of artisans.

Regarding the phrase "by which": he may perform various kinds of artisanal work (*kārukakarman*), such as carpentry and the like, as well as crafts (*śilpa*) such as lacquer-work and so forth—those actions by the performance of which twice-born men are excluded from their caste. (10.100)
A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path and is suffering from the lack of a livelihood, should practice this dharma. (10.101)

"Regarding the livelihood of a Vaiśya": one who, being oppressed by the absence of the Brāhmaṇa's own livelihood and falling into distress, resorts to the livelihood of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, should—while remaining within his own [prescribed] order—perform the following work for subsistence that is about to be described. Consequently, for a Brāhmaṇa, accepting gifts from others is better than [adopting] another's livelihood; as it has been said: "Better is one's own duty, though deficient. (10.101)
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that the means of purification should become defiled—this is not logically tenable according to the Dharma. (10.102)

"From all [sources]" means that a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from these [classes] in order, whether they be censurable or not; for it is not possible—according to the established tenets of the scriptures—that things such as water from the Gaṅgā or other purifying substances become defiled. And thus, a Brāhmaṇa does not incur sin by accepting gifts from unworthy persons when he is in distress. 10.102.
No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts—even those that are censured—for they are like fire and water. 10.103

"Not from teaching" means that even for Brahmins, no demerit arises from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or accepting gifts if these acts are censurable. Therefore, by virtue of their purity, they are equal to fire and water. 10.103.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from here and there, is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not smeared by mud. (10.104)

"Regarding 'the end of life': he who has reached the point of death and eats food even from an outcaste is not tainted by sin, just as the atmosphere is not defiled by mud. This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) concerning the conduct of others. 10.104
Ajīgarta, driven by hunger, approached to kill his own son;
