yet, while performing this remedy for his hunger, he was not defiled by sin. (10.105)
Regarding "Ajīgarta": the sage named Ajīgarta, being famished, set about to kill his son Śunaḥśepha; yet, even while thus seeking to counteract his hunger, he was not defiled by sin. (10.105)
Desiring to eat dog-flesh out of distress, Vāmadeva—who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma—was not defiled, for he did so to preserve his life. (10.106)

"Desiring dog-meat": the seer named Vāmadeva, who knew what ought and ought not to be done, being afflicted by hunger and desiring to eat dog-meat for the sake of preserving his life, was not smeared by sin. (10.106)
But Bhāradvāja, the great ascetic, afflicted by hunger along with his sons in the lonely forest,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.

Regarding the name Bhāradvāja: the high-minded sage known as Bhāradvāja, together with his son, while dwelling in a lonely forest, accepted many cows from a carpenter named Vṛdhu when he was oppressed by hunger. (10.107)
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
"Afflicted by hunger": Viśvāmitra, though knowing what ought and ought not to be done, being tormented by hunger, took a dog's haunch from the hand of a Caṇḍāla and resolved to eat it. (10.108)
Whether from receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or even from teaching—receiving gifts is the lowest of these and is censured for a Brahmin after death. (10.109)

Regarding the phrase "from accepting gifts": because of the forthcoming statement, "Sin is removed by recitations and burnt offerings even from causing misfortune," among the three—condemned officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and accepting gifts—it is shown that for a Brāhmaṇa, accepting gifts from the wicked is the most base cause for hell in the next world. Therefore, in times of distress, one should first turn away from officiating at sacrifices for the wicked and from teaching them; only in their absence is accepting gifts from the wicked permissible. This is the intended meaning of verse 10.109.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed using refined speech;
however, the acceptance of gifts is performed even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "officiating at sacrifices and teaching. Officiating at sacrifices and teaching are performed by the twice-born alone, whether in times of distress or not; however, receiving gifts may be done even from a Śūdra of inferior birth, and for that reason, it is censured. (10.110)

Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings; however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed only by renunciation and austerity. (10.111)

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by means of recitations and burnt offerings": the sin produced from accepting gifts from unworthy persons or from officiating at sacrifices for the unworthy is removed by recitations and burnt offerings in the manner that will be described in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*). However, the sin generated by accepting gifts from the unworthy is pacified by the renunciation of that property and by the ascetic practices (*tapas*) to be described later, such as "drinking milk in a cow-pen for a month.
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grains from various sources;
gleaning ears of corn is better than receiving gifts, and picking up individual grains is praised even more than that. (10.112)

Regarding the phrase "gleaning ears of grain" (śiloñcha): A Brāhmaṇa, unable to subsist by his own proper means of livelihood, may accept gleaned ears even from those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakins), but he should not maintain himself through the acceptance of gifts from the wicked when such [proper means] are available. For the gathering of gleaned grains is more praiseworthy than accepting gifts from the wicked; and even better than that is the gathering of individual grains of corn one by one. (10.112)
A lord of the earth should be entreated by *snātaka* Brahmins who are sinking and desiring base metals or wealth; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned. 10.113.

Regarding the phrase "by those who are sinking": when *snātaka* Brahmins, due to a lack of wealth, are undergoing the ruin of their righteous families, they may request from a king—whether he be a Kṣatriya or even a non-Kṣatriya who acts contrary to the scriptures—either worthless goods useful for the household, such as bedding, seating, and food, or wealth consisting of grain, gold, and so forth. [The rule] "one should not dwell in the territory of one who does not give" applies here. This is intended to authorize [the acceptance of gifts] in times of distress (*āpad*), whereas it is prohibited in normal times (*anāpad*) by the verse: "One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the *Rājanya* caste; he who accepts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures [is reborn] as a worm in excrement. (10.113) Thus, what is forbidden for a non-Kṣatriya king who acts contrary to the scriptures in times of no distress is permitted in times of distress.
From a cultivated field, one may take unprepared grain; likewise, a cow, a goat, or a sheep; gold, grain, and food—each preceding item is free from blame.

Regarding "unprepared": when accepting [gifts] from a ploughed field, one should accept what is unploughed and unsown; likewise, among cows, goats, sheep, gold, and grain, each preceding item is less blameworthy than the following. In the absence of the former, the latter should be accepted.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, the application of labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. 10.115

Regarding the word "seven": [the phrase] "the practice and all forms of acquisition" refers to the seven lawful sources of wealth (*dhanāgama*). Among these, *dāya* (inheritance) is wealth acquired through lineage; *lābha* (gain) is understood as the discovery of a treasure or something obtained from some source; *kraya* (purchase) is well known. These three are lawful for all four social classes (*varṇas*). *Jaya* (conquest) by means of war is lawful for the Kṣatriya. The lending of money for the sake of interest, as well as agriculture and trade, are lawful for the Vaiśya. *Satpratigraha* (acceptance of gifts from the virtuous) is lawful for the Brāhmaṇa. This being the case, because these are designated as "lawful," this verse is stated here with the following purpose: when these [primary] means of livelihood are not available, one should engage in those [secondary] occupations that have been declared as permissible in times of distress; and even when those are unavailable, one may resort to the [next] ones mentioned in the context during a time of calamity. 10.115.
Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood. (10.116)

Regarding the term *vidyā* (knowledge): because of the context of distress and the specific mention that these are "means of livelihood," they are permitted for one who would otherwise have his livelihood forbidden in times of non-distress by the rule of study; such a person is permitted to resort to them in times of distress, just as a Brāhmaṇa might be permitted to act as a paid teacher. This is what is permitted here as well. The same should be understood regarding *śilpa* (crafts) and the rest. *Śilpa* is the practice of arts such as perfumery and the like; *bhṛti* is receiving wages; *prekṣya* is attendance; *sevā* is service; *citrānuvartanam* is following various [arts]; *gorakṣā* is cattle-herding; *vipaṇi* is trade; *kṛṣi* is agriculture performed by oneself; *abhidhṛti* is contentment—for when this exists, one can live even with very little. *Bhakṣyam* (food) is permitted even for a *snātaka*; and *kusīdam* is the lending of money at interest, even if done by oneself. By these ten means, one may maintain one's life in times of distress. (10.116)
Neither a Brahmin nor even a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may indeed give a small amount at will to a person of evil character.

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should not lend money for the sake of interest even in times of distress; however, if he desires to pursue his religious duties (*dharma*) in that situation, he may lend at a small rate of interest for a base activity. (10.117)
Even when taking a fourth share during times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.

Now he states the fourth [rule] regarding the duties of a king in times of distress (*āpaddharma*): "In times of distress, a king may take even a fourth part of grain and other produce for the sake of taxes. By protecting his subjects with the utmost effort, as prescribed by rules such as taking an eighth part of grain in normal times, he does not incur the sin of collecting excessive taxes. (10.118)
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he must not turn his back in battle. Having protected the Vaiśya with his weapon, he may indeed collect the lawful tribute from him.

Why, then, is protection enjoined even when one has fallen into misfortune? Because it is his own duty (*svadharma*). For a king, the defeat of enemies is his own duty; and for one engaged in protecting the subjects, if there should be danger from any quarter, he must certainly not turn his back on battle. And thus, having protected the Vaiśyas from robbers with his weapons, the Kṣatriya should collect from them a tax that does not deviate from righteousness, through trusted men. (10.119)
From the Vaiśyas, the toll on grain shall be one-eighth, and on other goods, one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa;
likewise, Śūdras who are laborers, artisans, and craftsmen [shall pay this].

"What is that dharma? To this he says: "The eighth part of grain. For Vaiśyas who live by agriculture, he should collect as tax the eighth part of their grain from the increase; for gold and other goods ending with the kārṣāpaṇa coin, [he should take] the twentieth or the fourth part. (10.120)
But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek to live. (10.121)

"And the Śūdra. If a Śūdra, unable to subsist by serving Brāhmaṇas, should desire a means of livelihood, he should then serve a Kṣatriya. In the absence of that, he should seek to live by serving a wealthy Vaiśya. In the absence of even that, in times of extreme distress, he may perform the crafts mentioned [for other castes]. Thus, the service of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is for the Śūdra both for the sake of livelihood and for the sake of dharma. (10.121)
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both, he should indeed propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has attained the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his purpose.

"For the sake of his own [well-being]" means for the sake of obtaining a livelihood, or else out of a desire for both heaven and a livelihood; thus, for the sake of both, a Śūdra should serve the Brāhmaṇas alone. Because he is supported by the Brāhmaṇas, he becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose through that very designation which has arisen from such instruction. || 10.122 ||
Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him. (10.123)

Since this is so, therefore [the text says] "service to Brahmins alone. Service to Brāhmaṇas alone is declared in the scripture to be the distinguished duty of a Śūdra among all other duties; for whatever work he performs apart from this becomes fruitless for him. This is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) of the preceding matter, not intended to exclude other activities, since *pākayajña* sacrifices and the like are prescribed for him. 10.123.
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family estate as is appropriate, having considered their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they support. (10.124)

"Having provided," [means]: having considered the capacity for service of that *śūdra* who desires to serve—his diligence and the extent of his dependents such as sons and wife—the Brahmins should provide him with a suitable livelihood from their own homes.
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, the dregs of grain, and dilapidated household utensils. (10.125)

Furthermore, regarding the term "leavings" (*ucchiṣṭa*): for this aforementioned dependent Śūdra, the Brāhmaṇa should give what remains after he has eaten from the vessel. And thus, the rule "one should not give advice to a Śūdra, nor his leavings" is explained as referring to a Śūdra who is not dependent. Likewise, worn-out clothes, inferior grain, and worn-out beds and so forth are to be given to him. (10.125)
There is no sin for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve the sacramental rites;
he has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against dharma for him. (10.126)

"Not a Śūdra": no sin whatsoever accrues to a Śūdra from the eating or non-eating of garlic and such things; for it has been stated that the rules regarding "what is fit to be eaten and what is not" apply to the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Because [the rules] such as "non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing" are universal in scope, they do not apply [exclusively] to Brāhmaṇas and the other [twice-born classes]. Furthermore, he does not deserve the sacrament known as initiation (*upanayana*), because the time for it—beginning with the eighth month of pregnancy—is prescribed specifically for the three higher castes. Nor is he entitled to the *śrauta* duties such as the *agnihotra*, because his marriage is of a different type. Yet, there is no prohibition against him performing the *smārta* duties, since he is authorized to do so as their performer. Thus, it is said: "The four [castes exist]; it is certain that the Śūdra does not fall [from dharma], nor is he unworthy of sacraments here; he is not enjoined by the Veda, yet he partakes in dharma, and there is no prohibition of him from dharma in the Smṛti. And so, since this dharma is established even for the deceased, this verse is a restatement intended for what follows. (10.126)
But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who practice the dharma of the virtuous, do not incur blame when acting except by means of sacred mantras; rather, they receive praise. (10.127)

And thus he shows: "those desiring dharma. Furthermore, those Śūdras who know their own duty and desire the attainment of dharma, having resorted to the unprohibited conduct associated with the three higher castes, do not incur sin when performing rites such as the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) and the *pākayajña* sacrifices without mantras; however, they do not perform the initiation (*upanayana*), because it has been stated that "the fourth caste is born once only," and they nevertheless attain renown in the world. (10.127)
For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct, in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the world beyond. 10.128

"Yathā" means: because a Śūdra who is free from reproach performs the conduct of the twice-born as prescribed, provided it is not forbidden, he—being beyond censure—attains fame in this world and heaven in the next world. 10.128.
For even a Śūdra who is capable should not amass wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves. (10.129)

Regarding the phrase "by one who is capable": even a Śūdra who is capable of acquiring wealth must not engage in the accumulation of riches; rather, this statement is intended to mean that he must invariably give wealth to the Brāhmaṇa upon whom he depends. Thus says Gautama: "Whatever wealth he may rely upon for his maintenance, even if he is impoverished by that, he should have a store of that wealth for the sake of his superior. In this regard, there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda): "The Śūdra deserves [to be supported]; therefore, having acquired wealth, the Śūdra—due to his lack of knowledge of the scriptures—might become arrogant with wealth and cease his service. (10.129)
These are proclaimed as the specific duties of the four social orders;
by performing them correctly, people attain the supreme goal. 10.130

"These" refers to the duties to be performed by the four castes in times of distress (*āpad*); these have now been declared. By practicing them correctly, and through self-protection and the attainment of true knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*), they attain Brahman. (10.130)
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter I shall declare the auspicious rule for expiation. 10.131
"Regarding this": that which constitutes the performance of dharma by the four castes has all been explained. Now, hereafter, I shall declare the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta). 10.131.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of those Born of Inverse and Direct Orders," in this commentary on Manu composed by Govindarāja, the son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Mādhava, which follows the intention of Manu.

Now begins the eleventh chapter: One who seeks progeny, one intending to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one seeking to support a teacher, one seeking to support his father or mother, one seeking to study the Vedas, and one who is afflicted by illness—[these may accept gifts]. || 11.1 ||
One should indeed recognize those Snātakas and Brāhmaṇas who live as seekers of dharma;
gifts should be given to these destitute ones according to the excellence of their learning. (11.2)

Although the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*) should now be discussed—since the table of contents states, "I shall next proclaim the auspicious rules for penance for the castes"—nevertheless, this [section on] various duties (*uccāvaca-dharma*) must first be addressed so that the rules for penance may apply to their transgression. Regarding the term *sāntānika*: because its purpose is progeny, a *sāntānika* is one seeking marriage. Likewise, one who desires to perform obligatory sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, or one who is returning from such a sacrifice and has exhausted his provisions; a *sarvavedas* (one who has given away all his property) is one who has given away his entire wealth in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, according to the view of Gautama; and those who beg for the sake of a teacher of knowledge, a father, or a mother, or for clothing and other necessities at the time of Vedic study; and the sick (*upatāpin*); these nine types of Brahmins following the *Dharmaśāstra* should be known as *bhikṣus* (mendicants) and *snātakas*. One must invariably give to these indigent persons according to their learning. Therefore, by failing to do so, there is demerit (*adharma*), and because this rule is fulfilled through a specific substance, the fruit belongs to that substance. (11.1–2)
For food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, it is said that cooked food should be given outside the sacrificial altar (bahirvedi).

"From these": that which is to be given to these Brahmins should be given after having fed them; however, cooked food other than this is prescribed as being for giving elsewhere. But regarding the gift of wealth, there is no such restriction. (11.3)
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon the Brahmins learned in the Vedas as is appropriate, and likewise provide sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice. 11.4.

"Regarding 'all kinds of jewels': furthermore, the king should always give all the gems, pearls, and so forth—whatever is suitable for a sacrifice—as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sake of the sacrifice, to those Brāhmaṇas who know the Vedas, in accordance with their learning as previously described. (11.4)
If one who already has a wife obtains another wife by begging for her, his reward is merely sensual pleasure; however, the offspring belongs to the giver of the wealth. || 11.5 ||

Regarding the phrase "one who has taken a wife": according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba, one who already has a wife should take another only if that wife is endowed with both virtue and progeny, or if there is a deficiency in either; otherwise, he should not. Therefore, if a man, without such a cause, begs for and performs a further marriage merely out of lust, the fruit for him is only sensual passion, whereas for the giver of the wealth, there will be the offspring born from that union—this is the extreme censure intended. Such another marriage should not be performed, nor should one beg for wealth for that purpose, nor should it be given as a matter of rule to such a person; this is the meaning. (11.5)
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents, or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma. || 11.6 ||

Regarding the phrase "of whom": he for whom there is food and so forth sufficient to maintain those who must necessarily be supported, and which is capable of lasting three years or even more than that, is entitled to perform the optional *somayāga*. However, as for the obligatory (*nitya*) sacrifice, because it must be performed by any means whatsoever, this prohibition does not apply. (11.6)
Therefore, that twice-born man who drinks the Soma when the substance is very small, even if he has previously drunk the Soma, does not obtain its fruit.

And thus he shows: "Therefore, it is even smaller. When one possesses wealth less than what is required for three years' maintenance, if he performs a Soma sacrifice, even his first Soma sacrifice becomes unfulfilled in its obligatory nature, let alone its optional (kāmya) aspect. Therefore, an optional sacrifice must not be performed by one who has such meager wealth. || 11.7 ||
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own people live in misery— this is a deceptive semblance of dharma, like honey at first taste but poison in its effect.

"Capable": one who, though possessing the means to give wealth to those of his own kind who are destitute, gives it instead to others—his gift is like honey fit for first consumption because it brings prosperity and fame, yet in the next world it is equivalent to the transformation of poison such as falling into hell; therefore, this is a mere semblance of dharma and not true dharma, and thus one should not act in this manner. 11.8
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by oppressing one's dependents results in unhappiness both while living and after death. (11.9)

Regarding the phrase "of dependents": when one performs acts such as giving for the sake of the next world while being oppressed by the necessity of supporting children, a wife, and others who must be maintained, that results in an unhappy fruit for him, whether he is living or dead. (11.9)
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by a single component,
especially that of a Brahmin while a righteous king is in power— (11.10)
If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice.

Regarding the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*): if for a Kṣatriya or other [caste] who is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the sacrifice, its performance, or the completion of the sacrifice should not be obstructed by the absence of even a single component, then a Vaiśya who possesses abundant wealth such as cattle may take it by theft for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice. And this should be done when the king is preeminent in righteousness (*dharma*), for he overlooks one who is following the scriptures. (11.10–11)
One may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for a Śūdra has no proprietary right in sacrifices. || 11.12 ||

"He should take it": when there is a deficiency of two or three constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, he should take those three or two parts without hesitation. And because of the mention of a *śūdra*, he should take it by theft, since a *śūdra* has not even the slightest connection with the sacrifice. Wealth exists for the sake of the sacrifice; thus, wealth was created by the Creator for the purpose of sacrifice. Consequently, there will be a prohibition regarding wealth begged from a *śūdra*, but not [a prohibition] against wealth for the sake of sacrifice coming from a *śūdra*. (11.12)

If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not established the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—one may take from the households of both of them without hesitation. (11.13)

"Whoever"—meaning one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) but possesses wealth amounting to a hundred cows, or even one who has maintained the fires (*āhitāgni*) but has not performed the Soma sacrifice and possesses wealth amounting to a thousand cows—from the houses of either of these two, he shall quickly seize two or three *madgu* birds as prescribed. Since seizing from a Vaiśya has already been mentioned and seizing from a Brāhmaṇa will be mentioned later, this rule pertains specifically to a Kṣatriya. (11.13)
One may take from a person who is constantly taking [from others] and who does not give, provided they do not offer it themselves;
in this way, one’s fame spreads and one’s merit increases. 11.14

"From one who is constant in receiving": he whose constant practice is the receiving of wealth through acceptance of gifts and so forth is "one constant in receiving"—that is, a Brāhmaṇa devoid of the performance of sacrifices, charitable works, or the giving of gifts. If such a person, when requested for a portion of the sacrificial requisites, does not give, one may take it by theft; in this way, the fame of the taker is proclaimed and his merit increases. (11.14)
In the same way, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one who follows the rule of not providing for the morrow may take food from a person of low conduct.

"So be it. Because of the instruction to eat both evening and morning, he does not eat for three days; then on the fourth morning, at the seventh meal-time, he should take as much as is sufficient merely for his daily sustenance—free from ritual acts such as sacrifice—in such a way that there is no obstruction to his sacrificial duties. (11.15)
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found—if he asks, one must tell that to him who inquires. (11.16)

Regarding the word "from a threshing floor" (*khalāt*): it should be taken from a threshing floor, a field where grain and so forth are pounded, or from whatever other place it is obtained through a connection with lowly labor; or, if the owner of the wealth asks about it, then for that questioner, the theft is considered to have a specific motive (*sanimittaka*). (11.16)
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa; however, he is entitled to take the property of a robber or of one who neglects his religious duties if he cannot otherwise subsist. 11.17.

"Regarding 'the property of a Brāhmaṇa': even when the aforementioned causes for seizure exist, the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa must not be taken by a Kṣatriya; by implication, it must also not be taken by Vaiśyas or Śūdras. However, in the case of extreme distress, a Kṣatriya may take the property of two Brāhmaṇas who have committed forbidden acts or failed to perform prescribed duties. (11.17)
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a raft and enables both of them to cross over. 11.18.

"Who" refers to one who bestows [wealth] upon those of inferior conduct and so forth; having made himself a boat by taking away the aforementioned wealth—the limbs of sacrifice and the like—from those for whom it was prescribed as a cause, he gives it to the virtuous, such as the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others. He thus delivers both from suffering: him from whom he takes it, from the pain of guarding wealth, and him to whom he gives it, from poverty and the like. In this way, having made himself a boat, he liberates both of them from suffering. (11.18)
The wise know that the wealth of those devoted to sacrifice is the property of the Vedas;
but the riches of those who do not sacrifice are said to be the property of the Asuras.

Because it is said, "the wealth that belongs to those whose nature is sacrifice": the wise consider whatever substance belongs to those whose very essence is the performance of sacrifice to be the property of the gods (*devasva*), due to its application toward sacrifices and other such rites. On the other hand, whatever substance belongs to those devoid of sacrifice is related to the *asuras* because of its application to improper acts and the absence of dharma. Therefore, having seized that [wealth], one must make it the property of the gods by completing sacrifices. (11.19)
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of the Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger. (11.20)

"No," [he said]. "In that case, when a Brāhmaṇa is committing theft due to such causes, the king, whose primary concern is righteousness, should not inflict punishment; for it is through the stinginess of giving that a Brāhmaṇa falls into the exhaustion of hunger. (11.20)

Having ascertained his circle of servants and his own family members, and having understood their learning and character, the lord of the earth should provide them with a righteous means of livelihood.

And so it is said: "Of him" (tasya). Having ascertained the extent of the dependents, such as sons and others, whom that Brāhmaṇa must necessarily maintain, the king shall provide from his own treasury a livelihood consistent with that requirement and not departing from righteousness, for the purpose of the Brāhmaṇa’s performance of religious duties.
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from one who is thus protected, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit of dharma.

"Having provided for"—that is, having established a livelihood for this Brāhmaṇa, he should constantly protect him from enemies, thieves, and the like; for from a Brāhmaṇa who is protected, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit acquired by him. || 11.22 ||
A Brahmin should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for by begging, a sacrificer is born as a Caṇḍāla after death. (11.23)

"A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice. A Brāhmaṇa who understands the Dharma should not beg wealth from a Śūdra for the purpose of accomplishing sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma. For he who performs a sacrifice after begging wealth from a Śūdra is born as a Caṇḍāla in another birth. (11.23)
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all,
goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of sacrifice": he who, having begged for wealth for the purpose of accomplishing a sacrifice, does not give it all to the Brahmins at that sacrifice, attains the state of a crow or a vulture for a hundred years. 11.24.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of Brahmins—that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures. || 11.25 ||

Regarding the phrase "the property of the gods": since the relationship between a word and its meaning is known solely through the usage of elders, that person in the world who, out of greed, seizes the property of the gods—that is, the wealth of Brāhmaṇas—is of sinful nature; in another birth, he lives upon the leavings of those related to him as a vulture in a birth connected to that other life. (11.25)

At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the purpose of expiating any failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.

Regarding the phrase "the sacrifice" (iṣṭi): when the spring season arrives at the start of the year, if animal sacrifices and Soma sacrifices—which are enjoined by the scriptures—cannot be performed, a twice-born man should always perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, or the Vaiśvānaryā and others mentioned in the Gṛhya-sūtras, as a means to remove the fault of non-performance during times of distress; this constitutes the nature of the rite to be practiced. This is optional in conjunction with Śrauta expiations, just as the Aśvamedha and the twelve-year penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa are optional alternatives between Śrauta and Smārta expiations. || 11.27 ||

If a twice-born man performs a religious duty according to the rules for times of distress when he is not in distress, it has been determined that he does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter. (11.27)

Regarding the "rule for times of distress" (āpatkalpa): it has been deliberated by Manu and others that if a twice-born man performs rituals such as the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice during various emergencies according to the procedure prescribed for distress, his action becomes fruitless in the next world. || 11.27 ||
By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great Ṛṣis,
fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for the sacred ordinance was established.

Regarding the word "viśvaiḥ" (by all): by the Viśvedevas, the gods, the Sādhyas, as well as the great ṛṣis, and the Brāhmaṇas who were afraid of death, a substitute for the primary rites such as the Soma sacrifice—namely the Vaiśvānarī and others—was performed during times of distress. Therefore, this [substitute] should be employed when the primary rite is impossible, but not when it is possible. 11.28.
The lord of the primary rule who conducts himself according to a secondary rule—
no fruit pertaining to the hereafter exists for that man of evil intellect.

Regarding the word "prabhuḥ" (the master): this is stated again for the sake of summary—that for that person of poor intellect who, while being capable of the primary performance, performs the rite through a substitute when impelled by distress, there is no spiritual prosperity or absence of transgression in the next world; thus, even though this was already expressed by the phrase "that dharma which [is prescribed] for times of distress," it is mentioned once more. 11.29.
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king regarding those human disciples who have done him harm; he should deal with them by his own power alone. 11.30

"No," [says the opponent]. A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report even the slightest collection of offenses to the king; rather, he should subdue those offending men by means of his own power through the performance of the malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) to be described hereafter. This is the duty of the body (*śarīradharma*); therefore, when a grave offense has been committed against the limbs of Vyāsa, the performance of malevolent rites against those to be targeted is not a fault. Thus, this passage is intended to convey that much, and it neither enjoins the practice of infidelity (*vyabhicāra*) nor prohibits reporting to the king. Why, then, is it stated in this way? (11.30)
One's own prowess is more powerful than the prowess of a king;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own prowess alone. (11.31)
"Because of his own prowess" means: because he possesses royal power and personal strength, being preeminent due to his self-mastery, therefore the Brāhmaṇa should subdue his enemies. || 11.31 ||
One should employ the hymns of the Atharva-Angirases without hesitation;
for the speech of a Brahmin is indeed a weapon, and with that, the twice-born may slay his enemies. (11.32)

Regarding the phrase "the Śrutis": one should perform without hesitation those spells for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) taught by the Atharvans and Aṅgirases; because the speech of a Brāhmaṇa, consisting of the utterance of malevolent mantras, is indeed his weapon due to its capacity for action, a Brāhmaṇa may thereby subdue his enemies. (11.32)
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through silent recitation and burnt offerings.

Regarding the term "Kṣatriya": a Kṣatriya may overcome the calamity characterized by defeat at the hands of an enemy through his own prowess; however, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra must do so by paying wealth to the king and recording the legal proceedings, while a Brāhmaṇa, as stated, does so through *abhicāra* (malevolent) oblations. 11.33.
One who is a provider, a teacher, a speaker, and friendly is called a Brāhmaṇa;
one should not speak anything unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words.

Regarding the word "vidhātṛ": a Brāhmaṇa is called one who benefits all beings, whose conduct leads even those who perform their own duties to engage in acts such as theft when they are destitute. Therefore, O King, he should not speak of his undesirable faults, saying, "Let this man be punished," nor should he utter words of abuse in the form of verbal punishment. || 11.34 ||
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool;
nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, should be the officiating priest of the Agnihotra. (11.35)

"No. A girl, a youth, one who has studied little, a fool, those afflicted by disease and so forth, and those who have not been initiated (anupanīta) shall neither perform the Śrauta morning and evening oblation (sāyaṃprātar-homa) themselves nor cause it to be performed by another. Because of this scriptural understanding, one may cause them to perform the oblation through a substitute; therefore, this prohibition applies to girls and the others as well. 11.35.
For these fall into hell, as do he who offers the oblation and he for whom it is offered;
therefore, the officiating priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.

"Regarding 'hell': these [persons], such as virgins and others, go to hell if they perform the *homa*; and he for whose sake they perform the *agnihotra* by way of substitution also goes to hell. Therefore, one who is proficient in the Śrauta rituals and has studied the entirety of the Vedas should be appointed as the *hotṛ* priest. (11.36)

If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, does not give the horse as the sacrificial fee for the Agnyādheya rite dedicated to Prajāpati, he remains one who has not established the sacred fires. 11.37.

Regarding the term *prājāpatya*: at the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), a Brāhmaṇa becomes one who has not yet established the fires (*anāhitāgni*) only after he has prepared and given to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) a horse dedicated to Prajāpati as a sacrificial fee (*dak�ṣiṇā*). Therefore, when there is sufficient wealth, a Brāhmaṇa must give a horse in addition to the scripturally prescribed sacrificial fees, in accordance with the traditional injunctions. 11.37.
One who is faithful and has conquered the senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, one should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees.

Regarding the phrase "meritorious acts": one who is faithful and has mastered his senses should perform meritorious acts other than sacrifices; however, he should never perform a sacrifice here after giving the scripturally prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to them, because the fee is intended for the purpose of hiring. In response to the doubt that the hiring might be accomplished even with a very small amount, this statement [is made].
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice. (11.39)

Regarding the "faculties": a sacrifice with small sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) destroys the faculties—the eye and so forth—as well as life, the reputation for longevity in heaven after death, offspring, and cattle. Therefore, one should not perform a sacrifice by giving small sacrificial fees. 11.39
If a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should abandon those fires out of his own will,
he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month, for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.

"An Agnihotrī who abandons the fires... A Brāhmaṇa who has established the sacred fires may, at his own will, abandon the fires and perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month, because this act is equal to the killing of a sacrificer (yajamāna). Although this occurs in the section on self-restraint within the context of the performance of sacrifices, the mention of the "month" is a restatement for the sake of emphasis; others, however, connect it with the phrase "abandoning for a month. 11.40.
Those who, having obtained wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—they are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on the Veda. (11.41)

"Those who"—that is, those who, having acquired wealth by begging or not begging from a Śūdra, perform the Agnihotra preceded by the formal establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—are censured in the context of defining the nature of the Supreme Self, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) to be stated later in verse 11.42: "of those who serve the fire of a Vṛṣala. They are the officiating priests for Śūdras, but no fruit whatsoever accrues to them from that. 11.41.
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of the low-born, the donor shall cross over all difficulties.

"Of them" means: by placing his foot upon the heads of those fools who serve the wealth of Śūdras or those who maintain the sacred fires (agnihotra) for them, that donor—the Śūdra—constantly crosses over from sufferings in the next world by means of that gift; however, no fruit arises for them from it. 11.42.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured, and becomes attached to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to expiation. (11.43)

Having thus stated the entire section [on forbidden acts], he now says "akurvan" (not performing) in order to define the eligibility for penances (*prāyaścitta*). "A man who, becoming attached to the objects of the senses, fails to perform the rites enjoined as duties—such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*)—and performs prohibited acts such as violence, and who cultivates a capacity for the objects of sensory enjoyment, namely forbidden things like forms and so forth, that man, being merely human, deserves penance. [Objection: Since there is a prohibition stating, "One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire," the phrase "becoming attached to the objects of the senses" is already covered by the mention of "blameworthy acts" (*nindita*); therefore, it need not be stated separately. [Response: It is said: Because this is recited within the context of the *snātaka* vows, and because the introduction there is made in the form, "He should observe these vows," it pertains to injunctions (*vidhi*) and thus possesses the nature of a sacrificial act. Consequently, it does not touch upon prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), which is why it is prescribed separately. Furthermore, if this were not present, only Brahmins would be subject to penance due to their eligibility for the *snātaka* vows, and not others. (11.43)
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some say it is also required for one committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scriptures. (11.44)
"Unwillingly" means that Prajāpati spoke for the purpose of expiation for sins committed without prior conscious intent; such is the meaning of the Vedic scripture. 11.44
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites.

"Unwillingly" means that sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas; however, that which is committed intentionally due to delusion caused by passion, hatred, and so forth, is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). This is stated for the purpose of reinforcing what was previously mentioned, as it is a section defining the specific eligibility for these rites, and not for the purpose of dividing the subject matter, because the expiations are about to be introduced starting from this point—beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin—and because both types of sin are prescribed in both places [the earlier and later sections]. 11.45.

Having incurred the state of requiring expiation, whether by fate or by his own past actions, a twice-born man shall not associate with the virtuous as long as that expiation has not been performed. (11.46)

"Let him perform penance. A man who has committed evil deeds acquired in a previous birth becomes eligible for penance through the scriptural injunction regarding discolored teeth and other such marks; having incurred this state either through past actions or through negligence in this present body, once the penance has been performed, he should not enter into association with the virtuous, such as joint Vedic study and other social interactions. || 11.46 ||
In this world, certain evil-minded men encounter a transformation of their physical form due to their own misconduct, as well as by what was done in previous lives. (11.47)

"Here" means: certain wicked-minded humans here obtain physical defects such as deformed nails through contrary conduct, while others obtain them through misdeeds accumulated in previous births. (11.47)
A thief of gold suffers from deformed nails; a drinker of liquor, black teeth;
a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease.
An informer suffers from a foul-smelling nose; a slanderer, from a putrid mouth; a stealer of grain, from physical deformity; and one who adulterates goods, from an excess of limbs. (11.49)
The stealer of food suffers from disease; the stealer of speech becomes mute;
the stealer of cloth becomes white (leucoderma); and the stealer of a horse becomes lame.
Thus, by the particularity of their karma, they are born despised by the virtuous—stupid, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance. (11.51)

And so it is with the thief of gold, the slanderer, and the thief of grain. [The text states: "The thief of grain suffers from deficiency of limbs; the mixer [of goods] suffers from redundancy; the thief of food suffers from indigestion. Regarding "in this manner": a Brāhmaṇa who steals gold acquires deformed nails; one who drinks forbidden liquor acquires black teeth; a killer of a Brāhmaṇa acquires consumption; one who violates the wife of his guru acquires a discharging organ; one who proclaims the faults of others acquires a foul-smelling nose; one who imputes false faults acquires a foul-smelling mouth; a thief of grain suffers from deficiency of limbs; one who mixes other substances with grain and the like suffers from redundant limbs; a thief of food suffers from chronic indigestion; one who studies without permission suffers from impairment of speech; a thief of clothing suffers from leprosy; a thief of horses suffers from lameness of foot. Thus, those who have committed acts that cause defects in the intellect, speech, eyes, ears, or form are censured by the virtuous. They are born with these conditions due to the residue of evil deeds performed in previous lives and experienced in the house of Yama. (11.48–51)
Therefore, one must always perform penance for the sake of purification;
otherwise, those whose sins have not been expiated are born in this world endowed with censurable physical marks. 11.52

"Because one must conduct oneself in this way": since those who have not performed [atonement for] their sins experience various sufferings in hell in the next world, and by the remainder of their unrighteousness (*adharma*) are reborn bearing contemptible marks such as deformed nails, therefore the penances (*prāyaścitta*) intended for the removal of sin do not merely terminate in being occasional rites; rather, they are for the purpose of producing a qualification for another state of existence through differentiation. For it is seen that "karman is not exhausted without yielding its fruit"; thus, because they fall solely within the domain of the scriptures, the very arising of sin is what constitutes its removal. (11.52)
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife, and association with those who commit such acts—these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka). 11.53.

"Killing a Brāhmaṇa," etc. They call [these] great sins (mahāpātaka), as well as association with those [who commit them]. Killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking forbidden liquor, stealing a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, and violating the wife of a guru—by associating with these for one year, one falls, according to the manner that will be described; thus they call these "great sins. This designation of names is for the sake of brevity, and it should be understood to apply to the minor sins (upapātaka) and so forth as well. 11.53.
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, backbiting directed toward the king, and persistent deception of one's teacher are equal to the killing of a Brahmin. (11.54)

"Falsehood": regarding the exaltation of one's caste, falsehood consists in saying "I am a Brāhmaṇa" when one is not a Brāhmaṇa; and regarding the royal domain, it consists in being a slanderer—resulting in the most grievous fruit—and causing agitation of the king's mind, as well as producing a false accusation against a teacher. As Gautama states, "A false accusation against a teacher" is equal to a mortal sin (*pātaka*); these [acts] are equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. 11.54.
Abandoning one’s Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, and eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. 11.55.

"Abandoning Vedic study" (*brahmōjjhatā*) means disregarding the Veda one has studied by resorting to false treatises. As for the statement that "abandoning one's teacher, mother, sacred study, the sacred fires, and one's son" constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*), this is to be understood as applying specifically to the abandonment of the Veda due to being preoccupied with other worldly activities in this life, and not to other instances. "Censuring the Veda" (*vedanindā*) is the disparagement of the Veda through an adherence to atheism (*nāstikya*). "Giving false testimony" (*kūṭasākṣitva*) refers to a legal proceeding where the death penalty would fall upon either the plaintiff or the defendant. "Killing a friend"—even if he is a non-Brāhmaṇa—and "eating forbidden things," such as onions and other unwholesome foods, or impure substances like excrement: these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. (11.55)
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as [the theft] of men, horses, and silver, and of land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.

Regarding the phrase "of a deposit": the theft of a deposit consisting of gold other than that belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is equal to the theft of gold. (11.56)

They consider the emission of semen into women of one's own kin, into virgins, into women of the lowest castes, and into the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the bed of a teacher. (11.57)

"Seminal emission in one's own female relatives": they say that approaching a sister, an unmarried girl, the wife of a friend, a daughter-in-law, or women such as Cāṇḍālas and others, is equal to violating the teacher’s wife. This equalization of these acts with that [violation] is for the purpose of prescribing for each the same penance as that which has been equalized with it. However, as for false testimony and the killing of a friend, which he will later state involve the extension (*atideśa*) of the penance for killing a Brahmin, that is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, the prescription of the penance for violating the Guru’s bed for "false persistence against the Guru"—which has been equalized with the killing of a Brahmin—is for the purpose of making known that for those acts equalized [with a more serious crime], the penance is less than that [of the primary offense]. Just as in common worldly usage, when it is said, "The minister is equal to the king," the inferiority of the minister is understood; so too here, among the *upadeśika* (directly taught) and *ādeśika* (extended by analogy) offenses, the *ādeśika* are less than the *upadeśika*, and the equalized offenses are even less than those. (11.57)

The killing of a cow; officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice or sacrificing for one who should not be sacrificed for; adultery; selling oneself; abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, or son; and neglecting the private recitation of the Vedas or the sacred fires—[these are minor sins]. (11.58)

The state of being superseded by a younger brother when he is unmarried, as well as the act of superseding him; the giving away of a daughter to those two, and officiating at a sacrifice for those very two. (11.59)
Violating a maiden, usury, the breaking of a vow, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child; 11.60.
The state of being a *vrātya*, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for wages, receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that ought not to be sold; 11.61.

Exercising authority over all types of crafts, operating great mechanical devices, dealing in harmful medicinal herbs, living off women, performing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and performing root-rites (*mūlakarman*). (11.62)
Felling trees that are not yet dry for the sake of fuel, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating food that is censured. (11.63)
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts, studying heterodox scriptures, and the practice of the arts of the stage; 11.64.

The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; the habit of drinking liquor or consorting with forbidden women; the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka).

The killing of a cow; being a younger brother who marries before his elder brother (*parivitti*); [the marriage of] a maiden; being a *vrātya*; working in all types of mines; cutting wood for fuel; not maintaining the sacred fires; studying false scriptures; engaging in the vices of the arts; stealing grain, base metals, or livestock; associating with women who drink liquor; killing a cow; officiating at sacrifices for those corrupted by birth or conduct; adultery; selling oneself; failing to perform service toward one's mother, father, or teacher; abandoning Vedic study; and abandoning the *smārta* fire established by tradition. Regarding the *śrauta* fires, because it is stated, "The *agnihotrī* who neglects the fires," there is the failure to provide for the consecration and maintenance of a son. Regarding the elder brother’s status as a *parivitti*, it is as described in the passage beginning, "When the younger brother marries first," where the younger brother marries while the elder remains unmarried, and likewise the giving away of a maiden, the instruction on the performance of marriage rites and *homa* for those two, the piercing of the female organ (excluding sexual intercourse), the emission of semen, and the exercise of authority regarding non-vaginal emissions upon virgins—all as previously mentioned. Living by usury that is prohibited; sexual intercourse for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*); selling tanks, gardens, wives, or children; not performing the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) at the proper time, as it is said: "Beyond this, these three, if not consecrated at the proper time... [become outcasts]; failing to show deference to paternal relatives such as uncles; teaching or studying on the basis of a wager; selling what should not be sold; exercising royal authority over gold mines and other places of production; undertaking the construction of dams and the like—which cause the obstruction of great water flows—without a spiritual purpose; the destruction of green plants; and the habitual practice of intentional injury, which involves heavy expiation for plants known to be sentient, as will be explained later. Furthermore, living off women; performing malevolent magic against those who should not be harmed using spells, herbs, and so forth; cutting down green trees for visible purposes like cooking, but not for unscriptural fire-rites or for one's own sake—the prohibition "he eats alone" applies to the mere act of cooking, and thus the rule must be interpreted accordingly. Eating once unintentionally food that is censured, such as onions; but eating such forbidden food habitually and intentionally; failing to maintain the sacred fires despite having the right to do so, such as when one has sons; theft other than that of a Brahmin’s gold; failing to discharge debts, as stated in the verse on the "three debts"; teaching contrary to the *śruti* and *smṛti*; becoming an actor or singer; stealing grain, copper, iron, and the like, as well as livestock; enjoying a woman who drinks liquor; killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and the belief in the non-existence of actions intended for unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*)—each of these is a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Since the abandonment of maternal relatives is already included under the term "abandonment of kin," its separate mention here is for a specific purpose; thus, in the case of abandoning paternal uncles and others, this same expiation is required, though perhaps a lesser one. Furthermore, since the theft of grain and other items is already covered by the general term "theft," their separate enumeration is explained as follows: where a term is used in both a general and a specific sense—as in "injury to plants"—there are two expiations, and a choice between them depends on whether the act was intentional or unintentional, or repeated. Where a term is used in a specific sense in both instances—as in "having killed a donkey, a horse, a camel, a deer, or an elephant, [one should give] a one-year-old [cow]"—the same principle applies. However, where one thing is mentioned generally in one place and specifically in another—as in "having performed the sacrifice for *vrātyas*, who are fit for sacrifice and unfit for sacrifice"—then the specific cases must be distinguished from the general. Finally, where a single name is used for different acts in sentences with different agents, but a distinction is made elsewhere, that general term must be interpreted as referring specifically to those particular acts. For example, "killing a Brahmin," "drinking liquor," and "theft of a Brahmin’s gold" are each defined as a "great sin" (*mahāpātaka*); by assuming a single root for these, there is brevity, whereas otherwise, by assuming separate roots for the general and the specific, prolixity would result. (11.59–65)

Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste (jātibhraṃśakara). 11.66.

"Of a Brāhmaṇa": causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling garlic and the like as well as intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male in the mouth or other such places—each of these is recorded in tradition as causing loss of caste. (11.66)
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats, sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa). 11.67.

Regarding the phrase "of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants": the killing of each of these—donkeys, horses, camels, deer, elephants, goats, sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes—should be understood as an act that causes loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*). || 11.67 ||
Accepting wealth from those who are censurable, engaging in trade, serving a Śūdra, and speaking untruths—these should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa). || 11.68 ||

"From those who are censured" means: receiving gifts from those from whom one ought not to accept them, engaging in trade, serving a Śūdra, and declaring oneself to be outside the vows—each of these is to be understood as an act that renders one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa). || 11.68 ||
The killing of worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.

"By killing worms, insects, or birds": *kṛmayaḥ* are Śūdra creatures that take refuge in the earth; slightly larger than them are *kīṭāḥ*, which include both those with wings and those without. The killing of these and of birds, as well as eating anything whatsoever—whether it has come from some source for the sake of a meal—that has been mixed with liquor, but not that which is merely touched by liquor; for even though water situated in a vessel for *surā* or a vessel for liquor is not itself touched by liquor, we see that a heavy penance is prescribed merely due to contact with a liquor vessel. Likewise, the theft of fruits, wood, or flowers—even when the loss is slight—is to be declared as an extreme offense; each of these acts individually causes defilement. (11.69)
Learn now correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins, each individually, are expiated. (11.70)
"Regarding these": listen to the vows exactly as they are, by which specific penances all the aforementioned sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others, are removed. 11.70.
A slayer of a Brahmin, having built a hut in the forest, shall dwell there for twelve years,
subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, having made a human skull his banner.

The *brahmaheti* (the weapon for killing a Brahmin): He who has killed a Brahmin should construct a small hut of grass, leaves, and such in the forest, and make a skull related to a corpse his emblem. He should enter seven houses that have not been visited before and are not intended for others; he should do so slowly when the smoke has ceased and the people have finished their meals. He should go about for alms once a day and drink [water] according to the rule of Yama; thus, for the sake of removing his own sin, he shall live for twelve years. (11.71)
Or he may become the target for weapon-wielders, according to his own wish;
or he may cast himself headlong three times into a kindled fire. (11.72)

"Regarding the term 'target' (lakṣyam): for those bearing weapons such as bows and arrows while engaged in combat, he should stand as a target at their will, knowing that 'this one is [the object of] atonement. He remains so until he is killed or rendered near-death in battle; being struck down as a target in combat, he attains purification. For according to the view of Yājñavalkya, even if he survives, he is purified by the pain of the wounds. Or, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba, he should throw his body into a blazing fire three times with his face downward, casting himself in such a way that he dies; thus he should throw himself. 11.72.
Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.

"One should sacrifice" means one should perform the sacrifice known as the Aśvamedha; and in this case, the qualification belongs to a sovereign king who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), but the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) need not be performed for the sake of an expiation. The two expiations are the Abhijit and the Viśvajit; [the former] is with the *trivṛt* [laud], that is, with the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice characterized by the *trivṛt-stoma*. "Stoma" is not mentioned here, as it refers to a collection of hymns (*stotra*). (11.73)
Or one may travel a hundred *yojanas* to Japan or any other [sacred place], eating sparingly and with senses restrained, in order to expiate the sin of killing a Brahmin. (11.74)

"Reciting"—meaning one of two [Vedas] from among the Vedas, he should go for a hundred *yojanas* while reciting it, eating little and with his senses restrained, in order to expiate the killing of a Brahmin. (11.74)
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas; for wealth sufficient for livelihood, a house, clothing, and household goods [should also be given]. (11.75)

"His entire property" (*sarvasvam*). He should give his entire property to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas—property that is sufficient for livelihood, whether it be wealth or household requisites; since it includes wealth, grain, and so forth, by which one enjoys the house, he should give his entire property, including the house and its furnishings. Because of the statement "sufficient for livelihood," he should give his entire property only to the extent that it is adequate for living, and not less than that. (11.75)
Or, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), he may follow the Sarasvatī river against its current;
or, with his diet restricted, he may recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.

"An eater of sacrificial food (*haviṣyabhuj*). This means one who eats sacrificial grains such as *nīvāra* and the like. Beginning from the famous spring (*prasravaṇa*) up to the western ocean, the noble one (*ārya*), eating moderately during the day, should recite the Vedic Saṃhitā three times along every stream of the Sarasvatī. In this manner, these are the thirteen penances (*prāyaścitta*). One should prescribe the penance after considering the caste, capacity, and qualities [of the offender], as well as whether the act was committed intentionally, and having understood the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) and so forth.

Because of this traditional teaching of Devala, these rules must be understood as having fixed applications based on the caste, capacity, qualities, and circumstances of the perpetrator, or based on the qualities of the victim; they are not optional alternatives, for that would result in the redundancy of the heavy penances. Some maintain that all persons are ineligible for any of these rites here, and that when a single cause of the same nature occurs, one should perform only a single expiation with a mantra; but that is incorrect, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "For sins, there are both light and heavy [penances]. Furthermore, it is seen in the Veda: "Or, having committed a full [sin], one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra. From this first injunction, double the penance is prescribed for the second offense; for the fourth, there is no atonement by means of a mantra. (11.76)
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village or in a cow-pen,
in a hermitage or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.

Now, because of the concluding statement, "when the twelfth year has been completed," he states this rule for the qualities [of the student] who has finished the twelve years: "having shaved his hair" (kṛtavāpana). Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails clipped, the Brāhmaṇa, performing services, should dwell near a village—either in a cow-pen, a sacred spot, at the foot of a tree, or in one of the aforementioned forest huts—as an alternative residence. 11.77.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should properly sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a cow or a Brahmin is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

"Regarding 'for the sake of a cow': when the twelfth year has begun, one who unhesitatingly gives up his life for the purpose of rescuing a Brāhmaṇa assailed by a king, a thief, fire, water, or the like, or for the purpose of lifting up a cow, is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa; or, having rescued a Brāhmaṇa from that [danger], he is released even if he dies. (11.78)

One who attempts to prevent a Brahmin from losing his three lower castes, or who recovers his entire property after it has been seized, or who does so even at the risk of his own life for that purpose, is liberated from sin.

Regarding the term "at least three times" (*tryavaram*): when the entire property of a Brāhmaṇa is being stolen by thieves and others, if one attempts to recover it and engages in combat for no more than three rounds—provided that the property has not been taken away—he is released from guilt. Alternatively, having recovered his entire property, he is released even if the combat has occurred fewer than three times. Or, if the Brāhmaṇa loses his life, or if for some other reason his life is spared because of that [attempted recovery], he is likewise released. (11.79)
Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly practicing celibacy and concentrated in mind,
removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin at the completion of twelve years.

"Thus" means: in the manner described, one who is firm in his vow at all times, abstaining from sexual intercourse with women and possessing a restrained mind, removes the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa when twelve years have been completed; and in this way, all such cases—including for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, for the sake of a cow, and so forth—should be understood as pertaining to one who has undertaken the twelve-year penance. (11.80)
Or, having confessed his own sin in an assembly of kings before the gods of the earth, he is liberated from it after bathing in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.

Regarding the phrase "having instructed": when the officiating Brahmins of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) assemble with the king, he may declare his own sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) and, having bathed in the water-offering (avabhṛtha)—which is an ancillary part of the ritual—be liberated from that sin. This is an optional expiation because it is mentioned as a primary alternative; furthermore, since it is stated after the conclusion of that [twelve-year penance], it is understood to be an ancillary part of the twelve-year penance itself. However, it is more logical that this [bath] is an ancillary to all expiations except for the horse-sacrifice. Thus, if one who has commenced the twelve-year penance or similar expiation undergoes the intermediate avabhṛtha bath, purification is achieved by that alone. (11.81)
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Rājanya its summit. Therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified. 11.82.

Regarding the phrase "of dharma": since the Brāhmaṇa is the cause of dharma—because when its instruction exists, it is practiced—and since the King is said by Manu and others to be its culmination—because when he exists, that [dharma] is completed—therefore, when a Brāhmaṇa and a King have come together at a horse sacrifice, one becomes pure after confessing one's sin, provided one has not yet performed the final purificatory bath (*anabhṛthasnāta*). (11.82)
By his very birth, the Brahmin is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā himself is the cause in this matter.

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": by his very birth, a Brāhmaṇa is worthy of worship even by the gods, let alone by humans and the world at large. He is a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as if through direct perception; whatever he teaches must be practiced. This is because the Veda itself is the sole basis for the authority of the Brāhmaṇa, since he is the instructor of the meaning of the Veda. (11.83)
To them, you should say, "Even these three [sins] have a perfect expiation; that shall serve for their purification, for the word of the learned is indeed purifying. (11.84)

Since this is so, therefore [the text says] "of them": that speech of theirs is purifying because the speech of the learned is indeed pure. Those three types of Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda—how much more so those who are even more qualified—their speech, being connected with the learned, serves for the complete purification of evildoers because it is purifying; and for this reason, approaching an assembly (*parṣad*) of those learned in determining public penances must necessarily be performed as an ancillary part of the penance. However, there is no such thing as a secret penance in this case, because it would follow that the quality of its secrecy would be destroyed. (11.84)
Therefore, by resorting to any one of these, a self-controlled Brahmin, through his mastery of the self, removes the sin committed by killing a Brahmin. || 11.85 ||

"Therefore" means: by resorting to one of these penances other than death, a Brāhmaṇa or others, with a restrained mind and through the state of a purified soul, removes the sin committed by killing a Brāhmaṇa. (11.85)

Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also in the case of killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows [the Veda], or a woman who is the wife of an Ātreya.

Regarding the word "having killed" (*hatvā*): having killed a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are engaged in a sacrifice, or a woman of the Ātreya lineage; and because of the context, having killed a Brāhmaṇa fetus whose gender as male or female is unknown, or having killed a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya when they have commenced a sacrifice—[one commits a minor offense]. As for the "woman of the Ātreya lineage" (*ātreyī*), Vasiṣṭha records: "They call her *ātreyī* who is menstruating and in her fertile period (*ṛtumatī*), for in her the future offspring exists" (VaDh 20.35–36); Viṣṇu records: "or a woman of the Atri clan" (ViDh 50.12); and Śaṅkha records: "and she is both an *ātreyī* and a Brāhmaṇī. Having killed such a Brāhmaṇī who is an *ātreyī*, the killing constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*), as stated in the rule regarding the killing of women, Śūdras, and Kṣatriyas. This is what is referred to in the verse by the phrase "the killing of a woman or a friend."
Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin; the same applies to one who kills an Ātreyī woman.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Aṅgiras, this refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, a devoted wife, and a Brāhmaṇa woman who is his spouse. (11.86)
Having given false testimony, having reviled a guru, having embezzled a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend; 11.87.

Having said this: "In a case where, by giving false testimony, one incurs the penalty for murder—there, having spoken an untruth, or having caused a false curse to be pronounced upon a guru, or having stolen even a Brāhmaṇa’s gold deposited with him, or having committed the killing of a woman as previously described, or having slain a Brāhmaṇa friend, one shall perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa. (11.87)
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
no atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa.

"This" refers to this expiation which has been declared for the unintentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa. For the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, purification through penance is not taught. Others, however, maintain that there is a penance even for intentional Brāhmaṇa-killing based on the indicative mark of the Vedic text beginning with "Indra [struck] the Yatis," and they explain this [verse] as being intended to show reverence for the avoidance of Brāhmaṇa-killing. (11.88)
Having drunk liquor through delusion, a twice-born man shall drink liquor that is the color of fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then liberated from that sin.

Regarding the word "surā": if, being utterly deluded by the excessive fragrance of the twice-born [caste], one drinks the primary *surā* made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) out of desire, one should drink *surā* that has been touched by fire. When one is burnt by that *surā*, the twice-born is liberated from that sin. || 11.89 ||
Or he should drink cow’s urine that has the color of fire, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung until death. (11.90)
Regarding "cow's urine": one should drink any one of the substances—cow's urine, water, cow's milk, ghee, or the liquid from cow dung—after it has been touched by fire, until death. 11.90.
Or he may eat grains for a year, or oil-cake once at night;
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks and carrying a skull-topped staff, for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor. (11.91)

"Grains," it is said. Alternatively, one who wears clothing made of cow-hair and the like, who has matted locks, and who bears the mark of a liquor vessel, should eat the dregs of rice and the dregs of sesame once at night for one year in order to remove the sin of drinking liquor. This should be understood as applying to the unintentional drinking of the primary types of liquor, and not as an optional alternative to the previous [penance], because this one is lighter. 11.91.
Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and it is called sin;
therefore, the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya shall not drink surā. (11.92)

"Yes. Because it can be produced even from rice flour (*taṇḍulapiṣṭa*), *surā* is "food-impurity" (*annamala*); and by the word "impurity," sin is meant. Since the prohibition is already established by the rule, "Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas shall not drink *paiṣṭī* *surā*," the penance beginning with "having drunk *surā*" applies to the transgression of this [specific] rule. Furthermore, the statement that *surā* is "food-impurity" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Moreover, in common worldly usage, only the *paiṣṭī* (rice-based) liquor is the primary meaning of *surā*; the terms *gauḍī* (molasses-based) and *mādhvī* (honey-based) are applied to it only figuratively. (11.92)
Surā is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that made from honey (madhvī).
Just as one is so are all; none of them should be drunk by the best of the twice-born.

Regarding the term *gauḍī*: liquor made from molasses (*guḍa*)—that is, from sugarcane juice which is its cause—is of this kind; just as the *paiṣṭī* (liquor made from flour), which was prohibited in the preceding verse, so too all such liquors must not be drunk by Brāhmaṇas. Because of the use of the term "best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*) here and the use of the term "Brāhmaṇa" in the subsequent verses, the designation of "liquor" (*surā*) is applied figuratively to both *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*. (11.93)
The food of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas—namely liquor, meat, wine, and spirits—must not be consumed by a brāhmaṇa who eats the sacrificial oblation of the gods. (11.94)
