"Food for Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas" refers to liquor other than *surā*, meat that is unfit for consumption, and the three kinds of *surā*—namely, *āsava*, *ariṣṭa*, and so forth. This "food for Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas" is food associated with them; therefore, it must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who eats the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) according to the injunctions of the Veda, based on the indicative mark (liṅga) that he is eating the oblation for the gods. Some say that the prohibition against liquor applies only to the male Brāhmaṇa and not to the woman; however, that is incorrect. For [the texts state]: "Liquor, garlic, onion, and *gṛñjanaka* are foods not to be eaten; a Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks liquor, the gods do not lead her to the world of her husband; right here she is of evil mind, her merit exhausted, born from the water, or [born from] sour gruel. Thus, it is forbidden for women as well.
That brahmin woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of Brahmā;
even in this very life, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, or a sow.
Thus, because Śaṅkha, Vasiṣṭha, and Yājñavalkya record a prohibition even for a Brāhmaṇī woman. 11.94.
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brahmin might fall into impurity, or he might recite the Veda, or he might perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication. (11.95)

"Regarding the term 'impure': if a Brāhmaṇa, being intoxicated, should fall into impurity, or utter a Vedic passage, or, deluded by intoxication, commit an improper act such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa—for these reasons, liquor must not be drunk by him; this is another explanatory statement (arthavāda). (11.95)
He whose Brahman residing in the body is once drenched by intoxicating liquor loses his status as a Brahmin and attains the state of a Śūdra. (11.96)

"Of him"—of that [person], his Brahminhood departs; he descends to the state of a Śūdra. That Brahmin in whose body the Veda, which resides in the form of sacred refinement (*saṃskāra*), even once becomes filled with fat—that person's Brahminhood vanishes and he goes to the condition of a Śūdra. This also has the same meaning as the previous verse. (11.96)
This manifold expiation for the drinking of spirituous liquor has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.

Regarding the word "this": various forms of purification for the sin produced by drinking liquor have been stated; therefore, hereafter I shall declare the purification for the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold. (11.97)
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should proclaim his own deed and say: "May your majesty punish me. (11.98)

Regarding the phrase "one who has committed the theft of gold": according to the legal tradition of Yājñavalkya, "But one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa," the thief of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, having approached the king and making public the act of stealing the gold, should say, "Inflict punishment upon me. (11.98)
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by this execution the thief is purified, but a Brāhmaṇa is purified only through ascetic penance.

"Having taken," as it is said: "Skanda having taken up the mace," and so forth; having taken the mace offered by him, and having declared that one must never kill that thief if he is a Brāhmaṇa, the king may kill him once, provided he is not a Brāhmaṇa, and that thief is liberated from that sin by the execution. If a Brāhmaṇa is killed by the king after he has performed the penance to be described—which consists in transgressing the prohibitions—then he too is indeed purified. (11.99)
But a twice-born man who desires to remove the impurity born of stealing gold should,
clothed in bark garments, perform the vow of Brahmā in the forest.

But a twice-born man who desires to remove by austerity the impurity born of stealing gold shall, clothed in rags, perform in the forest the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin; for a twice-born man wishing to destroy through austerity the sin produced by the theft of gold, being covered with pieces of cloth, he should perform that twelve-year vow which was first mentioned in the case of killing a Brahmin. (11.100)
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
but he shall expel the sin of approaching the wife of his teacher by means of these same vows.

Regarding the word "by these": a twice-born man shall remove the sin produced by the theft of gold through these vows. Now, since two halves of penance have already been mentioned, the plural "by these" is intended to indicate that even though not explicitly stated, other methods such as those of Manu and others are also to be understood. Furthermore, the sin caused by approaching the wife of a guru shall be removed by the expiations that will be described hereafter. The term "guru" refers to both the preceptor (ācārya) and the father. (11.101)
Having addressed the sin of violating the teacher’s bed, he should lie down upon an iron bed;
or he should embrace a glowing metal image (sūrmi); by death, he is purified. 11.102.

Regarding the phrase "one who violates the Guru’s bed": having declared the sin of approaching the Guru’s wife, he should lie down upon a heated iron bed. According to the traditional teaching of Saṃvarta, "or [he should embrace] a woman-shaped image made of black iron," he must indeed embrace a glowing iron figure; thus, through death, he is purified. (11.102)
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms, he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until he collapses. (11.103)

"By himself" means: having himself extracted his own penis and testicles and held them in his cupped hands, he should go with clear strides toward the south-western direction until the fall of his body. 11.103.
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard and dwelling in a lonely forest, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind. (11.104)

Regarding the term *khaṭvāṅgī*: covered with a piece of cloth from a part of a bedstead, with his beard and body hair grown, and with his mind restrained, he should spend one year in a solitary forest performing the *prājāpatya* penance or the *kṛcchra* penance which will be described hereafter. || 11.104 ||
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (havis) or barley-gruel, in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.

Regarding the *cāndrāyaṇa*: Alternatively, for the purpose of expiating the sin of approaching the wife of a guru, one who has restrained his senses should perform *cāndrāyaṇa* penances for three months, subsisting on wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like, or on flour mixed with milk and so forth. Here too, these penances are to be determined according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional, whether the guru was primary or secondary, and whether the woman was his own wife or another’s, as well as the degree of contact. Since it is impossible for the wife of a guru to be "another's wife," there is no separate penance for approaching the wife of another in this context. However, where entry occurs unavoidably, multiple penances may apply due to the convergence of several causes. One who approaches the wife of a guru—whether she belongs to the same lineage (*sagotrā*), is menstruating, is unapproachable, or is unwilling—even if it is during the new moon or by day, or if he does so while impure from eating, becomes liable to penance for each individual cause. (11.105)
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
however, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) [may do so] by means of these various kinds of vows.

"By these": by means of these aforementioned vows, those who have committed great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin may remove their transgressions. Furthermore, those who have committed secondary sins (upapātaka) such as the killing of a cow may remove them by means of the various forms that will be described hereafter. 11.106.
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
He should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with his senses restrained, he should perform his ablutions with cow urine. (11.108)
By day he should follow those cows, and while standing upright, he should inhale the dust they raise;
having performed service and paid homage, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
While they stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should follow;
likewise, while they sit, he should sit, self-restrained and free from envy. (11.110)
One should rescue with all one's strength a woman who is ill or accursed, or one threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one who has fallen or is stuck in the mud. (11.111)
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently, one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability. (11.112)
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking. (11.113)
The cow-killer who follows a cow according to this rule removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months. (11.114)
"Connected with minor offenses"; "at the fourth meal-time"; "during the day"; "while [the women] are standing"; "until the cows have returned"; "in the heat"; "of oneself"; "by this."

A cow-killer, having committed a minor offense (*upapātaka*), shall drink barley in the form of groats or gruel for one month. For another two months, he shall eat food daily that is free from salt and substances such as molasses, and on the second day, he shall eat only a small amount in the evening. Covered with a cow-hide, with his hair and other parts shorn, bathing with cow-urine, and with his senses restrained, he shall dwell for three months in the company of cows. During the day, when those cows in whose pen he dwells go far from the pen, he shall follow behind them; while following them, standing still, he shall inhale the dust raised upward by their hooves. Having returned to the pen with them, he shall serve them by scratching them and so forth, and after bowing to them, he shall sit down at night where he is not forbidden. Likewise, if they are threatened by causes of fear such as thieves or tigers, or have fallen into a pit, or are stuck in mud, he shall rescue them with all his might. Similarly, whether the sun is scorching in the heat, or it rains, or the wind blows fiercely, he shall protect the cow to the best of his ability rather than seeking protection for himself. Furthermore, in the house, field, or threshing floor of himself or others, he shall not speak out against a cow or calf eating crops or a calf drinking milk. By following this prescribed method, the cow-killer who follows the cow shall remove the sin committed by killing a cow within three months. (11.107–114)
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

"Eleven bulls": if one has cows of which a bull is the eleventh, he should give them according to his desire as part of that expiation. If such wealth is not available, he should give his entire property to those learned in the Vedas. (11.115)

Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka) should perform this very same vow for the sake of purification, with the exception of the emission of semen, or else they may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

"Regarding this [verse]: other men as well—those who have committed offenses belonging to the category of minor sins (upapātaka), excluding the *vakīrṇin* whose penance will be described later—should perform this very same penance for killing a cow for the sake of removing their sin. (11.116)
But one who has spilled his seed shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*.
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rules, and finally having come together with the *ṛc* verse,
he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni.

Regarding the term *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy): having performed the oblation (*hutvā*), the *avakīrṇin*, as will be described, shall sacrifice to the deity named Nirṛti at a crossroads at night, using a one-eyed donkey according to the ritual procedure of the *Pārvaṇa*. Having performed the offerings of the omentum (*vapā*) and so forth from that donkey as required, he should then offer clarified butter with a dipping-spoon (*sruva*) from these fires, reciting the verse beginning with "saṃ mā siñcantu" and the mantra beginning with "māruta-indra-bṛhaspate. (11.117–118)
The knowers of dharma and exponents of the Veda declare that for a twice-born man established in a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow. (11.119)

Because it is not well-known, he states the definition of *avakīrṇin* with the words "through desire" (*kāmataḥ*). Those who know the Dharma and are intent on defining the nature of Brahman have declared that the intentional emission of semen by a twice-born student constitutes a violation of his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). (11.119)
The fourfold Brahmanic splendor of one who has broken his vow approaches Māruta, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka.

Regarding the term "mārutam": this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the injunction concerning the oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*), stating that one who has violated his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) should offer four oblations of clarified butter to Marut, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni, from whichever [of the two sets] are appropriate, as a means of expiation for the spiritual luster (*tejas*) produced by the student’s observance of study and his vows and restraints. 11.120.
When this sin has been incurred, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.

Regarding the phrase "in this": when the sin known as *avakīrṇa* (the violation of celibacy) has arisen, one should perform the previously mentioned sacrifice of the donkey and so forth; then, having covered oneself with the hide belonging to that donkey and proclaiming one's own deed by saying "I am an *avakīrṇin*," one should go for alms at seven houses while announcing one's own action. 11.122.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year. (11.122)

Regarding the phrase "from them": by subsisting on alms obtained from those houses, taking food only once a day, and performing ritual ablutions in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, he who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin) becomes purified within one year. (11.122)
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra; if done unintentionally, the Prājāpatya.

Regarding the phrase "causing loss of caste": acts such as "inflicting physical injury upon a Brāhmaṇa" and so forth have been described as causing loss of caste; having intentionally committed any one among those, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance to be described hereafter. However, having committed it unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance to be described hereafter. (11.123)
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness of receiving alms, purification is achieved by the lunar penance (Aindava) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.

Regarding the phrase "acts causing mixture [of castes] (saṃkara) and acts rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātra)": acts such as taking wealth from those censured—such as from donkeys, horses, camels, and so forth—are said to cause mixture and to render one unworthy of receiving gifts; having intentionally committed any one among these, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for purification even if the act was committed unintentionally. Regarding the acts said to cause defilement (malinīkaraṇīya), such as killing worms, insects, or birds: having intentionally committed any one among these, one should drink barley-gruel (yāvaka) for three days. Yāvaka is a liquid preparation made from barley, resembling thin gruel, which one should drink while it is warm. (11.124)
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part is required for a Vaiśya who abides by his duty, while for a Śūdra it should be known as a sixteenth part. (11.125)

Regarding the term "fourth" (*turīya*): A fourth part of the twelve-year penance prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa is ordained for the killing of a Kṣatriya; for a Vaiśya of good conduct, an eighth part; and for a Śūdra who is killed, a sixteenth part is to be understood. This refers to the case of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra of virtuous conduct, because of their superior status. As for the penance for the murder of men—namely, "the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya"—this is an alternative *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance differentiated by whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and it applies to the case of a wicked Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra, because of their inferior status. And this [sixteenth-part rule] applies to an unintentional killing, since he stated this in reference to a fourth part of the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa. (11.125)
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born, having observed his vows well, should give a thousand cows with one bull.
"Unintentionally": furthermore, having unintentionally killed a Kṣatriya, one should give a single bull among a thousand cows to Brāhmaṇas for the sake of his own purification. (11.127)
Or, for three years, one who has killed a Brahmin shall perform the vow with self-restraint, wearing matted hair,
dwelling at a great distance from the village, and making his abode at the root of a tree.

Regarding the phrase "for three years": the rule that "the slayer of a Brahmin shall perform [penance] for twelve years," and so forth, ending with "he shall practice this for three years," is an alternative to the rule "but this [is for] unintentional [killing]. Since it is observed that "if one is unable [to provide] a thousand cows as a gift, the purification from the killing of snakes and other creatures is by means of giving," the meaning is that wearing matted hair, dwelling far from a village, and residing at the foot of a tree constitute another limb of the penance due to the firmness of the vow; however, in the case of the fourth part of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter, all of this becomes a constituent part of the twelve-year penance. (11.127)
An excellent twice-born man who has killed a Vaiśya established in his duties should perform this very same penance for one year, or he should give one hundred and one cows.

Regarding the phrase "this very same": the vow that was prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa—namely, "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall perform [the penance] for twelve years"—is indeed applicable here due to the context of intentional agency; thus, having unintentionally killed a Vaiśya of virtuous conduct, a wealthy man should perform the penance for one year as prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa and others, and furthermore, he should give a hundred cows along with one additional bull. This is because the term "bull" is mentioned in both the preceding and following verses. (11.128)
A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or he shall give ten white cows and a bull to a Brāhmaṇa.

"Regarding this": the vow that was stated as "the slayer of a Brahmin [shall perform] this very vow for twelve years"—that vow, accompanied by a bull, he shall perform after having unintentionally killed a Śūdra of virtuous conduct, because the context concerns unintentional acts. Furthermore, one who possesses wealth shall give to a Brāhmaṇa white cows, eleven of which include a bull. 11.129.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
or even a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, or an owl, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.

Regarding the phrase "the cat and the mongoose": having killed each one of these—the cat (*biḍāla*), the mongoose (*nakula*), the blue jay (*cāṣa*), the frog (*maṇḍūka*), the monitor lizard (*godha*), the owl (*ulūka*), and the crow (*kāka*)—one should perform the vow for the killing of a Śūdra. According to the rule "the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya" constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*), one should perform the penance for a minor offense, which is the vow for cow-killing or the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. However, this should be understood as sixteenfold in the case of a Śūdra, by way of extension (*atideśa*), because that is the logical conclusion. If this is so, why has this [group of animals] not been recited in the very list of cow-killing and the rest? It is not so; for if they were included there in the recitation, their mention would have had to be repeated in the passage concerning drinking milk for three nights (*payah pibet trirātram*). Some say that since this penance applies to the killing of all [animals] together, it stands in optional alternative (*vikalpa*) with the subsequent lighter penances such as drinking milk, because that is logical. But that is incorrect, because no word expressing a collective aggregate (*samuccaya*) is heard, and because a regulated option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) is possible based on distinctions such as intention (*jñāna*) and so forth. Furthermore, it is illogical for a very heavy penance to stand in optional alternative with a much lighter one based on distinctions of intention and so forth. In cases such as "one should throw oneself into fire," or "one should give the house and its furnishings to a Brāhmaṇa," this [penance] does not apply to the collective [killing]. And since the subsequent [penances] refer to each individual [animal], the word "or" (*vā*) is appropriate in the sense of "one should drink milk for three nights, or [perform another penance]. Therefore, due to the gravity of the situation, this penance is to be applied according to one's own choice: for one who is capable of intense austerity but does not kill intentionally, and for one who is utterly incapable of intense austerity. This is the penance for a righteous person (*dhārmika*). The subsequent [penances], however, apply in some way to one whose transgression arose through negligence and who is extremely righteous and utterly capable of austerity. Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana, or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn dedicated to the waters (Ab-daivata-sūkta). || 11.131 ||

Regarding the term "milk": for the unintentional killing of these animals, such as cats and the like, one should drink milk for three nights. If one is unable to do that due to internal weakness or other reasons, one should travel a journey's distance on the prescribed path for three nights; if one is unable even for that, one should bathe in a river for three nights; and if one is incapable even of that, one should mutter the hymn beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭha* for three nights. (11.131)
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.
A spade, a load of straw, a piece of lead, and a masha of silver for a eunuch. || 11.132 ||
For killing a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a curlew, a three-year-old calf.

Regarding "a jar of clarified butter": when a boar has been killed, one should give a jar filled with clarified butter; when a bird called a partridge has been killed, one should give two hundred palas of sesame seeds; when a parrot has been killed, a two-year-old calf; and having killed a bird called a curlew, one should give a three-year-old calf. (11.133)
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, and even a peacock, as well as a monkey, a hawk, and a vulture, one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. 11.134.

"Having killed" means: having killed any one of the birds known as the *haṃsa*, *balāka*, *baka*, peacock, monkey-bird (*vānarapājika*), or *bhāsa*, one should give a cow to a Brahmin. "Touching" refers to the act of giving. Here too, some say that because the cow is a large animal, this expiation applies only to the killing of all [the aforementioned birds] together; but that is incorrect, because for the killing of a *krauñca* crane, the gift of a three-year-old calf is prescribed. (11.134)
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; and having killed a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, one should give a one-year-old calf.

Regarding "clothing": having killed a horse, one should give a garment; having killed an elephant, one should give five dark-colored bulls; having killed a goat or sheep, one should give a bull; having killed a donkey, one should give a calf one year old. (11.135)
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous ones, a heifer; but having killed a camel, one should give a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.

Regarding the term *kravyādān* (meat-eaters): having killed wild animals such as tigers and others that consume raw flesh, one should give a cow that has recently calved and yields abundant milk. Having killed wild animals such as the *sāraṅga* deer and others that do not consume flesh, one should give a cow whose calf has recently emerged from the birth-cord. Having killed a camel, one should give a *raktikā* of gold. (11.136)
Having killed women of the four castes who were not protected by their husbands, one should give a bow of Jina, a bull, a horse, and a goat respectively for the sake of purification. (11.137)

"Regarding the phrase 'a bow of a Jina, a goat-skin bag, and a ewe' [11.137]: women belonging to the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas do not fall [from their status] by having intercourse with men who are either superior or inferior; however, if they have somehow killed [an animal] unintentionally, they should give, for the sake of purification, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, and a sheep respectively."

If a twice-born man is unable to expiate the killing of snakes and other such creatures through the gift of wealth, he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove his sin. (11.138)

Regarding the phrase "by means of a gift": because there is no [specific] sacrificial vessel (*puṭa*) and so forth, one who is unable to remove the sin of killing a snake or similar creature through a gift must perform the first *kṛcchra* penance among those beginning with the *prājāpatya* for the purpose of removing the sin from killing a Brāhmaṇa or others individually. Furthermore, snakes and the like are included starting from the rule: "one should give a ploughshare of black iron" (*abhrikārṣṇāyasīṃ dadyāt*).
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate beings,
or for a full wagon-load of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.

"Of those possessed of bones": because of the association with "boneless," this refers to the killing of a thousand small creatures possessing bones, such as lizards and the like; for their slaughter, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra. For the killing of boneless small creatures, such as bedbugs and the like, when they amount to a full cartload, one should perform this very same penance.
But for killing a vertebrate creature, one should give something to a Brahmin;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma).

"Something" (*kiṃcit*): For the killing of each individual small creature possessing bones, such as lizards and the like, one should give a *paṇa* to a Brāhmaṇa, because of the traditional teaching of Sumantu: "For the killing of each [creature] possessing bones, a *paṇa* is to be given. However, for the killing of each boneless creature, there is expiation by means of *prāṇāyāma*: "One should recite three times the Gāyatrī together with the *praṇava*, along with the *Śiras*, while restraining the breath; that is called *prāṇāyāma*."
Thus, one is purified according to the characteristics described by Vasiṣṭha. || 11.140 ||
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.

Regarding "the giving of fruit": for the cutting of fruit-bearing trees such as mangoes, or of creepers with many leaves that have produced flowers, one hundred *liṅga* verses must be recited for the expiation of the sin. (11.141)
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete purification.

Regarding the phrase "of those born from food": for all living beings produced from flour and the like, as well as those produced from molasses and the like, and those arising from fruits and flowers such as the *udumbara* and *madhūka*, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) serves as a purification. Since expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) are intended for the purpose of heating the body, the injunctions to consume clarified butter, drink milk, and so forth, exclude other types of food. However, when the consumption of clarified butter is for the sake of bodily purification—as in the case of approaching a woman during her courses or touching a corpse—other meals would not be excluded. (11.142)
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.

Regarding the phrase "of those grown in plowed land": for cultivated plants such as *ṣaṣṭika* rice and the like, and for wild-grown grains such as *nīvāra* and the like found in the forest, when they are cut down without purpose, one who subsists on milk should follow a cow for one day. 11.143.
By these vows, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear concerning the eating of forbidden food.

"By these": indeed, by means of these penances, the sin produced by violence shall be removed; now listen to how all the sin produced by eating—whether done intentionally or unintentionally—is likewise dispelled. 11.144.

Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite alone; but for intentional drinking, there is no instruction [for purification], as the established rule is that it ends only with life. (11.145)

"Through ignorance": because there is a gradation in the commission of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), this [penance] does not refer to the primary types of *surā* (distilled liquor), but rather to *gauḍī* (molasses-based) and *mādhvī* (honey-based) liquors. Therefore, having unintentionally drunk *gauḍī* or *mādhvī*, one undergoes shaving, the girdle, and the staff; and because of the prohibition of these ancillaries of initiation, one is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance—consisting of milk, clarified butter, water, or air, each heated, to be consumed daily for three days—as stated in the Smṛti of Gautama: "For drinking [liquor] unintentionally, he shall perform the *taptakṛcchra*; thereafter his consecration (*saṃskāra*) [is performed]. Thus, he is purified by means of the *taptakṛcchra*. Furthermore, even in the case of intentional drinking of *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* once, a penance ending in death (*prāṇāntika*) is not to be prescribed; such is the limit of the scriptures. This was stated previously—that [death] is not to be prescribed—in order to dispel the suspicion that the phrase "having drunk *surā*" might apply to all varieties of *surā*. (11.145)
If one drinks water contained in a vessel for *surā* liquor, or likewise situated in a vessel for intoxicants,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.

Regarding the term *apaḥ*: water contained in a vessel for *surā* or a vessel for intoxicants, provided it is devoid of the taste and smell of *surā* or intoxicants; or milk boiled with the addition of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* herb—which is indeed like clarified butter (*havis*) because of the word "boiled" (*śṛta*)—one should drink this milk, not water, for five nights after having consumed [forbidden substances]. Since different penances are observed for the direct consumption of *surā* and intoxicants, one should avoid equating the objects here as well by failing to distinguish between intentional and unintentional acts. 11.146.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rules,
or having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.

Regarding the word "having touched": having touched or given liquor (surā), and having accepted it after performing the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*) and other preliminary rites, as well as having drunk all waters left over by a Śūdra—because of the inclusion of the term "having accepted"—a Brāhmaṇa shall drink water boiled with *darbha* grass for three days. (11.147)
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor, becomes pure by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter. (11.148)

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa who has performed the Soma sacrifice, having smelled the fragrant breath from the mouth of one who has drunk *surā* liquor, becomes purified by performing three *prāṇāyāmas* in the midst of water and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). 11.148.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite once again. (11.149)

"Through ignorance": since pigs and other such animals will be mentioned later, this refers to unintentionally eating the urine or feces of a human being, or consuming something touched by *surā* (liquor) when its taste is not perceived. For the three twice-born castes, they deserve the rite of re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) along with the *taptakṛcchra* penance, according to the traditional law of Gautama: "And likewise for the consumption of urine, feces, a corpse, or semen. Furthermore, regarding consumption, it has been stated: "One should perform a *kṛcchra* for [eating] semen, feces, and urine even for a Brāhmaṇa"; that too should be understood as being devoid of the *Gautamīya* sacramental rite. Moreover, due to this scriptural statement, the penance for intentional and unintentional consumption is indeed unequal. (11.149)
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.

Regarding "shaving": for the twice-born at their initiation, the shaving of the head, the girdle, the staff, wandering for alms, the observances, the fire-ritual, and the avoidance of honey, meat, and so forth, do not take place when performed for the purpose of penance. (11.150)
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women and Śūdras, or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights. (11.151)

Regarding the phrase "of those whose food is not to be eaten": having eaten the food of those declared unfit to be fed—such as those at whom a sacrifice has not been offered by a *śrotriya* (as mentioned in the preceding verses)—and having also consumed the leavings of women of the twice-born castes (since these are included by the very mention of the *śūdra*), and having eaten meat that is forbidden—such as that of carnivorous animals, pigs, and camels, for which no optional penance has been prescribed—one should drink barley in the form of groats or gruel for seven nights. (11.151)
Even after drinking fermented acids and astringent decoctions, though they are purifying, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that [substance] has not passed downward. (11.152)

Regarding "sour liquids" (*śuktāni*): those substances which have acquired their own natural acidity, or which become sour through contact with other substances intended for fermentation or through the process of aging, are called *śukta*. These include astringent decoctions such as *harītakī* and the like. Even though these are not explicitly forbidden, a twice-born man becomes impure by drinking them until that food and drink has been digested. (11.152)
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Regarding the phrase "of village pigs, donkeys, and camels": having consumed the urine or excrement of village pigs, donkeys, camels, jackals, monkeys, or crows, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (11.153)
Having eaten dried meats, terrestrial fungi, or anything from a slaughterhouse that was unknown, one should observe this very same vow. (11.154)

"Regarding 'dry' (meats)": having eaten dried meats such as *vallūra* and the like, which have been desiccated by wind, the sun, and so forth; and having consumed mushrooms growing from the earth; and having unintentionally eaten meat from a slaughterhouse, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (11.154)
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks,
as well as that of hell-beings, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.

Regarding the phrase "of carnivorous animals, pigs, and camels": for eating the raw flesh of those who eat raw meat, such as vultures and others, as well as village pigs, camels, domestic cocks, humans, crows, and donkeys, the purification is the *taptakṛcchra* penance which will be described hereafter. (11.155)
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher’s house should eat food belonging to a monthly Śrāddha, he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day. (11.156)

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the monthly [śrāddha]": one who has been invited may eat at will; thus, having received permission to eat at the *amāvāsyā* śrāddha, if a Brāhmaṇa who is a student (*brahmacārī*) should eat at a *ekoddiṣṭa* performed for the sake of the monthly rite before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, he shall fast for three nights and dwell for three days thereafter in the midst of fire and water. (11.156)
But he who, while observing a vow, should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever, shall perform the ordinary Kṛcchra penance and then complete the remainder of his vow. (11.157)

Regarding the phrase "one who observes a vow": if a student (brahmacārī) should eat honey or meat either unintentionally or in times of distress, he must perform the Prājāpatya penance; thereafter, he should complete whatever remains of his interrupted vow of studentship. (11.157)
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a mouse, or those of a dog or a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink the Brahmasuvarcalā plant.

"Regarding the phrase 'the leavings of cats, crows, and mice': having eaten food that has been defiled by contact with the hair or insects of cats, crows, mice, dogs, or mongooses, or food that is impure because it was not prepared for sacrifice, one should boil *brahmasuvarcalā* and drink its juice from the remainder for one day as a means of purification. (11.158)
One who desires self-purification must not eat food that is unfit to be eaten;
however, if it has been consumed through ignorance, one should either fast for a day or quickly purify oneself by means of purificatory rites. (11.159)

"Regarding 'not to be eaten': one who desires his own purity must not forcibly consume food that is forbidden. If it has been consumed through negligence, it must be vomited; if that is impossible, he must quickly purify himself through penances. However, even when vomiting or casting it out occurs, there is a light penance. (11.159)
Thus has been declared the various rule for the vows regarding the abstention from eating;
now hear the rule for those vows which remove the fault of theft.

"Regarding this": those penances which are prescribed for eating what is forbidden to eat have been declared here in their various forms. Now, let the prescription of the penances that remove the sin of theft be heard. 11.160.

Having committed thefts of grain, food, or wealth out of desire from the very house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year. (11.161)

"Regarding the theft of grain, food, and wealth": if a Brāhmaṇa, out of desire—and not under the delusion that it belongs to him—takes from the house of a Brāhmaṇa items in the form of grain, items such as cooked food, or thefts of wealth, he becomes purified by performing the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance for one year. This penance is to be determined according to the considerations of time, place, the transformation [of the object], the substance, the location, and the quality or poverty [of the victim]; thus it should be understood that this same principle applies to subsequent cases involving houses and so forth. (11.161)
But for the abduction of women, as well as for the seizure of fields, houses, and the waters of wells or tanks, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the purification. (11.162)
Regarding "of men":

having committed the theft of articles of small value in another's house, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that [stolen property]. (11.163)

Regarding the phrase "of substances": having committed theft from another's house of substances that are of low value, of little utility, such as tin, lead, and the like, for which no specific penance has been mentioned, one should—after returning that stolen substance to its owner—perform the *sāntapana* *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of self-purification as will be described hereafter; the word "having returned" (*niryātya*) is the understood supplement. (11.163)
For the theft of edible foods, whether chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats,
and for the theft of flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.

Regarding "the theft of foodstuffs to be chewed or eaten": for the theft of *bhakṣya* (food to be chewed, such as sweetmeats), *yāna* (vehicles, such as carts), *śayyā* (beds, such as couches), *āsana* (seats, such as stools), flowers, or roots, the purification is the *pañcagavya* consisting of cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter. (11.164)
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.
Regarding "of grass, wood, and trees": the theft of grass, wood, trees, molasses, cloth, leather, meat, and dried food such as rice and the like, shall require a fast for three nights. (11.165)
For gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron,
bronze, and stones, one should subsist on grains for twelve days.

Regarding "of gems, pearls, and corals": for the theft of gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, bronze, and stones, one must subsist on rice and fruit for twelve days. In all these cases, one must avoid any inequality in the application of the penance by taking into account whether the act was a single instance or repeated, the time and place, the nature of the substance, and the poverty or status of the owner; this applies specifically to the theft of superior materials. 11.166.
For cotton, silk-worms, and worn-out items; for animals with cloven hooves and those with uncloven hooves; and for birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope—one must drink milk for three days.

Regarding the phrase "of cotton, silk, wool, [the products] of two-hoofed animals such as horses and the like, of birds such as parrots and the like, of fragrant substances such as agallochum and so forth, of medicinal herbs such as *guḍūcī* and the like, and of ropes made of *muñja* grass and the like": in the case of stealing these, one should subsist on milk for three days. (11.167)
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
but he shall cast off the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these same vows.

"By these": by means of these aforementioned expiations, a twice-born man shall remove the sin produced by theft; however, he shall eliminate the sin caused by approaching those with whom one should not have intercourse by means of the expiations that will be described hereafter. 11.168.

Having emitted semen into women of his own kin, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, he shall perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed. (11.169)

Regarding the phrase "the vow for violating the Guru’s bed": having approached sisters born of the same womb, the wives of friends, daughters-in-law, young maidens, and Cāṇḍālas or other outcaste women, one should perform the penance prescribed for approaching the Guru’s wife. In each of these cases, the specific penance for violating the Guru’s bed should be understood according to the degree of repetition and other factors. The mention here is not redundant with the rule "emission of semen among one's own female kin" (11.170), as it serves the purpose of providing a specific remedy for that case. 11.169.
Having approached the daughter of his father’s sister, the daughter of his mother’s sister, or the daughter of his own maternal uncle, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (11.170)

Regarding the term "pitṛṣvasreyī": having approached the daughter of one's father’s sister or mother’s sister—that is, the daughter of one's own maternal uncle—one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (11.170)
A wise man should not take these three as wives;
for knowing them to be such, he who approaches them falls downward. 11.171

"Regarding the word 'these': these three, beginning with the father's sister, should not be married by the wise for the sake of a wife. Because they are kinswomen (*jñāti*), they must not be wed; for by approaching them, a man goes to hell. Since the prohibition is already established by the rule, 'But she who is not a *sapinda* of the mother,' this repetition is for the sake of reinforcement, based on the observation of the customs of the Southerners. (11.171)

Having discharged semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper site for conception, or indeed into water, one shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. (11.172)

Regarding the phrase "among non-human females and those lacking sexual organs": among non-human females such as mares and the like—but not in a cow, according to the view of Gautama—and in a cow, because a penance as heavy as that for violating a teacher's bed is prescribed; or among those "lacking sexual organs," meaning hermaphrodites who possess neither female nor male characteristics, and likewise with a menstruating woman, and when the emission of semen occurs outside the vagina or in water, one shall perform the *Sāntapana* penance. (11.172)
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman, a twice-born man shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a bullock-cart, in water, or during the daytime. (11.173)

Regarding "sexual intercourse": having engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman by means of the thighs, the middle of the body, the armpits, or other parts of a man, whether in a vehicle yoked with oxen such as a cart, in a water-vehicle such as a boat, or during the daytime, one shall perform a bath with one's clothes on. (11.173)

By approaching women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, by eating their food, or by accepting gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them]. (11.174)

Regarding the phrase "of a Cāṇḍāla": having approached a Cāṇḍāla or a Mleccha woman, or having eaten [their food] unknowingly, or having accepted gifts from them knowingly—if this is done habitually, one falls [from caste]. Consequently, the penance for a fallen person applies to him; furthermore, by doing this repeatedly, he attains equality with them. Therefore, there is no other penance for him [beyond that]. (11.174)
A husband should confine a corrupt wife in a single room;
he should compel her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man who has committed adultery with another's wife. (11.175)

"Regarding the term *vipraduṣṭām* (corrupted): having confined a corrupted woman, he should keep her until she has performed penance. And whatever penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) is prescribed for a man who has approached the wife of another of his own caste, that very same penance he should cause her to perform. (11.175)
If, however, she should become corrupted after being solicited by one of equal status,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification.

She [is called] *seti*. If that woman, having once committed an offense by approaching a man of her own caste and having performed the penance therefor, should again engage in intercourse with that same man of her own caste when solicited by him, then both the *prājāpatya* and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances shall apply for her purification. (11.176)
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night, he removes that by eating only permitted food and constantly reciting prayers for three years. (11.177)

Regarding the word "yat" (which): because of the hearing of scriptural passages expressing intense condemnation, such as "A Brāhmaṇa who has taken a Śūdra woman to his bed goes to a low state" and "One who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste] according to Atri," [this penance applies] to the service of a Śūdra woman married out of order. Whatever sin one acquires in a single night, that he removes in three years by subsisting on alms and constantly performing recitation (*japa*). As for the claim that the term *vṛṣalī* here refers to a Caṇḍālī, that is incorrect due to its lack of established usage; and thus Āpastamba, having begun with "Bearing [the burden of] a non-Aryan woman's bed," says: "Whatever sin a Brāhmaṇa incurs in a single night by serving a dark-complexioned [woman], he destroys that sin in three years by eating only at every fourth mealtime and subsisting on water. (11.177)
This is the expiation even for the four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who have associated with the fallen. || 11.178 ||

"This" refers to the following: this purification has been declared for the four types of great sinners—those who commit violence, those who eat forbidden food, thieves, and those who approach women who should not be approached—as well as for others. Now, listen to these purifications that will be described for those who associate with outcasts (patitas). 11.178.
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food. (11.179)

"By a year": one who officiates at a sacrifice for a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), or one who is officiated by such a person; one who teaches the Veda to him, or is taught by him; one who gives a daughter to him in marriage, or marries a girl given by him—such a person falls [from his caste] within a year. This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama that "falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation," meaning he is excluded from the entitlement to rites intended for transcendental results or for the fulfillment of desires. However, if one performs the acts of traveling, eating, or residing together with an outcaste, one falls after a year; yet even beyond that, these acts are lighter offenses. (11.179)
Whatever person among these who has fallen, a man who enters into association with him must perform that very same vow for the sake of purification from that association. (11.180)

"Whoever"—meaning that man who engages in "association," as previously described in the preceding verse, with these four types of outcasts beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin, such as teaching them and so forth—he shall perform the penance prescribed for that [original sinner], namely "the slayer of a Brahmin [shall undergo penance] for twelve years," and so on; he must perform this very penance arising from the sin produced by contact. (11.181)

The sapinda relatives and kinsmen shall perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day, in the evening, in the presence of his agnates, officiating priests, and teachers. (11.181)

Regarding the phrase "water for one who has fallen": for a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*) while still alive, that very same water-rite (*udakakriyā*) must be performed by the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* having assembled in the presence of kinsmen, officiating priests, and teachers, on an empty day such as the ninth lunar day and so forth, at the end of the day, according to the procedure to be described. (11.181)
A female slave should overturn a water-pot full of water with her foot as if for a dead person;
[the relatives] should observe impurity together with their kinsmen for a day and a night.

"A female slave"—according to the traditional teaching of Gautama, "A female slave employed by a sapinda or a samānodaka [relative] shall say, 'I make this jar full of water waterless,' while naming the deceased; having spoken thus, she should kick it with her foot toward the south, as one does for a dead person. Thereafter, those sapindas, together with the samānodakas, should observe the period of ritual impurity (śauca). 11.182.
From that point on, however, there shall be a cessation of conversation and shared seating, as well as the giving of inheritance and even ordinary social intercourse. (11.183)

"They shall turn back. This means that the inheritance and even ordinary worldly hospitality should not be given to him; one must not engage in conversation or cohabitation with that outcast; no wealth should be given to him; nor should he be invited to festivals and the like—no worldly social interaction whatsoever should be performed with him. (11.183)
Seniority shall cease, as shall that wealth acquired by the eldest;
even a younger brother who is superior in virtue shall receive the portion of the eldest. (11.184)

Regarding the term "eldest-hood": the duties of an eldest son, such as rising to greet him and so forth, are no longer his duty; nor should the preferential share (*uddhāra*) obtainable by an eldest son be given to him. This fact, already established previously, is restated here for the purpose of granting [the rights] to the younger brother. And his younger brother, being the most eminent in the group, receives that portion of the preferential share belonging to the eldest. (11.184)
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe in a sacred body of water and cast a new pitcher full of water into it along with that very person.

Regarding the term *prāyaścitta*: when the penance has been performed by the outcaste, his sapinda and samānodaka relatives should bathe together with him in a new water-vessel filled with water that has been purified by that very same penance, and then they should pour [the water] over him. Here, because of the mention of "new," it is understood from the phrase "the slave-girl's jar" (*dāsīghaṭa*) that the jar previously used is intended. (11.185)
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home, he should perform all the duties of his kin as before. || 11.186 ||

"He" refers to him who has performed the penance; having thrown that aforementioned jar into the midst of water, he should then enter his own home and perform all the duties toward his kinsmen as before. || 11.186 ||
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be given clothing, food, and drink, and they should live near the house. 11.187.

"This is the very same vow. Yājñavalkya has stated a specific distinction regarding women: "Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming the husband—these also certainly constitute grounds for the loss of caste specifically for women. Thus, when women have become outcasts (*patita*), one might ask what should be done regarding the water-libation (*udaka*) and other rites mentioned [in the previous verse]; however, one should provide them with food, clothing, and drink, as well as a dilapidated house or similar dwelling near their home for the sake of their residence. (11.187)
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins until they have been purified; yet once they have undergone purification, one should never despise them. (11.188)

"With those who have committed sins" means that one should not perform acts such as giving gifts or receiving them in common with evildoers who have not performed penance; nor should one ever entertain any association with those who have performed penance. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman, even if they are pure according to the Dharma.

"Killers of children": one who has killed a child, one who has destroyed a favor by failing to act upon it, one who has killed someone who came seeking protection, and one who has killed a woman—one should avoid living together with these, even if they have attained purification through penance and expiation. (11.189)
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.

Regarding the phrase "of those": for those Brāhmaṇas and others for whom the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has not been performed according to the scriptures even during the period of secondary eligibility, one should cause them to perform three *prājāpatya* penances and then initiate them according to the scriptures. (11.190)
This same penance one should prescribe even for those twice-born men who perform forbidden acts, for Brahmins who have abandoned their duties, and for those who desire to perform expiation. (11.191)

Regarding "expiation": this threefold *kṛcchra* penance should be prescribed even for those twice-born men who live by performing forbidden acts and wish to perform expiation, or for those who have not studied the Vedas. (11.191)
Whatever wealth Brahmins acquire through a censurable action, they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by silent recitation and austerity. (11.192)

Regarding the word "yat": by the renunciation of that wealth which Brāhmaṇas acquire through censurable austerity, such as actions like accepting improper gifts, and by means of the recitation of prayers and austerities to be described hereafter, they are purified. (11.192)
Having recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

"Having recited," it is said: having diligently recited three thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī, while subsisting on milk, dwelling in a cow-pen, and remaining seated, one removes the sin produced by accepting improper gifts. (11.193)
But when he has returned from the cow-pasture having observed his fast, they should question him as he bows down: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (11.194)

"Regarding the phrase 'performed by fasting': when he has returned from the cow-pen with his body purified solely by a diet of milk and the cessation of other food, being humble, the Brahmins should inquire about his dharma, saying: 'O virtuous one, do you desire equality with us? Do you no longer engage in the acceptance of improper gifts? (11.194)
But having spoken the truth before the Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for the cows;
when the ford has been established by the cows, they should perform his formal reception there.

"Truly," he says. Having declared to the Brahmins, "I shall henceforth not accept gifts from the wicked," he should scatter fodder for the cows. Then, because that spot where the grass was eaten has been purified by the cows, the Brahmins—having descended into that very *tīrtha*—should grant their consent for his reintegration into social intercourse. (11.195)

Having performed sacrifices for Vrātyas, having performed funeral rites for others, and having practiced malevolent magic or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes the taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances. (11.196)

Regarding the term "of the Vrātyas": for those Vrātyas who have lost their eligibility for initiation (*upanayana*)—referring to those previously mentioned as "these three and so forth"—having performed the *Vrātyastoma* and other sacrifices, and having performed the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) for those other than their fathers or gurus; since it is stated that speech is the weapon of a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform [the rite] with non-malevolent acts such as the *Śyena* and others. Having performed a specific sacrifice such as the *Dvirātra*, which is devoid of birth and death, he becomes purified by three *Kṛcchra* penances. (11.196)
Having abandoned one who has come for refuge and having caused the Veda to be corrupted, a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.

Regarding the phrase "one who has come for refuge": if a twice-born man, being capable, does not abandon one who has come for refuge—whether he be sinless, seeking protection, or arrived to perform penance—and instead teaches him the Veda which ought not to be taught, or for the sake of wealth speaks a portion of the Veda while seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka-yoga*) at a place of examination, that twice-born man removes the sin produced by that act by subsisting on barley for one year. (11.197)
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals, as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma). 11.198.

"By dogs, jackals, and donkeys," etc.: one who has been bitten by dogs, jackals, donkeys, humans, horses, camels, pigs, or by village-dwelling animals such as cats that eat raw meat, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma). 11.198.

Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*, as well as constant *Śākala* oblations, are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals. (11.199)

Regarding the phrase "eating at the sixth meal-time" and "the Śālaka oblations": for those individuals mentioned in the passage beginning with "those unworthy of the company (apāṅktya)—thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and so forth"—for whom no specific expiation has been prescribed by name, the purification consists of this combined practice: eating only once on the evening of every third day for one month; reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā; and daily offering eight oblations of wood chips with Yajus formulas such as "Thou art the expiation of the sin committed against the gods. || 11.199 ||
Having mounted a camel vehicle or a donkey vehicle,
a Brahmin who has bathed while naked becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
"Camel-vehicle," [so it is said]. 11.200.
If one is distressed and finds neither water nor is within water, one should deposit the bodily excrement and, having bathed outside with one's clothes on and touched a cow, becomes pure. 11.201.

"Even without water, or even in water when distressed, having voided bodily excrement"—meaning that if one is in the midst of water or in a place where water is not available and is overcome by an urgent need, having discharged urine or feces, he becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on outside the village in a river or similar body of water, and by touching a cow.
In the case of the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda,
and upon the violation of the vows of a Snātaka, the expiation is fasting.

Regarding the phrase "of those declared in the Veda": for the omission of the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) prescribed by the Veda—such as the *agnihotra* sacrifices—for which no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is recorded in the Śruti, and for the failure to perform the *snātaka-vratas* (the vows of one who has completed his studies), such as "he should carry a bamboo staff" and so forth, fasting is the prescribed expiation. 11.202.
Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" or an elder with "tvaṃ," one should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and seek their favor by offering salutations.

Regarding the word *huṅkāra*: having spoken "hum" thus with anger to a Brāhmaṇa, and having likewise addressed one who is superior in wealth and so forth as "you," he should, while fasting for the remainder of that day until the completion of the act, perform a bath and appease him by clasping his feet once the anger has subsided. || 11.203 ||
Having struck him even with a blade of grass, or having bound him by the neck with a cloth, or having defeated him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by prostrating before him. (11.204)

"Having struck," and "even by means of a dispute": having struck even with a blade of grass out of anger a common Brahmin or one of higher status, or having bound him by the neck with a cloth during a quarrel, and having won the dispute, one should cause his anger to subside by prostrating oneself. (11.204)
But by threatening a Brahmin for a hundred years, or by striking him for a thousand, one falls into hell through the intent to kill. (11.205)

Regarding the phrase "having threatened": by raising a staff or similar weapon with the intent to kill a Brāhmaṇa, one falls into hell for a hundred years; by striking him again with that staff or similar weapon, one falls for a thousand years. || 11.206 ||
For as many particles of dust as the blood collects upon the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of years shall the perpetrator go to hell.

"However many particles of dust the blood of the twice-born man collects," means that when a Brāhmaṇa has been struck, for as many thousands of years as there are grains of dust on the ground that the blood coagulates into, the one who caused that blood to flow shall remain in hell. (11.206)
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him, the Atikṛcchra;
and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra.

"Having threatened," etc.: having raised a staff or similar weapon against a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance; having struck him with a staff or the like, one should perform the *atikṛcchra*, which will be described later; and having caused blood to flow, one should perform both the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra*. (11.207)
But for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been stated, one should prescribe an atonement after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin. (11.208)

"Regarding those for which no expiation has been stated": for the removal of those sins for which no penance has been prescribed—such as the killing of those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) and the like—one should determine the appropriate expiation to be described hereafter, having regard for the capacity of the perpetrator in terms of body, wealth, and so forth, and having also considered the nature of the sin in terms of whether it was committed intentionally or unintentionally, once or repeatedly, and its attendant circumstances. || 11.208 ||
I shall describe to you those means by which a human being removes his sins—means practiced by the gods, sages, and ancestors. (11.209)
Regarding the phrase "by which": those means by which a person dispels sins—those means practiced by the gods, sages, and ancestors for the sake of removing sin—I shall declare to you. 11.209.
For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should eat food given unasked;
for the final three days he should not eat at all—this is the *prājāpatya* penance performed by a twice-born man.

Regarding the phrase "for three days": a twice-born man performing the *kṛcchra* penance known as *prājāpatya* should eat at the beginning of the day for the first three days; on the next three days he should eat at the end of the day; on another three days he should eat what comes unasked; and for the final three days he should not consume anything at all. In this regard, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama—"In the morning he should eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*)"—he must consume sacrificial food. As for the number of mouthfuls: "Twelve mouthfuls are prescribed for the evening, fifteen for the morning;
thirty-six are to be eaten when food is unasked; beyond that, fasting is prescribed."
This is to be understood according to the statement of Parāśara. 11.210.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, followed by a fast for one night—this is known as the *sāntapana* penance. (11.211)

Regarding "cow urine": one should consume cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *darbha* grass, one at a time each day, along with a fast. In this manner, over seven days, one should drink all these on a single day and observe a fast on another; thus for three days. Because both views are seen, Yājñavalkya has declared that this penance known as *sāntapana* is a *kṛcchra*. (11.211)
A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should eat a single morsel for three periods of three days as before, and should fast for the final three days. (11.212)

"One by one" means: "And he should fast for three days. A twice-born man performing the penance called *atikṛcchra* should eat one morsel each in the morning and evening for three periods of three days respectively in the manner of not begging; furthermore, for another three days, he should not eat anything at all. (11.212)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind. (11.213)
Regarding the *taptakṛcchra*: when a Brāhmaṇa or others perform the penance known as *taptakṛcchra*, they should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air for three days each.
Having drunk three *palas* of water, one should drink three *palas* of milk;
then, for three nights, one should consume one *pala* of ghee and inhale hot air.
Thus, performing the bath once with the quantities prescribed by Parāśara, one who is self-controlled should drink either warm air or warm water. 11.213.
For one who is self-controlled and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called Parāka, which removes all sins.

Regarding the phrase "self-restrained": for one whose desire for food has departed and whose senses are controlled, fasting for twelve days is the penance known as *parāka*. Depending on the degree of repetition and the nature of the sin—whether manifest or unmanifest, heavy or light—it removes all sins. (11.214)
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three periods of the day, this is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (11.215)

"One by one" means that he should perform his ablutions in the evening, the morning, and at midday. On the full moon day, he should eat fifteen morsels, according to the measure prescribed by Gautama: "The size of a morsel is such that it does not distort the cheeks" (GDh 27.10). Thereafter, during the dark fortnight, beginning from the first day, he should reduce the intake by one morsel each day until he eats only one morsel on the fourteenth day; having fasted on the new moon day, he should then increase the intake by one morsel each day during the bright fortnight, beginning from the first day, until there are fifteen on the full moon day. This is the *cāndrāyaṇa* known as "ant-like" (*pipīlikā-madhya*). 11.215.

One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, being self-restrained from the beginning of the bright fortnight, should carry out this entire procedure in its entirety during the "barley-shaped" (yavamadhya) variety. || 11.216 ||

"Practicing this entire rule" means that, having undertaken the vow, one should perform this very rite of increasing the mouthfuls of food and bathing three times a day during the *yavamadhya* (barley-shaped middle) *cāndrāyaṇa*, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight. On the first day (*pratipad*) one should eat one mouthful, on the second two, and so on until fifteen are eaten on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). Thereafter, starting again from the first day of the dark fortnight, one should decrease the mouthfuls by one each day until there is only one on the fourteenth; finally, there is a fast on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).
Restraining his self and eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), one performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa should eat eight morsels when the sun has reached the meridian. (11.217)

"Eight," it says; "with self-restraint, he should eat sacrificial food. Performing the lunar penance known as the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*, one who is free from the scent of ordinary food should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food—such as boiled rice—at the time of midday. (11.217)
A Brahmin, composed in mind, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set; this is remembered as the Śuddhacāndrāyaṇa.

Regarding the word "four": one who performs the *cāndrāyaṇa* known as the *śuśucāndrāyaṇa*, such as a Brāhmaṇa or others, being self-restrained, should eat four mouthfuls at the beginning of the day and four more when the sun has set. || 11.218 ||
By eating, with a concentrated mind, eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in some manner or other for one month, one attains the same world as the Moon. || 11.219 ||

"In whatever manner" means that by consuming two hundred and forty mouthfuls of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*)—such as *nīvāra* rice and other grains associated with sacrificial offerings—in an unrestricted way, sometimes one, sometimes five, sometimes sixteen, or sometimes fasting entirely, and so forth; by eating in such a manner for a month, one who possesses self-restraint attains the world of the Moon (*candraloka*). For this reason, this practice should be performed even for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). || 11.219 ||
The Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts, together with the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.

"Regarding this": Rudra, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Maruts, and the Ṛṣis performed this vow called Cāndrāyaṇa for the removal of all sins—whether manifest or unmanifest, grave or light—in accordance with the degree of repetition based on the gravity of the sin.
One should personally perform the fire-oblation every day with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
one should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness. (11.221)

"With the great utterances" (mahāvyāhṛtibhiḥ) means with these: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. According to the author of the Sūtra’s statement, "When no specific oblation is prescribed, clarified butter (*ājya*) is used," he should himself perform the daily burnt offering (*homa*) with clarified butter. Although non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and freedom from crookedness have been taught as goals for human life, he should practice them as constituent parts of his vow (*vrata*). 11.221.
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
nor should he ever speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.

"Three times during the day and three times at night"—this means that at the beginning, middle, and end of both the day and the night, he should enter a river or other body of water with his clothes on for the purpose of bathing; and this excludes the *pipīlikā-madhya-cāndrāyaṇa* penance, because it is stated therein that one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśan*) at the three sessions (*triṣavaṇa*). Furthermore, he should never engage in conversation with women, Śūdras, or outcasts (*patita*) as long as the vow lasts. (11.222)
He should pass his time standing or sitting; if unable, he may lie down on the ground.
He should be a celibate observer of vows, worshipping his guru, the gods, and the twice-born. || 11.223 ||

Regarding the phrase "by means of standing and sitting": based on the traditional teaching of Gautama, "He should stand during the day and remain seated at night," he should conduct himself by standing during the day and sitting at night; or, due to incapacity, he may sleep upon the bare ground. Free from sexual intercourse with women and observing his vows, and because of the observation of Śaṅkha that one should possess a girdle, staff, and water-pot, and perform the fire-ritual, he should be equipped with a girdle and other such items, and be a worshiper of his guru, the gods, and Brahmins. (11.223)
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to his ability;
in all such vows, he should thus be diligent for the sake of expiation. (11.224)

Regarding the *sāvitrī*: one should recite the *sāvitrī* at all times, even at night, and one should recite purificatory prayers (*pavitra*) according to one's ability. Likewise, in all penances such as the *kṛcchra*, one who is diligent should perform all acts, such as the fire-oblation (*homa*), with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* for the sake of expiation. In the cases of the *taptakṛcchra* penances, the rule of bathing at the six periods of the day (*ṣaṭsavana*) does not apply by extension (*atideśa*), because it would contradict the direct injunction (*aupadeśika*) that "one should bathe once. (11.224)
The twice-born whose sins have been made public should be purified by these vows;
however, those whose sins have not been made public, one should purify with mantras and burnt offerings. 11.225.

"By these": by means of these aforementioned penances for sins, twice-born men whose sins are known to the world are to be purified by the assembly (parṣad) to be described hereafter. However, in the case of secret killing, the assembly should purify those who have committed it—so as to avoid the destruction of its secrecy—by means of recitations and burnt offerings (japa-homa) to be described later, under the pretext of being disciples and so forth. 11.225.
