By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study, as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil. (11.226)

"By confession": when one's actions are known to two or three people, one confesses one's sin to others who are unaware of the transgression; this confession serves as a manifest auxiliary [to purification], not a secret one, for if it were secret, its status as such would be lost, leading to the painful thought, "Alas, what have I done? Furthermore, by remorse that likewise serves as a manifest auxiliary, by austerity (*tapas*) of the aforementioned kind such as the *kṛcchra* penance, by recitation (*japa*) which is primarily a manifest auxiliary, and by the efficacy of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the sinner is released from sin through giving (*dāna*). || 11.226 ||
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act,
confesses it, to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin.

"Yathā yathā" means: when a person, having committed a sin, confesses that very sin by himself, saying "I have done this evil deed," and censures it—then, because the *kṣetrajña* residing in the body is the locus of both merit and demerit, he is liberated from that sin like a snake from its worn-out skin; this is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of confession. (11.227)
To the extent that his mind reproaches the evil deed,
to that same extent his body is released from that unrighteousness.
"In whatever manner [he acts], in that very manner he is released from that body by means of that unrighteousness. (11.228)
For having committed a sin and felt remorse, one is indeed released from that sin;
however, by desisting with the thought, "I shall not do this again," one is purified. (11.229)

"Having committed a sin": it has been stated that if remorse arises in one who has committed a sinful act, then he is liberated from that sin. Furthermore, that sinner is purified by the resolve to desist from committing sin again, thinking, "I shall not commit sin once more. This [verse] is intended for the prescription of the rules regarding the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of penance (*prāyaścitta*), both public and private, once [the sin] has ceased. 11.229.
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death, he should constantly perform virtuous deeds through his thoughts, speech, and physical form. (11.230)

Thus it is said. Having thus reflected with the mind upon the arising of desired fruits in the next world from wholesome and unwholesome actions, one should perform only wholesome action through mind, speech, and body. Because [the fruit] is desired, one should not perform the unwholesome; for [unwholesome acts] produce unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) for those who have not performed atonement, and even the performance of atonement is of the nature of suffering. (11.230)
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a censurable deed, one who seeks liberation from it should not perform a second such act. (11.231)

"Out of ignorance": having performed a censurable act either through negligence or intentionally, one who seeks liberation from that sin should not commit further evil deeds. This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) intended for desisting [from such acts]. 11.231.
If, after performing a certain action, there should be a lack of lightness in his mind, he should perform penance for that until it brings about satisfaction. (11.232)

Regarding the phrase "in whatever action one has acted wrongly": even when a proscribed penance has been performed for a particular misdeed, if the mind should still feel hesitant or doubtful, one should perform that very same penance again, or another suitable one, until the mind reaches a state of supreme clarity. (11.232)
All happiness, whether divine or human, has austerity as its root;
it is declared by the wise, who perceive the Vedas, that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.

"Asceticism is the root": this means that whatever happiness belongs to all gods and humans, asceticism is its cause in the beginning, middle, and end; thus, this description of the majesty of asceticism is for the purpose of praising penance as an expiation. (11.233)
For a Brāhmaṇa, austerity is knowledge; for a Kṣatriya, austerity is protection;
for a Vaiśya, austerity is agriculture and trade; and for a Śūdra, austerity is service. (11.234)

"Of the Brāhmaṇa," etc. For a Brāhmaṇa, the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas is austerity (*tapas*); for a Kṣatriya, the protection of subjects according to dharma is austerity; for a Vaiśya, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are austerity; and for a Śūdra, service to Brāhmaṇas is austerity. Although these have been mentioned previously, they are stated here again for the purpose of being constituent parts of the penance (*prāyaścitta*). (11.234)
Sages who have subdued their selves and subsist on fruits, roots, and air perceive the three worlds, with all that is moving and unmoving, through asceticism alone.

Regarding the word "ṛṣis": Ṛṣis are those endowed with speech, mind, and body, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air; by means of austerity alone, while remaining in a single location, they behold with excellence the three worlds in their entirety—consisting of the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven, along with all that is moving and stationary. This is a statement regarding the greatness of austerity. These two subsequent verses should also be understood as being for the purpose of praising penance as a means of expiation (prāyaścitta). 11.235.
Medicines, antidotes, sciences, and the various states of divine power—
all these are accomplished through austerity alone, for austerity is indeed their means of attainment.

Regarding "medicines": medicines are substances that alleviate disease, antidotes, and substances that remove poison; and according to the Śruti, the knowledge of Brahman—which consists of the inquiry into the Self through austerity (tapas)—as well as various forms of existence associated with the gods situated in heaven and other realms, all these are attained through austerity alone. Therefore, austerity is the cause for their attainment. 11.236.

Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—all that can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed insurmountable. (11.237)

Regarding the word "that" (*yat*): that which is crossed over with difficulty, such as the misfortunes of planetary afflictions or calamities; that which is attained with difficulty by means of that very body, such as the status of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth; that which is reached with difficulty, such as the summit of Mount Meru and so forth; and that which is accomplished with difficulty, such as drinking the ocean and so forth—all this can be achieved through austerity (*tapas*), because in the performance of exceedingly difficult tasks, austerity possesses unimpeded power.
Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed forbidden acts, are liberated from that evil through well-performed austerity. (11.238)

Regarding the term "those who have committed great sins" (*mahāpātakinaḥ*): those who have committed such acts as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as others who have committed minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and so forth, are liberated from that sin by means of penance (*tapas*) performed properly in the manner described. This statement, although already mentioned [previously], is intended as a praise for the penance that serves as expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even stationary beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.

"Kīṭāḥ" (insects). Insects, snakes, locusts, animals, birds, and stationary beings such as trees and shrubs go to heaven by the greatness of austerity (*tapas*), as shown in the Itihāsas in the story of the insect (*kīṭopākhyāna*) and others. By this statement regarding the greatness of austerity, the subsequent verses are to be understood as a praise of penance (*prāyaścitta-tapas*). || 11.239 ||
Whatever sin people commit through thought, word, or deed, those whose wealth is austerity quickly consume it all by means of austerity alone. (11.240)

"Whatever" means: whatever slight sin of men—whether mental, vocal, or physical—occurs which would otherwise persist without expiation, if it somehow arises for those engaged in uninterrupted austerity, then all of that is quickly destroyed by that very austerity performed as a constant practice, even without formal expiation. || 11.240 ||
For a Brahmin purified by austerity alone, the denizens of heaven accept his offerings and fulfill his desires. (11.241)

Regarding the word "tapasā" (by austerity): it is only for a Brāhmaṇa whose impurities have been destroyed by the austerity of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) that the gods accept sacrifices such as the *puroḍāśa* and nourish their desired objects. (11.241)
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity. (11.242)

Regarding the term "Prajāpati": even Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of the origin and maintenance of all beings, composed this treatise only after performing ascetic penance (tapas). Likewise, the sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others attained mastery over the granting of mantras through penance alone. 11.242.
That which the gods proclaim as the great majesty of austerity—beholding the holy origin of all this from austerity. (11.243)

"Thus, 'the gods [arise] from austerity'—seeing that whatever auspicious birth there is in this entire world comes from the presence of austerity, the gods proclaim this greatness of austerity, beginning with 'this whole world has austerity as its root. This is the complete praise of austerity. (11.243)
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability and the performance of the great sacrifices destroy sins quickly, even those born of the most heinous crimes. (11.244)

"Recitation of the Vedas": daily study of the Veda according to one's ability, the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and the *aparādhamarṣaṇa* [mantra]—these quickly destroy even those sins arising from mortal transgressions (*pātaka*), let alone others. This is stated for the purpose of making known that the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) is a cause for the destruction of subtle, unperceived sins. (11.244)
Just as fire consumes whatever fuel it encounters in an instant by its heat,
so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge.

"Just as fire consumes fuel that has reached it with its brilliance. Just as fire, having reached pieces of wood, burns them away completely with its brilliance in an instant, so too does the knower of the meaning of the Vedas burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge. This is stated for the purpose of making known that the knowledge of the Self is the cause for the destruction of evil. 11.245.
Thus has the expiation for these offenses been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret sins.
Now he states the secret penances with the words "iti" (thus). 11.246.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), performed daily with the Vyahritis and the Praṇava for a month, purify even the slayer of an embryo. (11.247)

"Accompanied by the vyāhṛtis" means: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*, *mahar*, *janas*, *tapaḥ*, and *satyam*—these are the sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*) consisting of all the vyāhṛtis together with the syllable *oṃ*.
"With the vyāhṛtis, with the *praṇava*, and with the head [of the Gāyatrī], one should recite the Gāyatrī three times while holding the breath; that is called *prāṇāyāma*."

Thus, when performed daily for a month according to the procedure of *kumbhaka*, *pūraka*, and *recaka* as defined by Vasiṣṭha, these practices remove even the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), and by the use of the word "even" (*api*), they remove all other such transgressions as well. In this context, *kumbhaka* is the restraint of the entry and exit of the external and internal breaths from the chest; *pūraka* is the filling of the chest with external air; and *recaka* is the continuous expulsion of the air from the chest. The eligibility for secret penances (*rahasya-prāyaścitta*) belongs only to twice-born males, and not to Śūdras or women, because of the predominance of *japa* (recitation) and *homa* (fire-offering) among secret penances. Regarding secret penances:
He who teaches or even recites [the Veda] without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity,
or the application, becomes a sinner.

Because of this traditional teaching of Vyāsa, learning is not required for anything other than either the application of penance or the mere understanding of the true nature of reality regarding deities and so forth; for one who is authorized to perform rituals, there is no utility for knowledge pertaining to other rites beyond the performance and observation of the Vedic rituals. (11.247)
By muttering the Kautsa hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the Vāsiṣṭha verse beginning with "prati," the Māhitra hymn, and the Śuddhavatī verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified. (11.248)

"Having muttered the *Kautsa* [hymn] beginning with *apa naḥ śośucad agham*—that is, the *Māhendra* hymn seen by the seer Kutsa—and the *variṣṭha*-seen triplet beginning with *pratistomebhiḥ*, as well as the hymn beginning with *māhā indro ya ojasā* and these *Śuddhavatī* verses beginning with *eto nv indraṃ stavāma*: having muttered these every day for the prescribed month sixteen times, even a drinker of *surā* is purified; and because of the word "even" (*api*), one who is authorized as a teacher and the like is also purified. (11.248)
By reciting the Vāmīya hymn and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once,
one who has stolen gold becomes stainless in an instant.

Regarding the word "once": having stolen gold, a Brāhmaṇa becomes free from taint immediately after reciting once every day this established hymn, *asya vāmasya*, as well as the *śivasaṃkalpa* hymn, *yaj jāgrato dūram udaiti daivam*. || 11.249 ||
By practicing the Haviṣyāntīya hymn and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and by reciting the Puruṣa Sūkta, one who has violated the teacher's bed is liberated from sin.

Regarding the *haviṣyāntīya*: by reciting daily with repetition throughout the prescribed month these hymns—the *haviṣyāntam ajaraṃ na tamaṃ ho na duritam*, the *iti me manaḥ*, and the *sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*—one who has committed adultery with the wife of his teacher removes that sin. 11.250.
Desiring the removal of gross and subtle sins, one should mutter for a year either the verse beginning with "Having known" (avet) or that beginning with "Whatever this" (yat kiṃcedam). || 11.251 ||

Regarding the phrase "enasām" (of sins): one who desires to effect the removal of gross sins—that is, mortal transgressions (*mahāpātaka*)—should mutter for a year this *ṛc*, "ava te heḷo varuṇa namobhiḥ," and also this [verse], "yat kiṃ cedam varuṇa devyāi janaḥ.
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
Regarding the phrase "having accepted": having consumed forbidden gifts such as liquor and the like, a twice-born man becomes purified in three days by reciting the *taratsamandī* hymn. 11.252.
But one who has committed many sins becomes purified by reciting the *Somāraudra* hymn for a year;
likewise, by performing his bath in a flowing river while reciting the three-verse hymn beginning with "aryamṇām. (11.253)

Regarding the verse beginning with "To Soma and Rudra": by reciting daily for a month this hymn, "O Soma and Rudra, uphold the power of the Asuras," as well as the verse beginning with "Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Mitra," while bathing in a river, one who has committed a sin is purified.
One who has committed an offense should mutter the seven verses beginning with "Indra, lord of the waters" (abdārtham indram).
But having performed an act that is not praiseworthy, one should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of expiation": because it remains [to be addressed], one who has committed any one of all the sins should mutter this group of seven verses beginning with "Indra as a friend" for six months; and having performed sexual intercourse in the midst of water, he should subsist on alms for one month. (11.255)

Having offered clarified butter for a year with the mantras used for the Śakala-homa, a twice-born man destroys even the most grievous sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "Namaḥ. (11.255)

"By means of mantras": having performed an oblation of clarified butter for one year with the mantras prescribed for the offering of wood chips, beginning with "Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods," and having muttered for one year this verse, "Homage indeed to the fierce one," he removes even a mortal sin (mahāpātaka). 11.255.
One who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī hymns for a year and subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.

"Regarding the phrase 'one joined with a mortal sin' (mahāpātakasaṃyukta): one who has committed a mortal sin is purified by subsisting on alms for one year, by reciting the *Pāvamānī* verses beginning with *svādiṣṭhayā*, and by performing the cow-following penance (*govadhavrata*) as prescribed. (11.256)
Or, having purified himself with three *parāka* penances, one who is self-restrained recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest; he is released from all sins. (11.257)

Regarding the phrase "in the forest": having removed his sins by means of the three *parāka* penances, he who, possessing self-restraint, recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the wilderness destroys all transgressions, including even the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and secondary sins (*upapātaka*). || 11.257 ||
One who, being self-controlled, fasts for three days and approaches water three times a day,
is released from all sins after reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.

"Three days" means that, performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, while muttering three times during each bath in the midst of the water this hymn beginning with "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ cābhīddhāt," one should fast for three days with a concentrated mind; by doing so, one is released from all sins, including the great mortal transgressions (mahāpātaka). || 11.258 ||
Just as the horse-sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.

"Yathā" means: just as the Aśvamedha is the best of sacrifices, effecting the destruction of all sins, so too is the entire Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the destroyer of every blemish; this is the preceding explanatory praise (arthavāda). || 11.259 ||
Even if he were to kill these three worlds and eat [their inhabitants] here and there, a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever. (11.260)

"Having slain" means that even after killing every living being existing within the three worlds, and even eating from the hands of a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste, one incurs no sin whatsoever by practicing the *Ṛgveda*. This is a praise of the practice of the *Ṛgveda* for the sake of what follows. 11.260.
Having recited the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā three times with a concentrated mind, or the Yajus formulas, or the Sāmans together with their secret doctrines (rahasya), one is liberated from all sins. (11.261)

Regarding the phrase "the Ṛk-saṃhitā": by reciting three times with self-restraint either the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā or the Yajurveda-saṃhitā, or the Sāmavedic collection—the *Sāmārcika* consisting of the Sāmans studied in the Āraṇyakas—one destroys all sins. (11.261)
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does every evil deed sink away when one has mastered the threefold Veda.

"Yathā" (as): Just as a clod of earth, having fallen into a vast lake, meets its destruction, even so all evil deeds reach their end within the Veda through its three constituent parts consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas; this is the preceding explanatory praise (arthavāda). 11.262.
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the various Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.

In order to define the threefold nature of the Veda, he says: "The Ṛks and Yajus are to be recited first. One should understand that this threefold Veda consists of the primary Ṛks and Yajus found in the *saṃhitās*, as well as the Brāhmaṇas when studied, and the Sāmans in their many varieties such as the *ārcika* and *stomika*; he who knows the Veda in this threefold way is a knower of the Veda, and no other. (11.263)
That which is the primordial Brahman of three syllables, in which the triple Veda is established—
that other secret threefold Veda, he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the threefold nature (*trivṛttva*) of the Veda, he says "the first" (*ādyam*). That which is called *Oṃ*—consisting of the collection of the three syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*—is Brahman, because it denotes the Supreme Brahman. In that *Oṃ*, the threefold knowledge consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas is supported; for according to the Śruti: "Just as all leaves are held together by a stalk, so all speech is held together in the *Oṃ*. That secret form is the supreme threefold Veda. He who knows this—who understands this threefold [Veda]—is a knower of the Veda. (11.264)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter in this commentary on Manu, composed by Govindarāja, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Mādhava, which follows the intention of Manu and serves as the foundation for the conduct of the four castes.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
"O sinless one, you have fully declared this dharma of the four social orders (cāturvarṇya).
Now, tell us truly the supreme result that arises from actions. (12.1)

"Regarding the four castes": "O sinless one, this entire dharma of the four castes—Brahmins and the others—along with those born of intermediate origins, has been declared by you. Now, tell us in its ultimate sense about the attainment of the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions arising in future births," thus did the great sages speak to the seer Bhṛgu. (12.1)
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action. (12.2)
"He" refers to Bhṛgu, the descendant of Manu, who is preeminent in dharma; he said to those great seers, "Listen to the determination of the fruits of this entire bond of karma. (12.2)
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, yields auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
the destinies of men—superior, inferior, and middling—are born of action. (12.3)

Regarding "the fruit of the auspicious and the inauspicious": action (karman) consists of mental, vocal, and physical causes, characterized by volition, expression, and activity; it takes the form of what is prescribed or prohibited and has pleasure and pain as its fruit. Furthermore, with that action as their cause, there arise for human beings the attainment of future births—superior, middling, or inferior—in the forms of gods, humans, animals, and so forth. (12.3)

One should know that for this embodied being—who possesses these three types [of action], who has three bases, and who is endowed with ten characteristics—it is the mind that is the instigator. (12.4)

Regarding the word "of that" (tasya): one should know that the mind is the instigator of that action—which pertains to the body, which is of three kinds (superior, middling, and inferior), and which rests upon the mind, speech, and body—by means of this tenfold characteristic that will be described hereafter; for indeed, nothing can be done or spoken that has not been conceived by the mind. 12.4.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehood—this is the threefold mental action. (12.5)

Thus, in order to demonstrate that action possesses ten characteristics, he says "regarding the property of others. In what manner? The mental action that has an impure result is threefold: the thought, "How might I steal the wealth of another? the desire for the destruction of another, and the misconception that the results of actions taught in the scriptures do not exist. The opposite of this—the lack of longing for another's wealth, compassion, and the conviction that the results of actions taught in the scriptures do exist—constitutes the action with a pure result. This is because both pure and impure action have been introduced as the subject matter. (12.5)
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form, and incoherent prattle—these constitute the fourfold nature of speech. (12.6)

Regarding "harshness": verbal action that results in impure fruit is of four kinds—speaking what is unpleasant, speaking untruth, being offensive in every way, and speaking that which is external, untrue, and purposeless. The opposite of this—speaking what is pleasant, true, beneficial, and consistent with the study of the scriptures—is that which results in pure fruit. (12.6)
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the rules, and adultery with another's wife—this is remembered as the threefold bodily [evil]. (12.7)

"Of things not given" means that the taking of another's property, violence not sanctioned by the scriptures, and sexual intercourse with another's wife—these three types constitute bodily action with inauspicious results. Its opposite—giving, protection, and restraint of the senses—constitutes action with auspicious results. (12.7)
One experiences the mental [karma], whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the mind itself;
the action performed by speech through speech, and that which is bodily through the body alone. (12.8)

Regarding "mental": whatever wholesome or unwholesome action has been performed by means of the mind, its fruit—whether in the form of pleasure or pain—is experienced swiftly through the door of the mind by one who is born night after night, depending on other actions. Likewise, the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome vocal actions is experienced through the door of the body itself, such as by being free from illness or by suffering from it. (12.8)
Through the defects of action born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, he becomes a bird or a beast; and through those of the mind, he attains birth among the lowest castes.

Regarding the phrase "born of the body": by the passage beginning with "of dogs, pigs, donkeys, and camels," it will also be stated that bodily, vocal, and mental actions have the attainment of an internal state as their fruit. This [verse] says: "If he mostly practices dharma... This should be explained with the intention that there is a small amount of dharma due to the abundance of evil. By means of bodily misdeeds committed in abundance, a human being attains the state of an immobile being (*sthāvara*). By means of verbal acts committed in abundance, one attains the state of a bird or a wild beast. And by means of mental acts committed in abundance, one attains the state of a *caṇḍāla* and so forth. (12.9)

The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body—he in whom these are firmly established for the sake of spiritual growth is called a "triple-staffed one" (tridaṇḍin). 12.10.

Regarding the term "vāgdaṇḍa" (the restraint of speech): he whose [restraint] regarding the impure intentions and activities of speech, mind, and body is established in his intellect is called a *tridaṇḍin* (one who possesses the triple staff), and not merely by virtue of possessing the three physical staffs alone. 12.10.
Having laid aside this triple staff among all living beings and having thoroughly restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.
Regarding the "three staffs":
the staff of speech destroys discernment; the staff of mind [destroys] the supreme goal;
but the staff of action destroys the three worlds for one who fails to protect them.
One should observe silence as a punishment for verbal transgression, fasting as a punishment for physical actions,
and breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed as a punishment for mental transgression.

The yogi should carry the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) pertaining to the body, but not that made of bamboo; likewise, he should properly maintain the triple staff of speech, body, and mind according to the rules.

Thus, having restrained the mind—which has all beings as its object—regarding these impure things such as speech and so forth, and having likewise controlled desire and anger for the sake of subduing them, even a human being attains the acquisition of auspicious fruits; however, we do not see this occurring while the body itself is still performing actions. And since that [body] is perishable, who is it that attains perfection? To this he says: || 12.11 ||

Those who, having fashioned this self of his, designate it as the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field), while that which performs actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise. (12.12)

Regarding the word "ya" (who): the wise call him the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) who is the instigator of the actions of that which is known in the world as the self, namely the body; furthermore, he who performs this activity is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the learned, because the thing called the body consists of the elements such as earth and the rest. || 12.12 ||
There is another inner self, distinct [from the body], known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.

Regarding the term "designated as the *jīva*": distinct from the body and the *kṣetrajña*, there is another self within the body called the *jīva*, existing for the sake of the [individual] self. This *jīva* is innate to all *kṣetrajñas* until the attainment of liberation. And it is through them—the *kṣetrajñas*—acting as the cause by means of their respective yogas, that [the *jīva*] experiences pleasure and pain in every birth; and here, it is this *manas* that is indicated by the word *jīva*. This is known from the use of the instrumental case in the word "by which" (*yena*), and because in the subsequent verse it says, "both those minds and the *kṣetrajña* itself," referring to the Great One (*mahat*) through its direct function.
Intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), cognition of objects (arthavijñāna), and the first transformation—
these are proclaimed as synonymous terms for the Great Principle (mahat).
Thus, because the Great Self is synonymous [with these states]. 12.13.
Both of these—the Great One (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they remain pervading that which abides within high and low beings.

"Those two": these two, the mind (*manas*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), joined with the elements known as earth, water, fire, air, and ether, abide pervading the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) which is about to be described and which exists established among the superior and inferior [beings]. Or rather, since the Supreme Self is that which is to be pervaded by everything, it is said that "they abide pervading Him. And so Vyāsa says:
"There are these two persons in the world, the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*).
The perishable consists of all beings; the unchanging (*kūṭastha*) is called the imperishable."
But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self (Paramātman),
who, as the imperishable Lord, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
You are the imperishable, the knower of the field, and the unchanging; and you are [the cause] of her attainment of liberation through the cessation of agency and enjoyership.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.

"Numberless" means that from the body of that Supreme Self, like waves stirred by the wind from the ocean, infinite individual souls (kṣetrajña) emerge according to the manner described in the Vedānta; these [souls] always cause superior and inferior bodies to engage in actions. 12.15.
After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from the five elements alone, intended for their torment.

"From the five": for men who have committed evil deeds, another body—distinct from the [ordinary] womb-born and other types of bodies, produced for the purpose of torment, and solid—is said to arise in the next world from the very same five elemental portions, namely earth and the others, which are designated as "measures. (12.16)
Having experienced those torments with the body here in the world of Yama,
they dissolve part by part back into those very same elemental constituents.

"By that" means: by means of that body, those torments belonging to Yama are not experienced by the doer of evil deeds. Those elements, such as earth and the rest, which constitute the origin of that body, dissolve back into their respective elemental portions known as *tanmātras*. || 12.17 ||
Having experienced those faults born of attachment to sense-objects which result in unhappiness, he,
with his defilements removed, approaches those two who possess such great majesty.

"He" refers to that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Having experienced in the world of Yama the sufferings arising from the enjoyment of objects known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—which result in the emergence of unhappiness—he thereafter, his impurities destroyed, takes refuge in those two alone: the Great One and the Supreme Self, who possess great power. 12.18.
Vigilantly observing both his merit and his sin together, they behold that by which one,
when joined with them, attains happiness or misery both here and after death.

"Those two" refers to the Great Principle (mahat) and the Supreme Self (paramātman), who are themselves terrified; they reflect upon the merit and demerit of that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), joined with which the Knower of the Field experiences happiness and suffering in this world and the next. 12.19.
Insofar as he practices dharma and for the most part avoids adharma, though in small measure,
he enjoys happiness in heaven, enveloped by those very same elements.

Regarding the phrase "as he conducts himself": if that *kṣetrajña* predominantly practices dharma and only a small amount of adharma, then, composed of those very elements—earth and the rest—he experiences happiness in heaven in a body made of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*). || 12.20 ||
But if one generally practices unrighteousness and righteousness only slightly,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if, moreover, that *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) predominantly practices unrighteousness (*adharma*) and only a small amount of righteousness (*dharma*), then, abandoned by those elements (*bhūta*) that constitute the body in this life, he undergoes the tortures of Yama with a solid body, according to the principle stated in the passage beginning, "from the five subtle elements alone. By this, the following is meant: through the predominance of unrighteousness, one experiences the tortures of Yama; furthermore, when the fruit of righteousness is experienced in the next world due to the predominance of unrighteousness, one experiences the fruit of unrighteousness in this very world. 12.21.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from defilement,
returns once again to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.

"Regarding the word *yāmīḥ*: that knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), having experienced those torments of Yama with that cruel body, then—being freed from evil—returns once more to those portions of the elements such as earth which initiate other bodies, such as those born from a womb, and takes up a physical body in this world; this is the meaning. (12.22)
Having observed with his own mind these destinies of the living being resulting from both righteousness and unrighteousness, he should always fix his mind upon righteousness.

"These" refers to these attainments of desirable and undesirable bodies in heaven and other realms, which have dharma as their cause. Having understood these through his own intellect, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) should apply himself to the practice of dharma; for it is joined with these that the Great-Souled One remains, pervading all these objects—both stationary and moving—without exception, because of his omnipresence. 12.23.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the self;
pervaded by these, the Great One (*mahat*) stands encompassing all these states without exception. (12.24)

Regarding the term *sattva*: one should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—the three attributes of the self whose characteristics will be described hereafter—are those by which the Great Self (Mahātman) is so called; for, being omnipresent, it remains pervading all these objects without exception, whether they be stationary or moving.
Whichever of these qualities predominates entirely within the body, it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality. (12.25)

Regarding the word "ya" (which): among these qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, whichever quality, by virtue of past karma, becomes predominant in the body at a particular time—that quality makes that *kṣetrajña* subject to its own control at that time; and consequently, unrighteousness (*adharma*) proceeds together with it. || 12.25 ||
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is said to be attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings.

Now he states the characteristics of *sattva* and the others, beginning with "sattvam": Knowledge that is the true nature of things as they are is *sattva*. Its opposite, ignorance, is *tamas*. The mere pride of longing for sense objects is all *rajas*. This is the inherent nature of these qualities—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—which is ever-present and inseparable from all living beings. (12.26)
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself as associated with joy, tranquil and appearing pure—that one should understand to be the quality of *sattva*. (12.27)

He states that there are other [qualities] with such characteristics as well, using the word "therein" (tatra). One should know that *sattva* is that experience within that self which, even without a cause for pleasure, is accompanied by joy, in which afflictions have subsided, and whose nature is not manifest. 12.27.
But that which is joined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, know that to be *rajas*, ever carrying away embodied beings against their will. (12.28)

Regarding the word "yat": furthermore, that experience which, though arising from suffering, does not produce self-joy for the sake of purifying the mind of the wise—which is like a living being—and which always generates a craving for sense objects in the embodied soul, one should know that to be *rajas*, because it is difficult to ward off and its opposite is not present. (12.28)
But that which is conjoined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense objects, inconceivable, and unknowable—one should understand that to be *tamas*. (12.29)

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): furthermore, one should know that to be *tamas* which is devoid of the discrimination between existence and non-existence, whose nature is unreal due to its indistinct objective form, whose essence cannot be reasoned out, and which cannot be understood by the two internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And thus, for the purpose of determining the true nature [of the self], one should be diligent in remaining established in the function of *sattva*. || 12.29 ||
And I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruit for each of these three qualities— whether it be superior, middling, or inferior.
"Of the three": I shall explain exhaustively how these three—sattva and the others—produce effects that are respectively superior, middling, and inferior. 12.30.
Study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self—these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva. 12.31.

Regarding "the study of the Vedas": the practice of Vedic study, the performance of penances such as the *kṛcchra*, comprehension of the scriptures, purification with earth and water, restraint of the senses, and the performance of duties such as charity—this constitutes the activity associated with the quality known as *sattva*. (12.31)

Delight in undertaking new projects, lack of steadfastness, clinging to what is improper, and constant indulgence in sense objects—these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa). 12.32.

"Delight in undertaking [actions]" means: the repeated exertion in beginning actions for the sake of results; agitation even over a slight misfortune; the performance of actions contrary to the scriptures; and the incessant enjoyment of objects such as sound and so forth—this is the effect of the quality designated as *rajas*. (12.32)
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct, mendicancy, and negligence—these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas). || 12.33 ||

Regarding greed (*lobha*): devotion to material wealth, excessive sleepiness, cowardice, cruelty, the notion that dharma and other virtues do not exist, the neglect of proper conduct, a habit of begging, and a lack of attention toward dharma and the like—these are the effects of the quality known as *tamas*. (12.33)
And for these three qualities abiding in the three [states], this should be known as the summary definition of their characteristics in due order. (12.34)

"Of the three" means: this definition of the qualities (guṇalakṣaṇa), which is about to be stated and is relative [to one another], is to be understood as applying respectively to these three qualities—sattva and the others—when they exist throughout the three times: past, future, and present. || 12.34 ||

Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even when intending to do it—all that should be known by the wise as characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas). 12.35.

Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even when about to do it—whether that action pertains to the past, present, or future, or to any one of these times, or to two of them, or to all times—if it produces shame in the agent, all such action should be understood by the knower of the scriptures as characterized by the quality designated as *tamas*, because it is an effect of *tamas*. 12.35.
That action by which people desire abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve when it fails to succeed— that should be known as rajasic.

"By which": that action which one performs in this world solely for the purpose of attaining great fame—neither for the sake of the next world nor because one becomes distressed by the failure to accomplish that action—that is to be known as the effect of *rajas*. (12.36)
That which one desires to know in its entirety, that which one does not feel shame in practicing,
and that by which one’s own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic of the quality of a virtuous being.

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): when desire for an object of knowledge arises in its entirety, and when one does not feel shame at any time—past, present, or future—while performing an action, and by means of which action being performed satisfaction arises within him, that is the characteristic of the quality known as *sattva*. 12.37.
Lust is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while wealth is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Among these, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding.

Regarding the verse beginning with *tamasah*: the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*), while for these [qualities], superiority follows their respective order. The characteristic of *tamas* is the predominance of desire (*kāma*), and the characteristic of *sattva* is steadfastness in righteousness (*dharmaniṣṭhatā*). Furthermore, among these—desire and the rest—there is a mutual hierarchy of superiority: purpose (*artha*) is superior to desire, because desire is rooted in purpose; and even a small amount of righteousness (*dharma*) is superior to those two, because it is rooted in *sattva*. (12.38)
I shall now briefly describe, in their proper order, those qualities by which one enters into these various states of worldly existence.

Regarding the word "by which": from among these qualities, such as goodness (sattva) and the rest, by whichever quality it is cultivated, the person attains certain destinies; those destinies of the entire world I shall describe briefly and in due order. 12.39.
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans;
and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals eternally—such is this threefold destiny.

Regarding "the state of a deity": those who abide in the mode of existence characterized by *sattva* attain the state of a deity; moreover, those who abide in the mode of existence characterized by *rajas* attain the state of a human being, while those who abide in the mode of existence characterized by *tamas* are eternally [born as] animals. || 12.40 ||
This secondary course of action should be understood as being threefold and of three kinds:
inferior, middling, and superior, according to the specific nature of one's karma and knowledge.

"Threefold" means: this threefold course of existence (gati) which has been described as being caused by the qualities (guṇa) such as sattva and so forth, should be understood as being further divided into three types—superior, middling, and inferior—due to distinctions of place, time, and so on; due to the distinctions among karmas that serve as the cause of saṃsāra; and due to the specific differences among deities and others who constitute the auxiliary factors (aṅga) of those karmas. || 12.41 ||
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
cattle, and wild animals— this is the lowest state of darkness.

Regarding the term "stationary" (sthāvara): stationary beings are trees and the like; more gross than those are worms, minute creatures dwelling in the earth, insects, as well as fish, snakes, tortoises, domestic animals, and wild beasts—for these, there is an inferior state of existence caused by ignorance (tamas). 12.42.
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas; lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the intermediate state of darkness (tāmasī gati). || 12.43 ||

"Elephants," etc.: "elephants, horses, Śūdras, Mlecchas, lions, tigers, and boars"—this intermediate state, caused by darkness (*tamas*), is censured; this is a restatement of the nature of the Mlecchas. (12.43)
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and deceitful men, as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas—these are the highest destination among those in the quality of darkness (tamas). || 12.44 ||

Regarding "the wandering performers" (cāraṇā): these are actors and the like; "the well-winged one" (suparṇa) is the specific bird known as Garuḍa; and those men who practice deceitful dharma, such as Rākṣasas and Piśācas—this is the superior destination among the tamasic humans. || 12.44 ||
Jhallas, mallas, and naṭas, as well as men who live by the sword,
those addicted to gambling and drinking— this is the lowest state belonging to rajas.

"Jhallas, mallas, and naṭas—these are men of evil conduct. Jhallas and mallas are said to be born from a Vratya of the Kṣatriya caste; thus they are called jhalla-malla-naṭas. Because they stand outside the scriptures, these men are unfit for instruction. Furthermore, those addicted to gambling and liquor—at the end [of their lives] there is a low rebirth caused by passion (rajas). (12.45)
Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings,
as well as those whose primary concern is the science of war— this is the intermediate Rājasa path.

Regarding "kings": kings who have been consecrated, as well as unconsecrated Kṣatriyas, royal priests who delight in disputes over the meaning of the scriptures, and those fond of battle—this is the middling *rājasī* destiny caused by kings. 12.46.

The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are followers of the gods, as well as all the Apsarases—this is the highest destination among those born of the quality of passion (rājasa). || 12.47 ||

Regarding "gandharvas": the gandharvas, guhyakas, yakṣas, and other specific classes of beings who follow the gods, such as the vidyādharas and others; the apsarases, the celestial courtesans born from the waters and others—among these, the highest rebirth is among humans who possess a rajasic nature. (12.47)
Ascetics, yogis, brahmins, and the hosts of celestial beings who dwell in aerial chariots,
as well as the lunar mansions and the Daityas— this is the first, the sattvic state of existence.

Regarding the term *tāpasāḥ*: ascetics (*vānaprastha*), mendicants (*bhikṣu*), Brahmins, those specific classes of gods who travel in celestial chariots such as the *puṣpaka*, the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and the class of beings called *daityas*—this is an inferior state caused by *sattva*, because it is based on the practice of asceticism and other such duties; yet even that is caused solely by the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva*. This is what is shown by the word *tāpasāḥ*. However, there is no such thing as a caste of ascetics (*tāpasa-jāti*) or a caste of renunciants (*yati-jāti*). From the perspective of historical tradition, there do exist specific classes of beings residing on Mount Meru and elsewhere, such as the *yatis* and so forth. And it is heard in scripture: "Indra gave the *yatis* over to the hyenas. (12.48)
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, sattvic goal.

Regarding the term "sacrificers" (*yajvānaḥ*): the Ṛṣis who are habitually engaged in sacrifice, the deities who preside over the Vedas and possess embodied forms as described in the Itihāsas within the assembly of Brahmā, the luminaries such as Dhruva and the others, and the years—all these, according to the perspective of the Itihāsas, possess embodied forms. The Pitṛs, beginning with the Somapās, and the Sādhyas, who are specific classes of gods—this is the intermediate state (*madhyamā gatiḥ*) caused by the quality of goodness (*sattva*). (12.49)
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, and the Great Unmanifest—
wise men declare this to be the highest state characterized by sattva.

"Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest itself"—the wise declare this to be the supreme goal characterized by goodness (*sattva*). They mean: Hiraṇyagarbha, Marīci and the other Prajāpatis, Dharma embodied, the deity presiding over the specific principle known as Mahat who possesses a form, and that which pertains to the Unmanifest, namely Pradhāna; they call this the exalted state caused by *sattva*.
Thus has been fully described the entire transmigratory existence consisting of all living beings, which is threefold and of three kinds, arising from the three types of action.

"This" refers to the entire range of specific destinies pertaining to all living beings, which has been described in its entirety as "belonging to all creatures" (*sārvabhautika*) because of that designation. This destiny is threefold according to the division of the three types of action—verbal, mental, and physical—and is further characterized by the three forms of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Although not explicitly mentioned here, other destinies are also to be understood as being included for the sake of illustration.
Through attachment to the senses and by failing to practice the Dharma, the ignorant and lowest of men go to sinful states of existence. 12.52

Regarding the phrase "of the senses": through attachment to the objects of the senses and by practicing what is forbidden, those who are contemptible, deluded in the cycle of rebirth, and have not performed expiation become outcasts among men. 12.52.
Learn now all that specific womb into which this living soul enters in this world, and by what particular karma it goes there, in due succession. (12.53)

Regarding the word "ya" (who): this verse is intended to introduce the description of the fruits of performing prohibited actions; it means that hear, in their proper order, whatever womb the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) attains in this world by whichever specific action performed here—that is, the fruit of that action. (12.53)
Having endured these terrible hells for many series of years, upon their exhaustion,
those who have committed great sins enter back into this cycle of transmigratory existence.

Regarding the word "many": those who have committed great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, after reaching terrifying hells for many series of years, attain these wombs to be described below upon the exhaustion of their evil deeds, when only a slight remnant of their wickedness remains. (12.54)
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, a camel, a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a mouse; he also enters the wombs of Caṇḍālas and Pukkasas.

"Of dogs, pigs, donkeys, and camels": the slayer of a Brahmin incurs the birth-status of those belonging to the species of dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, cattle, goats, sheep, wild animals, birds, and Cāṇḍālas born of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra. || 12.55 ||
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures.

"Of worms, insects, and moths": the Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor goes to the womb associated with worms, insects, and locusts; with birds that feed on excrement; and with living beings such as tigers and others that are by nature violent. 12.56.
A Brahmin who is a thief [becomes] thousands of times a spider, a snake, a lizard, or aquatic animals, as well as predatory beasts and Piśācas. (12.57)

"Of spiders, snakes, and lizards," and "of aquatic creatures such as crocodiles and others," and "of the flesh-eating *piśācas*": a Brāhmaṇa who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa incurs [the fate] belonging to these. (12.57)
One who violates the Guru’s bed must undergo hundreds of births as grasses, shrubs, creepers, and even as fanged beasts that perform cruel deeds.

"Of grasses, shrubs, and creepers": one who approaches the wife of his guru undergoes a hundred births among grasses such as *dūrvā*, among shrubs (*gulma*) which are plants without woody trunks such as *kupyaka* and the like, among those that eat raw flesh such as vultures and the like, among fanged creatures such as lions and the like, and among those who perform cruel deeds such as the *śabara* tribes and the like. (12.58)

Those who eat the flesh of others become carnivorous predators; those who consume impure things become worms; thieves become creatures that devour one another; and those who consort with women of the lowest castes become pretas.

Regarding the term "cruel" (hiṃsrā): those whose nature is the slaughter of living beings become vultures and the like, who feed on raw flesh. Those who eat what is unfit to be eaten are born as worms. Those thieves who have committed crimes other than the great sins (mahāpātaka) arise as fish and other creatures that prey upon one another. And those who have sexual intercourse with women such as Caṇḍālas and others become specific types of beings known as *pretas*. (12.59)
By entering into union with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa.

Regarding "conjunction": for as long as it takes to fall [into hell], having engaged in association with the four beginning with Brahmā for that duration, having approached another's wife, and having stolen the property of a Brahmin other than gold, one is born as a specific class of spirit called a *brahmarākṣasa*. (12.60)
Having stolen gems, pearls, corals, and various other jewels out of greed, a man is born among the workers in gold.

"Jewels, pearls, and corals": through greed for various gems such as rubies (*padmarāga*), as well as pearls and coral, and diverse precious stones such as lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*) and diamonds (*hīraka*), one is born in the womb of a goldsmith. They call this very being the bird known as the "goldsmith. (12.61)

By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl; by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing juice, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.

"Grain": having stolen grain, one becomes a mouse. Having stolen bell-metal, one becomes a swan. Having stolen water for the purpose of irrigation and so forth, one becomes a bird called *plava*, *śakaṭa*, or *bila*. As for honey—regarding which it is said "it is like a crow's [beverage]" because the *stokaka* bird also shows an excessive desire for drinking it—one is born as an insect called a gadfly after stealing it. Having stolen milk, one becomes a crow. Having stolen juice related to sugarcane, *āmalaka*, and so forth, one is reborn as a dog. Because molasses, salt, and other such items are mentioned separately, one becomes a mongoose after stealing clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (12.62)
The vulture [takes] meat, the cormorant the fat, the oil-drinking bird the oil,
the cricket the salt, and the crane the curd.

Regarding "meat": having stolen meat, one becomes a bird called a vulture; having stolen fat, one becomes a bird called a *maṅga*; having stolen oil, one is reborn as a bird called a *tailapaka*; having stolen salt, one becomes a loud-sounding insect called a *cīrīvāka*; and having stolen curd, one is born as a bird called a *balākā*. (12.63)
Having stolen silk, a partridge [is reborn as such]; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; having stolen a cow, an iguana; and having stolen molasses, a guḍa-worm.

Regarding "silk" (kauśeya): having stolen fine silk produced by the *kauśa* insect, one is born as a bird called a partridge (*tittiri*). Having stolen cloth made from flax (*kṣumā*), one is born as a frog. Having stolen a woven garment made of cotton thread, one arises as a bird called a curlew (*krauñca*). Having stolen a cow, one becomes a creature called a monitor lizard (*godhā*). Having stolen molasses, one becomes a bird called a *vāgdomantha*. (12.64)
The chuchundarī [eats] auspicious fragrances; the peacock, leafy vegetables; the porcupine, various kinds of prepared food; and the hedgehog, likewise prepared food. (12.65)

Regarding the term *chucchundarī*: having stolen fragrant substances such as camphor and the like, one becomes a musk-rat (*chucchundarī*) known as the "daughter of the king"; having stolen leafy vegetables, mustard seeds, and so forth, one is born as a peacock. (12.65)
By stealing fire, one becomes a cricket; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder;
and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.

"Regarding the crane (baka): having stolen fire, one is born as a bird called a crane. Having stolen household items such as jars and mortars, one becomes a house-builder, a worm known as a *rūḍhamakṣikā*. Having stolen garments dyed with safflower and the like, one becomes a bird called a *jīvajīvaka*.
The wolf [seizes] the deer, the tiger the elephant, the monkey the fruit and root, the bear the woman, the cuckoo the water, the camel the vehicles, and the goat the livestock. || 12.67 ||

Regarding the word "wolf": having stolen a deer or an elephant, one becomes a creature called a wolf; having stolen a horse, one becomes a tiger; having stolen fruits or roots, one is born as a monkey; having stolen a woman, one becomes a bear—a specific kind of ape; having stolen water for drinking, one is reborn as a *stokaka* or *cātaka*, a bird that is extremely thirsty; having stolen vehicles such as carts and the like, one becomes a camel; and having stolen livestock, one is born as a goat. (12.67)
Having forcibly seized any property whatsoever belonging to another, or having consumed an oblation intended for the gods, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal. (12.68)

Regarding the word "yad" (that which): whatever insubstantial wealth belonging to another a person may desire, having stolen it and consumed offerings such as the *puroḍāśa* cake given as a sacrificial portion, he becomes mindless and attains the state of an animal. (12.68)
Women also, by taking [property] according to this same rule, incur guilt;
they become wives of those very same creatures.

Regarding the word "women": even women, by this same method, having taken the property of another through desire in such a form, incur sin; and by that sin, they attain the female state of the aforementioned beings. (12.69)
For when the social classes fall away from their respective duties in times of no distress,
they pass through sinful transmigrations and enter into servitude among bandits.

Having thus described the fruits of performing prohibited acts, [the author] now states the ripening of the non-performance of prescribed duties with the words "from their respective... (svebhyaḥ svebhyaḥ). Brāhmaṇas and the other castes who, in the absence of distress, abandon their duties such as Vedic study and so forth, reach the base wombs that will be described; thereafter, in another birth, they fall into servitude among their enemies. (12.70)
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta with a mouth like a flaming torch that eats what has been vomited;
and a Kṣatriya who is deceitful and impure becomes a preta that eats filth and corpses.

"Eater of vomit": a Brahmin who has fallen from his own duty becomes a specific kind of spirit called Agnipiśāca, whose mouth is a flame and who feeds on vomit. A Kṣatriya, moreover, who has fallen from his duty, is born as a specific kind of Piśāca called Pūtanā, who eats odors, mucus, and all kinds of excrement. (12.71)
The Vaiśya Maitrākṣijyotika becomes a preta that feeds on pus;
and the Śūdra, fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.

Regarding the "cloth-eater" (*cailāśa*): a Vaiśya who has fallen from his duty becomes a specific type of *piśāca* named Maitra or Jyotika; for the sake of finding shelter, he dwells in holes and feeds on pus. Furthermore, a Śūdra who has fallen from his own duties is born as an insect called the "cloth-eater" (*cailāśaka*), which feeds upon the cloth in which it is produced. (12.72)
To whatever extent those whose nature is focused on sense objects indulge in them, to that same extent skillfulness arises in them regarding those very objects. 12.73

"According as... means: just as those who increase the enjoyment of objects such as sound practice the habit of enjoying those objects, so too does proficiency in those very objects—meaning a state of single-minded absorption—arise for them. (12.73)
Due to the repeated practice of those evil deeds, those of small intelligence encounter sufferings in various wombs here in this world. (12.74)

And thus, regarding "of actions": to the extent that those of little wisdom practice the enjoyment of forbidden objects, to that same extent they experience suffering in various births such as those of animals, in accordance with the degree of that practice. (12.74)
There is wandering through the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
and [suffering] in the Forest of Sword-leaves and other places, as well as the cutting of bonds.

"In the Tāmisra and other [hells]" means that they undergo complete plundering in the terrible hells mentioned in the fourth chapter, such as the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana) and others also mentioned in the fourth chapter—namely, those hells characterized by the cutting of their own bodies. The phrase "they undergo" is supplied from the preceding sentence and connects here with the subsequent one as well. 12.75.
And various torments indeed, such as being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of burning sand mixed with grit, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.

"Various" means they undergo manifold kinds of torments, such as being split apart like wood, being devoured by crows and owls, and the heat of burning sand mixed with molten bronze; they encounter forests in cauldrons that cannot be endured through suffering. (12.76)
And he [experienced] births in various wombs that are mostly full of suffering, as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and manifold fears. || 12.77 ||

Regarding "from births": they undergo births in species such as those of animals, which are constantly abounding in suffering; therein they encounter various forms of affliction from cold and heat, as well as manifold kinds of fears. || 12.77 ||
Repeatedly dwelling in the womb and undergoing dreadful births, as well as painful bondages and even the state of being a servant to others. (12.78)

"Repeatedly" means: they undergo painful bonds and even the state of being servants on the other shore; many times they experience birth in the womb, which brings extreme suffering; and once born, they encounter harsh bonds such as being strangled by a rope around the neck and so forth, as well as falling into further servitude. (12.78)
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people; the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies. (12.79)

"They experience separation from loved ones" means that they encounter separation from kinsmen and friends, dwelling together with wicked people, the hardship of acquiring wealth, the loss of wealth, the hardship of seeking friends, and the appearance of enemies. (12.79)
He beheld old age, which is indeed beyond remedy; the torment of various diseases; those manifold afflictions; and death itself, like a wicked enemy.
"Regarding 'old age': they encounter old age that cannot be resisted, the affliction by diseases, various kinds of distress such as hunger and thirst, and death, which is impossible to avoid. (12.80)
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action, with a body of that same nature one experiences its corresponding fruit. (12.81)

"By whatever state of being"—meaning, by whatever kind of mind, whether characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*, one performs an action such as bathing or sacrifice, by a body of that same character—whether abounding in *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*—one experiences the respective fruit of that bathing and so forth. (12.81)
This entire arising of the fruits of actions for you has been fully described;
now learn this action which brings about the highest good for a Brahmin.

"Regarding this: 'Learn this rule of action for the supreme good of a Brahmin. This entire origin of auspicious and inauspicious actions has been declared to you. Now, listen to this practice of action which is about to be described for the sake of heaven, liberation, and so forth, pertaining to the Brahmin. (12.82)
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.

Regarding "the study of the Vedas": the repeated practice of the Veda in both its text and meaning, the performance of austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance, knowledge of the Self, mastery over the senses, avoidance of violence, and service to the teacher—this is the preeminent means for accomplishing the category of wealth (*artha*). (12.83)
And among all these auspicious actions here, a certain action has been declared to be more conducive to welfare for a person. (12.84)

Regarding the word "of all": through the deliberation that among these—such as the study of the Vedas and ritual acts—the internal practice might be the means for a person’s supreme good by virtue of its excellence, the sages gave rise to a desire to know; and by means of what follows, a definitive conclusion was reached. || 12.84 ||
And for all of these, self-knowledge is remembered as supreme; for that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained from it. 12.85

"Of all"—that is, among all those [means] such as the study of the Vedas and so forth, the ascertainment of the nature of the Supreme Self through the meditations taught in the Upaniṣads is remembered as the most excellent; because that is the principal among all branches of knowledge, and since liberation is attained from it. 12.85.
Of these six aforementioned types of action, it should be known that the Vedic rite is always more conducive to welfare, both in this world and after death.

"But of all six indeed": among these six previously mentioned actions, beginning with the study of the Vedas, it should be understood that Vedic action—in comparison to Smārta (tradition-based) action—is the most excellent means for achieving heaven and other goals in both this world and the next. Because self-knowledge has immortality as its fruit, is prescribed by injunction, and is Vedic, this [Vedic action] is said to be superior to other Vedic actions; however, it is superior specifically in comparison to Smārta action. 12.86.
But in the Vedic path of action, all these [stages] without exception are included, respectively, within each specific ritual injunction.

"Vedic" means that it is included, in due order, within the performance of rituals taught in the Vedas, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma. Thus, the study of the Vedas is included in the Śrauta and Smārta rites and so forth; austerity (tapas) is included in the consecration, the Upasad, the milk-vow, and the like; knowledge (jñāna) is included through its conjunction with self-knowledge, since Vedic action has the suppression of obstacles as its fruit; and restraint of the senses is included because it is stated as an auxiliary to ritual action in such injunctions as "one should not eat meat" and "one should not engage in sexual intercourse. Non-violence (ahiṃsā) is also included because it is designated as a part [of the sacrifice] in the passage, "Therefore, on this night one should not cut off the breaths of living beings. Service to the teacher is included as it leads to the acquisition of the Veda, which is the cause for performing the rituals. In this way, all these qualities exist through connection with the Veda. (12.87)

Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the path of active engagement and the path of withdrawal.

"Leading to worldly prosperity (*sukhābhyudayika*). Action that results in happiness, such as from obtaining a village and so forth, because it causes one to rise up [to higher states], is called "leading to worldly prosperity"; it is known as the cause for the continuation of *saṃsāra*. Likewise, "Vedic action" refers to that which leads to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), which is liberation (*mokṣa*); action for that purpose is "leading to the highest good," and because it is the cause for the cessation of *saṃsāra*, it is known as "cessation. Thus, Vedic action should be understood as being of two kinds. 12.88
Action performed with desire for results here or hereafter is proclaimed as "active" (pravṛtta);
but that which is free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as "withdrawn" (nivṛtta).

To clarify this very point, he says "and here" (iha ca). That which is performed with desire for fruits pertaining to this world or the next, such as heaven and so forth, is called *kāmya* (desirable). However, that which is performed without desire and preceded by knowledge is called *nivṛtta* (renounced), because it is the cause of the cessation of saṃsāra. || 12.89 ||
By practicing active karma, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renunciation, one indeed transcends the five elements.

"By practicing *pravṛtta* karma, one attains equality of power with the gods. This means that through the practice of *pravṛtta* karma, one attains a state of equal destiny with the gods. Furthermore, by the practice of *nivṛtta* karma, one transcends the elements that initiate the body and attains liberation (*mokṣa*). || 12.90 ||
Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, he who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty. (12.91)

Regarding the phrase "in all beings": when one performs those various sacrifices that must necessarily be performed, if one considers that the Self alone—just like other deities such as Agni—abides in that very form as light (*jyotis*), then such a person is an "officiant of the Self" (*ātmayājī*). Thinking thus, "I myself am established in all beings," consisting of both the stationary and the moving; and thinking, "all beings abide in me"—by perceiving all things with such equality, he attains independence from sacrificial animals. He does not possess the dependence associated with the body and so forth; rather, knowing this and possessing self-knowledge, he is liberated. (12.91)
Even having abandoned the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas.

"Even those prescribed [acts]" means that even though he has abandoned the Agnihotra and other rites enjoined by the scriptures, a Brāhmaṇa should exert effort in self-knowledge, mastery of the senses, and the study of the Vedas, while performing them according to the manner of the scriptural texts shown in the fourth chapter, beginning with "As long as a person shines," and so forth. 12.92.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of birth, especially for a Brahmin;
having attained this, a twice-born man has truly accomplished his purpose, and not otherwise.

Regarding the word "this": because this [practice] produces the fruitfulness of the birth of the twice-born through the study of the Vedas and so forth, it constitutes the specific fruitfulness of birth, especially for the Brāhmaṇa; for once a twice-born person has accomplished this, he has fulfilled his duty, and not by performing other ritual acts. 12.93.
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is impossible to master and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture.

Regarding the phrase "of the ancestors, gods, and humans": since we are the givers of *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors), and this is known through the Vedas, it is impossible to act [against them]; furthermore, the Vedic scriptures cannot be invalidated because their subject matter is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), and it is impossible to study the entire collection of those scriptures—such is the established conclusion. 12.94.
Whatever scriptures are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all these are fruitless after death, for they are remembered as being grounded in darkness.

"Those which are outside the Veda" means those treatises that are in contradiction with the Veda and thus have the appearance of pseudo-scripture (*āgamābhāsa*), as well as any philosophical systems (*darśana*) that, even without being based on scripture, are merely fallacious causes for liberation and so forth; all of these are fruitless in the next world because they are remembered by Manu and others as having hell as their result. (12.95)
Whatever other things there may be besides these, which arise and perish,
they are fruitless and false because they belong to the past.

Regarding the statement "they arise": whatever treatises exist apart from the Vedas arise because they originate from human beings; for this very reason, they perish quickly. Because they are of recent origin, they are fruitless and unreal in nature. Since the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda, there is no room for such an objection. 12.96.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life in their distinctness—the past, the present, and the future—all these are established from the Veda. 12.97

Regarding the phrase "the fourfold caste" (*cāturvarṇyam*): just as the mutual distinction between cows, buffaloes, and so forth is within the range of the senses, yet that fourfold caste is established through the Veda alone; and just as the earth and the worlds are established by both the Vedas and non-Vedic means because they serve as the locus for experiencing the fruits of Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*, so too the four stages of life (*āśrama*), beginning with the student (*brahmacārin*), are established through the Veda alone, since they fall within the domain of mutually distinct Vedic injunctions. Furthermore, according to the principle of the oblation cast into the fire, whatever has passed, is present, or will be—everything is established as authoritative through the Veda alone. (12.97)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are produced from the Veda alone; their origin is from the qualities and actions [of the elements].

Regarding the word "sound" (*śabda*): those objects such as sound and so forth, which are desired as things to be enjoyed and are variously classified as heaven and so on, are established through the Veda alone by means of the performance of rituals—such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice—which are conducive to the production of the enjoyment of those desired objects, based upon their manifold qualities and actions.
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of a living being.

"It sustains": the eternal Vedic scripture constantly supports all beings. Just as an oblation is poured into the fire, that fire satisfies the sun; the sun then rains through its rays, and from that food comes into being. From that, indeed, the origin and maintenance of beings here are understood—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, I know this scripture to be the preeminent scripture of the Veda, for it is the preeminent means of accomplishing the goals of man for this qualified person. (12.99)
One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the office of a magistrate, and even the lordship over all the worlds.

"Generalship" means the command of an army, sovereignty, the office of a magistrate, and the lordships of universal emperors; thus, this praise of the Veda asserts that only one who knows the Vedic scriptures is worthy of all such visible human goals. 12.100
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees, so does one who knows the Veda burn away the faults of his own karma. 12.101
