Regarding the word "yathā" (as): just as a fire that has grown exceedingly great burns even moist trees, so too, by the power of knowledge of the Veda, one destroys the evil born of failing to perform what is prescribed and of practicing what is forbidden for oneself; and thus, it is not only the cause for attaining what is seen in the Veda, but also the cessation of the undesirable. 12.101.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
becomes fit for absorption into Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

"One who knows the true meaning of the Vedic scriptures" means one who knows the ultimate meaning of the Vedas; when there is no longer ignorance regarding the defects of sense-objects and so forth, through the expulsion of passion and other such impulses, he—remaining established in whichever stage of life (āśrama) such as celibacy (brahmacarya), and staying in this very world with this very body—attains the state of Brahman. 12.102.

Those who possess the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them are better than those who merely possess them; those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who practice with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge. (12.103)

Regarding the phrase "to the ignorant": since both [the learned and the ignorant] are praiseworthy, the term *śreṣṭha* (superior) is applied here to distinguish one from the other within the scope of Vedic study; thus, those who have studied only slightly are called "ignorant" in this context. However, they are not utterly foolish. Compared to them, those who merely recite the texts are superior; compared to them, those who have dispelled [their ignorance] through practice are more excellent; compared to them, those who know the meaning of the texts are better; and compared even to them, those who perform the rites are the most excellent. (12.103)
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
by austerity he destroys sin, and through knowledge he partakes of immortality.

Regarding "austerity" (tapa): austerity such as the *kṛcchra* penance and self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) are the preeminent means for attaining the highest good for a Brahmin; for by austerity one destroys evil, and by self-knowledge one attains liberation. 12.104.
Perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions—these three must be thoroughly understood by one who desires purity in dharma. 12.105

Regarding "perception" (*pratyakṣa*): by one who desires the realization of the true nature of *dharma*, the scripture—consisting of the Vedas and the Smṛtis, and divided into many types of mantras—must be thoroughly understood through perception and inference. For, once the nature of perception and inference is understood, it is appropriate to possess the most profound knowledge of the substances, qualities, and genera that serve as the means for performing ritual acts. (12.105)
He who examines the instruction on dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the Shastras—he, and no other, knows dharma. (12.106)

Regarding the term *ārṣa*: that which was seen by the seers (*ṛṣi*) is the Veda, and the Smṛti is the instruction on Dharma. When there arises a doubt concerning their interpretation or a suspicion of redundancy, one who investigates those two through reasoning in a manner consistent with the Veda and Smṛti knows Dharma; however, one who is ignorant of such reasoning does not. (12.106)
This action leading to supreme bliss has been declared in its entirety;
now the secret of this treatise of Manu shall be taught.

Regarding the term "liberation" (*naiḥśreyasa*): that which leads to liberation and other such goals has been correctly explained above through the complete exhaustion of ritual action (*karman*). Hereafter, a portion of this treatise for the human being, consisting of the Upaniṣads, will be set forth with the purpose of instructing on the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*). 12.107.
If it should be asked how one should act regarding dharmas not explicitly mentioned, that which learned Brahmins declare shall be the dharma, free from doubt. (12.108)

Having thus promised to speak of the secret [tradition], he raises the concern that his promise might be violated by not mentioning all ritual acts, saying "in the case of those not mentioned" (*anāmnāteṣu*). Since tradition possesses a dual nature—both with and without a formal text—there may arise a doubt regarding those duties not taught, as well as those taught but lacking a specified procedure: "Should these be performed or not? Or, if they are to be performed, how? If such a doubt should arise, then whatever the cultured *brāhmaṇas* (the learned) declare shall be the settled duty.

Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered according to the Dharma, they are to be known as cultured Brahmins, who are the authorities for both scripture and direct perception. (12.109)

"Attained through the Dharma": those by whom the Veda has been studied—augmented by the limbs [of the Vedas], Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, Purāṇas, and so forth—and according to the prescribed procedure for the holy life (brahmacarya), they are to be understood as *brāhmaṇas*; they are the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) ones who serve as the cause for the instruction on the categories of objects within the scope of the Veda. (12.109)
Whatever dharma an assembly of at least ten members may determine, or even one of at least three who are established in virtuous conduct—that dharma one should not unsettle. (12.110)

Regarding the phrase "ten at the minimum": if there are young men present, then that assembly in which ten learned persons—as will be described—reside, or in their absence, three, should determine the righteous conduct and Dharma; that [determination] is to be established as the Dharma. (12.110)
One who possesses the threefold knowledge, a logician, a dialectician, a reciter of the Dharma, and the three types of ascetics—these ten, or more, constitute a formal assembly (pariṣad). 12.111.

Regarding the term "traividya": those who have studied the three branches of the three Vedas, those who know the treatises on logic (*nyāya*) that are not in contradiction with *śruti* and *smṛti*, those endowed with the intellectual capacity for reasoning and refutation, those who know etymology (*nirukta*), and those who study the *dharma* of Manu and others—namely, students (*brahmacārin*), householders (*gṛhastha*), and forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*)—this shall constitute an assembly (*pariṣad*) of at least ten members. (12.111)

One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—this assembly of at least three is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts regarding dharma. (12.112)

Regarding the phrase "one who knows the Ṛgveda": since those who know the meaning of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are required for the purpose of dispelling doubts concerning dharma, an assembly of at least ten persons should be understood [as necessary]. (12.112)
Whatever dharma even a single best of the twice-born who knows the Vedas may determine, that is to be known as the supreme dharma; it is not [dharma] proclaimed by tens of thousands of ignorant men.

"Even in the absence of that [large number], 'one' [is sufficient]" means: even a single person who knows the meaning of the Veda, whatever dharma he may determine, that should be understood as preeminent; it is not [determined] by what is said even by ten thousand (ayuta) of those ignorant of the Veda. An *ayuta* is ten thousand. 12.113.
For those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist on mere birth—even if they have gathered by the thousands—no true assembly exists. (12.114)

Regarding the phrase "of those who are without vows": even if thousands of individuals who merely subsist on the basis of their Brāhmaṇa birth—being devoid of the vows of a student (*brahmacārin*) such as the *Sāvitra* and being empty of Vedic study—should become united, they do not constitute an assembly (*pariṣad*), because they lack the capacity to determine the Dharma. (12.114)
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the fools who do not know the Dharma, proclaim as such, that sin becomes tenfold and follows after those who spoke it. (12.115)

Regarding the word "yat" (which): that expiation which foolish people—who, due to a lack of discrimination, are of the nature of darkness (*tamas*) and ignorant of dharma, yet perform sinful acts—prescribe, becomes a hundredfold sin for those givers of expiation, as it results from their very act of prescribing it. (12.115)
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
the Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.

"‘This’ means: this entire preeminent dharma leading to the highest good has been declared to you all. By practicing this, a Brāhmaṇa or anyone else attains heaven, liberation, and so forth; thus, this is the complete summary of dharma. (12.116)
Thus that Blessed One, the God, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of the Dharma.

"So be it. That Blessed One, the divine Manu, endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and other qualities, has thus declared to me, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, this entire ultimate truth of Dharma in the manner just described; so said Bhṛgu to the great seers. 12.117.
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
for by perceiving everything within the self, one does not set one's mind upon unrighteousness. 12.118

Now, explaining that which was stated—that the secret of the Mānava Śāstra will be taught—he says "all": having become one-pointed, one should see that everything—whatever is formed, such as earth and the rest, and whatever is formless, such as space—is unified within the Self (ātman), thinking, "I indeed am all this. By contemplating in this way, because of the absence of passion and hatred, the mind does not engage in unrighteousness (adharma). 12.118.
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings. (12.119)

Regarding the term "Self" (*ātman*): Indra and all other deities are indeed the Supreme Self; there are no deities existing apart from or distinct from the Self. Thus it is heard in scripture: "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa. The sages speak of the One Reality in many ways; they call him Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan. Furthermore, the entire world is dependent upon the Supreme Self, because the Self alone—through the scriptural injunctions and the performance of actions prescribed therein—establishes the connection for these individual knowers of the field (*kṣetrajñas*) with the cause of the world. And so says the venerable Vyāsa:
This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or even to hell.
Thus he said. 12.119.
One should place space within the cavities; wind within movement and touch; fire as the supreme [element] in digestion and sight; water in moisture; and earth in solid forms.
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, Viṣṇu in the ears, Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.

Now, regarding what was stated—that one should perceive everything within oneself—the author states a specific detail therein, beginning with "the ether" (*kham*) and "in the mind" (*manasi*). One should contemplate the Brahmic ether as being identical with the ether within the body; likewise, one should contemplate the identity of the external air with the bodily air which is the cause of movement and touch; the identity of the supreme light—composed of fire, the sun, and so forth—with the ocular radiance; the identity of water with the bodily fluids; and the identity of the external earth with the solid, earthly parts of the body. Furthermore, one should contemplate the identity of the moon with the mind (*manas*), Viṣṇu’s virility with the sense of hearing, the Lord Bhagavat (or Īśvara) with the organ of speech, and Hiraṇyagarbha with the organ of excretion (apāna). In this manner, one should contemplate the identity of the elemental and divine principles with the internal, corporeal principles.

|| 12.120–121 || The king, having heard that speech, was filled with joy; he then spoke these words to his ministers: "I shall go myself to see the son of Daśaratha. || 12.120 || Then, having summoned all the ministers, the king, together with them, set out for Ayodhyā. Having reached Ayodhyā, the king entered the city, which was adorned with flags and banners. || 12.121 ||
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep. 12.122.

"Of the Ruler": [this refers to] the one who establishes the order of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. Furthermore, regarding the instruction on this very Imperishable, the *Gārgī-Brahmaṇa* states that it is subtler than even an atom because it is formless; its nature is pure like gold. Having cast off hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death, one should know the Supreme Self—whose true nature is comparable to consciousness during the state of deep sleep—as described in the initial *Brahmaṇa*. One who desires to see [the Self] should know the Supreme Self to always have such a form for the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) in the state of deep sleep, wherein all particularities of pleasure and pain have subsided. Deep sleep is that state devoid of the perception of dreams. (12.122)
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman. (12.123)

"This one" (*etam*): the ritualists (*yājñika*) worship this Supreme Self as Fire. Thus, the Brāhmaṇa says, "The Adhvaryus worship Him as Fire. Furthermore, because He rises even from the Self at every moment, and because of the Vedic texts concerning His preeminence and His being the prototype of the Manu-narrative, others worship this Self as Prāṇa; yet others worship Him as the form of the perishable Supreme Self. Thus, since the Supreme Self consists of all things, some worship Him in one particular form or another. And so the Brāhmaṇa states: "Therefore, we know Him thus; by whatever [means] they worship Him, [so do they find Him]."
Pervading all beings with his five forms,
he perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.

"This one" refers to this Supreme Self. Having taken hold of all living beings by means of the five elements, beginning with earth, which constitute the body, He—taking into account the karma acquired in previous births—perpetually joins them to birth, maintenance, and destruction, which recur simultaneously like the wheel of a chariot and so forth, until liberation. 12.124.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self, having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state. (12.125)

"Thus": in the manner described by the verse beginning with "and [he who sees] himself in all beings," he who perceives the Self abiding in all beings by means of his own self attains the abandonment of passion and hatred and reaches the supreme state, Brahman; that is to say, he is liberated. || 12.125 ||
A twice-born man who recites this Mānava Śāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu becomes constantly possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal. (12.126)

Thus [ends the section]. This treatise composed by Manu has been fully expounded by Bhṛgu. A twice-born person who studies this treatise becomes learned and, performing what is enjoined while avoiding what is prohibited, shall thereby attain in the hereafter his desired goal, such as union with the Blessed Maheśvara and others. (12.126)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Three Qualities, Occupations, Castes, Hells, and the Praise of the Vedas," in this commentary on Manu composed by Śrī Govindarāja, the son of Śrī Bhaṭṭa Mādhava, which follows the intention of the venerable Manu.
